title: Documenting Science
contributors: Ron Kurtz, Julia Van Haaften, John Durant
description:
Illustrated in tritone throughout. Fascination with the scientific advances that were rapidly changing the world motivated Berenice Abbott to use photography as "the friendly interpreter of science".

Documenting Science explores this work, beginning in 1939 with Abbott's early experiments with scientific imagery, continuing with science-based commercial assignments, and culminating in 1958 with the Physical Science Study Project at MIT which illustrated a new series of physics textbooks. This spectacular body of work is arguably Abbott's most innovative and creative. Both beautiful and instructive, these images often illustrate some basic scientific principle. They are a marriage of science and art, and have fundamentally changed the way thousands of students visualize complex principles of physics. Berenice Abbott, born in Springfield, Ohio in 1898, was a dominant figure in twentieth-century American photography.

Abbott moved to Paris from New York in 1921, and in 1923, after many false starts, was hired by her friend Man Ray.He was looking for an assistant who knew nothing about photography whom he could teach. Abbott learned quickly and within a year was taking her own photographs. Her first solo exhibition in 1926 was a success, and for the next 65 years Abbott mastered a wide range of subjects. Highlights of Abbott's career include the monumental project Changing New York (1935-1938), photographing rural America including US Route 1 from Maine to Florida, photographically interpreting scientific and natural phenomena, establishing the reputation of Eugène Atget, and founding the first university photography program in the United States. Steidl published the two-volume retrospective Berenice Abbott in 2008. Co-published with Commerce Graphics, New York
tags: Music, Photographers, Photography, Science, Technology, architecture

title: Berenice Abbott: Changing New York
description:
Berenice Abbott's Changing New York is the fullest record of the Federal Art Project commission that defined her career: a systematic photographic survey of a city remaking itself in the 1930s.

Between 1935 and 1939, working under the Federal Art Project, Abbott photographed Manhattan's old tenements and elevated trains alongside the steel frames rising to replace them, using a large-format view camera to hold both foreground and skyline in sharp focus. This edition reproduces more than 300 of those duotones, arranged geographically in eight sections that trace her route through the city, alongside period maps and line drawings. Text by Bonnie Yochelson, former curator of prints and photographs at the Museum of the City of New York, draws on WPA field notes to annotate Abbott's compositional choices block by block.

Abbott had spent the 1920s in Paris making portraits before Eugène Atget's street photographs turned her toward the built environment as a subject in its own right. Changing New York is the project she is remembered for, and it set the terms for the documentary tradition that later photographers of American cities, from Walker Evans to the New Topographics, would work within.

notes: Federal Art Project (WPA) commission, 1935–1939; text by Bonnie Yochelson, Museum of the City of New York.

title: Berenice Abbott
contributors: Sarah Miller , Jeu de Paume (Paris) , Terri Weissman
description:
This catalogue accompanied the first major European retrospective of Berenice Abbott's photography, staged at the Jeu de Paume in Paris in 2012 and traveling to the Ryerson Image Centre and the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto the same year.

Edited by curator Gaëlle Morel with essays by Sarah Miller and Terri Weissman, the book surveys Abbott's full working life: her Paris portraits of the 1920s, her advocacy for Eugène Atget's archive, the WPA-funded Changing New York series, and the scientific photographs she made for MIT in the 1950s and 1960s. Running 223 pages, it draws on the Ryerson Image Centre's Abbott archive and reproduces vintage prints alongside contact sheets and studio ephemera, arguing for a photographer whose work in portraiture, urban documentation, and science has rarely been shown together.

Abbott died in 1991 having spent six decades moving between these registers, and this catalogue was among the first to treat that range as a single body of work rather than three separate careers.
notes: Exhibition catalogue for Berenice Abbott's 2012 retrospective at the Jeu de Paume, Paris, and the Ryerson Image Centre at the Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto.

title: Paris Portraits
description:
The photographs that launched Abbott's career: portraits of artists and writers in prewar Paris, from Jean Cocteau to James Joyce This is one in a series of books to be published by Steidl that will explore Berenice Abbott’s oeuvre.

Abbott began her photographic career in Paris in 1925, taking portraits of some the most celebrated artists and writers of the day, including Marie Laurencin, Jean Cocteau, Peggy Guggenheim, Coco Chanel, Max Ernst, André Gide, Philippe Soupault and James Joyce. Within a year her work was exhibited and acclaimed. Paris Portraits 1925–1930 features the results of Abbott’s earliest photographic project and illustrates the philosophy of all her subsequent work. For this landmark book, 115 portraits of 83 subjects have been scanned from the original glass negatives, which have been printed in full.

title: The Movement of Clouds around Mount Fuji
description:
376 pages, 4 lbs. In the late 1920s, Japanese physicist Masanao Abe built an observatory with a view of Mount Fuji.

From it, over the course of fifteen years, he recorded the clouds that surrounded the mountain. He was interested in the scientific question of how the air currents around Fuji could be visualized by means of film and photography. Albeit unintentionally, Abe’s motifs fit into a long iconographic tradition: the mountain and the clouds. For decades his archive was left untouched in a Tokyo garden shed.

Helmut Völter, who discovered Abe’s legacy while working on his book Cloud Studies, sifted through the images of the passionate cineaste who saw a combination of individual images, moving pictures and stereo recordings as the ideal form of scientific evidence. The mere contemplation of these dynamic cloud photographs centring on snow-covered Fuji seems to lift the viewer into the air.
tags: clouds, earth, mountain, time series, Photography

title: Anaesthesia
description:
curated and edited by Valentina Abenavoli, signed, edition of 500 copies.

With a text by Veronique Pin Fat. Rather than a traditional photo book, Valentina Abenavoli’s “anaesthesia” is a care- and thoughtful recontextualisation of images of war and terror. Words from writers such as T.S. Eliot, Rousseau, Zizek and screenshots from war footage and execution videos are edited and arranged to form an engaging narrative.

“Anaesthesia is a lament of several voices, a symphony of the evil in us, cinematically edited screenshots from videos, an engagement with the media, an open criticism to war and terrorism, a declaration of neutrality, an act of rebellion to the ego, where one stands alone prevented to feel anything else beyond his own finitude. Nothing would be more painful than not suffering anymore, dropping the burden of sensations, withdrawing from living and bonding. In the lyricism of the agony of mind, in the longing for a break in the inner solitude, what is more ambiguous than the desire to feel others? When confronted with others, personal pleasure as much as personal pain become absolute and universal. What remains is the love for horror and the horror of love.”

title: Gertrude Abercrombie
contributors: Robert Storr (Author), Susan Weininger (Author), Robert Cozzolino (Author), Dinah Livingston (Author), Studs Terkel (Author), Dan Nadel (Editor), Gertrude Abercrombie (Artist)
description:
4.4 pounds. This is the most comprehensive book ever published on the Chicago surrealist Gertrude Abercrombie (1909–77), a key figure in midcentury American surrealism.

From the late 1930s until her death, Abercrombie made paintings populated by objects of personal significance―moons, towers, cats, pennants, Victorian furniture, shells, snails and doors―to create allegories for her own often precarious psychological states. Often presiding over these symbols was Abercrombie herself, who appears in numerous pictures as proud observer or witchy caricature.

Abercrombie exhibited in Chicago and New York in the 1940s and ‘50s, and her salon became a center of Midwestern culture, hosting jazz musicians (such as her close friend Dizzy Gillespie), writers and artists. This book includes new scholarship by Robert Cozzolino a memoir of Abercrombie by Robert Storr the artist's own writing a definitive text by art historian Susan Weininger and a memoir by the artist's daughter, Dinah Livingston.

title: Rita Ackermann & Andro Wekua: Chapter 4
description:
red mylar, perfect binding, offset printed, color, Chapter 4” is published in conjunction with an exhibition of the same title at Fergus McCaffrey Tokyo (May 1 – July 3, 2021).

It was in 2002 that Swiss-based Georgian artist Andro Wekua and New York-based Hungarian artist Rita Ackermann were introduced and began a fruitful creative collaboration with each other. Their remote communication, fuelled by mutual experiences of pictures, music, poetry and plain talk, resulted in the publication of zine-like art books – first self-published (“Chapter 1”), then published by Swiss publisher Nieves (“Chapter 2” and “Chapter 3”). This “Chapter 4”, published by Fergus McCaffrey and Tokyo-based Case Publishing, continues serving as a platform to showcase Ackermann’s and Wekua’s mutual artistic fruits. The large-format book includes paintings, drawings and collages of the two artists, created between 2008 and 2021. “Ackermann and Wekua are part of a lineage that includes their fellow ‘Easterners’ Georg Baselitz and Sigmar Polke, in that they borrow widely from folk and fairy tales, invoke high and low culture, and navigate a path between state-mandated realism and the perceived allure of American gestural abstraction. Further, it is impossible not to reference two earlier displaced Europeans: Willem de Kooning and Mark Rothko, who seem to provide material and spiritual nutrition in finding a path between figuration, landscape, and pure abstraction.

Wekua begins with collages of animals, palm trees, inwardly consumed adolescents, and abandoned domestic spaces that become gradually obliterated and transformed under layers of bright pinks, purples, acid yellows, turquoises, and magentas that evoke the color palette of Rothko. His vibrant hues contain all of the elder artist’s contradictions in the apparent elation and the tugging sense of desperation. It is a personal art drawn from a specific place and time, but which has universal resonance despite or because of its stubborn evasiveness. Though Wekua’s scale of works and methods are significantly different, both feel psychically fraught and born of struggle. Scraped down and distressed in the making, Wekua’s means are very evident to behold loaded with materials and meaning. Portraiture and self-portraiture are amongst Wekua’s most pressing concerns, and a sense of unease and discomfort is evoked that whispers of alienation and longing. (…) Ackermann shares the same layering, coding, and disclosure of source imagery, which often appears distracting and at odds with itself, perhaps reflecting a layer of self-defense against prying eyes and pervasive surveillance. ” The book also includes an essay by curator Gianni Jetzer. All texts are included in English and Japanese translation

title: Sketchbook II (A Midsummer Night's Dream)
description:
Illustrated. Hardcover, Printed by Pureprint, London, U.K.. Sketchbook II (A Midsummer Night’s Dream), was inspired by Max Reinhardt’s film, A Midsummer Night’s Dream from 1935.

For a brief moment there were vehement ideas to re-stage the iconic masterpiece during the summer of 2020. As the first pages could almost be read as direct references to the film or notes for future productions, this tangible approach quickly evaporates from the following pages and the illustrative elements gradually fade into free assocaitions to just about anything, anytime, anywhere, under the title “A Midsummer Night’s Dream”.

description: Sketchbook V (Twitchy), the fifth and final installment of Ackermann's sketchbook series. Long time collaborator and friend of Ackermann's Harmony Korine created a foundation of drawings for Ackermann to rework within the pages of this sketchbook. The cover bears Twitchy, a character created by Korine.

title: Rita Ackermann
contributors: by Rita Ackermann (Author), Bonnie Clearwater (Author), Harmony Korine (Author), Felix Ensslin (Author), John Kelsey (Author)
description:
Illustrated. A native of Hungary, Rita Ackermann moved to New York City in the mid-1990s.

She arrived to find a culture (and art world) in transition: rave and zine culture was in full swing collaborations between artists, musicians, and magazine and book publishers were pervasive and the dawning of the Internet age was upon us. Within a few short months after settling in New York, the artist received widespread attention for her work, particularly a group of canvases populated with figures inspired by the cult German film We Children from Bahnhof Zoo about the heroin subculture of the 1970s.

Her work forged a new visual language: paintings, drawings, and collages which telescoped between a virtuoso—and sometimes brutalistic—expressionism and taut, precise figurative drawing. Ackermann’s work explores the paradoxical relationship between fragility and violence, as she derives inspiration from literature, film, philosophy, and popular culture.

title: Gone?
description:
Robert Adams calls Gone? his most personal book: a return to the semi-rural stretch of Colorado where he grew up, photographed decades after he first left it.

The 116-page volume collects 119 black-and-white photographs of the Front Range foothills, land Adams had already documented as it filled with tract housing in the 1970s. Here he goes back to what is left of the open country of his childhood, framing subdivisions, scrub, and irrigation ditches with the same unhurried attention he once gave to unbroken plains. Adams has described photography as a melancholy vocation, and this book carries that weight directly, revisiting a landscape that keeps being taken away while insisting that something of its light survives.

Adams built his reputation on exactly this kind of return: to the American West as a site of loss and habitation both, first in The New West and across the decades that followed. Gone? closes that arc on the ground where it started, published by Steidl in 2010 as a cloth-bound hardcover.
notes: Robert Adams's return to the semi-rural Colorado landscape of his childhood, revisited decades after his earlier documentation of its suburbanization.

title: Dreaming is Heavy Metal
description:
Grace Ahlbom's Dreaming is Heavy Metal reworks the imagery of Norwegian black metal fandom into a set of staged photographs, made after a chance visit to a record shop shrine to the scene's 1990s originators.

Ahlbom found the basement of Helvete, a Norwegian record store, converted into a memorial to the bands that formed there decades earlier, its walls covered in records, T-shirts, and photo-shoot props. Not a fan of the music herself, she approached the subculture as an outsider drawn to its devotion, painting the faces of two of her regular subjects in corpse paint and photographing them moving through crowds near London tourist sites. The resulting square-backed softcover, designed by Ben Ganz, was published by Soft Opening in 2018 in an edition of 300 and shown first at the gallery's unusual home inside Piccadilly Circus Underground Station.

Ahlbom, a New York-based photographer who often works with subcultures and their rituals of belonging, has trained her camera on skaters, black metal devotees, and pop idols alike, treating fandom itself as a subject worth close observation.
notes: Square-backed softcover, 4-color, 1st edition of 300, designed by Ben Ganz. Original catalogue description ("square Backed, 4 Color.") was the collector's own shorthand and has been expanded here.

title: CDMX
description:
CDMX collects Grace Ahlbom's photographs of a group of boys skating through Mexico City, made on a Supreme trip in the spring of 2019 and printed the following year as she went back through her archive in quarantine.

The fourth zine in Dashwood Books' ongoing series with Ahlbom, this staple-bound, four-color publication runs 18 pages at 5 1/4 by 8 inches, issued in an edition of 300. Ahlbom has said the photographs read differently now than when she took them: what looked like a routine afternoon of skating in public space became, seen from indoors during lockdown, a record of a freedom that had briefly disappeared. Proceeds from the zine went to LGBT Books to Prisoners.

Ahlbom, who holds a BFA in photography from Pratt Institute, has built a body of work around teenage boys and the subcultures they form, and skating has been a recurring subject since her work first drew attention in fashion and photography circles.
notes: Fourth zine in Dashwood Books' series with Grace Ahlbom. Proceeds from sale benefited LGBT Books to Prisoners. Original catalogue description ("staple bound, 4 Color. Dashwood zines.") was the collector's own shorthand and has been expanded here.

title: Monument For Nothing
description:
Makoto Aida's Monument for Nothing gathers two decades of a practice built on refusing to settle into one style, medium, or position.

Published by Graphic-sha in 2007 to accompany a survey of Aida's work, the 245-page volume runs text in Japanese and English and includes a chronology alongside an introductory essay by curator Gabriel Ritter, "True Colors." It moves across the paintings, installations, video, and drawing that make up Aida's output, work that has taken on Japanese nationalism, war memory, pornography, and the art world's own conventions, often within a single piece. The book follows no single thread through this range; instead it lays out the contradictions side by side, letting a nationalist history painting sit near a cartoonish self-portrait.

Aida trained at Tokyo University of the Arts and has remained one of Japan's most argued-over artists since the 1990s, as comfortable provoking with dark satire as painting in a deliberately classical, nihonga-derived style.
notes: Text in Japanese and English; includes a chronology and an introductory essay, "True Colors," by Gabriel Ritter.

title: Hello Future
description:
Dividing her time between Brooklyn and Dubai, Emirates artist, Farah Al Qasimi’s is a bright and rising multidisciplinary artist whose work examines postcolonial structures of power, gender and aesthetic in the Persian Gulf states and global cultural confluence and migration at-large.

Hello Future is a culmination of Al Qasimi’s photographic, performance and film practice, unified within her keen focus on surface and texture, and the revealing visual influences of the splashy and florid. The monograph includes an essay by Negar Azimi and conversation between Al Qasimi and artist Meriem Bennani. Designed by Studio Lin. Farah is recipient of the third annual Capricious Photo Award

title: Arrival, The Third Line, Dubai
description:
Farah Al Qasimi's Arrival uses the imagery of horror cinema to stage jinn folklore drawn from across the United Arab Emirates.

Self-published in a signed edition of 100 for Al Qasimi's third solo exhibition at The Third Line in Dubai, running September through November 2019, the softcover book gathers the photographs shown alongside her first feature-length film, the horror-comedy Um Al Naar (Mother of Fire). That film follows a fictional reality-television crew producing a segment on a Ras Al Khaimah jinn, using the format to trace the region's shift from Portuguese and British naval occupation to a national identity built around tolerance and rapid cultural change. The photographs in Arrival extend that same interest in belief, spectacle, and everyday transformation, staging domestic and public scenes as though something unseen were already in the frame.

Al Qasimi studied photography and music at Yale, and her work, held in the collections of MoMA, Tate Modern, and the Guggenheim, has consistently treated the Gulf's rapid modernization as a subject for the uncanny rather than the merely documentary.
notes: Self-published photobook made for Al Qasimi's 2019 exhibition "Arrival" at The Third Line, Dubai, which also premiered her film Um Al Naar (Mother of Fire). Signed edition of 100.

title: General View
description:
saddle stitch. "General View“ investigates conceptions of a new reality that continuously departs from the indexical referent towards an ever-changing rendering of a world that is yet still routed in the photographic image.

Inspired by photographs of Yosemite National Park, one of the most intensely mediated nature sites on earth, the series toys with the question regarding the necessity of traveling to a place that has been photographed innumerable times, the need to record additional photographs. If countless images of a specific place are downloadable or can be screenshot, have I been there already?

The series concentrates on the reenactment of glitches on Google Street View in a gesture similar to the concepts of Warhol's Brillo Box or Fischli & Weiss‘ reversed Ready-mades, the malfunctions are appropriated and reenacted via pre- and post-photographic processes – to test their sculptural qualities, their ability to become an autonomous entity, potentially independent from their indexical referents. The unintended glitches (as well as the originally intended blurs to conceal faces or car plates) appear as a trace of the algorithmic merging and altering of photographic images without direct human control an early potential glimpse into, a herald for a post-human understanding of the concept of the image or its redundancy and disappearance.

title: Formulation: Articulation
description:
Josef Albers spent his final years on the Formulation: Articulation portfolios, a two-part set of silkscreens that stands as his own summary of a lifetime spent testing what color does to the eye.

This 2006 Thames & Hudson edition, introduced by T.G. Rosenthal, reproduces all 127 screenprints across the portfolios' full sequence at 168 pages, tracking Albers as he revisits the nested squares of Homage to the Square and the linear studies that preceded it. Printed between 1972 and his death in 1976, the plates function as a retrospective in a medium Albers controlled completely, each color relationship built up in flat, unmodulated screens so that the interaction between adjacent hues, not any illusion of depth, carries the image.

Albers taught color theory at the Bauhaus, Black Mountain College, and Yale, and the systematic thinking behind Interaction of Color, his best-known text, runs through this late portfolio as a kind of visual index to everything he had argued in the classroom.
notes: Reproduces the complete Formulation: Articulation silkscreen portfolios (127 prints), made 1972–1976.

title: One black & white and nineteen colour photographs
description: One black & white and nineteen colour photographs by Miles Aldridge. First edition (2014). First impression. Large format paperback in new condition. Signed by The Cabinet by Miles Aldridge to back of cover. No markings. This is a brand new book. Please see pictures. PayPal accepted, any questions please get in touch.
tags: Art, Miles Aldridge, Photography, Portrait Photography, Signed Photography, fashion photography

title: Please return Polaroid
description:
clothbound, 117 images. Please Please return Polaroid is Miles Aldridge’s ongoing love letter to Polaroid, a process once integral to the craft of many photographers but now more or less extinct, apart from the rare and out-of-date material still traded on eBay.

The sequel to Aldridge’s Please Return Polaroid of 2016, this book presents new and vintage Polaroids from his more than 20-year archive in a seemingly random sequence shaped by a dreamlike logic and surprising juxtapositions. Please Please return Polaroid explores Aldridge’s dedication to analogue processes where cut-and-paste is still a manual process, made with scissors, gaffer tape, intuition and not a little patience.

Aldridge continues to use Polaroids as part of his work-in-progress “sketches,” often scratching, tearing and taping them together, even drawing over them each mark part of the creative act. Known for creating immaculate photos of a less than perfect world, Aldridge revels in these unpolished images, transforming some into extreme enlargements filling double pages with their re-worked and damaged surfaces.

Inkjet printed by AJM (Brussels), Risograph printed by Chez Rosi (Brussels), Recycled paper and Fedrigoni paper, Screen-printed paper envelope by Atelier l'Appât (Brussels). 515.05 by Alex GD is an experimental copy machine project about surveillance, image control, identity and numeric filing. Who are the real criminals here the people in the pictures or the one that controls de CCTV?

title: Dirty Windows
publisher: Art Pub Inc First Edition, First Printing
description:
Merry Alpern's Dirty Windows reduces surveillance photography to its rawest form: forty-some black-and-white frames shot through a bathroom window, aimed at a makeshift brothel used by Wall Street traders after hours.

In 1994, Alpern set up a medium-format camera in the bathroom window of a friend's apartment overlooking an air shaft off Wall Street. Over several months she photographed a room used for paid sex and drug use by financial-district men and the women they hired, working without her subjects' knowledge. The pictures are cropped tight and grainy, closer to surveillance footage than composed photography. Scalo published the sequence as a small monograph in 1995, its plain grid layout keeping the evidentiary tone of the source material intact.

Alpern had worked as a documentary photographer before turning her camera on that window, and she has said the project began as an exercise in looking rather than a statement about gender or class. Its covert method and its subject, sex for sale steps from the New York Stock Exchange, made Dirty Windows one of the most argued-over photobooks of the 1990s, still cited in debates over consent and the ethics of an unseen camera.
tags: New York City, prostitution, sex, sex-work downtown, Surveillance, Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One
notes: Cataloguer's publisher field ("Art Pub Inc First Edition, First Printing") is retained from the existing record; secondary sources (Setanta Books, OpenLibrary) identify the actual publisher as Scalo, Zurich, 1995. Kept as a possible different-printing note rather than overridden. One of two copies in the collection; see id 2337 for the boxed, numbered copy.

title: M by Ralf Christofor
description:
Text (German/English) by Ralf Christofori, 84 pages with 95 coloured illustrations.

Yoshitaka Amano was born in Shizuoka in 1952 and, on leaving the production company Tatsunoko at the tender age of 30, had already become a star in the firmament of Japan’s Manga-scene. His early animation series »Speed-Racer« and »G-Force«, as well as the later »Final Fantasy« proved to be immensely popular, becoming permanent fixtures in 70s TV entertainment schedules, particularly in the USA. The mass Japanese animation and comics market’s insatiable appetite has subsequently turned Amano into a fully-fledged superstar. With a few notable exceptions, contemporary art in Japan has continually been reproached for its style of imitative appropriation, until that is a new batch of artists burst onto the scene at the end of the 90s. On their own admission they owe a lot to Amano, be it Mariko Mori’s futuristic barbie-esque dreamscapes and performances or Takasha Murakami and Yoshitomo Nara for instance, in whose paintings the graphic borrowings from Manga proliferate in the funny faces or as unformed babies and little bears. Next to his work on further Mangas for a variety of new applications, be they films, as book illustrations, ceramic designs or as video games, Amano has recently revisited the 700 year old painting tradition of sumi-e.

This technique using ink on fine rice paper is based upon expression, brush stroke and absolute precision, leaving no room for error. The Zen idea of penetrating to the essence of the matter is coupled here with an automatism, which construes the thing being painted as a kind of second nature, or as (American) critical opinion has described it: »the introverting of something extrovert in the form of an applied mutation …and, as a merging of different ideas of time, allowing past and future to coalesce.« Amano has Mangas coming out of his ears, Mangas he can use and fashion everywhichway in a variety of guises, situations and modes of expression. In between however, he has been fascinated by the challenge of transferring pictorial elements derived from the ancient sumi-e painting tradition onto highly polished placards. And here, aside from of any skill involved, his supra-dimensional eyes and chins, furrowed brows, silhouettes and details appear to be drawn from the same inexhaustible but anonymous reservoir, from which modern pictorial language also feeds they have quite literally lost their Japanese innocence and have become universal ciphers in a universalistic culture. Were one to ask Amano where he is currently living, it is indeed fitting that he should reply: mostly Tokyo, New York and Paris.

title: Ghada Amer: Painting in Revolt - by Susan Thompson
description:
New York-based painter and embroiderer Ghada Amer (born 1963) was raised in Cairo, Egypt, and later educated in Nice and Paris, France.

Her experiences with sexism in both locations served as the impetus for her to forge new ground in a range of mediums, from painting and sculpture to ceramics and earthworks. With a background in abstract painting, Amer eventually turned to embroidery as a strategy for infiltrating the male space of painting with a material traditionally associated with women.

Her work is frequently based on the images of female figures found in magazines, through which she explores the constructions of gender, sexuality and eroticism. Her embroidery is intentionally loose, with threads dangling from the canvas, provoking a pictorial effect not unlike Pollock's splattered paint. More recent works introduce a verbal element, with quotations and aphorisms. This volume reproduces these pieces along with a selection of works from across her career.

title: Christopher Anderson -: SON
description: With this book, Magnum photographer Christopher Anderson, renowned for his documentary work from conflict zones all over the world, presents a very personal body of work: "These photographs are an organic response to an experience that is at the same time the most unique and the most universal of experiences: the birth of a child. . . . Through my son, my role as the son took on new meaning and my senses were hypertuned to the evidence of my own life passing."

title: Christopher Anderson: Stump
description:
Christopher Anderson's Stump collects color and black-and-white pictures from the 2012 U.S. presidential campaign trail, close-cropped portraits that catch politicians mid-gesture, between rehearsed composure and unscripted strain.

Anderson followed the Obama and Romney campaigns as a photojournalist, but sequenced the resulting images here as something closer to theater criticism than reportage. Faces of Barack and Michelle Obama, Mitt Romney, Paul Ryan, Bill Clinton, and rally crowds appear without captions, interspersed with fireworks, flags, and the other stagecraft of a campaign. Removed from its original news context, the material reads as a study of political performance itself. RM published the book in 2014 with an essay by journalist John Heilemann.

Anderson, a member of Magnum Photos, built his early reputation on war reportage, including his 1999 crossing with Haitian refugees that earned him a Robert Capa Gold Medal. Stump belongs to a later, more personal turn in his career, one that also produced Son and Capitolio, in which he trains a documentary eye on subjects closer to home, whether family or the machinery of American power.
notes: Some secondary sources (josefchladek.com) list this as a 2013 Barcelona edition; the catalogue's 2014 date is retained.

title: Approximate Joy
description:
paper wrapped, Silk screened, 68 Images (CMYK). Christopher Anderson’s photographs portray a contemporary China in the midst of perpetual reinvention.

"I have seen the future and it is now and it is China. There is no need for the past. It can be erased. A new happiness is being constructed, an approximation of joy, better than the real thing.” - Christopher Anderson The images are tightly cropped and extremely close up, bringing the viewer to an intimate distance where all context is removed, except for the ambient artificial light that illuminates the faces, giving only the sensual information of the physical form allowing the viewer the indiscreet pleasure of staring at another human face and wondering who the individual might be or what they might be thinking about at the moment of the photograph.

These photographs are not a documentary about what people do. Rather they are a search for connection and recognition of self.
tags: Fine Art Photography, Portrait Photography, Still Life Photography, Photography

title: COP
description:
Christopher Anderson began photographing New York City cops in the wake of 9/11, as the visual landscape of the city he called home began to change.

Bomb blast barriers went up, cops carrying larger guns seemed to be everywhere, and whilst the increased presence of security was designed, in part, to make New Yorkers feel safe, it reminded Anderson that something was deeply wrong. Then, in the wake of Occupy Wall Street, the death of Eric Garner and the election of Trump, Anderson found himself making photographs of cops on the streets of New York City once again, as a form of unconscious protest on a larger sense of authority. On assessing the images he was making, Anderson began to see them as something entirely different than a protest or commentary on power - there was almost a sentimentality.

“I saw a portrait of a working class, immigrant America. The uniform only served as a thread on which to hang a cross section sample. The photographs felt more like a love letter to New York”—Christopher Anderson Anderson is a member of Magnum. He first gained recognition in 1999 when his poignant images of the rescue of Haitian refugees taken onboard a sinking wooden boat won him the Robert Capa Gold Medal. His previous book Approximate Joy was widely regarded as one of the best books of 2018.

title: Bleu Blanc Rouge
description:
In Bleu Blanc Rouge, Christopher Anderson lays out a decade of color pictures made across the United States and Europe like pages torn from an unfinished magazine, image after image left to argue its own case.

The photographs move between New York, France, Italy, Spain, and Germany, mixing portraits, street moments, and still lifes with no fixed narrative thread. What holds the sequence together is a set of recurring visual notes: the color red, repeated shapes, and the low light of late afternoon. Some pairings tell a clear story; others sit apart, and Anderson leaves the reader to decide whether they belong together at all. Hatje Cantz published the book with text by Nadine Barth, alongside an exhibition of the same title at The Ravestijn Gallery in Amsterdam.

Anderson has spent two decades moving between photojournalism, fashion, and art photography as a member of Magnum Photos, a career that also includes Son, Capitolio, and Stump. Bleu Blanc Rouge sits at the loosest end of that body of work, less a project than a working method laid bare.
notes: Several bookseller and gallery sources list a 2018 publication/exhibition date; the catalogue's 2019 date is retained.

title: Disobedient Bodies
description:
JW Anderson built Disobedient Bodies as a second exhibition on paper, pairing sculpture by Barbara Hepworth and Henry Moore with the fashion he designs for a living.

The book documents Anderson's 2017 exhibition at The Hepworth Wakefield, where he set works by Hepworth, Moore, Constantin Brancusi, Eileen Gray, and Sarah Lucas alongside garments by Jean Paul Gaultier, Christian Dior, Helmut Lang, and his own label. Rather than reproduce the show's wall-by-wall layout, the publication recombines the material into new page pairings not seen in the gallery, an approach Anderson describes as asking his collaborators to be "disobedient" within their own disciplines. Bound with an elastic tie around a single interleaved section, the 142-page book was printed by InOtherWords in an edition of 2,000.

Anderson, the founder of his own label and creative director of Loewe, has built a body of work that treats the body's shape as unstable territory, an interest this project extends from the runway into sculpture and museum display. Disobedient Bodies remains one of the clearest statements of how he thinks across those fields rather than within any one of them.
notes: ISBN 9780993223822 taken from the cover barcode; not previously in the catalogue record.

title: Letters From Mayhem
description:
Roger Andersson's book Letters from Mayhem is an artist's book made of 26 duotone watercolors, each depicting one letter of the alphabet.

Printed on thick board in the format of a children's ABC primer, each letter is embedded in a fairytale setting in which wispy long-haired teenagers lie around stoned, sniffing glue, listening to heavy metal, and so on.

This garden of vices overgrown with weeds and entangled vines forms a strange foil for imagery drawn from drug culture, anarchy, heavy metal, and children's cartoons, rendering every scene both innocent and corrupt. Full of messages hidden within plants, ponds and clouds, Andersson's drawings evoke a soft nostalgia for childhood tempered by images of soft-edged romantic decadence.

title: Swedish Girls: A Tribute
contributors: Nina Tahko (Designer), Louise Enhörning (Photographer), Nina Andersson (Photographer)
description:
Swedish Girls: A Tribute gathers five years of portraits by photographers Nina Andersson and Louise Enhörning, each working independently to picture young women across Sweden.

Between them, Andersson and Enhörning photographed one hundred women, building a loose collective portrait of what it meant to be young and female in Sweden in the early 2010s rather than following any single subject. Sequenced together without a shared narrative, the pictures accumulate into something closer to a group document than a conventional monograph, arranged across two hundred pages of Swedish-language text. Argent Books published the book in 2014.

Both photographers worked largely outside the gallery system on this project, and Swedish Girls remains their best-known collaboration, an example of portrait photography used as a form of collective record-keeping rather than individual authorship.
notes: Photographs by Nina Andersson and Louise Enhörning. A third name, Nina Tahko, appears in some bookseller records as an additional credit but could not be confirmed.

title: Strip
description:
Kathryn Andrews' Strip turns snapshots of the Hollywood Walk of Fame into a flip-book of tourists, street performers, and the traffic lights between them.

Andrews photographed Hollywood Boulevard at street level, then laid the pictures out in overlapping rows that shift left and right as the reader turns the page, mimicking the look of a film strip. The layered images never quite resolve into a single coherent scene; instead a fragmented version of the boulevard keeps reassembling itself in new combinations. Published by UCCA and Koenig Books in 2015 and edited by Karen Marta and Brian Roettinger, the book was made for "The Los Angeles Project," a 2014 exhibition at the Ullens Center for Contemporary Art in Beijing that asked seven Los Angeles artists to each produce an artist's book.

Strip was Andrews' first artist's book, made in the tradition of John Baldessari and Edward Ruscha's photographic studies of the Los Angeles street. It marked an early instance of the found-object and appropriation strategies that later defined her sculpture and installation work.
notes: Made as part of a group exhibition ("The Los Angeles Project," UCCA Beijing, 2014) that commissioned individual artist's books from seven Los Angeles artists.

title: Black Panther Coloring Book
contributors: Corey Presha (Reissue Artist), Bill Sullivan (Reissue Artist)
description:
The Black Panther Coloring Book is a 1968 pamphlet whose true origin is still disputed: was it Black Panther propaganda, an FBI forgery meant to discredit the Panthers, or an internal Panther drawing the FBI later weaponized against its own creators.

The 46-page booklet, drawn in the style of Panther Minister of Culture Emory Douglas, traces a march from the kidnapping of Africans through the Party's founding to armed confrontation with police drawn as pigs. FBI memos describe distributing the book to white households as part of COINTELPRO, the Bureau's campaign to "expose, disrupt, misdirect, discredit, or otherwise neutralize" Black nationalist groups. Historian Ward Churchill later traced the drawings to Party member Akinsanya Kambon, whose artwork was reportedly ordered destroyed by Panther leadership before a Los Angeles chapter member distributed copies anyway. This edition reprints the imagery with its original text stripped away.

Regardless of who drew it first, the book endures as a document of COINTELPRO's methods and of how easily political image-making can be turned against the people it was made to serve. Its 2016 reissue by artists Corey Presha and Bill Sullivan asks viewers to look again at images once judged too violent for the Panthers' own children.
notes: Publication year for this reissue is given as 2015 by one retailer (Perimeter Books) and 2016 by another (edcat); 2016 used here. Original 1968 pamphlet's authorship is genuinely contested in the historical record (FBI COINTELPRO vs. Black Panther Party member Akinsanya Kambon); both accounts are presented in the description rather than resolved.

title: I Am Woman
contributors: Patrik Andersson, Charlotte Cotton, Lars-Erik Hjertström Lappalainen
description:
Lotta Antonsson's I Am a Woman (Art and Theory Publishing, Stockholm, 2016) gathers the Swedish artist's collages and montages, cutting fashion and erotic photography from vintage print sources and pairing the fragments with natural forms: a shell pressed over a sleeping face on the cover, driftwood, minerals. The work reads eroticism and ephemerality through the same cut.

Designed by Aoki, the 128-page softcover reproduces the work in full color and black and white. Patrik Andersson's essay locates the work in the “documentary and fiction blur” of the late 1960s and '70s, where the social and sexual revolutions of that era resurface in Antonsson's analogue cuts and repetitions Charlotte Cotton and Lars-Erik Hjertström Lappalainen contribute additional texts.

Antonsson works across photography, sculpture, and collage, returning often to found and appropriated imagery to examine the gendered histories embedded in mass media. I Am a Woman continues that inquiry, freeing fashion and erotic photography from their original contexts to expose the clichés, and the allegorical potential, locked inside them.

title: Blue Period / Last Summer
description:
Blue Period / Last Summer pairs two chapters of Nobuyoshi Araki's ongoing photographic diary, its cover a nude print overpainted by the artist in raw washes of color. The hand-applied intervention recurs throughout his later work.

Published by Dashwood Books in December 2017, the paperback gathers photographs alongside earlier negatives reworked with paint and other additions, a method Araki has used to layer new marks onto images made years apart. Its two titled sections each trace a season, a blue period and a last summer, continuing his habit of dating and naming bodies of work as entries in one continuous private record rather than as discrete, self-contained series.

Araki has published several hundred books since the 1970s, moving between the erotic, the domestic, and the elegiac often within a single volume; his self-portraits, images of his late wife Yoko, and his hallmark kinbaku rope photography sit alongside street and sky pictures in an oeuvre organized less by genre than by the calendar of his own life. Blue Period / Last Summer belongs to the later period of that project, in which the photograph becomes raw material for further mark-making rather than a finished, untouched object.
notes: Published by Dashwood Books, December 2017; also credited to Session Press and Arakinema. Page count, dimensions, and print run were not confirmed by any source consulted. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Araki by Araki
description:
Araki by Araki is Nobuyoshi Araki's own retrospective selection of his photography, a career-spanning survey chosen and sequenced by the artist himself rather than an outside editor or curator.

Across 568 pages the book moves through the subjects that recur across Araki's five-decade output: Tokyo street life, food, faces, flowers photographed with an erotic intensity, and the rope-bound bodies of his kinbaku work. Araki has described the bondage photographs as a collaboration with his subjects, built on conversation rather than direction, and the sequencing here plays that vocabulary of restraint and release against his gentler still lifes and portraits.

Published by TASCHEN with text by Jérôme Sans, the book is one of several Araki has titled around his own name, distinct from the earlier Kodansha volume Araki by Araki: The Photographer's Personal Selection issued for his sixtieth birthday. Araki has published more than 500 books since the 1970s, and this edition stands as one of the most widely available single-volume overviews of that output.
notes: TASCHEN retrospective selected and sequenced by Araki himself, text by Jérôme Sans; published in English, French, and German. Distinct from the earlier 2003 Kodansha volume of the same short title, 'Araki by Araki: The Photographer's Personal Selection.' Dimensions not confirmed by any source checked. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Araki Teller, Teller Araki
description: Araki Teller, Teller Araki was published to coincide with the two artist's collaborative exhibition at the Ostlicht Galerie fur Fotografie in Vienna. This large tome, the first artist's book conceived and designed jointly by Araki and Teller, consists of over 300 pages of photo-jousting by two of the most original and influential voices working in photography today. Each, in their own way, exploring existential questions of physicality and sexuality

title: Monochrome Paradise
description:
Monochrome Paradise gathers seventy-five black-and-white photographs in which Nobuyoshi Araki turns dolls, dying flowers, and toy animals into a small theater of decay and desire.

Published by Adachi Press in 2015, the book continues Araki's long-running "Paradise" project, begun after his wife Yoko's death with A's Paradise and carried forward through qARADISE and It Was Once a Paradise. Still-life arrangements of plastic figurines and cut flowers alternate with portraits, among them Umezu Kazuo, Setouchi Jakucho, Araki's longtime muse Kaori, and a cameo appearance by Lady Gaga. Text runs in Japanese and English.

Araki has spent more than five decades photographing Tokyo, sex, flowers, and mortality with the same directness, and the "Paradise" series is one of his most sustained treatments of aging and bodily decline. Monochrome Paradise stands with his diaristic bondage work and city photographs as one more entry in a body of work he keeps reworking from a small set of fixed obsessions.
notes: Part of Araki's ongoing 'Paradise' series, which began with A's Paradise (1998) after the death of his wife Yoko and continued through qARADISE (2011) and It Was Once a Paradise (2011). Designed by Isao Mitobe.

title: Theater of Love
editor: Designed by Yoshihisa Tanaka, Printing by Hakkou Art Co., Ltd.
description:
The series consists of around 100 photographs taken around the year 1965, when Araki was working at advertising giant Dentsu.

The photos, first shown at an exhibition at Taka Ishii Gallery in February 2011, are presented as a postcard-sized book, hidden in a Fuji photographic paper box replica, the same way Araki discovered his old prints.

"I've found a cabinet box, labelled 'Theater of Love'. Opening it, there were about 150 prints inside. They must have been taken around '65, back when I was clicking away on an Olympus Pen F, experimenting with thermal development, fooling around with printing and film developing techniques. The photos are a record of me, the women and the life and the places of that era. Seems like I called them 'Theater of Love' in those days. But either way — good stuff. Good photos. You can't get this with digital." — Nobuyoshi Araki

title: Nobuyoshi Araki: Vintage Prints
description:
Nobuyoshi Araki: Vintage Prints documents a rare New York showing of prints Araki made himself, close to the time each picture was taken, rather than the later reprints through which most of his work is known.

Published by Dashwood Books with Taka Ishii Gallery on the occasion of Araki's first solo exhibition at the gallery's New York space (April 4–28, 2018), the 48-page softcover reproduces all twenty-one vintage prints in the show, designed by Alex Lin of Studio Lin and issued in an edition of 500. The selected images move from the 1970s, when Araki left a career in advertising to photograph Tokyo with a tripod-mounted Pentax and a fixed 55mm lens, through the streetscapes later published as Life and pictures from Tokyo, in Autumn, Pseudo-Diary, Tokyo Story, and The First Year of Heisei.

Vintage prints — made close to the date of the negative rather than later, for exhibition or sale — are unusual in Araki's practice given the sheer volume of his output, and this catalogue offers a rare document of his working prints across four formative decades, tracing the shift from his early, Atget- and Walker Evans-influenced cityscapes toward the diaristic, intimate mode for which he later became known.
notes: Catalogue for the exhibition at Taka Ishii Gallery, New York, April 4–28, 2018. Designed by Alex Lin (Studio Lin). Edition of 500 copies. No ISBN found. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Nobuyoshi Araki: Eros Diary
description:
Eros Diary collects eighty-seven new photographs in which Nobuyoshi Araki turns from provocation toward something quieter: an old man taking stock of loss.

Published by Anthony d'Offay in 2016 to accompany Araki's exhibition of the same name at Anton Kern Gallery in New York, the book reproduces seventy-seven black-and-white and ten color images. Each photograph carries a timestamp keyed to the date of Araki's marriage to his late wife Yoko, which also falls on Tanabata, the Japanese festival built around a folktale of separated lovers reunited for one night a year. The recurring date threads the book together and keeps Yoko present in her absence.

Araki made the pictures while dealing with prostate cancer, the loss of sight in one eye, and the death of his cat Chiro, and that accumulation of grief gives Eros Diary a softness rare in his catalogue of erotic and urban photography. Coming more than four decades into his career, it reads as a late, private counterpart to the diaristic work that made him famous.
notes: 10 color and 77 black-and-white plates. Each image is timestamped to the anniversary of Araki's marriage to Yoko, who died in 1990.

title: Tokyo Blues 1977
description: 43 illustrations. This catalog was published for the solo exhibition ‘Tokyo Blues 1977’, held at Taka Ishii Gallery in August 2013. After their exhibition at Nikon Salon in 1977, these works remained untouched in Araki’s storeroom until their recent rediscovery. This book includes 43 photographs loosely centered about a woman from Kyushu who Araki had just met. It captures the languidness and blues of Japan in the 1970’s

title: Araki Teller, Teller Araki
publisher: eyesencia, MATCH and Company Co., Ltd.
description:
Published to coincide with the exhibition "Araki Teller Teller Araki" held at OstLich Gallery (April-May 2014) in Vienna Austria, Nobuyoshi Araki and Juergen Teller present their first jointly conceived and designed book.

The publication assembles more than 300 photographs including works shown at the exhibition which were previously unpublished. The book brings together two of the most important photographers of our time, showing new works conceived for the exhibition. Both artists are united in this publication in their radical artistic attitude and their almost insatiable hunger for images as reflections of their personal experience of the world. Includes texts written by Nobuyoshi Araki and Juergen Teller which they have each dedicated to one another.

title: Magazine Work
description:
Diane Arbus: Magazine Work collects the photographs Arbus made on assignment for Esquire, Harper's Bazaar, and other magazines between 1960 and 1971, work she never separated from her personal projects.

Edited by Doon Arbus and Marvin Israel with an essay by Thomas W. Southall, the book was first published by Aperture in 1984 and reprinted several times since; this is the 2005 impression. It reproduces the tear sheets and layouts alongside the original photographs, showing how portraits of figures such as Mae West, Jorge Luis Borges, and Norman Mailer moved from Arbus's camera into print. The magazine format gave her steady access to strangers and public figures alike, and she used it the same way she used the street.

Arbus died in 1971, and this volume, assembled well after her death by her daughter and her friend and editor, argues against any hard line between commercial photography and art. It sits with Diane Arbus: An Aperture Monograph and Revelations as one of the primary sources for how her published work actually looked on the page.
notes: Collects photographs originally made for magazine assignment, edited posthumously by Doon Arbus and Marvin Israel; first published 1984, reprinted through at least a 2005 (fourth) impression, the edition catalogued here.

title: Diane Arbus In the Beginning Early Photographs 1956 1962
description:
illustrations. Catalog of the exhibition held at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, July 12-November 27, 2016 and at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, January 21-April 30, 2017.

Includes bibliographical references (pages 261-263) and index.

"Diane Arbus (1923-1971) is one of the most distinctive and provocative artists of the twentieth century. Her photographs of children and eccentrics, couples and circus performers, female impersonators and nudists, are among the most recognizable images of our time. This book is the definitive study of the artist's first seven years of work, from 1956 to 1962. Drawn primarily from the rich holdings of the Metropolitan Museum's Diane Arbus Archive--a remarkable treasury of photographs, negatives, appointment books, notebooks, and correspondence--it is an essential contribution to our understanding of Arbus and her oeuvre. diane arbus: in the beginning showcases over 100 of the artist's early photographs, more than half of which are published here for the first time. The book provides a crucial, in- depth presentation of the artist's genesis, showing Arbus as she developed her evocative and often haunting imagery. The photographs featured in this handsome volume reveal an artist defining her style, honing her subject matter, and in full possession of the many gifts for which she is now recognized the world over." -- Publisher's description
tags: Art, Photography, exhibition, moma, street photography

title: On the Street: 1980-1990
description:
Between 1980 and 1990, over five hundred of photographer Amy Arbus's impromptu and edgy portraits of New Yorkers appeared in the Village Voice's monthly fashion feature, "On the Street."

The column's missive was to document the city's most adventurous trednsetters as they lived their lives. But Arbus's photographs tell much more than a style story. From the friendliest to the grittiest, every one of these images is a potent tribute to self-expression. Taken as a whole, they reflect an era of contradictions, a time in America when urban individualism and raw creativity were courageously fighting for breathing room and holding their own in a culture ruled by wealthy conservatism and Republican politics. For the first time since that hard-to-define decade, this time-capsule collection of images is being revisited. On the Street features seventy of the most revealing and expressive images taken by Arbus on the city’s fashion-fertile sidewalks.

From the unknown to the unmistakably famous, her subjects are all equally unforgettable. Arbus’s ubiquitous lens captured the most influential style-makers, from The Clash on the set of Martin Scorsese's King of Comedy and Madonna on the same day her single “Everybody” hit the charts, to Anna Sui, Joey Arias, Phoebe Legére, and countless other local artists, actors, costume designers, shop owners, musicians, make-up artists, graffiti artists, and downtown scenesters. From eyewear to underwear and schoolgirl skirts to backless shirts from women dressed like men to men that are barely dressed from lipstick to just plain “schtik,” there is no aspect of 80’s style that goes unrepresented.

title: The Fourth Wall
description:
What happens when a performing actor leaves behind his lines, staging, sets, and lighting, and steps beyond the fourth wall?

For three years, Amy Arbus has been exploring this question in a series of dramatic portraits of celebrated actors, both on and off Broadway. Fully costumed but stripped of their context, Arbus's actors remain in character as they step outside the fiction of theater into the reality of the world beyond. Staged in anonymous public spaces--in theater lobbies, on city streets, in parks, and in stage door alleys--Arbus's images achieve an unexpected blend of spectacle and high art formality and sontaneity vulnerability and pretense. Collected in The Fourth Wall are some of the modern stage's most gifted actors, including Alan Cumming in Cabaret, John Malkovitch in Lost Land, Liev Schreiber in Talk Radio, Ed Harris in Wrecks, Cherry Jones in Doubt, Christine Ebersol in Grey Gardens, and Ethan Hawke and Martha Plimpton in The Coast of Utopia.

Actors are included from such successful and ambitioud productions as Wicked, The Light in the Piazza, Hedwig and the Angry Inch, Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, and The Color Purple, to name but a few. Portraits are accompanied by synopses of the plays as well as quotes from a number of the actors portrayed.In 2006's critically acclaimed book On the Street, Arbus focused her lens on those who dressed to express themselves--now she turns her attention to those who dress to become someone else. The result is a collection of potent photographs that pay remarkable tribute to contemporary theater and the performers who bring fantasy to life.

title: Pickpocket
contributors: David Rudnick, Emiel Penninckx, Maharani, Yasmine Putri, and Mozes Mosuse in Terrain
description: 228 pages, 5 individually bound inserts, offset width.4 colour offset litho, 3 spot colours screenprinted mylar clear outer jacket 578 images total. The first monograph of the work of New York-based photographer Daniel Arnold. Pickpocket is comprised of a "Prestige Edit" titled The Woods, and five additional "Alleyways" – GALA, Cell Out, Fuck Ups, 47th Street, and ElseWhere. With liner notes by Daniel Arnold and an afterword by Josh Safdie.

title: Morena No. 2
description: Lais Ribeiro. This second issue of Morena was shot in different sessions during 2014 by Guy Aroch. Aroch is one of today's most influential fashion photographers, his photography is recognized by its plastic values and proximity, creating evocative works. Guy's editorial partners include British Vogue, Muse, Harpers Bazaar UK, Centrefold, French, British GQ , L'Officiel, The New York Times, LA Times and WWD.

title: Medianoche
description:
Medianoche photographs the small rituals of a night out: the glance, the touch on an arm, the drink held a beat too long, staged in the bars and clubs where courtship still runs on old signals.

Rafael Arocha shot the series between 2009 and 2011 in Belgrade, Madrid, Barcelona, and other Spanish cities, working close and in available light. He self-published the fifty-two black-and-white images as an 84-page hardcover in 2014, in an edition of 500, with no text, and the book is distributed by Dalpine. The design keeps the pictures unbroken by captions, so the sequence itself carries the narrative of a night moving toward its later hours.

Arocha, born in Gran Canaria in 1978 and based in Barcelona, considers Medianoche his first book. It won first prize at the 2015 Cordoba Biennial for Self-Publishing and was a finalist for the Rencontres d'Arles Book Award, and it remains the work most identified with his nocturnal, observational approach to street photography.
notes: Winner, 1st Prize, Cordoba Biennial for Self-Publishing, 2015; finalist, Rencontres d'Arles Book Award, 2015. No dimensions found in available sources.

title: Jeddah Diary
description: Olivia Arthur’s debut, Jeddah Diary, was published by Fishbar and documents the lives of young Saudi women in Jeddah.

title: Artificial Nature
description:
Artificial Nature is the catalogue for a 1990 group exhibition that read the American and European fascination with genetics, plastic surgery, and processed food as a single project: the replacement of nature with its manufactured image.

Curated by Jeffrey Deitch and designed by the graphic artist Dan Friedman, the show ran at the DESTE Foundation's space at the House of Cyprus in Athens from June to September 1990 and brought together seventeen American and European artists, among them Ashley Bickerton, Jeff Koons, Martin Kippenberger, Robert Smithson, Andy Warhol, and Meg Webster. The 152-page catalogue, printed in English and Greek, pairs installation views and artist plates with Deitch's essay on how consumer culture had already substituted its own version of the natural world.

Friedman, known for his design work with Warhol and for the retail interiors he built at Fiorucci, gave the catalogue the flat, saturated look of advertising rather than an art book. That choice carries the exhibition's argument onto the cover itself. Artificial Nature remains a key document of Deitch's early curatorial voice, several years before he opened his own gallery in New York.
notes: Group exhibition catalogue; seventeen artists included Ashley Bickerton, Clegg & Guttmann, Walter de Maria, Laura Grisi, Martin Kippenberger, Jeff Koons, Liz Larner, Tatsuo Miyajima, Peter Nagy, Pino Pascali, Edward Ruscha, Manuel Saiz, Robert Smithson, William Stone, Thanassis Totsikas, Meg Webster, and Andy Warhol.

title: Liz Johnson Artur
description:
This self-titled 2016 monograph was Liz Johnson Artur's first book-length survey, drawing on three decades of photographing Black communities across the African diaspora, from her Black Balloon Archive.

Published by Bierke in an edition of 700 clothbound copies with a photograph tipped into the cover, the book presents a cross-section of images made in London, Moscow, Accra, New York and elsewhere since the late 1980s, moving between portraiture, street photography and the everyday life of the communities she photographs. It was named to The New York Times' Best Photo Books of 2016.

Johnson Artur was born in 1964 in Sokhumi, then part of the Soviet Union, to a Russian mother and Ghanaian father, and has lived and worked in London since 1991. Her practice centers on the long-running Black Balloon Archive, the source for this book as well as her later titles I Will Keep You in Good Company (SPBH Editions/Mack) and PDA (Bierke), and for Dusha, her first solo museum exhibition, shown at the Brooklyn Museum in 2019 and the Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis in 2020.
tags: Photography, Portraiture, African Diaspora, Documentary Photography
notes: Page count reported inconsistently across dealer listings; approximately 130 pages is the more plausible figure.

title: Leviathan
description:
cloth bound. This series emerged from Morgan Ashcom’s experiences at a remote community in south-eastern Ohio, an outsiders’ oasis.

Originally, he saw the potential to reconcile two opposing but familiar scenes: the urban skating culture he had once been part of, and the rural surroundings of his youth. But the identity of things seemed slightly altered – it was a warped doppelganger of his childhood home. So he stepped away from his presumed knowledge of where he was. Themes of escape and confrontation with the unknowable began to appear in the pictures. The sequence of images suggests a subjective narrative where disparate cultures and geographies converge.

title: Monsanto: A Photographic Investigation
description:
Monsanto has had a rapid rise and a more-than-colorful history, marked by cover-ups and scandals: dioxins in PCB coolants, genetically modified products such as the bovine growth hormone Posilac, and the production of the defoliant Agent Orange.

The company is still highly controversial, irritating scientists, environmental organizations and human rights associations and acting in a way that makes people doubt the harmlessness of its products. As a manufacturer of food and animal feed, seeds and chemical products, Monsanto is relentlessly developing and marketing new technologies. The monopoly it has arguably secured by dubious means bears no relation to its negligence with regard to potential risks. Particularly in light of the devastating consequences that are still causing suffering to people and the environment in many places, the company ' s self-portrayal as a forward-looking, omnipotent force for good seems cynical. The photographer Mathieu Asselin has tried his hand at the daunting task of exploring the issues surrounding Monsanto. His investigative photographic study manages to capture the complexity of this topic, creating links between past, present and future and illuminating many different aspects from a variety of perspectives.

His photos and texts raise awareness of the problems involved. Throughout the book, Asselin seems to be concerned about who is actually responsible and who is affected by the consequences. Recognising that passing the buck is a useless game, his photos show that there are victims on all sides: physical deformities in Vietnam, families plagued by death and disease in the US, illegal waste dumps, depopulated regions, destroyed cornfields and farmers whose livelihood has been ruined. The photos are complemented by a wealth of archival material, extracts from press releases, court files, and image campaigns, as well as different slogans and stills from commercials, which in comparison seem as glib and farcical as Disneyland. These expose Monsanto's absurd attempts to pass itself off as a company interested in satisfying today's demands and preserving the earth for future generations.

title: Transformations
description:
The manifold entanglements of African and Western culture are a central motif in the oeuvre of the Algerian-French artist Kader Attia.

The influence of traditional African architecture on European modernism forms the background for his voluminous spatial installations, videos and photographs, as much as the reappropriation of North and South American black music within African Jazz and Pop of the 1960s up to the 1980s.

His work manifests the productivity of dissonance where African masks, stuffed animals, scientific instruments, and historical artifacts seemingly have nothing in common, the artist unearths connections between Europe’s handling of its own colonial history, current migration politics, and the urbanistic realities of its metropolises of today. Based on Kader Attia’s solo show Repair: 5 Acts at the KW Institute for Contemporary Art, Berlin, this publication focuses on works from the years 2008–2013 and places them in a broader art historical concept.
notes: One of two copies in the collection.

title: Tauba Auerbach ― S v Z
description:
Part artist's book, part exhibition catalog, this book chronicles Tauba Auerbach’s multimedia syntheses of abstraction, science, graphic design and typography Tauba Auerbach studies the boundaries of perception through an art and design practice grounded in math, science and craft.

Published in conjunction with the first major survey of the artist’s work, this volume, designed by Auerbach in collaboration with David Reinfurt, spans 16 years of her career and her interest in concepts such as duality and its alternatives, interconnectedness, rhythm and four-dimensional geometry.

title: An Autobiography
description:
An Autobiography tells Richard Avedon's life story entirely through photographs, without a written narrative to explain them.

Published by Random House in 1993, the book gathers 284 duotone plates spanning Avedon's career from the 1940s through the early 1990s, printed unpaginated in a large folio bound in brown cloth beneath a clear acetate jacket. In his two-page preface, Avedon describes the sequence as tracking "three crucial illusions" in his life, starting with what he calls the illusion of laughter and a young man's discovery of how close it sits to panic. Portraits of the famous run alongside pictures of people no one would otherwise have known, arranged so the pairings argue with each other across the page.

The book functions as a working catalogue raisonné of Avedon's photography and was reprinted quickly after its first run. A signed, limited edition followed the next year to mark his retrospective at the Whitney Museum, and An Autobiography remains the fullest single volume of his portrait work, from fashion pages to the plainspoken faces of In the American West.
notes: Unpaginated, 284 duotone plates. A signed limited edition (stated 250, roughly 100 actually produced) was issued in 1994 alongside the Whitney retrospective.

title: this is a raincoat like anybody else’s
description: 6.5 lb./2,9kg.. a collection of projects that explore language, people, narratives, couples, human intention, softness, failure, self-awareness, peculiar situations, the printed (and unprinted) page, and which question the format and purpose of the book in portland, oregon.

title: Organs of a Divided Labour
description:
Organs of a Divided Labour: Pipes and Fittings reprints the studio photography of a stainless-steel tubing catalogue and asks what happens to authorship when the pictures are this anonymous to begin with.

Jeremy Ayer, a Zurich-based photographer, appropriated the original commission images of pipe fittings, valves, and joints and rebuilt them into a 224-page book that is, page for page, close to indistinguishable from the industrial source. Mörel Books published it in 2021 with text by Leila Peacock and a conversation between Ayer and curator David Campany, printed in tritones with gloss and matte varnish so the plates keep the sheen of the original product shots. By claiming this commercial work as his own, Ayer puts a name to labour that catalogue photography almost never credits.

The book won a Swiss Design Award in 2022 in the photography category and became the first volume in Ayer's ongoing Organs of a Divided Labour project, which he continued with a second book built from flower photography shot in the same deadpan, product-catalogue style.
notes: Full title on the publisher's own listing is 'Organs of a Divided Labour – Pipes and Fittings'; catalogued here with the subtitle folded into the display title. Winner, Swiss Design Award 2022 (Photography category). First volume in Ayer's ongoing 'Organs of a Divided Labour' series, followed by a second book of flower photography.

title: Encyclopedia of Flowers: Flower Works by Makoto Azuma photographed by Shunsuke Shiinoki
description:
Flowers have been a universal cultural object for millennia.

They are an important aesthetic element in everyday life worldwide, and have played a highly symbolic role in art throughout the ages. Over the past few years, Makoto Azuma has created a furor in the art world with his floral installations, in which he creates unusual new shapes from plants and flowers and their component parts.

Inspired by the Japanese tradition of ikebana―the art of flower arranging―Azuma creates novel and previously unseen aesthetics by bringing together unusual plants that wouldn’t usually meet in nature―some of them exotic ―in extraordinary arrangements. Shunsuke Shiinoki, who opened the “haute-couture” florists Jardin des Fleurs in Tokyo in 2002 in association with Makoto Azuma, captured these exceptional floral installations in extraordinary photographs.

title: Encyclopedia Of Flowers Part 2 - Makoto Azuma  Shunsuke Shiinoki
description:
Flower artist Makoto Azuma and botanical photographer Shunsuke Shiinoki present a second edition of their vibrant anthology, two years after the first.

Focusing on the ephemeral nature of flowers while working to conserve in a concrete, tangible form the passage of time they embody, the authors use two techniques. The first highlights the flowers features and sense of presence by picturing them from overhead. The second applies a lateral perspective to capture the life force of plants as they stretch towards the sun. In contrast to the first edition, natural light sources were used as much as possible to illuminate the exceptionally dense and colourful palettes on display.

title: Encyclopedia of Flowers III (English and Japanese Edition)
description:
Makoto Azuma and Shunsuke Shiinoki collaborate once again to further their pioneering Encyclopedia of Flowers series, which focuses in part on market-related changes that impact floristry, such as the disappearance and new emergence of species, as well as on changing the common perception of flowers.

Following the first volume in 2011 and the second in 2015, this third dazzling instalment features a greater variety of styles, reflected in photographs divided into seven chapter-categories that include Coexistence , Hybrid , Chiaroscuro , and Autogenesis . The myriad arrangements done in Azuma s singular style are expertly captured by Shiinoki s camera.

title: SNOW
contributors: Gregor Muir (Editor), Beatrix Ruf (Editor), Sophie von Olfers (Editor), Lutz Bacher (Artist)
description:
Ever since her career began in the 1970s, this Bay Area artist has drawn upon fragmentary information from popular culture and her own life to produce works that play with the instability of identity and the all-around trickiness of images.

In artist's books, installations, sculptures, videos, photographs, paintings, and screen prints, Bacher uses images and objects in a physical, visceral manner. Bacher's mixture of bodies and ideas, pop and personal, while always remaining somehow elusive, feels entirely relevant to problems in art and life now.

In this publication, she has compiled her work from 1975 to 2013 into a hefty volume of seemingly digital files from an inventory. It is accompanied by a new essay by Caoimhín Mac Giolla Léith. The book is published with Kunsthalle Zürich, Portikus, Frankfurt am Main, and the Institute of Contemporary Arts, London

title: Late Paintings
description:
Encompassing more than twenty-five paintings that Francis Bacon made in London and Paris during the last two decades of his life, this book serves as a companion to the 2015 exhibition at Gagosian Gallery, New York, and is the first in-depth exploration of the innovations of the artist’s late work.

In his late paintings, Francis Bacon refined themes that had long obsessed him. He quoted reflexively from his oeuvre, reworking subjects to strip them to the bare essentials. This stunning new book features over 150 color illustrations of the artist’s work and related materials, including reproductions of ephemera from Bacon’s Hugh Lane studio.
notes: One of two copies in the collection.

title: Incunabula
description:
Incunabula reproduces the working material Francis Bacon kept locked away in his London studio: torn photographs, magazine pages, film stills, and book plates that he tore, folded, and stained before turning them into paint. The book gives the clearest evidence yet of how directly Bacon's imagery depended on found sources rather than observation from life.

Drawn from thousands of items recovered from 7 Reece Mews after Bacon's death and now held at the Hugh Lane Gallery in Dublin, the volume reproduces over two hundred of these source documents in full-page plates. Martin Harrison and Rebecca Daniels group the material by subject: photographs of the body and of sculpture, stills from Eadweard Muybridge's motion studies, and news images of violence that recur across Bacon's paintings. Barbara Dawson contributes a foreword, and Harrison's essay traces how each category of image entered Bacon's studio practice.

Harrison, editor of the Francis Bacon catalogue raisonné, and Daniels, an art historian who worked with the Bacon estate, treat the studio itself as an archive of the artist's private research. Read against Bacon's finished canvases, Incunabula shows him less as an inventor of images than as an obsessive editor of the ones already in circulation.
notes: US edition dated 2009; some sources list a UK first printing in 2008. Page count and dimensions per catalogue record; some bookseller records give slightly lower page counts (199-224pp), likely inconsistent counting of unnumbered plate sections.

title: Francis Bacon
description:
Francis Bacon’s style was so personal and distinctive that his influence lay more in the intensity of his commitment to art itself than in any direct stylistic legacy.

The British artist developed a way of portraying the human body that was unique in the history of painting—usually in isolation, at moments of extreme tension or even pain, distorted like figures from a fantastical nightmare. He remains a towering example to those dedicated to the depiction of the human figure. In addition to 250 full-color plates, this publication also reveals Bacon’s low-art inspirations, including magazine tear sheets, photographs, and imagery from films.

title: Water Maters
description:
Swimming is a delicate balance between flying and sinking This quote by Burkhard Strassmann opens Julia Baier's book ›Water Matters‹.

Her pictures show what people do with water, and even more, how water affects people and the animals, too. Not on the whole, but in the immediate encounter. When bathing, diving, splashing and spraying, in rain, snow and ice, in the city and in the countryside.
