And as the water itself the photographer seems to get to wherever it flows and foams, drips, bubbles and reflects or where the water and its derivatives form into mysterious and beautiful abstractions - in Budapest or Bremen, in Passau or Paris, Chicago or Sovata. Julia Baier's book is a refreshing and fluid trip through the international water world - with surface tension, cliffs, swirls, pull and draft.

title: Novokuznetsk
description:
Paper Wrapped, Tipped-on Image. During the 1980s by the Siberian artist Nikolay Bakharev worked as a mechanic and communal services factory photographer in the USSR.

To supplement his income he would solicit work as a black market portrait photographer on the public beaches of Eastern Russia. If the shoot went well, he would invite his subjects to make further images in a more intimate setting, compelling his subjects over several hours into contorted, erotically charged poses, which at the time was highly illegal. After the the fall of the Iron Curtain, Bakharev began to work more openly as an artist, although often being admonished as a pornographer.

His photographs from this time reveal more than just the bodies of his subjects, but the longing and dampened dreams of the inhabitants of an industrial town and the desires of an unrelenting artist. "It would be easy to misinterpret these images as simply the pornographic imaginings of a manipulative and dirty old man, yet there is something else within them — in the subjects’ eyes, in their frankness, in their curiosity and collusion, as well as in their surroundings – that suggests that much more is going on here, and that what is both at stake and in evidence stretches far beyond the realms of explicit sexuality, voyeurism and mere titillation." — Aaron Schuman

title: Baldessari Sings LeWitt
description:
Baldessari Sings LeWitt is graphic designer Toom Tragel's complete transcription of a deadpan 1972 performance in which John Baldessari sang the tenets of conceptual art.

In the original film, Baldessari sits with a sheaf of papers and sings each of Sol LeWitt's thirty-five Sentences on Conceptual Art to a different pop melody, after the model of Ella Fitzgerald Sings Cole Porter. Tragel's softcover book, published by Rollo Press in Zurich, prints Baldessari's spoken introduction and every musical score in full, with LeWitt's sentences set as lyrics beneath the notation, and preserves Baldessari's on-camera asides and self-corrections.

The piece is one of Baldessari's most cited works from his early conceptual period, using pop-song structure to expose both the earnestness and the absurdity of translating LeWitt's philosophical statements into performance. It sits alongside his contemporaneous text and photo-text pieces as an example of his sustained, wry interrogation of what conceptual art claims to be.
notes: No ISBN found; sources disagree on exact page count (40 vs. 44) and edition history (first edition 2009, later editions through 2012). Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Pure Beauty
description:
A major figure in contemporary art, John Baldessari is widely considered one of the most influential artists to emerge since the mid-1960s.

From his early text-and-image paintings to his more recent photo collages and installations, Baldessari has continued to make art that addresses the social impact of mass culture, often playfully through strategies of appropriation and deconstruction. Baldessari's lifelong interest in language, written and visual, and the interaction between the two, raises questions about the nature of communication and perception.

More than 400 illustrations are presented in full colour in this monograph published in conjunction with a major exhibition organised by the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and Tate Modern in London. Eleven essays by critics, curators, art historians, and an artist and former student of Baldessari's round out this volume. Few contemporary artists have achieved the range and relevance of Baldessari's oeuvre, which is finally given its due in this elegant retrospective book.

title: A Print Retrospective from the Collections of Jordan D. Schnitzer and his Family Foundation
publisher: Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco-Legion of Honor/Jordan Schnitzer Family
description:
Conceptual art veteran John Baldessari (born 1931) began making prints in the mid-1970s, and has placed printmaking at the center of his appropriative practice, in which found photographs of people are amended with colorful dots that blot out the heads of the subjects, redirecting the viewer's attention towards marginal detail.

For Baldessari, keen as he is to minimize or erase his own manual presence, printmaking also helps to flatten out these collaged additions and interventions, heightening their sense of estrangement and beguiling anonymity. Many of Baldessari's prints series have been extremely influential, such as the 1970s Raw Prints series, for which he amended photos of Santa Monica mallgoers with abstracted shapes printed above the images that replicate details from them this series was pivotal in democratizing photo-based prints in the art world.

Since then, Baldessari has gone on to collaborate with some of the world's great printmakers, such as Brooke Alexander, Gemini G.E.L., Cirrus Editions, Edition Jacob Samuel, Mixographia and Crown Point Press. An essential volume in any contemporary art library, this first full survey of Baldessari's four-decade printmaking career is the definitive volume on the prints, and boasts 140 color plates alongside testimonies from his printmaking collaborators.
tags: Prints & Multiples, Conceptual Art, Contemporary Art, Printmaking

title: Visionaire No. 64: Art, Baldessari Red Edition
description:
In Henry Joost and Ariel Schulman's short film A Brief History of John Baldessari, the world-renowned conceptual artist suggests that he will be best remembered as "the guy who put dots over people's faces."

Baldessari recalls: "I felt like it [the dot] leveled the playing field"--surely an ironic claim to fame in an age of self-obsession and self-celebration. Especially from the early Renaissance, when mirrors became more readily available, through today--an age of constant surveillance in which nearly every pedestrian carries some form of camera--the auto portrait has become an inevitability that, to varying degrees, finds its way into the practice of many working artists. For its 64th issue, Visionaire invites a roster of contemporary actors, entertainers and personalities to contribute a self-portrait. The participants include artists Ai Weiwei and Ed Ruscha models Gisele Bundchen and Kate Upton actors Scarlett Johansson and James Franco singer Miley Cyrus filmmaker Pedro Almodovar fashion designers Kate and Laura Mulleavy (Rodarte) and Riccardo Tisci (Givenchy) athlete Lionel Messi, and many more.

Their self-portraits are printed in black and white, and then silkscreened with shapes and colors created by Baldessari. The resulting collection of images offers a snapshot of contemporary iconography, bridging technology and craftsmanship, high art and pop culture, digital and analogue, new and old. Visionaire No. 64: Art is available in three different editions, each themed by a color, and featuring a different selection of contributors. All of the editions are presented in a beautifully printed cloth box. The red edition includes contributions by James Franco, Miley Cyrus, Marina Abramovic, Ranveer Singh, Yuna Kim, Karlie Kloss, Pedro Almodóvar, Drew Barrymore, G-Dragon and Ed Ruscha.

title: John Baldessari Catalogue Raisonné: Volume One: 1956–1974
description:
The first volume of the complete catalogue of works by John Baldessari The pioneering conceptual artist John Baldessari (b. 1931) began his career as a painter in the 1950s, but in the subsequent decades he expanded his practice in a new and groundbreaking direction by juxtaposing texts with found photography or appropriated images.

These texts questioned the nature of art and the art-viewing experience, suggesting new meanings for the images they accompanied. This interaction of words and images remained a critical aspect of Baldessari's work, even as he branched into other media, such as site-specific installations, drawings, video, sculpture, prints, and multiples. The first of a projected four-volume set, this lavishly illustrated book features about 500 works and chronicles an important shift in Baldessari's thinking during these formative years.

Included are such landmark works as the Cremation Project (1970), where Baldessari incinerated the "body" of work he had made between the years 1953 and 1966. The ashes of the cremated works were then baked into cookies, and the rest sealed in a book-shaped urn, which he then presented along with a plaque announcing the "life" and "death" dates. Baldessari's work and teaching have been greatly influential on a subsequent generation of artists. The book features an essay by Yve-Alain Bois considering Baldessari's ethos as a generator of his artistic practice. Also included are an interview with Christopher Knight and a detailed chronology of the artist's life and work.

title: No Joke
description: 37 black-and-white photographs. Asger Carlsen and Roger Ballen exchanged ideas, sketches and works and reworked them manually and digitally, blurring the lines of authorship and process. Both artists are known for their blurring of the line between the real world and the fictional. In NO JOKE they lead each other into what eventually becomes something larger then expected.

title: The Prototype Works
description:
clothbound. Beginning in 1965, but especially in the years between 1967 and 1971, Lewis Baltz made a body of work concentrated on the dialectic between simple, regular geometric forms found in the postwar industrial landscape, and the culture that generated such forms.

Stucco walls, parking lots, the sides of warehouse sheds or disused billboards baked in the steady Californian sunlight. Baltz called his works "Prototypes," by which he meant replicable social conventions as well as model structures of replicable manufacture. Marking Baltz's preliminary forays into a minimal aesthetic, The Prototype Works continued his work to capture the reality of a sprawling Western ecology gone wild.

title: Nevada
edition_printrun: staple-bound, with title embossed on front, Oblong size: 21,5 by 26,5.
description:
Nevada is Lewis Baltz's 1978 survey of the tract housing and scrubland edging Reno and Sparks, issued not as a conventional photography book but as a spare, self-published pamphlet.

Designed by David Smoak and released through Castelli Graphics in an edition of 2,000, the book collects fifteen black-and-white plates, unpaginated, staple-bound in matte grey wrappers with the title embossed on the cover. The oblong format holds daylight views of new construction alongside Baltz's long-exposure nightscapes of streetlit intersections and model homes. Castelli also distributed a related portfolio of individual prints from the same series, sold through the gallery to collectors.

Nevada extends the flat documentary approach Baltz established in The New Industrial Parks near Irvine, California (1974) and points toward the larger surveys Park City (1980) and San Quentin Point (1985). Grouped with Robert Adams and the other photographers of the 1975 New Topographics exhibition, Baltz used Nevada's speculative subdivisions to track a single subject across an expanding American landscape: land steadily reorganized by development.
notes: This copy is signed. The stapled, embossed-wrapper pamphlet described here is Baltz's 1978 first-edition publication (edition of 2,000), not a separate gallery handout, though its slim format resembles an exhibition program.

title: Lewis Baltz: Rule Without Exception / Only Exceptions
description:
This progressive book object combines two volumes and covers the sweep and depth of Lewis Baltz's influential oeuvre.

Rule Without Exception is a re-issue of Baltz's award-winning mid-career retrospective book which accompanied a travelling exhibition of the same name in 1991. The book surveys Baltz's work from "The Prototype Works" of 1967 through to "Sites of Technology" of 1991, showing the range of his images of industrialised landscapes and technological sites. Each section of the book is accompanied by installation views as well as texts by distinguished writers, some newly commissioned for this edition.

Only Exceptions is a new book chronicling Baltz's work - now usually site-generated commissioned works - from 1992 to the present and is published on the occasion of an exhibition organized by the Kunstmuseum, Bonn. Only Exceptions includes Baltz's work in California, Leipzig's "Black Triangle", Reggio Emilia, Groningen, Rome, Venice, and two projects with Jean Nouvel in France and Italy.

title: Lewis Baltz
description:
Published in Paris in 1993, Lewis Baltz pairs a compact survey of Baltz's photographs with a single sustained essay by the French critic Bernard Lamarche-Vadel, one of the closest European readings of Baltz's cool, procedural landscapes.

Issued by Éditions de la Différence as the seventh volume in its "Classiques du XXIe siècle" series, the hardcover gathers black-and-white plates spanning Baltz's industrial parks and tract housing alongside Lamarche-Vadel's French text. Its release coincided with Rule Without Exception, the artist's retrospective at the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris that same year, which went on to travel to venues in the United States.

Lamarche-Vadel, a novelist and critic active in French debates on photography and conceptual art, places Baltz among the American photographers who turned documentary technique into a form of institutional critique. The book is one of the few sustained European readings of Baltz's work published during his lifetime.
notes: Text by Bernard Lamarche-Vadel. Published by Éditions de la Différence in the series "Classiques du XXIe siècle" (no. 7), 1993.

title: At The / In Der Albertina
description:
At the / In der Albertina documents a two-part exhibition of Lewis Baltz's photographs staged jointly by the Albertina in Vienna and Galerie Thomas Zander in Cologne, built around a recorded conversation between the artist and curator Walter Moser.

Published by Walther König in 2014, the bilingual German and English paperback combines installation views from both venues with a transcribed interview in which Moser, chief curator of the Albertina's photography collection, questions Baltz about the arc of his career. Thirteen color plates supplement the discussion, giving the book the character of a working record of the exhibition rather than a conventional retrospective catalogue.

The interview lets Baltz speak directly about the concerns that ran through five decades of work, from the deadpan surveys of Southern California development that made him a central figure of the New Topographics group to the digitally composed color panoramas of his later career. Published the year of Baltz's death, it captures one of his last extended conversations about that career.
notes: Distinct from an earlier, similarly titled 2012 Kestnergesellschaft/Albertina catalogue (ISBN 9783863352387); this is the 2014 Walther König edition tied to the Albertina/Thomas Zander showing.

title: Lewis Baltz
contributors: Walead Beshty (Essay), Urs Stahel (Essay), David Campany (Interview)
description:
Steidl's 2017 Lewis Baltz is the first comprehensive monograph to appear after the photographer's death in 2014, assembling five decades of work into a single retrospective volume.

Co-published with Fundación Mapfre to accompany the first full-scale exhibition of Baltz's photography since his death, the 320-page clothbound book moves chronologically through his interlocking series: the early Prototypes and tract-house studies, the black-and-white surveys Park City, San Quentin Point, and Candlestick Point, and the later color panoramas made in Europe, including Venezia Marghera. Essays by Walead Beshty and Urs Stahel, plus an interview conducted by David Campany, read the work as a single continuous project rather than a set of separate bodies of work.

Baltz emerged in the 1970s as one of the sharpest voices of the New Topographics generation, photographing tract housing and industrial parks with a flatness that treated the built environment as evidence rather than scenery. This volume places that early work alongside his later, more painterly color series, tracing how one deadpan method carried across four decades and two continents.
notes: Out of print per distributor listing. Steidl's own site lists 330 pages; Artbook/D.A.P. lists 320 pages, used here.

title: The New Industrial Parks Near Irvine, California
edition_printrun: First edition, first printing; limited to 960 unnumbered copies (a separate signed limited edition of 100 hand-numbered copies also exists)
description:
Lewis Baltz's The New Industrial Parks Near Irvine, California is one of the founding documents of the New Topographics movement, a body of work that gave a critical, deadpan eye to the man-altered landscape spreading across California's former agricultural land.

The book presents fifty-one uniform black-and-white photographs of suburban industrial buildings, shot in a flat, minimalist style with no evidence of human life, printed on heavy coated stock. First published by Leo Castelli/Castelli Graphics in 1974 in an edition of 960 unnumbered copies, it was designed by Thomas F. Barrow and issued alongside a related Castelli Graphics print portfolio of the same fifty-one images in an edition of forty. A separate signed limited edition of 100 hand-numbered copies, signed by Baltz, was also produced.

The work placed Baltz at the center of New Topographics, the movement named for the 1975 George Eastman House exhibition that also included Robert Adams, Stephen Shore, Henry Wessel Jr., and Bernd and Hilla Becher; its cool, glacial view of suburban development shaped landscape photography in the United States, Germany, and Japan for decades afterward.
notes: Landmark New Topographics photobook, first published by Leo Castelli/Castelli Graphics in 1974 (edition of 960; a separate 100-copy signed limited edition also exists); reissued as a Steidl/Castelli facsimile. No ISBN on the original edition. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Politics of Bacteria, Docile Bodies, Ronde de Nuit
description:
This exhibition catalogue gathers three of Lewis Baltz's large-scale color trilogies: Ronde de Nuit, Docile Bodies, and The Politics of Bacteria, the body of work in which he traded the black-and-white seriality of his early career for saturated, multi-panel color installations.

Published by the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles with Ram Publications to accompany Baltz's first American presentation of the three trilogies together, the catalogue reproduces the panels in four-color and black-and-white plates across sixty pages, with an essay by curator Cornelia H. Butler. The exhibition followed Baltz's internationally traveled retrospective Rule Without Exception and marked his turn toward subjects drawn from surveillance, medicine, and information technology.

Where Baltz's 1970s work treated the American landscape as a record of unchecked development, these color trilogies apply the same procedural eye to the interiors of laboratories, hospitals, and control rooms. Butler's essay reads the shift as a continuation of his earlier interest in institutional power, now traced through the body and the network instead of the tract house.
notes: Museum and bookseller records consistently date this MOCA/Ram Publications catalogue to 1998; the catalogue's on-file year (2017) is retained per house convention but the two do not reconcile, and this may be a data-entry conflation with the unrelated 2017 Steidl "Lewis Baltz" monograph.

title: Candlestick Point
description:
Candlestick Point is Lewis Baltz's stark inventory of a marginal California landscape, one of the defining works of the New Topographics movement and a touchstone for photography's turn toward the built and the discarded.

First published in 1989 and long out of print, the 2011 Steidl edition returns Baltz's black-and-white photographs of an undeveloped strip of San Francisco Bay shoreline scarred by drainage channels, dumped rubble, and abandoned infrastructure to print. Designed by Baltz, Bernard Fischer, and Gerhard Steidl, the clothbound volume adds a new text by Wolfgang Scheppe, Lewis Baltz and the Garden of False Reality, situating the pictures within the artist's broader inquiry into land, waste, and surveillance.

Baltz emerged in the 1970s as a central figure of New Topographics, photographing tract housing, industrial parks, and the anonymous edges of the American West with a cool, deadpan rigor drawn as much from Minimalism and Conceptual art as from documentary photography. Candlestick Point extends that project into the terrain of landfill and reclamation, and remains one of his most sustained bodies of work.
notes: 2011 Steidl reissue of the 1989 original; adds an essay by Wolfgang Scheppe not present in the first edition. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Wall and Piece
description:
Wall and Piece collects the stencils, photographs, and captions that made Banksy the best-known street artist working under anonymity, gathering roughly a decade of unauthorized work into a single illustrated volume.

First published in the mid-2000s and built from Banksy's earlier self-issued books Banging Your Head Against a Brick Wall, Existencilism, and Cut It Out, the collection adds material from gallery shows in London, New York, and Paris, plus documentation of his intervention on the separation wall in the West Bank. Photographs of the stencils in situ are paired with one-line captions and short texts, organized into loose chapters: Monkeys, Cops, Rats, Cows, Art, Street Furniture.

Banksy came up through Bristol's stencil graffiti scene in the late 1990s, and by the time Wall and Piece appeared he had moved from illegal night work into gallery exhibitions and international press coverage without ever revealing his identity. The book remains the clearest single record of the visual vocabulary, rats, policemen, monkeys, and children, that carried his work from the street into museums and auction houses.
notes: First UK edition published by Century in 2005 per most bookseller records; on-file year (2007) retained and may reflect a later printing.

title: Talk Story
edition_printrun: First edition, numbered edition of 555 copies
description:
Cole Barash's Talk Story is a photographic study of the North Shore of Oahu, made in close proximity to a young John John Florence at the moment professional surfing's expectations were beginning to weigh on him.

Shot entirely on film over six weeks spent wandering the North Shore with Florence, the book turns away from the noise and hype of action photography toward vulnerability, family life, and the subculture surrounding the sport. The self-published volume runs 76 pages plus cover, perfect bound, and combines five paper stocks with offset and digital printing, released in a numbered edition of 555 copies designed by Tucker Phillips.

The project marked a turning point for Barash, who came up through snowboard and action-sports photography before shifting toward documentary, subculture-driven work; the book was accompanied by exhibitions at Picture Farm Gallery in Brooklyn and Venice Arts Gallery in Los Angeles.
notes: First edition, signed and inscribed copy per Dashwood Books listing; numbered edition of 555. No ISBN identified for this self-published title. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Blues
description: 80 pages with col. Illus.. Collection of photographs published in conjunction with the "blues" exhibition held at agnès b by American photographer Tim Barber.

title: Site Specific (site specific_03 13)
description:
Site Specific is a summary of Italian photographer Olivo Barbieri’s ten-year project to record the world’s cities in aerial photographs.

On the one hand, the book offers remarkable documentation, by one of today’s most thrilling image-makers, of 25 cities throughout the world. On the other, it is a narrative of Barbieri’s ever-evolving approach to photography and his thoughts about the nature of the medium. Presented chronologically, the book begins with the distinctive tilt-shift photographs of Italian cities with which Barbieri first established his reputation, and which launched a popular stylistic movement for selective-focus photographs.

As the series continued, with portrayals of cities all over the world, Barbieri introduced other devices and approaches to distort perceived reality—such as playing with color, registration and the deletion or discoloring of particular details—to dramatic effect. The result is a remarkable photo essay about twenty-first-century urban space and about photography itself. Stunningly designed and presented in a luxuriously large format, the book is introduced by Christopher Phillips.
tags: Olivo Barbieri, Photography, Still Life Photography, landscape photography

title: Beyond Drifting: Imperfectly Known Animals
description:
59 color and numerous additional illustrations. Beyond Drifting: Imperfectly Known Animals is an astounding piece of work, one in which Barker takes the most humdrum of things – plastic detrius – inserts it into an intriguing, multilayered historical narrative, lends its physical form a gossamer, airy beauty, and presents the whole to us in the form of a book.

Not just any book, but a replica of an old science publication from the 1800s, including mould-spotted pages, a library lending form and specimen labels.” – Lucy Davies, V&A Magazine May 2017 Now, 170 years after Atkins, another British woman has produced an important photobook that echoes Victorian-era science even as it exposes a contemporary environmental crisis. Mandy Barker’s Beyond Drifting: Imperfectly Known Animals similarly occupies that liminal space where art and science converge, and its impeccable presentation exemplifies how book design can extend content. – Laura M. André, review on Photo-eye “Mandy Barker’s work on plastic has been developing for some time.

In its latest advance, she looks at micro-particles of plastic as a species of a lunatic plankton, floating about the sea, and she has included a rather wonderful pastiche book of old-fashioned science as a way of getting us into her subject.” – Francis Hodgson, Photography critic “Her images could be mistaken for Victorian glass-plate photographs in fact they are ornate, long-exposure studies of the plastic debris that pollutes beaches in and around Cobh in Cork Harbour, Ireland.” – Tom Seymour, British Journal of Photography “Beyond Drifting is a clever critique of a massive environmental problem – and, in focusing in on one small area of Ireland in particular, Barker highlights a global issue.” – Mark Sinclair, Creative Review

title: ADAC
description: ADAC is a collaborative book by Matthew Barney and Brandon Stosuy commemorating the lives of NFL/Oakland Raiders legend Al Davis, who died on October 8, 2011, and Seth Putnam, vocalist of the grindcore band Anal Cunt, who died on June 11, 2011. Published by Dashwood Books

title: Scene
description:
Scene collects Jeannette Montgomery Barron's portraits of the artists, musicians, and downtown regulars who defined New York's early-1980s underground, a record of a social world made from the inside rather than observed at a distance.

Published by powerHouse Books in 2013, the hardcover pairs Montgomery Barron's close, plainly lit portraits, made between roughly 1983 and 1987, with brief recollections of the nightclubs and restaurants where the pictures were taken: Area, the Palladium, the Mudd Club, Warhol's Factory, and the Odeon. Her subjects include Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring, Andy Warhol, Robert Mapplethorpe, Cindy Sherman, William Burroughs, and Willem Dafoe, most photographed as friends and peers rather than as sitters for a formal commission.

Montgomery Barron worked alongside her subjects rather than around them, and Scene reads less like a survey of famous names than a photo album kept by someone who knew everyone in the room. Three decades later, the book stands as an intimate visual record of a downtown scene that has since become historical shorthand for the era.

title: Jean-Michel Basquiat
contributors: Keith Haring (Essay), Francesco Clemente (Essay), Henry Geldzahler (Essay)
description:
This 1999 exhibition catalogue assembles more than a hundred paintings by Jean-Michel Basquiat alongside recollections from artists and critics who knew him, and it captures a career that lasted less than a decade yet reshaped American painting.

Published by Charta in Milan for an exhibition at the Museo Revoltella in Trieste, the bilingual English and Italian volume was edited by curator Luca Marenzi. It pairs critical essays with an interview and a detailed chronology of Basquiat's life. Contributions come from artist Keith Haring, frequent collaborator Francesco Clemente, and curator Henry Geldzahler, each writing from direct experience of the artist and his work. The book is printed as a softcover quarto, matching the scale of the exhibition it documents.

Basquiat began as a graffiti writer under the tag SAMO before turning to painting in the early 1980s, drawing on jazz, boxing, and Black history to build a vocabulary apart from the era's other Neo-Expressionists. His collaborations with Andy Warhol and Clemente placed him at the center of New York's art world. He died in 1988 at twenty-seven, and catalogues built from testimony of people who worked alongside him, like this one, remain a primary record of that brief career.
notes: Bilingual English/Italian exhibition catalogue published by Charta (Milan) for the 1999 Museo Revoltella show in Trieste.

title: Basquiat
editor: Dieter Buchhart, Jean-Louis Prat, Susanne Reichling
description:
This 2010 monograph traces Jean-Michel Basquiat's eight-year career through more than three hundred color plates, brought together to mark what would have been the artist's fiftieth birthday.

Published by Hatje Cantz for an exhibition at Fondation Beyeler in Riehen, near Basel, that ran from May to September 2010, the book was edited by curator Dieter Buchhart with Jean-Louis Prat and Susanne Reichling, and includes an essay by longtime friend and writer Glenn O'Brien. A chronology situates the plates within Basquiat's short working life. The oversized hardcover runs 224 pages with 334 color images, and its cover reproduces the 1985 painting Now's the Time, a black tondo built around the shape of a vinyl record.

Basquiat moved from the graffiti tag SAMO to gallery walls in barely three years, forming close ties with Andy Warhol, Keith Haring, and Madonna along the way. His paintings pulled from jazz, boxing, anatomy, and Black history to stand apart from the Neo-Expressionism and Conceptual art around him. He died in 1988 at twenty-seven, and this catalogue, built around a major European retrospective, remains one of the fuller surveys of that compressed body of work.
notes: Catalogue for the 2010 Fondation Beyeler retrospective marking Basquiat's fiftieth birthday; the cover reproduces the 1985 painting Now's the Time.

title: Words Are All We Have Paintings by Jean-Michel Basquiat
description:
Language in the art of Jean-Michel Basquiat, from graffiti to word as motif In the wild New York of the 1980s, Jean-Michel Basquiat was the first African-American artist to receive art-world attention.

The complexity and trailblazing innovative power of his paintings has been widely discussed, but this book focuses on the treatment of language in Basquiat’s ouevre. With its complex structures, spontaneous rhythms and sampled, collage-like manifestations, his work was drawn into the orbit of the Beat Generation poets and the protagonists of the musical avant-garde.

The multitalented Basquiat created a shimmering, syncopated fabric of images and text, which the American curator and critic Robert Storr aptly called “eye rap.” It was with this unpretentious and spontaneous way of working that Basquiat rewrote art history.

title: The Notebooks
description:
facsimile edition of the artist's fascinating working notebooks Brooklyn-born Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-88) was one of the most important artists of the 1980s.

A key figure in the New York art scene, he inventively explored the interplay between words and images throughout his career, first as a member of SAMO, a graffiti group active on the Lower East Side in the late 1970s, and then as a painter acclaimed for his unmistakable Neoexpressionist style. From 1980 to 1987, he filled numerous working notebooks with drawings and handwritten texts. This facsimile edition reproduces the pages of eight of these fascinating and rarely seen notebooks for the first time.The notebooks are filled with images and words that recur in Basquiat's paintings and other works.

Iconic drawings and pictograms of crowns, teepees, and hatch-marked hearts share space with handwritten texts, including notes, observations, and poems that often touch on culture, race, class, and life in New York. Like his other work, the notebooks vividly demonstrate Basquiat’s deep interests in comic, street, and pop art, hip-hop, politics, and the ephemera of urban life. They also provide an intimate look at the working process of one of the most creative forces in contemporary American art.

title: The Naked Eye
description:
Erica Baum photographs the fanned, aging edges of paperback books rather than their covers or spines, and this 2015 monograph gathers the first full survey of that ongoing series, begun in 2008.

Published by Crevecoeur in Paris with Bureau in New York, the 144-page hardcover reproduces fifty-eight color photographs in an edition of 1,200, designed by Myriam Barchechat. Baum turns old softcovers on their side, so the camera catches strips of colored page edges and slivers of interrupted text instead of a legible page. Two essays frame the work: Jean-Max Colard's "Filmo-Biographemes" and Cathleen Chaffee's "Erica Baum's Contemporary," reading the photographs against a wider history of picture-text collision in her practice.

Baum has spent two decades mining overlooked printed sources, from library card catalogs to art-historical indices and antique parlor games, for the fragments of language and image lodged inside them. The Naked Eye pushes that method to its most abstract point, cropped so tightly that the books themselves nearly disappear, leaving only color, edge, and the trace of type. Chaffee calls the result a photographic present, gone the instant the shutter closes.
notes: First comprehensive monograph on Baum's Naked Eye series (2008-present); edition of 1,200, printed by NPN Drukkers, Breda, NL. 144 pages, with 58 colour and 11 black-and-white plates.

title: Dashwood Book Series (LTD EDITION - VOL 1)
edition_printrun: Condition: As new in sturdy slipcase stamped with names of artists and their projects. # /20. 20 copies
description: Janette Beckman, Sam Falls, Andreas Laszlo Konrath, Jim Mangan, Ari Marcopoulos, Betty Tompkins & Archive of Modern Conflict

title: Hans Bellmer
contributors: Agnès de la Beaumelle (Author), Alain Sayag (Author), Wieland Schmied (Author), Michael Semff (Editor), Anthony Spira (Editor)
description:
The Surrealists' fascination with dolls and machines that resembled humans is especially evident in the work of Hans Bellmer (1902-1975), the subject of this comprehensive monograph.

Rejecting the Nazis' Aryan ideals, the artist spent the years after 1933 creating disturbing dolls out of wax, wood, flax, plaster and glue--equipped with wigs and glass eyes. Photographs of these fetishistic simulacra were published in Minotaure, the Surrealists' magazine, and eagerly supported by members of Andre Breton's circle.

After immigrating to Paris, Bellmer continued to develop his erotic obsessions through his art, now influenced by the writings of the Marquis de Sade and Georges Bataille, and began to collaborate with his companion, the German artist Unica Zurn. Deeply involved in Freudian discourse, his drawings, lithographs and photographs investigate psychoanalytic theories around hysteria and transference and reveal a singular exploration into the relationship between language and the body.

title: The Book of Veles
description: Photographs of contemporary Veles are intertwined with fragments from an archaeological discovery also called ‘the Book of Veles’ ― a cryptic collection of 40 ‘ancient’ wooden boards discovered in Russia in 1919, written in a proto-Slavic language. It was claimed to be a history of the Slavic people and the god Veles himself―the pre-Christian Slavic god of mischief, chaos and deception

title: Polaroids
editor: by Dagon James (Editor), Vincent Fremont (Editor), Anastasia Rygle (Editor)
contributors: by Dagon James (Editor), Vincent Fremont (Editor), Anastasia Rygle (Editor), Brigid Berlin (Photographer), Bob Colacello (Introduction), John Waters
description:
Brigid Berlin (born 1939) was one of the most prominent and colorful members of Andy Warhol’s Factory in the 1960s and 1970s.

Her legendary personal collection of Polaroids is collected here for the first time and constitutes an intimate, beautiful, artistic, outrageous insight into this iconic period. This wild photographic odyssey featured a foreword by cult filmmaker John Waters, who writes, “Brigid was always my favorite underground movie star big, often naked, and ornery as hell ... The Polaroids here show just how wide Brigid’s world was her access was amazing. She was never a groupie, always an insider.” Berlin knew everyone and her lens captured them all: celebrities, Superstars, artists, herself and, of course, Warhol.

As Waters observes, through her snaps, “Andy was uncovered and revealed like never before.” The book also features an introduction by Bob Colacello, editor of Warhol’s Interview magazine and features writer for Vanity Fair, who notes: “In recording life, she captured our times. By myopically depicting her own transgressions and self- indulgences, she has prophetically reflected the narcissism and exhibitionism, the craving for fame and confusing of fame and infamy that have become the staples of American popular culture.” In discussing her style, he reflects, “This is the opposite of fashion photography or studio portraiture. Brigid was a realist. What she saw is7

title: Wallace Berman: American Aleph
contributors: by Tosh Berman (Introduction), Wallace Berman (Artist), Claudia Bohn-Spector (Contributor), Sam Mellon (Contributor), Ken Allan (Contributor)
description:
Commemorating the 40th anniversary of the artist’s accidental death at age 50, this volume offers the first substantial survey of the entire oeuvre of Wallace Berman (1926–76) from the late 1940s until 1976.

Berman has been long heralded as one of the most significant and influential artists to emerge in Southern California. Spiritually inclined yet steeped in popular culture and the political events of the day, he conducted reconnaissance far beyond the borders of California, mining the American psyche and broadcasting his ideas through mail art, publications, photographs and multilayered art works. Berman intersected with several intriguing cultural moments, starting with his first Los Angeles solo show in 1957 at Ed Kienholz and Walter Hopps’ Ferus Gallery.

He also participated in an important 1966 group exhibition in London at the legendary Robert Fraser Gallery, whose other artists included Richard Hamilton, Bruce Conner and Peter Blake--who put Berman’s face among the notable crowd in his cover for the Beatles’ Sgt Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band.As interest in West Coast art has increased over the past 40 years, scholars have viewed Berman as a quintessentially Californian artist whose entourage of likeminded friends was essential to the formation of his creative vision. This volume takes a broader view, reassessing Berman’s significant contributions to the history of 20th-century American art.

title: Disco The Bill Berstein Photographs
description:
Stunning photography by Bill Bernstein. Containing many previously unpublished photographs, Disco takes the viewer on an access-all-areas tour of late 70s New York nightlife.

Bernstein's eye was drawn to the characters that lived for the night, rather than the celebrities, the unknown men and women who were transformed by the nightlife haze. The pictures in this book are a document of an incredibly exciting and creative time in music and in social, political and fashion history.

title: Japanese Whispers
description:
Zaza Bertrand spent time inside Japan's rabuho, the anonymous "love hotels" where sex and romance are kept deliberately apart, and Japanese Whispers is the document she brought back.

Published by Art Paper Editions in 2016, the 96-page softcover holds seventy color plates printed offset and bound with linen thread, its spine and back cover blind-embossed and its front cover carrying a tip-in image under a printed dustcover. Bertrand photographed the hotels' guests, whom she calls models rather than subjects, in the beds, mirrors, and karaoke rooms built for a few anonymous hours. She could not speak with most of them, and that distance sits inside every picture: a foreign observer granted access but never explanation.

The Belgian photographer built the series over repeated visits, working a subject that Japanese media itself treats with a mix of embarrassment and fascination. Japanese Whispers won the Ibasho Photo Competition and traveled to RIOT in Ghent and Ibasho Gallery in Antwerp, and it established the approach Bertrand later carried into Dreamlands, her series on the gated desert communities of wealthy Egyptians.
notes: Winner of the Ibasho Photo Competition; exhibited at RIOT (Ghent) and Ibasho Gallery (Antwerp).

title: Breaking the Codex: Bookwork, Collage, and Mixed Media
publisher: Etc. Etc. The Iconoclastic Museum Press
description:
Doug Beube calls himself a biblioclast, an artist who takes the book apart to see what it is still capable of, and this 2011 monograph surveys three decades of that work in bookwork, collage, and mixed media.

Published by Etc. Etc. The Iconoclastic Museum Press in Brooklyn and edited by Marian Cohn, the 220-page hardcover reproduces more than 275 illustrations across Beube's altered books, carved volumes, map pieces, and organic-material sculptures. An introduction by curator David Revere McFadden opens essays by Betty Bright, Allan Chasanoff, Buzz Spector, and others, each taking up a different strand of the work: the book as an art medium, the mechanics of cutting and rebinding, the specific bodies of work built from carved pages and found maps.

Beube treats the codex, an old technology still doing real work in a digital age, as a fixed structure to cut against, pasting and rerouting its pages the way a programmer might route around a hardwired constraint. Breaking the Codex traces that method from his early altered books through the sculptural and photographic pieces that followed, and stands as the fullest account in print of a practice built on taking books apart.
tags: Art, and sculpture., book art, collage, mixed media, Photography
notes: Retrospective monograph covering three decades of Beube's altered-book and collage practice; edited by Marian Cohn, introduction by David Revere McFadden.

title: Tom Bianchi: Fire Island Pines, Polaroids 1975-1983
description:
Tom Bianchi carried a Polaroid SX-70 to Fire Island Pines through the second half of the 1970s and into the early 1980s, and the pictures gathered in this 2013 book are as close as photography gets to a diary of that place.

Published by Damiani in 2013, the 210-page hardcover reproduces Bianchi's instant-film images of the men who summered in the Pines: on the beach, on decks, in bed, at parties that ran past sunrise. Bianchi pairs the pictures with his own written recollections, tracing how he first read about Fire Island in a magazine as a teenager and eventually made it his home after law school. Edmund White contributes a companion text, situating the Polaroids within the wider literature of gay life on Fire Island in that period.

The Pines in these years functioned as a rare space where gay men could be openly affectionate and undressed without consequence, and Bianchi's camera, small and immediate, let him work without staging or self-consciousness. Shot in the years just before AIDS reshaped that community, the book has become one of the primary photographic records of Fire Island's gay culture at its most unguarded, and it remains the best-known of Bianchi's several Polaroid collections.
notes: Pairs Bianchi's Polaroid photographs of Fire Island Pines (1975-1983) with his own memoir text and a companion piece by Edmund White.

title: Czech Photography VIII: Europeans
description:
Three generations of Czech documentary photography meet in Europeans, a 2009 book built around Vladimir Birgus, Jindrich Marco, and Jindrich Streit's shared eye for ordinary life across the continent.

Published by KANT for an exhibition at the Leica Gallery in New York in 2009, later shown at the Month of Photography festival in Vienna, the book gathers work by three photographers spanning half a century of Czech practice. Marco, who died in 2000, contributes postwar images of central European cities rebuilding after 1945; Streit brings his long-running documentary studies of rural village life; Birgus, who also edited the volume, adds a more recent body of street and social photography. The three series together read as a survey of European daily life from the ruins of the war years to the present.

The book carries the number VIII in KANT's Czech Photography series, the project through which Birgus has become the leading historian and anthologist of Czech photography, later producing the wide-ranging survey Czech Photography of the 20th Century with Jan Mlcoch. Europeans belongs to that larger effort to place Czech documentary work, long isolated behind the Iron Curtain, alongside the European tradition it always belonged to.
notes: Volume VIII of KANT's Czech Photography series; group exhibition catalogue for three photographers rather than a single-artist monograph.

title: Psychobuch
edition_printrun: EPF N° 149 (1 of 2 copies). Out of print
description:
It all started when Beni Bischof began publishing laser-copied artist's magazines in 2005 as an independent means of distributing his drawings, collages, and texts.

The speed of production suited his impetuous, prolific output. It was not long before he found an additional, three-dimensional outlet for his obsessions by adding sculpture, painting, and installations to his repertoire. Often using everyday objects, Bischof creates bizarre objects whose coherence he reinforces with plaster and paint.

He applies similar techniques of combining, reassembling, and reworking to images appropriated from fashion magazines, trivial literature, LP covers, and the like, overpainting them and modifying them digitally or even mechanically. Psychobuch presents an extensive and unusual survey of Beni Bischof's oeuvre. It is a wildly rampant, multimedia conglomerate, held together by a dense network of recurring themes and motifs. The elaborate book is both an overview of Beni Bischof's output to date and an artist's book in its own right.

title: 1-130 Nour Bishouty Selected works Ghassan Bishoutyaha b. 1941 Safad Palestine d. 2004 Amman, Jordan
description:
Which images are made manifest across an artist’s practice and which are the ones that disappear?

How do objects, whether seen or unseen, and the knowledge they possess traverse across place and time to avow their resistance? These are amongst the questions asked by artist Nour Bishouty in her artist’s book 1—130, a project that draws upon her ongoing research into the works of her father, Ghassan Bishouty (b. 1941 Palestine – d. 2004, Jordan). In 1—130, she borrows from methods of indexing and object classification to act as figurative codes for identification and cross-reference within the contexts of value and legacy. All the while employing paratactic strategies of text and image to understand the life and work of an artist faced with the discontinuity of deracination. 1—130 constitutes reflexive encounters with a series of 130 selected paintings and sculptures made circa 1965-2004 in Lebanon and Jordan, and concludes with an afterword by editor and curator Jacob Korczynski. 1—130 is designed by Laura Pappa & Lotte Lara Schröder and co-published by Art Metropole & Motto Books.

Nour Bishouty is a visual artist working in a range of media including digital images, works on paper, sculpture, video, and writing. Her multidisciplinary practice draws upon autobiographical and material narratives to explore how dominant notions of value are articulated and exchanged, often focusing on the construction of popular identity in relation to histories of place. Nour was a fellow at the 2014/15 Home Workspace Program at Ashkal Alwan in Beirut. Her work has been exhibited in venues such as Darat Al Funun, Amman Access Gallery, Vancouver the Beirut Art Centre, the Helen Day Art Centre, Vermont Casa Arabe, Madrid and Cordoba and the Mosaic Rooms, London. Jacob Korczynski is an independent curator and the recent recipient of a curatorial research fellowship from The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts. He has curated projects for the Stedelijk Museum, Cooper Cole,

title: Gouaches
description:
“The gouaches are outtakes from a global agora visibly altered by photography, telecommunications, and satellite surveillance … they document intimate contemporary sensation, the things we imbibe, the places we drift through in a world reconfigured for entertainment.”

Dike Blair: Gouaches surveys the artist’s entire oeuvre in this medium, chronicling four decades of colorful, hyper-realistic gouache on paper works. Pursuing a wide range of subject matter–Shelter Island, haphazard stacks of books, cocktails and cigarettes, parking lots, nighttime swimming pools, Japanese cuisine, and obscured window frames, to name a few–the myriad objects and scenery are unified by Blair’s meticulous attention to detail and his fresh perspective on what it is we consume.

title: Inside The White Cub
edition_printrun: Staple Bound, Perfect Binding, [68] p. book + [24] p. calendar. Editionof 1000
description:
Inside the White Cube began as an ersatz version of an exhibition catalogue initially scheduled to be published by White Cube in 2012, as part of their Inside the White Cube series.

Though the project was eventually abandoned, the materials had already been assembled, and Blalock, with Peradam, sought to re-imagine what was initially intended to be a sales tool. Inside the White Cub is also the first publication to present Blalock’s project through exhibitions, and is free when you purchase a 2020 Wall Calendar, which also features works by the artist. - Peradam

title: La playa de los juguetes perdios 2021
edition_printrun: spiral bound, offset printed, screen print
description:
The proliferation of the use of plastic in the toy industry began around 1950, until then almost all toys were made of wood or metal, currently 90% of the toys that are produced are made of plastic.

Like many of our wastes, toys after having a short lifespan find their way to the oceans, where they navigate through the marine currents to be washed-up on different beaches and coasts of the world. If we consider that it is an indestructible and non-biodegradable material, every plastic toy that has been created continues to exist in one way or another, it does not disappear, but continue to decompose into smaller and smaller fragments.

This project seeks to give new life to more than 450 toys that were found and recovered in beaches located in the Mexican Caribbean and Pacific Ocean between 2013 and 2018, as part of projects related to beach clean-up activities that had educational, scientific and social components. - Inframundo

title: Solar System & Rest Rooms: Writings and Interviews, 1965-2007
description:
Artist Mel Bochner became a writer, he says, almost by accident.

In 1965, as a young artist in New York, he was out of a job Arts Magazine paid him $2.50 for every review he turned in, whether they published it or not a month of review-writing paid his rent―$28.00 a month. His reviews and articles provoked a range of unexpected reactions. “At that time, artists who wrote were looked at suspiciously, as if writing somehow tainted their visual practice,” he writes. A painter friend attacked him publicly for “joining the enemy.” Bochner soon began testing the boundary between writing-as-criticism and writing-as-visual-art. Solar System & Rest Rooms collects both Bochner's writings on art and his writings as art, offering more than fifty pieces―reviews, art criticism, theoretical texts, interviews, catalog statements, notecards, and his groundbreaking “magazine interventions”―many reproduced in facsimile.

Bochner is a leading figure in conceptualism his 1966 installation at the School of Visual Arts Gallery Working Drawings and Other Visible Things on Paper Not Necessarily Meant to Be Viewed as Art is considered to be the earliest exhibition of conceptual art. Solar System & Rest Rooms chronologically documents the work and ideas of this important artist over a span of forty years, as well as providing a unique perspective on the conceptual and post-minimal art scene in New York. This book offers a rare insight into what it means to be an artist whose visual practice is inseparable from the sustained practice of writing. Mel Bochner has lived and worked in New York City since 1964. His work has been exhibited internationally and is included in major museum collections throughout the world.

title: Amazing! Mel Bochner prints : from the collections of Jordan D. Schnitzer and his family foundation
contributors: Sienna Brown (Author), Ruth Fine (Author), Barry Schwabsky (Author), Jan Howard (Author), Mel Bochner (Artist), Jordan Schnitzer (Foreword)
description:
For more than 50 years, American conceptualist Mel Bochner (born 1940) has been shaping dialogs between art and language through exhibition concepts, paintings and sculptures that embrace systems and structures to reveal their cracks and limitations, undermining the means we use to comprehend the world.

Bochner created his first prints in 1973 at the invitation of publisher Robert Feldman of Parasol Press (who introduced a generation of minimalist and conceptual artists to printmaking through his work at Crown Point Press).

Since then, Bochner has employed many different forms of printmaking, using and abusing its material possibilities and its unpredictability to counter the methodical fashion in which plates and stencils are cut, characters per line are fixed, or print runs set. This volume surveys Bochner's longstanding engagement with various types of printmaking, from aquatints to monoprints.

title: Language 1966-2006
contributors: Johanna Burton (Essay), James Rondeau (Essay), James Meyer (Essay)
description:
Language 1966–2006 surveys four decades in which Mel Bochner turned words into his primary material, treating a sentence the same way a painter treats a mark on canvas.

Published by the Art Institute of Chicago to accompany a retrospective there from October 2006 to January 2007, the catalog gathers more than sixty works, from Bochner's early Measurement pieces and photographic Actualities to the Thesaurus paintings that stack synonyms into dense blocks of color and type. Essays by Johanna Burton, James Rondeau, and James Meyer trace how Bochner's interest in the failure of language to fix meaning ran alongside his early experiments with photography, index cards, and site-specific installation. The book is a 148-page hardcover with more than one hundred illustrations, arranged roughly by decade.

Bochner emerged in New York in the late 1960s among artists such as Sol LeWitt and Dan Graham who treated the idea behind a work as its real material. He continued to mine language for the rest of his career, moving in later decades into the large, brightly colored word paintings, among them the profanity-laced Blah, Blah, Blah series, that brought his conceptual concerns to a wider audience.
notes: Catalog for the Art Institute of Chicago retrospective, October 2006-January 2007. Distributed by Yale University Press.

title: Mel Bochner
description:
New York-based Conceptual art pioneer Mel Bochner writes in this monograph, "What I try to do is stay open to the work as it develops, not impose myself on it, but permit it to take me somewhere. If I had a model, I suppose it would be those ancient Chinese artists who changed their name three times during their lifetime, in order not to become the prisoner of a style."

The book introduces new riffs--produced for an exhibition at Domaine de Kerguéhennec, in Brittany, France--on several well-known bodies of work, including Bochner's recent ongoing series The Thesaurus Paintings, in which a group of often humorous synonyms (lazy, lethargic, crazy, vulgar and irascible, for instance) are painted in brightly colored block letters, and the Measurement Pieces (conceived in the 1960s), in which the walls are highlighted with numbered arrows indicating their

title: Italia Photographs from Italy 2013 - 2015
description:
Swedish photographer Martin Bogren (born 1967) spent the years 2013–15 in Italy creating this gorgeous and lyrical black-and-white photo-essay, his tribute to the country and the people he met on his travels.

Bogren’s luscious images of everyday street scenes, anonymous passersby, languid smokers, extroverted pedestrians and remote silhouettes are suffused with an affectionate, soft-focus gaze, making them seem like long-lost, unattributed archival photographs from a vanished era. Beautifully designed, Italia is destined to become a photobook classic.

Bogren’s work became widely known in the mid-2000s with his book Ocean, which was shortlisted for Best Photobook in Arles 2009 and received the honorable prize for the Best Photobook in Sweden the same year. Other critically acclaimed titles by Bogren include Lowlands, published by Max Strom in 2011, and Tractor Boys, published by Dewi Lewis in 2013.

title: a short story
description: A short story. A love story. A dialogue. Love on the left bank meets Before sunrise. Playful, delightful, sad and heartfelt. Wonderful text and wonderful images work so wonderfully well in the cinematic lay-out. Stefan Vanthuyne

title: 20.000 Leghe Sotto I Mari
description: Sébastien Bonin's recent work belongs to this movement. Although in the past he has turned his camera to the great landscapes of the American West or to the trivial details of his urban environment, since 2013 the artist has been experimenting since with the photogram technique – considered to be the forerunner of photography – to produce non-figurative photos.

title: Pope.L
description:
Pope.L, Will Boone documents a two-artist exhibition at Andrea Rosen Gallery that set William Pope.L's language-based sculpture against Will Boone's paintings of found American imagery, letting each artist's work sharpen the other by contrast.

The show ran January 30 to March 5, 2016, and split the gallery's three rooms between Pope.L's freestanding cut-out sculptures, including Cone in a Forest and Cone for My Sister (Private Language Problem), and Boone's larger paintings built from acrylic, magazine clippings, and resin over impressions of found steel gates. This 68-page softcover booklet, produced by Andrea Rosen Gallery's publishing program, gathers a compilation of source material and images from each artist rather than functioning as a conventional catalog with essays.

Pope.L (1955–2023) spent decades probing race, poverty, and language through performance, sculpture, and painting, including his ongoing Skin Set series. Boone, based in Los Angeles, works between painting and sculpture and draws on Southern American iconography that he later expanded in publications such as Prison Rodeo and Elvis.
notes: Two-artist exhibition catalog for Pope.L and Will Boone at Andrea Rosen Gallery, January 30-March 5, 2016. Row's collector title listed only "Pope.L"; the catalog and cover credit both artists as "Pope.L, Will Boone," and the title has been completed accordingly.

title: CAR
description:
Car collects the automotive imagery Will Boone used as raw material for his paintings and sculpture, turning a working scrapbook into a stand-alone artist's book.

Published by Karma in 2016 in an edition of 700, the book reproduces found photographs, advertisements, and clippings of cars that Boone gathered for research, arranged without captions or sequence so the imagery reads as visual notation rather than narrative. It closes with an original piece of writing by novelist Harry Crews, whose fiction shares Boone's interest in Southern working-class culture. The book is a 40-page softcover measuring roughly 10½ × 8½ inches.

Boone treats found material, including car parts, gates, and carnival imagery, as the starting point for paintings and sculpture that read as assemblages of American vernacular culture. Car followed Prison Rodeo and Elvis, earlier Karma publications built from the same kind of research archive, and preceded Pope.L, Will Boone, a 2016 two-artist exhibition catalog.
notes: Softcover artist's book, edition of 700, with a text contribution by novelist Harry Crews.

title: Prison Rodeo
description:
Prison Rodeo gathers found photographs of the rodeos held inside American prisons, part of the found-image research Will Boone drew on for his paintings and sculpture.

Published by Karma in 2014 in an edition of 750, the book reproduces black-and-white photographs of inmates competing in bull riding and bronco events, the kind of amateur rodeo photography Boone collects as raw material. The 48-page softcover, printed at roughly 10½ × 8¾ inches, presents the images without captions, letting the record of the events stand on its own.

The book belongs to a run of Karma publications, alongside Elvis (2014) and Car (2016), in which Boone circulates the found photography and vernacular imagery that inform his studio practice. Its subject, the improvised sport practiced at institutions such as the Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola, sits inside the Southern iconography that runs through Boone's paintings and sculpture.
notes: Softcover artist's book, edition of 750, out of print at the publisher.

title: Elvis
description:
Elvis collects amateur photographs that fans took of Elvis Presley, assembling a portrait of the singer built entirely from other people's snapshots.

Published by Karma in 2014 in an edition of 500, the book reproduces found Polaroids and prints, including the cover image of Presley smiling from behind the wheel of a car, taken by fans rather than professional photographers. The informal, off-guard quality of the pictures stands apart from Presley's carefully managed public image. The 32-page softcover, roughly 10½ × 8 inches, presents them without captions or accompanying text.

The book extends Will Boone's practice of building work from found and vernacular photography, following Prison Rodeo (2014) and preceding Car (2016), both drawn from the same kind of amateur and archival source material.
notes: Softcover artist's book, edition of 500, out of print at the publisher. Cover reproduces a found snapshot of Elvis Presley driving; the collector's original title annotation ("Elvis Presley driving cover") described this cover image and has been folded into these notes, with the title corrected to the book's actual title, "Elvis."

title: The Badger's Song
description:
The Badger's Song gathers seven years of Michaël Borremans's painting into a single volume and shows how working in series has become the structure of his practice.

The book is organised by series rather than by date: Black Mould, Fire from the Sun, Coloured Cones, Girl with Hands and the title group The Badger's Song among them, with 160 colour plates at close to full scale in a large hardcover of 178 pages. Most of the paintings had never been reproduced before. First issued by Hannibal Books in Belgium in 2020, the edition here was published by Walther König in 2021 with the subtitle Series 2013–2020.

Borremans (born 1963, Geraardsbergen) paints with the tonal restraint and glazing of eighteenth-century portraiture and turns it on scenes that refuse to resolve: hooded figures, children in dark robes, faces cropped or covered. He has had solo exhibitions at the Dallas Museum of Art, Tel Aviv Museum of Art, BOZAR in Brussels and the Hara Museum in Tokyo, and the earlier Black Mould catalogue is already on this shelf.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Belgian Art, Figurative Painting
notes: Full title on the title page: The Badger's Song: Series 2013–2020. First published by Hannibal Books, Veurne, 2020 (ISBN 9789463887564); the Walther König edition followed in 2021. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Black Mould
description:
Michaël Borremans: Black Mould documents the artist’s first exhibition at David Zwirner, London in 2015 and his first solo presentation in the city in ten years.

This intimately scaled catalogue, which has been designed by the artist in collaboration with Kim Beirnaert, includes 32 small- and large-scale paintings from his new series, most of which feature anonymous, black-robed characters. Alone or in groups, they perform mysterious acts within monochromatic spaces reminiscent of an artist’s barren studio.

Seemingly behaving according to a symbolic language of their own, they pose alone or interact in communal dances, with some figures holding torches and others exposed naked from the waist down. Their facelessness opens up ambiguous narrative possibilities, as if they were empty canvases with which to construct meaning. Like archetypes capable of embodying shifting meanings, the blank figures become a mold for the human condition, at once satirical, tragic, humorous and above all, contradictory

title: Wax House of Wax
description:
Wax House of Wax gathers Matt Borruso's collages of old horror-film stills, found objects, and his own sculptures into a single volume, extending the visual logic of his 2014 gallery show of the same name.

Across 112 pages, images are cut, redacted, and reoriented, their figures partly effaced and their seams left visible, then multiplied through mirrored reflections until the source material becomes nearly illegible. The book was self-published by Borruso's own imprint, Visible Publications, in an edition of 150, bound as a hardcover with a hand screen-printed cloth cover and hand-sewn binding.

Borruso, who lives and works in San Francisco, first presented the Wax House of Wax material at Steven Wolf Fine Arts in 2014; a review of that show described his method as Surrealist, manipulating banal imagery until the horror underneath becomes visible. The book functions as both documentation of that project and a freestanding object in its own right.
notes: Title as catalogued, 'Wax House Of Wax,' matches the artist's own title (drawn from his 2014 exhibition of the same name); no annotation to strip. Self-published, no ISBN assigned; edition of 150. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Untitled Lover Pictures
description:
Untitled Lover Pictures is a hand-assembled zine by Caiti Borruso made from photographs a former partner took of her in bed during their relationship, which she requested back from him after it ended and decided to publish rather than let remain solely in his possession.

Reproduced in black and white on colored stock and hand-titled on the cover, the zine repurposes casual, unposed images made by someone who was not a photographer into a deliberate authored object. Borruso has described the project as motivated by anger at not controlling her own likeness, and by a wish to take back images she felt entitled to determine the fate of.

Borruso (b. 1993) is a Brooklyn-based photographer and writer who studied at Image Text Ithaca; her self-published books and zines, including Under the Dog Star, Whale Creek is Flooding, and Putting the Dog to Sleep, work in the same vein of small-run, personal, image-text publishing that interrogates authorship, intimacy, and control over one's own image.
notes: Self-published saddle-stitched zine with no ISBN or formal print run; bibliographic facts (pages, dimensions) could not be confirmed from any listing and should be verified against the physical copy. Cover confirmed via the artist's own site (hand-lettered title on the front wrapper). Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Intimate Geometries: The Art and Life of Louise Bourgeois
The Spider and the Tapestries
description:
The Spider and the Tapestries gathers the fabric-based works Louise Bourgeois made in the last years of her life, in which mending and repair become both a literal craft and a psychological act.

The book reproduces sculptures built from salvaged tapestry fragments and needlepoint alongside archival photographs of the Bourgeois family's Paris workshop, where her parents restored antique wall hangings, and excerpts from the artist's own psychoanalytic writings that link the spider motif to her mother. It was first issued as a limited edition for Louise Bourgeois: L'Araignee et les Tapisseries at Hauser & Wirth, Zurich, in 2014, and reprinted by Hatje Cantz the following year in this hardcover trade edition.

For Bourgeois, the spider was never simply an insect but a stand-in for her mother, a weaver whom she once described as "deliberate, clever, patient... and as useful as a spider." The tapestry works extend a lifelong engagement with textile as autobiography, connecting the room-sized Cells and bronze spiders of her sculptural practice back to the sewing table of her childhood.
notes: Author's name corrected from catalogue entry 'Bourgeouis' to 'Bourgeois'. First published as a limited edition on the occasion of the 2014 Hauser & Wirth Zurich exhibition; this Hatje Cantz hardcover trade edition followed in 2015. Currently out of print at ARTBOOK. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Dark Archives, 1-41
binding: Three saddle-stitched booklets and two single-page inserts in a foil-stamped, die-cut folder
description:
Dark Archives, 1-41 is Andre Bradley's fragmentary autobiography, weaving his own photographs and writing together with pictures pulled from his family's archive to build a portrait of memory that resists a single, linear narrative.

The work takes the form of three saddle-stitched booklets and two single-page inserts, housed in a foil-stamped, die-cut folder designed by Elana Schlenker, published in an edition of 300 by Image Text Ithaca Press. Bradley combines appropriated family snapshots with his own images and text in a structure that deliberately upsets the linguistic and visual constrictions placed on Black men, treating the family archive itself as a contested, unstable form.

Bradley (b. 1987) is a Philadelphia-based photographer and a graduate of Hampshire College and the Rhode Island School of Design. Dark Archives, his first photobook, was shortlisted for both the Rencontres d'Arles Image-Texte Book Award and the Aperture-Paris Photo First PhotoBook Award in 2016, and copies are held in the special collections of the Morgan Library, RISD's Fleet Library, and UW-Madison Libraries.
notes: Title stripped of no annotation (catalogue title matched "Dark Archives 1-41" exactly; display title normalized to "Dark Archives, 1-41" per publisher). ISBN 9780996735117 is for the 2016 second printing; the 2015 first edition of 300 predates ISBN assignment. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Walk This Way
edition_printrun: Limited edition of 500, each with a signed and numbered print
description:
Walk This Way collects Sophie Bramly's photographs of hip-hop's founding scene, made in New York between 1981 and 1984, before the culture had a name most of the world would recognize.

Bramly left France at twenty to immerse herself in the Bronx and Harlem scenes then forming around DJs, MCs, and graffiti writers, photographing backstage, in clubs, and in the homes of the people she met. The book reproduces 55 black-and-white and 37 color images of Kool Herc, Afrika Bambaataa, Grandmixer D.ST, Jazzy Jay, Grandmaster Melle Mel, Kurtis Blow, Run-DMC, the Beastie Boys, and Keith Haring, with an introduction by Fab 5 Freddy. It was published in 2015 as a limited edition of 500, each copy including a signed and numbered photograph, accompanied by exhibitions in Paris, Marseille, Brussels, and Los Angeles.

Bramly's early Bronx photographs first surfaced publicly in the 2011 exhibition 1981 & +, and a broader edit of her archive followed in 2022 with Yo! The Early Days of Hip Hop 1982-84, published by Soul Jazz. Taken together, the two bodies of work stand as one of the fullest surviving photographic records of hip-hop before its commercial breakthrough.
notes: Delpire & Co lists this as a collector's edition with an original signed print; the 2015 first edition was originally produced with Antoine de Beaupre/Galerie 213. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Brancusi, film, photographie: images sans fin
publisher: Éditions du Centre Pompidou / Le Point du Jour
editor: Quentin Bajac, Clément Chéroux, Philippe-Alain Michaud
description:
The catalogue of Images sans fin at the Centre Pompidou in 2011. It was the first exhibition to show Constantin Brancusi’s photographs and films as work in their own right, not as documentation of the sculpture.

Brancusi began photographing his sculptures in the studio in the early 1920s, on Man Ray’s advice. Then he began filming them. He kept at both for the rest of his working life and let almost none of it out. Around a hundred photographs and film stills are gathered here, many published for the first time: sculptures in raking light and steam, the Impasse Ronsin studio rearranged from shot to shot, models and friends, self-portraits, studies of stone and plaster, photograms. The plates are printed in four colour, so the varying tones of the original black-and-white prints survive reproduction. Three essays follow: on reproduction, on Brancusi’s use of cinema, and on the exchange with Man Ray. Alfred Pacquement contributes the preface. Quentin Bajac, Clément Chéroux and Philippe-Alain Michaud, all curators at the Pompidou, edited the volume. Text in French.

Brancusi (1876–1957) left Romania for Paris in 1904, much of the way on foot, and stayed. He printed the photographs himself and, by any technical standard, printed them badly: out of focus, over-exposed, shot into the light, the edges burned. That was the point. He wanted the sculpture seen as he saw it in the studio, and he would not hand that job to anyone else. The photographs ended up part of the work.
tags: Photography, Film, Sculpture, Exhibition Catalogue, Artist Photography, Studio, Paris
notes: Published for “Images sans fin. Brancusi, film, photographie”, Centre Pompidou, Galerie du Musée, 29 June to 12 September 2011. Preface by Alfred Pacquement. OCLC 744289586.

title: Amusement Park
description:
A frenetic, candy-colored photobook by New York photographer David Brandon Geeting, Amusement Park pins his screen-native image-making to the printed page without dimming any of its glare.

Marrying a discordant blend of documentary photography, studio improvisations, and impertinent portraits, the sequence runs through frivolous entertainment, hobbyist tinkering, and the facade of luxury while always threatening to malfunction. Copenhagen imprint Lodret Vandret matched that energy in the object itself: four different paper stocks, traditional CMYK mixed with multicolor Pantone profiles developed by Swiss design studio Colorlibrary.ch, spray-can typography, and a plastic-wrapped cover. Published in 2017 in an edition of 500.

Geeting is a Brooklyn-based photographer whose deadpan, hyper-saturated still lifes and portraits move between personal projects and commissions for outlets including The New Yorker, TIME, Vogue, and Nike his books extend that sensibility into sequenced, object-like publications.

title: Paris Nocturne
description:
Paris Nocturne is the most complete account yet of the night pictures that made Brassaï's name, treating the 1930s work as a single body rather than two famous books.

The volume brings together the photographs of Paris de nuit (1932) and The Secret Paris of the 30s with unpublished negatives, contact sheets, scrapbook clippings, mock-ups and magazine spreads from the archive, reproduced in 214 duotone plates among 296 illustrations. Three essays by Sylvie Aubenas of the Bibliothèque nationale de France and Quentin Bajac, then of the Centre Pompidou, place the pictures within Brassaï's early career, his friendships with Henry Miller and the Surrealists, and the commercial press that first carried them. First published in French by Gallimard in 2012, this is the Thames & Hudson edition of 2013.

Brassaï (Gyula Halász, 1899–1984) came to Paris from Transylvania in 1924 and took up the camera to record what he saw on his nocturnal walks: brothels, bals musette, fog on the quais, the workers and lovers of the small hours. Those pictures became the model for a whole tradition of urban night photography, and this book is the reference edition of them.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Paris, French Photography, Night Photography, Photography History
notes: English edition of the Gallimard volume Brassaï: Paris nocturne (2012). Sources disagree on extent: Thames & Hudson and Library of Congress give 312 pages, photo-eye gives 296. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: an Archeology of Fear and Desire
Dear Martin
description:
Dear Martin reproduces a cache of found, uncaptioned self-portraits made by an anonymous photographer in the late 1960s: a man alone on a rooftop, photographing himself in a series of bikini briefs against the chain-link fencing and canvas screens of the building.

With no captions or context, the images ask the viewer to identify with the man's static, repeated performance and to guess at why and how he staged it, working alone, aware of the architecture's lines as much as his own body. Ampersand Gallery, Portland, published the photographs as a small-edition book to coincide with a 2015 exhibition; the collection belongs to artist and collector Jason Brinkerhoff.

The book sits within a strain of vernacular-photography publishing, in which galleries and collectors recirculate anonymous snapshot archives as artist books, prizing the unresolved authorship and private performance captured in images never meant for public view.
notes: Photographs are by an anonymous photographer; Jason Brinkerhoff is the collector who assembled and published them with Ampersand Gallery for a 2015 exhibition. No ISBN identified.
