title: Stills
publisher: Yale University Press / Art Institute of Chicago
description:
Stills presents, for the first time in full, Sarah Charlesworth's 1980 series of fourteen photographs depicting figures falling or jumping from buildings, each print exceeding six feet in height.

Charlesworth appropriated the source images from newspapers and re-photographed them, stripping away captions and context to isolate the suspended instant of the fall. Seven works debuted in 1980 at Tony Shafrazi's gallery; the remaining seven existed only as negatives until Charlesworth printed them as artist's proofs for the Art Institute of Chicago in 2012. This 2014 publication, with an essay by curator Matthew S. Witkovsky, was issued alongside the museum's exhibition of the complete set.

A key figure of the Pictures Generation, Charlesworth used appropriation to interrogate how mass-media images construct meaning, a concern she shared with contemporaries such as Cindy Sherman and Richard Prince. Stills resurfaced in 2011 in the group exhibition September 11 at MoMA PS1, where its unattributed, ambiguous falling bodies took on new and unavoidable resonance.
notes: One of two copies in the collection. Catalogue title corrected from 'Still' to 'Stills', the series' and publication's actual title. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Stills
publisher: Yale University Press / Art Institute of Chicago
description:
This slim, haunting volume gathers for the first time the complete Stills, Sarah Charlesworth's 1980 series of fourteen large-scale photographs depicting anonymous figures caught mid-fall or mid-jump from buildings, images she appropriated and re-photographed from newspaper wire sources.

Charlesworth printed the images at over six feet tall, a scale that turns a fraction-of-a-second news photograph into a suspended, almost architectural event. Seven of the fourteen were shown in 1980 at her dealer's apartment; the remaining seven were not printed until 2012, when Charlesworth made a unique artist's proof edition from her original negatives for the Art Institute of Chicago. This book, with an essay by curator Matthew S. Witkovsky and a foreword by Douglas Druick, is the first time the full series has been reproduced or exhibited together.

Charlesworth (1947-2013) was a central figure of the Pictures Generation alongside Sherrie Levine, Richard Prince, and Cindy Sherman, using appropriated mass-media imagery to interrogate representation, spectacle, and the photographic image itself. Stills remains one of the starkest and most direct works of that circle.
notes: One of two copies in the collection. First full publication of the complete Stills series (1980); half the prints were not made until 2012 from Charlesworth's original negatives. Cover already present from an earlier ingest pass. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Cherchez la femme (Search for the Woman)
Cherchez la Femme
description:
Cherchez la Femme brings together Luc Chessex's photographs of Cuban women, made during the fourteen years he spent living and working in Havana.

Chessex left Lausanne for Cuba in 1961, drawn by the revolution, and stayed until 1975, working as a photographer for the Ministry of Culture and as artistic director of the magazine Cuba Internacional. The photographs collected here move past political iconography to observe Cuban women directly, on the street, at work, at leisure, forming a counterpoint to the propaganda imagery more commonly associated with the period. The book, drawn from the Musee de l'Elysee's collection with text by Daniel Girardin, is presented in French and English.

The series later formed one quarter of CCCC (Castro, Coca, Che, Cherchez la Femme), a 2014 exhibition at the Musee de l'Elysee in Lausanne that surveyed Chessex's Cuban years alongside his portraits of Fidel Castro and his images of Coca-Cola signage and Che Guevara iconography, situating Cherchez la Femme within his broader documentary record of the revolution.
notes: Publication year not confirmed by any source checked; distributed alongside the Musee de l'Elysee's 2014 CCCC exhibition, which surveyed this and three related bodies of work from Chessex's years in Cuba. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Dark Room
description:
Phyllis Christopher’s fearless and tender photographs fuse lesbian sex and queer protest against the backdrop of a city in flux.

Relocating to San Francisco from her hometown Buffalo in the late-1980s, Christopher began to collaborate with her subjects to make images in which documentary and performance converge. Dark Room brings together fifteen years of Christopher’s work, negotiating street, club, and studio, with camera in hand, to compose a portrait of a community simultaneously defining radical articulations of queer lesbian sexuality and defending its bodily autonomy in the face of right-wing politics, the AIDS crisis and urban gentrification.

Reproducing photographs of startling intensity and sensuality alongside new writing by Susie Bright, Laura Guy, Michelle Tea and an interview with Shar Rednour, Dark Room is a heartfelt record of Christopher’s devotion to an analogue tradition, to the pleasures of photographs and the community that made them.

title: Guantanamo: If the Light Goes Out
description:
Guantanamo: If the Light Goes Out is Edmund Clark's three-year investigation into the naval base and prison camp at Guantanamo Bay, told through three interlocking environments: the American base community, the detention camp complex, and the homes of former detainees who were never charged with a crime.

Working within severe restrictions on what he could photograph, Clark deliberately chops and interweaves the three settings into a disjointed sequence, evoking the disorientation the camp was designed to produce. Rather than portraits, he photographs domestic interiors, drawing on the vanitas tradition of Dutch still-life painting, and the book includes texts by Julian Stallabrass and former detainee Omar Deghayes. Its title comes from a former detainee's statement: that when the light goes out unexpectedly in a room, he is back in his cell.

Clark is a British photographer known for long-form investigations into secrecy and incarceration, including Control Order House and The Mountains of Majeed. Guantanamo: If the Light Goes Out won Best Photographic Book at the 2011 New York Photo Awards and the Royal Photographic Society's Hood Medal.
notes: Full display title restored from catalogue's shortened "Guantanamo" to the publisher's "Guantanamo: If the Light Goes Out." Winner, Best Photographic Book, 2011 New York Photo Awards; Royal Photographic Society Hood Medal, 2011. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Chuck Close Prints: Process and Collaboration
description:
Chuck Close Prints: Process and Collaboration was the first full survey of Close's printmaking, and it made the case that the prints, not the paintings, are where his method is most visible.

Organised technique by technique, the book follows three decades of work in mezzotint, etching, woodcut, linocut, silkscreen, pulp-paper multiples and the Japanese and European traditions Close revived, showing progressive and state proofs beside the editioned image so that the decisions can be read. Terrie Sultan's introduction and an essay by Richard Shiff frame interviews with Close and the printers he worked with. Published by Princeton University Press in 2003 for the exhibition at Blaffer Gallery, the Art Museum of the University of Houston, which then travelled to the Metropolitan Museum of Art and other venues; a softcover of 160 pages with 110 colour plates, 38 black-and-white illustrations and a double gatefold.

Close (1940–2021) built his career on the gridded, enormously enlarged portrait head, and printmaking gave him a way to make the grid and its incremental labour the subject. The exhibition kept touring for a decade, and Prestel issued an expanded edition in 2014.
tags: Art, Printmaking, Contemporary Art, Portraiture, Exhibition Catalog, American Art
notes: Catalogued as Prints. An expanded hardcover edition was published by Prestel in 2014 (ISBN 9783791349664). Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Everything_1
edition_printrun: First edition, limited to 500 signed copies
description:
Everything_1 is Kenta Cobayashi's debut photobook, a hallucinatory index of glitched, layered images that redraws his native Tokyo as a shifting, screen-lit dreamscape.

Published by Newfave in 2016 in a signed edition of 500, the unnumbered 80-page softcover is bound with neon-orange elastic cord and offset-printed. Roughly ninety heavily layered color images, assembled from iPhone photographs, MacBook webcam stills, screen captures, and photo-booth strips, depict Cobayashi's circle of friends digitally warped into a nearly abstract, hallucinogenic register somewhere between the futuristic and the corrupted.

Cobayashi (b. 1992) treats Everything as an ongoing project, first developed as a daily photo blog before taking book form here and later in the 2020 sequel Everything_2. The book helped establish his reputation for genre-defying, glitch-driven photography that has since informed advertising and collaborative work for Louis Vuitton and Dunhill.
notes: First edition, limited to 500 signed copies; illustrated softcover with neon-orange elastic string binding, 80 unnumbered pages. A 2020 bootleg reprint and the sequel Everything_2 also circulate; this record is for the 2016 Newfave first edition. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Friends Forever
description:
Friends Forever is an early self-published photobook by Kenta Cobayashi, documenting the young artists and friends who passed through his shared house in Shibuya, Tokyo.

The 56-page softcover book was self-published in Tokyo in 2014, part of a run of small, quickly produced photobooks — alongside titles such as Daydream and The Scrap — that Cobayashi issued outside any commercial publisher during the early years of his career. Cobayashi photographs his circle candidly and close-up, treating the shared house itself as a recurring subject.

Cobayashi has since become known for a more processed, glitch- and collage-based approach to color photography, shown internationally and applied to commercial work for brands including Louis Vuitton and Adidas. Friends Forever predates that shift, capturing his earlier, more straightforwardly documentary mode.
notes: Self-published, Tokyo, 2014; no ISBN. Listed in the artist's own biography under his 2014 artist's-book output but no longer listed on the current books page of his site. No usable cover image found from any source checked (the only located non-text reference was a YouTube video thumbnail, not a photograph of the physical book) — cover to be photographed. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: A Real Bronx Cheer
edition_printrun: Edition of 1000 copies (plus 22 deluxe copies with original drawings). Book design by Brendan Dugan
description:
A significant collaboration between two artists and a music impresario, featuring Colen's sculptures of cement-filled whoopie cushions, Kenny's collaborative cartoon drawings of an inflatable God, and Delsener's humorous captions.

The drawings depict contentious moments in the relationship between a priest and his inflatable God, who is rendered in the tradition of a blow-up sex doll. The book is about the inherent utility of air and humor as our greatest defense mechanism against the unanswerable questions we all carry. The cement-filled whoopee cushions represent the faith an artist places in any object he creates, capturing something ephemeral and abstract. The book contains numerous gag cartoons and whoopie cushion imagery.

title: Trash
description:
Trash is the first book devoted to Dan Colen's paintings built from studio detritus — chewed gum, dirt, and refuse worked into the paint surface as both subject and material.

Published by Gagosian and Rizzoli in October 2014, the 302-page hardcover reproduces the series in full-page plates with close-up details that register the built-up texture of each surface. Colen has spoken of incorporating found and discarded material as a way of ceding some authorship to the object itself: gum wrappers, cigarette butts, and studio sweepings arrive with their own history embedded, functioning as active collaborators in the composition rather than raw pigment alone, registering what he has called real time and visceral experience directly on the canvas.

The book accompanies a body of work that extended Colen's long engagement with unconventional materials, following earlier series built from chewing gum, flowers, and confetti. A member of the generation of New York artists who emerged around the Bowery in the 2000s, Colen has continued to test how far from traditional painting materials a picture can travel while still functioning, formally, as one.
notes: Text by Josh Smith. Hardcover, 302 pages, 9 × 12 in. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Women with Cameras (Anonymous)
description:
Women with Cameras (Anonymous) assembles eighty found photographs of women photographed in the act of taking a picture, turning a private, repeated gesture into a study of who gets to hold the camera.

Collier sourced the images — amateur snapshots spanning the 1970s through the early 2000s — from flea markets and thrift stores, then sequenced them without captions or identifying information beyond the pose they share. The book was published by Karma, New York, and Studio Voltaire, London, as a 168-page softcover with an essay by Hilton Als, and preserves the plain, undesigned quality of its source snapshots.

The project extends Collier's long-standing interest in photography's own conventions and apparatus, seen elsewhere in her studies of book covers, album sleeves, and camera manuals. By collecting only images of women behind the lens, Women with Cameras (Anonymous) quietly reframes the history of amateur photography as a history of female authorship.
notes: Co-published by Karma (New York) and Studio Voltaire (London); essay by Hilton Als. A companion volume, 'Women with Cameras (Self Portrait)' (ISBN 9781949172003), exists as a separate publication and should not be conflated with this one. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Ink Drawings
description:
Exhibition catalog documenting George Condo's monumental ink drawings created over a six-month period in 2013-2014. They marked a significant new direction in his practice. Published for Condo's solo exhibition at Skarstedt Gallery London (February 11–April 5, 2014), this catalog features full-plate images, details, and foldouts revealing the artist's exploration of "the extreme possibilities of ink on paper." Working with transparent color layers, Condo positioned his signature distorted figures within abstract spaces, drawing conceptual inspiration from color field painting techniques while maintaining his distinctive psychological intensity.

Born in 1957, George Condo pioneered "Psychological Cubism," his groundbreaking approach that departs from classical Cubism by representing multiple emotional and psychological states simultaneously within single figures rather than multiple spatial perspectives. Emerging from the 1980s East Village art scene alongside Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring, Condo developed his signature "Artificial Realism," a synthesis of Old Master painting techniques with American pop sensibility and cartoon aesthetics. His distorted figures with bulbous faces, skewed limbs, and protruding eyes authentically represent the emotional complexity and psychological contradictions of modern life.

This body of ink drawings demonstrates Condo's continued investigation into the relationship between abstraction and figuration. The monumental scale of these works on paper, many approaching the size of paintings, allowed Condo to explore layered transparency and color interaction in ways distinct from his oil paintings. By positioning figures within abstract color fields, he created a dialogue between gestural abstraction and his psychological portraiture, expanding his vocabulary while remaining true to his exploration of "the disjointed human psyche."

The 64-page catalog, illustrated in color throughout with details and foldouts, provides intimate access to this exceptional series. Condo's work is held in major museum collections including MoMA, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Whitney Museum, Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Albright-Knox Art Gallery, Corcoran Gallery, and The Broad. Published by Skarstedt Gallery in an edition of limited availability.
notes: Exhibition at Skarstedt Gallery, London (February 11–April 5, 2014). Format: 26 × 21 cm (10.25 × 8.25 inches), 64 pages. Paperback, illustrated in color throughout. Published July 1, 2014. ISBN: 978-0-9575297-2-4. Monumental ink drawings created over six-month period exploring transparent color layers and abstract space. George Condo (b. 1957) coined the term "Psychological Cubism." His work is in collections at MoMA, Metropolitan Museum, Whitney Museum, Louisiana Museum, and The Broad.

title: George Condo: Painting Reconfigured
description:
The definitive monograph on George Condo's career from 1984 to 2015, written by art historian and curator Simon Baker working in close collaboration with the artist. This comprehensive 288-page volume combines biographical, chronological, and thematic approaches to survey Condo's outrageous, unorthodox painting practice. With over 250 illustrations, the book includes an introductory essay on Condo's contradictory nature, a chapter exploring his phenomenal early career in the 1980s East Village scene, and three thematic chapters tracing his systematic reconstruction of painting techniques from Abstract Expressionism to Old Master traditions.

Born in 1957 in Concord, New Hampshire, George Condo emerged as a pioneer of Neo-Expressionist revival, coining the term "Psychological Cubism" to describe his approach of representing multiple emotional and psychological states simultaneously within single figures. Unlike classical Cubism's multiple spatial perspectives, Condo's fragmented faces and distorted bodies depict the internal contradictions and psychological complexity of his subjects. His "Artificial Realism" synthesizes Old Master technical precision with American pop culture, cartoon aesthetics, and visceral psychological content—creating what he describes as authentic representations of "the disjointed human psyche."

The volume explores Condo's relationship to abstraction, examining how he alternates between figuration and pure abstraction while maintaining psychological intensity throughout. Baker analyzes the darker dimensions of Condo's iconography: the grotesque faces, violent distortions, and unsettling humor that characterize his portrait subjects. The book traces influences from Velázquez, Goya, and Picasso to de Kooning and Guston, revealing how Condo reconstructs painting history through his distinctive lens. His approach combines technical virtuosity with deliberately crude passages, academic precision with cartoon simplicity, beauty with horror.

Published by Thames & Hudson in hardcover format with 288 pages and over 250 color illustrations. George Condo's work is held in major museum collections including MoMA, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Whitney Museum, Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Albright-Knox Art Gallery, Corcoran Gallery, Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, and The Broad. Major retrospectives have been presented at New Museum (2011), Hayward Gallery (2011-2012), and Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris (2025-2026). This monograph represents the most comprehensive study of Condo's painting practice to date.
notes: Published December 7, 2015 by Thames & Hudson. 288 pages, over 250 color illustrations. ISBN: 978-0-500-09394-8. Hardcover format: 32.0 × 24.4 × 3.0 cm. Text by Simon Baker. Comprehensive monograph covering Condo's career from 1984-2015, exploring his "Psychological Cubism" approach and systematic reconstruction of painting techniques. George Condo (b. 1957) is in collections at MoMA, Metropolitan Museum, Whitney Museum, Louisiana Museum, Guggenheim, and The Broad. Major retrospectives at New Museum, Hayward Gallery, and Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris.

title: Mental States
description:
Major exhibition catalog surveying George Condo's career from 1982 to 2011, published for his landmark touring retrospective at New Museum (New York), Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen (Rotterdam), Hayward Gallery (London), and Schirn Kunsthalle (Frankfurt) in 2011-2012. This comprehensive 168-page volume focuses on Condo's portrait paintings while including sculptural busts in materials including gold and bronze. Organized thematically with 125 color illustrations, the book explores Condo's engagement with art history, popular culture, and contemporary society through essays by Ralph Rugoff (New Museum Director), Laura Hoptman (MoMA curator), novelist Will Self, and fiction writer David Means.

George Condo (b. 1957) pioneered "Psychological Cubism," his term for representing multiple emotional and psychological states simultaneously within single figures, a departure from classical Cubism's spatial fragmentation. Emerging from New York's 1980s East Village scene alongside Basquiat and Haring, Condo developed "Artificial Realism," synthesizing Old Master techniques with pop sensibility and cartoon aesthetics. His distorted portraits with bulbous faces, multiple eyes, and fractured features authentically depict what he calls "the disjointed human psyche": the emotional complexity and psychological contradictions of modern existence rendered through virtuoso painting combined with deliberately crude passages.

The "Mental States" exhibition and catalog examine Condo's systematic investigation of psychological portraiture across three decades. His subjects, whether based on observation or pure invention, exist in states of psychological flux, their features rearranged to express simultaneous, contradictory emotions. This approach extends to his sculptural busts in gold and bronze, which translate his painted distortions into three-dimensional form. The works engage art historical precedents from Velázquez and Goya through Picasso and de Kooning, while incorporating references from American popular culture, advertising, and cartoons to create what Condo terms "composites of the imagination."

Published by Hayward Gallery Publishing and distributed by D.A.P. in North America. Hardcover format, 11 × 11.75 inches, 168 pages with 125 color illustrations. Contributors: Ralph Rugoff, Laura Hoptman, Will Self, David Means. Condo's work is held in major collections including MoMA, The Metropolitan Museum, Whitney Museum, Louisiana Museum, Guggenheim, Tate, Centre Pompidou, and The Broad. This catalog represents the most significant survey of Condo's psychological portraiture from the early 1980s through 2011.
notes: Exhibition catalog for touring retrospective: New Museum, New York (January–May 2011) Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam (June–September 2011) Hayward Gallery, London (October 2011–January 2012) Schirn Kunsthalle, Frankfurt (February–May 2012). Published April 30, 2011 by Hayward Gallery Publishing. Hardcover, 11 × 11.75 inches (28.0 × 29.8 cm), 168 pages, 125 color illustrations. ISBN: 978-1-85332-289-1. Essays by Ralph Rugoff, Laura Hoptman, Will Self, David Means. Focus on portrait paintings and sculptural busts 1982-2011. George Condo (b. 1957) coined "Psychological Cubism." Collections: MoMA, Met, Whitney, Louisiana, Guggenheim, Tate, Pompidou.

title: Thirty-Four Reverse Telescopes and Three Buttons
description:
Thirty-Four Reverse Telescopes and Three Buttons catalogs the artist’s recent body of colored Plexiglas works, made between 2013 and 2016, introduced obliquely with a poem by Ben Estes.

Painter Matt Connors (born 1973) is known for combining a modernist visual vocabulary of grids and tense, minimal compositions with influences from design, poetry and music. Connors’ recent series of works brings this sensibility into the play of media: paintings in acrylic on paper are mounted on colored matte board, framed behind colored Plexiglass, creating an effect of nested colored forms in space.

Both objects and paintings, the deeply hued, mixed-media pieces have been reproduced in Thirty-Four Reverse Telescopes and Three Buttons in black and white as well as color. The two treatments show the works’ complex tonality along with their dynamic coloration.

title: A Bell Is a Cup
edition_printrun: 1st Edition of 1000. Four different colours for both the dust jacket and cover have been produced, allowing each dust jacket to be interchanged to create a new color combination. Sixteen different color combinations can be created in total.
contributors: Peter Eleey, Michel Leiris, Jack Spicer, Gertrude Stein
description:
A Bell is a Cup has been published by Rainoff to coincide with the exhibition "Impressionism" by Matt Connors, held at MoMA PS1, New York.

Alongside texts by Peter Eleey, Michel Leiris, Gertrude Stein and Jack Spicer, the publication presents the first comprehensive gathering of Connors' work to date. In his essay, Eleey writes that Connors' paintings "bear traces of one another, but they also some- times prop each other up or lean into each other, as if to physically reinforce, in painterly terms, Jack Spicer's ideas about the interdependence of poems. 'There is really no single poem,' Spicer came to believe he argued that 'poems should echo and re-echo against each other.'"
tags: Contemporary Art, Painting, Poetry, Artist Books

title: Public, Private, Secret: On Photography and the Configuration of Self
Selected Works from 1990's
description:
Selected Works from 1990's puts a slice of the William Crawford archive into circulation as a zine, which is close to the form the drawings originally took.

Thirty-two pages of black-and-white offset reproductions, staple-bound at 19 by 13 cm and published by Innen in Switzerland in 2016 in an edition of 500. The drawings are graphite on paper: interiors, couples and groups, women in heels and hats, a recurring man with a short afro and a moustache who is presumably the artist. Several sheets in the source archive carry captions or fragments of dialogue, the remains of sequences of thirty or more drawings that once read as stories.

Nothing is known of Crawford beyond the work. Roughly 950 drawings were found in an abandoned house in Oakland, California; some are on the backs of prison roster sheets dated 1997, cut down the middle so the institution cannot be identified, and San Francisco landmarks appear in the backgrounds. He signed a few sheets as Bill, William or WM Crawford. The archive was first shown in 2015 and has since been published by Innen and by Ampersand in Portland, and this zine is its most portable form.
tags: Art, Drawing, Zines, Outsider Art, Erotica
notes: Catalogued as "Selected works from 1990's - 2000"; the printed title is Selected Works from 1990's. No ISBN. Page count from a dealer listing; Printed Matter records the pamphlet without an extent. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Silhouettes
edition_printrun: Signed and numbered edition (sources give 100-120 copies)
description:
Silhouettes is Fred Cray's 2016 continuation of his long-running Unique Photographs project, in which mass-produced snapshots are altered into one-of-a-kind objects.

For this book, Cray ran 4 x 6 machine prints through a desktop printer a second time, layering silhouettes, and their photographic negatives, over his own photographs, found snapshots, and images of posters, graffiti, and murals. Published in a signed and numbered softcover edition, each copy comes with at least one unique inserted photograph, so that no two copies are identical.

Since 2008, Cray has scattered more than 26,000 individually altered photographs in public places worldwide as part of Unique Photographs, and his small-run books, including Cray Cray and Silhouettes, extend that project's interest in chance encounter and the single, irreproducible print into book form. His work is held in the collections of the Brooklyn Museum, the George Eastman Museum, and the New York Public Library.
notes: Page count and physical dimensions not found; sources disagree on edition size (Dashwood Books states 120 signed/numbered copies, other sources state 100). Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Money
description:
Money is the first joint artist's book by Tania Prill, Alberto Vieceli, and Sebastian Cremers, the Zurich design studio Prill Vieceli Cremers, built entirely from the pictures printed on the world's banknotes.

Across 256 pages and 300 color images, the book collects and compares the political subject matter, historical milestones, distinguished figures, status symbols, and landscapes that appear on paper currency, treating banknotes as mini-posters proclaiming an idealized world. It traces recurring visual patterns, such as the Euro's bridges standing for a united Europe, or the pathos formulae used again and again to depict strong, happy, laboring figures with access to education, arguing that monetary iconography functions as a form of visual propaganda that imprints value on otherwise worthless paper.

Prill Vieceli Cremers has designed numerous books for Edition Patrick Frey since 2006; Money, published by the same house, extends the studio's design practice into an authored, research-driven artist's book on the visual language of the state.
notes: First edition 2015, reprinted through a third printing in 2017. Studio name (Prill Vieceli Cremers) kept as the catalogued author; "Cremers" and "Prill Vieceli" used as last/first for sort purposes. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Disss-Co (A Fragment)
description:
Disss-Co (A Fragment) is Douglas Crimp's fragmentary memoir of gay disco culture in 1970s New York, a personal counterpart to the criticism that made him one of the era's most influential voices on art, sexuality, and AIDS activism.

Subtitled From Before Pictures, A Memoir of 1970s New York, the essay was published by MoMA PS1 in 2016 as part of the reader series edited by Jocelyn Miller accompanying the fourth iteration of the museum's Greater New York exhibition. In brief, tactile fragments, Crimp recalls nights at downtown discotheques, recreating the ecstatic, anonymous release of the dancefloor in prose as precise as his art criticism.

Crimp (1944-2019) was Fanny Knapp Allen Professor of Art History at the University of Rochester and the author of On the Museum's Ruins and Melancholia and Moralism: Essays on AIDS and Queer Politics. This first-person fragment extends the same attentiveness to bodies, desire, and loss that runs through his critical writing into memoir of pre-AIDS gay New York.
notes: Part of MoMA PS1's Greater New York reader series, edited by Jocelyn Miller, accompanying the exhibition's 2015 iteration; subtitled 'From Before Pictures, A Memoir of 1970s New York.' Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Arc
edition_printrun: Edition of 500. Perimeter Editions 007. Out of print.
description:
The debut book of the Melbourne artist Zoë Croggon, whose photographic collages set the human body against the geometry of modernist architecture, and the winner of the 2015 Asia-Pacific Photobook Prize.

Croggon works with found images drawn from the histories of modernist and minimalist architecture, dance, gymnastics and athletics. Each collage is made with the fewest possible cuts: a torso meets a concrete plane, a limb continues the line of a stair. The pairings are formal rather than narrative, and the book keeps that economy, giving each work a full page on white. Eighty pages, softcover with flaps, in an edition of 500, published as Perimeter Editions 007 in September 2015 and co-published with the Asia-Pacific Photobook Archive, Melbourne.

Croggon is represented by Daine Singer, Melbourne, and has exhibited widely in Australia. Arc established the vocabulary she has continued in later work, including the 2024 Perimeter title How to Cut an Orange, where the same cut-and-abut method is applied to a wider range of source material.
tags: Art, Photography, Collage, Contemporary Art, Limited Edition, Australia
notes: Edition of 500; Perimeter Editions 007. Co-published with the Asia-Pacific Photobook Archive, Melbourne. Winner of the 2015 Asia-Pacific Photobook Prize. Record repaired from empty stub. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: I Refuse to be Invisible
description:
This catalogue is the first publication to focus on the work of Nigerian-born, L.A.-based artist Njideka Akunyili Crosby.

It accompanied an exhibition of the artist's work held at the Norton Museum of Art in West Palm Beach, FL January 28 - April 24, 2016. Contents include an introductory essay by exhibition curator Cheryl Brutvan, Taiye Selasi's "Bye-Bye, Babar (Or: What Is An Afropolitan?)", artist interview, artist's chronology, and select bibliography and exhibition history. With full color reproductions of all works in the exhibitio

title: Predecessors
publisher: Tang Contemporary Arts Center in Cincinnati
contributors: Contributors: Ian Berry, Steven Matijcio, Malik Gaines
description:
30 color reproductions. Njideka Akunyili Crosby: Predecessors unites works from the artist’s Predecessors series.

Investigating the confluences, contact zones, and third spaces of culture, Akunyili Crosby represents the people and places closest to her: the women of her family, her partner, the interiors of her grandmother’s home and her own. Even in the midst of such personal themes, Akunyili Crosby opens these painted worlds to her viewers, and invites them to reflect upon their own experiences, memories, and emotions.

title: Robert Cumming: The Difficulties of Nonsense
description:
Robert Cumming: The Difficulties of Nonsense is the first comprehensive publication to survey the artist's landmark conceptual photographs of the 1970s, work that remains a touchstone for artists still working with illusion and staged fiction.

Working from Los Angeles, Cumming built props and functional-looking but ultimately useless constructions expressly to be photographed with his 8-by-10 camera, manipulating proportion, angle, light, and mirrors so that a picture invites a viewer to look, then look again and second-guess what they saw. The 184-page hardcover monograph gathers 135 black-and-white and color photographs alongside an essay by Sarah Bay Gachot and an interview with the artist by David Campany.

Cumming trained first as a painter before moving into sculpture and photography, and his layered, trick-of-the-eye images sit at the intersection of conceptual art, photography, and printmaking; his work is held in major museum collections including MoMA. He died in 2021.
notes: First comprehensive monograph on Cumming's 1970s conceptual photography, published by Aperture in a first edition limited to 2,500 copies. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: John Currin: The Complete Works: New Paintings
Glass Life
description:
Cwynar’s research-driven and visually complex images constitute the hallmarks of contemporary post–Pictures Generation work―in which photography is pursued in relation to film, sculpture, digital culture, and the cultural and technological history of image-making.

Cwynar’s work revolves around her interest in subjective notions of beauty through images the fetishization of consumer objects and colors and the exploration of the informal image archives that have emerged around the industrialization and capitalization of these ideas.

As part of her core practice, Cwynar collects, arranges, and archives her eBay purchases and creates studio studies of these consumer objects, exploring how images circulate online and how the lives and purposes of both physical objects and their likenesses change over time. Sara Cwynar: Glass Life is a must-have sourcebook for understanding the multilayered practice of this celebrated, multidisciplinary artist.
notes: One of two copies in the collection.

title: Pictures of Pictures
edition_printrun: Printed Matter Emerging Artists Publication Series
description:
Pictures of Pictures is Sara Cwynar's early taxonomy of found photographic ephemera, a slim artist's zine that previews the archival, image-about-images method that would define her later work.

Published through Printed Matter's Emerging Artists Publication Series in 2014 in an edition of 350, the fold-only booklet gathers photographs Cwynar found in discarded printed matter, camera advertisements, darkroom manuals, instructional pamphlets, arranged in an indexical, yearbook-like grid and bound in navy bookcloth with a gold foil-stamped cover. Drawing on Roland Barthes's writing on photography's "that-has-been," the sequence foregrounds the way a picture both revives and mourns its vanished subject.

Made while Cwynar was beginning her MFA at Yale, Pictures of Pictures belongs to a run of independently published books, including Kitsch Encyclopedia, that established the research-driven, image-archaeology approach she later expanded into large-scale photographic installations and, in 2021, the Aperture monograph Glass Life.
notes: Printed Matter Emerging Artists Publication Series, edition of 350; navy bookcloth cover with gold foil stamp, fold-only booklet with rubber-band binding. Page count differs between sources (92 pp. per the print studio's spec sheet vs. 24 pp. reported elsewhere); trim size (6 x 8.75 in / 15 x 22 cm) is consistent across sources. Out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Mexico
contributors: Paco Taibo (Author), Nicolas Arraitz (Author), Bruno Le Dantec (Author), Tania Bohorquèz (Author), Alfonso Morales (Author),
description:
This book is a record of the photographer’s Mexican travels, a tense, immobile diary of his experiences in the devastated landscapes of an increasingly volatile criminal society.

Still images, cinematographic narratives and texts make up a personal diary that, through intimate, sexual and narcotic encounters, constructs an increasingly sickening reality. Mirroring his journey as he wanders through a lonely and marginal world, d’Agata’s photographic language seems to fracture and degenerate page by page.

As a whole, Mexico presents a complex, difficult portrait of a period that has been constructed as a time of lawlessness and criminality in Mexican society. D’Agata structures the book around six photographic movements, relating directly to different times in the contemporary history of Mexico. These chapters suggest ruptures in the continuity of history, even as D’Agata creates a narrative of descent into pain and savagery.

title: A - New York 1989-93
edition_printrun: Leporello, 62 pictures. First edition. Design by Joao Linneu
description:
French photographer Antoine d'Agata departed his homeland in 1983 to begin a series of travels.

He has since gained notoriety with a body of work that deals with addiction, sex, personal obsessions, darkness, prostitution, and other topics widely considered taboo. D'Agata studied photography at the International Center of Photography of New York City in 1990, under the tutelage of Larry Clark and Nan Goldin. This publication offers a personal visual reflection of that time. Designed as a 48-page leporello with an insert containing 20 pages of text, including a letter written in 1991, it includes self-portraits, scratched out journal snippets, and grainy photographs of drug use.

This booklet is the first in a series of twelve books which opens the space for A's crossings, his physical journey through his wanderings, his drifts, his strained advances, his encounters. Form, if it can surprise at first, spins the redeployement of this road, begun one day which does not seem to have an end. We must imagine this booklet, related to the leporello, deploying in a jet of images, presence blown, unfolded situations, temporal suspensions. It is not a chronology, even if the images are grouped in sequences, here New York 1989-1993 each time an atmosphere, a climate, that are given in a mix of images, a confronting mixture that creates tension and calls for the energy and desire for life that emanate from it.
tags: New York City, Photographer Monographs, Street Photography, Photography, Addiction, Autobiography, Documentary Photography

title: Index
description:
Index turns the A7 between Paris and Marseille into a confessional, with the rest areas as stations and the family history surfacing mile by mile.

The book runs 1,215 small colour photographs across 256 pages at 13.5 by 18 cm, most of them made at night in lay-bys, service stations and cabs, against wide margins of white page that carry d'Agata's journal and letters. Other voices cut in: parents, women, the CB radio of the truckers. The countryside is treated as an extension of the body and the highway as a mirror in which the photographer sees his own path and his forebears' repeating. Parts of the work were shown in S'il y a lieu je pars avec vous at Le Bal, Paris, in autumn 2014; André Frère Éditions published the complete work that December, co-edited with D.Books, in French.

D'Agata (born 1961, Marseille) studied with Larry Clark and Nan Goldin and has been a member of Magnum Photos since 2004. His books, from Mala Noche and Insomnia to Anticorps, are made from the inside of the situations they record, and Index applies that method to the road home.
tags: Photography, French Photography, Documentary Photography, Diaristic Photography, Magnum Photos, France
notes: Text in French. Co-edition André Frère Éditions / D.Books; the publisher dates it December 2014, some retailers 2015. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: VIRUS
description:
From the ﬁrst day of conﬁnement ensuing the outbreak of the Covid-19 epidemic, Antoine d’Agata roamed the streets of Paris with a thermal camera to record, in his own unique way, the viral epidemic that turned the city into a strange theatre of wandering souls, bowed heads and ﬂeeing bodies.

Initially attracted by the way in which the thermodynamic device records the various infrared rays (heat waves) emitted by bodies, which vary according to their temperature, the artist was soon fascinated by a process that reduces human subjects to essential ﬁgures, devoid of superﬂuous characteristics or speciﬁcities.

Living and working for two months out of the Paris ofﬁce of the Magnum Photos agency and gallery, he used the thermal technique to document the impregnation of the deserted city existing under conﬁnement: a city plunged into silence, traversed by bodies with stereotypical attitudes, inhabited above all by the homeless who appear – in these images – as the last truly living and resistant bodies, austere and ﬂame-tinged compositions offering an alternative and dystopian vision of the emptying streets.

title: Easternsports
publisher: Institute of Contemporary Art, University of PennsylvaniaKarma
description:
Longtime friends and first-time collaborators Alex Da Corte and Jayson Musson created a major new commission for ICA in 2014.

Nearly two and a half hours in length, this in-the-round video installation was scripted by Jayson Musson, directed by Alex Da Corte, and with a score by composer Devonté Hynes. Easternsports is amorality tale for the digital age. Both deadly serious and heartbreakingly flippant, it embraces Gap commercials and grand jury rulings, middle-class aspirations and global imperialism. And it transforms a decade-long conversation between Musson and Da Corte into a work awash in the neon glow of their American milieu. This expansive catalogue includes an essay by ICA curator Kate Kraczon.

title: Two Perspectives on Tokyo
description:
Two Perspectives on Tokyo pairs two photographers based in the same city into a single publication, setting Motoyuki Daifu's family-centered snapshots against Kenta Cobayashi's images of the young artists and friends sharing his Shibuya house.

Issued as a set of two 28-page zines rather than a single bound book, the project captures fragments of Tokyo as each photographer encountered it in 2015: Daifu's practice has centered on staged, cluttered scenes of his own family and girlfriend, while Cobayashi documents the loose, communal life of his share-house circle in blog and zine form. Newfave published the set in 2016 in an edition of 100.

The pairing places two distinct strands of contemporary Japanese snapshot photography side by side: Daifu's domestic maximalism and Cobayashi's more glitch- and collage-inflected documentary style, both artists working in the self-published, small-run tradition that has defined much of the Tokyo photobook scene since the 2000s.
notes: Catalogue record combined the two photographers' names into a single garbled author field ('Daifu Cobayashi, Kenta' / 'Motoyuki'); corrected here to two separate authors, Motoyuki Daifu and Kenta Cobayashi. Issued as a set of two zines rather than one bound book; no ISBN. Sold out at time of research. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Night and Day
description:
First Edition of 1000, Signed. Night & Day brings together a selection of iconic Kodachrome pictures from David Armstrong's archive of the late 70's and early 80's New York scene.

The images illuminate an intimate and carefree epoch of innocent-bohemian wilderness -a time just before the tumultuos 80's. Dispersed through out the series are images of generation of youngsters which changed culture - including Rene Ricard, Philip-Lorca diCorcia, Jean-Michel Basquait, John Waters to mention a few.

Vernacular yet with a undeniable ability to capture and create timeless images, David Armstrong's Night & Day tells tales of a bygone era. The book contains 110 images, including a facsimile of an original poem typed out in 1979 by Rene Ricard. We also tracked down Rene to design the cover of the book and have a conversation between David Armstrong and Jack Pierson!

title: May the Circle Remain Unbroken
contributors: Charlotte Cotton (Essay), Glenn O'Brien (Text), Pablo Ferro (Cover typography)
description:
May the Circle Remain Unbroken gathers previously unpublished early photographs by Corinne Day, whose unflinching, snapshot-style documentation of friends, lovers, and youth culture reshaped fashion photography in the 1990s, including her controversial 1993 Vogue images of a teenage Kate Moss.

Collated by her husband Mark Szaszy after Day's death in 2010, the book presents personal, unguarded pictures of friends dressing up, lounging in worn-down flats, and swimming in lakes, images that blur the line between documentary and staged photography and capture the post-rave counterculture Day moved through before her fashion career. Published as a cloth-bound hardcover in a limited edition of 1000, with essays by Charlotte Cotton and Glenn O'Brien and cover typography by Pablo Ferro, it accompanied an exhibition of the same title at Gimpel Fils Gallery, London.

Day (1962-2010) became known for pioneering so-called grunge fashion photography before a period of exile from mainstream fashion media, later returning to acclaim with work collected and exhibited internationally. This was her first book published after her death, revisiting the personal, unpolished images that first defined her eye.
notes: Posthumous publication collated by the artist's husband, Mark Szaszy; limited edition of 1000 copies with a contact sheet laid in. Accompanied the 2013 exhibition of the same title at Gimpel Fils Gallery, London. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Accidental Fold
description:
The Accidental Fold is Saskia de Brauw's debut artist book, a diaristic record of small discarded things she picked up and scanned over roughly six years on the road.

Working with a handheld scanner she carried between fashion shoots and travels, de Brauw assembled images of a playing card found in Cambodia, a broken sandal seen in Marrakech, a rusty nail from Marfa, Texas, and threads swept from a Chanel fitting-room floor, objects she calls "evidence of presence." The book was designed in close collaboration with art director Erik Haberfeld, French-bound with a visible glued spine, and issued in January 2016 as a first edition of 500 softcover copies housed in a recycled-cardboard slipcase with a folded, poster-format dust jacket.

De Brauw studied fine art at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie in Amsterdam before becoming known internationally as a fashion model, and has continued to move between the two practices throughout her career. The Accidental Fold marks her return to an object-based collecting practice rooted in her training as an artist, and was followed in 2018 by a second book, Ghosts Don't Walk in Straight Lines.
notes: Catalogue listed no first name; confirmed as Saskia de Brauw. Self-published first edition of 500 copies, Amsterdam, January 2016; softcover in a recycled-cardboard slipcase with folded poster dust jacket, designed with Erik Haberfeld. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: A Way of Living: The Art of Willem de Kooning
binding: Oversized oblong hardcover in slipcase with bright blue cloth boards
edition_printrun: First edition and first printing. Heavy oversized book
description:
Willem de Kooning was a leading exponent of Abstract Expressionism.

This is the most wide-ranging and comprehensive monograph available on this artist. Sumptuously illustrated and produced, the book encompasses his major works and periods, including his controversial 'Woman' paintings, as well as a wealth of accompanying sketches and preparatory drawings. An illustrated chronology maps de Kooning's life, career, and work, with photographs from the artist's archive interspersed throughout the book, enriching the reader's understanding of the wider art-historical context of his paintings.

Judith Zilczer's critically acclaimed monograph is an essential addition to the libraries of a new audience of readers and de Kooning enthusiasts, offering an unprecedented and compelling examination of his body of work. The book features a comprehensive, richly illustrated exploration of de Kooning's influential paintings, sketches, and career, with an analysis of his major works and periods.

title: I Loved My Wife (Killing Children Is Good for the Economy)
binding: Softcover with 24-page booklet in a two-pocket folder
edition_printrun: Every copy hand-finished by the artist with a red cross stamped on the cover
contributors: Joachim Naudts (Essay), Erik Thys (Essay), Herwig Czech (Essay)
description:
I Loved My Wife (Killing Children Is Good for the Economy) confronts a largely unexamined chapter of the Holocaust: the Nazi program that murdered tens of thousands of children in Austrian psychiatric institutions between 1939 and 1941, framed by the regime as mercy killing.

De Lathauwer traveled to sixteen former care centers and psychiatric institutions across Austria, combining his own in-situ photographs with stills from Nazi propaganda films on euthanasia, digital collage, and images of historical objects. The book is a 112-page softcover with a separate 24-page booklet in a two-pocket folder; every copy is finished by hand, with the artist stamping a red cross on the cover, the mark once used to designate patients for elimination. Its title is drawn from a line spoken by a man in Nazi propaganda footage, boasting of having sacrificed his wife for the fatherland.

De Lathauwer is a Belgian photographer whose work investigates suppressed histories through archival research and in-situ documentation. I Loved My Wife won the Unseen Dummy Award in 2016 and was longlisted for the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2018.
notes: Every copy is hand-finished by the artist with a stamped red cross on the cover, referencing the mark historically used to designate patients for elimination. Winner, Unseen Dummy Award 2016; longlisted, Deutsche Börse Photography Prize 2018. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: This is What Hatred Did
description:
This Is What Hatred Did is Cristina de Middel's staged photographic response to Amos Tutuola's 1954 novel My Life in the Bush of Ghosts, restaging its hallucinatory vision of Lagos as a threshold between the living and the spirit world.

Working with Nigerian sign painters, wrestlers, market traders and studio photographers, de Middel built tableaux that borrow the visual language of hand-painted film posters and Nollywood melodrama to picture Tutuola's ghosts, monsters and shape-shifting bush spirits. The resulting images sit deliberately between document and invention, refusing to resolve into either straight reportage or pure fiction. The book was published as a 180-page hardcover by RM in 2015, sequencing the photographs without captions so the narrative unfolds the way Tutuola's own prose does, digressively and without apology to Western logic.

De Middel came to international attention with The Afronauts (2012), her staged retelling of Zambia's 1964 amateur space program, and has continued to build a body of work that treats myth, propaganda and collective belief as material for photography rather than obstacles to it. This Is What Hatred Did extends that method to West African literature and popular image-making.
tags: Photography, Contemporary Art, Staged Photography, West African Photography
notes: Inspired by Amos Tutuola's 1954 novel My Life in the Bush of Ghosts; shot on location in Lagos, Nigeria. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Vanity of Certain Flowers Part Two
description:
The Vanity of Certain Flowers Part Two continues a project Peter De Potter began in an earlier volume, working across still life, fashion photography and collaged found imagery.

As with the first part, the book builds meaning through juxtaposition rather than narrative, setting flowers and other still-life motifs against fragments of fashion and popular imagery to worry at ideas of beauty, artifice and decay. It was published by the Amsterdam gallery and bookshop MENDO, which has produced several of De Potter's artist books and shown his collage work.

De Potter is a Belgian artist and graphic designer whose practice moves between collage, photography and self-published books, frequently reworking fashion and advertising imagery into new, often unsettling compositions. Full bibliographic detail for this title (year, pagination, format) could not be independently confirmed this session and should be checked against the copy.
notes: Second part of a two-volume artist book; bibliographic detail (year, pagination, dimensions) unconfirmed this session. Cover to be photographed. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Complete Papers
description: Texts by Jeffrey Eugenides, Neville Wakefield, Julia Franck, Russell Ferguson, Adrian Searle, Francesco Bonami, inter alia. The Complete Papers is an extensive volume encompassing all of Thomas Demand’s work over the past 28 years, together with the primary texts written about his practice. The book includes previously unseen early works from 1990, together with reference reproductions on every one of his pieces.

title: Los Angeles Standards
description:
Los Angeles Standards is a photographic portrait of Los Angeles that presents the city through 15 ordinary typologies characteristic of its urban fabric.

1300 photographs taken between 2008 and 2012 by Caroline and Cyril Desroche, French architects who came to live and work in Los Angeles, are presented like a documentary. Organized in chapters, they make it possible to establish comparisons, analogies and correspondences between archetypes such as freeways, car parks, streets, construction sites, billboards, mini-malls, homes.

Each of these images is referenced by its address. As Los Angeles is embarking on a process of greatly increasing its existing density and transforming its infrastructure, this book is a visual testimony of its current state, its contemporary form and its urban history.

title: Los Angeles Standards
description:
Los Angeles Standards is a photographic portrait of Los Angeles which offers a way to view the city through 15 typologies which identify this unique city environment.

The 1300 photographs were taken between 2008 and 2012 by French architects Caroline and Cyril Desroche during the years they live in Los Angeles. They are organized in order to compare and contrast the design archetypes that they have identified, including Mini-Malls, Billboards, Freeways, Parking Lots and Stilt Houses. Each picture is accompanied by its address for research and travel.

title: Take a Swing on the Thread of Life
description:
Take a Swing on the Thread of Life gathers the Polish artist Jan Dobkowski's largest single body of drawing, a set of 383 works in pencil made over ten years and united by an obsessive, symmetrical figuration.

Each drawing is worked on handmade paper at a uniform 36 by 47 cm, the figures built from mirrored, sagittal repetitions that let one body part stand in for another: a toe or a tongue swells into a bulb recalling a glans, an ear coils into a double, information-spewing form. The book was published by Kodoji Press in a softcover edition of 400 to accompany the premiere exhibition, and includes an essay by the critic Janusz Zagrodzki, who reads the work as a record of inner transmutation from analysis to synthesis, a contemplation in which the sacred and the erotic stay bound together.

Dobkowski (b. 1942) emerged in the Polish neo-avant-garde of the 1960s and has worked across painting, drawing, and object-based art since, consistently returning to the body as a site where biomorphic invention and pointed eroticism meet. Take a Swing on the Thread of Life represents the fullest late statement of that preoccupation, distilled into a single obsessively repeated cast of figures.
notes: Accompanies the 2014 exhibition of the same title at Galeria Bielska BWA, Bielsko-Biała, with an essay by Janusz Zagrodzki. Edition of 400 softcover copies. Page count and physical dimensions were not given by any source checked; edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Go West Young Man
description:
Go West Young Man is the catalogue for Peter Doig's 2006 exhibition at the Museum der bildenden Künste Leipzig, surveying the Scottish-born painter's dreamlike, densely worked landscapes and isolated figures.

Published by Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König to accompany the Leipzig show, the bilingual German/English paperback reproduces paintings exhibited at the museum alongside essays by curator Hans-Werner Schmidt and critic Rudolf Fuchs, tracing Doig's recurring motifs of canoes, snow, and lone figures set against thickly built-up, luminous grounds.

Doig (b. 1959) trained in London and spent two decades living in Trinidad, developing a signature technique of translucent, layered paint that recasts memory and found photographic imagery as hallucinatory scenes. By 2006 he was among the most acclaimed painters of his generation, and this exhibition placed his work within a German institutional context alongside his ongoing gallery presentations in London and New York.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Exhibition catalogue for Peter Doig's show at Museum der bildenden Künste Leipzig, 17 September-26 November 2006; bilingual German/English text with essays by Hans-Werner Schmidt and Rudolf Fuchs. A 2007 English-language paperback printing shares the same ISBN and page count is recorded as 67 or 68 pages depending on the printing. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Blizzard Seventy-Seven
contributors: Terry R. Myers (Essay), Hans-Werner Schmidt (Essay), Felicity Lunn (Essay)
description:
Blizzard Seventy-Seven is the catalogue for Peter Doig's first major European survey, gathering the image-saturated landscape paintings that established his reputation over the previous decade.

Published by Kerber Verlag to accompany a 1998 touring exhibition at Kunsthalle zu Kiel, Kunsthalle Nürnberg, the Whitechapel Art Gallery in London and Contemporary Fine Arts in Berlin, the book reproduces the paintings alongside bilingual German and English texts by Terry R. Myers, Hans-Werner Schmidt and Felicity Lunn. Its title is drawn from Blizzard, Seventy-Seven, one of the included canvases, in which a city skyline dissolves behind a static-like scatter of white paint.

Doig (born 1959, Edinburgh, raised in Trinidad and Canada) had by the late 1990s become known for reworking found photographs and film stills into thickly worked, half-remembered landscapes, many drawn from the Canadian housing developments of his childhood. This catalogue documents him just before the wider international attention that followed, and remains an early record of the body of work that built his critical and market standing.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Bilingual German/English catalogue for a 1998 touring exhibition. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Dead Children Playing
description:
Dead Children Playing collects a body of paintings and prints Stanley Donwood made between 2003 and 2006, appropriating the flat lettering of British road signage and the blunt language of wartime propaganda to answer the rhetoric of the war on terror.

Black grounds are stencilled over with slogans and warnings lifted from official signage and government messaging, arranged like a city of hoardings gone wrong. The title itself is cut from a British road sign reading "dead slow, children playing," trimmed down to something closer to a headline. The book was published by Verso in 2007 as an 80-page hardcover, and several of the works were made jointly with Dr. Tchock, a pseudonym under which Donwood and Radiohead's Thom Yorke have collaborated since the late 1990s.

Donwood has been Radiohead's resident visual artist since The Bends in 1995, producing the artwork for every album through Hail to the Thief and beyond, work that draws on the same vocabulary of warning signs, maps and official typography assembled here. His practice moves between painting, printmaking, album design and land art, and this book presents that protest imagery as a standalone artist's publication rather than as sleeve art.
tags: Art, Illustration, Graphic Design, Political Art
notes: Catalogued as "Stanley Doonwood"; corrected to Donwood. Several works co-credited to Dr. Tchock, a pseudonym of Radiohead's Thom Yorke. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: End.
description:
End. completes the trilogy of self-published books Eamonn Doyle made about Dublin's inner city, following i (2014) and On (2015).

Working around the same stretch of O'Connell Street that runs through the earlier volumes, Doyle photographs its everyday crowds, in cropped, high-contrast frames that pull figures out of the flow of the street and turn them into something closer to portrait or apparition. As with the previous two books, the design (by Niall Sweeney's studio Design Action) and sequencing favour repetition and rhythm over documentary narrative. Exact pagination and format for the copy on this shelf could not be independently confirmed this session.

Doyle (born 1969, Dublin) worked for years as a DJ and record label owner before turning to photography, and the trilogy's episodic, almost musical structure carries some of that background. The three books were later brought together and re-edited as the exhibition and book Made in Dublin.
notes: Third book in Doyle's self-published Dublin trilogy (i, On, End.). Self-published titles in this series were not issued with a standard ISBN; exact pagination/dimensions unconfirmed this session. Cover to be photographed. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: i
description:
i is Eamonn Doyle's self-published debut photobook, a document of elderly residents photographed from above on the streets around Dublin's Parnell Street and Moore Street, and the book that reintroduced street photography as a serious contemporary form for a new generation.

Shot low-angle and often looming over its subjects, inspired in part by the rhythms of Samuel Beckett's prose, the photographs isolate figures against Dublin's pavement and shopfronts, turning ordinary passers-by into monumental, almost sculptural presences. Doyle self-published the book in Dublin in 2014 in an edition of 750 copies; it is the first of a trilogy completed by ON (2015) and End (2016), and it won the Author Book Award at Rencontres d'Arles and a Kraszna-Krausz Book Award.

Doyle, born in Dublin in 1969, spent fifteen years running the D1 Recordings label before returning to photography in 2008 and turning his camera on the same north inner-city streets he grew up around. Martin Parr called i the best street photobook in a decade, and the trilogy's success led to a later career survey, Eamonn Doyle (RM Verlag/Fundación MAPFRE, 2020), and the compilation Made in Dublin (Thames & Hudson).
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Portraiture, Irish Photography
notes: First of the self-published Doyle trilogy (i, ON, End); no ISBN found for the original 2014 self-published edition of 750 copies. A later boxed compilation was issued as Made in Dublin (Thames & Hudson) and a career survey as Eamonn Doyle (RM Verlag/Fundación MAPFRE, 2020). No usable cover image could be located through publisher or distributor channels; cover to be photographed. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Unknown #2: Tentative d'épuisement d'un livre
edition_printrun: Standard edition; a 16-copy numbered deluxe edition included a signed original print
description:
Unknown #2: Tentative d'épuisement d'un livre is Stéphane Duroy's account of a single book he could not stop remaking, turning a discontinued edition of his own photography into an open-ended material process.

In 2007 Filigranes published Duroy's Unknown, photographs from his trips across the United States. A printing flaw left him with roughly a hundred unsellable copies, and in 2009 he began working back into them with collage, press cuttings, anonymous photographs and abstract painting, tearing and rebuilding the original pages. Between 2009 and 2017 this produced twenty-eight distinct book-objects. Unknown #2, a 64-page bilingual leporello with 63 color photographs, gathers this reworking and was co-produced with Le Bal for the exhibition Again and Again, shown at Le Bal and the Espace Photographique Leica in Paris in early 2017.

Duroy began as a press photographer for the Sipa agency before turning to long-term documentary projects on Thatcher-era England, divided Berlin and its aftermath, and the United States, work recognized with a World Press Photo award. Unknown #2 marks a turn from documentary photography toward the book itself as a site of ongoing revision.
notes: Catalogued author name corrected from "Duray" to "Duroy." Owner's copy noted as signed; a 16-copy deluxe edition included a numbered, signed original print (18 × 24 cm) alongside the standard trade copies. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Moments of Vision: The Stroboscopic Revolution in Photography
The Democratic Forest
edition_printrun: Ten clothbound volumes in a slipcase.
description:
The Democratic Forest runs to ten volumes and more than a thousand photographs. It is the fullest account of the work William Eggleston made in the 1980s, cut from a body of some twelve thousand pictures that had gone almost entirely unpublished.

The first volume stays in Louisiana. The rest follow Eggleston out from Memphis and Tennessee to Dallas, Pittsburgh, Miami and Boston. They reach the pastures of Kentucky and, at the far edge, the Berlin Wall. The last volume turns back south, to small towns and cotton fields, the battlefield at Shiloh, and Andrew Jackson's house in Tennessee. The democratic of the title means a democracy of vision, in which a freezer door gets the same attention as a monument. Mark Holborn and Eggleston spent over three years on the edit. Steidl published the set on 24 November 2015: ten clothbound volumes, 1,328 pages, in a dark blue slipcase. Holborn contributes a new introduction, and Eudora Welty's essay from the 1989 edition is reprinted.

That 1989 Doubleday volume ran to fewer than two hundred pages. It stood for the whole project for twenty-five years. Steidl's set is the third and largest part of its reassessment of Eggleston's archive, after Chromes (2011) and Los Alamos Revisited (2012). A one-volume selection drawn from it followed as The Democratic Forest: Selected Works.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Monograph, Color Photography, American South, Box Set
notes: Signed by the photographer. Ten volumes in a slipcase. Edited by Mark Holborn and William Eggleston, with an introduction by Holborn and Eudora Welty's essay reprinted from the 1989 Doubleday edition (ISBN 9780385266512). Not to be confused with the one-volume selection, The Democratic Forest: Selected Works, catalogued separately.

title: Los Alamos Revisited
edition_printrun: Three clothbound volumes in a linen slipcase.
description:
Los Alamos Revisited is the complete edit of the pictures William Eggleston made on the road with Walter Hopps between 1965 and 1974, and it replaces the single Scalo volume of 2003 that showed only part of them.

Eggleston photographed while Hopps drove, working out from Memphis through the South and west across Texas into New Mexico, where the town of Los Alamos gave the series its name. The two men later edited the pictures into five portfolio boxes of dye-transfer prints, but the negatives ended up divided between them, with roughly half staying in Hopps' hands. What came back to the Eggleston Artistic Trust in Memphis was catalogued as Box #17. A second box turned up after Hopps died in 2005 and was catalogued as Box #83. William Eggleston III and Mark Holborn worked through the reunited negatives in 2011 and settled the sequence with Winston Eggleston at Steidl the following year. Steidl published it in September 2012 as three clothbound volumes in a linen slipcase, 12.5 inches square.

Eggleston began shooting colour negative film in Memphis in 1964 and moved to dye-transfer printing in the early 1970s. The 1976 exhibition John Szarkowski gave him at the Museum of Modern Art is the usual marker for colour being taken seriously in the medium. Los Alamos Revisited is the middle part of Steidl's reassessment of his archive, between Chromes (2011) and the ten-volume The Democratic Forest (2015).
tags: Photography, Photobook, Monograph, Color Photography, American South, Box Set
notes: Signed by the photographer. Three volumes in a linen slipcase. D.A.P. gives the extent as 432 pages; some reviewers count 588 across the three volumes. Supersedes the 2003 Scalo edition of Los Alamos (ISBN 9783908247692), which carried only part of the series. The record previously read "Los Altos" and named Gagosian Gallery as publisher; corrected 2026-09-05 on the collector's identification of the shelf copy.

title: From Black and White to Color
Olafur Eliasson: Reality Machines
contributors: Daniel Birnbaum (Contribution), Timothy Morton (Essay), Matilda Olof-Ors (Essay)
description:
Olafur Eliasson: Reality Machines documents a three-decade practice built on the conviction that art can turn thinking into doing, tracing sculpture, photography, film, and installation shaped by a deep interest in perception, movement, and embodied experience.

Published by Koenig Books and Moderna Museet to accompany the exhibition Verklighetsmaskiner / Reality Machines in Stockholm, the book was conceived and designed by Irma Boom as an artist's book in its own right, with essays interacting with tactile papers and transparent films rather than a conventional plate-and-text layout. It includes writing by philosopher Timothy Morton and curator Matilda Olof-Ors, a conversation between Eliasson and Moderna Museet director Daniel Birnbaum, and Anders Sune Berg's installation photography of the exhibition.

Eliasson (b. 1967) works from a large Berlin studio with architects, engineers, and designers, extending his practice beyond the museum into architectural and civic projects worldwide. This volume situates the Stockholm exhibition within that broader trajectory, from early works like Beauty (1993) through the large-scale environmental and perceptual installations for which he later became known.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Sculpture, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Exhibition catalogue for Verklighetsmaskiner / Reality Machines at Moderna Museet, Stockholm; designed by graphic designer Irma Boom as an artist's book with mylar and tactile paper elements. Listed as out of print by its distributor. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Revoir
edition_printrun: cloth binding, 174 b/w and color images
description:
“In 2004, I made the book Trying to Dance, designed by Patric Leo and published by Journal.

Since then, it has lived a life of its own, just as books should do. For me, Trying to Dance is more than a book – the photographs on which it was based constitute an image universe of its own. Photography then had a liberating effect on me as a visual artist. I lived mostly in New York, but also in Värmland, Sweden, and travelled a lot in the United States and Europe. Mentally, I was in between worlds, between realities, between the urban and the rural. This was also a period when I questioned and doubted the importance and relevance of photography for me – actually. The freedom I so strongly experienced in the process of making Trying to Dance, largely answered my doubts and became a compass for my continued creativity. To start with, I was not at all certain when Gösta Flemming at Journal, Patric Leo and Christian Caujolle, suggested going back to the Trying to Dance negatives.

But when I started looking through the files – so many images, so many that were not used in Trying to Dance, and so many new combinations that hit me it was then that I decided that we should publish Revoir. Revoir is a completely new book, a revision, a revisit to that period between the mid-90s and the early 2000s. The book has been made in close and enjoyable collaboration with all the people that I worked with on Trying to Dance. Around two thirds of the photographs have not been published before. For the first time I have scanned the negatives, together with Ewa-Teréz Gölin, and allowed the present to guide me in the printing for Revoir. Christian Caujolle has written a text for the book. This makes me especially happy, since he was the first to whole-heartedly embrace and recognise the photographs then, almost 17 years ago.” / JH Engström

title: Ende und Anfang (Early Trips)
description: I took these photographs before the turn of the century while travelling across Europe and the United States. My eye was good-hearted. The time that has passed since then is, at least, something we all have in common. As the time I was astonished. I still am. /JH

title: Mitch Epstein State of the Union
Roe Ethridge and Zin Taylor: The Ceremony and the Spirit
Throughout the Universe in Perpetuity
