title: Hamburger Eyes -The continuing Story of Life on Earth
Boardwalk
description:
Max Farago's self-published Boardwalk is an unruly document of a decade spent photographing the far West Coast of America, taking the temperature of a culture running on plastic, impulse, and image-saturation.

The book moves through surfers, addicts, fluid sexuality, take-out food, corporations, and roadside coincidence, assembling a loose, diaristic portrait of California as the internet accelerated the careless spread of images. Published in Los Angeles in 2017 as a spiral-bound softcover of 174 pages, it was released in a signed edition of 200 copies and debuted at Dashwood Books in New York before touring to the Yvon Lambert Bookshop and Claire de Rouen Books in Paris.

Farago works across fashion and editorial photography, and Boardwalk compiles roughly ten years of personal, off-assignment images shot along the coast. The book sits among a current of diaristic, vernacular American photobooks that treat the beach and its fringe characters as a barometer for national mood.
notes: Self-published, signed edition of 200 copies, spiral-bound softcover. No ISBN was issued for this limited self-published title. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Harun Farocki: Diagrams Images from Ten Films
Wolfgang
description:
Using photographs drawn from the archives of the CERN laboratory, David Fathi builds Wolfgang around a piece of scientific folklore: the "Pauli Effect," the belief that physicist Wolfgang Pauli caused unexplainable equipment failures simply by entering a room.

The book gathers accidents, malfunctions and unexplained anomalies from the CERN archive; some images are left untouched, others manipulated by the artist, so that art, science and history run together and the reader is left to sort myth from record. Skinnerboox published the 164-page hardcover in an edition of 500 in September 2016, designed by Ramon Pez with text by Jeffrey Ladd. It was named a best photobook of the year by The Guardian, LensCulture and several photobook critics.

Fathi, a French artist working with appropriated and archival photography, treats found imagery as raw material for invented histories rather than documentary evidence. A second, reworked edition, Wolfgang², followed in 2018.
notes: Standard hardcover first edition (September 2016, edition of 500), not the 2018 second edition Wolfgang². Named a best book of 2016 by The Guardian, LensCulture, Erik Kessels and others. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Louis Faurer
contributors: Agnès Sire (Introduction), Walter Hopps (Text), Susan Kismaric (Text)
description:
Louis Faurer is the first monograph in fifteen years devoted to a photographer whose darkly romantic pictures of 1940s and '50s New York have long been overshadowed by the better-known work of his contemporaries.

Working first for fashion magazines like Harper's Bazaar before turning his camera on Times Square and the streets around it, Faurer built an empathetic, ironic body of street photography full of graphic contrasts, reflections and distortions borrowed from film noir. The book gathers roughly one hundred plates across 208 pages in a green linen hardcover with a tipped-in portrait on the cover, published by Steidl with the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson, Paris, in 2016, with an introduction by Agnès Sire and texts by Walter Hopps and Susan Kismaric.

Faurer (1916–2001) worked alongside Robert Frank in New York in the early 1950s and drew on Walker Evans before him, developing a sensibility for marginal figures and emotional ambiguity that Walter Hopps recognized as the work of, in his words, a master of the medium. Long under-recognized relative to Frank and Evans, Faurer's reputation has grown steadily through retrospectives like this one.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Portraiture, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Published in association with the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson, Paris; the first major Faurer monograph in fifteen years. Currently out of print at Steidl (listed as "Vergriffen"). Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Rachel Feinstein
contributors: Kelly Taxter (Introduction), Marc Jacobs (Contribution), Lisa Yuskavage (Contribution), Florence Welch (Contribution)
description:
Rachel Feinstein is the first full-scale monograph on the American sculptor and installation artist, tracing two decades of work that fuses baroque ornament, Americana, and pop imagery into a singular vision of kitsch and elegance.

Published by Rizzoli Electa in 2019, the 240-page hardcover surveys Feinstein's sculpture, painting, pastel, and drawing practice, illustrating recurring subjects — carnival architecture, biblical and mythological women, dollhouses, and stage sets — realized in mirror, wood, plaster, and metal. An introduction by curator Kelly Taxter is joined by contributions from Marc Jacobs, Lisa Yuskavage, Florence Welch, Sofia Coppola, and other figures from art, fashion, and film who have collaborated with or been influenced by Feinstein's work.

Feinstein (b. 1971) emerged from New York's 1990s downtown art scene, developing a practice that moves fluidly between fine art and the worlds of fashion and design, including a long-running collaboration with Marc Jacobs on window and runway installations. This volume positions her as one of the defining sculptors of contemporary American kitsch, following her evolution from early carved-wood tableaux to the large-scale mirrored sculptures for which she is best known.
notes: Catalogued title 'R/Electa' is a garbled fragment of the book's actual title, 'Rachel Feinstein', and its publisher, Rizzoli/Electa. Author name corrected from 'Rachael' to 'Rachel' to match the artist's published name. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Album
description:
Album is Hans-Peter Feldmann's wordless survey of the personal image archive he assembled over decades, presenting roughly 3,000 photographs in sequence with no text beyond the title page.

Published by Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König as a cloth-bound hardcover, the book opens with a photograph of Feldmann's own archive boxes, accumulated from magazines, advertising, photography books, postcards, and curios, then interleaves these found images with his travel photographs, family snapshots, and pictures of friends. The sequencing itself becomes the artist's gesture, building narrative and rhythm from juxtaposition alone.

Feldmann (1941-2023) built a body of work around collecting, archiving, and re-presenting ordinary photographs, arguing that images should be cheap and easy to produce rather than precious or unique. Album extends the interests of earlier projects like Voyeur and his postcard collections. He is one of the key figures to treat the found photograph as raw material for art.
notes: Wordless artist's book of roughly 3,000 found and personal images from Feldmann's archive; no essay or text beyond the title page. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Frauen
description:
with tipped in images on front and back cover, b/w and color illustrated throughout.

“80 per cent of artists are dealing with mother issues.” In this personal interview the internationally praised German artist Hans-Peter Feldmann muses on the magnetic power of women, and shares how he has used art as both escape and therapy. Images of women attract Feldmann, who claims that the majority of artists are dealing with mother issues: “It’s always about women, about mothers, images of women.” As an example, he points out how public toilets for men are similar to ancient caves with their many drawings of vulvas.

The repetitive function of collecting pictures is therapeutic to Feldmann, and makes things clear and tangible for him. Many artists use their art as a form of therapy, “as a flight to another world someone from the old world can’t access.” As for Feldmann, who too had mother-issues and grew up during the war and the post-war years, this was also the case: “… the images opened a world to me that was very, very lovely.”

title: Buch/Book No. 9
contributors: Inka Schube (Essay), Martin Clark (Essay), Martin Hochleitner (Essay)
description:
Buch/Book No. 9 is the ninth in Hans-Peter Feldmann's numbered book series, a survey that treats the artist's collections of found and made photographs as a body of work in their own right.

Published by Walther König in a bilingual German/English hardcover of 208 pages to accompany exhibitions at the Sprengel Museum in Hannover, the Landesgalerie in Linz and the Arnolfini in Bristol, the book moves without captions or hierarchy between anonymous snapshots, studio still lifes, appropriated pictures and Feldmann's own photographs, with essays by Inka Schube, Martin Clark and Martin Hochleitner.

Feldmann (1941-2023, Düsseldorf) spent five decades collecting, arranging and re-photographing ordinary images to strip them of their original context, treating curation itself as an artistic method. The numbered Buch/Book series, of which this is the ninth volume, remains one of the clearest statements of that practice, sitting alongside his better-known postcard and toy-collection projects.
tags: Art, Photography, Conceptual Art, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Ninth volume in Feldmann's numbered Buch/Book series; the catalogue title on this row ("Book\\Buch #9") is standardized here to the publisher's own "Buch/Book No. 9". Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Milky Way
description:
Milky Way follows the French photographer Vincent Ferrané's wife and newborn child through six months of breastfeeding, an act he found himself struck by after the birth of his first child and set out to document without concealment or gloss.

The 62 colour plates were shot with a single small camera chosen for its embedded flash and clean definition, so the images could sit as comfortably in an intimate book as printed large. Ferrané frames the project against the Greek myth in which the galaxy was formed from the milk of the goddess Hera, reading the everyday choreography of feeding as its own kind of world-building; the geometry the act imposes on two bodies recurs picture to picture, echoing older icons of nursing motherhood without tidying up the moment. Libraryman published the book as a clothbound hardcover in 2017, in a first edition of 500 with a smaller signed special edition in a screen-printed slipcase.

Ferrané (b. 1974) works across fashion and personal documentary photography; Milky Way, made from material closest to home, was followed by Visitor (2018), a series of portraits of women artists in their studios, also published by Libraryman.
notes: First edition of 500; a special edition of 25 copies plus 6 artist's proofs, numbered and housed in a screen-printed slipcase with a signed print, was issued alongside it. Both printings are now out of print. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Tribeca 9/11/01–9/11/11
description:
This is a self-produced photographic record Donna Ferrato made of Tribeca in the decade following September 11, framed by the title itself: 9/11/01 to 9/11/11.

Ferrato lived and worked in Tribeca, the Lower Manhattan neighborhood a few blocks from the World Trade Center site, and turned her camera on its recovery over the years that followed. Beyond the title's date span and a printer credit (Grafiche dell'Artiere, Italy), no formal publisher, ISBN, or print run has been located for this volume. It appears to have been produced independently rather than through a trade publisher, which matches how little record of it exists outside dealer listings.

Ferrato is best known for Living with the Enemy, her record of domestic violence made over more than a decade inside the households she photographed. This Tribeca record extends that same method, sustained, personal, neighborhood-level observation, to her own corner of New York.
notes: No ISBN or trade publisher identified; printer credit only (Grafiche dell'Artiere, Italy). Publication year (2011) inferred from the title's date span; confirm against the physical copy.

title: The Beat Poets By Larry Fink
Paintings: 1998–2011, 2012–2015, 2016–2017
binding: Paperback, 3 volumes housed in a slipcase
editor: Priya Bhatnagar, Jaime Gecker, Abby Haywood, Angela Kunicky, Annie Roft, Natalie Skinner
description:
Paintings is the first retrospective publication devoted solely to Urs Fischer's work on canvas, gathering two decades of output that runs from photographic collage to trompe-l'oeil illusion.

Issued as three paperback volumes covering 1998–2011, 2012–2015 and 2016–2017 and housed together in a slipcase, the set reproduces every painting Fischer made through 2017, prints many works to scale relative to one another, and includes select details printed 1:1. Published by Kiito-San in 2019, the 572-page set includes over six hundred color plates and early collage works that had not been exhibited in years.

Fischer (born 1973, Zurich) is best known for large sculptural and installation gestures — wax effigies that burn down over an exhibition's run, cast bronze fruit and vegetables, holes punched through gallery floors — and his paintings extend the same interest in illusion and appropriated imagery, often built from photographs, historical artworks and studio detritus layered digitally before being printed onto canvas.
notes: Housed in a slipcase as three paperback volumes spanning 1998–2011, 2012–2015 and 2016–2017 — the shelf record's annotation "(3 books)" refers to this set. Described by the publisher as the first retrospective devoted solely to Fischer's paintings. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Flowers and Mushrooms
edition_printrun: Original edition, 1999 (the collection also holds the 2016 Walther König reprint as a separate record).
description:
Flowers & Mushrooms is a hallucinatory double-exposure portfolio by the Swiss artist duo Peter Fischli and David Weiss, bursting with saturated color that navigates the fine line between beauty and kitsch.

Working between 1997 and 1998, Fischli and Weiss spent countless hours photographing gardens and mushroom patches, layering the images into superimposed double exposures that dissolve petals, stamens, berries, weeds, and fungi into vivid fields of color. The photographs first appeared as an artist's book published for the pair's 1999 exhibition at the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris; this edition reprints that 160-page softcover in full, with 40 color plates printed on folded, unbound sheets.

Fischli (b. 1952) and Weiss (1946–2012) worked together from 1979 until Weiss's death, building a body of work — from the film The Way Things Go to their rubber and polyurethane sculptures — on a deadpan slippage between the mundane and the absurd. Flowers & Mushrooms extends that sensibility to still-life photography, treating two of art history's most conventional subjects with a strain of hallucination distinct from either.
notes: This copy is catalogued as the original 1999 edition, published for the Fischli & Weiss exhibition at the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris. No bibliographic record for that printing could be confirmed; the ISBN, extent and cover held in the collection's other record belong to Walther König's 2016 reprint. Edition to be verified against the copy. Cover to be photographed. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: 800 Views of Airports
description:
800 Views of Airports documents a lengthy series of work by Peter Fischli (born 1952) and David Weiss (1946-2012), comprising 1,010 photographs to date, all of which appear here complete for the first time.

For this ongoing documentary project, the artistic duo photograph the airports they passed through in their travels around the world over nearly 25 years, in a quest for exotic banality throughout different cultures. Their images of these nondescript airports focus on the humdrum aspect of air travel: the fuel vehicles, the baggage trucks, the daily routines of airport workers, the long antiseptic corridors and sprawling tarmacs surrounded by panoramic views of empty vistas.

Whether presenting a Lufthansa airplane sitting idle in a yellowy light, a Swiss Air plane waiting in a neon-haunted dusk or an Air France plane getting its belly filled in the dead of night, Fischli and Weiss's images present the evanescence of any national identity when reduced to a symbol on a vertical stabilizer. 800 Views of Airports reveal the non-places encircling our world, and the non-journeys that have come to define our contemporary life in transit, while simultaneously offering carefully composed images that are strangely placid and restful.
tags: Conceptual Art, Travel Photography, Photography, Airports, Contemporary Art, Documentary Photography

title: Flowers and Mushrooms
description:
Flowers and Mushrooms is a reprint of an artist's book by the Swiss duo Peter Fischli and David Weiss, built from multiple superimposed photographic exposures of gardens and mushroom patches shot between 1997 and 1998.

Published by Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König, the 160-page book reproduces 40 color images beautifully printed on folded, unbound sheets, a format that mirrors the loose, layered logic of the double exposures themselves. The superimposed images of berries, grasses, flowers, weeds, and mushrooms in saturated color produce a hallucinogenic effect, with the artists navigating, as one critic put it, the line between beauty and kitsch.

Fischli (b. 1952) and Weiss (1946-2012) worked together from 1979 until Weiss's death, becoming known for deadpan, absurdist, and often technically inventive projects spanning sculpture, film, and photography, including the acclaimed film The Way Things Go. Flowers and Mushrooms belongs to their recurring interest in the natural world rendered strange, sitting alongside related bodies of work such as their touring rock sculptures and studio still lifes.
notes: 2016 reprint of Fischli/Weiss's 1999 artist's book; printed on folded, unbound sheets rather than a conventional bound format. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: PDA
description:
PDA is Todd Fisher's document of couples caught in the open, unguarded gestures of affection staged not for the camera but for each other.

Shot in New York's bars, clubs and on its sidewalks, the photographs work close and low-lit, favoring the grain and color shifts of available light over staged setups. The sequence moves through embraces, kisses and half-hidden moments, building a loose portrait of a city's nightlife through its physical intimacies rather than its faces or venues. The book was self-published through Fisher's own imprint, 0-100 Editions, in a run of 100 copies, in keeping with the small, hand-produced photobooks that defined much of the early 2010s New York independent scene.

Fisher is a New York-based photographer whose work has appeared in Dazed, Juxtapoz and IMA, and who exhibited at Signal Gallery and the New York Photo Festival in the years around PDA's release. It sits alongside his other small-press books, including Someone Cuts My Hair While I Sleep and Winter, in a body of work built from close, diaristic observation of the people around him.
notes: Self-published by the artist's own imprint, 0-100 Editions, in an edition of 100 copies; no ISBN. Pagination, format and dimensions could not be confirmed this session. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Now Here Then
description:
Now Here Then collects photographs Huger Foote made over years of travel and daily life, prints whose stains, tears and scorch marks became part of the finished work, a book about the passage of time as much as about the pictures in it.

The images were shot around the world, then archived and re-edited over several years as Foote worked back through boxes of prints, sorting and resorting them until a sequence emerged. Some prints were damaged in that process, and Foote kept the damage rather than replacing it, letting stained and scorched surfaces stand alongside the photographs. Dashwood Books published the result in 2015 as a signed hardcover edition of 1,000 copies, designed by Hans Seeger with texts by Glenn O'Brien and Susan Minot.

Foote was born in 1961 in Memphis, Tennessee, and has held solo exhibitions in London, New York, Paris and his hometown. Now Here Then is his second monograph, following My Friend from Memphis (Booth-Clibborn Editions, 2001), and extends his loose, diaristic approach to color photography across a wider span of years and places.
notes: Author corrected from the catalogue's 'Hugur Foote' to Huger Foote (misspelling). Page count and physical dimensions could not be confirmed this session. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Jonah Freeman & Justin Lowe: Black Acid Co-op / Bright White Underground / Stray Light Grey / Artichoke Underground
contributors: Glenn O'Brien (Text), Jan Tumlir (Text), Mark Flood (Text), Hamilton Morris (Text), Ali Subotnick (Interview), Gianni Jetzer (Interview), Todd Eberle (Photographs), Greg Kessler (Photographs), Joshua White (Photographs)
description:
This inaugural monograph documents the collaborative practice of Jonah Freeman and Justin Lowe, whose mazelike, fully built installations turn gallery interiors into fictional worlds assembled from found objects and invented products.

The book surveys four major works: Black Acid Co-op, Bright White Underground, Stray Light Grey and Artichoke Underground. It presents them through photographs by Todd Eberle, Greg Kessler and Joshua White alongside texts by Glenn O'Brien, Jan Tumlir, Mark Flood and Hamilton Morris and interviews with Ali Subotnick and Gianni Jetzer. Published by Glenn Horowitz Bookseller in 2015, it runs 224 pages in a clothbound edition with 232 color and 32 black and white plates, edited by Lauren Miller Walsh.

Freeman (born 1975) and Lowe (born 1976) have collaborated since 2007 on installations that read as abandoned outposts of imagined subcultures: drug labs, communes, backrooms built with the density of film sets and photographed as though documenting a real place. The book is their first sustained document of a decade spent building these immersive, narrative-driven environments.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Installation Art, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Inaugural monograph documenting the Freeman/Lowe collaborative practice since 2007, covering the immersive installations Black Acid Co-op, Bright White Underground, Stray Light Grey and Artichoke Underground. The shelf record's title fragment "GHB" could not be identified as a title, room, or edition marker for this or any other Freeman/Lowe work and is not part of the published title; retained here as an open question. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Wilder Mann: The Image of the Savage
description:
Charles Fréger's Wilder Mann catalogues one of Europe's stranger and oldest living traditions. Men dress as beasts, straw giants, and horned spirits for winter masquerades that survive in villages from Portugal to Bulgaria.

Fréger spent two winters, 2010 and 2011, traveling through nineteen European countries. He photographed around fifty of these costumed figures. Most are tied to pre-Christian solstice and Carnival rites that predate the church holidays now layered over them. He shot each figure alone, in daylight, against a plain outdoor backdrop. The method is flat and frontal. It treats a straw bear or a horned Krampus with the same deadpan attention as a passport photograph. Dewi Lewis Publishing released the book in 2012, with an accompanying text by the novelist Robert McLiam Wilson and graphic contributions from Geneviève Gauckler.

Fréger was born in France in 1975. He has built his career around long-running typological series that photograph groups defined by a shared uniform or role: sailors, wrestlers, cheerleaders. He extended the method into later projects like Yokainoshima, on Japanese festival costumes, and Cimarrón, on Latin American masquerade traditions. Wilder Mann remains the series that established that approach and his best-known body of work.

title: The Nudes: A Second Look
edition_printrun: 84 nudes. Layout and design by Katy Homans. New separations by Thomas Palmer. Expands on the 1991 Cape edition which is long out of print.
description:
Lee Friedlander's exploration of one of photography's most enduring genres began almost by chance, in the late 1970s, when a teacher colleague at Rice University in Houston lined up a regular schedule of nude models for his students.

Almost immediately, Friedlander found that he preferred to photograph the models at their homes, and ingeniously deployed household objects such as bedside lamps, potted plants and sofa fabrics to play off against the angular poses of the models and the emphatic framing of the overall composition. Friedlander's nudes show every blemish, every contour that makes each body unique, while his flash often serves to counter this realism with a softening effect that often recedes the body's shadow right up to its outline.

With the publication of Friedlander's nude portraits of Madonna (prints of which fetch huge sums), the series became among the photographer's best known work, and eventually saw publication in 1991, from Jonathan Cape. Lee Friedlander: The Nudes significantly expands on the Cape edition (itself long out of print), with a total of 84 nudes, plus a new layout and design by Katy Homans and new separations by Thomas Palmer. As such, it offers the most lavish presentation of this key series in Friedlander's massive oeuvre.
tags: Nude Photography, American Photography, Contemporary Photography

title: Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Sailor: Jim French Polaroids
description:
Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Sailor: Jim French Polaroids collects vintage Polaroid studies of the male figure made between 1964 and 1967, offering an intimate, working view of pre-Stonewall underground photography.

Published by Antinous Press in 2013 as a limited first-edition hardcover, the 144-page volume reproduces French's Polaroids of soldiers, sailors, cowboys, and other archetypally masculine figures on pictorial boards with a dust jacket, letting the images stand with no accompanying text. French made the photographs as working references for the homoerotic drawings he sold through his mail-order company, Luger and Arion, turning to the instant format because commercial photo labs of the era would not reliably process, and could report, explicitly gay imagery.

French built on this practice through the 1960s: in 1967 he bought out his business partner and, under the pseudonym Rip Colt, founded Colt Studio, which became one of the most influential producers of physique photography, drawing, and film of the era. This volume of early Polaroids offers a rare look at the working method behind French's later, more polished Colt output.
notes: Limited first-edition hardcover, printed in Italy; pictorial boards and dust jacket, no text. Reproduces Polaroids c. 1964-67 predating French's founding of Colt Studio. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Malls Across America
description:
Throughout the 1980s, as Americas downtown districts declined in importance and the big-box stores began their slow march across the country, malls became increasing central to American popular culture, dominating the social life of a large swath of the population.

In 1989 Michael Galinsky, a twenty-year-old photographer, drove across the country recording this change: the spaces, textures and pace that defined this era. Starting in the winter of 1989 with the Smith Haven Mall in Garden City Long Island, Galinsky photographed malls from North Carolina to South Dakota, Washington State and beyond.

The photos he took capture life in these malls as it began to shift from the shiny excess of the 1980s towards an era of slackers and grunge culture. Malls Across America is filled with seemingly lost or harried families navigating their way through these temples of consumerism, along with playful teens, misfits, and the aged.

title: Facsimile Cabinet of Woman Origin Stories - Reflections
publisher: DelMonico Books/Colby College Museum of Art

title: Theaster Gates by Kavi Gupta and Theaster Gates
Theaster Gates (Contemporary Artists)
description:
The first monograph of Chicago-based Theaster Gates, one of the most exciting and highly regarded contemporary artists at work today.

Theaster Gates has developed an expanded artistic practice that includes space development, object making, performance and critical engagement with many publics. Gates transforms spaces, institutions, traditions, and perceptions. Gates's training as an urban planner and sculptor, and subsequent time spent studying clay, has given him keen awareness of the poetics of production and systems of organizing. Playing with these poetic and systematic interests, Gates has assembled gospel choirs, formed temporary unions, and used systems of mass production as a way of underscoring the need that industry has for the body. Gates refers to his working method as 'critique through collaboration' and his projects often stretch the form of what we usually understand visual art to be. His focus is also on the availability of information and the cross-fertilization of ideas. His multi-faceted exhibitions investigate themes of race and history through sculpture, installation, performance and two-dimensional works, furthering the artist's interest in a critique of social practice, shared economies and the question of objects in relation to political and cultural thought.

Gates' recent exhibition and performance venues include the Seattle Art Museum, Art Basel Miami Beach, Milwaukee Art Museum, Contemporary Arts Museum Houston, and the Whitney Biennial in New York. Gates was a participating artist in Documenta 13 in Kassel (2012) with his total-living installation 12 Ballads for Huguenot House. Other notable solo exhibitions include An Epitaph for Civil Rights at the Los Angeles Museum of Contemporary Art (2011) and My Labor Is My Protest, at White Cube Bermondsey, London (2012). Parallel to his artist career, Gates is also Director of Arts and Public Life Initiative at the University of Chicago and a board member of the city's South Side Community Center. Recently commissioned as the 2012 Armory Show Artist and a Loeb Fellow at Harvard Graduate School of Design in 2011, Gates has received awards and grants from Creative Capital, the Joyce Foundation, Graham Foundation, and the Bemis Center for Contemporary Art.

title: Theaster Gates - The Black Image Corporation
editor: Editor: Theaster Gates Associate Editor: Chiara Costa Introductory text by Theaster Gates conversation between Theaster Gates and Linda Johnson Rice.

title: Theaster Gates: 12 Ballads for Huguenot House (dOCUMENTA) by Michael Darling (2012-10-31)
And Another Thing
description:
And Another Thing compiles seven years of collage work and studio materials by London-based artist Anthony Gerace, functioning as much as an artwork in itself as a record of one.

Published by Aint-Bad in an edition of 700, printed in the Netherlands, the 128-page hardcover was sequenced by Gerace as both creator and editor, pairing finished collages with the degraded printed matter, tiny repeated squares, and studio ephemera from which they emerge. An essay by Laura May Todd frames the book's recurring concern with the physical life and reinterpretation of printed images, described by the publisher as tracing an image-death subverted through actions repeated incessantly. The book coincided with an exhibition of the same title at Klompching Gallery, New York, in May 2017.

Gerace works primarily in collage, portraiture, and landscape, building compositions from found and altered printed matter that foreground the wear and reprocessing of the source material itself. And Another Thing remains his most extensive monograph, distilling nearly a decade of that practice into a single sequenced object.
notes: Edition of 700, printed in the Netherlands; essay by Laura May Todd; coincided with the exhibition of the same title at Klompching Gallery, New York, May 2017. Cover photographed at an angle for the catalogue image; corrected via crop. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Bücherwald
description:
Bücherwald ("book forest") is a small illustrated zine by the Zurich artist Ingo Giezendanner, published under his GRRRR alias, that turns a page of dense pen-and-ink drawing into a literal thicket of books and branches.

Issued by the Zurich art-book publisher Nieves in a softcover pocket format, the zine continues the hand-drawn, black-and-white style Giezendanner has used since the late 1990s to document cities and invented landscapes in obsessive linear detail. It sits within a long run of self-published GRRRR zines and artist's books that Nieves has issued alongside his murals and installations.

Giezendanner (born 1975, Zurich) is a member of the Kroesos Foundation collective and has documented the urban environments of places he has lived and travelled, from Zurich to New York, New Orleans, Cairo, Nairobi, Karachi and Colombo, in ink on paper and in large-scale wall paintings. Bücherwald is a compact example of the same practice turned toward an invented, book-filled woodland.
notes: The catalogue's title ("Buchenwald") is corrected here to Bücherwald ("book forest"), the actual title of Giezendanner's GRRRR-alias zine; no title matching the original spelling exists in his bibliography. Self-published via Nieves, Zurich. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Moscow Terminus
description:
Bruce Gilden's Moscow Terminus is an unpublished dispatch from Komsomolskaya Square, the frenetic three-station plaza where Moscow's rail lines converge, rendered in the photographer's signature close, flash-lit street style.

The pictures move through the commuters, hustlers, and travelers gathered around Yaroslavsky Station, terminus of the Trans-Siberian Railway, and its neighboring terminals, catching faces mid-startle in the flash's sudden light. Dashwood Books published the project in New York in December 2014 as a 52-page softcover, in a first edition of 1000 copies, alongside a companion poster limited to 150.

Gilden built his reputation on unflinching, close-range flash photography of New York street life beginning in the 1980s and has carried that method to subjects abroad as a longtime Magnum photographer. Moscow Terminus extends that practice to a foreign transit hub, joining other works such as Facing New York and Haiti in his ongoing record of cities under pressure.
notes: First edition softcover, 1000 copies, published December 2014. No ISBN found for this title; a companion poster (150 copies) was released alongside it. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Coming up for Air: Stephen Gill – A Retrospective
publisher: Nobody Books, in association with Arnolfini
description:
Coming up for Air is the fullest account so far of Stephen Gill's photography, drawing together four decades of work, from 1982 to 2021, into a single retrospective.

The 604-page clothbound hardback holds over 600 images — roughly 450 in colour and 150 in black and white — sequenced by Gill across his best-known series (The Pillar, Talking to Ants, Hackney Flowers) as well as lesser-seen projects such as Invisible, Russian Women Smokers and Audio Portraits, plus early photographs from his Bristol childhood. Designed by Greger Ulf Nilson, the book is bound in cloth with foil embossing and a tipped-in cover image, and was published by Gill's own Nobody Books alongside a retrospective exhibition at Arnolfini, Bristol.

Gill (born 1971, Bristol) has spent his career working against the grain of straightforward documentary photography, burying negatives, layering exposures and letting chance intervene in the printing process. Long based between Bristol and Sweden, he has published most of his work himself through Nobody, and this volume gathers that output into one place for the first time.
tags: Photography, British Photography, Documentary Photography, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Published to accompany the retrospective exhibition of the same name at Arnolfini, Bristol, 2021. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Pillar
binding: Foil-embossed, three-part clothbound hardback with accompanying 12-page saddle-stitched booklet
description:
The Pillar is Stephen Gill's five-year study of the birds that came to perch on a wooden post he installed in a Swedish field, a quiet, sustained act of observation built entirely around one fixed point in the landscape.

Between 2015 and 2019 Gill positioned a camera trap on the pillar and let birds trigger their own portraits across the seasons, resulting in 31 color plates and 95 quadtone black-and-white plates of the species that landed there. Published by Gill's own imprint Nobody in 2019, the book is a foil-embossed, three-part clothbound hardback of 224 pages, including a gatefold and monoprinted endpapers, accompanied by a 12-page saddle-stitched booklet of text by Karl Ove Knausgård.

Gill (born 1971, Bristol) has spent much of his career working in and around a single patch of land near Bristol or, as here, returning obsessively to one site until it yields an entire book. The Pillar won the 2019 Rencontres d'Arles Author Book Award and extends the patient, process-driven method of earlier projects like Buried and Night Procession.
notes: Documents birds observed at a wooden pillar Gill installed in a Swedish field, 2015–2019; text by Karl Ove Knausgård. Winner of the 2019 Rencontres d'Arles Author Book Award. Housed as a three-part clothbound hardback with an accompanying 12-page booklet (132 x 210 mm). Catalogued shelf title "The Piller" corrected to "The Pillar". Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Please Notify the Sun
edition_printrun: clothbound, with 111 color plates, Includes a 132 x 210 mm yellow saddle stitched booklet with an essay by Karl Ove Knausgård.

title: Public
contributors: Glen Luchford (Photographer), Nadine Fraczkowski (Photographer), Vivien Solari (Photographer), Benjamin Lennox (Photographer), Greta Ilieva (Photographer), Alice Neale (Photographer)
description:
Public is a fashion journal founded and designed by the creative director Alex McWhirter, its first issue built from five distinct photographic portfolios shown side by side rather than folded into a single house style.

Issue 1 pairs Glen Luchford's Sequence with Nadine Fraczkowski's Identity, Vivien Solari's Immersion, Benjamin Lennox's Artifact, and Greta Ilieva's Flyoverland, alongside further images by McWhirter and Alice Neale, across 112 pages. The publisher's note frames the project as a reaction against an image culture in which, in its words, everything has been fine-tuned until indistinctiveness prevails and taste is easy to place a pulse on; the five portfolios are left to argue for a rougher, more specific alternative. McWhirter Studio issued the journal in a numbered edition of 250, spiral-bound behind a clear acetate cover.

McWhirter, originally from London, worked as art director at V Magazine in New York before collaborating with Raf Simons and Pieter Mulier at Calvin Klein; Public is his own editorial platform, continuing as an occasional publication built around a rotating cast of photographers and stylists.
notes: Issue 1 of the fashion journal Public, edited and designed by Alex McWhirter; numbered edition of 250. The catalogue record originally combined McWhirter's name with contributor Glen Luchford's; corrected here. Whether this copy is signed or numbered is unconfirmed; edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Folding Space / Pressing Time
description:
Folding Space / Pressing Time sets two artists' responses to the same flood of online imagery side by side, one working in paint and one in photography.

Dan Gluibizzi's contribution reworks grids of images gathered from Tumblr into loose, warm watercolors of the human form, drawn from amateur and selfie-sourced photographs. Zefrey Throwell's photographs give physical form to recurring dreams of time travel, with the same erotic disorientation running through Gluibizzi's paintings. Published by Ampersand in Portland in 2012 in a softcover edition of 200 copies, the book accompanied the gallery's two-artist exhibition There Is No Finish Line, standing as a conceptual counterpart to the show rather than a catalogue of it.

Gluibizzi, an MFA graduate of the University of Cincinnati based in Portland, has shown at Ampersand and in group shows at Compound Gallery and Froelick Gallery; his illustration work has appeared in the New York Times and Vogue. Throwell, based in New York, works across video, painting and performance and has shown solo at the Leopold Hoesch Museum. Folding Space / Pressing Time is one of two books Ampersand produced around Gluibizzi's work, alongside his earlier solo title Our Time.
notes: Catalogued as two authors merged into one garbled field ("Gluibizzi Zefrey Throwell" / "Dan"); corrected to Dan Gluibizzi and Zefrey Throwell as co-authors. Title corrected from the catalogue's "Folding Space / Depressing Time" to "Folding Space / Pressing Time," matching the publisher (Ampersand); Dashwood Books' listing spells it "Depressing Time," which appears to be a mishearing/typo of the publisher's own title. No ISBN traced; pagination and dimensions unconfirmed. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Burning Images - A History Of Effigy Protests Vis-A-Vis Series
description:
Effigy hanging and burning, a specific theatrical form of political protest, has become increasingly visible in the news media, particularly in protests against United States military operations in Afghanistan and Iraq, in US domestic politics, and in the Arab Spring.

Taking these events as points of departure, Florian Göttke investigates the conditions of this visual genre of protest, its roots and genealogies in a number of countries, its aesthetics, and politics. The book delves deeply into the different practices, iconologies, rituals, protest and media strategies, as well as into politics.

title: Peekaboo
description:
Peekaboo collects the monochrome paintings from Tomoo Gokita's 2018 exhibition of the same name at Tokyo Opera City Art Gallery, a body of work built entirely around surprise and withheld information.

Published by 888 Books in Tokyo, the book reproduces canvases worked in acrylic gouache in Gokita's collage-like manner, black, white and grey passages built up and scraped back until faces and figures blur toward abstraction. The subjects continue his long engagement with 1960s and 1970s American counterculture and underground magazines, filtered through pulp illustration and pin-up photography rather than reproduced directly.

Gokita (born 1969, Tokyo) trained as a graphic designer before turning to painting, and has shown with Blum and Taka Ishii Gallery among others. Peekaboo extends the vocabulary of erasure and disguise that runs through his work, in which recognisable source imagery is worked over until only a residue of gesture and expression remains.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Japanese Art, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Published by 888 Books, Tokyo, to accompany Gokita's solo exhibition Peekaboo at Tokyo Opera City Art Gallery. No usable cover image could be sourced online; cover to be photographed. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: A House Without A Roof
edition_printrun: Edition of 700. Offset print. In English, Hebrew and Arabic. Printed by Shapco. Shortlisted: 2017 Kraszna-Kraus Foundation Photography Book of the Year Award, 2016 Paris Photo-Aperture Foundation First Book Award, 2016 Mack First Book Award
description:
A House Without a Roof is a photographic book and installation of images and texts which looks at the deeply intertwined histories of violence and displacement connecting Europe to Israel and the Palestinian Territories.

Between 2011-2016, Golfer photographed and conducted fieldwork in the Baltic States, Britain, Germany, Israel, and the Occupied West Bank. He photographed varying landscapes of contention spanning from Jericho to Nuremberg, to the house in Siauliai, Lithuania where his grandmother was born before the war. Photographing and working in archives, he collected imagery and ephemera whose incompleteness, irony and poetic sensibilities point to ruptures in history, and occupy a place where the lines between myth and fact become difficult to distinguish. Framed by the relationship between his grandfather (a Jewish-Lithuanian survivor of Dachau), his dad (who briefly lived on an Israeli kibbutz in the 1970s) and himself, A House Without a Roof wrestles with contradictory narratives and points of view.

Histories and time fold into one another as the mythologies and memories of his family become entangled with the ongoing narratives of violence, trauma and mass displacement which continue to play out in present-day Israel and Palestine. Multiple short stories appear dispersed throughout the book, reflecting events that either actually occurred or could have. They grapple with the anxieties of attempting to understand histories which have a myriad of truths and inhabit a dream-like space where his own memories and visions of the past, present and future blur together.
tags: Documentary Photography, Diaspora, History, Israel, Migration, Palestine, Photography, WWII, Holocaust, Baltic States

title: Specific Objects Without Specific Form
contributors: by Elena Filipovic (Author), Danh Vo (Author), Carol Bove (Author), Tino Sehgal (Author), Felix Gonzalez-Torres (Artist)
description: This comprehensive 656-page catalogue documents the traveling retrospective Felix Gonzalez-Torres: Specific Objects without Specific Form, which showcased work from throughout the artist's career including paintings, sculptures, photographic works, and public projects. The exhibition employed an innovative format where it was re-installed by a different invited artist midway through its run at each venue, resulting in multiple distinct versions. Overall curator: Elena Filipovic.

title: American Surveillance: Someone to Watch Over Me

title: Still Lifes, Portraits & Parts
description:
Still Lifes, Portraits & Parts brings together three interlocking bodies of work in which Daniel Gordon builds his subjects out of paper before he ever points a camera at them.

Gordon prints photographs scavenged from internet image searches and magazines, then cuts, crumples, curls and pins them into three-dimensional constructions: fruit bowls assembled from mismatched textures, geometric heads built from strangers' skin and features, sitters cobbled together from wallpaper and wrapping paper. He photographs the resulting sculpture under studio light and discards it, so the finished print is the only record of an object that otherwise no longer exists. The book was published by Morel Books in 2013 as a 102-page hardcover, with an accompanying essay by curator Eva Respini.

Gordon emerged from the New York photography scene of the mid-2000s as part of a generation reworking the studio still life and photomontage for an image economy built on search and appropriation. Still Lifes, Portraits & Parts remains one of the clearest statements of that method, treating the camera as the last, not the first, step in making a picture.
tags: Photography, Contemporary Art, Still Life, Collage, Portraiture
notes: No cover image located through available sources; cover to be photographed. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Who Do You Love: Twelve Reproductions
description:
Who Do You Love presents twelve unique pieces John Gossage made through the 1990s and set aside for two decades, work he calls "photographic distractions" that refuse to sit squarely in either photography or collage.

Each gelatin silver print is combined with color elements, tissue paper and handmade marks on backing board, breaking the usual photographic illusion of a window onto another place and time and returning attention to the surface of the object itself. Fraenkel Gallery published this catalogue of the 2014 exhibition in a small hardcover of 32 pages, bound in kraft board with a paper title label, and including an interview with the artist.

Gossage (born 1946) has spent a five-decade career photographing overlooked and marginal American and European landscapes, in books including The Pond and Berlin in the Time of the Wall. Who Do You Love shows a private, more experimental side of that practice, made concurrently with his straight photographic work but not exhibited until years later.
notes: Catalogue for Gossage's 2014 exhibition of the same name at Fraenkel Gallery; no ISBN was issued for this gallery publication. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Mariposas Nocturnas: Moths of Central and South America, A Study in Beauty and Diversity
description:
Mariposas Nocturnas gathers fifteen years of Emmet Gowin's photographs of moths from Central and South American cloud forests, a late-career turn from the landscapes and family portraits that made his name.

Working with biologists in Bolivia, Brazil, Ecuador, French Guiana and Panama, Gowin photographed live moths in natural poses against backgrounds drawn from the natural world and art history, arranging them in typological grids of twenty-five to a sheet; many species had never before been photographed alive. Published by Princeton University Press in 2017 with a foreword by Terry Tempest Williams, the 144-page hardcover reproduces ninety color and two black-and-white plates at 11 x 14 inches, with an accompanying essay by Gowin on the project's collaborative and philosophical dimensions.

Gowin (born 1941) is best known for the aerial landscapes of mining sites and nuclear test grounds that occupied him for decades, and for his early portraits of his wife Edith and her family in Danville, Virginia. Mariposas Nocturnas won the 2018 PROSE Award in Popular Science and was named one of the British Journal of Photography's Best Books of 2017.
notes: Fifteen-year project documenting more than a thousand moth species across Bolivia, Brazil, Ecuador, French Guiana and Panama, arranged in typological grids of twenty-five. Winner of the 2018 PROSE Award in Popular Science; named one of the British Journal of Photography's Best Books of 2017. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Does Yellow Run Forever?
description:
Does Yellow Run Forever? is Paul Graham's meditation on desire and belief, following the color yellow from the promise of gold at a rainbow's end to the storefronts that turn hope into hard currency.

Published by MACK in 2014 as a debossed, faux suede-bound hardback, the 96-page book interweaves three groups of images: rainbows photographed in western Ireland, a sleeping dreamer, and cash-for-gold stores across the United States. The imagery moves between fact and reverie, refusing a single reading and holding love, wealth, and beauty in the same uncertain light — there is no singular meaning, and no gold waiting at the end of the rainbow, only startling visions in the everyday.

Graham (b. 1956) has spent four decades photographing everyday American and British life with a documentary eye alert to political and social undercurrent, in books including New Europe, American Night, and the twelve-volume a shimmer of possibility. Does Yellow Run Forever? extends that practice into a more allegorical register, using color itself as its organizing idea.
notes: Debossed faux-suede hardback with gilt page edges, 31 color photographs; the copy was catalogued to be checked for whether it is a signed or unsigned printing (MACK issued both). Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Western Front
description:
The Western Front is Stanley Greene's record of the San Francisco punk scene he lived inside as a young photographer in the 1970s, black-and-white pictures taken from within a music culture rather than at its edge.

Greene moved to San Francisco in 1975 and began photographing the bands, clubs and roommates around him, including the Mutants, the Dead Kennedys and other figures tied to the San Francisco Art Institute, shooting almost nightly with a Leica. The negatives and contact sheets sat unprinted for decades until designer Teun van der Heijden, who had worked on Greene's book Black Passport, rediscovered them. André Frère Éditions published the resulting 176-page hardcover in 2013, pairing English and French text with 110 duotone photographs, to mark the 25th anniversary of Visa pour l'Image.

Born in Brooklyn in 1949, Greene spent most of his career as a war photographer, covering Chechnya, and won the W. Eugene Smith Prize and five World Press Photo awards before co-founding the Noor agency. The Western Front is an outlier in that body of work, a return to the young, undocumented photographs he made before conflict photography became his subject.
notes: Also referenced in press as 'Never Quiet on the Western Front.' Released to mark the 25th anniversary of Visa pour l'Image; contact sheets predate publication by decades. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Jenna Gribbon: The Honeymoon Show!
description:
The Honeymoon Show! is Jenna Gribbon's third monograph, built around tender, theatrically staged portraits of her wife and muse set against scenes from their honeymoon in Thailand.

Published by Lévy Gorvy Dayan to accompany the exhibition of the same name at the gallery's New York space, the paperback juxtaposes documentary honeymoon imagery with a new series of posed portraits of the musician Mackenzie Scott, who performs as Torres, working through the dichotomies of fact and fiction, public and private, spontaneity and forethought. Clare Preston edited the volume, with an essay by Alison M. Gingeras on the reciprocal act of looking that structures Gribbon's paintings.

Gribbon (born 1978, Knoxville, Tennessee) has built her practice around domestic and intimate scenes of Scott, painted from a consciously subjective, often low or looking-up vantage point that reverses the usual position of painter and muse. The Honeymoon Show! extends that project into a more explicitly staged and theatrical register.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Portraiture, Queer Culture
notes: Third monograph by Gribbon, published to accompany the exhibition of the same name at Lévy Gorvy Dayan, New York. Edited by Clare Preston, with an essay by Alison M. Gingeras. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Beryl Chen: A Jamaican Girl
description:
Beryl Chen: A Jamaican Girl gathers Rene Groebli's portrait studies of a young woman, printed from negatives that sat in the Swiss photographer's archive for decades before this book brought them into view.

The pictures hold the same close, attentive quality found throughout Groebli's early work: patient studio and location portraiture built on trust between photographer and sitter rather than on staging. The book accompanies the images with text by Teo Schlachter and was issued as a slim 44-page hardcover by Sturm & Drang Publishers in Zurich in 2015, one of several volumes through which the press has been re-surfacing corners of Groebli's archive that were never published in his lifetime.

Groebli, born in 1927, established his reputation with Rail Magic (1949) and the frankly intimate honeymoon diary The Eye of Love (1954), photobooks now regarded as landmarks of postwar European photography. Sturm & Drang's subsequent volumes, including Early Work 1945-1955 and New York 1978, have restored attention to a career that also spanned commercial, industrial and colour photography in Zurich.
notes: Catalogued title "Beryl Chen" is the German National Library's short title; full title is "Beryl Chen: A Jamaican Girl". No cover image located through available sources; cover to be photographed. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: 16 Pictures
description: 16 Pictures is the latest in a series of photobooks by American artist Robert Grosvenor (born 1937). Included here are color photographs of vehicles, scale models and ordinary objects. Sometimes blurry, sometimes overexposed, and very often brightly colorful, the photographs depict scenes that may be staged or chanced upon.
tags: Contemporary Art, Karma, New York City, Photobook, Photography, Art

title: 32 Pictures
edition_printrun: Special Edition, signed and painted with collaged photographs
description:
The first in Karma's series of publications of Robert Grosvenor's photography.

This work presents itself as a manifest extension of his sculptural work. The 32 images in this book reveal an artist interested in the space between objects, as much as the objects themselves, and how form and texture can be combined in the natural world.

At times, no intervention is necessary for a deadpan humor to effortlessly assert itself, as when Grosvenor takes a picture of concrete steps which have been painted a light sky blue. Other times Grosvenor seems to be implying a performance in mid-play, in others wonder a beguiling mystery suggests that perhaps it's all being staged for our viewing. We can't help but wonder if the world, more often than not, arranges itself to be seen.
tags: Contemporary Art, Karma, New York City, Photobook, Photography, Art

title: 27 Pictures
description:
The second in Karma's series of publications of Robert Grosvenor's photography.

This work presents itself as a manifest extension of his sculptural work. The 27 images in this book reveal an artist interested in the space between objects, as much as the objects themselves, and how form and texture can be combined in the natural world.

At times, no intervention is necessary for a deadpan humor to effortlessly assert itself. Other times Grosvenor seems to be implying a performance in mid-play, in others wonder a beguiling mystery suggests that perhaps it's all being staged for our viewing. We can't help but wonder if the world, more often than not, arranges itself to be seen.

title: Eindhovenseweg 56
description:
When the mother of photographer Ton Grote died in 2007, his father stayed behind in a large house.

Their parental home where his parents lived since 1969 and he grew up with his brother and sister. Eindhovenseweg 56, a house full of memories and dreams. When his father started to clean up, Ton Grote decided to photograph all the loose items his parents owned: teapots, old cameras, power strips, glasses, and a worn out football. Treasured things they grew up with and the objects his parents used: everything was recorded. The result is a photo archive of more than five thousand photos, of which 2,262 made it into the book.

title: Lovers Ten Tears On
description:
In 1984 SUNIL GUPTA’s first long term relationship broke down in shortly after he arrived in London in 1984.

He had met his lover in the early 1970’s when the impact of the gay movement upon the consciousness of gay men was just gaining ground. Then, gay was good, and gay was proud. The laws against gay sex had been turned back. The definition of homosexuality as a psychiatric disorder was successfully challenged. The commercial scene and the visibility of gay men expanded to unprecedented levels. Although, while all this change provided the individual with the means for unstigmatised sexual experimentation in relatively safe venues, simultaneously it hardly dented social attitudes and legal structures which oppressed gay relationships. The arrival of HIV/AIDS changed all that. Gay men came under attack, from the state and its various channels. The media mounted a vicious campaign to label gay men as sick and irresponsible. Gay men were almost exclusively represented as ill. Patients of some incurable disease that had been equated with their sexuality.

On the strength of this fallacy once again there was talk of reinstating repressive laws. Once again “expert medical advisors” were in on the act with their labels and talk of “containment.” Couples though had come into their own. Gay self-help groups encouraged a change in sexual behaviour and a reduction in the number of partners. However, still without legal recognition, with the new emphasis on monogamy, with social attitudes reverting to hostility and given the invisibility of day-to-day life for gay men within relationships, being a partner in the 1980s proved to be as difficult as it had been decades ago. “These photographs were made in London. The couples define themselves as such by various criteria some live together, some don’t, some have been together a short time, some a very long time, and soon. I believe the relationship between gay men is an important but often neglected component central to their lives.” - Sunil Gupta
tags: Gay, London, Portraits, Queer Culture, Photography

title: Black Paintings
description:
Wade Guyton makes his Black Paintings by running raw linen canvas through a large-format inkjet printer, layering black ink pass after pass until the surface approaches an even, saturated black.

This 800-page book, published by JRP|Ringier in 2011, reproduces the series at length, tracking the small variations, streaks, misfeeds and printer artifacts that survive within an image that reads at first glance as a single flat colour. A text by the critic and Reena Spaulings co-founder John Kelsey accompanies the plates. The paperback volume's unusual length mirrors the repetitive, industrial logic of Guyton's process itself.

Guyton (born 1972, Hammond, Indiana) has worked since the early 2000s at the boundary between painting and mechanical reproduction, printing X's, flames and fragments of text onto canvas with office and studio printers. He represented the United States at the 2013 Venice Biennale and had a career survey at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 2012–13.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Conceptual Art
notes: Catalogue stub listed the title simply as "Black"; identified as Black Paintings (JRP|Ringier, 2011), the only Wade Guyton title matching that description. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: 1 Month Ago
description: 1 Month Ago documents the contents of the hardcore blog Sfcrewcut one month after a single painting of Guyton's appeared in its feed. Making the digital tactile, the publication examines the realm of re-appropriation amongst online subcultures.
tags: Contemporary Art, Digital Culture, Karma, New York City, Re-appropriation, Art, Digital Art

title: Wade Guyton im Josef Alpers Museum
Wade Guyton, Seth Price, Josh Smith, Kelley Walker
description:
This exhibition catalog documents Wade Guyton, Seth Price, Josh Smith, Kelley Walker's 2007 group show at Kunsthalle Zürich, an early survey of four artists whose work reshaped ideas of authorship, appropriation, and process in painting after 2000.

Published by Kunsthalle Zürich in 2007 as a 192-page softcover in English and German, with a red handprint stamped across its cover, the book reproduces the four artists' paintings, sculptures, and printed works as installed for curator Beatrix Ruf's exhibition, alongside an essay by writer and dealer John Kelsey.

Guyton, Price, Smith, and Walker emerged together from New York's early-2000s gallery scene — Guyton and Walker for their inkjet- and screen-printed canvases, Price for his vacuum-formed reliefs and internet-derived imagery, Smith for his loose, repeated self-portrait paintings — and this show remains a touchstone reference point for their generation's rethinking of painting through mechanical reproduction.
notes: Catalogued title 'Guyton Smith Walker' drops co-artist Seth Price; corrected here to the book's full title, matching all four artists credited on the cover. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Das New Yorker Atelier
description:
Das New Yorker Atelier documents a significant new body of work by Wade Guyton, moving beyond his signature repeated letterforms into paintings built from a diverse range of digitally captured imagery.

Published by Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König to accompany Guyton's 2017 exhibition at Museum Brandhorst, Munich, the 356-page hardcover reproduces large-format inkjet paintings made from cell-phone snapshots, screenshots, and digital enlargements, including recognizable subjects such as newspaper homepages and views of his Bowery studio alongside passages that dissolve into abstraction under extreme magnification. Edited by Achim Hochdörfer with essays by Hochdörfer, Johanna Burton, and Bernhard Maaz, the book examines how the work registers what it calls the rapid expansion of digital code into all areas of life.

Guyton (b. 1972) works at the boundary of painting and photography, feeding raw linen through large-format Epson printers to produce paintings that are simultaneously mechanically reproduced and materially unique. This volume extends a long-running series of exhibition publications documenting his studio practice, following his 2007 Walther König debut monograph and subsequent gallery and museum catalogues.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Full 356-page Museum Brandhorst edition (2017), distinct from the shorter 92-page 'Das New Yorker Atelier, Abridged' catalogue issued for the 2017-2018 Serpentine Galleries showing (different ISBN). Cover to be photographed: no confirmed cover image for this specific edition could be located. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Wade Guyton: Zeichnungen von Drama und Frühstück im Atelier Vol. II
description:
Zeichnungen von Drama und Frühstück im Atelier Vol. II is the second half of a two-volume catalogue documenting Wade Guyton's studio floor as both subject and support, this volume tied to the condensed London restaging of a Munich exhibition.

Volume I, published by Walther König in 2017, accompanied Wade Guyton: Das New Yorker Atelier at Museum Brandhorst in Munich; this second volume documents its abridged restaging as Das New Yorker Atelier, Abridged at the Serpentine Gallery, London, from September 2017 to February 2018. Both books continue the format of Guyton's earlier trilogy of studio catalogues, photographing stacks of his inkjet-printed "drawings" - pages torn from art history books and overprinted - laid on the glossy floor of his studio, painted black for this iteration.

Guyton (born 1972, Hammond, Indiana) has worked since the mid-2000s with a large-format inkjet printer as his primary tool, feeding book pages, canvas and linen through it to produce paintings built from a mechanical, repeatable process. These studio-floor catalogues treat the accumulating printed sheets themselves as a subject, extending that inquiry into the space where the work is made.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Second of a two-volume exhibition catalogue; Vol. I (ISBN 9783960980971) accompanies the Museum Brandhorst exhibition in Munich, Vol. II documents its condensed restaging as Das New Yorker Atelier, Abridged at the Serpentine Gallery, London. Page count and trim size are estimated from the companion Vol. I edition and should be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Wade Guyton: Zeichnungen von Drama und Frühstück im Atelier
description:
Zeichnungen von Drama und Frühstück im Atelier documents an exhibition at Museum Brandhorst in Munich, extending Wade Guyton's ongoing Zeichnungen (drawings) series of artist publications built entirely from the debris of his own studio floor.

The book gathers book pages, photographs, bitmap files and screen captures that had piled up on the floor of Guyton's studio, run through the same industrial inkjet printers he uses to make his large linen paintings. Presented for the exhibition, which ran from 28 January to 30 April 2017, the pages read as a single continuous sequence rather than a conventional catalogue of works. It was published as a 130-page softcover ("flexi") volume by Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König.

Guyton has spent two decades feeding raw canvas and paper through Epson printers to make paintings that register the machine's own drips, banding and misregistration as much as the source imagery. The Zeichnungen series translates that same process onto the printed page, a body of work later anthologized in Wade Guyton: Two Decades MCMXCIX-MMXIX (2022) and shown at institutions including the Serpentine Galleries and the Punta della Dogana.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Conceptual Art, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Solo exhibition catalog, Museum Brandhorst, Munich, 28 Jan - 30 Apr 2017. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Polaroids
description:
Polaroids collects instant photographs François Halard has taken over the course of his career shooting interiors and artists' homes for magazines such as Vogue and AD.

Rougher and more immediate than the large-format editorial work he is known for, the Polaroids function as private notes: quick studies of light, colour and detail made on location, later kept as a personal archive rather than published assignments. The Name Books, a Zurich imprint devoted to photographers' informal and archival work, issued this 60-page hardcover selection in 2016.

Halard (born 1961, Paris) has spent four decades photographing the homes and studios of artists, designers and writers, from Cy Twombly and Nathalie du Pasquier to his own family's house in Arles. The Polaroids sit alongside that larger body of interiors photography as a looser, more diaristic counterpart.
notes: Not to be confused with Halard's later Art & Flowers (Rizzoli, 2025). Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Man Who Never Returned
description:
The Man Who Never Returned takes a folk tale about a man who disappeared and turns it into an image-fiction that treats photographs as pure information, expanding and collapsing single moments until the picture itself starts to fail.

Andrew Hammerand built the book from digitally altered street photographs made in Boston: figures blur, ghost, and fracture inside the frame as data drops out mid-exposure. The disruptions read as glitches in surveillance itself, undercutting any confidence that a camera records a stable truth during a period of mass data collection. The Table, a small exhibition and publishing project run out of a Phoenix home, issued the book in 2014 to accompany Hammerand's exhibition of the same title: a staple-bound paperback of 48 pages in an edition of 250.

Hammerand, based in Boston, has built a body of work around privacy, authority, and digitized culture, most visibly in The New Town, made using a municipal surveillance camera and shown in Watching You, Watching Me at the Open Society Foundations in New York. The Man Who Never Returned extends that same scrutiny of the camera as an instrument of control into an explicitly fictional register.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Surveillance, Digital Culture, Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One
notes: Published by The Table, a small exhibition and publishing project in Phoenix, AZ, in an edition of 250; staple-bound paperback, 48 pages. No ISBN was issued for this small-press edition. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: September
description:
Ren Hang's September is one installment in a self-published monthly photo-book project the Chinese photographer and poet undertook in 2016, releasing a new booklet each month for a year.

The 32-page softcover collects photographs made in Beijing that September, continuing Ren Hang's spare, deadpan studio style: young bodies arranged in tight, sculptural embraces against plain backdrops, printed without captions or accompanying text. It was distributed independently in a first edition of 100 copies, the way most of his books reached readers before larger publishers took an interest.

Ren Hang (1987-2017) photographed friends and acquaintances nude and semi-nude, treating the body as raw material for tableaux that were frank about desire while sidestepping pornography's conventions. His images circulated online and in self-published books like this one years before institutions such as the Multimedia Art Museum, Moscow, and the Kansas State University art museum acquired his work, and before Taschen issued a posthumous retrospective monograph in 2020.
notes: Annotated in the collector's records as 'September (signed) by Ren Hang'; signed copy. Self-published softcover booklet, first edition of 100 copies, part of Ren Hang's 2016 project to release one photo-book per month. No ISBN was assigned. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Huang Jiaqi
description:
Ren Hang's Huang Jiaqi is a self-published record of a Berlin encounter with his partner, a work as intimate as it is unrepeatable.

The 32-page hardcover, produced in Beijing and issued with an accompanying poster, gathers photographs Ren Hang made of Huang Jiaqi during their time together, continuing the direct, unguarded nude portraiture that defined his practice. Huang, later credited alongside Ren Hang as image editor on the book New Love, appears here as both subject and collaborator, and the book was never reprinted.

Ren Hang (1987–2017) photographed friends and lovers nude against ordinary domestic backdrops, work that drew repeated police scrutiny in China for its casual defiance of official modesty codes. Huang Jiaqi's portrait from this book was later chosen for the cover of Ren Hang's posthumous Taschen retrospective, and Huang has since continued working as a photographer in his own right.
tags: Photography, Chinese Photography, Portraiture, Queer Culture
notes: Collector's annotation "(signed) by Ren Hang" stripped from the catalogued title; the library's copy is signed. Sources agree the book was self-published in Beijing; one retailer dates it 2013, another lists 2016 (likely a later distribution date rather than the original printing) — 2013 used here. No ISBN was ever assigned. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: May
description:
Ren Hang's May is one installment in a self-published, month-by-month photobook project the Beijing photographer set for himself in 2016, printing a new book for each month of the year.

Following his stated plan to publish "one photo book every month," each volume gathered pictures made that month in a single city; May collects images shot in Paris, continuing Ren Hang's recurring subjects of nude and semi-nude friends photographed in stark, matter-of-fact settings. The book was issued as a softcover of 28 pages in an edition of 100 copies, printed and distributed by the artist himself outside the conventional publishing system.

Ren Hang (1986–2017) was a self-taught photographer and poet whose direct, often explicit images of the body made him one of the most closely watched, and in China most censored, photographers of his generation. The monthly series that includes May sits alongside his larger monographs, such as the Taschen retrospective, as a record of the fast, prolific, self-published working method that defined his short career.
notes: Self-published monthly photobook (May 2016), part of Ren Hang's year-long one-book-per-month project. Catalog title "May by Ren Hang" simplified to the book's actual title. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: March
description:
A self-published photobook by the Chinese photographer and poet Ren Hang, part of a year-long project of monthly volumes that stands among the most personal work of his brief career.

In 2016 Ren Hang set out to publish a small softcover book every month, an informal diary running alongside his more widely exhibited series. March, forty pages in an edition of 100 copies, gathers images shot that month in New York and Hong Kong: the nude and semi-nude bodies of friends and lovers set against plain interiors, rendered in the flat, saturated color and deadpan framing that mark his work throughout the series. Ren described the project simply as being about survival and love.

Ren Hang (1987-2017) worked outside China's official art system for his entire career, photographing nudity, gender, and homosexuality in a context where such images could not be publicly exhibited at home. The monthly books of 2016, made the year before his death, sit alongside better-known volumes like Republic and Athens Love as part of a body of work built largely through self-publishing and international gallery shows rather than commercial distribution.
tags: Photography, Chinese Photography, Queer Culture, Zines
notes: Self-published softcover, edition of 100; no ISBN was assigned. Part of a series of twelve monthly photobooks (January-December) Ren Hang produced in 2016. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: November
description:
Ren Hang's November is one installment in a yearlong project the Beijing photographer set for himself in 2016: to self-publish a photobook every month, each one a compact record of the people and desire that filled his life that year.

The booklet gathers photographs made in Beijing in November 2016, continuing Ren Hang's practice of photographing friends and lovers nude and unguarded in cramped apartment rooms, on rooftops and around the city, printed without captions or a stated sequence. It was issued as a first edition of one hundred copies, a thirty-two-page softcover booklet following the stripped-down format of the rest of the 2016 series: a single cover photograph, minimal typography, no accompanying text.

Ren Hang (1987-2017) built a body of work around explicit, often startling nudity photographed among friends, circulating first through Chinese social media before it reached galleries and magazines internationally, including Aperture and Foam. He died in February 2017, shortly after completing this monthly series, leaving its twelve booklets among his last self-published projects.
notes: Catalogue annotation "(signed)" retained; this copy is signed. Self-published edition of 100 copies, part of Ren Hang's 2016 monthly photobook series. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: August
description:
August belongs to a run of monthly zines Ren Hang self-published through 2016, each one a snapshot of a single month spent shooting the bodies of friends and collaborators.

The photographs, all made in Tokyo in August 2016, show nude figures alone or in small groups, staged with the flat flash light and blunt, matter-of-fact framing that runs through Ren Hang's work.
