The artist described the year-long series simply as a shooting plan about survival and love. This copy is a first-edition softcover booklet of 48 pages from an edition of 100, signed by the photographer.

Ren Hang (1987-2017) was a Beijing-based photographer and poet whose nude portraits of young Chinese men and women, made outside any studio system and often on rooftops or in domestic interiors, drew both international acclaim and repeated censorship at home. The monthly zines of 2016, of which August is one, were made in the final year of his life alongside larger monographs such as Nude and Athens Love.
tags: Photography, Zines, Nude Photography, Chinese Photography
notes: Catalogued as 'August (signed) by Ren Hang'; this copy is signed by the artist. Self-published softcover booklet, first edition of 100 copies, part of a series of monthly zines Ren Hang produced through 2016. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: October
description:
Ren Hang's October is another installment in the self-published monthly photo-book project the Chinese photographer and poet ran through 2016, releasing a new booklet each month for a year.

The 44-page softcover gathers photographs made in Beijing that October, continuing the deadpan, sculptural nude studies that define the series: bodies knotted into tight, geometric arrangements against plain backdrops, printed without captions or supporting text. It was distributed independently in a first edition of 100 copies, the way most of his books reached readers before larger publishers took an interest.

Ren Hang (1987-2017) photographed friends and acquaintances nude and semi-nude, treating the body as raw material for tableaux that were frank about desire while sidestepping pornography's conventions. His images circulated online and in self-published books like this one years before institutions such as the Multimedia Art Museum, Moscow, and the Kansas State University art museum acquired his work, and before Taschen issued a posthumous retrospective monograph in 2020.
notes: Annotated in the collector's records as 'October (signed) by Ren Hang'; signed copy. Self-published softcover booklet, first edition of 100 copies, part of Ren Hang's 2016 project to release one photo-book per month. No ISBN was assigned. Cover image reproduced from an archival scan carrying a source watermark; edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Physical Borderline
description:
Physical Borderline is the catalogue Three Shadows Photography Art Centre published for Ren Hang's 2014 exhibition of the same name, a body of work that pushes his nude portraiture toward its most contorted, sculptural extreme.

Produced in a single printing of 500 copies to accompany the Beijing exhibition, the 128-page book collects images in which Hang arranges his mostly unclothed subjects into improbable, interlocking shapes, treating the body as raw material rather than as a site of modesty or shame. It is one of the more substantial of Hang's self-published and small-press catalogues.

Ren Hang (1987–2017) worked almost exclusively with friends and acquaintances as models, photographing them nude in domestic interiors and on rooftops with a directness that repeatedly drew the attention of Chinese authorities. Physical Borderline sits alongside his other Beijing-published titles, including Huang Jiaqi, among the small run of books that circulated before his death in 2017.
notes: Format is listed variously as hardcover (Dashwood Books) and softcover (Josef Chladek archive); no ISBN was assigned to this 500-copy exhibition catalogue. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: June
description:
June is another installment in Ren Hang's self-published, month-by-month photobook project, the Beijing photographer's plan in 2016 to print and issue one book for every month of the year.

The cover spells the title letter by letter across pages of dense green sea foam and rock, paired inside with a small set of photographs made in Los Angeles that month; Ren Hang described the series as "all about survival and love." It was issued as a softcover of 32 pages in an edition of 100 copies, self-produced outside the conventional publishing system.

Ren Hang (1986–2017) was a self-taught photographer and poet whose direct treatment of the nude body made him one of the most closely watched, and in China most censored, photographers of his generation. The monthly series that includes June records the fast, prolific, self-published working method that defined his short career, running alongside more widely distributed monographs such as the Taschen retrospective.
notes: Self-published monthly photobook (June 2016), part of Ren Hang's year-long one-book-per-month project; photographs made in Los Angeles. Catalog title "June by Ren Hang" simplified to the book's actual title. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Private Room
description:
Pamela Hanson's Private Room gathers portraits of eight women photographed over two years at Lafayette House, a small hotel in downtown New York, framing undress and repose as a matter of interior life rather than performance.

Working with stylist Susan Winget inside the hotel's rooms, Hanson built a sequence of sixty color photographs across the book's ninety-six pages, treating each woman's session as its own closed world: tousled bedding, half-drawn curtains, the ordinary furniture of a rented room standing in for privacy itself. Damiani published the book as a suede-bound hardcover with an accompanying text by the artist Jack Pierson, extending the language of fashion portraiture into something closer to a diary.

Hanson has shot editorial for Vogue, Marie Claire and GQ over a three-decade career, with prints held in the Smithsonian American Art Museum's permanent collection. Private Room stands apart from that commercial output as a personal, self-directed project, continuing an interest in female intimacy she had explored in earlier books.
notes: Published by Damiani; sources place the release between 2016 and 2017, with 2017 and this ISBN confirmed via a D.A.P./Artbook.com listing. Damiani also issued a small numbered collector's edition with a signed print; edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Two Years of Bluto
description:
In January of 2017, self-taught artist Erik Hanson decided to try something new.

He set aside the conceive/execute way of working and decided to live in the moment with no plans and no internal critique, giving himself the freedom to do whatever he wanted to do in the studio with no road-map. Within the first week a friend had sent him an image of a Bluto toy and as he painted it, Hanson soon found himself immersed in the concepts he had learned as a little kid parked in front of the TV. The floodgates opened and he was on his way to a monumental meditation on “Good Guys and Bad Guys”
tags: Art, Cartoon, Popeye, Queer Culture, luto

title: Hier
description:
Hier ("here") gathers Jitka Hanzlová's long look at the Ruhr, a landscape built and rebuilt for industry until nature is reduced to whatever gaps are left over.

The book pairs 47 color plates of people and places across 96 pages, moving between tender, direct portraits and views of trees, verges, and scrubland that seem to insist on their own presence inside a heavily managed environment. Hanzlová began the project after settling near Essen and returned to it over more than a decade, from 1998 through 2010. Walther König published this hardcover edition in 2014, with an introduction by the novelist Terézia Mora.

Hanzlová, born in 1958 in Czechoslovakia, fled to Germany in 1982 and studied photography at Essen from 1987 to 1994; her work returns to the relationship between landscape, civilization, and the places that shape identity, from her early series on her home village of Rokytník to Hier's study of her adopted region. She has had solo exhibitions at the Museum Folkwang, Fotomuseum Winterthur, and Fundación MAPFRE, and won the BMW-Paris Photo Prize in 2007.
notes: Photographs made 1998 and 2003-2010 around Essen, Germany. Named a TIME Best Photobook of 2013 pick despite the 2014 D.A.P. distribution date. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: 31 Subway Drawings
description:
A fascinating look at Keith Haring's New York City subway artwork from the 1980s.

Celebrated artist Keith Haring (1958-1990) has been embraced by popular culture for his signature bold graphic line drawings of figures and forms. Like other graffiti artists in the 1980s, Haring found an empty canvas in the advertising panels scattered throughout New York City's subway system, where he communicated his socially conscious, often humorous messages on platforms and train cars. Over a five-year period, in an epic conquest of civic space, Haring produced a massive body of subway artwork that remains daunting in its scale and its impact on the public consciousness.

Dedicated to the individuals who might encounter them and to the moments of their creation, Haring's drawings now exist solely in the form of documentary photographs and legend. Because they were not meant to be permanent--only briefly inhabiting blacked-out advertising boards before being covered up by ads or torn down by authorities or admirers--what little remains of this project is uniquely fugitive. Keith Haring: 31 Subway Drawings reproduces archival materials relating to this magnificent project alongside essays by leading Haring experts.
tags: Art, Biography, Contemporary Art, Graffiti & Street Art, Popular Culture

title: Keith Haring (Rizzoli Classics)
editor: Jeffrey Deitch, Julia Gruen, Suzanne Geiss
description:
Keith Haring gathers the fullest published account of the artist's decade-long career, developed from a book concept Haring had begun sketching out before his death in 1990.

Across 528 pages, the volume draws on more than ten years of research into Haring's archive, reproducing drawings, studio photographs, and journal entries alongside finished work. It follows his trajectory from chalk drawings made in New York's subway system through murals in Pisa and Berlin, his body painting of Grace Jones, and his engagement with AIDS activism, illiteracy, and apartheid. This edition reissues Rizzoli's 2008 monograph in the publisher's compact Rizzoli Classics series.

Keith Haring (1958-1990) moved from unsanctioned subway drawings in the early 1980s to a practice that spanned murals, sculpture, and design, using a graphic vocabulary of radiant babies, barking dogs, and dancing figures to address social and political subjects directly. Julia Gruen, a former studio assistant, has directed the Keith Haring Foundation since Haring's death, and Jeffrey Deitch has represented the estate; both worked from Haring's own outline for the book this monograph completes.
notes: Reissue, under Rizzoli's 'Rizzoli Classics' imprint, of the 522-page first edition Rizzoli published in 2008 (ISBN 9780847831395, 30.4 x 27.6 cm); this 2014 printing is 528 pages at a standard 9 x 10 in trade size. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Keith Haring Journals
description:
Keith Haring Journals collects the artist's private writing from 1977 until shortly before his death in 1990, a first-person record that runs alongside the drawings for which he became famous.

This Penguin Classics Deluxe Edition reprints the journals in full across 464 pages, illustrated with ninety black-and-white reproductions of Haring's work and previously unpublished Polaroids, with a new foreword by Shepard Fairey and Robert Farris Thompson's original introduction. The entries move from Haring's arrival in New York and his early subway drawings through the School of Visual Arts years, the Club 57 and Pop Shop period, and his 1988 AIDS diagnosis, in his own unfiltered voice rather than as retrospective narrative.

Haring (1958–1990) turned the New York City subway system into a public canvas with chalk drawings before moving into painting, murals and the Pop Shop, building an image vocabulary of radiant babies, barking dogs and dancing figures that became inseparable from 1980s downtown culture. The journals, first published by Viking in 1996, remain the primary written source for how he understood his own work and the AIDS crisis that shaped his final years.
notes: Edition catalogued here is the Penguin Classics Deluxe Edition (2010, ISBN 9780143105978); earlier hardcover (Viking, 1996) and paperback (Penguin, 1997) editions also exist under different ISBNs. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Against All Odds: Keith Haring in the Rubell Family Collection
Keith Haring: Manhattan Penis Drawings for Ken Hicks
Iran: A Picture Book
description:
Between 2011 and 2014 the German photographer Oliver Hartung travelled across Iran to document its public monuments, murals and memorials, publishing the results as Iran / A Picture Book.

Working in a typological, deadpan style, Hartung records the visual culture that has filled Iranian public space since the 1979 revolution: war memorials to the 1980–88 conflict with Iraq, portraits of the ayatollahs painted on building facades, and the odd, often absurd civic sculpture. A wheat sheaf doubles as a street lamp in Damghan. A hand grenade in Isfahan is stamped with an internet icon. Captions give each location in English. The book was published by Spector Books in Leipzig as a thread-sewn paperback of 340 pages carrying 470 colour images, designed by Hartung with Helmut Völter.

Hartung, born in 1973 and based in Berlin and Leipzig, has worked since 2007 on a long-term project surveying the Middle East through its built and painted public imagery; Iran / A Picture Book followed his earlier Spector Books title on Syria, Syria Al-Assad, and extends the same typological method to a different state's visual propaganda.
notes: Also listed by some retailers under the alternate title "Iran Monuments"; the book's own title is "Iran / A Picture Book." Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Naoya Hatakeyama: Excavating the Future City
description:
The first English-language survey of Naoya Hatakeyama, whose thirty-year study of cities and the materials that build them has made him one of the defining photographers of the transformed Japanese landscape.

Organized around five chapters, the book brings together twenty-four of Hatakeyama's series, from labyrinthine city views and high-speed images of exploding limestone quarries to studies of architectural maquettes and documentation of the damage left by the 2011 tsunami in his hometown of Rikuzentakata. Essays by Yasufumi Nakamori, Toyo Ito, and the artist himself accompany the plates. Aperture published the volume for the exhibition Excavating the Future City: Photographs by Naoya Hatakeyama at the Minneapolis Institute of Art in 2018.

Hatakeyama represented Japan at the 49th Venice Biennale in 2001 and had his first solo museum show outside Japan the following year at Kunstverein Hannover; his work was also part of the Golden Lion-winning Japanese pavilion at the 2012 Venice Architecture Biennale. This survey gathers his full arc, from early quarry and city studies through the tsunami work that marked a turn toward his own history.
tags: Photography, Japanese Photography, Architecture, Landscape, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Published with the Minneapolis Institute of Art for Hatakeyama's 2018 survey exhibition, curated by Yasufumi Nakamori. Page count listed as 276 on the publisher's own site; some retailers cite 280. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Preston Bus Station
edition_printrun: First edition of 2,000 copies, including a numbered edition of 100 with a print
description:
Jamie Hawkesworth's Preston Bus Station collects portraits of commuters and passersby photographed inside one of Britain's largest Brutalist bus stations, made after Hawkesworth learned the 1969 building was under threat of demolition.

Returning to his hometown for a month, Hawkesworth walked the station's single continuous loop every day, approaching whoever caught his eye among the travelers passing through on the Megabus route north and south. The resulting portraits, made without a fixed plan beyond that daily circuit, were brought together into a 196-page hardcover published by Dashwood Books in 2017, designed by Hans Seeger, in a first edition of 2,000 copies that included a numbered issue of 100 sold with a print.

The project traces back to 2010, when Hawkesworth first photographed the station as a student working with tutor Adam Murray, producing a newspaper of teenage portraits that helped launch his career in fashion and portrait photography. This monograph gathers seven years of return visits into his first full-length book, anchoring his later editorial work in the same instinct for unplanned encounter.
notes: First monograph edition, following an earlier 2015 Loose Joints edition and a 2010 self-published newspaper of the same project; this copy is the 2017 Dashwood Books hardcover. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Lessons in Posing Subjects
description:
Lessons in Posing Subjects takes the stock gestures of commercial photography apart, one deadpan caption at a time.

Between 1981 and 1982, Robert Heinecken rephotographed models and families from mail-order catalogues onto Polaroid SX-70 film, then wrote his own sober, faux-instructional texts beneath each image, describing invented rules of posture and expression as though transcribing a professional manual. This book reproduces the series' 41 plates in full for the first time, co-published by Triangle Books and WIELS to accompany the exhibition of the same title, the artist's first solo show in the UK. It is a spiral-bound softcover of 56 pages, with an essay by curator Devrim Bayar, in an edition of 1000.

Heinecken (1931-2006) called himself a "paraphotographer," someone who examined photographic meaning while rarely touching a camera, working instead with found and appropriated commercial imagery across collage, offset lithography and Polaroid. Lessons in Posing Subjects sits alongside related bodies of work from the same period as some of his most direct engagements with advertising's grammar of gesture.
tags: Photography, Appropriation Art, Polaroid, Exhibition Catalog
notes: One of two copies in the collection. Catalogued as 'Lessons in Public Posing'; the published title of the book and series is Lessons in Posing Subjects. Co-published by Triangle Books and WIELS in an edition of 1000 to accompany the 2014 exhibition; the show later traveled to Open Eye Gallery, Liverpool, and Fri Art Kunsthalle, Fribourg. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Lessons in Posing Subjects
description:
Lessons in Posing Subjects reproduces, complete and for the first time, the series Robert Heinecken assembled between 1981 and 1982 from photographs he found in mail-order clothing catalogues.

The spiral-bound, 56-page volume pairs each appropriated image of a model with a deadpan instructional caption, mimicking the language of posing guides while exposing the poses' underlying artifice and address to a consuming eye. Published by Triangle Books with WIELS in Brussels in 2014, in an edition of 1,000 copies, the book accompanied an exhibition of the same title curated by Devrim Bayar, who also contributed the accompanying text; the show later traveled to Fri Art Kunsthalle Fribourg and Open Eye Gallery, Liverpool.

Robert Heinecken (1931-2006) worked mostly without a camera, instead cutting, rephotographing, and recombining images already circulating in magazines, catalogues, and advertising, describing his practice as that of a 'paraphotographer.' Lessons in Posing Subjects belongs to a broader body of appropriation work from the late 1970s and early 1980s, made alongside his Polaroid-based projects, that treats commercial photography's conventions of femininity as material to be dismantled from within.
notes: One of two copies in the collection. Published to accompany the WIELS exhibition of the same title, curated by Devrim Bayar; first edition of 1,000 copies, now out of print through the publisher. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Forever
description:
Forever follows the daily movements of homeless residents through downtown Los Angeles and the neighborhoods of Compton, Watts and South Central, photographed from the vantage point of the street rather than as a record of what people leave behind.

Made between 2007 and 2012, the 128-page hardback gathers Anthony Hernandez's color photographs of underpasses, chain-link fences, tarps and makeshift shelters, framed so the camera occupies the same low, exposed position as its unseen subjects. The title and approach return to ground Hernandez covered two decades earlier in Landscapes for the Homeless (1996), a project begun after a conversation with photographer Lewis Baltz; here he notes that the population he first photographed has only grown.

Hernandez (born 1947, Los Angeles) has spent his career photographing the city's overlooked infrastructure and the people who inhabit its margins, work held in the collections of the Museum of Modern Art and the Getty. Forever, published by MACK in 2017, extends a body of work concerned less with individual portraits than with the built environment homelessness produces.
notes: Published by MACK, London, 2017. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Beyond Blonde
description:
Steve Hiett's Beyond Blonde gathers five decades of the British photographer's fashion work, most of it never before collected in book form.

Arranged by decade from the late 1960s to the 2000s, the book moves through Hiett's magazine work for British, French and Italian titles, built around his signature use of hard, off-camera flash against blown-out skies and bleached urban backdrops. The pictures favour saturated colour and off-centre framing over conventional glamour, turning studio and street alike into sets for images that read as fragments of unstated stories. Beyond Blonde was published by Prestel in 2015 as a 280-page hardcover with an essay by Philippe Garner, edited by Patrick Remy, following an exhibition of the same body of work at the Hyères International Festival of Fashion and Photography.

Hiett has worked as a fashion photographer since the late 1960s, contributing to Vogue Paris, Per Lui and Cosmopolitan among others, and is closely associated with the plein-air, saturated-colour style that shaped a generation of fashion photographers who followed him, from Guy Bourdin to Miles Aldridge.
notes: Catalog title corrected from "Beyond Blond" to the book's actual title, "Beyond Blonde." Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Le Feu
description:
A found-image artist book by the French photographer Pauline Hisbacq that treats desire and fantasy as material already circulating online, waiting to be re-cut into a new sequence.

Rather than shooting original photographs, Hisbacq assembled Le Feu from pictures collected from the internet, arranging them across forty pages by affinity, shock, and ricochet rather than narrative logic. The sequence moves through desire, fantasy, and eroticism with the loose momentum of a flirtation, treating the internet's flow of images as its own kind of imagination. Designed by François Santerre, the softcover edition of 100 copies is bound with an elastic band and was published by September Books in Paris in 2018.

Hisbacq trained in philosophy before studying photography at the École Nationale Supérieure de la Photographie in Arles and, later, the International Center of Photography in New York. Le Feu followed her first book, Natalya (7 Editions, 2016), and preceded Amour adolescente (Rayon Vert, 2019) and further collaborations with September Books, forming part of a body of work that returns repeatedly to appropriated and found imagery as a way of examining desire.
notes: Softcover, elastic-band binding, edition of 100. Made from appropriated internet images rather than original photographs. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Open Nightly
description:
Open Nightly is a self-published photobook by the Chicago photographer Liv Hoffman, distributed through Dashwood Books in New York in 2016 as a softcover first edition, signed, and sold out shortly after release.

At 480 pages, it is the longest of the small run of self-published titles, including Irving Dreams and Crash, that Hoffman released in the mid-2010s through the same independent photography bookshop, part of a body of self-distributed work built outside gallery or publisher structures.

Hoffman studied photography at the Art Institute of Chicago and has shown installations and prints from her Pilsen Series at Parasol Projects in New York, alongside a photography award from the musician Juicy J that led to a Vice magazine feature. Her pictures have also appeared in National Geographic and the Miami Herald, work that runs alongside the small-run photobooks she continues to self-publish.
notes: Self-published through Dashwood Books, New York, 2016; softcover first edition, signed, 480 pages. No cover image located; cover to be photographed. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Dignity
description:
An artist's book by the American artist Christian Holstad, Dignity was published by Snoeck of Cologne in 2004 in a limited edition of 1,000 copies.

The book draws on Holstad's alterations of found newsprint: its cover sets the title in ornate lettering over a collage of newspaper obituary columns, framed by a stitched, doily-like border and overlaid with a flocked gold tree — mourning ornamented into something domestic and handmade. The softcover volume documents the body of collaged and embellished works surrounding this practice.

Holstad (b. 1972) works across collage, textile, performance, and his signature eraser drawings, salvaging the printed ephemera of American life into tender, queer reworkings he is represented by Andrew Kreps Gallery, New York. The library also holds his related material in the Collage collection.

title: Matador
binding: Hardcover, sewn binding, with attached booklet
description:
Matador borrows its title from the bullfighter's trick of concealing a blade inside a cape, using that image of hidden intent to frame a book about escape and the erasure of evidence.

Nicolas Hosteing sequences photographs of motorcycle and car riders burning rubber into full-bleed landscapes thick with fog or smoke, then closes with a series of helmet studies shot from shifting angles, so that concealment and disclosure keep trading places across the book. Études Books published it in Paris in 2012 as the third title in its Blue Books series, a clothbound hardcover with sewn binding and an attached stapled booklet carrying a text by Julien Perez, in a numbered edition of 300 copies.

Hosteing, born in 1985 and based in Paris, studied art history at Bordeaux and photography at the University of Paris 8. Matador belongs to a body of work built around fiction, staged evidence, and the unreliability of the photographic document, continuing the Blue Books series' interest in young French photographers working at the edge of narrative.
notes: Third title in Études Books' Blue Books series. Numbered hardcover edition of 300 copies with an attached stapled booklet carrying Julien Perez's text. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Travel for the Adventurous and Self-Involved
Peter Hujar: A Retrospective
description:
Peter Hujar: A Retrospective is the catalogue published by Scalo in 1994 to accompany the first major museum retrospective of the photographer's work, organized by the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam and Fotomuseum Winterthur.

Edited by Urs Stahel and Hripsimé Visser with a critical essay by Max Kozloff, the volume gathers Hujar's portraits of cultural figures from his downtown New York circle—including Susan Sontag, William S. Burroughs, David Wojnarowicz, John Waters, and Andy Warhol—alongside his unsentimental studies of farm animals, dogs, seascapes, and architectural interiors.

Hujar (1934–1987) photographed his subjects with what one writer called "undramatic concentration," pursuing essences rather than personality and treating animals, landscapes, and people with the same formal gravity. Released seven years after Hujar's death from AIDS-related illness, this catalogue marked the beginning of the international institutional recognition that had largely eluded him during his lifetime, and it remains the foundational survey publication on his work.
tags: Photography, Peter Hujar, Portraits, New York City, Downtown Scene, Animals, Landscapes, Queer Culture, 1970s, 1980s, Scalo, Retrospective, Catalogue
notes: Catalogue for the touring retrospective Peter Hujar organized by the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam and Fotomuseum Winterthur, 1994 — the first major posthumous museum survey of Hujar's photography. English-language edition published by Scalo (Zürich/Berlin/New York) German edition published as "Peter Hujar: Eine Retrospektive" with separate ISBN 9783980385107. Edited by Urs Stahel (then director of Fotomuseum Winterthur) and Hripsimé Visser (curator of photography at the Stedelijk). Contains 128 illustrations across 207 pages 9.5 × 11.5 inches (24 × 30 cm), hardcover with dust jacket.

title: Love & Lust
contributors: Jeffrey Fraenkel (introduction), Vince Aletti (essay), Stephen Koch, Fran Lebowitz (interview)
description:
Peter Hujar: Love & Lust is the first monograph dedicated to Hujar's photographs of eroticism and intimacy, published by Fraenkel Gallery in 2014 in conjunction with the exhibition of the same name.

Made between 1969 and 1986, the thirty-six tritone plates gather Hujar's male and female nudes, embraces, and unguarded studio portraits—work that, in the words of the gallery, has come to define a certain era in New York and is widely considered to be his finest and most radical. Jeffrey Fraenkel introduces the volume Vince Aletti contributes a newly commissioned essay placing Hujar's work alongside the downtown New York scene of artists, writers, and performers he photographed Stephen Koch contextualizes Hujar's relationship to friends and lovers and a candid interview with Fran Lebowitz closes the book.

Hujar (1934–1987) photographed his subjects with the same exacting black-and-white tonalities and unsentimental gaze that distinguished his portraits and animal studies, and Love & Lust assembles, for the first time in book form, the side of his practice most closely tied to the body.
tags: Photography, Peter Hujar, Nudes, Eroticism, Portraits, New York City, Downtown Scene, Queer Culture, 1970s, 1980s, Fraenkel Gallery, Tritone
notes: Published by Fraenkel Gallery on the occasion of the exhibition Peter Hujar: Love & Lust at Fraenkel Gallery, San Francisco, January 4–March 8, 2014. First monograph devoted specifically to Hujar's photographs dealing with sex and eroticism, drawn from work made between 1969 and 1986. Thirty-six tritone reproductions, 11 × 14 inches, softcover with slipcase. Hujar (1934–1987) is held in major collections including MoMA, the Whitney, the Museum of Fine Arts Houston, and SFMOMA.

title: Red Flower, The Women of Okinawa
Lingering Ghosts
description:
Lingering Ghosts collects Sam Ivin's portraits of 28 people from 28 countries then waiting on asylum decisions in the UK, their eyes scratched out of every print.

Ivin began the project in 2013 at a drop-in centre in Cardiff while still a documentary photography student, later extending it across England; his sitters, from Albania, Eritrea, Kashmir, Palestine, Syria, Zimbabwe, and elsewhere, had by then been waiting between five months and 21 years for their applications to be resolved. Ivin scratched the c-type prints by hand with sandpaper and a knife, erasing the eyes to stand for the state of limbo asylum seekers are held in, neither seen nor able to move forward. The book reproduces the full series and opens with the text of Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which guarantees the right to seek asylum; it was published by Fabrica in a first edition of 500 copies.

Ivin is a UK documentary photographer whose work focuses on social issues and the people living inside them; Lingering Ghosts, developed after he was selected in a Magnum/Ideas Tap competition for young photographers, remains his best-known project and has been exhibited and published internationally since its release.
notes: Published by Fabrica, Treviso, in a first edition of 500 copies. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: A Series of Utterly Improbable, Yet Extraordinary Renditions
publisher: Serpentine Galleries, the Store X, Julia Stoschek Collection, and Koenig Books
edition_printrun: 117 color and 51 b&w images. Exhibition catalogue. Design by OSK
contributors: Fred Moten, Tina M. Campt, Ernest Hardy, John Akomfrah, and many others
description:
Over the past three decades, the American filmmaker, cinematographer and artist, Arthur Jafa, has developed a dynamic and multidisciplinary career that is centred upon questions of identity and race.

Jafa creates films, artefacts and happenings that reference and question the universal and specific articulations of Black being. Through his research, he asks how we might identify a specific set of aesthetics that is modelled on the centrality of Black music to America's cultural history. Building upon Jafa's image-based practice, this volume comprises a series of visual sequences that are cut and juxtaposed across its pages.

The artist has been collecting and working from a set of source books since the 1990s, seeking to trace and map unwritten histories and narratives relating to black life. Punctuating this visual material is a series of commissioned texts partnered with a rich compendium of essays, short stories and poetry that has informed Jafa's artistic practice. This catalogue is published to accompany Arthur Jafa's exhibition at the Serpentine Galleries (8 June – 10 September 2017) that travelled to the Julia Stoschek Collection in Berlin (11 February – 25 November 2018).
tags: Black Artists, Exhibition Catalogues, Black Identity, African American Art, Contemporary Art, Photography, Film

title: PRINT / Issue Two
binding: Softcover, perfect bound, in corrugated cardboard box
contributors: David Sims (Photographer), Jamie Hawkesworth (Photographer), Zoë Ghertner (Photographer), Hugo Scott (Photographer), Terry Richardson (Photographer), Ari Marcopoulos (Photographer), Bill Henson (Photographer), Colin Dodgson (Photographer), Karim Sadli (Photographer), Suzanne Koller (Contributor), Spike Jonze (Contributor)
description:
PRINT / Issue Two is the second issue of the fashion magazine produced by stylist Francesca Burns and creative director Christopher Simmonds, a single object that treats a magazine as a physical archive rather than a stack of pages.

Issued in a numbered edition of 1,000, the issue arrives as a thick, perfect-bound volume packed inside a corrugated cardboard box together with additional zines, posters and badges. Photography comes from a large roster of contributors including David Sims, Jamie Hawkesworth, Zoë Ghertner, Terry Richardson, Ari Marcopoulos, Bill Henson, Colin Dodgson and Karim Sadli, alongside written contributions; no page numbering or masthead conventions structure the issue.

PRINT grew out of Burns's work as a fashion editor and Simmonds's practice as a creative director, positioning the magazine closer to an artist's edition than to a newsstand title. Its object-based distribution — sold through art bookshops such as Dashwood Books rather than magazine racks — places Issue Two alongside other independent, small-run fashion publications of the period.
notes: The catalogued author field ("Zoe Ghertner Jamie") is a data-entry merge of two contributing photographers' names (Zoë Ghertner and Jamie Hawkesworth); reassigned to NA VA per house convention since this is a various-contributor magazine, not authored by a single artist. Numbered edition of 1,000 copies, Summer/Autumn 2017. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Four Thousand Threads
description:
Dick Jewell's Four Thousand Threads is a survey of the artist's decades-long habit of collecting and arranging found and appropriated photographs, brought together as digital photography multiplied the volume of images in circulation.

The book groups pictures, drawn from the artist's own archive and from the wider flow of images shared online, into visual "threads": recurring gestures, poses and scenarios such as planking, upside-down stunts, or people photographed with animals, laid out across the page in dense grids. Jewell has described his long-standing interest as being not in single images but in the relationships between them, and the book extends that interest to internet-driven photographic trends. It was self-published by the artist in London in 2015 as a large-format paperback.

Jewell has worked since the 1970s across photography, film and collage, repeatedly returning to vernacular and found imagery (party photobooths, tourist snapshots, amateur pornography) as raw material; Four Thousand Threads continues that practice into the era of social media and mass image-sharing.
tags: Photography, Contemporary Art, Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One
notes: First edition, self-published large-format paperback; page count not independently confirmed this session. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Order of Appearance
description:
A second look into Jim Jocoy's archive of San Francisco punk photographs, this one turned toward the quiet moments between the poses that made his earlier work famous.

Structured in three short chapters spanning 1977 to 1980, Order of Appearance moves like vignettes from a single long night, tracking its subjects from delight to despair, sober to wasted, and back toward morning. Where Jocoy's earlier work captured club-scene style and spectacle, this selection favors tenderness: love, loss, and daily life among the young musicians and fans of the emerging West Coast punk scene. The book is bound in foil-embossed cloth with a tipped-on cover image, 84 pages and 44 full-color plates, published by TBW Books in an edition of 1,000.

Two decades earlier, Jocoy's photographs formed the core of We're Desperate, assembled with Thurston Moore and Marc Jacobs and widely regarded as a defining document of early West Coast punk fashion. Order of Appearance returns to that same archive to draw out what the first book left aside, with a blurb from Moore and a reflection from the photographer Jim Goldberg, who recalled Jocoy's stacks of Polaroids and prints as raw, intimate, and ahead of their time.
notes: Foil-embossed hardcover with tipped-on cover image, edition of 1,000. Companion volume to Jocoy's earlier monograph We're Desperate, drawn from the same 1977-1980 archive. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Photobooks &: a critical companion to the contemporary medium
description:
Matt Johnston's Photobooks & takes stock of the contemporary photobook at a point of real excess, asking what happens to a medium once its supply of makers, small presses, and specialist fairs has outpaced any settled way of reading it.

Across chapters on the photobook's post-digital and post-photographic condition, the purposes of self-publishing, and the practical business of encountering and reading a photobook, Johnston draws on interviews with editors, publishers, and critics across the field alongside his own decade running The Photobook Club project. Onomatopee published the 210-page softcover in 2021 as number 220 in its list, closing with a proposed framework for a more accountable reading culture around the form.

Johnston teaches photography at Coventry University's School of Media and Performing Arts, where his research has tracked the photobook's post-millennium ecology for over a decade. Photobooks & consolidates that research into an extended critical companion, aimed at makers and readers navigating a landscape it argues has grown too large to survey by instinct alone.
notes: Author's name is Matt Johnston (catalogued as "Matt Johnson"), per Onomatopee/Perimeter Books listings. Onomatopee 220. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Ray Johnson c/o
description:
Ray Johnson (1927–1995) was a renowned maker of meticulous collages whose works influenced movements including Pop Art, Fluxus, and Conceptual Art.

Emerging from the interdisciplinary community of artists and poets at Black Mountain College, Johnson was extraordinarily adept at using social interaction as an artistic endeavor and founded a mail art network known as the New York Correspondence School. Drawing on the vast collection of Johnson’s work at the Art Institute of Chicago, this volume gives new shape to our understanding of his artistic practice and features hundreds of pieces that include artist’s books, collages, drawings, mail art, and performance documentation.

In keeping with Johnson’s democratic, rhizomatic, and antihierarchical ethos, this indispensable resource on the artist’s oeuvre contains 700 illustrations, many of them never before published, and twenty-one short essays by various contributors that allow readers to dip into and out of the book in a nonlinear manner.

title: Briney Breezes
description:
Briney Breezes pairs Charles Johnstone's black-and-white topographies with Aaron McElroy's colour interiors, and the two bodies of work together describe a place that never existed built out of one that did.

It is the second title in Series 1, S U N's experimental run of two-artist books issued in editions of 100. Johnstone's contribution comes from an older series photographed between 2004 and 2006; McElroy's, often sexually charged and shot close in, was made in the year before publication. The contrast between the surveyed landscape and the interior carries the sequence across 72 pages, printed digital offset and Japanese stab bound in a linen soft cover.

Johnstone is a New York photographer and publisher whose books include Libby and The Girl in the Fifth Floor Walk-Up, both built around a single recurring subject. McElroy (b. 1978) has published more than a dozen monographs, among them The Devil May Care and Reds, working between abstraction and the nude in pictures he keeps deliberately anonymous and open-ended.
tags: Photography, Collaboration, Landscape, Interiors, Limited Edition, New York, Self-Published
notes: S U N Series 1, second title. One of 100 copies. Sun New York archiving 2026.

title: The Girl in the Fifth Floor Walk-Up
description:
The Girl in the Fifth Floor Walk-Up casts a set of Polaroids as a paperback noir, building a fictional case file around a single recurring character.

Charles Johnstone photographed Heather Malesson, his longtime muse and collaborator, then designed the book around an excerpt from Raymond Chandler's Farewell, My Lovely, using 1940s pulp typography and layout to cast the pictures as evidence in an invented case. The linen hardcover was published by S_U_N_ in New York in 2014 as a signed first edition of 200 copies, 64 pages; a later deluxe octavo edition of 10 numbered copies included an original Polaroid, alongside a trade edition of 150 copies in red cloth signed by both Johnstone and Malesson.

Johnstone, a New York-based photographer who has self-published more than a dozen photo books, built the project as a companion to his earlier Libby, another Polaroid-based book centered on Malesson. Both works trace a documentary and performative collaboration between photographer and subject that has continued across more than a decade.
notes: First edition, signed, one of 200 copies, linen hardcover. Companion to Johnstone's earlier self-published Libby. No ISBN found for this small-press edition. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Libby
edition_printrun: First edition, signed and numbered, limited to 35 copies
description:
Libby gathers Charles Johnstone's Polaroid portraits of Elizabeth Schoettle, made over seven years of an ongoing friendship and collaboration.

The book was initiated in 2011 by 70South's Corey Presha, who was looking through Johnstone's archive of Polaroids and recognized a project distinct from the deadpan architectural typologies of his earlier self-published books. The 47 photographs, made between 2002 and 2009, are interleaved with reproductions of and excerpts from letters Schoettle wrote Johnstone over the same years, so the book reads as an exchange rather than a one-way study; Johnstone has described it as being 'as much about how I saw Libby as how Libby saw herself.' It was published by 70South in 2013 as a signed and numbered hardcover, limited to 35 copies, bound in black cloth with a Polaroid reproduced on the front cover.

Libby was the first of what Johnstone calls his Walkup Series, three books each built around a different woman in his life, followed by The Girl in the Fifth Floor Walkup and Je ne sais quoi. Together they mark a shift in his practice away from the typological documentary projects, such as Thirtyfour Basketball Courts and Brooklyn Fences, that established his earlier work.
notes: Published by 70South in a signed, numbered edition of 35 hardcover copies, black cloth boards with a Polaroid reproduced on the front cover; this copy's own signing and number to be confirmed. Page count and trim size were not given by any source checked. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: JR: Can Art Change the World?
Transformations
description:
The manifold entanglements of African and Western culture are a central motif in the oeuvre of the Algerian-French artist Kader Attia.

The influence of traditional African architecture on European modernism forms the background for his voluminous spatial installations, videos and photographs, as much as the reappropriation of North and South American black music within African Jazz and Pop of the 1960s up to the 1980s.

His work manifests the productivity of dissonance where African masks, stuffed animals, scientific instruments, and historical artifacts seemingly have nothing in common, the artist unearths connections between Europe’s handling of its own colonial history, current migration politics, and the urbanistic realities of its metropolises of today. Based on Kader Attia’s solo show Repair: 5 Acts at the KW Institute for Contemporary Art, Berlin, this publication focuses on works from the years 2008–2013 and places them in a broader art historical concept.
notes: One of two copies in the collection.

title: Surf Goddess: Beauty Meets the Beach
JK Sitting
description:
JK Sitting gathers the vintage photographs of John Kayser, an unknown California photographer who spent decades photographing nude women seated on pies, cakes, fish bowls, cats and vegetables. It was an obsessive private practice that stayed out of sight until after his death.

Designed by Peter Miles and published in a numbered edition of 400 copies, the softcover book reproduces Kayser's staged studio and street pictures, made in and around Los Angeles through the 1960s and '70s, largely without commentary beyond the images themselves. The project came to light only through the photographs Kayser left behind rather than through any exhibition or publication during his lifetime.

Little biographical information about Kayser survives; he worked as an amateur, using his own house and the streets of Los Angeles as sets, and made no attempt to exhibit or publish the pictures collected here. JK Sitting, produced by Peter Miles Studio in association with Steidl, remains the only book to bring this body of work into circulation.
notes: Peter Miles Studio's own project archive lists the book as a Steidl-Miles collaboration; numbered edition of 400 copies, New York, 2016. Little is confirmed about Kayser's biography beyond what the publisher and booksellers describe. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Vicky
description: with tip-in. Vicky: ‘Fucking Glad I met You’ is a personal and raw collection of portraits and mobile phone snapshots shot in the summer of 2020 by Dutch photographer Ilja Keizer. The images were made during an intense journey that led them around Europe in a little over 3 months, with the trip ending in a tiny Polish village where Vicky lives. The result is a highly personal document, including a signed print and various inserts.

title: Passengers
description:
Passengers gathers photographs Dagmar Keller and Martin Wittwer made at a bus station at night while travelling through Poland, of riders seen through the ice-covered windows of an idling coach.

Fogged, stained and lit only by the station's pale lamps, the windows turn each passenger into something closer to a painted figure than a photographic subject — faces softened by condensation, expressions read as melancholy or unguarded joy, distance and intimacy held in the same frame. The book collects 114 colour photographs from the series across 164 pages, published by Spector Books in Leipzig as a clothbound hardcover with dust jacket.

Keller and Wittwer are a Swiss artist duo working primarily in photography and video, frequently focused on transit and waiting — bus stations, airports, the spaces where people are briefly held between destinations. Passengers was followed by a related book, Point de Départ, which turned the same method on commuters boarding buses in Paris.
notes: Work by the Swiss artist duo Dagmar Keller & Martin Wittwer; the catalog's author field had combined the two names into one. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Collecting Colour
description:
A conservator's tour through one of the world's working pigment archives, told by the scientist responsible for keeping it useful to painters, restorers, and historians alike.

Narayan Khandekar directs the Forbes Pigment Collection at Harvard's Straus Center for Conservation and Technical Studies, an array of more than three thousand natural and synthetic colouring agents assembled over a century of technical art research. Collecting Colour traces the origins of individual pigments and their cultural uses, arguing for pigment as a basic material fact underlying any work of art. The book, designed by Thijs Verbeek and printed with high-pigment ink, grew out of Khandekar's Mondrian Lecture delivered in Rotterdam for the Sikkens Prize awarded to designer Hella Jongerius.

Khandekar also directs the Center for the Technical Study of Modern Art and heads the Analytical Laboratory of the Harvard Art Museums. Published by ArtEZ Press as the fourth title in the Sikkens Foundation series, Collecting Colour extends that research past the laboratory into a compact, image-driven volume for a general readership.
notes: Fourth volume in the Sikkens Foundation series; grew out of Khandekar's 2017 Mondrian Lecture. Page count and image totals vary slightly by retailer (136-152 pages cited); figures here follow the publisher's own listing. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Die Buchstaben
description:
Our civilization would be inconceivable without letters. In a meaningful way, words, sentences and scripts are strung together, especially the printed word that shapes our existence.

Anselm Kiefer deals with this power of the word in his work The Letters, to which this publication is dedicated. Sunflowers that grow out of a printing machine, rolls of film that spill on the floor, letters that are scattered on the floor combine to create a space-filling installation. The artist develops an ambiguous symbiosis from the surprising combination of technical object and natural organism. Numerous large-format detailed images enable intensive immersion in this complex, poetic spatial staging.

title: Puss Puss Issue 5
contributors: Heathermary Jackson (Guest Curator), Juergen Teller (Photographer), Gia Coppola (Photographer), Ren Hang (Photographer)
description:
Issue 5 of Puss Puss, the London fashion and culture biannual, was guest-curated by Heathermary Jackson and released with four alternating covers, one of them Sandy Kim's photograph of the artist and actress India Salvor Menuez.

Alongside Kim's cover story, the issue carries Juergen Teller's portrait of Grace Coddington, Gia Coppola's photograph of the model Jane Moseley, and a shoot by Ren Hang, to whom the issue was dedicated following his death earlier that year. Editorial content runs from an interview with the sound artist Michel Gaubert to a profile of the artist Sue Webster, alongside further photography and styling from a rotating list of contributors.

Sandy Kim's photography is built on close, unguarded pictures of friends and lovers, shot on flash-lit film in a snapshot style that carried her from zines and Rookie Mag into fashion and magazine editorial. This issue's cover story, a portrait of India Salvor Menuez, sits within that same body of work, made the same year Kim's photographs began appearing more widely in magazines such as Puss Puss.
notes: Catalogued under photographer Sandy Kim, whose photograph of India Salvor Menuez is one of four alternating covers for this guest-curated issue; other covers by Juergen Teller, Gia Coppola and Ren Hang, to whom the issue was posthumously dedicated. No ISBN/ISSN located for this issue. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Four Oranges, Some Office Buildings, Woman's Legs
Belgravia
binding: Hardcover, paper wrap, tipped-in image, protective jacket
description:
Belgravia collects Karen Knorr's portraits of a London neighborhood's rich and titled residents, each image paired with a scrap of their own speech, so the work turns into a study of power told partly in its subjects' own words.

Made between 1979 and 1981 while Knorr was a student at the Polytechnic of Central London, the series pictures interiors and their occupants at a fixed, neutral distance, closer to inventory than portraiture, with quotations recorded during the sittings running beneath each plate. Stanley/Barker published the complete 26-image series for the first time as a monograph in 2015: a large hardcover of 58 pages, printed on heavy stock and issued in a protective transparent jacket, with an afterword by the artist, in a first edition of 1000 copies.

Knorr's own family lived in Belgravia, and the series' second image is a photograph of her mother and grandmother in their Lowndes Square flat. She followed Belgravia with Gentlemen (1981-1983), photographing London's private clubs; both series were shown together at Tate Britain in 2014-15, and Knorr's later work has continued to examine institutions, class, and power through staged and archival photography.
tags: Photography, Portrait Photography, British Photography, Social Commentary
notes: First monograph publication of the complete 1979-1981 Belgravia series, with an afterword by the artist. First edition of 1000 copies. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Test the West
edition_printrun: Signed and numbered, limited to 150 copies
description:
Test the West is a self-published photobook by Misha Kominek, produced in a signed, numbered edition of 150 copies through his own Berlin imprint.

The softcover volume, bound in yellow cloth, was published by Kominek Gallery in 2017. Its title echoes the German cigarette advertising slogan used to court East German consumers after reunification, a phrase closely tied to Berlin's post-1989 landscape, though the publisher's own description of the book's specific photographic content was not available from the sources checked. It stands as one of four monographs Kominek has produced of his own photography, following First Journey Home (2013) and Strangers in Paradise (2013) and preceding Photocopies from Tokyo (2014).

Misha Kominek is a Polish-born, Berlin-based photographer, publisher, and curator who emigrated to Germany at twelve, studied photography at IEFC in Barcelona, and founded Kominek Books + Gallery in 2007 after running SCOPE magazine from 2001. His own photographic work, including First Journey Home, a 1997 road trip retracing his childhood in Poland, often returns to questions of displacement and return between Eastern and Western Europe.
notes: Catalogued title corrected from 'Test The Wind' to 'Test the West', the book's actual title. Self-published by the artist's own Kominek Gallery, Berlin, signed and numbered, edition of 150; no ISBN identified. Page count, dimensions, and a publisher description of the photographic content were not found in the sources checked. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Japan Works
description:
Aglaia Konrad’s photographic work probes the social, cultural, economic, political, and historical parameters that inform architecture and urbanism.

Japan Works is the result of her journey through Japan in the autumn of 2019. Using a pre-compiled list of places with exceptional architecture, Konrad took thousands of photos in Tokyo, Itoigawa, Kyoto, Nagoya and Osaka.

In addition to mostly iconic, post-war Metabolist architecture, Konrad also took a large number of photos of nonspecific architectural moments and infrastructure that, with the same intensity, give their own impression of the architectural landscape in Japan. Free associations of full-page photographs alternate with contact sheets documenting her itinerary. These are informed by postscript glosses written by architect and critic Julian Worrall.

title: THE NEW YORK YEARS 1971 to 1994 (regular edition) – Eric Kroll
Barbara Kruger : Thinking of You, I Mean Me, I Mean You
publisher: DelMonico Books/Los Angeles County Museum of Art
description:
Since the mid-1970s, Barbara Kruger (born 1945) has been interrogating consumer culture in works that often combine visual and written language.

In her singular graphic style, Kruger probes aspects of identity, desire and consumerism that are embedded in our everyday lives. This volume traces her continuously evolving practice to reveal how she adapts her work in accordance with the moment, site and context.

The book features a range of striking images—from her analogue paste-ups of the 1980s to digital productions of the last two decades, including new works produced on the occasion of the exhibition. Also featured are singular works in vinyl, her large-scale room wraps, multichannel videos, site-specific installations and commissioned works

title: Black Threads from Meng Chiao
description:
20 tritone plates. In a true collaboration, Justine Kurland and John Yau shared photographs and poems throughout the making of Black Threads from Meng Chiao, each reacting to the work of the other many times over.

The result is a revelation for each: Kurland's intimate interior black-and-white images offer a new side of an artist known for large-format color pictures of landscapes both peopled and not Yau's spare, precise language is given room to reveal multiple layers of meaning over the three distinct formal sections that comprise the title poem. A friendship between these two was born several years ago after Yau - also a renowned critic - wrote about Kurland's photographs, but an artistic partnership wasn't contemplated until they recently found themselves in similar mental and emotional situations born of quite different logistical circumstances. Yau was housebound while recuperating from knee and neck surgeries, and Kurland was off the road (her accustomed place of working), caring for her son in the East Village. It was, in Kurland's words, a period of "house arrest, or being shipwrecked" for both.

Kurland turned away from the 4x5 film camera and its slow working process to embrace the immediacy of a digital SLR and its instant results, producing tight interior shots as claustrophobic and caged as she felt. Through the magic of email, she shared the raw results with Yau, who responded both to the specifics of her images and to the way he was feeling as a person whose full, unfettered mobility had been temporarily removed from him. The idea of Meng Chiao's Black Threads came from that poet's late poems, in which he wrote sequences comprised of interconnected (or, to Yau's thinking, echoing) lyrics. Yau started the sequence after he was unable to find the book in his library, and took this as a sign to begin writing in the space of its absence. In turn, the photographer internalized the poet's ideas to spur the making of new pictures, and the process was repeated several times. Kurland says the result is like "staring out a window at a brick wall across the alley" - finding some way to deal with adverse situations and making sense of them through the creation of something new in the world.

title: Concrete and Sex
description:
Concrete and Sex pairs nude snapshots with the post-industrial, post-Soviet architecture of Kyiv, Sasha Kurmaz's third publication and a clear statement of the juxtaposition that runs through his early work.

Printed as a 32-page stapled booklet in an edition of 500, the book sets youthful nude bodies against concrete surfaces, political icons and flags. Kurmaz calls his earliest self-published works "funzines," and Concrete and Sex carries that directness: it moves between raw eroticism and a more pointed commentary on ideology stamped onto the built environment.

Kurmaz (born 1986, Kyiv) works across photography, collage, video and public intervention, and has continued to build conceptual artists' books from found and archival material alongside his own images. Concrete and Sex, published by Pogobooks in Berlin in 2013, belongs to the run of small, quickly produced zines through which he first circulated his photography before moving into gallery and institutional contexts.
notes: First edition of 500 copies, Pogobooks, Berlin, 2013; some retailers list the title inverted as "Sex and Concrete." Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Event Horizon
binding: Softcover, Japanese binding, foldout poster dust jacket
description:
Quentin Lacombe's Event Horizon takes its title from the boundary around a black hole beyond which no event can be observed, and builds a private cosmology out of photography, digital rendering and collage.

Full-bleed pictures of trees, animals, unidentifiable technology and houses lit in surreal night colour open the book, giving way gradually to two- and three-image collages that wrap around the edge of the page as the sequence pushes toward its own horizon line. Lacombe combined photograms, 3D renders and studio photographs to blur where documentary description ends and invented image begins. First self-published in 2016, the book was reissued in 2017 by the Paris publisher RVB Books as a 118-page softcover with a foldout poster dust jacket and Japanese binding, carrying 72 colour photographs and a short text by the artist.

Lacombe, born in France in 1990, trained first in architecture before completing a photography degree at ECAL in Lausanne; Event Horizon, his first book, was shortlisted for the Aperture–Paris Photo First PhotoBook Award and was later staged as an immersive installation in the group exhibition Transformer: A Rebirth of Wonder in London.
notes: Originally self-published in 2016 (shortlisted for the Aperture–Paris Photo First PhotoBook Award) before this RVB Books edition. Cover photographed at an angle by the seller and cropped; edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: A Field Measure Survey of American Architecture
description:
Drawing from the nearly half a million photographs and documents comprising the Historic American Buildings Survey held in the US Library of Congress, this book constructs a fictional ‘one-way road trip’ across the United States, weaving north and south across the Mason-Dixon line while tacking west.

In A Field Measure Survey of American Architecture, Jeffrey Ladd uses the HABS archive as a surrogate in order to manifest a portrait of his former country at a moment when its democracy seems imperiled.

title: The Mechanism
description:
A melancholic black-and-white sequence that treats the contemporary city as evidence of a story already underway, one about surveillance, infrastructure, and the machinery threaded through daily life.

Mårten Lange made The Mechanism across multiple cities, cutting back and forth between tight architectural details and wider urban views to build what reads as a filmic, almost narrative sequence. Rather than documenting any single place, the photographs use recurring structural motifs, grids, scaffolding, surveillance apparatus, glass and steel, to trace how technological development presses on ordinary experience, landing somewhere between reportage and speculative fiction. The book was published by MACK in 2017 as a hardcover bound in Japanese paper, 96 pages of tritone plates at 22 x 28 cm.

Lange (b. 1984, Gothenburg) studied photography at the University of Gothenburg and the University for the Creative Arts in Farnham. The Mechanism followed earlier MACK and Études Books titles including Another Language and Citizen, along with self-published volumes such as Machina and Chicxulub, extending Lange's recurring interest in built and natural structure as a way of reading the present.
notes: Hardcover bound in Japanese paper, tritone plates. Page count and trim size differ slightly by retailer (96pp/22x28cm per MACK, Shashasha, and Ensemble vs. 108pp/28x20.5cm per Perimeter); figures here follow the publisher's own listing. No text contributor or essayist found despite a flag on the source list; edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Byways & Through Lines
description:
Byways & Through Lines treats the photobook as a set of loosely related paths rather than a single narrative, letting drawing, scanning, and photography sit side by side without settling into one method.

Pierre Le Hors builds the book from images made by several means at once: pencil marks and paint alongside pictures produced on a flatbed scanner and more conventional photographs, sequenced so that connections between spreads bisect and separate rather than accumulate toward a single subject. Dashwood Books published it in 2013 as a 4-color offset, saddle-stitched softcover of 44 pages, in an edition of 500, as part of its ongoing Dashwood Book Series of small-run artist publications.

Le Hors, born in France in 1981 and based in Brooklyn, graduated from the ICP-Bard MFA program in 2010. Byways & Through Lines followed his earlier Firework Studies (Hassla, 2011) and continues his interest in the photobook as a physical, constructed object rather than a straightforward vehicle for images.
notes: Part of Dashwood Books' Dashwood Book Series of small-run artist publications. No ISBN found for this small-press edition. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Grassland
description:
Grassland follows a year inside Humboldt County's cannabis-growing community, photographed by an artist working under the pseudonym H. Lee.

Lee lived among growers in the towering redwood country of Northern California, gaining access on the promise that the work would be published under a pseudonym and that anyone who wished to remain unidentified would have their face concealed. The 112-page hardcover moves through a full growing season, from fields and greenhouses to drying houses and trim rooms, presenting cannabis as agricultural labor and cash crop rather than as spectacle, with 75 color plates and captions gathered at the back. Published by Kehrer Verlag in 2014 with texts by Glenn O'Brien and Emily Brady, author of Humboldt: Life on America's Marijuana Frontier, the book appeared as California's decades-old prohibition culture was giving way to legal cultivation.

Working anonymously let Lee document a community still wary of exposure even as its economy moved toward legitimacy, producing an insider's record of a subculture rarely photographed from the inside. Grassland was named among the best photobooks of 2014 by several publications on its release.
notes: Photographer works under the pseudonym 'H. Lee' to protect the identities of the growers photographed. Published in a regular signed edition alongside limited deluxe and collector's editions with hemp packaging and prints, not represented by this copy. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Women
binding: Hardcover with dust jacket and obi
description:
Women collects nude and intimate portraits Saul Leiter made of women in his life across two decades, photographs that stayed in his East Village apartment until they surfaced after his death.

Published by the Japanese label Space Shower Books in 2018, the 160-page hardcover reproduces images taken between the late 1940s and late 1960s in the homes and private spaces Leiter shared with his subjects, scanned from his original silver prints, alongside a small number of his painted nudes. An eight-page essay by Michael Parillo of the Saul Leiter Foundation, printed in Japanese and English, accompanies the plates, and the edition carries the obi band and reference paper typical of Japanese photobook production.

Leiter (1923–2013) spent decades photographing New York in color for magazines while working largely unrecognized as a fine artist until a wave of late-career attention beginning in the early 2000s. Women was published the same year as the related Steidl title In My Room, both drawn from the archive of nudes Leiter kept private, and both realizing a book of nude studies he had first planned, but never completed, in the 1970s.
notes: Published by Space Shower Books, Tokyo, 2018, with obi band; distinct from the Steidl title In My Room (also 2018), which draws on the same body of nude photographs. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: All About Saul Leiter
contributors: Margit Erb (Text), Pauline Vermare (Text), Motoyuki Shibata (Text)
description:
All About Saul Leiter surveys the full arc of Saul Leiter's work, from the street photographs he began making in New York in the 1940s to the fashion pictures, nudes and late paintings that followed.

Drawing on some 200 images, the book moves through Leiter's early black-and-white street photography, his pioneering colour work made on Kodachrome and shot largely around his own neighbourhood of the East Village, and the commercial photography he produced for Harper's Bazaar, Esquire and other magazines, interspersed with quotations from the artist. It was compiled with texts by Margit Erb, Pauline Vermare and Motoyuki Shibata, first published in Japan by Seigensha in 2017 and issued the following year in this English-language paperback edition by Thames & Hudson.

Leiter (1923–2013) largely withdrew from professional photography in the 1980s and was rediscovered only after the 2006 monograph Early Color brought his Kodachrome street work to wide attention; All About Saul Leiter extends that rediscovery into a fuller picture of a practice that ran across editorial fashion work, unpublished colour photographs and painting.
notes: UK (Thames & Hudson) edition; the book was also released in editions from RM/Seigensha (US), Editorial RM (Spain), Will Books (Korea) and Éditions Textuel (France), and originally published in Japan by Seigensha in 2017. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.
