title: Roy Lichtenstein: History in the Making, 1948-1960
Lichtenstein Posters
description:
A survey of the poster as a working medium for Roy Lichtenstein, tracing how the same benday-dot vocabulary that defined his paintings moved into printed ephemera for exhibitions, films, and public causes.

The book gathers 68 full-color posters spanning Lichtenstein's career, opening with the poster he designed for his first exhibition at Leo Castelli Gallery in 1962 and closing with the last one he completed, the year of his death. A further section draws on a private collection of ephemera, reproducing posters and flyers produced worldwide using Lichtenstein's motifs for music and film festivals, theater, museums, and public-service messages. Jürgen Döring, curator of the exhibition the book accompanied, contributes an essay tracing Lichtenstein's movement between low and high culture, alongside an illustrated biography.

Originally published by Prestel for an exhibition at the Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg in 2008-2009, Lichtenstein Posters sits alongside the artist's paintings and sculpture as evidence of how thoroughly Pop art's commercial vocabulary ran through his practice, from gallery announcements to mass-produced flyers.
tags: Art, Pop Art, Prints, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Originally published for a 2008-2009 exhibition at the Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg, curated by Jürgen Döring, who wrote the accompanying essay; this 2019 Prestel paperback is a reissue of that catalogue. Multiple prior editions exist (2009 hardcover, 2013 paperback) with the same page count. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Greene Street Mural
contributors: Camille Morineau (Essay), Robert McKeever (Interview), Brian O'Leary (Interview), Alison McDonald (Interview), Bob Adelman (Photographer)
description:
In December 1983, Roy Lichtenstein painted an eighteen-by-ninety-six-and-a-half-foot mural directly onto the walls of Leo Castelli's Greene Street gallery, a temporary work destroyed at the close of its six-week run. Gagosian's 2015 exhibition recreated it at full scale, introducing the piece to a generation that had only known it through photographs.

This book documents both versions, layering the mural's signature motifs, marbled composition-notebook patterns, cartoon brushstrokes, Swiss cheese, filing cabinets and folding chairs, across 180 pages. It includes an essay by the curator Camille Morineau, a conversation between Lichtenstein's former studio assistants Robert McKeever and Brian O'Leary and Gagosian's Alison McDonald, and photographs by Bob Adelman documenting the original mural's creation in 1983.

Lichtenstein (1923-1997) built his reputation on the comic-derived Pop paintings of the early 1960s, but continued experimenting with scale and site through the 1980s, of which the Greene Street Mural was among the most ambitious and most fleeting. The book situates the piece within a fuller account of his large-scale wall projects across his career.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Documents both the destroyed 1983 mural at Leo Castelli Gallery and Gagosian's 2015 recreation at 555 West 24th Street; published by Gagosian, distributed by Rizzoli. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Girls
contributors: Richard Hamilton (Text), Jeff Koons (Conversation with Dorothy Lichtenstein), Richard Prince (Artist's book contribution)
description:
Girls documents an exhibition built around one of Pop Art's founding subjects: the anonymous, mass-produced face of the romance comic heroine.

The catalogue reproduces fifteen paintings and two ceramic sculptures shown at Gagosian's 980 Madison Avenue space in New York in 2008, alongside related studies and the newspaper and comic-book source images Roy Lichtenstein worked from when he began this body of work in the summer of 1961. The book runs 94 pages and includes a conversation between Dorothy Lichtenstein and Jeff Koons, a tribute by Richard Hamilton, and an artist's book contribution by Richard Prince, with graphic design by Graphic Thought Facility; it was co-published by Gagosian and Yale University Press.

Lichtenstein (1923-1997) built his reputation on paintings that translated the Ben-Day dots and cropped compositions of commercial printing into fine art, and the women of his romance-comic paintings, alongside Warhol's celebrities, became one of Pop Art's central images of mass-media femininity. Girls revisits that early-1960s body of work through the Gagosian exhibition and the ongoing scholarship of the Roy Lichtenstein Foundation.
tags: Art, Pop Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Published to accompany Gagosian's Girls exhibition, May 12-June 28, 2008, at 980 Madison Avenue, New York; co-published with Yale University Press. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Tender Mint
description:
Tender Mint gathers three years of photographs Lynn Alleva Lilley made after moving to Amman, Jordan, with her husband and two children in 2011.

Far from home while her father was ill, Lilley used photography to make an unfamiliar country legible, photographing Jordanian citizens alongside Syrian and Iraqi refugees, animals kept in private zoos and farms, bird migrations, a biodynamic vineyard near the Syrian border, a veterinary clinic in Petra, and landscapes at the Dead Sea. The 144-page softcover, bound in linen, interleaves these images with two poems, by Jane Hirshfield and Samih al-Qasim, and two of Lilley's own personal anecdotes, building a picture of displacement, entrapment, and adaptation alongside unexpected beauty. It was published by The Eriskay Connection in Breda in 2017, designed by Rob van Hoesel, in a first edition of 750 copies funded in part through Kickstarter.

Tender Mint was Lilley's debut photobook. An American photographer drawn to place and to the photobook as an intimate form, she has continued to work at the intersection of personal experience, displacement, and landscape in the projects that followed it.
notes: Published by The Eriskay Connection, Breda, in a first edition of 750 copies, part-funded via Kickstarter; the artist's debut photobook. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: A Different Vision on Fashion Photography
Scugnizzi
description:
A photobook by the English photographer Brett Lloyd, Scugnizzi documents the street kids who overrun the town beaches of Naples, Italy each summer. The project marked the start of Lloyd's long engagement with the city.

Shot over two extended summers, the black-and-white photographs are vignettes of daily drama on the beach: local kids Lloyd described as "cunning and lively," caught mid-motion against a backdrop of lampposts and festival decorations. The pictures channel the neorealist Italian cinema of the 1940s and the bawdy Naples that drew Caravaggio into exile. The book was edited with Another Man creative director Alister Mackie and designed by Francesca Grassi, published by Dashwood Books, New York, in a softcover first edition limited to 500 copies.

Lloyd went on to spend five years living in and photographing Naples, resulting in his later, more expansive book Napoli, Napoli, Napoli, published by Mörel; Scugnizzi remains the project's origin point.
notes: Catalogue title carried a "(PRE-ORDER A COPY)" annotation; stripped for the record. Softcover first edition, limited to 500 copies. No ISBN identified — small-press photobook. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Damaged Negatives
description:
Glen Luchford's Damaged Negatives turns an archival disaster into the substance of the book itself, presenting fashion and portrait photographs that were left to rot in a flooded storage unit for months before anyone noticed.

Luchford shot for Vogue, The Face and Arena through the 1990s, building a reputation for clean, narrative-driven fashion photography. The negatives collected here, including images of a young Kate Moss, were never meant to survive in this state: standing water, humidity and mold left oxidation blooms, burn-like marks and cigarette-hole patterns across the frames, obscuring faces and grounds alike. Rather than discard the ruined archive, Luchford and Dashwood Books published it as found, reproduced in duotone across sixty unpaginated pages in a softcover first edition of 1,000 copies.

The result sits apart from Luchford's commercial work, closer to the damaged-material tradition explored by photographers who treat chemical accident as authorship. Damaged Negatives was published in 2013 by Dashwood Books, New York, with design and creative direction by DJA.
tags: Photography, Fashion, Black and White Photography
notes: Softcover, unpaginated, first edition of 1000 copies. No ISBN was assigned to this Dashwood Books release. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Seventh Dog
description:
The Seventh Dog is Danny Lyon's own account of a fifty-year career, told backward from the present to his 1960s beginnings — as much a self-portrait in fragments as a survey of one of American documentary photography's defining bodies of work.

Working in reverse chronology, Lyon interleaves black-and-white and color photographs with letters, contact sheets, collages, and other personal ephemera, much of it printed here for the first time, alongside his own written commentary. The 240-page hardcover moves from recent work back through his years in New Mexico and Haiti, his filmmaking, The Destruction of Lower Manhattan, Conversations with the Dead, and The Bikeriders, arriving finally at his photographs of the early-1960s civil rights movement, made as the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee's first staff photographer. Phaidon designed the cover as a collaged tribute to Kelton Labs, Lyon's printer of several decades.

Lyon (b. 1942) helped establish the immersive, participatory strain of American documentary photography, living for extended periods among the people he photographed rather than observing from outside. The Seventh Dog joins the library's holdings of Conversations with the Dead and The Bikeriders, supplying the connective narrative between Lyon's individual bodies of work in his own voice.
tags: Photography, Documentary Photography, Civil Rights, Memoir
notes: First published by Phaidon in 2014. Retailer listings mostly give 240 pages; one review (Conscientious Photography Magazine) cites 228. Elisabeth Sussman contributes text. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Danny Lyon: Message to the Future
contributors: Elisabeth Sussman (Essay), Alexander Nemerov (Essay), Ed Halter (Essay), Danica Willard Sachs (Essay)
description:
Danny Lyon: Message to the Future is the first in-depth examination of Danny Lyon, a central figure in postwar American photography whose immersive, participatory approach to picture-making redefined documentary practice.

The catalogue accompanies the first comprehensive retrospective of Lyon's career in twenty-five years, organized by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco and presented at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 2016 before traveling to San Francisco, Winterthur, and Berlin. Across 288 pages and roughly 250 illustrations, it surveys Lyon's work with the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, the Chicago Outlaws motorcycle club, and the Texas prison system, alongside his films and photomontages, with essays by Julian Cox and Elisabeth Sussman and further contributions on his work in Knoxville, his films, and his earliest published books.

Lyon (b. 1942) worked as an embedded participant rather than a detached observer, a method he carried from The Bikeriders and Conversations with the Dead through his later work in film and collage; this volume situates that body of work within a single, sustained account of his career.
tags: Photography, Documentary Photography, Exhibition Catalog, Film
notes: Retrospective catalogue; a separate edition of this exhibition traveled to the de Young (Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco), Fotomuseum Winterthur, and C/O Berlin. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Bikeriders
description:
Danny Lyon's The Bikeriders is a founding document of American New Journalism photography: a first-person portrait of the Chicago Outlaws Motorcycle Club made by a photographer who rode with them rather than watched from outside.

Between 1963 and 1967, Lyon joined the Outlaws as a member, photographing initiations, funerals, cross-country runs, and ordinary downtime, then paired the pictures with transcribed interviews in the riders' own words. First published in 1968, the book combines 48 duotone black-and-white photographs with oral history, a hybrid of documentary photography and reportage that anticipated the immersive nonfiction of the following decade. This edition, reissued by Aperture, restores the original journal-sized format and sequence.

Lyon began his career photographing the civil rights movement for SNCC before turning his camera on the incarcerated in Conversations with the Dead and on New York's vanishing built environment in The Destruction of Lower Manhattan. The Bikeriders established the embedded, participant-observer method that runs through his later work and inspired the 2024 feature film of the same name.
notes: Aperture reissue of the 1968 original; edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Saša J. Maechtig: Systems, Structures, Strategies
description:
Saa J. Mächtig is one of the most prominent creative forces in Slovenian industrial design.

His best-known and most influential work is Kiosk K67, whose modular design and complex system of elements represents the very essence both of his larger design philosophy and practice. Mächtigs approach is systemic, with individual products and design strategies consistently conceived as part of a wider system that can develop, grow and change.

According to him, urban space should not be furnished with individual, self-sufficient objects, but should instead offer open systems of flexible structures to create active areas that facilitate daily rituals, exchange of information and the participation of all. The publication reflects Mächtigs systemic thought, interdisciplinary work, concept designs and end products, while showcasing the process of creation, from first concepts and project variations to extensive research, testing in public space and marketing campaigns.

title: Welcome 2 my Room
description:
Maki made these portraits by pointing a Polaroid camera at his own computer screen, photographing the sex workers he was talking to on a Philippine webcam site.

Welcome 2 my Room was published in Marseille in May 2010 by Média Immédiat, the mini-photobook imprint Maki founded that year, in an edition of 72 signed and numbered copies: 28 pages, 24 pictures, digitally printed on satin stock at 10.5 x 7.6 cm. The starting point was a Philippine peep-show site he found in 2006, where several hundred people worked from home or from shared studios; over the years that followed the exchange became something other than a transaction, and the pictures (Polaroids of a screen, twice removed from the person in front of the lens) hold that ambiguity rather than resolving it. The title was issued as a trilogy of three mini books, and separately as a loose-leaf portfolio in a slipcase.

Born in Marseille in 1964, Maki is a photographer, publisher, DJ and composer of electroacoustic music who has exhibited in Belgium, Switzerland, Japan, Canada and the Czech Republic. Média Immédiat, which he founded in 2010, has since published Onaka Koji, Morten Andersen, Ed Templeton and Ichiba Daisuke. His other books include Gûyu — Allegory and Timeshow Cinq from Timeshow Press, and Mono Vol. 1 from Gomma Books.
notes: Issued both as a trilogy of three mini photobooks from Média Immédiat and as a separate portfolio edition of 30 numbered copies in a cardboard slipcase holding loose inkjet prints and an original Polaroid. Edition to be verified against the copy. Cover to be photographed. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: New Reproductions
contributors: Mirene Arsanios (Essay), Maria Fusco (Essay), Karl Larsson (Essay), Sidsel Nelund (Essay), Jonas Zakaitis (Essay)
description:
New Reproductions is an artist book by the Croatian artist David Maljković (b. 1973, Rijeka), published to accompany his solo exhibition of the same name at the Contemporary Art Centre (CAC), Vilnius, from 19 November 2013 to 12 January 2014.

The exhibition presented six new reworkings of earlier Maljković projects — spanning animation, slide projection, collage, and sculpture — assembling filiations between works separated by time and by the artist's shifting concerns with re-reading, remembering, incompleteness, and exhaustion as artistic positions. The book, designed by Åbäke and edited by exhibition curator Jurga Daubaraitė, reproduces Maljković's collaged images alongside poetic and fictional text responses commissioned from Mirene Arsanios, Maria Fusco, Karl Larsson, Sidsel Nelund, and Jonas Žakaitis.

Maljković's work examines the politics of memory and how historical narratives are constructed to serve present-day social and economic agendas, frequently returning to the turbulent twentieth-century history of Croatia and the unrealized futures of Yugoslav modernism. New Reproductions extends that inquiry by literally re-presenting and recombining his own earlier images and objects.
notes: Published on the occasion of the artist's solo exhibition New Reproductions, Contemporary Art Centre (CAC), Vilnius, 19 Nov 2013–12 Jan 2014. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Local Time
publisher: The Center for Ongoing Reasearch & Projects

title: A Minor Wrong Doing (signed)
binding: Softcover with embossing and silver ink on black paper
description:
Slowly but steadily we become immersed in what Henrik Malmström saw and photographed from the window of his living room.

The pages of A Minor Wrongdoing unfold as a hypnotic sequence of candid shots taken at the neighbourhood of St. Georg in Hamburg, between 2011 and 2014. Hundreds of them, they record the last remains of street life in an urban area that is currently undergoing fierce gentrification after recent official law enforcement against street-based prostitution. Malmström used a cheap digital camera forcing its ISO levels to reproduce in each scene the raw effect of a surveillance cam.

The grainy monochromatic material of his voyeuristic enterprise has been put together in this voluminous book replicating a messy police report archive. Printed in sharp dots, the grain adds a grade of unprecedented abstraction and beauty to the sequence whereas the quantity of images breaks with the conventional linear story structure. There is an uncanny feel in it. And obsession: the unconfessed obsession of a photographer who happened to be in the right place at the right time. We do not get to see much of what he photographed but we can still imagine pretty much happening in this obscure underworld of transactions.
tags: Street Photography, Photography, Hamburg, St. Georg, Surveillance, Gentrification, Urban Life, Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One

title: Life is One Live it Well
description:
Henrik Malmström's Life is One Live it Well documents the barroom culture of St. Georg, a Hamburg district long associated with street prostitution and, more recently, rapid gentrification.

Over four years Malmström frequented bars including Mickey Mouse, Windstärke 11 and Zum Frühaufsteher, befriending the regulars, bartenders and clients until he was accepted as one of them. Shot in close-up color with on-camera flash, the photographs read like a drinker's own snapshots: balloons, velvet cushions, faded wallpaper and spilled champagne stand in for a fading era, while the people Malmström photographs, often dismissed by outsiders as the neighborhood's prostitutes, pimps and petty criminals, appear instead as people wanting company, a drink and a bit of peace. The publisher has likened the tone to Rainer Werner Fassbinder's fatalism crossed with Aki Kaurismäki's deadpan warmth.

The book is the first installment of Malmström's St. Georg trilogy, continued with A Minor Wrongdoing and OK Cloth Shop, both also published by Kominek after the Finnish photographer relocated to Hamburg. This copy is signed and numbered from the edition of 375.
notes: Embossed hardback with tipped-in cover image; signed and numbered, edition of 375. Catalogue annotation "(signed)" refers to this copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: People in Cars
description:
People in Cars collects Mike Mandel's spontaneous close-up portraits of Los Angeles drivers and passengers, shot through open car windows at a single Van Nuys intersection. It is a study of the automobile as a stage for unguarded, fleeting encounter.

Mandel began the project around 1970, positioning himself at a busy corner on Victory Boulevard with a wide-angle 28mm lens on his 35mm camera, close enough to the glass that his subjects reacted in real time, with surprise, amusement, and occasional annoyance. Stanley/Barker's 2017 edition, produced with Robert Mann Gallery, gathers 34 duotone reproductions in a softback, Swiss-catalogue-bound volume, left unsequenced by narrative so each image stands as its own self-contained meeting between photographer and stranger.

Mandel (b. 1950) made his name in the 1970s alongside Larry Sultan on the conceptual road-trip project Evidence and the billboard series Seven Days, and has continued to treat vernacular American subjects (baseball cards, driver's-ed manuals, freeway culture) as material for photographic play. People in Cars revisits this early, largely unpublished body of work decades later, restoring an overlooked chapter of his California period.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, California, Vernacular Photography
notes: The first edition of 1000 copies is signed by Mandel on the title page as issued (a bumper sticker is laid in at the rear cover); this is not a separate signed edition. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Robert Mapplethorpe: Portraits
description:
Robert Mapplethorpe: Portraits is the catalogue for a 2009 exhibition at Palm Springs Art Museum devoted specifically to Mapplethorpe's studio portraiture, a body of work usually read in the shadow of his flowers and figure studies.

Published without a dust jacket and printed in black and white throughout, the book gathers portraits from across his career with an essay by Gordon Baldwin and additional text by Daniell Cornell. It tracks the sitters, the poses, and the formal control that carried into his portrait work the same rigor he applied to still life: direct gazes, plain grounds, sculptural lighting. The exhibition traveled from Palm Springs (January-April 2009) to the Tucson Museum of Art (summer 2009) and the San Jose Museum of Art (fall 2010).

Mapplethorpe (1946-1989) trained at Pratt Institute before moving from mixed-media collage into photography in the early 1970s. Working first in Polaroid, he built a reputation through studio portraits, flowers, and explicit documentation of New York's S&M subculture that drew both acclaim and censorship fights. The Whitney Museum mounted his first major American retrospective in 1988, the year before his death from AIDS-related illness. The Robert Mapplethorpe Foundation, which he established that same year, now maintains his archive and supports museum photography programs and HIV/AIDS research.

title: Action
description:
When his 24-hour film The Clock was awarded the Golden Lion at the 54th Venice Biennale in 2011, Christian Marclay's hour had struck.

Christian Marclay's Actions Series is a vibrant exploration of the intersection between sound and visual art. These works employ onomatopoeic words in comic-strip style, transforming auditory expressions into visual forms.

Each piece in the series captures the dynamic energy of sound through bold graphics and vivid colors, inviting viewers to experience the artwork both visually and sonically. Marclay's innovative approach continues his career-long investigation into how sound can be represented and perceived in a visual medium, challenging traditional boundaries between auditory and visual experiences.

title: To Be Continued
description:
To Be Continued is an artist's book by Christian Marclay built entirely from collaged fragments of comic books, with each page functioning as a graphic score to be read and played aloud.

Published by Klangspuren Schwaz in 2016 in an edition of 2,000, the 48-page stapled softcover assembles panels of comic-book figures caught mid-shout, mid-scream, or mid-noise into a sequence that musicians can interpret for guitar, woodwinds, double bass, and percussion, with each page allotted roughly thirty seconds. It was conceived for Ensemble baBel, with whom Marclay has collaborated since 2012, and premiered at Klangspuren Schwaz in September 2016 in a version for the group.

Marclay (b. 1955) has worked at the intersection of sound and visual art since the early 1980s, turning records, comics, and photographs into instruments and scores; To Be Continued extends the line of graphic-score works that let performers translate images directly into sound.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Comics, Sound Art
notes: Artist's book conceived as a graphic score for Ensemble baBel; edition of 2,000. No standard trade distribution, so edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Portraits From the Studio and the Street
edition_printrun: 2017 IDEA reissue, limited to 500 signed copies
description:
Ari Marcopoulos's Portraits From the Studio and the Street is a document of downtown New York in the 1980s, caught at the moment when Pop Art's established figures rubbed shoulders with the emerging worlds of street art and hip-hop.

The book gathers black-and-white portraits made on the sidewalks and in the studios Marcopoulos moved through as a young photographer newly arrived in the city, mixing recognizable figures such as Willem Dafoe, Roy Lichtenstein, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Queen Latifah with anonymous New Yorkers identified only by a first name or a street corner. First published in 1987 by Bert Bakker in Amsterdam, this 2017 IDEA edition is styled as a photocopy of the original, bound in cloth boards, and adds previously unseen images alongside a new introduction by the writer Glenn O'Brien.

Marcopoulos began working as a photo printer in Andy Warhol's studio after moving to New York in the early 1980s, and went on to build a career photographing skateboarding, snowboarding, hip-hop, and graffiti culture from the inside. Portraits From the Studio and the Street is an early record of the eye O'Brien called "soul photography," the same embedded, unglamorous attention Marcopoulos later brought to his work with musicians, athletes, and his own family.
notes: 2017 IDEA reissue of the 1987 Bert Bakker original, styled as a facsimile with added images; limited to 500 signed copies. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Epiphany
description:
Epiphany is a limited-edition photobook made by Ari Marcopoulos while embedded with Gucci's pre-fall 2016 shoot, one of a string of outsider collaborators creative director Alessandro Michele brought into the house's orbit.

Marcopoulos spent seven days photographing the collection inside a palazzo, deliberately working against the romance of the setting: flash rather than soft light, direct rather than composed. The book mixes black-and-white and color sections and was issued in a hand-numbered edition of 1,000, each copy including one of sixteen glossy snapshot cards tucked into a glassine pocket on the cover, a folded poster, and pink bubble-wrap packaging with a snake decal. The title plays on Dionysus, the god for whom the collection's signature bag was named.

Marcopoulos, born in the Netherlands and based in New York since 1980, has spent his career photographing the margins of American culture, skateboarders, graffiti writers, hip-hop and hardcore musicians, and figures like Jean-Michel Basquiat and the Beastie Boys, and Epiphany carries that same loose, unposed eye into a fashion-house commission.
notes: Published by IDEA in collaboration with Gucci to accompany the pre-fall 2016 collection; hand-numbered limited edition of 1,000. No ISBN was assigned. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Impala
edition_printrun: Numbered edition of 300 copies, risograph printed
description:
A photobook by the Amsterdam-born, New York-based photographer Ari Marcopoulos, Impala takes its title from the undercover police cars the artist repeatedly encountered around Flatbush, his Brooklyn neighborhood.

Marcopoulos photographed the unmarked Crown Victorias and Chevy Impalas from the side whenever he spotted them, deliberately avoiding high or low angles or any added interpretation; through repetition, he has said, the car loses its specific significance and becomes an outline, a shape, a repeated form that can register as authority or its misuse depending on context. Those pictures are interspersed with local pickup basketball games and street photographs made along his everyday walking loop through the neighborhood. The book was published by the independent Paris imprint Red Lebanese in 2014 as an oblong, risograph-printed softcover, numbered and limited to 300 copies.

Marcopoulos has published well over 200 books and limited-edition zines over his career, working in a fast, diaristic mode across skateboarding, hip-hop, and street subjects since the 1980s. Impala sits within that prolific self-published output, a small, direct record of one recurring observation from his own block.
notes: Softcover, risograph-printed, numbered edition of 300 copies. No ISBN — small-press, self-published title. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Book of Images 1970
description: The forgoing suite: work same shapes only so I can push differences more. work faster work them all together ponder them all as group push differences and samenesses at same time. A facsimile of one of Brice Marden's journals from 1970, this publication contains images of clippings, drawings, and hand written notes that focus on the political and cultural events of the era, creating a unique guide for the artist's panel paintings from the same period.

title: Notebook Feb. 1968-
description:
Facsimile of American artist Brice Marden's personal journals.

On every page, a patchwork of clippings, drawings, renderings and handwritten notes reveal the painter's thought process and document the political and cultural events of the era. A prolific notetaker, Marden filled his journals with subject matter as familiar as references to Italian film director Federico Fellini and as esoteric as "looking at an object in nature and running lines around it."

The constant throughout is the work–deliberate, studied rectangles of graphite and ballpoint pen allude to the monochrome paintings that earned the artist fame and are a precursor to the panel paintings to come. Each journal is a unique guide to Marden's artistic output from that period as well as a distinct reference to the city–at that time bustling with artists such as Robert Rauschenberg and Jasper Johns–where he painted.

title: Notebook Sept. 1964-Sept. 1967
description:
Mars black, lemon yellow, use muddy white. Don't forget the young blonde in La Dolce Vita.

Scenes in country cafe and post orgy on the beach. She is the one Benno calls the 'Purity symbol.' Orange green grey. This and other reflections make up Brice Marden: Notebook Sept. 1964-Sept. 1967, facsimiles of American artist Brice Marden's personal journals. On every page, a patchwork of clippings, drawings, renderings and handwritten notes reveal the painter's thought process and document the political and cultural events of the era.

A prolific notetaker, Marden filled his journals with subject matter as familiar as references to Italian film director Federico Fellini and as esoteric as "looking at an object in nature and running lines around it." The constant throughout is the work–deliberate, studied rectangles of graphite and ballpoint pen allude to the monochrome paintings that earned the artist fame and are a precursor to the panel paintings to come. Each journal is a unique guide to Marden's artistic output from that period as well as a distinct reference to the city–at that time bustling with artists such as Robert Rauschenberg and Jasper Johns–where he painted.

Rebel Without A Cause
description:
Rebel Without A Cause is a project by artist Stefan Marx and distiller Christoph Keller.

It features Keller's exorbitant collection of over 150 traffic tickets and regulatory warnings that he accumulated over the last 20 years. These acts of misconduct and unpleasant letters by the authorities transform into art with Stefan Marx’ associative drawings layered on top of each ticket.

The originals were exhibited at Galerie Karin Guenther in Hamburg, where each drawing was released against the fine it was made from multiplied by seven, so that the penalty was converted into an artwork. A special edition of fifteen copies was issued, each containing an original drawing.

title: Gordon Matta-Clark: Anarchitect
description:
Published with the Bronx Museum of the Arts, Gordon Matta-Clark: Anarchitect surveys the practice of an artist who treated the building itself, cut open, gutted or partially demolished, as his primary material.

After training as an architect at Cornell, Matta-Clark returned to New York and coined the term "anarchitecture" to describe site-specific interventions staged in the economically devastated South Bronx. His Cuts series sliced through the walls and floors of abandoned buildings, turning demolition into an anatomical study of urban decline; Conical Intersect, made in Paris on row houses slated for demolition ahead of the Centre Pompidou's construction, became one of his best-known works of artistic protest. The volume reproduces 90 color illustrations alongside essays placing these projects within architectural and urban history.

Matta-Clark (1943-1978) worked at the edge of the Anarchitecture group and the downtown New York scene of the 1970s, and this book, edited by Antonio Sergio Bessa and Jessamyn Fiore with Cara M. Jordan and Xavier Wrona, situates his short career as a founding contribution to social practice and relational aesthetics.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Architecture, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Published in association with the Bronx Museum of the Arts. 90 color illustrations. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Short Term Eternity
edition_printrun: 500, The book was published in two separate editions, in English and in Estonian.
description:
Short Term Eternity brings together two artists, Gordon Matta-Clark (1943–1978, USA) and Anu Vahtra (1982, Estonia), whose practices are related to each other in many ways, even if they were born in different times and locations.

The aim of the book is to describe the circling of ideas and strategies in the art world from a non-hierarchical perspective rather than to compare the two bodies of work. The book was published on the occasion of Gordon Matta-Clark: Anarchitect. Anu Vahtra: Completion through removal, an exhibition at the Kumu Art Museum in Tallinn, 22.02. – 8.06.2019, curated by Sergio Bessa, Jessamyn Fiore, and Anu Allas. As a contrast to the large-scale installations in both Matta-Clark’s and Vahtra’s practice, the book is small in size. The content is printed on thin paper and is divided into three parts.

It starts with Completion through removal, a series of photographs by Anu Vahtra showing the spatial intervention realised in the Great Hall in Kumu and ends with the illustrated script of Vahtra’s performance piece Open House Closing. A Walk. The middle section of the book includes three thoroughly illustrated essays, where the images are printed overleaf from the text and are only visible through the page in a gap in the text at their intended location. These gaps or cuts in the text refer to the empty space, characteristic for the practices of both Matta-Clark and Vahtra.

title: You Haven't Seen Their Faces
description:
You Haven't Seen Their Faces borrows the visual language of a police wanted-poster and points it at power rather than poverty, presenting the hundred most influential figures in the City of London as though they were suspects in an ongoing investigation.

Prompted by the surveillance imagery London police circulated after the 2011 riots (grainy CCTV stills of young, often working-class suspects), Daniel Mayrit sourced public images of London's leading bankers, financiers, and executives and reworked them into the same coded aesthetic: cropped, gridded, stamped with case numbers. Designer Verónica Fieiras bound the 101-page book in brown kraft paper, screw-bound like an evidence file, its cover printed with the line "These are the faces of the 100 most powerful people in the City of London. Use these images at your own discretion." RIOT BOOKS published the project in Madrid in 2015 in a signed, numbered edition of 350.

Mayrit, a Madrid-based photographer working between documentary and conceptual practice, builds his projects around surveillance, bureaucracy, statistics and other institutional image systems, and how they assign guilt or invisibility. You Haven't Seen Their Faces won the Paris Photo–Aperture First PhotoBook Award the year of its publication and remains his best-known work.
tags: Photography, Surveillance, Politics, Spanish Photography, Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One
notes: Catalogue title carried a '(SIGNED)' annotation, recorded here: the edition is signed and numbered, 350 copies, screw-bound in brown paper mimicking a case file. No ISBN found across several sources (RIOT BOOKS listings, Princeton University Library catalog, photo-eye, PlacArt Photo) — this small-press edition appears not to have one. Winner, Paris Photo-Aperture First PhotoBook Award, 2015. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Paul McCarthy: Between Beauty and the Beast
description:
Between Beauty and the Beast: Sculptures, Drawings and Photographs is the catalogue for a 2006 exhibition surveying the scatological, cartoonish, and violent imagery central to Paul McCarthy's work.

Published by Foundation 20/21 in 2007 to accompany a show held at Thread Waxing Space, New York, from October 28 through December 30, 2006, the 56-page hardcover reproduces sculpture, drawing, and photography drawn across McCarthy's practice, with text by Sam Lipsyte and editing by Tim Nye. The book's wood-veneer boards, rounded corners, and bubble-lettered title mimic a children's book, a design choice that sets its scatological and phallic imagery against a register of innocence.

McCarthy (b. 1945, Salt Lake City) has used performance, sculpture, and video since the 1970s to stage grotesque inversions of consumer and entertainment culture, work shown at the Moderna Museet, the New Museum, and Tate Modern; this catalogue gathers strands of that practice around the recurring pairing named in its title.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Sculpture, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Wood-veneer boards with a silhouette of one of McCarthy's sculptures printed on the cover. Copies were number-stamped in an edition of 2,500. Now out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Sex, Drugs and Magick
description:
Gareth McConnell's Sex, Drugs and Magick looks past the sunlit cliche of Ibiza to the people who built its rave and club culture, rendered in grainy, high-contrast black and white.

McConnell shot the island's clubbers, DJs, and dawn stragglers over repeated visits, then pushed the images through a photocopier to strip out tonal nuance and leave faces as near-abstract fields of grain, a process he used to unify the sequence and hold it apart from documentary reportage. The book is accompanied by an essay from Matthew Collin, author of Altered State: The Story of Ecstasy Culture and Acid House, situating the pictures within the island's role in the spread of dance-music culture from the 1980s onward. It was published by Sorika in a limited edition.

McConnell, a Northern Irish photographer based in London, has worked across club culture, landscape, and portraiture, including further Ibiza-set projects that return to the same territory in a darker register. Sex, Drugs and Magick remains the clearest statement of his interest in subcultures viewed from the inside rather than as spectacle.
notes: Catalogue title carried a trailing "(?)" annotation, stripped here. Identified as the 2014 Sorika first edition (523 copies); a related later Ibiza volume exists under a similar title, so edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Ground: A Reprise of Photographs from the Farm Security Administration
contributors: Jock Reynolds (Introduction), Rosanne Cash (Text), Wendell Berry (Text), DJ Hellerman (Contribution)
description:
Ground assembles photographs from the Farm Security Administration archive that were never meant to be seen: negatives Roy Stryker rejected by driving a hole punch through the frame rather than discarding the film.

Bill McDowell first came across a print made from one of these "killed" negatives in an article on Michael Lesy's Long Time Coming and returned to the FSA archive to build a book around the mark itself. Ground gathers duotone reproductions, many previously unpublished, including 1936 photographs Walker Evans made toward Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, alongside work by Russell Lee, Ben Shahn, Marion Post Wolcott, John Vachon, Paul Carter, Theodor Jung, Carl Mydans, and Arthur Rothstein. McDowell sequenced the 176-page hardcover by how the black hole sits in and abstracts each image, with an introduction by Jock Reynolds and texts by Rosanne Cash and Wendell Berry.

A photographer and University of Vermont professor, McDowell treats Stryker's punch as a found intervention, a bureaucratic mark that reads, eighty years on, as a contemporary gesture of erasure laid over Depression-era documentary photography.
notes: Cover reproduces John Vachon's "Homesteader at Roanoke Farms, North Carolina" (1938) and Russell Lee's "Mr. Tronson, farmer near Wheelock, North Dakota" (1937). Named a notable photography book of 2016 by Mother Jones and Artnet. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Sweet
description:
Sweet is the point at which Aaron McElroy sets aside the muted colour and diaristic drift of his earlier work and reduces the nude to line, form and the coarse grain of a laser print.

Published in 2015 by S_U_N, the photographers' cooperative McElroy helped found, the book gathers older and recent nudes in black and white. It is his first to work exclusively that way. The figure is handled as much through the texture of the printing as through the exposure: the off-register tones and flattened blacks of laser output are part of the picture rather than a compromise in reproducing it. Fifty-one pages, 21 x 28 cm, wire-bound in a plain yellow cover with the title set alone in italic, in an edition of 50 copies.

Sweet opens what McElroy calls the Sugar series, completed by Candy later in 2015 and Sugar in 2016 — three books that together survey the nudes his practice is built on. His work has circulated largely through Dashwood Books in New York and through small-run publication rather than trade distribution, and the imprint has been listed variously out of New York and Los Angeles.
notes: First volume of the three-part Sugar series (Sweet, Candy, Sugar). Edition of 50. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: You Can Count On Me
contributors: Aaron McElroy (Photographer), Andreas Laszlo Konrath (Photographer), Ben Rayner (Photographer), Jim Mangan (Photographer), Aaron Stern (Photographer), Brian Merriam (Photographer), Samantha Casolari (Photographer), Jordan Sullivan (Photographer), Daniel Arnold (Photographer)
description:
You Can Count On Me is the zine catalogue for the group photography show that opened 205 A, the short-lived project space Aaron Stern and Jordan Sullivan ran in a vacant storefront at 205 Avenue A in the East Village in September 2014.

Curated by Stern and Sullivan and published by 205-A, Brooklyn, in 2014, the softcover zine gathers nine New York photographers: Aaron McElroy, Andreas Laszlo Konrath, Ben Rayner, Jim Mangan, Aaron Stern, Brian Merriam, Samantha Casolari, Jordan Sullivan and Daniel Arnold. The cover is a photograph of a woman face down in white sheets, her hair across the pillow, with the title set over it in pale lowercase type. Inside, the work runs a few pages per artist, from a grid of photobooth-style portraits to street and studio pictures. A second edition followed in 2015. Both were sold through Dashwood Books and ICP and are out of print.

205-A lasted little more than a season, but its zines record a loose circle of New York photographers who were also publishing each other through Dashwood, S_U_N and Pau Wau. The library holds McElroy's Sweet and The Devil May Care, his Briney Breezes with Charles Johnstone, and Konrath's Tupsu (V1).
tags: Photography, Zines, Group Show, Exhibition Catalog, New York, Self-Published
notes: Zine catalogue for the inaugural group show at 205 A, curated by Aaron Stern and Jordan Sullivan. Contributors include Aaron McElroy and Andreas Laszlo Konrath.

title: Life Adjustment Center
description:
Life Adjustment Center pairs two strands of Ryan McGinley's work from the same period: staged black-and-white nude studio portraits, often shared with live animals, set against the loose, saturated color photographs he made travelling with friends across the American landscape.

The first sequence, drawn from the series Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere, stages models nude in the studio alongside wild animals, extending McGinley's long interest in the vulnerability and theater of the unclothed body. The second returns to the open-road photography that made his name in the early 2000s — bodies in motion, campfires, water, and light, shot on the move rather than staged. Dashwood Books published the hardcover in blue cloth boards with red stamped titling in November 2010, alongside a signed, numbered edition of 100 copies.

McGinley (b. 1977) became, at twenty-five, the youngest artist to have a solo show at the Whitney Museum, built on exactly this territory: youth, nudity, and motion photographed with the immediacy of a snapshot and the ambition of a tableau. Life Adjustment Center sits between his early road-trip books and his later animal and studio work, showing the two strands developing side by side.
notes: Standard trade hardcover, ISBN 9780984454617; distinct from Dashwood's separate signed, numbered edition of 100 (ISBN 9780984454624). Page count and dimensions (95pp, 24.5 x 18 cm) are from a secondary retailer listing, not the publisher's own page, which lists no specs. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Theatrical Properties
description: Dennis McGrath is a LA and San Francisco-based photographer who is also the master printer for Ed Templeton. "Theatrical Properties" is a very unique and cool series that focuses on "props" scattered in countless adult movie sets. Ed Templeton is in charge of designing this book. Limited to 500 copies.

title: Ceremony
description:
A documentation of the British Army ceremonial troops through the eyes of a fashion photographer In 2006, acclaimed fashion photographer Alasdair McLellan spent a month capturing the ceremonial soldiers of the British Army for a magazine assignment, and published the expanded series in this photobook in 2016.

McLellan’s images, verging between portraiture and documentation, capture the details and import of their uniforms as well as the soldiers wearing them, accompanying them into their private living spaces and off-duty as they groom their horses. The series is an open testament to the appeal McLellan sees in the traditional uniforms and the values they embody, as well as the centuries of history that went into their colors and design.

“You can imagine that this is what Ralph Lauren has always dreamed Britain to be like the barking of dogs, the clip-clopping of horses, the gleaming silverware, royal thank-you notes on the walls and awfully kind and polite people. Of course, we know that by and large Britain is not like this now—and somehow doubt if it ever really was like this at all. Yet it most definitely is like this here, an affirmation that a time actually did exist in the past when such things went on, and what we are witnessing now isn’t just for show.” (from Jo-Ann Furniss’ introductory essay)

title: Ultimate Clothing Company
description:
Being from the North of England Alasdair McLellan's youthful curiosities channeled romantic notions about being English and Northern since he began to photograph in 1986.

He has admired those who have directed generations through their own similar obsessions such as Bruce Weber’s playful and sexually charged imagery of America and Steven Patrick Morrissey’s unfaltering melancholy and mythological observations. McLellan’s work maintains both the edginess of these influences as well as the unashamedly lyrical pulse which makes the work a tune for the masses.

The Northern, working class aesthetic of Bradford’s Buttershaw Estate, immortalized in Alan Clarke’s classic film Rita, Sue and Bob Too! has continually had a pull for McLellan. His photographs play with the tension of the ordinary in a similarly unselfconscious way as it's writer Andrea Dunbar. Alasdair McLellan’s Ultimate Clothing Company is both an intimate and introspective monograph edited and designed by art directors Mathias Augustyniak and Michael Amzalag M/M (PARIS) and beautifully printed in a numbered limited edition of 2,000 with a poster-wrap dust jacket

title: so8os: A Photographic Diary of a Decade
A Tale of Two Cities: Disco Era Bushwick
contributors: Catherine Kirkpatrick (Introduction), Charles Dickens, John A. Dereszewski, Judith DeLong, Vanessa Mártir, Adam J. Schwartz, Emanuel Xavier
description:
NYC in the late 1970s and early 80s could best be described using Charles Dickens' phrase 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.'

Meryl Meisler's photographs documented it with compassion and humor. As the city neared bankruptcy, crime rates rose, epidemics of arson and crack made the Big Apple seem like it was rotting to the core. In the midst of it all, a scintillating groundbreaking disco nightlife culture arose. Crossing the most exclusive clubs' velvet gates, Meryl danced and photographed with her medium format camera. July 13, 1977, while she was en route to Studio 54, a blackout shuttered NYC. A few days later, the disco beat was back while headlines and radios blasted news about a neighborhood she had never heard of before, Bushwick, where looting and rioting erupted in the darkness and went on and on. Fast forward to 1981 Meryl arrives at her new teaching position in a Bushwick Public School.

On the surface the neighborhood epitomized urban decay. The beauty of natural light and those who loved and thrived in the destruction were captured with a point and shoot camera as Meryl walked to and from the subway and school. A Tale of Two Cities: Disco Era Bushwick juxtaposes Meryl's disco and Bushwick photographs with the writing of authors who grew up amongst the rubble. The accounts of Bushwick historians and educators, Disco Divas and Dickens' narrative contribute to this true-life story and remind us that many of the same issues reverberate today. Meryl's images of Bushwick are the largest known documentation of the neighborhood during a desperate decade. Her disco photographs have never been shown before.
tags: Bushwick, Disco Era, Documentary Photography, NYC Photobooks, NYC Photography, 1970s-80s

title: Immersion / Visions
description:
Immersion / Visions is the catalogue for a two-part exhibition of Joel Meyerowitz's work staged at La Piscine, the art and industry museum in Roubaix housed in a former Art Deco swimming pool.

Published by Winch in 2014, the 94-page volume documents the exhibition's two halves: Immersion, installed in the museum's former changing cabins beside the pool basin, gathered pictures grouped by theme (swimming pools, full-length beach portraits, underwater images, skies, and bays) drawn from Meyerowitz's long attention to water as subject. Visions presented a retrospective of his career as a single photographic fresco more than 23 meters long, developed with graphic designer Christian Scheibling.

Meyerowitz (b. 1938) began photographing in color on the streets of New York in the early 1960s and has since worked across street photography, large-format landscape, and still life; this catalogue's pairing of thematic and chronological display reflects a career built on both immediacy and patience.
notes: Catalogue's title appears on Meyerowitz's own publication list as "Immersion / Visions"; the shelf copy is annotated "Visions/ Immersion," so the display title has been set to match the confirmed published order. Cover to be photographed: no reproducible cover image could be located online. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.
