author_full_name: Enrique Metinides ed. Misha Kominek text by Véronique Ricardoni
title: Series
description:
"Series" presents Enrique Metinides' iconic crime and disaster photography through a cinematographic lens, organizing 100 photographs—both color and black & white duotone—across fourteen thematic sequences.

The book examines works including "Explosion," "The Tower Suicide," and "The Lovers of Chapultepec," revealing how Metinides captures human reactions to tragedy: the faces and postures of survivors after their lives have been fundamentally altered. The sequential arrangement transforms tabloid images into a compassionate documentation where survivors become the focus rather than sensationalism. Metinides' fifty-year career documenting Mexico City's tragedies reveals the city's juxtaposition of mechanical brutality, opulence, and poverty.
tags: disaster, emergency, photojournalism, Mexico City, nota roja, crime photography, Photography
notes: Text by Véronique Ricardoni (English/Spanish), translated by Shawn Volesky. Recognized by TIME Magazine photo editors, the British Journal of Photography, photo-eye and others as one of the best photobooks of 2011. Enrique Metinides (1934-2022) earned the nickname "El Niño" (The Boy) after publishing his first photograph at age twelve. He worked from 1949 to 1979 as a photographer for La Prensa and other Mexico City tabloids.

title: Earthly Delights
description:
Ray K. Metzker's Earthly Delights catalogs a body of close, dense black-and-white studies of foliage and undergrowth, a quieter register from a photographer best known for stark urban abstraction.

Produced for Metzker's exhibition at Laurence Miller Gallery in New York, on view October 19 through December 3, 1988, the catalog reproduces ten black-and-white photographs from the Earthly Delights series, made in the eastern United States, alongside an introduction by Tom Goodman, brief biographical notes, a list of Metzker's previous exhibitions, and a list of public collections holding his work. It is a modest, stapled wrappers publication rather than a full monograph, sized to accompany the gallery show.

Metzker studied at Chicago's Institute of Design under Aaron Siskind and Harry Callahan and spent his career pushing photographic technique toward abstraction, through multiple exposures, composite prints, and dense tonal fields. The Earthly Delights series was later folded into Ray K. Metzker: Landscapes, Aperture's 2000 retrospective of his landscape work, situating these close-up studies within his broader engagement with the American landscape.
notes: Gallery exhibition catalog, not the later Aperture retrospective that also reproduces this series. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Storyteller: The Photographs of Duane Michals
publisher: DelMonico Books / Prestel, with Carnegie Museum of Art
contributors: Allen Ellenzweig (Essay), Marah Gubar (Essay), Adam Ryan (Essay), Aaron Schuman (Essay)
description:
Storyteller: The Photographs of Duane Michals is the catalogue for a retrospective that treats Michals less as a photographer than as, in his own description, a teller of stories who happens to use a camera.

The book reproduces more than 75 works spanning Michals's career, from the early sequences The Spirit Leaves the Body, Paradise Regained, and Chance Meeting to later series such as The Bewitched Bee and Who Is Sidney Sherman?, alongside the handwritten texts and poems Michals inscribed directly onto his prints. Essays by Linda Benedict-Jones, Allen Ellenzweig, Marah Gubar, Adam Ryan, and Aaron Schuman situate this work within twentieth-century photography and take up Michals's recurring subjects of sexuality, sensuality, and childhood, closing with an annotated biographical timeline drawn from archival material.

Michals (born 1932, McKeesport, Pennsylvania) broke from the documentary mainstream of 1960s photography by building narrative sequences and adding text to the photographic surface itself. The volume accompanied a retrospective that opened at Carnegie Museum of Art in November 2014 before traveling to the Peabody Essex Museum.
notes: Catalogue author spelled "Michaels" in the catalogue record; corrected to Michals. A softcover edition was also issued (ISBN 9783791365428, 240 pp.); the copy has not been checked against either binding. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Tulips
edition_printrun: First edition, embossed cover with plastic Tulips logo, edition of 1000
description:
A photobook by the American photographer Andrew Miksys, Tulips gathers color photographs made in and around a chain of roadside cafes called Tulips scattered across rural Belarus — modest social hubs where village life plays out in the absence of much else.

The book collects 118 color photographs across 164 pages, published in a red, embossed hardcover stamped with a plastic Tulips logo evoking the cafes' own signage, with text by the writer Laimonas Briedis and design by Claudia Ott. It was produced by ARÖK Books, the imprint Miksys runs to publish his own long-term projects, in a first edition of 1000 copies.

Miksys has built a body of work documenting social spaces and vernacular culture across Lithuania and the wider Baltic and Belarusian region, including Disko, on village discotheques in Lithuania, and Baxt, on the Lithuanian Roma community. Tulips extends that documentary project across the border into Belarus.
notes: Hardcover, embossed with a plastic Tulips logo; edition of 1000. Text by Laimonas Briedis, design by Claudia Ott. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The First March of Gentlemen / Kolekcja Wrzesińska
A Spiritual Good Time
description:
The source of the photographs in A Spiritual Good Time is from various surfing magazines published before 1990.

The appropriated images from mass-printed surf culture is a meditation on the perpetual pursuit of pleasure. It is a blending of fear and desire within a sport that often focused on the heterosexual gaze, hyper-masculinity, localism and the gossamer tipped dream of all inclusiveness and spirituality. Through tight cropping and editing of the editorial tropes of surf photography, the images are re-contextualized into a loose narrative of the contradictory forces at play.

title: Plush
description:
Plush is Marilyn Minter's first artist's book, a direct, close-up set of photographs devoted to a single subject that had largely vanished from popular imagery: female pubic hair.

Minter has described the project's premise plainly: in the nineteenth century, "plush" was slang for pubic hair, and she wanted to make beautiful images of a subject that had become taboo, asking models of every race and color to grow theirs out before she photographed and later painted from the resulting images. The book gathers those photographs in a softcover bound in bright pink paper-wrappers, with the title set in bold black type across the cover. It was released on December 3, 2014, at the Miami Beach Edition Hotel, in a signed edition of 500 copies plus 10 deluxe copies.

Plush also marks the end of an era: it was the last book published by Fulton Ryder, the secretive Upper East Side bookstore and imprint run by artist Richard Prince, before it closed in 2014. For Minter, better known for her enamel paintings and photographs of glamour, desire and the body's messier textures, the book extended a career-long interest in subjects that make viewers look twice.
notes: Signed first edition of 500 copies plus 10 deluxe copies; last book published by Richard Prince's Fulton Ryder Press before it closed. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Pretty/Dirty
contributors: Bill Arning (Essay), Elissa Auther (Essay), Eileen Myles (Contributor), Richard Hell (Contributor)
description:
Pretty/Dirty is the catalog for Marilyn Minter's first full-career survey, tracking four decades of work that renders glamour and desire in almost unbearable close-up — lip gloss, sweat, spit, jewelry, and grime rendered with the same hyperreal precision.

Organized by the Contemporary Arts Museum Houston, where the exhibition opened in April 2015 before traveling to the Denver Art Museum, the Orange County Museum of Art, and the Brooklyn Museum, the show and its 176-page catalog span Minter's early photorealist paintings of the late 1960s through her signature enamel-on-metal paintings, photographs, and video. Essays by curators Bill Arning and Elissa Auther sit alongside contributions from Eileen Myles, Richard Hell, Nick Flynn, K8 Hardy, Colby Keller, and others, with interviews conducted by Catherine Morris and Linda Yablonsky.

Minter (b. 1948) spent decades painting from the margins of the art world's comfort with female sexuality and commercial imagery before institutional recognition caught up with her practice in the 2000s. Pretty/Dirty marks that turn, presenting the full arc from her early, once-controversial Porn Grid paintings to the glossy, maximalist canvases that made her a reference point for a generation of artists working with appropriation and the body.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Photography, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Catalog for Minter's first career survey, organized by Contemporary Arts Museum Houston (April 17-August 2, 2015), traveling to the Denver Art Museum, Orange County Museum of Art, and Brooklyn Museum. Catalogue row's title 'Pretty Dirty' normalized to the book's actual stylization, Pretty/Dirty. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Miserachs Barcelona
description:
Xavier Miserachs photographed Barcelona as a city that was still being lived in rather than looked at, and this catalogue is the argument that his 1964 book belongs among the great European city books.

MACBA and RM Verlag co-published it in 2015 for the exhibition of the same name, which ran at the museum from 18 September 2015 to 27 March 2016 under the curator Horacio Fernandez. The 128-page volume reproduces 68 photographs selected from the 371 that made up Barcelona blanc i negre, Miserachs's own 1964 publication, and it is printed as a trilingual edition in Catalan, English and Spanish with a design by Ramon Pez and Laia Abril. The pictures are of families out walking, children in the streets, flea markets, workers leaving the factories and migrants' luggage stacked at the railway station, made by day and by night across the city's neighbourhoods, with William Klein and Francesc Catala-Roca as the acknowledged points of reference.

Miserachs (1937-1998) worked in Barcelona through the late Franco years and is now read as one of the central figures of Spanish photojournalism. A second, separate edition of this catalogue was issued for the same exhibition under the same title but with different contents; this is the library edition.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Documentary Photography, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Library edition, ISBN 9788416282395, confirmed by the collector. MACBA issued a second edition for the same exhibition under the same title (the Portfolio Edition, ISBN 9788416282333, 144 pages, 84 photographs), which is a different book. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: I Can Make You Feel Good
Some Thing Means Everything to Somebody
description:
Peter Mitchell's Some Thing Means Everything to Somebody tells an autobiography sideways, through faceless scarecrows standing alone in empty Yorkshire fields.

Mitchell photographed scarecrows he sought out specifically because they had no face, treating them as stand-ins for absence and memory, and interleaves these images with photographs of ordinary personal objects collected across four decades. Handcrafted typography and a deliberately disjointed sequence carry the narrative rather than explanatory text, so the book reads as a private history told through things rather than people. It was published by RRB Photobooks in Yorkshire in 2015, in a limited edition of 950 copies, some including a signed print.

Mitchell, a Leeds-based photographer associated with the British color-documentary tradition of the 1970s and 80s, first gained wider attention decades after making the work later collected in Strangely Familiar, his survey of Leeds's industrial edges and eccentric local characters. Some Thing Means Everything to Somebody extends that same close, particular attention to place into a more personal, autobiographical register.
notes: Limited edition of 950 copies; some copies include a signed print. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Joan Mitchell: I Carry My Landscapes Around with Me
description:
I Carry My Landscapes Around with Me is the first publication devoted to Joan Mitchell's multipanel paintings, the large-scale works she built by joining two to five canvases across four decades of practice.

The book accompanied a 2019 exhibition at David Zwirner in New York organized with the Joan Mitchell Foundation, drawing on paintings held in public and private collections as well as the Foundation's own holdings. Its 104 pages reproduce 57 works in color, including detail views that show the surface and brushwork up close, with new essays by Suzanne Hudson and Robert Slifkin examining how the multipanel format let Mitchell build continuity and rupture into a single field and open onto something closer to a remembered landscape than a depicted one. The title comes from Mitchell's own account of her process, written in 1958: she painted not nature itself but what it left her with.

Mitchell (1925–1992) was a central figure of second-generation Abstract Expressionism, known for a synesthetic, intuitive use of color and a reworking of the figure-ground relationship that set her apart from her peers; David Zwirner has represented the Joan Mitchell Foundation's holdings since 2018.
tags: Art, Painting, Abstract Art, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Hanon
description:
Yoshinori Mizutani photographs the great cormorants that have colonised the skies over suburban Tokyo, and lets them arrange themselves into something that reads less like a bird book than like a page of music.

Hanon was published by amana in Tokyo in 2016, the fourth of Mizutani's books with the imprint, and takes its title from Charles-Louis Hanon's nineteenth-century piano studies, The Virtuoso Pianist in Sixty Exercises. Shot in colour but reproduced so close to monochrome that it registers as black on white, the series flattens the city's power lines and steel lattice towers into a field with no perspectival depth, across which the birds sit strung out like notes on a stave. Sixty-four pages, softcover, 26 x 36 cm; the work was shown the same year in a solo exhibition at IMA CONCEPT STORE in Roppongi.

Mizutani came to attention with Tokyo Parrots (2014), his record of the feral parakeets nesting in the city, and Hanon extends that project's central interest: an expanding bird population read as a graphic incident in the urban fabric. amana published four of his books in three years — Tokyo Parrots, Colors and Yusurika before this one — followed by HDR_nature in 2018.
tags: Photography, Japanese Photography, Nature, Urban Landscape
notes: Signed copy; the catalogue title carried the annotation "(signed)". Published to coincide with the HANON exhibition at IMA CONCEPT STORE, Tokyo, 2016. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Tokyo Parrots
description:
Yoshinori Mizutani's Tokyo Parrots follows the feral rose-ringed parakeets, descended from pets brought to Japan in the 1970s, that now flock by the hundreds over Tokyo.

Mizutani has said his first encounter with an enormous flock left him afraid, "like I had fallen into the movie The Birds directed by Hitchcock." That apprehension drove the project: he tracked the birds' daily movements until he located one of their largest nesting sites in a ginkgo tree, then photographed them late in the day with heavy flash, lighting the foreground stark white against skies still carrying the last color of sunset. The resulting images, often freezing birds mid-flight with wings spread against green branches or darkening sky, give the familiar city an unfamiliar, almost hallucinatory charge.

Published by amana/IMA Photobooks in 2014, Tokyo Parrots was an early book from Mizutani, a Tokyo-based photographer whose subsequent work has continued to look at the unnoticed intersections of the urban and the wild. The book has been compared to Masahisa Fukase's Ravens as a color, lower-key counterpart within the same tradition of the city as animal habitat.
notes: First edition, hardcover, 90 pages. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Photographs 1934–1973
description:
Carlo Mollino: Photographs 1934-1973 is the fullest survey yet published of Mollino's photographic work. It spans four decades, from his earliest experiments to the images found in his studio after his death.

Mollino trained as an architect and made his name in Turin designing furniture, interiors, and buildings. Photography ran through nearly all of it. He photographed his own buildings and interiors as extensions of their design. He documented alpine skiing and mountain landscapes, an early passion of his. In his final years he made thousands of Polaroids of local sex workers in his apartment, never exhibited in his lifetime. Francesco Zanot edited this book, published by Silvana Editoriale in 2018. It draws on Mollino's full archive to trace these different bodies of work as a single, continuous photographic practice rather than a footnote to his design career.

Mollino (1905-1973) worked in Turin as an architect, industrial designer, and university professor. He also raced cars, flew planes, and skied. The library holds two narrower volumes drawn from this same archive. Polaroids collects the erotic Polaroid series from his final years. Giappone 1970 collects photographs from his 1970 trip to Japan for Expo '70. This survey is the wider frame those two sit inside.

title: Carlo Mollino: Polaroids
edition_printrun: Second edition (reissue of the 2002 first edition), new cover
contributors: James Crump (Foreword), Fulvio Ferrari (Text), Napoleone Ferrari (Text), Silvio Curto (Text)
description:
Polaroids gathers the private photographic practice Carlo Mollino kept almost entirely to himself: hundreds of Polaroid portraits of women, staged in his own Turin apartment and never intended for public view.

From around 1960 until his death in 1973, Mollino invited dancers and other women to late-night sessions in his apartment, art-directing each shot against elaborate backdrops, in costumes, wigs, and accessories he selected himself, then hand-finishing the resulting Polaroids with a fine brush to sharpen his idealized image of the female form. Of some 1,200 photographs found only after his death, this volume reproduces roughly 400, with texts by Fulvio Ferrari, Napoleone Ferrari, and Silvio Curto situating the work within Mollino's larger practice; James Crump contributes a foreword to Damiani's 2014 edition, a reissue of the volume first published in 2002.

Mollino (1905-1973) trained as an engineer before becoming one of mid-century Italy's most idiosyncratic architects and designers, equally known for the Turin buildings and furniture that made his reputation and for restless private interests in skiing, aviation, and photography — subjects he treated with the same obsessive control as his design work. Polaroids joins the library's other Mollino holdings as the most intimate and long-hidden part of that record.
notes: Damiani/Crump 2014 edition (foreword by James Crump), a reissue of the volume first published in 2002. Approximately 400 of Mollino's roughly 1,200 Polaroids are reproduced; the full body of work remained unknown until after his 1973 death. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Topographies
edition_printrun: housed in a slipcase, full bleed color plates, 54 full bleed black & white plates, 22 × 30.6 cm

title: Pictures from the Real World (Colour photographs) 1987-88
Record No. 34
description:
Record No. 34 is Moriyama at his least ceremonious: a working notebook issued to the public, without essay, theme or argument beyond the walk itself.

Akio Nagasawa Publishing issued this volume in 2017, 112 pages, softcover, at 27.8 x 22.0 cm. The pictures come from Moriyama's daily crisscrossing of central Tokyo, printed full-bleed in the grainy, high-contrast black and white he has used since the 1960s. His afterword records a doubt rather than a programme: that within the routine he is now and then overcome by a sense of bewilderment, asking what exactly he is trying to see through the finder, and what the photograph he has just taken actually is.

Moriyama began Kiroku in 1972 as a personal counterweight to his magazine work, stopped after five issues, and revived the series with Nagasawa decades later; it has run steadily since. The collection also holds Record No. 26, No. 31 and No. 32.
notes: Catalogue title carried a "(signed)" annotation, stripped here; this copy is signed. No ISBN was assigned to this journal series. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Record No. 32
edition_printrun: First edition, issued without dust jacket
description:
Daido Moriyama's Record No. 32 is one installment in a decades-long serial project, a photographer's working notebook issued to the public roughly twice a year rather than a single, discrete book.

Like the rest of the Record (Kiroku) series, this issue collects Moriyama's recent black-and-white street photographs, printed full-bleed throughout with no accompanying essay to direct the reading. The images move between Tokyo's streets, signage, bodies, and stray detail in the grainy, high-contrast, often blurred style Moriyama has used since the 1960s. Published by Akio Nagasawa in Tokyo, the volume is a softcover issued without a dust jacket, designed by Rie Shimoda and printed in Japan.

Moriyama began Record in 1972 as a self-published outlet outside the gallery and museum system, let it lapse, then restarted it in the mid-2000s as an ongoing numbered series that now runs past thirty issues. Associated early in his career with the short-lived Provoke journal and its rejection of polished documentary style, Moriyama has used Record to keep that raw, immediate working method continuously in print alongside his more widely distributed monographs.
notes: Catalogue title carried a "(signed)" annotation, stripped here; this copy is signed. Cover to be photographed: no reliable product-page image could be sourced. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Record No. 31
description:
Record No. 31 is one issue in Daido Moriyama's ongoing photo-journal series Kiroku (Record), a run of small, self-published volumes he has produced steadily since 2006.

Moriyama began Kiroku in 1972 as a personal counterweight to his commercial magazine work, let it lapse after five issues, and revived it decades later with the publisher Akio Nagasawa. This volume, printed full-bleed in black and white across 160 unpaginated pages, combines snapshots Moriyama made in Paris while there for an exhibition with pictures taken in Tokyo before and after the trip, what he called, in his own note on the book, "a tentative tale of two cities." It marks the point at which the compiled anthology Record (Thames & Hudson, 2017, covering issues 1-30) leaves off and the sequel Record 2, edited by Mark Holborn, picks up.

Moriyama (born 1938, Osaka) has worked in high-contrast, blurred, grainy black-and-white since the 1960s Provoke era, and the Record series functions as an open-ended, book-form extension of that same restless street practice, issue by issue rather than as a single fixed body of work.
tags: Photography, Japanese Photography, Street Photography, Zines
notes: Catalogue annotation "(signed)" refers to Moriyama's signature on the title page. No ISBN was assigned to this self-published journal issue. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Record No. 26
description:
This is the issue in which Moriyama finally turns his camera on his own neighbourhood, and finds it does not feel like Shinjuku at all.

Published by Akio Nagasawa Publishing in 2014, 90 pages, softcover, at 27.8 x 22.0 cm, Record No. 26 collects black-and-white street photographs made in Ikebukuro and the districts beside it. Moriyama explains in his afterword that he had moved into an old apartment building in what is now West Ikebukuro more than ten years earlier but had given his attention almost entirely to Shinjuku, rarely going there at all; a picture he happened to like, taken on a walk in the spring of 2013, made him aware it would be a waste not to shoot his home ground, and he spent more than a year prowling the area. What he found was that although both are major terminal districts, the air in the streets differs, and the body temperature of the people in Ikebukuro suits his own. He summarises the result as lovable Ikebukuro, redoubtable Ikebukuro.

Moriyama began Kiroku in 1972 as a private counterweight to his commercial magazine work, abandoned it after five issues, and revived the series with Nagasawa decades later. The collection also holds Record No. 31, No. 32 and No. 34.
notes: Catalogue title carried a "(signed)" annotation, stripped here; this copy is signed. No ISBN was assigned to this journal series. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: 2000.12.14.pm
description: "2000.12.14.pm" is a publication, specifically a photobook booklet by Japanese photographer Daido Moriyama. It was published by HYSTERIC GLAMOUR in 2002 and is associated with a larger set or documentary project titled "Near Equal". Documentary on Japanese photographer Daido Moriyama. It is a booklet that was issued with a set of four prints as part of the "Near Equal Moriyama Daido" project.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One

title: Daido Moriyama: Mirage
description:
Mirage collects color photographs Daido Moriyama shot in the 1970s and left unpublished for four decades, presenting the film's chemical decay as inseparable from the images themselves.

The pictures, drawn from commissioned work including images made for the Japanese edition of Playboy alongside more personal frames of the city at night, survive only as slides that have mildewed and discolored in storage. Editor Hisako Motoo describes the effect as looking at the scenes "through a blur of frosted glass," the warm, bruised color shifts standing in for the passage of time itself. Rather than restore the images, the book, the fourth in an annual series produced by Moriyama with art director Satoshi Machiguchi and Motoo under the MMM imprint, prints them as found: a slipcased hardcover with a tipped-in cover photograph, each copy signed by Moriyama on the title page and numbered against the slipcase, in an edition of 1,000.

The book extends Moriyama's decades-long interest in the photograph as a degraded, grainy, blurred trace of experience rather than a clean record of it, a sensibility he has pursued since the 1970s across Tokyo street photography, self-published zines and major museum surveys alike.
notes: Fourth volume in the MMM annual limited-edition series with Moriyama, Satoshi Machiguchi and Hisako Motoo; signed and numbered edition of 1000, 200 distributed via Artbook|D.A.P. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Not Just Your Face Honey
description:
The series Not Just Your Face Honey by Austrian artist Stefanie Moshammer was produced in the USA nd reflects on the thin line between love and delusion.

Her photographic work is based on a love letter written to her in March 2014 by Troy C., a man she did not know. This text led the artist to explore questions of surveillance, stalking, and the image of the other. Her photographs mingle dreams, feelings, and obsessions, combining them into a web of visual associations embedded in a kind of American road movie. Stefanie Moshammer's series Not Just Your Face Honey won together with the art critic Andreas Prinzing the C / O Berlin Talent Award and is being exhibited at the venue from 7 July to 23 September 2018.

title: Tertium Quid
description:
Tertium Quid is Murray Moss's book of paired vintage press photographs, each image set beside another with which it forms an unplanned visual rhyme, a "third thing" produced by the meeting of two unrelated pictures.

Drawing on his personal archive of anonymous mid-century press photographs, Moss arranges the pictures in pairs he describes as duets, fugues, or conversations between strangers, reproducing each photograph at its original size with its annotated, stamped verso given equal weight to the printed front. August Editions published the 204-page hardcover in 2014 in a numbered edition of 1,250, with roughly 200 duotone reproductions across pairings that range from formal echo to pure coincidence.

Moss founded the SoHo design shop Moss in 1994 and spent a decade reshaping how American stores presented industrial design as a curatorial practice before turning, in later years, to collecting and recontextualizing vernacular press photography. Tertium Quid extends that same curatorial eye, pairing rather than authorship, to a body of found images whose original photographers and subjects are almost entirely anonymous.
tags: Photography, Vernacular Photography, Found Photography, Design
notes: Numbered edition of 1,250 copies. Moss is not the photographer of the images; the book pairs anonymous vintage press photographs from his own collection rather than presenting original photography. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Incoming
binding: OTA-bound softback with metallic silkscreened cover
description:
Richard Mosse's Incoming turns a weapon on its subject and asks what is left of a person once a camera can only see their heat.

The 280 metallic tritone plates are stills from Mosse's three-screen video work of the same name, made with a thermal imaging camera classed as a weapons component under international export law, able to detect a human body from some 30 kilometres away. Following migration routes across the Middle East, North Africa and Europe, the images show rescues off the Libyan coast, crossings of the Sahara and the burning of camps, all rendered as heat signatures in which faces, skin and clothing dissolve into a monochrome scale. MACK published the 576-page volume in 2017 as an OTA-bound softback with a metallic silkscreened cover, at 17.5 x 19.7 cm, with a text by the philosopher Giorgio Agamben.

Mosse has worked for over a decade at the point where documentary photography meets military optics, most visibly in Infra and The Enclave, which used discontinued Kodak Aerochrome infrared film to photograph the conflict in eastern Congo. He represented Ireland at the 55th Venice Biennale and won the Deutsche Borse Photography Prize in 2014. Incoming extends that method from a single conflict to the border apparatus itself.
tags: Photography, Documentary Photography, Contemporary Art, Surveillance Index
notes: Stills from the three-screen video work of the same name. Text by Giorgio Agamben. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Kraftwerk 45 RPM
description:
Toby Mott's Kraftwerk 45 RPM is a document of graphic design history read through the throwaway object of the 7-inch single sleeve.

The book reproduces Kraftwerk 45 RPM single sleeves and associated print ephemera assembled by Mott, presenting the group's cover art, national variants, and promotional material as a sequence of found design rather than a conventional discography. Published by Vinyl Factory Publishing in London in 2012, it appeared as a signed and numbered softcover edition, part of Vinyl Factory's program of small-run publications pairing music history with visual archives.

Mott is a British artist and collector best known for The Mott Collection, an extensive archive of punk, anarchist, and subcultural printed ephemera that he has exhibited and published under titles including Oh So Pretty: Punk in Print. Kraftwerk 45 RPM extends that same collector's eye for overlooked commercial graphics to a single band's record sleeves.
notes: Cover to be photographed: no reliable product-page image could be sourced. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Studio Paradiso
edition_printrun: First edition; issued with four different cover variants
description:
Studio Paradiso collects Max Natkiel's portraits of the people who passed through Amsterdam's Paradiso club across the 1980s, a decade he spent photographing its crowd rather than its stage.

Natkiel worked as a kind of house portraitist for the venue, pulling punks, new-wavers, rockers, mods, Rastafarians, squatters, and metal- and skinheads aside for direct black-and-white portraits against whatever wall or doorway was at hand. First circulated in small photocopied booklets at the time, the pictures are gathered here into a single 623-page volume of nearly 600 images, with trilingual text (English, Dutch, French) including an introduction by philosopher Dirk van Weelden. The book was issued with four different cover photographs distributed at random.

Natkiel's project sits alongside other social-documentary portraits of European subcultural nightlife, distinguished by its single fixed location and its long duration: one club, one photographer, one decade, returned to night after night.
notes: Catalogue listed author surname only ("Natkiel"); first name confirmed as Max. Cover art is one of four variants Voetnoot distributed at random; the copy's exact variant has not been confirmed. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: On Your Knees, Please.
description:
Raquel Nave works with her own body as her subject, and On Your Knees, Please. is one of a run of self-published books in which she turns the camera on herself.

First issued in 2014 and reprinted in softcover in New York in 2015, the book belongs to a sequence of small self-published volumes — Live Free In Hell (2010, through BCCKS), this title, and S.A.D. (2015) — made outside any publishing house and circulated through photography bookshops such as Dashwood Books in New York. The photographs are self-portraits, and Nave uses her own image to work on questions of identity, sexuality and, later, motherhood; the books are the form the work takes rather than a record of work made elsewhere.

Nave is an artist, actor and model based in New York, working across photography, video and performance. She has appeared in Abel Ferrara's Welcome to New York and Bizarre and in Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, and has been photographed for editorial work by Ellen von Unwerth, Jean-Baptiste Mondino and Rankin among others. In PIG (2019) she moved to digital and turned the camera off herself and onto her partner, the first of her books to look outward.
tags: Photography, Self-Published, Nudes, Performance Art, Identity
notes: First published 2014; the 2015 New York softcover is a reprint. Edition to be verified against the copy. Cover to be photographed. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Alice Neel: People Come First
contributors: Meredith A. Brown (Text), Julia Bryan-Wilson (Text), Susanna V. Temkin (Text)
description:
Alice Neel called herself a collector of souls, and this catalogue makes the case that her portraits are less likeness than testimony.

Published by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2021 for the retrospective of the same name, the book surveys seven decades of Neel's painting through more than a hundred works reproduced across 201 colour plates. The sequence moves from the Depression-era portraits and the Communist-affiliated work of the 1930s through the years in Spanish Harlem, where her sitters were neighbours, children and the people the art world was not looking at, and on to the later New York portraits of political organisers, queer artists, critics, pregnant women and her own family. Cityscapes, still lifes and erotic drawings are included alongside them. Essays by Kelly Baum and Randall Griffey and contributions from Meredith A. Brown, Julia Bryan-Wilson and Susanna V. Temkin take up her depictions of queer subjects, her mixture of abstraction and figuration, and her lifelong engagement with civil rights, feminism and the politics of who gets painted. The volume is a 256-page hardcover at 20.3 x 29.2 cm.

Neel (1900-1984) worked in obscurity for most of her career, given her first museum retrospective at the Whitney only in 1974, and has since become one of the defining American figure painters of the twentieth century. The collection also holds Alice Neel: Uptown and Alice Neel: Painted Truths.
tags: Art, Painting, Portraiture, Exhibition Catalog, American Art
notes: Catalogue for the Metropolitan Museum of Art retrospective, 2021. Distributed by Yale University Press. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Alice Neel: Painted Truths
publisher: The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston
description:
This is the book that argued Alice Neel belongs in a European lineage of figure painting, and it was the first survey to make that case at scale outside the United States.

Organised by the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston and published in 2010 with distribution by Yale University Press, Painted Truths accompanied an exhibition that travelled to the Whitechapel Gallery in London and the Moderna Museet in Malmo. Jeremy Lewison, formerly director of collections at Tate, edited the 296-page volume and led its reassessment, placing Neel's sitters alongside Munch, Kokoschka and the school of London rather than reading her only as an American realist working against the grain of abstraction. The plates cover the full span of her work, from the 1930s to the portraits of the 1970s and early 1980s, and the essays take up her handling of the nude, of pregnancy and of the sitter's psychological exposure.

Neel (1900-1984) painted the people around her for fifty years with almost no institutional support, and the run of exhibitions that began with this one has since made her a fixture of the museum canon. The collection also holds Alice Neel: Uptown and the Metropolitan Museum's Alice Neel: People Come First.
tags: Art, Painting, Portraiture, Exhibition Catalog, American Art
notes: Exhibition catalogue: Museum of Fine Arts, Houston; Whitechapel Gallery, London; Moderna Museet, Malmo. Distributed by Yale University Press. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Pud 3
binding: Hardcover, cloth-bound boards with foil-blocked title
description:
PUD 3 closes the trilogy in the same terms it opened with: a single lowercase word on a cloth board, and no explanation offered inside.

Dashwood Books published it in 2015, a year after the first two volumes. It is bound in navy bookcloth with pud blocked large across the front board in silver foil, the third colourway in a series that changes nothing but the cloth and the ink. Jason Nocito is a New York photographer whose books work by accumulation and abrupt cutting rather than by caption or narrative sequence; the Pud books are that method at its most compressed, and the uniform covers make the three read as one object issued in parts.

Dashwood has published most of Nocito's work, including the long End Or series of small books; twelve of those are in the collection along with all three Pud volumes.
notes: The artist's own bibliography styles this volume "PUD 3", titled here as "Pud 3" to match the other two; the catalogue records it as "PUD III". No ISBN was assigned and the page count is not stated by the publisher or the artist. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Pud 2
binding: Hardcover, cloth-bound boards with foil-blocked title
description:
Pud 2 arrived within months of the first, which is the point: the series works as a run of small books rather than as three separate statements.

Dashwood Books published it in September 2014 in an edition of 600. It runs to 40 pages, eight more than the first volume, and is bound in grey bookcloth with the lowercase word pud blocked large across the front board in pink, the same layout in a different colourway. Jason Nocito is a New York photographer whose books proceed by accumulation and abrupt cutting rather than by caption or narrative sequence, and the Pud books are that method at its most compressed.

Dashwood has published most of Nocito's work, including the long End Or series of small books; twelve of those are in the collection along with all three Pud volumes.
notes: The artist's own bibliography lists this volume as "Pud 2"; the catalogue records it as "PUD II". No ISBN was assigned. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Pud 1
binding: Hardcover, cloth-bound boards with foil-blocked title
description:
The Pud books are Jason Nocito's smallest and most obstinate objects: three short hardcovers that give you a word on the cover and nothing else to hold onto.

Dashwood Books published this first volume in 2014 in an edition of 600. It runs to 32 pages, bound in orange bookcloth with the lowercase word pud blocked large across the front board in blue, a treatment repeated in different colourways across the two volumes that followed. Nocito is a New York photographer whose books tend to work by accumulation and abrupt cutting rather than by sequence or caption, and the Pud trilogy is the compressed version of that method.

Dashwood has published most of Nocito's work, including the long End Or series of small books, twelve of which are also in the collection alongside all three Pud volumes.
notes: The artist's own bibliography lists this volume as "Pud 1"; the catalogue records it as "PUD". No ISBN was assigned. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Bomba
description:
Every February in San Juan de la Vega, men pack homemade explosive into the heads of sledgehammers and swing them at lengths of steel rail; Thomas Prior went and photographed it, and Bomba is what came back.

The Mexican town's festival commemorates a battle four centuries old. Hundreds of local men gather on an empty football field with hammers whose heads carry pockets of potassium chlorate; struck against the rails, they detonate in phosphorous smoke and flying grit. Prior works inside the cloud rather than at a safe remove, and the pictures hold their subjects still inside enormous motion — figures half-dissolved in smoke, arms raised, nearer the composition of history painting than of reportage. Self-published in 2016 in a signed edition of 250: 52 pages, 23 colour plates, no essay or accompanying text, bound in natural linen with a hammer blind-embossed on the front board, 10 x 12 inches. It was launched through Dashwood Books in New York.

Prior is a New York photographer whose editorial work has run in The New Yorker, Time, Vogue and Avaunt, and whose personal projects turn on athletes in motion and on landscapes altered by human intervention. Bomba was his first book; Amen Break followed from Loose Joints in 2020, and Slip Me the Master Key after it.
notes: The catalogue row filed this under Jason Nocito; Bomba is Thomas Prior's, absent from Nocito's own bibliography and present on thomasprior.com. Self-published, signed edition of 250, launched through Dashwood Books. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Cady Noland: Polaroids 1986-2024
description: Cady Noland: Polaroids 1986–2024 is an artist's book featuring previously unpublished photographs taken by the artist over the course of her career. This book was conceived of, edited, and designed by Cady Noland. It reproduces nearly one hundred Polaroids taken by the artist over the course of her career, which illustrate sculptures in process and exhibitions in development.

title: I Am A Lone Monk Walking The World With A Leaky Umbrella: Chinese Shadow-puppets 2012-2017
description:
Serge Onnen's I Am A Lone Monk Walking The World With A Leaky Umbrella documents twenty-one shadow-puppets the artist produced with Chinese craftsmen between 2012 and 2017, made in a folk tradition fading fast under China's rapid modernization.

Shadow puppet theatre, semi-transparent leather figures moved on sticks behind a lit screen, is among the oldest forms of projected moving image, and spread from its Chinese origins across Asia over centuries. Onnen traveled to China to research the craft and work directly with its remaining practitioners, producing puppets inspired by current global events rather than traditional folklore. The 184-page softcover book reproduces the puppets alongside short bilingual notes, in Chinese and English, on each figure, with Chinese numerology informing the book's structure. Text is contributed by Shuyu Chen.

The project extended beyond the book: the related film Cloacinae premiered at Rotterdam International Film Festival in 2017 and continued to travel the festival circuit. Onnen, a Netherlands-based artist and illustrator, works across drawing, film and craft-based collaboration reflecting a recurring interest in vanishing image technologies.
notes: Softcover, 184 pages, edition of 750; text by Shuyu Chen. Related film "Cloacinae" premiered at Rotterdam International Film Festival in 2017. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Eleventh Finger
description:
Eleventh Finger is a monograph of work by the Japan-born, Paris-based photographer Yuki Onodera, published by the Tokyo imprint Art Beat Publishers in a hardcover edition.

The 60-page volume gathers a body of Onodera's photographic work in the artist's characteristically conceptual register, in which everyday objects and staged tableaux are photographed in ways that ask viewers to reconsider what they are actually seeing. The book is produced to Art Beat Publishers' design standard for its run of small-edition artist titles, bilingual in Japanese and English.

Onodera trained as a photojournalist in Japan before moving to Paris in 1993, where she built an international practice spanning photography, sculpture and installation. Her work has been shown at institutions including the Maison Européenne de la Photographie and included in major surveys of Japanese photography; Eleventh Finger sits within a prolific run of small-edition artist books that punctuate her larger gallery and museum projects.
notes: No synopsis found beyond the bookseller listing; described from the physical object (hardcover, 60 pages, bilingual Japanese/English) and Onodera's general practice. Bilingual production is typical of Art Beat Publishers' artist-book series. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Catherine Opie
description:
Long awaited, the first survey of the work of one of America's foremost contemporary fine art photographers.

For almost 40 years, Catherine Opie has been documenting with psychological acuity the cultural and geographic identity of contemporary America. This unique artist monograph presents a compelling visual narrative of Opie's work since the early 1980s, pairing images across bodies of work to form a full picture of her artistic vision. With more than 300 beautiful illustrations and made in close collaboration with Opie, the book marks a turning point in the consideration of this artist's work to date.

title: I/O Underflow
description:
I/O Underflow documents Tony Oursler's site-specific commission for the Oude Kerk, Amsterdam's oldest building, in which the artist turned a seven-hundred-year-old church into a staging ground for questions about identity, surveillance, and machine cognition.

The book collects photographs of the installed video projections and sculptural elements alongside full dialogues drawn from the performances, an introduction situating the commission within Oursler's earlier work, and an in-depth interview conducted for the project, all illustrated with material from the artist's own archives. The exhibition used digitally produced video performances, projected onto figures set within the church's Gothic architecture, to layer surveillance imagery, distorted faces, and fragments of code over the building's existing ornament. Text appears in Dutch and English.

Oursler has worked since the late 1970s at the intersection of sculpture, video, and performance, projecting animated faces and eyes onto soft forms to unsettle the boundary between object and consciousness. I/O Underflow extended that vocabulary into an ecclesiastical space, using the church's own history of witness and confession as a frame for his ongoing inquiry into how machines watch, listen, and mimic human presence.
notes: Catalogue for Oursler's 2015 solo commission at the Oude Kerk, Amsterdam; edited by Jacqueline Grandjean and Petra Heck. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Imponderable: The Archives of Tony Oursler
editor: Tom Eccles, Maja Hoffmann, Beatrix Ruf
description:
Since the late 1990s, Tony Oursler (born 1957) has amassed a sprawling personal archive of objects and ephemera relating to magic, the paranormal, film, television, phantasmagoria, pseudoscience and technology. The project doubles as a family history and a historical inquiry into belief itself.

This English-only edition, published for two parallel exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art and Bard College, presents highlights from the collection: photographs, prints, historic manuscripts, rare books, letters and objects tracing threads from stage magic and spirit photography to the friendship between Oursler's grandfather, the author and publisher Charles Fulton Oursler, and Harry Houdini, along with a documented encounter with Arthur Conan Doyle. Essays by Jordan Bear, Karen Beckman, Branden Joseph and others situate the archive within histories of belief, technology and image-making.

Oursler, best known for his video and sculptural installations projecting distorted faces onto soft forms, has long treated the archive as an open resource for his own practice; Imponderable makes that private research collection public for the first time.
notes: English-only 2016 edition (520pp), published for parallel exhibitions at MoMA and Bard College. A separate bilingual 2015 first edition (ISBN 9783037644263, 666pp) also exists; this record follows the later English edition. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Laura Owens
description:
Owens's Whitney retrospective catalogue is less a companion volume than a work in its own right: 664 pages assembled with the artist, tracking twenty-five years of painting that has never settled into a signature style.

Published by the Whitney Museum of American Art for the retrospective organised by Scott Rothkopf, which opened in New York in November 2017 and travelled to the Dallas Museum of Art and the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, the book covers Owens's output from the early 1990s to the present. Rothkopf's text is set alongside an unusually dense apparatus of documentation - installation views, source material, correspondence and studio ephemera - reflecting the artist's own archival habits and her involvement in the book's making. It is the fullest published account of a practice that runs from wall-scaled clock paintings to silkscreened wallpaper grids.

Owens (b. 1970, Euclid, Ohio) lives in Los Angeles, where she co-founded the exhibition space 356 Mission. Her work is held by the Whitney, MoMA, MOCA Los Angeles and Tate, and she has since shown paintings in dialogue with Van Gogh at the Fondation Vincent van Gogh Arles.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication
notes: Published for the retrospective at the Whitney Museum of American Art, November 2017 – February 2018, which travelled to the Dallas Museum of Art and the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles. Cover to be photographed from the physical copy.

title: Questions of Faith
description:
Questions of Faith gathers three years of paintings and sculpture by the Belgrade-born, London-based artist Djordje Ozbolt, whose deadpan humor and magpie borrowings from folk art, art history, and popular imagery unsettle any single reading of belief, ritual, or authority.

Published by Hauser & Wirth to accompany exhibitions at the Holburne Museum in Bath and the gallery's Somerset space, the book reproduces 169 color and 28 black-and-white images across 160 pages, tracing how Ozbolt layers art-historical quotation, invented iconography, and slapstick wit into paintings and carved or cast sculptures that read as artifacts of an imagined culture. An essay by ArtReview International Editor Oliver Basciano situates the work within Ozbolt's broader interrogation of history, politics, and travel.

Ozbolt studied at the Slade School of Fine Art after training in Belgrade, and has exhibited internationally since the early 2000s, developing a body of painting and sculpture that treats museums, myth, and tourist souvenirs as equally suspect sources of meaning; Questions of Faith stands as one of the fullest surveys of that practice to date.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Collected Works. Study Edition, Volume 1: 1942–1948
editor: Peter W. Kunhardt, Jr., Paul Roth
contributors: Henry Louis Gates, Jr. (Text), Deborah Willis (Text), Maurice Berger (Text), Barbara Baker Burrows (Text)
description:
The first volume of the most extensive publication devoted to Gordon Parks (1912–2006), covering the years in which he taught himself photography and reached the staff of Life.

The volume runs from 1942, when Parks was photographing in Chicago and Washington, to 1948, when Life hired him as its first African American staff photographer. Its years hold the work he made under Roy Stryker at the Farm Security Administration and the Office of War Information. That includes the 1942 portrait of the government charwoman Ella Watson, standing with a mop and broom before an American flag. The fashion and portrait assignments he was taking at the same time run alongside it.

Parks went on to build the extended photo essay into a form for reporting on crime, poverty and segregation. He worked later as a composer, author and filmmaker (The Learning Tree, Shaft). Peter W. Kunhardt, Jr. and Paul Roth edited the Study Edition, a smaller-format reissue of the 2012 Collected Works. It runs to 1,084 pages across five clothbound volumes, arranged chronologically. The printed cardboard box they ship in is part of the design, not packaging. Texts across the set are by Henry Louis Gates, Jr., Deborah Willis, Maurice Berger, Barbara Baker Burrows, Paul Roth and Parks himself. The library holds Volumes 1 to 3.
tags: Photography, Documentary Photography, African American Photographers, Photobooks, Civil Rights
notes: Volume 1 of five. The five volumes were issued only as a set, so 9783958292628 is the set’s ISBN and the cover image shows the set’s printed cardboard slipcase. The library holds Volumes 1 to 3 of 5; Volume 4 (1952–1998) and Volume 5 (Life magazine, 1948–1970) are not held. Volume periods read from Steidl’s product photography of the volume spines. Out of print at Steidl. Gordon Parks has no separate official site; The Gordon Parks Foundation, which he co-founded in 2006, is the authoritative estate site.

title: Cityscapes
edition_printrun: Second edition, 2008. First published December 2006 for the Miami exhibition.
contributors: Manon Slome (text), Michael Betancourt (text), Stefan Ruiz (cover photograph)
description:
José Parlá’s first book, published for Cityscapes, his Miami solo debut, staged by Spoonfed during Art Basel Miami Beach in December 2006.

Some 150 pages of paintings and photographs follow Parlá’s calligraphic, layered surfaces back to the walls that inform them: weathered posters, scrawled tags and the palimpsest of the street, recorded in his own photographs and reworked in paint. An introduction by the exhibition’s curator Manon Slome and an essay by the theorist Michael Betancourt place the work between graffiti, abstraction and urban archaeology. Designed by Chris Rubino with the artist; cover photograph by Stefan Ruiz.

Parlá (b. 1973, Miami) grew up writing graffiti in Miami and Puerto Rico and has since produced large-scale public commissions, including murals for One World Trade Center and the Barclays Center. Cityscapes precedes the Hatje Cantz survey Walls, Diaries, and Paintings, also in the collection.

title: Bottom of the Lake
description:
Bottom of the Lake is Christian Patterson's book-within-a-book: an artist's book built inside a 256-page facsimile of the telephone directory his family used in Fond du Lac, Wisconsin — a town whose name literally translates as "the bottom of the lake" — printed in 1973, soon after the photographer's birth.

Patterson interleaves the directory's found markings, ads and inserted ephemera with his own photographs, drawings and marginalia, producing a dark, wryly funny portrait of his hometown that resists straightforward documentary reading. The book extends past its pages: a telephone number printed inside connects callers to more than a hundred field recordings, archival audio and staged performances re-imagining the town. TBW Books published it as Book 1 of its Annual Series 4, in an edition of 1,500; a larger, retitled edition, Fond du Lac / Bottom of the Lake, followed from Walther König in 2015.

Patterson, born in Fond du Lac in 1972, first drew international attention with Redheaded Peckerwood (MACK, 2011), which wove photography, archival material and reenactment around the 1958 Starkweather-Fugate killing spree. Bottom of the Lake continues that method of splicing document and invention within a single Midwestern landscape, this time turned toward his own family history.
notes: Original 2013 TBW Books edition (ISBN 9781942953098, edition of 1500); a differently titled reissue, Fond du Lac / Bottom of the Lake, was published by Walther König in 2015 under a separate ISBN — confirm which printing the shelf copy is before finalizing. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Solus Volume I: Concerning Atypical Beauty and Youth (Vol.1)
Gröna Lund
edition_printrun: New edition of Petersen's 1973 debut book Gröna Lund: om människor på ett nöjesfält, originally published by Fyra Förläggare, Stockholm
description:
Gröna Lund is a new edition of Anders Petersen's debut book, revisiting the photographs he made in the early 1970s at Stockholm's Gröna Lund amusement park, one of the oldest in Sweden.

First published in 1973 by Fyra Förläggare as Gröna Lund: om människor på ett nöjesfält, with text by Jan Stolpe, the project shares its enclosed, crowd-filled setting with Petersen's celebrated Café Lehmitz. This edition reworks the original sequence, favoring a more intense, melancholy selection of images over the fairground's built-in euphoria. The result is a rougher, more urgent extension of the visual language Petersen had begun to develop.

Petersen studied under Christer Strömholm at his School of Photography in Stockholm before turning his camera on Hamburg's Café Lehmitz in the late 1960s, work that established him as one of Europe's most influential documentary photographers. Gröna Lund stands as the origin point of that practice, made before Lehmitz but published here in a form shaped by everything that followed.
notes: Row title given without the diaeresis; corrected to Gröna Lund. This is a later French-language re-edition (2013) of Petersen's 1973 debut book; the retailer tags the publisher as Aman Iman, unconfirmed beyond that. Pages, trim size and print run not found in any source checked. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Raymond Pettibon: Homo Americanus: Collected Works
Untitled (Imprint 93)
description:
Untitled is Elizabeth Peyton's contribution to Imprint 93, the mail-art press Matthew Higgs ran out of London between 1993 and 1998, distributing more than fifty artists' editions to a small circle of friends and collaborators.

The zine reproduces a sequence of video-stills of Nirvana's Kurt Cobain performing in 1993, staple-bound and photocopied in black and white. It was first issued in 1995 on the occasion of Peyton's exhibition Drawings at the Prince Albert Public House in Brixton, organized by Cabinet Gallery; this copy is the second printing, produced by Printed Matter in 2018 in an edition of 100 plus 10 artist's proofs, on the occasion of an archival exhibition of the Imprint 93 project that originated at the Whitechapel Gallery.

Peyton became known in the early 1990s for intimate, often androgynous portraits of musicians, historical figures, and friends, rendered in a loose, romantic line. Cobain was a recurring subject in her painting and drawing of the period, and this zine's grainy, mediated stills sit alongside that body of work as a rawer, more disposable counterpart to it.
notes: Second printing (1995/2018) of Peyton's Imprint 93 contribution, a photocopied, staple-bound zine of Kurt Cobain video-stills; edition of 100 + 10 APs. Original title stub read "Imprint93"; catalogued here as Untitled with the series retained, since the work itself is untitled and Imprint 93 is what identifies it. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Here She Comes Now
description:
The catalogue of Elizabeth Peyton’s 2013 exhibition at the Staatliche Kunsthalle Baden-Baden, the first to gather her portraits of musicians as a body of work in their own right.

Rock performers such as David Bowie, Kurt Cobain, Jarvis Cocker, Pete Doherty, the Gallagher brothers, John Lydon and Keith Richards appear alongside opera singers including Jessye Norman, Jonas Kaufmann and Ludwig Schnorr von Carolsfeld, shown not in formal poses but in performance. The source snapshots and archival photographs are reproduced en face with the finished oils and works on paper, surveying twenty years of painting and drawing and making visible how Peyton edits a found image into a portrait. Texts by curator Johan Holten and Dodie Kazanjian; 64 colour plates, in English and German.

Peyton (b. 1965) came to prominence in the 1990s with small, jewel-toned portraits of friends, musicians and historical figures, and her painting has since been the subject of surveys at the New Museum, the Whitechapel Gallery and the National Portrait Gallery, London. Here She Comes Now sits alongside the collection’s other Peyton titles, including Aire and Angels and the Hatje Cantz monograph.
tags: Art, Painting, Portraiture, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Music
notes: One of two copies in the collection. Record filled from empty stub.

title: The Age of Innocence
description: 13 color ill.. Artist's book (12 paintings by Elizabeth Peyton). The title of this small volume by Elizabeth Peyton The Age of Innocence is taken from the early 20th century novel of the same name by Edith Wharton. It describes the claustrophobic, repressed, hypocritical atmosphere of New York society in the 1870's. In the novel passion is shown as the force that would make that highly ritualized world implode.

title: Ghost
description:
Famed for her intimate painted portraits, Elizabeth Peyton (born 1965) has also produced a wide range of prints over the past two decades — monotypes, lithographs, woodcuts and etchings worked across diverse paper stocks and inks. In contrast to the diminutive scale of her paintings, the prints, particularly the lithographs and monotypes, are notably large.

Published to accompany the exhibition Ghost: Elizabeth Peyton at the Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum, St. Louis, and Opelvillen Rüsselsheim in 2011, this monograph is the first sustained study of Peyton as a critical printmaker. Subjects include historical figures such as William Shakespeare, Oscar Wilde and Lord Alfred Douglas, and Richard Wagner; artists including Frida Kahlo, David Hockney, Andy Warhol and Robert Mapplethorpe; musicians from Eminem to Kurt Cobain; and Peyton's own circle of friends. The book includes essays by Sabine Eckmann and Hilton Als, and an interview with the artist conducted by Beate Kemfert.

More recently Peyton has turned toward still life, extending a practice long defined by an intensely subjective, romantic mode of portraiture that helped define figurative painting in the 1990s and 2000s.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Portraiture, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Also travelled to Opelvillen Rüsselsheim, Germany, Feb–May 2011. Cataloged by some distributors as 'Elizabeth Peyton: Ghost' or 'Ghost: Works on Paper'; the ISBN and edition are the same book. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Kembra Pfahler "Beautalism"
description:
After more than three decades in the New York underground scene, we finally have a book on the inimitable Kembra Pfahler, artist and lead singer of the interdisciplinary rock band, the Voluptuous Horror of Karen Black.

Cataloguing her recent projects for the 2008 Whitney Biennial--which included a huge rock show in the Park Avenue Armory--this volume also features her most notorious body-art performances and shocking Sewn Vagina and Wall of Vagina pieces. Numerous full-bleed photographs capture the making of the Biennial artworks, the preparation for her live show, the performance itself and the aftermath. Also included are images of her drawings, sculptural works and installations, alongside short texts by the artist and an essay by curator and sometimes Girl of Karen Black, Kathy Grayson.
tags: "karen black", music, New York City, Punk

title: Choli Cholie
contributors: ECAL (University of Art and Design Lausanne) (Workshop)
description:
Choli Cholie collects photographs made by graduate students at ECAL, the University of Art and Design Lausanne, during a 2014-15 workshop led by the Swiss photographer Walter Pfeiffer, and stands as a collective homage to his sensibility rather than a monograph of his own pictures.

Rather than a technical class, Pfeiffer's workshop centered on exchanges about beauty, intuition, and the process of building an image from shoot to edit; the book's title, an allusion to a phrase of encouragement he repeated to students, gathers the resulting photographs, instinctive, spontaneous, and resistant to easy classification, into a tribute to his teaching. RVB Books published the softcover in Paris, 78 pages, 22 × 31 cm.

Pfeiffer, born in Zurich in 1946, has photographed queer and youth subcultures since the 1970s with a warmth and immediacy that shaped generations of Swiss and international photographers; Choli Cholie extends that influence directly into the work of a new one.
notes: A collaborative workshop project: photographs by ECAL graduate students made under Pfeiffer's direction, not solely his own images. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Hustlers
description:
Hustlers gathers Philip-Lorca diCorcia's landmark series of staged portraits of male prostitutes, made in Los Angeles between 1990 and 1992 with support from a National Endowment for the Arts grant.

DiCorcia scouted motel rooms, vacant lots and street corners, then paid his subjects to pose within scenes he had already lit and composed, completing most shoots within the hour. Each photograph is titled with the sitter's name, age, hometown and fee, a device that folds the transaction itself into the work. Twenty-one images from the series were shown at MoMA in 1993 as diCorcia's first solo museum exhibition, Strangers; this volume, published by Steidl in 2013, reproduces the complete project of 66 photographs for the first time.

DiCorcia has spent his career working at the border between documentary and constructed photography, staging apparently candid street scenes with hidden strobes and elaborate setups. Hustlers sits alongside Streetwork and Heads as one of his best-known bodies of work built from anonymous strangers photographed in public space.
notes: Stripped catalogue annotation "(SIGNED)" from title; recorded as signed. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Unsigned Three
description:
Unsigned Three is a small, stapled zine by the photographer Valerie Phillips, produced to mark a signing event at Dashwood Books in New York.

Issued in a hand-numbered edition of 150 copies, the sixteen-page zine gathers black-and-white photographs in Phillips's characteristic snapshot style — informal, close, shot on the fly — continuing the diaristic portraiture of teenage girls and young women that runs through her wider body of work. It is one installment in an ongoing, loosely numbered Unsigned series Phillips has produced for Dashwood over several years, made specifically to accompany in-store signings rather than for general trade distribution.

Phillips, born in New York and based in London, built her reputation on a snapshot aesthetic that treats fashion photography like a teenage diary; her photographs have appeared on album artwork for musicians including PJ Harvey and Amy Winehouse. Unsigned Three sits alongside her published monographs, among them Baby Blue and Another Girl, Another Planet, as a smaller, more immediate counterpart to that book work.
notes: Catalogue title was 'Unsigned'; the numbered volume ('Three') was read off the front cover, where THREE is set in a rule box; it was not recorded in the catalogue row. No ISBN — self-published zine format. Edition to be verified against the copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-28.

title: Grandpa Goes to Hollywood
description:
Published for Brad Phillips’s first exhibition with de boer in Los Angeles, a book of paintings that treats the artist’s own life as material to be edited rather than reported.

The show ran from 24 April to 29 May 2021 and was hung in two rooms. Figurative canvases of the artist’s wife, the poet and artist Cristine Brache, filled the main gallery, among them Cristine in My Camo Shirt, April 2020 and Getting Dressed to Meet the Parents, Deauville Hotel, Room 413, Miami, Aug. 2015. Text paintings hung apart from them, in the domestic setting of the gallery’s private viewing room. One of those, No Gods, No Masters, restages Bruce Nauman’s The True Artist Is an Amazing Luminous Fountain (1966) and puts Daffy Duck, hands on hips, in the space Nauman left blank. Titles that read like dated diary entries hang against slogans borrowed from other people, and the book keeps both halves of the argument. Linen over boards, 8.5 by 11 inches, with a dust jacket carrying a painting detail. Edition of 100.

Phillips is a Canadian painter and writer whose first collection of stories, Essays and Fictions, was published in 2019 by Giancarlo DiTrapano’s Tyrant Books. The exhibition worked the way that book does, setting the true and the invented in one voice and declining to say which is which. The library also holds his Mother Nature Mother Creature (Perish Publishing, 2014).
tags: Painting, Portraiture, Text Art, Exhibition Catalogue, Limited Edition, Los Angeles, Canadian Art
notes: Published for the exhibition at de boer, Los Angeles, 24 April to 29 May 2021, the artist’s first with the gallery. One of 100 copies.

title: Mother Nature Mother Creature
description:
Mother Nature Mother Creature (2014) is the first book in which the Canadian painter Brad Phillips (b. 1974) presents work made entirely of original photographs, rather than the photo-sourced paintings for which he is best known.

Printed in risograph color by Perish Publishing in Toronto, the 84-page paperback follows two tattooed women as they undress, walk through a West Coast Canadian forest, and dress again. In a wry nod to the "naturalism" invoked by fashion editorials and vintage pornography alike, Phillips stages the nude body outdoors and lets the sequence sit with an idea he traces to Elizabeth Barrett Browning: that the naked body is sexual only a fraction of the time. The images read like outtakes from a cult photo album - casual and unglamorous, quietly at odds with the genres they borrow from.

Phillips lives and works in Toronto and is represented by Anat Ebgi in Los Angeles and New York. His paintings, drawn from his own snapshots, mine intimacy, addiction, and desire with equal parts vulnerability and dark humor Mother Nature Mother Creature extends that same material into a rare stand-alone photographic project, issued in an edition of 200.
tags: Collage, Photography, Nude Photography, Risograph, Self-Published, Canadian Art

title: It’s Not Him You See At Night In Your Dreams Valerie Phillips

description: This lookbook from London-based fashion photographer Valerie Phillips candidly and unaffectedly profiles model Sara Cummings in her Californian hometown. In her raw and intimate style, Phillips documents the androgynous, skater-chic Cummings in vintage threads amidst the Americana kitsch of roadsigns, carousels, and wood-panelled dives. The photographer has published several books profiling young models with a humanity and affection rarely found in the world of fashion photography.

title: Pierre et Gilles: Double Je, 1976–2007
description:
The summa of Pierre et Gilles' first thirty years, published by Taschen to accompany the duo's 2007 retrospective Double Je at the Galerie Nationale du Jeu de Paume in Paris: a devotional survey of the hand-painted photographs in which camp, pop, religious iconography, and queer desire fuse into a single, meticulously constructed glamour.

Nearly 460 pages gather work from 1976 through 2007, from early portraits of friends and lovers to the icon-making images of Iggy Pop, Madonna, Nina Hagen, Catherine Deneuve, Laetitia Casta, Marilyn Manson, and Mireille Mathieu, alongside a run of self-portraits and an illustrated biography. Paul Ardenne contributes the main text and Jeff Koons the introduction, in English, French, and German. The black boards carry the artists' names in silver glitter script above their 1991 self-portrait as space-suited cosmonauts adrift in flowers, a cover as staged and tender as the pictures inside the volume itself is a monumental quarto weighing over three kilograms.

Pierre Commoy (b. 1950, La Roche-sur-Yon), a photographer, and Gilles Blanchard (b. 1953, Le Havre), a painter, have been partners in life and work since meeting in Paris in 1976. Their method has never varied: sitters are photographed in elaborate sets built by hand in the artists' studio, and the resulting unique print is painted over until photography and painting are inseparable. Retrospectives at the Maison Européenne de la Photographie (1996), the New Museum in New York (2000), and the Jeu de Paume mark their institutional standing Taschen's earlier volumes The Complete Works 1976–1996 and Sailors & Sea chart the same territory this book completes. They are represented by Galerie Templon, Paris.
tags: Photography, Contemporary Art, Queer Culture, Portraiture, Painted Photography, Exhibition Catalog, Art
notes: Identified from spine description ('Pierre ♥ Gilles ... TASCHEN' in silver script on black): cover confirmed visually — black boards, silver glitter script 'pierre ♥ gilles', the duo's 1991 cosmonaut self-portrait, 'Taschen' in script at foot. This is the Jeu de Paume retrospective catalogue, not the Flammarion 'Pierre et Gilles: 40' (2017), which is a different publisher and cover. Accessioned 2026-06-21, catalogued 2026-08-05 (LGBT+ collection).

title: Tomorrow's Man, Lynn Valley 9
description:
The opening statement of Jack Pierson's (b. 1960) celebrated Tomorrow's Man artist-book series, which lifts its title from an infamous 1950s-60s bodybuilding magazine and repurposes the retro homoerotics of physique culture into a freewheeling visual anthology.

Co-published in 2014 by Bywater Bros. Editions and Presentation House Gallery as the ninth volume of the gallery's Lynn Valley artist-book series, the 84-page softcover sets Pierson's portraits against vintage physique publications, celebrity photographs and oddball printed matter, dropped into an unconventional layout that runs imagery across page breaks and centerfolds with cheerful disregard. Contributions by David Carrino, Florence Derive, Alex Jovanovich, Dan McCarthy, Ryan Sullivan and Evan Whale thread through the sequence, capped by Veralyn Behenna's short story "The Lobster."

Pierson emerged from Boston's storied circle of photographers alongside Nan Goldin, David Armstrong and Mark Morrisroe, and works across photography, collage and his signature found-letter word sculptures his work is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney and the Guggenheim. Tomorrow's Man would grow into a six-volume series, all held in this collection alongside his monographs The Hungry Years and Jack Pierson (Photology).
