Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin shoot Saint Laurent, Steven Klein photographs Jordan Roth, Gaspar Noé shoots Gucci and Torbjørn Rødland shoots Prada.

Claude Cahun, Pierre Molinier, Jürgen Klauke, Sylvie Fleury, General Idea, Cosey Fanni Tutti, Jack Smith and Linder Sterling supply the issue's argument that glamour has always been a queer invention.
tags: Magazines, Purple Magazine, Fashion, Art, Culture

title: Andre
description: Jack Pierson's Andre is a photographic exploration presented in an intimate format.

title: Array (Miami Beach)
description: Jack Pierson's Array (Miami Beach) is a collection of photographic works capturing the essence of Miami Beach.

title: MUG SHOT – guilty until proven innocent
description: MUG SHOT throws an eye on the wide range of forced identity photography we have stored in our historic archives. Whether these were of actual guilty criminals in the eyes of the law or innocent victims of persecution, racial agendas, political prisoners or war camp inmates. Our administrative records are filled to the brim with these representations of the person who acted against those in charge.

title: Absent without Leave
description: Christopher Wool: Absent without Leave. Published by DAAD (Deutscher Akademischer Austauschdienst) for Wool's 1992-93 residency in Berlin. Signed by the artist.

title: Christopher Wool: Camden Arts Centre 2004
description: Exhibition catalogue for Christopher Wool's solo exhibition at Camden Arts Centre, London, 2004. Signed by the artist.
notes: English

title: Christopher Wool: Guggenheim
description: Exhibition catalogue for Christopher Wool's major retrospective at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, 1998. Signed by the artist.
notes: English

title: Projects: Christopher Wool/Robert Gober
description: Early collaborative exhibition catalogue for Christopher Wool and Robert Gober at 303 Gallery, New York, 1988. Limited edition gallery publication. Signed by the artist.

title: Christopher Wool: 11/6/04 - 12/23/04
description: Exhibition catalogue for Christopher Wool's solo exhibition at Luhring Augustine gallery, New York, November 6 - December 23, 2004. Signed by the artist.

title: Christopher Wool: London 2006
description: Exhibition catalogue for Christopher Wool's solo exhibition at Simon Lee Gallery, London, 2006. Signed by the artist.

title: Maybe Maybe Not
description: Limited edition artist's book published by Inktree Editions, 2001. Edition of 300 copies, each signed and numbered by the artist. Signed by the artist.
notes: English

title: Pass the Bitch Chicken
description: Artist's book published by Holzwarth Publications, 2002. Signed by the artist.
notes: English

title: Christopher Wool: Porto-Köln 2006-2008
description: Exhibition catalogue documenting Wool's exhibitions in Porto and Cologne, 2006-2008. Published by Walther König, 2009. Signed by the artist.
notes: English

title: Secession
description: Exhibition catalogue for Christopher Wool's solo exhibition at the Wiener Secession, Vienna, 2001. Signed by the artist.
notes: English

title: 1965: Malcolm in Winter: A Translation Exercise
contributors: John Akomfrah, Zoé Whitley, Najha Zigbi-Johnson
description: Documents Theaster Gates's exhibition commemorating the centenary of Malcolm X's birth and 60 years since his assassination. Features archival materials from the Black radical archive of journalist Ei Nagata and partner Haruhi Ishitani. Silver screen-printed cover. Includes essays by Najha Zigbi-Johnson and conversation between Gates, Zoé Whitley, and John Akomfrah.

title: Safe Word
publisher: Les Éditions Rien Ne Va Plus
description: Muller's 300-page publication is an account of an obsessive, staggering practice of photography and self-publishing. His dark and raw work is intended to exist as a cross-section as well as a chronology within dense and dazzling archives. Maxime Muller advances on a fault line where image and violence collide, he speaks to us of politics and identity.
notes: Risograph Perfect Binding Accessioned 2026-06-21, catalogued 2026-08-05 (LGBT+ collection).

title: Revue Faire: 49: Lawrence Weiner
description:
The 49th issue of the critical graphic design journal is about Lawrence Weiner and his relationship with typography, titled We Are Ships at Sea, Not Ducks On a Pond and written by Joris Kritis.

Its glossy, full-colour pages honor Weiner's use of graphic design, which has always in turn fascinated graphic designers. What makes Weiner's work seductive is his resolutely non-apologetic method of displaying words without need for any explanation. A comparative analysis is made of different voices about Weiner's use of graphics and typography. Next to a speculative history of Weiner's formal language, two interviews with graphic designer Linda Van Deursen and artist Nora Turato discuss Weiner's enduring legacy.
notes: Staple Bound Black-and-White Mixed

title: Meta Cars
description:
In Meta Cars, Beni Bischof transforms found images of cars into visual distortions.

Through digital manipulation and radical simplification, the original shapes are abstracted – reduced to ghostly and ridiculous silhouettes that feel both familiar and alien. The result: automotive hybrids with an almost hypnotic pull. Drawing on the aesthetics of American muscle cars and the TV shows of the 1980s and '90s, Bischof taps into a retro sense of coolness – reframing it for the digital age with irony, intensity, and unsettling beauty.

title: Public Spaces NY
description: A sequel to Vacant Spaces NY, this volume documents and analyzes Manhattan's public realm—parks, streets, community gardens, POPS (Privately Owned Public Spaces), and waterfronts. It examines the legal, regulatory, and management structures that shape these spaces, arguing that public space is never neutral. The book includes detailed mappings and speculative illustrations on how design facilitates or hinders inclusion in the US's densest city.
tags: Architecture, Urban Planning, New York City, Design, Public Space

title: Lisa Yuskavage
description: Exhibition catalog from Museo Tamayo Arte Contemporáneo in Mexico City (June 22 – September 17, 2006). Features critical essays by curator Tobias Ostrander ("Taste") and critic Christian Viveros-Fauné ("Cursed beauty: the painting of Lisa Yuskavage and the goosing of the great tradition"), alongside full-color reproductions of her work. Bilingual Spanish and English text.
tags: Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog, Women Artists

title: Lisa Yuskavage (Contemporary Artists Series)
contributors: Ariel Levy, Barry Schwabsky, Lena Dunham Photography by Jason Schmidt
description: The definitive monograph on the innovative American painter Lisa Yuskavage, published as part of Phaidon's Contemporary Artists Series. Documents over two decades of her work, known for its bold, eccentric, and exhibitionist characters that challenge the conventions of figurative painting. Includes never-before-seen photographs of her studio by Jason Schmidt and essays that explore the tension in her work between the sacred and profane, high art and popular culture.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Women Artists

title: Portrait of J
description: A photographic survey comprising 111 portraits of Japanese citizens from 2002 to present

title: Scandinavian Mushroom
description: A photographic tribute to Ed Ruscha artist books featuring wild mushrooms from Scandinavia

title: Invisible Man: Gordon Parks and Ralph Ellison in Harlem
description: A collaboration between Gordon Parks and Ralph Ellison documenting life in Harlem

title: Born Black (Expanded Edition)
description: Expanded edition of Gordon Parks autobiography and photographic memoir

title: Felix Gonzalez-Torres Roni Horn
description:
This photographic essay explores the artistic dialogue between Gonzalez-Torres and Horn initiated in 1990 when Gonzalez-Torres encountered Horn's work Gold Field (1980/82).

The publication examines four iconic pieces including Untitled (For Stockholm) (1992) and Untitled (Blood) (1992) by Gonzalez-Torres alongside Well and Truly (2009-10) and a.k.a. (2008-09) by Horn. Images were captured during a 2022 exhibition at the Bourse de Commerce-Pinault Collection in Paris revealing both artists' radical visual vocabularies as well as their shared passion for language writing and poetry. The work emphasizes themes of doubling duality repetition and identity exploring the inexpressible the immeasurable.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Photography, Collaboration, Installation Art

title: Shoot
description:
This compilation collects all seven issues of a self-published zine produced between 2005-2008.

The work presents extended portrait experiments using contact sheets outtakes and text featuring the artist's friends and collaborators. Originally photocopied at various centers the volumes retain characteristic marks of the copy machine and the artist's hand reflecting queer zine traditions. The book demonstrates Sepuya's photographic methodology questioning portraiture singularity authorship race sexuality and medium structures.
tags: Art, Photography, Zines, Portraiture, Queer Culture, Contemporary Art

title: Otherhow: Essays and Documents on Art and Disability 1985-2024
description: A collection spanning four decades of writings by deaf artist Joseph Grigely examining ableism embedded in cultural and media production through various communication modes. The work includes essays lectures postcards and documentation exploring the intersection of disability and art with sections on advocacy and accessibility.
tags: Art, Disability, Essays, Accessibility, Contemporary Art, Criticism

title: BUTT Magazine #3
description:
Spring 2002, the third issue of the Amsterdam quarterly Gert Jonkers and Jop van Bennekom had started the year before, sixty-eight pages on pink paper.

Jonkers interviews the fashion designer Jeremy Scott, photographed by Dino Dinco, and the Dutch actor Martin de Wolf, photographed by van Bennekom. Peter de Potter reaches Jónsi Þór Birgisson of Sigur Rós by telephone in Iceland. Gregor Doll and Andrew Zega interview the filmmaker Alexandre Frédéric, and Bruce LaBruce writes on the photographer Ryan McGinley, who contributes a picture of his own. Bas Meerman supplies drawings from his diary, Viviane Sassen "Fist and Tree," Albert van Westing a portrait of a man named Valeri, and van Bennekom a fold-out poster of chest hair. Sico Carlier lists more than four hundred adjectives for the word boy.

The issue announces Kutt, a lesbian sister magazine started by Jessica Gysel, Martien Mulder and Marjolein Bijlevelt, an early sign of the editorial network BUTT would keep working with for the next two decades.

title: BUTT Magazine #4
description:
Summer 2002, subtitled "international faggot magazine for international men," and the first issue to run without an editor's letter.

Gert Jonkers interviews Casey Spooner of Fischerspooner, photographed by Ryan McGinley, and the German scriptwriter Patrick Schuckmann. Tim Groen talks to the Swedish writer Daniel Björk, Jim Gladstone to Al Eingang, and Lernert Engelberts to the British artist David Haines. Jop van Bennekom photographs Stuart, a New Zealand hand model, and files a portfolio called "Hand Jobs." Arnoud Holleman contributes drawings made from life, and Engelberts, van Bennekom and Jos van Heel stage the bear Pim as Burt Reynolds. Reader submissions come in from Sydney, Toronto, Amsterdam and New York.

Sixty-eight pages on pink paper. The reader submissions running between the features became BUTT's defining structural habit, and eventually a standing section of their own.

title: BUTT Magazine #5
description:
Autumn 2002, the issue that fixed BUTT's masthead line: "international faggot magazine for interesting homosexuals and the men who love them."

Danny Calvi and Jop van Bennekom interview Matmos in Los Angeles, photographed by Ryan McGinley. Gert Jonkers meets the fashion photographer Matthias Vriens in Paris, Andy Burmeister talks to the filmmaker Allan Brocka, Tim Groen to the South African Johno du Plessis, and Jim Gladstone to Rob Stephenson, photographed by Terry Richardson. Sico Carlier contributes "1980," shot in San Francisco, Slava Mogutin photographs Ben in New York, and Wolfgang Tillmans photographs a gay couple on holiday in Lucca.

Sixty-eight pages on pink paper. The contents list credits every contributor by the city they came from and the city they worked in, a conceit the magazine kept for several issues.

title: BUTT Magazine #6
description:
Spring 2003, sixty-eight pages on pink paper and the first issue to call itself a fagazine.

Jop van Bennekom interviews the Viennese artist Matthias Herrmann, who also supplies a portfolio. Michael Bullock talks to Louis Crespo, photographed by Slava Mogutin; Gert Jonkers interviews the fashion designer Edward Buchanan; Jonkers and van Bennekom talk to the party host Bauke Kortleve; and Arnoud Holleman interviews the artist Roger Payne, photographed by Andreas Larsson with drawings by Payne himself. Terry Richardson photographs Carl, Heinz Peter Knes and Robert Brecko shoot Heinz, and Wolfgang Tillmans contributes "A true encounter in a hotel room in the Middle East" and the closing Butt Page.

Reader pictures arrive from Amsterdam, Gothenburg, New York and San Francisco, including an envelope credited to the White House.

title: BUTT Magazine #7
description:
Summer 2003, a special oversized New York issue and the only BUTT printed outside the magazine's usual pocket format.

Gert Jonkers interviews Marc Jacobs, photographed by Willy Vanderperre, and Jop van Bennekom interviews AA Bronson, photographed by Bruce LaBruce. Danny Calvi talks to the musician Phiiliip, photographed by Hedi Slimane, and Andrew Richardson interviews the vintage couture dealer Keni Valenti. Marcelo Krasilcic photographs the porn actor Tommy DeLuca, Peter Maloney shoots Model Miek and assume vivid astro focus supplies the wallpaper. "The Gert Shirt" tracks a single shirt through seven photographers, among them Terry Richardson, Marcelo Krasilcic and Lernert Engelberts, shot in New York, Switzerland, Friesland and the Netherlands.

Sixty pages on pink paper. The editors' whole note reads: "This special issue of BUTT is about New York. It's bigger than average. Like, think big."

title: BUTT Magazine #8
description:
Autumn 2003, seventy-four pages on pink paper, opening with the Hidden Cameras singer Joel Gibb photographed by Viviane Sassen.

Alex Needham interviews Gibb, Jim Gladstone talks to the San Francisco writer and editor Matt Bernstein Sycamore, photographed by Jack Hunter, and Gert Jonkers interviews the Paris-based menswear designer Thomas Engel Hart, photographed by Katja Rahlwes. Billy Miller conducts what the magazine bills as the very last interview with the artist Asianpunkboy, illustrated with his own pictures. Lars Erik Frank interviews the Copenhagen activist Mads Ted Drud-Jensen, photographed by Erik Pold. Neal Franc documents a performance by Hailey Thompson, Albert van Westing contributes pictures and Sander Plug the double Butt page.

The editors' note for the issue runs to a single line: "It's Autumn 2003. It's October, November, December."

title: BUTT Magazine #9
description:
Spring 2004, the issue with Michael Stipe photographed and interviewed by Wolfgang Tillmans.

Tim Groen talks to the ballet dancer and choreographer Stephen Galloway, photographed by Viviane Sassen, and Alex Needham interviews Martin Degville, formerly of Sigue Sigue Sputnik, photographed by Andreas Larsson. Erik Hagoort interviews the florist Nard Wiegmans with portraits by Albert van Westing. Marcelo Krasilcic photographs Jake Shears of Scissor Sisters, Dean Sameshima contributes "Deaf Dude," Heinz Peter Knes files "1001" and Andreas Larsson shoots Calvin. BUTTSTUFF, the readers' section, appears for the first time under that name, carrying a sex review, a discovery by Neal Franc and Cock Talk with a reader from Amsterdam.

Seventy-four pages on pink paper, published under the strapline "fantastic magazine for homosexuals."

title: BUTT Magazine #10
description:
Summer 2004, the tenth issue, which the editors reckoned brought the magazine to about seven hundred pages of men, art, fashion and asses.

James Anderson interviews Peter Berlin, who supplies self-portraits and the opening picture. Alex Needham talks to Stephin Merritt of the Magnetic Fields, photographed by Marcelo Krasilcic, and Jop van Bennekom interviews the designer Lutz, photographed by Wolfgang Tillmans. Gert Jonkers conducts the second of Casey Spooner's recurring interviews, photographed by Terry Richardson; David Mills talks to the London performer Jonny Wooster, photographed by Andreas Larsson; and William Van Meter interviews Marcello, photographed by Slava Mogutin. A double-sided poster stages Michael as Al Parker, photographed by Joe Oppedisano.

Sixty-eight pages on pink paper. The editors sign off asking readers to enjoy the summer and be nice to other homos.

title: BUTT Magazine #11
description:
Autumn 2004, seventy-two pages on pink paper, with Roy Blakey's "Men in Color" shot in New York around 1980.

Marcel Musters interviews Dominic Vine, illustrated with Vine's self-portraits; Gert Jonkers talks to Luigi Murenu, Madonna's hairdresser; and Danny Calvi interviews the writer Robert Glück. Heinz Peter Knes shoots "Super Gays" in Berlin, Albert van Westing photographs "The Neighbour" and Paul Flynn contributes a story called "Andy Brooks." BUTTSTUFF carries a sex review by Peter and the Top Men, George and Oliver.

The editors' letter is one sentence long, which by this point in the run had become its own kind of house style.

title: BUTT Magazine #12
description:
Spring 2005, seventy-six pages on pink paper, with Bruce LaBruce interviewed in Berlin about punks, skinheads and German ancestors.

Jop van Bennekom conducts the LaBruce interview; Paul Tierney talks to the designer Antony Price in London about Roxy Music and arse pants; Gert Jonkers interviews Bruce Benderson in Paris; and Alex Needham interviews Dominic Masters, photographed by Wolfgang Tillmans. Van Bennekom interviews Mr Leather Europe, Roberto Menichetti, photographed in Antwerp by Andreas Larsson, and James Anderson talks to Jonjo, also shot by Larsson. Louis Zoellar Bickett II contributes "Haviland," Sander Plug "The Drawing Class" and Albert van Westing "Clash," a Spanish tourist photographed in Rome.

As in the Autumn 2002 issue, every contributor is credited by the city they came from and the city they worked in.

title: BUTT Magazine #13
description:
Summer 2005, the special BAD issue, which the editors made instead of skipping an unlucky thirteenth number.

Wolfgang Tillmans interviews John Waters, photographed by Ryan McGinley, and contributes "Bottoms." Thirteen contributors supply thirteen bad sex stories, among them Adam Baran, Vaginal Davis, Bruce Benderson, Billy Miller of Straight to Hell, Bruce LaBruce, Robert Glück, Stephin Merritt, William Van Meter and Shannon Michael Kane. James Anderson files a deliberately boring interview with a random gay stranger, Sander Plug an embarrassing one with a one-night stand, and Adam Baran a disgusting one with a toilet cleaner, photographed by Paul Moreno. "Normal Bodies" gathers submissions from around the world, Mathias Casado Castro shoots "Twink" and Donatien Veismann "Party Poopers."

Seventy-six pages on pink paper. The BAD issue is BUTT's only themed issue of the original run built around a refusal rather than a subject.

title: BUTT Magazine #14
description:
Autumn 2005, seventy-six pages on pink paper, with Walter Pfeiffer interviewed and given a portfolio of his own.

Jop van Bennekom interviews Pfeiffer, whose "Super Beauties" follows; Gert Jonkers talks to Christopher Ciccone, photographed by Naomi Fisher; James Anderson interviews the stylist Simon Foxton, photographed by Alasdair McLellan; and Luis Venegas interviews the German musician Justus Köhncke, photographed by Wolfgang Tillmans. Marcelo Krasilcic shoots "Go Go," Michael Bullock and Andreas Larsson file the story "Xevi," and Didier Barroso photographs Michiel. "Why Not?" collects submissions from around the world and BUTTSTUFF closes the issue.

Pfeiffer's appearance here begins a long association: he would still be contributing to BUTT seventeen years later, in the 2022 relaunch issues.

title: BUTT Magazine #15
description:
Spring 2006, seventy-six pages on pink paper, opening with Walter Pfeiffer's "Spring."

Jop van Bennekom and Gert Jonkers interview Viktor and Rolf together with Rufus Wainwright, photographed by Viviane Sassen. Adam Baran talks to the writer Mike Albo, with portraits by Derek Jackson, and to Ed Droste of Grizzly Bear, photographed by Andreas Larsson. Stephin Merritt interviews both halves of Kiki and Herb, Justin Bond and Kenny Mellman, photographed by Johnnie Shand Kydd. Jonkers writes on Paul Rutherford of Frankie Goes to Hollywood, now in New Zealand. Paul Mpagi Sepuya contributes "Boys," Juan-Dario "Cock" and Eduard Xandri "The Ball."

The last page is a piece of sheet music, "Nasty Fucker," composed by Mikael Karlsson.

title: BUTT Magazine #16
description:
Summer 2006, an issue given over to sex in its many settings, seventy-six pages on pink paper.

Paul Flynn writes on Julian Ganio, photographed by Wolfgang Tillmans, who also shoots Mark Simpson for an interview by Bruce Benderson. Gert Jonkers interviews the Portland singer-songwriter Holcombe Waller, photographed by Marcelo Krasilcic, who separately files a report from Portland, Oregon. Slava Mogutin interviews the Norwegian artist Bjarne Melgaard, photographed by Daniel Riera. "Buddies" documents gay cliques in Madrid, Berlin, Sydney and Los Angeles, shot by Luis Venegas, Heinz Peter Knes, Samuel Hodge and Dino Dinco. Christophe Chemin contributes four self-portraits.

The editors' note is a list of the issue's subjects and nothing else, one of the shortest they ever ran.

title: BUTT Magazine #17
description:
Autumn 2006, published five years after BUTT began and alongside the first BUTT Book, the anthology the editors made that summer.

Bruce LaBruce interviews Gus Van Sant. Stuart Comer interviews Wolfgang Tillmans, photographed by Heinz Peter Knes, in an exchange printed in German. James Anderson talks to the artist Jimmy Robert, photographed by Tillmans; William Van Meter interviews the porn actor François Sagat, photographed by Marcus Mam; David Mills talks to Ernesto, photographed by Johnnie Shand Kydd; and Gert Jonkers interviews Edmund White. Helmut Lang contributes a diary, Heinz Peter Knes shoots Ioannis and Shand Kydd files "Out."

Seventy-six pages on pink paper. The editors chose not to make it an anniversary issue, noting only that they had worked their asses off producing the book instead.

title: BUTT Magazine #18
description:
Winter 2006, seventy-six pages on pink paper, running two of the magazine's recurring formats and a portfolio of body hair.

Gert Jonkers interviews the porn director Michael Lucas and conducts the biennial Casey Spooner interview, photographed by Marcelo Krasilcic. Jop van Bennekom interviews Jason Whipple in Vermont, photographed by Miguel Villalobos. Ed Droste, interviewed himself earlier in the year, talks to Owen Pallett, photographed by Neal Franc. Adam Baran interviews John Cameron Mitchell, photographed by Wolfgang Tillmans, and Alex Needham interviews the punk historian Jon Savage, photographed by Jason Evans. Cesar Padilla writes on Rob Halford of Judas Priest, Robert Greene contributes "You Are So Hairy" and Matthias Vriens "The Couple."

Readers who first appeared in BUTTSTUFF and then returned as interviewers is a pattern this issue makes visible twice over.

title: BUTT Magazine #19
description:
Spring 2007, eighty pages on pink paper, the first issue to run past seventy-six.

Adam Baran interviews the artist Francesco Vezzoli, photographed by Marcelo Krasilcic, in what the magazine bills as a strikingly honest conversation about sex. Frank Rodriguez writes on the pornographer Joe Gage, Lernert Engelberts interviews Dirty Danny in Amsterdam, photographed by Jop van Bennekom, and Danny McFadden interviews Buck Angel. James Anderson contributes "66 sentences about Jim," photographed by Benjamin Alexander Huseby, who also supplies a portfolio. Walter Pfeiffer photographs Ricardo and Johannes, Luis Venegas files "Un hombre español," Derek Jackson "I Am Derek" and Daniel Riera a calendar of Spanish cocks.

BUTTSTUFF closes the issue, as it did every issue from BUTT 9 until the format was retired in 2008.

title: BUTT Magazine #20
description:
Summer 2007, the LA issue, made after the editors went back to Los Angeles for what they described as chill conversations and easy sunlight.

Jop van Bennekom interviews the art dealer Javier Peres, photographed by Jeppe Laursen. Gert Jonkers interviews Gore Vidal, the photographer and artist Jeff Burton, and the Danish musician Jeppe, photographed by Sean DeLear. Alex Needham talks to Perez Hilton, photographed by Dino Dinco, who also files "Los LA Amigos." Frank Rodriguez writes on the housecleaner Marco Flores, prvtdncr documents the graffiti artist Hollywood, and Matthias Vriens photographs "My LA Men" in a West Hollywood cottage. BUTTSTUFF contributes a single Los Angeles sex story.

Eighty pages on pink paper. The cover image is a vintage photograph the editors had already used once, in the debut issue of their other magazine, Fantastic Man.

title: BUTT Magazine #21
description:
Late autumn and early winter 2007, at eighty-four pages the longest issue of BUTT to that point.

Bruce LaBruce interviews Vaginal Davis in Berlin. Adam Baran talks to the California portraitist Don Bachardy, photographed by Matthias Vriens; Michael Bullock interviews the Canadian twins Ian and Marc Hundley, photographed by Marcelo Krasilcic; and Danny McFadden interviews the DJ Daniel Wang, photographed by Heinz Peter Knes. Sunil Gupta contributes "1976," photographs of Christopher Street; Régis Trigano photographs the French horticulturist Xavier; Andreas Larsson shoots East London lads and, with a text by James Anderson, "Kenny the Homo Dog"; and Shaun Fletcher photographs a bartender at the New York bear bar Big Lug.

Gupta's Christopher Street pictures would return to BUTT fifteen years later, when the relaunched magazine ran an interview with him in issue 30.

title: BUTT Magazine #22
description:
Spring 2008, seventy-six pages on pink paper, with a rather late interview with the pornographer Fred Halsted, who died in 1989.

William E. Jones conducts the Halsted piece. AA Bronson interviews the photographer Paul Mpagi Sepuya, illustrated with Sepuya's own pictures; Adam Baran interviews Peter Party, photographed by Miguel Villalobos; Jop van Bennekom talks to the celebrity photographer Gary Lee Boas, photographed by Marc Zaffuto; and Bruce Benderson writes on Ian and Joe. Cesar Padilla contributes "Drummers," Daniel Riera photographs Lernert Engelberts as the centerfold and Alessandro Di Giampietro files "Italiani."

Sepuya's first appearance in the magazine as a subject; he was still shooting for BUTT sixteen years later, in issue 34.

title: BUTT Magazine #23
description:
Summer 2008, the issue that introduced BUTT's waterproof cover and retired BUTTSTUFF.

Gert Jonkers interviews the New York designer Thom Browne about clothes and fetishes, photographed by Marcelo Krasilcic. Paul Flynn meets Andy Butler of Hercules and Love Affair, photographed by Andreas Larsson; Bruce Benderson interviews Sébastien, photographed by Marc Zaffuto; Adam Baran interviews Slava Mogutin, photographed by Terry Richardson; Alex Needham talks to Simon Napier-Bell, photographed by Johnnie Shand Kydd; and Angelo Flaccavento interviews the Italian actor and writer Filippo Timi. Alex Klesta photographs the London doorman Greg, and James Anderson writes forty-seven sentences about his friend Colin.

Seventy-six pages on pink paper. The revamped back section replaced BUTTSTUFF with random stories, cocks, faces, and a difficult-word list for readers who had written in to say the magazine was hard to read.

title: BUTT Magazine #24
description:
Autumn 2008, eighty-four pages on pink paper, the first issue to call itself The Homosexual Quarterly.

Gert Jonkers interviews Jake Shears of Scissor Sisters, photographed by Hedi Slimane. Dietmar Schwärzler meets the German director Rosa von Praunheim, photographed by Heinz Peter Knes; Michael Bullock interviews the creator of Thugs4thugsex.com about his Brooklyn sex parties; Billy Miller of Straight to Hell talks to the Canadian underwear designer Will Munro, photographed by Kyle Tryhorn; Cesar Padilla covers the Kentucky artist Stephen Irwin; and Luis Venegas interviews the Spanish teenager Íñigo. Terry Richardson photographs the Hungarian porn actor Arpad Miklos in New York, and the issue reprints a portfolio of Keith Haring's penis drawings, all made on one day in 1978 while he was still at art school.

Reader submissions run between the features throughout, the format the magazine kept after retiring BUTTSTUFF the previous issue.

title: BUTT Magazine #25
description:
Winter 2008/09, the twenty-fifth issue, whose cover returned the magazine to an ass: Juan, born in Colombia, raised in Miami, and the intern at BUTT's New York office.

Miguel Villalobos photographed Juan at Boiler Room on 23 October 2008 and persuaded at least twenty-five other men at the bar to drop their trousers, which supplies the "25 Butts" portfolio. Michael Bullock interviews John Holland of Salem, photographed by David Benjamin Sherry; Rupert Smith telephones the punk pioneer Jayne County in Georgia, photographed by Michael Fox; Jop van Bennekom interviews the Canadian painter Paul P., photographed by Scott Treleaven; Felix Burrichter interviews and photographs Craig P. Wern; and Adam Baran interviews a Czech convert, photographed by Martin Maryska. Adrian Gaut shoots a double-sided poster of the bathrooms at The Cock in New York.

Seventy-two pages on pink paper, with a poem by Shane Allison, a recipe by Mark Owen and a note recording that the two thousandth BUTTHEAD lives in Chicago.

title: BUTT Magazine #26
description:
Springtime 2009, ninety pages on pink paper, the longest single issue of BUTT's original run, and the one whose contents page turns the spotlight on its writers.

Ed Droste interviews the composer Nico Muhly. Adam Baran visits Vince Aletti, the collector of male nudes, photographed by Marcelo Krasilcic, and separately interviews the Japanese Pinkman, photographed by Dirk Zschunke. Paul Flynn meets the writer and performer Aiden Shaw in a London churchyard, photographed by Marc Wayland. Felix Burrichter interviews the two cover bears, Rick and Daren, from Texas; Adriano Sack interviews the Berlin artist Marc Brandenburg. Wolfgang Tillmans contributes a sixteen-page color portfolio titled "Der Unterwäschekatalog," Benjamin Fredrickson supplies Polaroids and Seth Bogart photographs Brontez Purnell, who also writes.

Both Purnell and Fredrickson would still be contributing when the magazine came back into print more than a decade later.

title: BUTT Magazine #27
description:
Fall 2009, the "straight" issue, an exception to what the editors describe as BUTT's unwritten rule that the magazine be a hundred percent homo.

The cover is Angel Hernandez, a forty-three-year-old carpenter and father from Queens. Gert Jonkers puts uncomfortable sex questions to the Dutch photographer Lard. Adam Baran goes to the Bijou Theater in Chicago, photographed by Jacob Meehan, and interviews its owner Steven Toushin. Jeremy Scott interviews Tony Ward in Los Angeles, with portraits by Robin Black. Cesar Padilla interviews a regular at his Louisville bar; Andreas Larsson photographs Stockholm men who look gay and are not; Gabrielle Mangeri contributes twenty pictures of her boyfriend; and Bruce Benderson writes an homage to breasts. "Heterosexualisms" gathers short pieces by Felix Burrichter, Jane Knox, Michael Bullock, Adriano Sack and Xevi Muntané.

Seventy-four pages on pink paper. The editors conclude that after making the issue they are less sure than before what heterosexuality means.

title: BUTT Magazine #28
description:
Spring 2010, seventy-eight pages on pink paper, the issue in which BUTT greets a new decade and introduces its blind date experiment.

Alex Needham interviews Kele Okereke of Bloc Party, photographed by Wolfgang Tillmans. Horacio Silva interviews Lorenzo Martone, photographed by Walter Pfeiffer; Michael Bullock talks to the video artist Ryan Trecartin, photographed by Paul Kopkau; and Paul Flynn interviews the former escort behind Greek Pete, photographed by Alasdair McLellan. The blind date experiment runs Thomas, Alexander, Paul, River and Joseph through the magazine's own matchmaking. Zoe Ghertner shoots "Fantasy," Juan-Dario files "Paris Is Cruising," and Corey Corey supplies an erotic massage guide photographed by Felix Burrichter. "Butt à la carte" profiles five men who cook, in Berlin, New York, Beijing, Spain and London.

This was the last issue before an absence of almost two years.

title: BUTT Magazine #29
description:
Autumn and Winter 2011, a double issue at a hundred and forty-four pages, published after nearly two years away and structured as an alphabet of homosexuality.

BUTT A–Z runs from A for Adriano, on Adriano Cintra by Danny Calvi and Marcelo Krasilcic, to XYZ by Gert Jonkers and Jop van Bennekom. Along the way: Wolfgang Tillmans on buzz cuts and on Karl, Cary Kwok on cum, Guy Trebay and Chris Beckham on Jonah Falcon, Paul Flynn and Alasdair McLellan on Jonny Pierce, Charlie Porter and Andreas Larsson on the calligrapher Paul Antonio, John Waters and Miguel Villalobos on Dina Martina, Gert Jonkers and Daniel Riera on Rick Owens, Michael Bullock and Marcelo Krasilcic on Telfar Clemens, and Cesar Padilla on vintage.

The issue carries two covers, both of Karl from Berlin, photographed by Wolfgang Tillmans. It was the last BUTT for eleven years.

title: BUTT Magazine #30
description:
Spring 2022, the issue that brought BUTT back into print after eleven years, made by an editorial club rather than by two editors.

Spyros Rennt photographs the DJ Babynymph. CL Mayers and Cameron Ugbodu write on Ajamu X and his Black Perverts Network in London; Felix Burrichter and Kuba Ryniewicz cover the hairdresser Holli Smith; AA Bronson and Victor Luque interview the porn actor Billy Vega; Karol Radziszewski and Ryniewicz document Homokomando in Poland; Prem Sahib and Ryniewicz interview Sunil Gupta about cruising with a camera; Erik Wong and Anton Shebetko talk to Richard John Jones; and Gert Jonkers interviews the actor Félix Maritaud, photographed by Rennt. Clifford Prince King and Willy Ndatira contribute "Sequence," Heinz Peter Knes "Joint" and David Lindert "Teargarten." Sean DeLear's 1979 diaries run as "Tony's Diary."

The masthead is a list rather than a hierarchy, and it names Jessica Gysel, who had started BUTT's lesbian sister magazine twenty years earlier.

title: BUTT Magazine #31
description:
Autumn 2022, the second issue of the relaunch, more than a hundred pink pages on what its contributors mean by freedom.

Bruce LaBruce interviews Jordan Firstman. Madison Moore and Ethan James Green cover the critic Hilton Als; Sophia Lamar and Bruno Staub interview Arca; Anton Shebetko and Vic Bakin talk to Stas Tweeman about war and techno; Michael Holt and Daniel Jack Lyons interview Leilah Weinraub in Los Angeles; Jordan Tannahill and Milan Zrnic meet Durk Dehner, who carries on Tom of Finland's legacy; Pierre-Alexandre Mateos and Staub interview the Paris artist Soufiane Ababri; and Andrew Pasquier and Shebetko interview Georgy Mamedov on queer communism. Wolfgang Tillmans photographs Matthew Blaise in Lagos and Juan Pablo Echeverri, Kuba Ryniewicz shoots Yoni in Newcastle, Zac Bayly interviews Max Arion, and Walter Pfeiffer contributes "Pussy."

Pfeiffer's contribution comes seventeen years after his first, and the issue's thanks go to Bottega Veneta, which has supported every issue since.

title: BUTT Magazine #32
description:
Spring 2023, an issue whose subjects run from an artist in a titty suit to a Czech tombstone engraver.

Zak Stone and Philip-Daniel Ducasse cover the stylist turned artist Akeem Smith. Brontez Purnell interviews Eileen Myles, photographed by Jack Pierson; Wilfrid Wood draws Oliver Sim for an interview by Gert Jonkers; Phillip Picardi, Billy Lobos and Benjamin Ackermann meet the Los Angeles sex worker Sharok; Steve Marais photographs Roman Hanak in the Czech Republic; Miloš Trakilović covers the Kosovar artist Astrit Ismaili; Zac Bayly interviews the accountant Katrina Summers; and Wolfgang Tillmans photographs LSDXOXO. Kuba Ryniewicz shoots "Trio Polski," Clifford Prince King "Favs!", Daisuke Nakashima "Arise" in Tokyo and Anthony O'Donoghue "Misc."

Eileen Myles and Katrina Summers appearing in the same issue is the clearest statement of the relaunched magazine's widened brief.

title: BUTT Magazine #33
description:
Autumn 2023, the thirty-third issue, given over to sex and what its contributors call the desire to create new queer worlds.

Michael Bullock and Torso cover the wrestler Sonny Kiss. Leendert Sonnevelt and Kotori Kawashima interview the Tokyo dressmaker Tomo Koizumi; Jordan Tannahill and Wolfgang Tillmans cover the DJ Grace Sands; Jop van Bennekom interviews the Thai photographer Harit Srikhao; Zak Stone and Rodrigo Álvarez meet Mexican Jihad in Mexico City; Evan Moffitt and James Emmerman interview the chef Andy Baraghani; Juliana Huxtable interviews Paul B. Preciado on body politics; Melanie Bonajo covers Young Boy Dancing Group; and Phillip Picardi and Matthias Vriens interview the painter Jwan Yosef. Benjamin Fredrickson contributes "Unzip" and Pol Anglada "Love You."

A reader submission, "Just a Hole, Sir," runs as a full feature, credited to Emil Cañita and Zac Bayly.

title: BUTT Magazine #34
description:
Spring 2024, an issue the editors summarise as running from ass to architecture to ass architecture.

Douglas Greenwood interviews the historian Jason Okundaye, photographed by Ajamu X. Zak Stone and Collier Schorr cover Hari Nef; Michael Bullock and Marcelo Krasilcic interview Dr Evan Goldstein; Kuba Ryniewicz photographs Gray Wielebinski and Asa Seresin and files "Play"; Matt Lambert shoots Frank Redieß of Ficken 3000; Evan Moffitt and Daniel Riera interview Marwan Kaabour; Andrew Pasquier and Raphaël Chatelain interview Constance Debré; and Gert Jonkers interviews Jean-Pierre Blanc, photographed by Marc Turlan. Chris Curreri contributes "Mouthful" and Paul Mpagi Sepuya "Hotshots," shot in the studio.

Sepuya first appeared in BUTT in 2008 as an interview subject; this is one of several returns the relaunch has made a habit of.

title: BUTT Magazine #35
description:
Autumn 2024, subtitled Pleasures, with contributors reporting from Tbilisi, Melbourne, Mexico City and a French dairy farm.

Zak Stone and Clifford Prince King interview Troye Sivan. Alberto Bustamante and Gustavo García-Villa cover Lalo Santos; Jeremy O. Harris and Alasdair McLellan interview Honey Dijon; Yasuyuki Shinohara writes on the Japanese artist Sadao Hasegawa; Michael Bullock and Reynaldo Rivera interview Gary Indiana; Anton Shebetko covers Giorgi Kikonishvili in Tbilisi; Ruby Zarsky and Lia Clay document trans strip nights in New York; Daniel Jack Lyons photographs Pierre the farmer; Evan Moffitt and Paul Mpagi Sepuya interview Dean Sameshima; and Andrew Pasquier and Raphaël Chatelain interview the Valencian artist Carlos Sáez. Kay Gabriel and Sam Clarke write on club sex, and Thyago Sainte photographs a Berlin allotment.

Dean Sameshima's first BUTT contribution was "Deaf Dude" in the Spring 2004 issue, twenty years earlier.

title: BUTT Magazine #36
description:
Spring 2025, subtitled Revelations, and the thickest issue the relaunched magazine had made.

Luis Venegas interviews the Spanish actor Omar Ayuso. AA Bronson and Daniel Jack Lyons conduct an intergenerational conversation with Joel Someone; Jesse Glazzard and Asa Seresin photograph Jill LeFlour; Felix Burrichter and Hildegard Titus report on Friedel Dausab's fight against Namibia's anti-sodomy law; Sam Max and Ethan Skaates interview Lilly Wachowski; Jordan Tannahill and Jo Fetto meet Filippo Sorcinelli, who designs vestments for the Pope; Sophia Al-Maria and Vic Lentaigne cover the wrestler Black Venus; Gert Jonkers and Kuba Ryniewicz interview the Welsh painter David Dawson; and Gustavo García-Villa photographs Sir Karim in Mexico. Raoul de Jong and Anton Shebetko retell an eighteenth-century anti-sodomy case, Zac Bayly reports from Melbourne, and Ryūdai Takano contributes "With Me."

Stéphane Gaboué photographs the Bordeaux couple Jérémy and Clément, one of the relaunch's recurring love-story features.

title: BUTT Magazine #37
description:
Autumn 2025, whose interview list pairs Martin Margiela with Jean Paul Gaultier and Nan Goldin with Édouard Louis.

Jordan Tannahill interviews Édouard Louis, photographed by Nan Goldin. Margiela interviews Gaultier, illustrated by Soufiane Ababri. Carlos Motta and David Mesa talk to Rubén Darío Gómez about running a towel-optional cultural institution; Amelia Abraham interviews Coco and Candela Capitán; Andrew Pasquier and Raphaël Chatelain interview the Hong Kong filmmaker Ray Yeung; Evan Moffitt and Daniel Jack Lyons meet the Los Angeles artist William E. Jones; Chico Felitti and Pedro Pedreira interview the Brazilian deputy Erika Hilton, in Portuguese; Michael Bullock and Daniel Trese interview Michael Rosey; and Bruce LaBruce interviews Omar Apollo. Ignasi Monreal contributes "Smart Ass Phones," Cary Kwok three paintings and Benjamin Fredrickson a portfolio of socks.

Erika Hilton's interview runs in Portuguese without translation, a first for the magazine.

title: Matera 1953
description:
Federico Patellani's photographic record of the making of Alberto Lattuada's 1953 film La Lupa stands as a rare document of Matera before its Sassi districts became an emblem of Italian poverty and resilience.

In the wake of Carlo Levi's Christ Stopped at Eboli, Matera drew writers, photographers, and filmmakers eager to confront a place history seemed to have overlooked. Lattuada and Patellani arrived in 1953 to shoot La Lupa, a melodrama shot through with Neorealist observation, and Patellani turned his camera on location scouting, the mechanics of the shoot, and the faces and streets of the city. Left in a drawer for decades, the reportage appears here in full for the first time, with texts by Matteo Pavesi, Alberto Crespi, and Giovanna Calvenzi. Humboldt Books issued it in its Time Travel series: a 96-page softcover with French flaps and an inserted booklet, bilingual in Italian and English.

Patellani was among Italy's foremost photojournalists, known for the reportage Italia Magica and for work that repeatedly crossed into cinema, including a turn as assistant director on La Lupa itself. Lattuada, who co-founded Milan's Cineteca Italiana with Luigi Comencini in 1947, moved between architecture, cinema, and photography across more than forty films.
tags: Photography, Italy, Matera, Cinema, Neorealism, Time Travel Series, Humboldt Books, Federico Patellani, Alberto Lattuada

title: USA 1972
description:
In the summer of 1972, Mario Bellini crossed the United States with a Hasselblad, and the resulting pictures read less like a designer's sketchbook than a candid portrait of an America already slipping into memory.

Bellini had come to New York that June for Italy: The New Domestic Landscape, the MoMA exhibition where he unveiled the Kar-a-sutra, his radical space-mobile concept. When the show closed, he set off coast to coast with Francesco Binfaré and Davide Mosconi, using a MoMA safe-conduct that opened doors from Andy Warhol's studio to Hugh Hefner's mansion. He photographed Mormon Salt Lake City, the utopian desert commune of Arcosanti, and mobile-home settlements strung along Midwest roads. The images sat unused for over forty years until Humboldt Books drew on them for this Time Travel volume: 168 pages plus an inserted booklet, 136 photographs, softcover with French flaps, bilingual in Italian and English, with texts by Mario Calabresi and Gianluigi Ricuperati.

Bellini, the architect and industrial designer behind the Cab chair, the Kar-a-sutra, and decades of work for Olivetti, Cassina, and B&B Italia, rarely worked as a photographer USA 1972 shows the same restless curiosity about how people actually live that shaped his furniture and interiors.
tags: Photography, USA, Road Trip, Design, Architecture, Time Travel Series, Humboldt Books, Mario Bellini

title: Italia 1945/1948
description:
Fifty black-and-white photographs by Luigi Comencini, taken in the years just before he became one of Italy's leading film directors, capture a country still absorbing the shock of war and unsure of what would come next.

Shot between 1945 and 1948, the pictures show navvies at work, farmers passing through town, an amateur painter at his easel, children playing or simply looking back at the lens: the suspended atmosphere of a nation in which nothing would be as it was, but the future was not yet imaginable. Comencini took them in the same Milanese years in which, with Alberto Lattuada, he helped found the Cineteca Italiana, the country's first film archive. Humboldt Books published the find in its Time Travel series to mark the centenary of his birth, a 92-page softcover with French flaps and an inserted booklet, bilingual in Italian and English, with an introduction by Cristina Comencini and essays by Giovanna Calvenzi, Giorgio Gosetti, and Mario Sesti.

Comencini went on to direct some of postwar Italian cinema's most enduring films, among them Bread, Love and Dreams, Everybody Go Home, and The Scientific Cardplayer. This early photographic work reveals the same attentive, unsentimental eye for ordinary life that his later films would turn on Italian family and society.
tags: Photography, Italy, Postwar, Cinema, Documentary, Time Travel Series, Humboldt Books, Luigi Comencini

title: Giappone 1970
description:
Three years before his death, the architect and photographer Carlo Mollino flew to Japan for Expo '70 and returned with a body of images that reads as a final, restless act of curiosity from one of twentieth-century design's most idiosyncratic figures.

On May 21, 1970, at age sixty-five, Mollino boarded an Alitalia DC-8 for Osaka, stopping in Athens, Karachi, and Bangkok along the way. Armed with a Leica and a Polaroid, he spent two weeks photographing a country suspended between ancient ritual and accelerating modernity: temples, gardens, and pagodas alongside the pavilions and crowds of the Expo. Humboldt Books' Time Travel edition also draws on photographs from his other journeys through Asia, with texts by Claudio Giunta, Corrado Levi, and Fulvio Ferrari examining Mollino's relationship to the camera. The volume runs 72 pages, softcover with French flaps and an inserted booklet, bilingual in Italian and English, designed by Teresa Piardi.

Mollino, based in Turin, moved across architecture, furniture and car design, skiing, and aviation with equal intensity, and photography ran through all of it, from his erotic Polaroids to his studies of the Alps. Giappone 1970 catches the polymath late in life, still looking outward.
tags: Photography, Japan, Architecture, Travel, Expo 1970, Time Travel Series, Humboldt Books, Carlo Mollino

title: Iran 1970
description:
Before he became the defining photographer of Europe's post-industrial landscapes, a young Gabriele Basilico, not yet twenty-six, set out from Milan toward Kabul in a Fiat 124, and the pictures he brought back from a trip that stalled in Iran already show the eye that would define his career.

In summer 1970, Basilico and a small group of friends drove the overland hippie route through Yugoslavia and Turkey, planning to sell a photo reportage to a magazine along the way. The car went off the road near Tehran the journey continued anyway, south to Qom and Shiraz, on to Persepolis during preparations for the 2,500th-anniversary celebrations of the Persian monarchy, then to Isfahan and back to Tehran. The negatives sat in Basilico's archive for over forty years before Humboldt Books published them in its Time Travel series, with an introduction by Luca Doninelli and an afterword by Giovanna Calvenzi, his travelling companion. The volume is 80 pages, softcover with French flaps and an inserted booklet, bilingual in Italian and English.

Basilico would go on to photograph the industrial edges of Milan, Beirut's war-scarred skyline, and cities worldwide with a detached, architectural rigor. Iran 1970 shows him before that vocabulary formed: what the publisher calls "Basilico pre-Basilico."
tags: Photography, Iran, Road Trip, Documentary, Time Travel Series, Humboldt Books, Gabriele Basilico

title: DER SPIEGEL – Hamburg Brandstwiete
description:
A deadpan architectural survey of the tower block that housed Der Spiegel, Germany's leading investigative newsmagazine, photographed in the years after the magazine moved out and before the building's fate was settled.

The Brandstwiete tower was designed by Hamburg architect Werner Kallmorgen and served as the magazine's editorial headquarters from 1969 to 2011, its interiors famously outfitted by Verner Panton in psychedelic color and form. Andreas Gehrke's photographs, made after the newsroom's departure, record empty corridors, stripped offices, and the traces of four decades of use with a flat, inventory-like precision that avoids nostalgia. Published by Drittel Books in an edition of 300 numbered copies with a foreword by Christine Dissmann and design by Katrin Oeding, the book is the first of a pair documenting the two Hamburg buildings the magazine occupied in succession.

Gehrke, a Berlin-based photographer and publisher, has built a body of work around vacant and transitional architecture, from his own imprint Drittel Books to series on Berlin's undeveloped lots and Brandenburg's postwar landscape. Der Spiegel extends that interest to corporate modernism, pairing this volume with Der Spiegel – Hamburg Dovenfleet and, in the wider trilogy, with his studies of the former IBM and Quelle headquarters elsewhere in Germany.
tags: Photography, Architecture, Modernism, Germany, Andreas Gehrke, Drittel Books, Hamburg, Der Spiegel

title: DER SPIEGEL – Hamburg Dovenfleet
description:
The companion volume to Der Spiegel – Hamburg Brandstwiete, turning the same dispassionate documentary eye on the second Hamburg tower the magazine occupied before its 2011 move.

The Dovenfleet tower was built in 1967 to a design by Werner Kallmorgen and first housed the German operations of IBM for nearly three decades before Der Spiegel relocated its staff there in 1995, remaining until 2011. Andreas Gehrke's photographs move through the vacated newsroom floors, stairwells, and service areas, treating the building as a layered record of two very different postwar institutions rather than as a single subject. Published by Drittel Books as a numbered edition of 300 alongside its Brandstwiete companion, with a foreword by Christine Dissmann and design by Katrin Oeding, the two volumes are sold and cataloged together as a single two-part publication.

Gehrke, who founded Drittel Books in Berlin, has repeatedly returned to buildings caught between uses: the empty lots and unclaimed edges of Berlin, the flat postwar terrain of Brandenburg, and, in this trilogy, the corporate headquarters of Der Spiegel, IBM, and the mail-order firm Quelle. Der Spiegel – Hamburg Dovenfleet completes the pairing begun with the Brandstwiete volume within that larger project.
tags: Photography, Architecture, Modernism, Germany, Andreas Gehrke, Drittel Books, Hamburg, Der Spiegel

title: QUELLE VERSAND – Nürnberg
description:
The third volume in Andreas Gehrke's survey of vacated West German corporate modernism, documenting the purpose-built mail-order headquarters of Quelle, once the country's largest catalogue retailer.

Designed by Ernst Neufert, a former Bauhaus student best known for his standardization handbook Bauentwurfslehre, the Nuremberg building served as Quelle's mail-order headquarters from 1956 until the company's insolvency in 2009. Gehrke's 27 photographs work through the emptied warehouse floors, dispatch halls, and office interiors of a building engineered for the logistics of a mid-century mail-order empire, now silent. Drittel Books published the book, the longest of the trilogy at 64 pages, as a numbered edition of 300 with a foreword by Christine Dissmann and design by Katrin Oeding.

Andreas Gehrke, a Berlin-based photographer who founded Drittel Books to publish this and related projects, has built a recurring practice around buildings suspended between use and obsolescence. Quelle Versand completes the trilogy begun with the Der Spiegel volumes on Hamburg's former Spiegel towers and IBM Campus on IBM Germany's Stuttgart headquarters, together forming a portrait of the physical infrastructure left behind by postwar West Germany's media, technology, and retail industries.
tags: Photography, Architecture, Modernism, Germany, Andreas Gehrke, Drittel Books, Nuremberg, Quelle

title: IBM CAMPUS – Stuttgart-Vaihingen
description:
A methodical photographic survey of IBM Germany's former campus outside Stuttgart, one of the country's most celebrated postwar corporate complexes, photographed empty after nearly forty years of continuous use.

Designed by Egon Eiermann, among the most influential architects of postwar German modernism, the Stuttgart-Vaihingen campus served as IBM's German headquarters from 1972 until 2009. Andreas Gehrke's 23 photographs move across the site's glass pavilions, entrance canopy, and interior office floors, cataloging fittings, signage, and furniture left behind in a building still structurally intact but stripped of its original purpose. Drittel Books published the work as a numbered edition of 300 with a foreword by Christine Dissmann and design by Katrin Oeding, the second title in the publisher's trilogy on dormant West German corporate modernism.

Andreas Gehrke, a Berlin-based photographer and the founder of Drittel Books, has consistently photographed architecture in the interval between use and demolition or renovation. IBM Campus sits alongside his companion volumes on the former Der Spiegel towers in Hamburg and the Quelle Versand headquarters in Nuremberg, together forming a survey of the vacated infrastructure of West Germany's postwar economic institutions.
tags: Photography, Architecture, Modernism, Germany, Andreas Gehrke, Drittel Books, Stuttgart, IBM

title: Static Magic [First Edition / Second Printing]: Current Editions No. 10
description:
In 1974 America's National Security Agency began publishing an internal publication called Cryptolog.

Written designed and printed by NSA employees the top secret project sought to address all disciplines within the cryptological sphere especially in how they could benefit the NSA. 136 issues were produced before production abruptly ended in 1997. Static Magic collects headers graphics and other visual detritus from Cryptolog's two decade run, a kaleidoscopic view into the design sensibilities of America's late-20th Century security state.

title: Posthume
edition_printrun: Limited edition of 750, signed and numbered
description:
A contemplative monograph exploring themes of death, memory, and transformation.

The work blends Western memento mori traditions with Día de los Muertos iconography, examining queer identity and Mexican American heritage through ambiguous imagery. Features 14 tri-tone printed, hand-tipped plates (8 × 10 inches each) with nude figures with obscured faces in stark landscapes. Wrapped in custom handmade paper created with artisan papermakers in Oaxaca, made from native agave fibers with embedded cempasúchil (marigold) flower petals. Housed in a box.
tags: Photography, Queer Culture, Mexican American, Death, Memory, Limited Edition
notes: Hardcover with handmade paper housed in box. 14 tri-tone printed, hand-tipped plates. Explores memento mori, Día de los Muertos iconography, queer identity, and Mexican American heritage.

description: Visual journal documenting Ethridge's month in Paris during spring 2021, between commissions. Paris was drained of tourists and under curfew. Ethridge walked the city thinking about NFTs and Eugène Atget, producing this distinctive visual journal of an in-between moment.

title: American Spirit
description:
An unabashedly gorgeous collection of mountainous vistas and meta-advertising spreads that riff on the name of the eponymous cigarette brand.

Wide-open views of Western peaks are interspersed with close-shot portraits, still lifes and consumer imagery, a Manifest Destiny atlas for the post-internet era. Features twenty-six pages devoted to pictures of Ethridge's drive through the Rocky Mountains in January 2017, with landscapes grouped according to the three-day period over which they were taken: January 19th, 20th, and 21st, the days before, during, and after the Presidential Inauguration.
tags: Photography, Landscape, American Photography, Conceptual Photography

title: Beach Umbrella

Positioned against the sun, shot from beneath, and cropped to the point of near abstraction, the umbrellas fill each image from edge to edge with vibrant color. Also includes photographs of sunflowers from a public school garden in Clinton Hill, Brooklyn, and images from a fashion story with model Maryel Sousa.

The title references the French expression "C'est pas du luxe," exploring the paradox of luxury as both superfluous and essential to existence. title: Daily Self-Portraits 1972-1973
description:
Complete series of 192 daily self-portraits photographed by Melissa Shook (1939-2020) in her Lower East Side apartment from December 1972 to August 1973.

Shot in medium format black and white, the project titled "To Prove That I Exist" stands at the forefront of conceptual feminist art from this formative period. The photographs capture Shook in a variety of intimate, irreverent poses that reject the tradition of female portraiture made from a male perspective, documenting the mundanity of everyday existence: nursing her ailing toe on the couch, sitting at the kitchen table with a friend, hair wrapped in a towel post-shower, dancing with her daughter.

Often includes her daughter and friends who populate her sphere. Shook pioneered diaristic approaches to photography that intertwined the personal and social, exploring identity, time, motherhood, and gender through daily documentation. Published posthumously as her first monograph. Nominated for First PhotoBook Award, Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards 2024. Work held in major collections including MoMA, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, and Moderna Museet Stockholm.
tags: Photography, Self-Portrait, Women Photographers, 1970s, Feminist Art
notes: First monograph by American artist Melissa Shook (1939-2020). Posthumous publication. Contains 198 duotone plates. Nominated for First PhotoBook Award, Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards 2024. Artist studied at Bard College and Art Students League of New York, based in Chelsea, Massachusetts. Project started as personal challenge to take self-portrait every day for a year.

title: The Mad and the Lonely
description:
Exhibition catalog for George Condo's "The Mad and the Lonely" at DESTE Foundation Project Space, Slaughterhouse, Hydra, Greece (June 18–October 31, 2024). This intimate presentation of small-scale paintings and sculptures explores themes of madness, loneliness, and psychological isolation through Condo's signature "Psychological Cubism" style. His groundbreaking approach departs from classical Cubism by representing multiple emotional and psychological states simultaneously within a single figure rather than multiple spatial perspectives.

Born in 1957, George Condo emerged from the 1980s East Village art scene alongside Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring as a pioneer of Neo-Expressionist revival. His work synthesizes Old Master painting techniques with American pop sensibility and cartoon aesthetics, creating what he terms "Artificial Realism." Condo's distorted figures carry exaggerated features: bulbous faces, skewed limbs, protruding eyes. They authentically represent the emotional complexity and psychological contradictions of modern life.

For this special installation at the historic Slaughterhouse venue on Hydra, Condo incorporated ancient polychromatic Greek painting methods with minimalist sculpture, creating a unique site-specific presentation. The works depict "disparate souls rejected by society," captured in portraits installed within the former animal cages of the slaughterhouse, a haunting architectural dialogue between containment, isolation, and psychological states. The exhibition represents Condo's ongoing investigation into what he describes as "the disjointed human psyche," offering both hideous examination and dark humor.

The DESTE Foundation for Contemporary Art, established in 1983 by Greek collector Dakis Joannou, operates the Slaughterhouse Project Space as an annual summer exhibition venue featuring site-specific installations by internationally significant contemporary artists. Condo's work is held in major museum collections including MoMA, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Whitney Museum, and Louisiana Museum of Modern Art. A major retrospective at Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris (October 2025–February 2026) surveyed his 50+ year career.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Sculpture, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Exhibition at DESTE Foundation Project Space, Slaughterhouse, Hydra, Greece (June 18–October 31, 2024). Format: 10 × 10 inches, 116 pages. 78 color and 7 b&w illustrations. Published May 26, 2026. George Condo (b. 1957) coined the term "Psychological Cubism" to describe his artistic approach. His work is in collections at MoMA, Metropolitan Museum, Whitney Museum, Louisiana Museum, Albright-Knox, Corcoran Gallery, and The Broad. Major retrospective at Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris (2025-2026). Signed copy.

title: Bedtime Stories for Bad Boys and Girls
description:
Collaborative artist book presenting photographs by Larry Clark paired with drawings by James Gilroy, documenting ten interconnected narratives shared between two lifelong friends who first met in downtown New York during the early 1970s. The stories span their parallel experiences from the 1950s through the 1970s and beyond, preserved as transcriptions of recorded conversations between the artists—candid recollections of youth, artistic life, danger, liberation, and survival in an era that claimed many of their peers.

Larry Clark (b. 1943, Tulsa, Oklahoma) pioneered confessional documentary photography with his groundbreaking photobook Tulsa (1971), which intimately documented drug use, sex, and violence among teenagers in his hometown between 1963-1971. The book caused a sensation within the photographic community and established Clark's raw, uninhibited approach that influenced generations of photographers including Nan Goldin and Ryan McGinley. His 1995 film Kids, written by 19-year-old Harmony Korine, became an instant classic that defined youth culture in 1990s New York. Clark's work fundamentally challenged boundaries of acceptable subject matter and photographer-subject relationships.

James Gilroy (b. 1948, New York City) is a contemporary abstract figurative painter formally trained at The New York Phoenix School of Design and Art Students League of New York, where he studied for over a decade. His practice emphasizes layered color that "transmutes and blends together as an alchemy of color," combining rigorous anatomical understanding with emotional expressionism. Gilroy represents the New York figurative expressionist tradition, bringing visual painting practice to complement Clark's photographic eye.

The two met through mutual connection Ralph Gibson in the early 1970s and "became fast friends" amid the social upheaval of downtown Manhattan. As Gilroy recalls: "Back then, you walked down the block and maybe ran into somebody or into a situation. We'd just get pulled into something every day." Economic conditions allowed them to "work two or three days and make enough cash for the month" then travel extensively. Many of their peers didn't survive the era's dangerous lifestyle. Now in their 80s and 70s, Clark and Gilroy remain "still standing," offering rare perspective on both the liberation and tragedy of that formative period.

Published by Dashwood Projects in conjunction with their March 25–April 4, 2026 exhibition. Dashwood Projects opened in 2024 as the exhibition and publishing extension of Dashwood Books, the influential independent photography bookstore founded in 2005 by David Strettell (formerly Cultural Director of Magnum Photos). The collaboration represents a mature, reflective perspective on an era that shaped contemporary photography and art, filtered through multiple artistic practices and decades of friendship.
tags: Photography, Art, Drawings, Collaboration, New York
notes: Exhibition at Dashwood Projects, New York (March 25–April 4, 2026). Book signing March 26, 2026. 94 pages softcover. Larry Clark (b. 1943) is renowned for Tulsa (1971), Teenage Lust (1983), and Kids (1995 film). James Gilroy (b. 1948) trained at Art Students League of New York. The artists met in downtown NYC in early 1970s through Ralph Gibson. Clark's work is foundational to confessional documentary photography and influenced Nan Goldin, Ryan McGinley, and contemporary photographers. This collaboration documents ten narratives from their shared experiences across five decades. Signed copy.

title: NONMEMORY
contributors: Text by Jay Ezra Nayssan and Mike Kelley. Introduction by Mike Kelley Foundation for the Arts. Conversations with Kelly Akashi, Meriem Bennani, Beatriz Cortez, Raúl de Nieves, Olivia Erlanger, Lauren Halsey, Max Hooper Schneider, Kathryn Andrews, Miriam Ben Salah, Daniela Lieja Quintanar, Ceci Moss, Ruba Katrib, Jova Lynne, and Mary Clare Stevens
description:
Exhibition catalog documenting "NONMEMORY" at Hauser & Wirth Los Angeles (2023-2024), presenting works by Mike Kelley alongside seven contemporary artists: Kelly Akashi, Meriem Bennani, Beatriz Cortez, Raúl de Nieves, Olivia Erlanger, Lauren Halsey, and Max Hooper Schneider. This collaborative presentation explores "the 'non-memory' of the various institutional spaces or built environments" encountered throughout these artists' practices, building upon Kelley's foundational concept and influential essay "Architectural Non-memory Replaced with Psychic Reality."

Mike Kelley (1954-2012) was one of the most influential American artists of his generation, known for his provocative investigations into American vernacular culture, repressed memory, psychological trauma, and institutional critique. Working across sculpture, installation, performance, video, drawing, and critical writing, Kelley challenged high/low cultural distinctions through his use of craft materials, stuffed animals, found objects, and references to popular entertainment. His work examined how cultural institutions such as educational systems, religious organizations, and entertainment venues shape and often damage individual psychology and collective memory.

"Architectural Non-memory Replaced with Psychic Reality," Kelley's seminal essay included in this volume, theorizes how institutional architecture produces collective amnesia while simultaneously encoding psychological experiences in built space. The seven contemporary artists featured alongside Kelley, each working with installation, sculpture, video, and mixed media, extend his investigations into institutional memory and architectural psychology. Their conversations with curators and scholars explore connections between physical spaces and psychic states, examining how contemporary artists continue to interrogate the relationship between built environments and buried memories.

Published by Hauser & Wirth Publishers in October 2024. Softcover, 29.2 × 21.6 cm, 216 pages. Text contributions by Jay Ezra Nayssan and Mike Kelley, with introduction by the Mike Kelley Foundation for the Arts. Features extensive conversations between the seven contemporary artists and curators including Kathryn Andrews, Miriam Ben Salah, Daniela Lieja Quintanar, Ceci Moss, Ruba Katrib, Jova Lynne, and Mary Clare Stevens. Mike Kelley's work is held in major collections including MoMA, Whitney Museum, Tate, Centre Pompidou, and Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Installation, Mike Kelley
notes: Exhibition catalog for Hauser & Wirth Los Angeles (2023-2024). Features Mike Kelley with Kelly Akashi, Meriem Bennani, Beatriz Cortez, Raúl de Nieves, Olivia Erlanger, Lauren Halsey, and Max Hooper Schneider. Published October 2024. Format: 29.2 × 21.6 cm, 216 pages, softcover. ISBN: 978-3-906915-84-5. Includes Kelley's foundational essay "Architectural Non-memory Replaced with Psychic Reality." Text by Jay Ezra Nayssan and Mike Kelley. Introduction by Mike Kelley Foundation for the Arts. Mike Kelley (1954-2012) was influential American artist known for institutional critique and cultural psychology investigations.

title: Letter to the World
contributors: Essay by Karen Tei Yamashita. Design by Zachary Fischman
description:
Exhibition catalog published for "Letter to the World," the inaugural U.S. solo exhibition of Japanese-Brazilian sculptor Megumi Yuasa at Ortuzar, New York (March 5–April 11, 2026). This fully illustrated catalog surveys six decades of practice, featuring approximately thirty works spanning from the early 1970s to 2025 across ceramic, metal, and stone mediums. Published in collaboration between Ortuzar and Gomide&Co, the volume includes a major essay by novelist and historian Karen Tei Yamashita reflecting on her fifty-year friendship with the artist.

Born in São Paulo in 1938 to Japanese immigrant parents, Megumi Yuasa developed a distinct sculptural language exploring the interconnection between matter, body, and the universe. His philosophy—"Everything is made from everything. Everything depends on everything"—manifests in works that range from compact early ceramic constructions to vertically oriented mixed-media sculptures investigating balance, suspension, and gravity. Working primarily with clay, Yuasa creates organic forms that blur boundaries between the natural and constructed, the solid and ethereal.

The exhibition and catalog trace Yuasa's evolution from early ceramic works like *Nuvem [Cloud]* (c. 1975) and *Tropical* (1980) through *Personagem Sensível [Sensible Character]* (1988) and his Espássaro and Árvores [Trees] series, culminating in *Elegia a Nova Iorque [Elegy to New York]* (2025), a new work created during his New York residency. These pieces demonstrate his continued investigation into clay's expressive possibilities and his engagement with themes of transformation, temporality, and the relationship between human presence and natural forces.

Karen Tei Yamashita's essay draws on five decades of friendship with Yuasa, providing intimate perspective on his artistic development and philosophy. The fully illustrated catalog documents each work in the exhibition, offering comprehensive visual access to this important survey. Published March 2026 by Ortuzar (5 White Street, New York) in collaboration with Gomide&Co (São Paulo). Design by Zachary Fischman. This publication marks a significant documentation of Yuasa's work for American audiences, introducing his six-decade practice to new collectors and scholars.

title: Double Bind
contributors: Conversation between Leigh Ledare and Rhea Anastas. Introduction by Rhea Anastas. Preface by Leigh Ledare. Edited by Alejandro Cesarco, assisted by Kylie Gilchrist
description:
Extended conversation between artist Leigh Ledare and art historian Rhea Anastas exploring Ledare's "Double Bind" installation, presented at The Box (Los Angeles, 2012) and Mitchell-Innes & Nash (New York, 2014). The publication documents their dialogue provoked by viewing the work, examining key concepts that structure both this project and Ledare's broader practice. Arranged in six thematic sections (viewing, systemic conditions, enactment, installation and mass media, genealogy, and affect), the book models "affective criticism" that responds across intimate and collective scales of artwork and viewership.

Ledare's "Double Bind" installation presents nearly one thousand photographs of the artist's ex-wife: half taken by Ledare, half by her current husband, according to a script conceived by Ledare and enacted by all three participants. These photographs are juxtaposed with a large collection of appropriated mass-media materials, creating overlaying comparative structures that investigate contradictions within cultural, psychological, and sexual dimensions of intimacy and heterosexual relationships. The work explores how personal relationships and representations exist within larger systemic and ideological frameworks.

The book features installation photography created exclusively by Ledare for publication, documenting the 2014 Mitchell-Innes & Nash exhibition. Anastas's introduction and Ledare's preface frame the dialogue, which unfolds as critical examination of the viewing experience and theoretical implications of the work. A chronology of "Double Bind" exhibitions and publications provides documentary context for the project's development across multiple iterations. The conversation format allows both participants to test ideas about social and aesthetic experience within an unfolding exchange.

Published by A.R.T. Press (A.rt R.esources T.ransfer) in 2015. Softcover, 6 × 9 inches, 264 pages. ISBN: 978-0-923183-50-9. Edited by Alejandro Cesarco with assistance from Kylie Gilchrist. Design by Kristian Henson (HWGL). Rhea Anastas is art historian and Professor at University of California, Irvine. Leigh Ledare's work examines social structures, intimacy, and representation through photography, installation, and conceptual practice. A Brooklyn Rail excerpt from the book appeared in February 2016.
