title: fierce pussy
contributors: Nancy Brooks Brody, Joy Episalla, Zoe Leonard, Carrie Yamaoka Editor: Jules Spector Design: Garrick Gott, Bryce Wilner
description:
fierce pussy is a collective of queer women artists formed in New York City in 1991 through their immersion in AIDS activism during a decade of increasing political mobilization around gay rights. All core members were involved in ACT UP (AIDS Coalition To Unleash Power) to fight the AIDS pandemic, bringing lesbian identity and visibility directly into the streets through guerrilla-style poster campaigns and public interventions.

The four original core members are Nancy Brooks Brody (1962–2023), Joy Episalla, Zoe Leonard, and Carrie Yamaoka. They continue to work together, joined at various times by a fluid and shifting cadre including Pam Brandt, Jean Carlomusto, Donna Evans, Alison Froling, and Suzanne Wright. Low-tech and low-budget, the collective responded to the urgency of those years using readily available resources: old typewriters, found photographs, their own baby pictures, and printing supplies accessible in their day jobs.

This publication compiles 39 posters spanning from works made during the urgent early days of the AIDS crisis through present-day advocacy for Queer and Trans rights. The spiral-bound design allows readers to tear out any poster to share, wheatpaste, scan, photocopy, and distribute, honoring the collective's original street-based practice. This expanded edition includes 25 additional posters beyond the 2008 Printed Matter original (which featured 14 posters).

fierce pussy's iconic projects included wheat-pasting posters throughout New York City, renaming streets after prominent lesbian heroines, re-designing the restroom at the LGBT Community Center, and distributing stickers and t-shirts. While most active between 1991 and 1995, the collective reformed in 2008 and continues to exhibit as historic examples of AIDS-related art and lesbian-identified art. Their work is held in the International Center of Photography collection and has been featured in major exhibitions including "AND SO ARE YOU" at Leslie Lohman Museum (2018) and "For The Record" at Visual AIDS/Printed Matter (2013).
tags: Art, Activism, Queer Culture, Posters, Feminism, AIDS Crisis, ACT UP, Street Art
notes: Expanded edition. Originally published by Printed Matter in 2008 with 14 posters this edition adds 25 more for 39 total. Core founding members: Nancy Brooks Brody (1962–2023), Joy Episalla, Zoe Leonard, Carrie Yamaoka. Additional members over the years: Pam Brandt, Jean Carlomusto, Donna Evans, Alison Froling, Suzanne Wright. Work held in International Center of Photography collection. Recent major exhibition: "arms ache avid aeon: fierce pussy amplified" at ICA Philadelphia (2024-2025).

title: Treatise of a Coat
contributors: Essays by Elfriede Jelinek, Eve Esfandiari-Denney, Claire Gilman, Felix Bernstein
description:
This inaugural monograph showcases Helen Marten's works on paper created between 2019 and 2025, gathering for the first time a comprehensive survey of the English artist's drawing and painting practice. The publication features works executed in colored pencil, watercolor, ink, airbrush, acrylic, and graphite, alongside more unusual media like sand, silicone, and olive oil. Together they make a sumptuous visual document of Marten's material investigations on paper.

Designed as an "unruly artist's book," Treatise of a Coat has multiple physical and linguistic folds. The title offers an oblique reference to Honoré de Balzac's Treatise on Modern Stimulants, embracing the desire for essayistic but paradoxical world building. The publication emphasizes the physicality of making a work on paper, with the word "coat" functioning both as literal garment and as verb signifying layers of visual material. As Marten herself notes, this "treatise" is no such thing, neither formal nor systematic with its subjects.

Helen Marten (b. 1985, Macclesfield, UK) is the youngest recipient of Britain's Turner Prize, which she won in 2016 alongside the inaugural Hepworth Prize for Sculpture. She studied at the Ruskin School of Drawing and Fine Art, University of Oxford, graduating in 2008. Her practice spans sculpture, painting, video, and writing, creating work that questions the stability of the material world and our place within it. Marten is also the author of the novel The Boiled in Between (2020) and is currently working on a second novel and a book of essays on containers.

The book includes essays by Elfriede Jelinek, Eve Esfandiari-Denney, Claire Gilman, and Felix Bernstein. Published in conjunction with Marten's 2025 exhibition at Sadie Coles HQ in London, this volume represents a major statement on her works on paper. Her work is held in collections including The Museum of Modern Art New York, Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Moderna Museet Stockholm, Julia Stoschek Collection Düsseldorf, and Astrup Fearnley Museet Oslo. She was included in the 2013 and 2015 Venice Biennales and is represented by Greene Naftali in New York and Sadie Coles HQ in London.
tags: Art, Drawing, Contemporary Art, Works on Paper
notes: First monograph of works on paper spanning 2019-2025. Published in conjunction with exhibition at Sadie Coles HQ, London (October-November 2025). Winner of Turner Prize 2016 (youngest recipient) and inaugural Hepworth Prize for Sculpture 2016.

title: Terminal Boundaries and A natural water course diverted reduced or displaced
contributors: Managing Editor: James Hoff Designer: Rick Myers
description:
Terminal Boundaries and A natural water course diverted reduced or displaced is a tête-bêche artist book by Lawrence Weiner, originally created in 1969 but never published until now. The manuscript contains two related bodies of work represented as typewritten statements on paper that Weiner pasted to the pages of a small composition notebook purchased in a European stationery store. Primary Information publishes this facsimile edition in Spring 2026, making available for the first time a pivotal work from one of conceptual art's founding figures.

Lawrence Weiner (1942-2021) was one of the central figures in the formation of Conceptual Art in the 1960s, exploring the potentials of language as a sculptural medium. In 1968, he published his influential "Declaration of Intent": "The artist may construct the piece. / The piece may be fabricated. / The piece need not be built." Terminal Boundaries marks a crucial inflection point in Weiner's practice, created just as he was making his decisive turn toward work centered in language. Despite being considered a founding father of Conceptual Art, Weiner rejected the label and preferred instead to call himself a sculptor.

The artist was traveling across Europe when this manuscript was composed in 1969, struck by the tumultuous times and critical illuminations about climate from the Club of Rome discussions. The works are concerned with the relationship of natural resources in relation to human beings, attempting to present something that is "not just about me," as Weiner stated, but about materials and the world we find ourselves in the here and now. The tête-bêche format—two books in one, read from opposite ends—reflects the duality of these concerns.

Weiner's work is held in major museum collections including MoMA, the Guggenheim, Tate Modern, and the Whitney Museum of American Art. His practice influenced generations of artists working with language, and he designed his own typeface, Margaret Seaworthy Gothic, to convey the particular poetic spirit of his work. This publication represents a significant addition to the artist's bibliography, revealing an early chapter in his development of language-based art that would define his five-decade career.
notes: Tête-bêche (double-ended) format. Original manuscript created in 1969, published posthumously. Weiner was traveling across Europe when composed. Concerned with natural resources and human relationships during tumultuous climate discussions.

title: Report a Concern - Nine Eyes 2008-25
contributors: Essays by Mathias Ussing Seeberg, Poul Erik Tøjner, Mieke Bal, Norman M. Klein
description:
This comprehensive catalogue accompanies the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art's fall 2025 exhibition "Report a Concern – The Nine Eyes Archives," presenting the most extensive showcase to date of Jon Rafman's groundbreaking Nine Eyes series. The exhibition features over 50 large-scale framed street views in scenographic environments designed in collaboration with the artist, displaying selections from Rafman's vast archive of Google Street View snapshots. Street View images are captured by a fleet of cars outfitted with a pole mounting nine cameras at its top—hence the project's title, Nine Eyes of Google Street View.

Jon Rafman (b. 1981, Montreal) is a Canadian artist renowned for multifaceted work that revolves around our relationship with digital technologies and surveillance. After studying literature and philosophy, he gained a master's degree in visual arts from The School of the Art Institute of Chicago. His complex practice encompasses video, animation, installation, and sculpture, focusing on everyday life, dreams, fantasies, loss, and grief in relation to digital technology. The story behind Nine Eyes dates back to 2007, when Google sent an army of hybrid cars on a never-ending mission equipped with nine cameras, GPS and laser scanners to photograph every highway, country road and dirt path in the world.

This 465-page publication features 450 color images alongside four essays by Mathias Ussing Seeberg, Poul Erik Tøjner, Mieke Bal, and Norman M. Klein, providing critical context for understanding Rafman's pioneering work. Rafman began creating an archive of these images in 2008, collecting them from countless blogs and websites, as well as becoming part of the culture and finding his own images. Nine Eyes is considered Rafman's breakthrough work and focuses on both the everyday and existential aspects of life in a digital surveillance society. The project is a never-ending work that continues to be updated by the artist, standing as a milestone both in Rafman's career and in the history of 21st century art.

Rafman's work is associated with the post-internet art movement and has been exhibited at prestigious biennales including the Venice Biennale, Lyon Biennale, and Berlin Biennale. His work is held in major museum collections including MoMA in New York, Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam, and MAXXI in Rome. This is the first full-scale museum presentation of the Nine Eyes project.
tags: Art, Photography, Digital Art, Post-Internet Art, Contemporary Art
notes: Exhibition catalogue for Louisiana Museum of Modern Art (Oct 8, 2025 - Jan 11, 2026). Nine Eyes project began in 2008. Contains 400 selections from Google Street View archive. Published in conjunction with most extensive presentation of the series to date.

title: Fury
contributors: Text: Guillaume Blanc-Marianne Design: Roger Willems
description:
Fury brings together a new series by Marie Quéau, winner of the 5th LE BAL/ADAGP Prize for Young Creation. The work focuses on bodies confronted with extreme states: stunt performers repeatedly thrown through windows, actors in trance within motion capture studios, freedivers in static immersion on the edge of drift, individuals giving free rein to their rage in a fury room. Through these settings, Quéau's work invites us to question our own perception of reality and what moments of confrontation with our limits, when body and mind waver between control and surrender, reveal about what binds us most intensely.

Marie Quéau (b. 1985, Choisy-le-Roi, France) studied art history at the Sorbonne before attending the École Nationale Supérieure de la Photographie in Arles, graduating in 2009. She has lived and worked in Paris since her residency at the Cité Internationale des Arts in 2017. Her practice explores the human body pushed to its limits, documenting extreme physical and psychological states with precision and poetic restraint. The title Fury came from David Fincher's film Alien 3 and the name of the planet "Fury 161" where the story takes place. At the very beginning of this project, Quéau imagined that the characters she photographed lived on this prison-planet, driven by extreme telluric forces.

This 140-page publication features text by Guillaume Blanc-Marianne and design by Roger Willems, published in conjunction with Quéau's exhibition at LE BAL (November 28, 2025 – February 8, 2026). The €20,000 LE BAL/ADAGP Prize for Young Creation is open to photographers and video artists under 40 living in France, recognizing emerging talent in contemporary visual arts. Quéau has pursued a personal approach while occasionally working on commissions for sports magazines such as L'Équipe and Entorse Magazine, bringing an athlete's understanding of physical extremes to her art practice.

Quéau's previous work has received significant recognition, including the 2012 Nofound Photo Fair/de Groot Foundation Prize for her series Gojira, the 2017 CNAP creation grants for contemporary documentary photography, and the 2018 Carré sur Seine Prize for Odds and Ends, which was also named among the finalists for the HSBC Photography Prize. Her work has been exhibited at PhotoLevallois Festival, Salon de Montrouge, International Festival of Fashion and Photography in Hyères, and various museums and institutions across France.
tags: Art, Photography, Contemporary Art, Documentary Photography, French Photography
notes: Winner of 5th LE BAL/ADAGP Prize for Young Creation (€20,000). Exhibition at LE BAL, Paris (Nov 28, 2025 - Feb 8, 2026). Copyright © Marie Quéau / ADAGP, Paris, 2025. Title inspired by David Fincher's Alien 3 and planet "Fury 161".

title: Hujar:Contact
contributors: Joel Smith (essays), Olivia McCall (job book annotations)
description:
Hujar:Contact is the catalogue accompanying the Morgan Library & Museum's exhibition of the same name (May 22–October 25, 2026), co-published with MACK.

Drawing on the Morgan's archive of more than 5,700 contact sheets and Peter Hujar's annotated job books spanning 1954 to 1987, the volume offers an unprecedented view of Hujar's working method and creative evolution. Critical texts by curator Joel Smith establish a chronology of Hujar's contact sheets, while Olivia McCall's transcriptions and annotations of the job books illuminate previously unseen images and early iterations of his iconic portraits—including those of Susan Sontag, David Wojnarowicz, Candy Darling, and others at the heart of New York's 1970s and 1980s downtown scene.

The contact sheets, many bearing Hujar's editing marks, function as intimate pictorial narratives traced across the cultural upheaval of Stonewall and AIDS. The Peter Hujar Collection at the Morgan was acquired through the Charina Endowment Fund in 2013.
tags: Photography, Peter Hujar, Contact Sheets, Portraits, New York City, Archive, Queer Culture, Exhibition Catalog, 1970s, 1980s
notes: Catalogue accompanies the exhibition Hujar:Contact at the Morgan Library & Museum, curated by Joel Smith, Richard L. Menschel Curator and Department Head of Photography (May 22–October 25, 2026). Exhibition presents over 110 contact sheets and 20 enlargements drawn from the Morgan's holdings of 5,700+ Hujar contact sheets. Peter Hujar (1934–1987) began filing and numbering contact sheets at age 21 his mature independent period (1974–1987) was based in the East Village. Co-published by MACK and the Morgan.

title: Portraits in Life and Death
description:
Portraits in Life and Death is the only photography book Peter Hujar published during his lifetime, originally released in 1976 by Da Capo Press and reissued in 2024 by Liveright with a new foreword by Benjamin Moser alongside Susan Sontag's original introduction.

The volume gathers forty-one black-and-white photographs in two sequences: twenty-nine portraits of creative figures from downtown New York—including Susan Sontag, William Burroughs, John Waters, Fran Lebowitz, Robert Wilson, and Divine—paired with eleven images of mummified bodies from the 19th-century Capuchin catacombs in Palermo, Sicily, photographed in 1963.

The juxtaposition turns the book into a meditation on mortality and presence, with Sontag praising Hujar's ability to capture "the inner spirit of his subjects" while sustaining "an air of nonchalance, even gaiety." Holland Cotter has called it "one of the most somberly beautiful and influential photography collections of its era," and the book stands as a defining artifact of post-Stonewall New York City.
tags: Photography, Peter Hujar, Portraits, New York City, Mortality, Catacombs, Palermo, Queer Culture, 1970s, Susan Sontag, Reissue
notes: First published 1976 by Da Capo Press (the only monograph Hujar published during his lifetime). Reissued October 2024 by Liveright Publishing Corporation with a new foreword by Benjamin Moser, retaining Susan Sontag's original 1976 introduction. Catacomb photographs were made in 1963 in Palermo, Sicily portraits date primarily 1974–1975. Hujar (1934–1987) died of AIDS-related illness ten years after the book's first publication.

title: Peter Hujar Curated by Elton John
description:
Peter Hujar Curated by Elton John presents a fifty-image survey of Hujar's photographic career as selected by the musician and longtime photography collector.

Spanning nearly two decades of work, the selection draws together portraits of Hujar's eclectic downtown New York circle, his landmark male nudes, atmospheric landscapes, and portraits of performers including Stevie Wonder, Peggy Lee, and Edgar Winter, alongside a moving image of the artist with his mother.

In his introduction, John reflects on the photographer's distinctive vision: "Hujar's humanity, depth and sensual insights aren't for everyone, and don't need to be, but once his pictures get into your bloodstream they are impossible to shake." Published by Fraenkel Gallery on the occasion of the 2022 exhibition of the same name, the book pairs a legendary collector's eye with a photographer whose mastery has only grown more widely recognized in the decades since his 1987 death.
tags: Photography, Peter Hujar, Portraits, Nudes, New York City, Performers, Curated Selection, Queer Culture, 1970s, 1980s, Elton John
notes: Catalogue published by Fraenkel Gallery on the occasion of the 2022 exhibition Peter Hujar: Curated by Elton John. Elton John selected fifty photographs from Hujar's career spanning nearly two decades and contributed the introduction. Includes performer portraits of Stevie Wonder, Peggy Lee, and Edgar Winter, along with Hujar's landmark nude studies, landscapes, and an image of the artist with his mother.

title: Speed of Life
contributors: Philip Gefter (essay), Steve Turtell (essay), Joel Smith (essay), Martha Scott Burton (curatorial assistant)
description:
Peter Hujar: Speed of Life is the major touring survey of the New York photographer published by Aperture in 2017 to accompany the retrospective exhibition organized by Joel Smith at the Morgan Library & Museum and Fundación MAPFRE.

Over 160 photographs gather Hujar's iconic portraits of the downtown New York artistic and underground community—Susan Sontag, William S. Burroughs, David Wojnarowicz, Andy Warhol, Candy Darling, and others—alongside his lesser-known studies of animals, landscapes, and the HIV/AIDS epidemic.

Hujar (1934–1987), a leading figure of the 1970s and '80s downtown scene, was a consummate technician whose exquisite black-and-white tonalities and uncompromising attitude toward work and life made him profoundly influential, though he remained underappreciated in his lifetime. Critical essays by Philip Gefter, Steve Turtell, and Joel Smith establish a thorough chronology of Hujar's biography and artistic practice. The exhibition traveled internationally, with stops in Madrid, Paris, New York, and Berkeley.
tags: Photography, Peter Hujar, Portraits, New York City, Downtown Scene, Queer Culture, AIDS, 1970s, 1980s, Aperture, Retrospective, Survey
notes: Catalogue published by Aperture in conjunction with the major touring retrospective Peter Hujar: Speed of Life, organized by Joel Smith for the Morgan Library & Museum and Fundación MAPFRE. Exhibition traveled to Fundación MAPFRE (Madrid), Jeu de Paume (Paris), the Morgan Library & Museum (New York), and the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (2017–2019). Hujar's work is held in permanent collections at MoMA, the Whitney, the Museum of Fine Arts Houston, and SFMOMA. Earlier major retrospectives mounted at the Stedelijk Museum (Amsterdam) and Fotomuseum Winterthur (Switzerland).

title: Peter Hujar: Behind the Camera and In the Darkroom
contributors: Gary Schneider (text and memoir), Peter Hujar (photographs), Nicolas Linnert (editor)
description:
Peter Hujar: Behind the Camera and In the Darkroom is Gary Schneider's intimate memoir of his friendship with Peter Hujar (1934–1987), written from the perspective of Schneider's later role as Hujar's posthumous printer.

Schneider (b. 1954) takes thirty-two of Hujar's photographs as starting points: portraits, nudes, animals, and downtown New York vignettes he has known from the contact sheet through to the final print. He uses each as the entry to a short essay on technique, biography, friendship, and grief. The result interleaves precise printerly attention with the social texture of pre- and early-AIDS-era downtown New York, where Schneider lived and worked alongside Hujar, David Wojnarowicz, and the wider circle of artists Hujar photographed.

Co-published with Delpire & Co (which handles European distribution) and distributed worldwide by D.A.P., the volume is one of the few Hujar publications written from inside the studio rather than the institutional vantage, and a rare extended account of how Hujar's photographs are made, on the wall and on the printing easel.
tags: Photography, Peter Hujar, Memoir, Darkroom, Printing, New York City, Downtown Scene, AIDS, Queer Culture, 1970s, 1980s, Delpire & Co, BookCrave Books
notes: Schneider was Hujar's friend, occasional subject, and—after Hujar's death in 1987—his posthumous printer the book draws on that printing practice. Published 2024 by BookCrave Books (the author's own imprint, ISBN 9798218371463) D.A.P. holds exclusive worldwide distribution. Delpire & Co distributes in France and co-publishes the European edition. Edited by Nicolas Linnert. 72 pages, 32 color reproductions, cloth hardcover, 8.75 × 11.25 in (22.5 × 29 cm).

title: Lost Downtown
description:
Peter Hujar: Lost Downtown is the Steidl / Pace MacGill Gallery monograph of twenty tritone portraits Hujar made of his closest friends and downtown New York peers between 1972 and 1985, with an essay by Vince Aletti.

The book draws together pictures of Joe Brainard, William S. Burroughs, Edwin Denby, Divine, Fran Lebowitz, Charles Ludlam, Susan Sontag, Paul Thek, David Wojnarowicz, Robert Wilson, and others—figures who, in Aletti's framing, populated a Lower East Side scene of artists, wannabe artists, and hangers-on "gathered from every town in America and relocated in the mean streets between Broadway and the Bowery."

Hujar (1934–1987) photographed them with the unsentimental gravity that defined his work: subjects recline, sit, stare back, give up the camera meets them at their level rather than mythologizing them. Published to accompany the exhibition Peter Hujar: Lost Downtown at Pace/MacGill Gallery, New York, in early 2016, the book is now out of print and serves, in Aletti's word, as a record of "a vanished world" that has since been claimed by gentrification, AIDS, and time.
tags: Photography, Peter Hujar, Portraits, New York City, Downtown Scene, Lower East Side, Queer Culture, AIDS, 1970s, 1980s, Steidl, Pace MacGill, Tritone
notes: Catalogue published by Steidl in association with Pace/MacGill Gallery on the occasion of the exhibition Peter Hujar: Lost Downtown at Pace/MacGill Gallery, New York (early 2016). Twenty tritone reproductions of portraits made between 1972–1985. Hardcover, 10.5 × 11 inches (26.7 × 27.9 cm), 56 pages. ISBN 9783958291065. Out of print. Cover portrait of Susan Sontag, 1975.

title: Twentysix Luxury Brands
description:
Twentysix Luxury Brands is a photographic zine by MarieVic, shot in New York City during election week 2020 as the country's high-end shopping districts boarded up their storefronts in anticipation of post-election unrest.

Plywood window coverings blanket the strip whose extroverted glassed windows are normally meant to speak a language of enticement instead, the brands appear behind raw plywood, unbranded for a week, identifiable only by location and embossed nameplates. The book takes its title and structure from Ed Ruscha's 1963 artist book Twentysix Gasoline Stations, the foundational gesture of conceptual photobook practice that traded fine-art subjects for the deadpan repetition of the American landscape.

MarieVic joins a long lineage of Ruscha homages—Mishka Henner's Eighteen Swimming Pools, Jeff Brouws's Twenty-four Former Filling Stations, and others—that adopt the "number-subject-location" formula and Ruscha's clinical typography to address consumerism, urban decay, and the passage of time. Here the formula meets a specific moment in 2020 New York, in which the architecture of luxury was briefly and bluntly remade as defensive infrastructure.
tags: Photography, Zine, MarieVic, New York City, 2020 Election, Storefronts, Boarded Up, Luxury, Conceptual Photography, Ruscha Homage, Blurring Books
notes: Self-published by MarieVic via her Blurring Books imprint, 2020. Made during U.S. election week 2020 in New York City documents twenty-six luxury storefronts boarded up in plywood ahead of the election. Title and structure are a deliberate homage to Ed Ruscha's Twentysix Gasoline Stations (1963) — part of the long Ruscha-tribute lineage that includes Mishka Henner's Eighteen Swimming Pools and Jeff Brouws's Twenty-four Former Filling Stations. 60 pages, 6 × 10 inches, softcover. ISBN not assigned (artist publication).

title: There Is No Light at the End of the Tunnel Because the Tunnel Is Made of Light
description:
Ryan Spencer's There Is No Light at the End of the Tunnel Because the Tunnel Is Made of Light is a 272-page paperback that imagines the visual companion to a film that was never made: the unrealized cinematic version of The Afghan Whigs' 1996 album Black Love.

Spencer assembles film stills culled from the deep catalogue of neo-noir Los Angeles cinema and arranges them so that the album's track titles and song-by-song narrative drive the sequence, making a found-image storyboard for a record that always wanted to be a movie. The accompanying fictional essay by Rebecca Bengal extends the conceit into prose Chummy Alexanian's illustrations punctuate the book with hand-drawn motifs that play against the cinematic source material.

Published in TBW Books' small-format paperback line with colored edges, the volume sits between artist book, music object, and pulp paperback. Its stylized object qualities are integral to its meaning. The result is at once a tribute to Greg Dulli's record, an essay on appropriation and cinephilia, and a meditation on the gap between what an album promises and what a film could have delivered.
tags: Photography, Found Photography, Film Stills, Cinema, Neo-Noir, Los Angeles, The Afghan Whigs, Black Love, Music, Pulp, Conceptual, TBW Books, 2024
notes: Published 2024 by TBW Books, Oakland. ISBN 9781942953630. 272 pages, paperback with colored edges, 4.25 × 7 inches (10.8 × 17.8 cm). Built around the unrealized film companion to The Afghan Whigs' 1996 album Black Love (Sub Pop / Elektra), with the album's track titles and narrative driving the sequence of appropriated film stills. Essay by Rebecca Bengal illustrations by Chummy Alexanian. Available in standard and signed editions from TBW.

title: FLOWERS
description:
FLOWERS is a collaborative artist book by Kenta Cobayashi and Tyrone Williams, published by Photobook Daydream Editions in a first edition of 100.

The work pairs the two photographers' practices through a shared image-language built at the seam where photographic capture meets generative AI: source photographs of flowers and floral arrangements are fed through the artists' respective digital processes, then iteratively transformed, first by the artists themselves, then extended further into computational realms, until the resulting images sit between document, painting, and rendered object.

The collaboration is in keeping with both photographers' wider concerns: Cobayashi (b. 1992, based in Tokyo) is known for warped, post-photographic image-making that pushes against the boundary between photograph and digital artifact, while Williams (based in New York) develops image work that interrogates surface, code, and abstraction. As a small softcover edition of 100, FLOWERS reads as a discrete proposition rather than a survey. It is a 64-page experiment in what intentional collaboration with AI tools looks like for two artists already working at the edges of computational photography.
tags: Photography, AI Art, Generative, Flowers, Collaboration, Kenta Cobayashi, Tyrone Williams, Japan, Computational Photography, Photobook Daydream Editions, Limited Edition, 2026
notes: Joint photobook by Kenta Cobayashi (b. 1992, Tokyo) and Tyrone Williams. Published 2026 by Photobook Daydream Editions in a first edition of 100, distributed through Book Dummy Press. 64 pages, softcover, 7 × 10 inches (17.8 × 25.4 cm). Source images of flowers transformed through the artists' processes and extended into AI/computational realms. No ISBN listed (limited artist edition).

title: Passports
description:
Passports is Keisha Scarville's first major monograph, anchored on more than three hundred reinterpretations the artist has made of her father's passport photograph.

Working over the original picture with paint, beads, gold leaf, glitter, and fragments of other Black bodies, Scarville turns a state-issued document of identification into a serial portrait practice, at once a private memorial and a public meditation on how citizenship, personhood, and Black diaspora are inscribed in and resisted by the bureaucratic image. The reworked passports are interleaved with archival photographs from her father's life in Guyana and New York between the 1960s and 1980s, his self-portraits, Scarville's own landscape photography, and transcripts of conversations with him before and after his death.

A new essay by Tina M. Campt, Professor of Humanities at Princeton and a leading voice on the visual culture of Black diaspora, situates the project alongside Campt's own thinking on listening to images and the quiet frequencies of Black archives. Published by MACK in May 2026 in a 280-page debossed Swiss hardcover, the volume is at once a daughter's elegy and a sustained argument that the archive is something we make, not something we receive.
tags: Photography, Keisha Scarville, Black Photographers, Diaspora, Caribbean, Guyana, New York City, Archive, Family, Collage, Mixed Media, Identity, Citizenship, MACK, 2026
notes: First major monograph by Keisha Scarville. Published May 2026 by MACK ISBN 9781917651486. 280 pages, debossed Swiss hardcover, 15 × 21.6 cm. Includes 300+ reworked iterations of the artist's father's passport photograph (paint, beads, gold leaf, glitter, photograph fragments), archival pictures of his life in Guyana and New York (1960s–80s), Scarville's landscape photography, and conversation transcripts. New essay by Tina M. Campt (Princeton). Available in unsigned and signed editions signed edition includes an additional artist-signed plate.

title: Richard Prince
contributors: Ralph Gleis (Foreword), Christian Liclair, Walter Moser, Nicole Scheyerer, Eva Kernbauer, Sydney Stutterheim, Thomas D. Trummer
description:
A retrospective catalog accompanying Richard Prince's major Albertina Museum survey (Vienna, on view through 16 August 2026), curated by Walter Moser.

The volume gathers approximately 150 works spanning Prince's practice from the 1970s to the present and presents his photographic work alongside forays into installation, drawing, painting, and collage. Iconic series (including the Cowboys, the Fashion pieces, and the rephotographed advertising images that established Prince as a central figure of Appropriation Art) appear alongside rarely seen and previously unpublished material.

Essays by Christian Liclair, Walter Moser, Nicole Scheyerer, Eva Kernbauer, Sydney Stutterheim, and Thomas D. Trummer address collage and montage technique, mythical masculinity, spiritual imagery, portraiture, and the conceptual stakes of appropriation. A foreword by Ralph Gleis frames the catalog within the Albertina's program. Prince's strategy, removing commercial context from images already saturated by media use and then re-staging them as art, interrogates authorship, originality, and the cultural codes embedded in American consumer imagery. 280 color illustrations.
tags: Art, Photography, Appropriation, Retrospective, Cowboys, American Art
notes: Catalog for Richard Prince retrospective at the Albertina Museum, Vienna exhibition on view through 16 August 2026. Approximately 150 works. Distributed in North America by University of Chicago Press for Hirmer Verlag.

title: New Cowboys
description:
A limited-edition artist's publication (edition of 500) from Karma continuing Richard Prince's decades-long Cowboys project, in which the artist rephotographs the lone, anonymous, often weathered cowboy figure from cigarette advertisements and other mass-market American sources.

This 24-page edition presents a new group of cowboy images that foreground the tears, scratches, and surface textures of Prince's source material — exposing the physical residue of the appropriated print as part of the picture itself. Prince's Cowboys works, begun in 1980, were among the foundational gestures of Appropriation Art and helped reframe rephotography as a critical practice rather than reproduction. Printed at a large 15¼ × 11½-inch trim, the publication functions as both an artist's edition and a distillation of Prince's continued investigation of the cowboy as American myth.
tags: Photography, Appropriation, Cowboys, Artist Editions, Limited Editions, American Art
notes: Edition of 500 copies. Part of Prince's ongoing Cowboys series (begun 1980), in which advertising images of cowboys are rephotographed and re-presented. Published by Karma (NYC).

title: Kiss of the Sun
description:
A catalogue published on the occasion of Lee Mary Manning's third solo exhibition at CANADA, New York (22 November 2024 – 11 January 2025).

The 100-page book features images of framed works from the show alongside collaged photographs and digital scans of ephemera, both objects included in the exhibition and material that did not end up on the wall. Manning's practice moves fluidly between photographic registers: daily diaristic shooting, found-image collage, and the digital flatbed scan. The catalogue mirrors that working method on the page rather than presenting only the framed end-products. Designed by Joe Gilmore. Published by CANADA, the artist-run gallery at 60 Lispenard Street founded in 1999.
tags: Photography, Exhibition Catalogs, Collage, Diaristic, NYC, Artist Editions, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Exhibition catalogue for Lee Mary Manning's third solo show at CANADA (60 Lispenard St, NYC), on view 22 November 2024 – 11 January 2025. Mixes installation views, collaged photographs, and flatbed scans of ephemera.

title: Cruising Pavilion: Architecture, Dissident Sex and Cruising Cultures
description:
Edited by Pierre-Alexandre Mateos and Charles Teyssou, Cruising Pavilion maps how cruising cultures have shaped architectural and urban environments.

The 432-page volume builds a typology of spaces produced by sexual subcultures — parks, restrooms, streets, sex clubs, bathhouses — alongside the virtual geographies that emerged with dating apps. Essays and case studies trace how artistic avant-gardes have worked at the intersection of sex, art, and architecture, following the eponymous curatorial project initiated by Mateos, Rasmus Myrup, Octave Perrault, and Teyssou, which travelled from Paris to Venice, New York, Fire Island, and Stockholm. Designed by Natasha Agapova. Thread-sewn softcover.
tags: Architecture, Queer Culture, Cruising, Sexuality, Urbanism, Curatorial Projects
notes: Curatorial project initiated by Pierre-Alexandre Mateos, Rasmus Myrup, Octave Perrault, and Charles Teyssou iterations in Paris, Venice, New York, Fire Island, and Stockholm.

author_full_name: Regina Bittner, Katja Klaus, Philipp Sack (eds.)
title: Pedagogies of Machine Learning: Schools of Departure Nr. 4
editor: Regina Bittner, Katja Klaus, Philipp Sack, Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau
designer: Yvonne Tenschert Offshore (Isabel Seiffert & Christoph Miler)
description:
The fourth volume in Spector's Schools of Departure series examines the use of technology in post-Bauhaus design education.

In the second half of the twentieth century, universities and research institutions were swept by a wave of cybernetisation as the triad of knowledge, technology, and progress surfaced again undaunted this book reflects on how designers and architects have conceptualised machines — and their relationship to them — across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Edited by Regina Bittner, Katja Klaus, and Philipp Sack for the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation. Designed by Yvonne Tenschert and Offshore (Isabel Seiffert & Christoph Miler). 192 pages, thread-sewn brochure, illustrated in colour.
tags: Design Education, Machine Learning, Bauhaus, Pedagogy, Technology, Cybernetics, Architecture
notes: Schools of Departure series, no. 4. Published in cooperation with Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau (Bauhaus Dessau Foundation).

title: (Inter)Faces of Predictions
description:
(Inter)Faces of Predictions, a collaboration between writer-researcher Megan Williams (b. 1995, London) and visual artist Sheung Yiu (b. 1991, Hong Kong based in Helsinki), examines how faces are read across cultural and technological contexts to attribute character traits and forecast the future.

The project sets East Asian face-analysis traditions and Western physiognomy alongside contemporary facial-recognition technology, with Yiu analysing his own face to show how historical belief systems and modern algorithmic procedures reproduce remarkably similar biases.

Archival material, photographic work, and technological methods are woven together to bridge historical discourse and contemporary AI critique. Co-published by Spector Books and the C/O Berlin Foundation in connection with the C/O Berlin Talent Award 2025. 640 pages, thread-bound softcover. Trilingual: English, Chinese, German.
tags: Photography, Machine Learning, Facial Recognition, Physiognomy, Technology, AI, C/O Berlin
notes: Co-published with C/O Berlin Foundation. C/O Berlin Talent Award 2025. Williams (b. 1995, London) is a writer, editor, and researcher Yiu (b. 1991, Hong Kong) is a visual artist and researcher based in Helsinki.

title: IDEA - KUTT Magazine (The Book)
description:
A facsimile edition collecting all three issues of KUTT, the cult dyke zine published between 2002-2003 in Amsterdam.

Originally conceived as the lesbian counterpart to BUTT Magazine, KUTT was founded by Jessica Gysel, Martien Mulder, and Marjolein Rams. The magazine's signature lilac pages featured it-girl actor Chloë Sevigny, acclaimed writer and activist Eileen Myles, experimental filmmaker K8 Hardy, and feminist queer icon Peaches (Merrill Nisker).

Photography by Ryan McGinley, Collier Schorr, Viviane Sassen, and Martien Mulder captured the burgeoning lesbian scene with the same bold spirit and tongue-in-cheek attitude as its sister publication. Despite lasting just three issues, KUTT quickly gained cult status among queer creatives, fashion insiders, and indie mag obsessives. Published by IDEA as a complete facsimile in an edition of 1,000 copies, reproducing the original issues page-for-page.
tags: Zines, Queer Culture, Photography, Dutch Publishing
notes: First edition facsimile of 1,000 copies. Original issues published Spring 2002-2003. Founded after dinner meeting with BUTT magazine team. Jessica Gysel went on to establish long-running queer magazine Girls Like Us. Distributor: https://havensurf.com/en-us/products/idea-kutt

title: Index #8
description:
The eighth issue of e-flux Index, a quarterly print journal surveying contemporary culture through e-flux's publishing on art, theory, architecture, film, criticism, activism, and art education.

This 560-page volume explores the fragmentary complexity of the current moment through eleven emergent thematic snapshots drawn from texts commissioned throughout spring 2025. Features 142 contributors including authors, artists, architects, filmmakers, poets, and educators—among them Evan Calder Williams, Fred Scharmen, Chris Murtha, Filipa Ramos, and Rory Rowan.

Each issue interweaves long-form essays, exhibition and book reviews, and critical discussions from various e-flux publications. Released January 2026, Index #8 continues e-flux's mission to capture the breadth and depth of contemporary cultural discourse in a substantial print format. Distributed by Antenne Books, Les presses du réel, Asterism Books, Art Metropole, The Book Society, and Buchhandlung Walther König.
tags: Art Theory, Contemporary Art, Criticism, Architecture, Cultural Studies, Quarterly
notes: Quarterly print journal, approximately 560 pages per issue. Launched 2024. Issue #8 released January 2026. Features 106 contributions from 101 artists, critics, filmmakers, theorists, and architects. Organized into eleven thematic "indications for reading." Available in print and digital download.

title: Brush Fires in the Social Landscape
contributors: Nan Goldin, Karen Finley, Kiki Smith, Vince Aletti, C. Carr, Fran Lebowitz, David Cole
description:
A seminal work begun in collaboration with David Wojnarowicz before his death in 1992 from AIDS-related complications.

This monograph demonstrates Wojnarowicz's extraordinary use of photography, often done in conjunction with writing or painting, to address the AIDS crisis and issues of censorship and homophobia.

The work includes contributions from artist and writer friends including Lucy R. Lippard, Nan Goldin, Karen Finley, Kiki Smith, and others, to David Cole, the lawyer who represented him in his case against Donald Wildmon and the American Family Association. Published as Aperture 137, this book captures Wojnarowicz's fierce engagement with political and social issues through his multimedia artistic practice.
tags: Photography, Art, AIDS, Queer Culture, Censorship, Social Commentary

title: Richard Prince: Untitled (couple)
description:
One Work is a unique series of books published by Afterall, with each presenting a single work of art considered in detail by a single author. The primary aim of the series is to provoke debate about significant moments in contemporary art's recent development.

By rephotographing an image from a magazine to make his 1977 work Untitled (couple), Richard Prince extracted the uncanny from the generic, locating the mysterious essence hidden behind the veil of advertisement. Working as a photo archivist at Time Life, Prince conceived his first body of appropriated work in 1977, creating what he would later dub "rephotography"—eliminating all surrounding text and imagery that would contextualize the image as an ad. In the process, Prince updated the readymade for the late 1970s and early 1980s, an age in which the image was the be-all and end-all.

Drawing on an unpublished interview with Richard Prince, Michael Newman analyses this seminal work, connecting it to ideas of allegory, simulacrum, and the formation of personal identity in a society of commodity and spectacle. Newman argues that the vintage TV series The Twilight Zone is crucial to understanding Prince's use of images. During the 1960s, structuralism recast the image as text Prince's work, Newman argues, revived the image in such a way that it is irreducible to text. The series questions issues of mass consumerism, reality vs. fiction in advertising, and identity formation in a commodity culture.

Richard Prince (b. 1949, Panama Canal Zone) is a member of the Pictures Generation of artists that emerged in the 1980s. His works are held in the collections of The Museum of Modern Art, the Art Institute of Chicago, the Goetz Collection (Munich), and the Victoria and Albert Museum (London).
tags: Art, Photography, Appropriation Art, Contemporary Art, Pictures Generation, Richard Prince, Conceptual Art
notes: Part of Afterall's One Work series examining single works of contemporary art. Newman's analysis draws on unpublished interview with Richard Prince. The 1977 Untitled (couple) series was one of Prince's earliest appropriation works, created while he worked as a photo archivist at Time Life magazine. Prince is considered a founding member of the Pictures Generation.

title: 13 Photographs
description:
Published in Hamden, Connecticut by Ives-Sillman in 1978, this is the prospectus booklet for Herbert Matter’s portfolio 13 Photographs, devoted entirely to the sculptor Alberto Giacometti.

The thirteen plates comprise a portrait of Giacometti and twelve photographs of his sculpture, drawn from the body of work Matter began in 1960 on his first visit to the artist’s Paris studio. Swiss-born photographer and graphic designer Herbert Matter (1907–1984) met Giacometti through Pierre Matisse in 1950 and was commissioned to photograph and design the Guggenheim’s 1955 Giacometti catalogue. Giacometti was astonished by the resulting images, writing that each was “a creation in itself” and that they revealed aspects of his sculpture he had never seen.

The portfolio carries texts by the painter and critic Louis Finkelstein and the photographer Baldwin Lee, who taught alongside Matter at Yale. The publication holds particular significance as the final edition issued by Ives-Sillman, the New Haven imprint of graphic designers Norman Ives and Sewell Sillman, appearing in 1978 shortly after Ives’s death. Matter’s two-decade Giacometti project was ultimately gathered in the monograph Giacometti (Abrams, 1987), completed after his own death in 1984.
notes: Prospectus for the Ives-Sillman portfolio thirteen images depict a portrait and twelve sculptures of Alberto Giacometti. Ives-Sillman’s final publication, issued 1978 after Norman Ives’s death. Texts by Louis Finkelstein and Baldwin Lee. Sources: J.N. Herlin, Inc. Guggenheim Museum Wikipedia.

title: 2000 BC: The Bruce Conner Story Part II
contributors: Kathy Halbreich, Bruce Jenkins, Peter Boswell
description:
Published by the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis, to accompany the 1999–2000 retrospective of the same name (Walker Art Center, October 9, 1999 – January 2, 2000, then touring to three further venues), this is the most comprehensive monograph to date on Bruce Conner (1933–2008), one of the most inventive and elusive figures in postwar American art.

Across roughly 280 pages it surveys five decades of Conner’s restless, cross-disciplinary practice: assemblage, found-object sculpture, drawing, collage, printmaking, photograms, and the pioneering experimental films (A Movie, Cosmic Ray, Crossroads) that made him a foundational figure in American avant-garde cinema. Edited by Joan Rothfuss, with essays by Walker director Kathy Halbreich and curators Bruce Jenkins and Peter Boswell, and designed by Andrew Blauvelt with Erin Mulcahy, the volume is profusely illustrated with 75 four-color and 175 black-and-white plates and finely printed in Germany by Cantz.

Extensive back matter includes an exhibition checklist, chronology, selected bibliography, filmography, and index. The catalogue received second prize in the 1999–2000 International Association of Art Critics (AICA/USA) awards. The playful title nods to Conner’s lifelong resistance to retrospective summary. It is a sequel to a “Part I” that never existed.
tags: Art, Assemblage, Experimental Film, Collage, Exhibition Catalog, Postwar American Art
notes: Exhibition catalogue for the Walker Art Center retrospective (Oct 9, 1999 – Jan 2, 2000), which traveled to three further venues. Issued in two bindings: softcover ISBN 9780935640632 (this record) and hardcover ISBN 9780935640618. 75 four-color + 175 b/w plates printed by Cantz, Germany. Second prize, 1999–2000 AICA/USA awards. Sources: Walker Art Center shop bookseller listings (Jeff Hirsch, Vincent Borrelli) WorldCat.

title: Nervous Breakdown
contributors: René Zechlin, Astrid Ihle (foreword) Max Dax, Robert Eikmeyer, Kim Gordon, Ulrich Loock (essays)
description:
Subtitled Album Covers, this is the first book to gather every record, CD, and cassette sleeve since 1979 to feature the artwork of Raymond Pettibon (b. 1957), the Southern California artist whose ink drawings became the visual signature of American punk and alternative music.

Spanning more than four decades, it traces his collaborations with Black Flag (whose logo and early sleeves he designed for his brother Greg Ginn’s SST label), Sonic Youth, Foo Fighters, Iggy Pop, Minutemen, and, more recently, Lana Del Rey, mapping Pettibon’s outsized influence on the look of alternative culture from the late 1970s to today.

Drawn from the Stefan Thull Collection, the volume reproduces 301 illustrations and carries a foreword by René Zechlin and Astrid Ihle and essays by Max Dax, Robert Eikmeyer, the musician and artist Kim Gordon, and Ulrich Loock. Designed by Studio Sven Michel, Berlin, and printed by VeronaLibri, it was published by David Zwirner Books with the Wilhelm-Hack-Museum to accompany the exhibition of more than 200 works from the Thull collection in Ludwigshafen, Germany.
tags: Art, Punk, Album Covers, Graphic Art, Music, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Subtitle: Album Covers. Published with the Wilhelm-Hack-Museum, Ludwigshafen, to accompany an exhibition of 200+ Pettibon-illustrated music sleeves from the Stefan Thull Collection. 301 illustrations designed by Studio Sven Michel, Berlin printed by VeronaLibri, Verona. Source: David Zwirner Books.

title: Magnetics
description:
A pocket-sized monograph on the Belgian painter Michaël Borremans (b. 1963), among the most admired painters of his generation, whose small, darkly lit canvases fuse the technique of the old masters with the framing of cinema and the displacements of Surrealism.

Published by Hatje Cantz for the exhibition Magnetics at BAWAG Contemporary, Vienna, the book presents a concise selection of about a dozen canvases made over the preceding five years, shown alongside related drawings and films. Its sixteen color plates concentrate on the enigmatic, psychologically charged portraits and figure studies for which Borremans is known — faces half-swallowed by shadow, gestures suspended mid-action, meaning withheld. A text by Christine Kintisch situates the work within Borremans’s wider practice. Compact at roughly 11 × 17 cm and 60 pages.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Belgian Art, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Published for the exhibition Magnetics at BAWAG Contemporary, Vienna. 16 color plates text by Christine Kintisch. Source: David Zwirner / Hatje Cantz.

title: Horse Hunting
description:
Published by David Zwirner on the occasion of Michaël Borremans’s second solo exhibition at the gallery (New York, March 7 – April 1, 2006), this hardcover catalogue documents a body of fourteen new paintings, among them the eponymous Horse Hunting (2005), a portrait of a young, fashionably dressed man holding a twig to each nostril, whose deadpan strangeness is typical of the Belgian painter (b. 1963).

Borremans’s pictures pair old-master technique with disquieting, hard-to-place imagery, resisting straightforward narrative or interpretation. Illustrated boards, no dust jacket as issued, with sixteen color reproductions and a text by the Belgian artist and curator Hans van Heirseele. Printed by Earth Enterprise, New York.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Belgian Art, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Catalogue for Borremans’s second David Zwirner solo show (Mar 7 – Apr 1, 2006), fourteen new paintings including Horse Hunting (2005). Illustrated boards, no dust jacket as issued 16 color plates text by Hans van Heirseele printed by Earth Enterprise, New York. Cover image: OpenLibrary. Sources: David Zwirner bookseller listings.

title: 121 Nurses
description:
A layered work of appropriation by the New York conceptual artist Eric Doeringer (b. 1974), best known for the “bootleg” miniatures of blue-chip artworks he sold on the street outside art fairs and for his Copycat Publications, which meticulously re-create rare conceptual artists’ books.

121 Nurses compiles the pulp nurse-romance paperbacks whose lurid covers Richard Prince scanned and reworked for his celebrated Nurse Paintings (2002–2008). The book is itself an appropriation: it borrows its design from Prince’s own 136 Nurses, the catalogue raisonné of those paintings — so Doeringer appropriates the source material Prince appropriated, and the form in which Prince catalogued it, folding authorship back on itself. Offset-printed in Los Angeles, 42 pages, perfect-bound, 21.5 × 14 cm. Issued without ISBN in the tradition of the artist’s book and zine.
tags: Artist's Books, Appropriation Art, Conceptual Art, Richard Prince, Zines, Art
notes: Copycat Publications is Eric Doeringer’s own imprint. Compiles the nurse novels behind Richard Prince’s Nurse Paintings design appropriated from Prince’s “136 Nurses” catalogue raisonné. Offset printed, Los Angeles. No ISBN. Held in MoMA Library, Whitney Museum Library, SFMOMA, NYPL and other collections per Printed Matter. Source: Printed Matter (catalog 62683).

title: Records
description:
Eric Doeringer’s remake of Ed Ruscha’s 1971 classic Records, and a companion in method to his other appropriations.

Ruscha’s original reproduced thirty records from his own collection, each spread pairing an album cover on the left with a photograph of the bare vinyl LP on the right. To make his version, Doeringer (b. 1974) tracked down copies of every record Ruscha had pictured and re-photographed them in the same sequence — but the two books are pointedly not identical: his copies carry their own histories of wear, price stickers, and doodles, and the labels differ in mono/stereo pressings and reissues.

The result turns a reproduction into a meditation on collecting, difference, and the impossibility of a true copy. It belongs to the now-sizeable genre of Ruscha-homage artists’ books — Doeringer has also remade Some Los Angeles Apartments, Real Estate Opportunities, and Stained. Self-published under his Copycat Publications imprint in an edition of 1,000, signed on the title page softcover, 72 pages, 7 × 5.5 in.
tags: Artist's Books, Appropriation Art, Conceptual Art, Ed Ruscha, Music, Vinyl Records, Art

title: David King Publications 1977–2019
publisher: Colpa Press / San Francisco Center for the Book
description:
The first published survey of the book projects and graphic design of David King (1948–2019), the English-born, New York– and San Francisco–based artist, designer, and musician best known for creating the Crass symbol.

King moved to New York in 1977 and made hundreds of flyers for clubs such as Danceteria, Pravda, and the Peppermint Lounge while playing in the no wave band Arsenal relocating to San Francisco in 1980, he designed for the I-Beam and played in the post-punk groups Sleeping Dogs and Brain Rust. Across four decades he produced dozens of cheaply made Xerox and offset zines — Suburbs of Hell, Too Many Zombies, Sleeping Dogs — collaging appropriated images from mainstream magazines, and, later, idiosyncratic small-run books issued through Colpa Press, &Pens, and Gingko Press.

This 120-page volume, co-published by Colpa Press and the San Francisco Center for the Book, gathers that work with an introduction by Matt Borruso and an essay by the design studio Experimental Jetset. It accompanied the first survey exhibitions of King’s output, at the San Francisco Center for the Book (October 25–December 22, 2024) and Printed Matter, New York (June 5–August 24, 2025). Not to be confused with the British graphic designer David King (1943–2016) of Soviet-design fame.
tags: Graphic Design, Zines, Punk, Artist’s Books, Ephemera, Small Press, Flyers, Art
notes: First survey of David King (1948–2019), designer of the Crass symbol English-born, active in NY and SF. Second printing of 1000. Co-published by Colpa Press and the San Francisco Center for the Book. Full-color offset on 120gsm Munken Lynx Rough 2-color cover on 240gsm Munken Lynx thread-sewn OTA binding. Exhibitions curated by Luca Antonucci and Matt Borruso (SF Center for the Book, 2024) and shown at Printed Matter, NY (2025). Distinct from David King (1943–2016), the Soviet-design historian. title: Record Culture Magazine Issue 11
description:
Record is a biannual print journal on the people at the center of the world’s niche music communities and the places those scenes meet art, fashion, and design Issue 11 (2026) runs 208 pages plus two bound supplements.

Built on candid longform interviews and photography made in its subjects’ homes and studios, the issue gathers conversations with Paul Takahashi, Nicolas Godin, Kiki Kudo, Jean Touitou, Ariel Zetina, OKO DJ, Sound Metaphors, and Fraser Cooke, among others, alongside Luke Jenner’s short story Plant Bar and the visual feature Eddie Ruscha: Sound / Waves. Two saddle-stitched booklets accompany the perfect-bound main magazine: The Invitations of Life... Child!, drawn from Nicky Siano’s Gallery-era archive (52 pages), and You Can Hear Your Own Heartbeat: A Day at Audio-Technica, photographed by Kento Mori (60 pages).

Founded in 2016 in New York’s Chinatown and now made across New York, Berlin, and Melbourne with its publisher in Cork, Ireland, Record pairs archival features on musical ephemera with original illustration and design under art director Holly Canham. Issue 11 continues the magazine’s approach of treating record culture as a lens on wider visual and social life rather than as genre coverage.

title: Index
binding: 11 saddle-stitched softcover books in a silkscreened fluted slipcase
description:
The first-edition boxed set of Index, the career-spanning self-anthology by the Magnum photographer Christopher Anderson (b. 1970): eleven saddle-stitched volumes housed in a silkscreened fluted slipcase, published by STANLEY/BARKER in 2026 and designed by Brian Roettinger.

Rather than a linear retrospective, Index breaks three decades of work into eleven separate booklets (Afghanistan, Haiti, China, France, Cars, Self Portrait, Holiday, New York, Trouble, White House, and 9 East 71st Street) that can be read in any order, juxtaposing war, migration, politics, and domestic intimacy like entries in an index. The 320-page set measures 255 × 225 mm this copy is signed by Anderson.

Anderson won the Robert Capa Gold Medal in 1999 for photographs made aboard a sinking boat of Haitian migrants bound for the United States, then covered Afghanistan, Iraq, and Israel/Palestine before turning toward family, cities, and self-portraiture, work that moves fluidly between reportage and the personal. A member of Magnum Photos, he built the monographs Capitolio, Son, Stump, and Approximate Joy Index draws that full arc together and was widely noted on release, including in The Guardian and Le Monde.
notes: Signed by Christopher Anderson. First edition, first printing. Boxed set of 11 saddle-stitched softcover volumes in a silkscreened fluted slipcase, designed by Brian Roettinger 255 × 225 mm, 320 pages, 2000 g. Volumes: 1 Afghanistan, 2 Haiti, 3 China, 4 France, 5 Cars, 6 Self Portrait, 7 Holiday, 8 New York, 9 Trouble, 10 White House, 11 9 East 71st Street, NY. Christopher Anderson (Magnum) won the Robert Capa Gold Medal in 1999. Reviewed in The Guardian and Le Monde. No ISBN found on publisher or distributor listings.

title: Folk Songs
description:
The catalogue for Folk Songs, Richard Prince's 2025 exhibition at Gagosian in New York: a 136-page softcover with a die-cut reproduction of one of the paintings tipped into its kraft cover.

Published by Gagosian in 2026 to accompany the show at 555 West 24th Street (November 6–December 20, 2025), the book documents handmade paintings, drawings, and collages made between 2018 and 2023 together with five sculptures dating from 2007 to 2025, reproduced in color plates and installation views. An essay by the art historian Sydney Stutterheim reads Prince's recurring methods (self-reference and appropriation, buried meanings and apocrypha) against a palette of soft pinks, magentas, and reds set against black. Designed by Graphic Thought Facility, London, and printed by Pureprint.

Richard Prince (b. 1949) is among the central figures of the Pictures Generation, whose rephotographed Marlboro Cowboys, Nurse paintings, joke canvases, and Instagram New Portraits made appropriation a defining strategy of postwar art. His work is held by the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney, the Guggenheim, and Tate Folk Songs extends the looser, hand-made register of his recent painting.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Appropriation, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Exhibition catalogue for 'Richard Prince: Folk Songs,' Gagosian, 555 West 24th Street, New York, November 6–December 20, 2025. Essay by Sydney Stutterheim. Designed by Graphic Thought Facility, London printed by Pureprint Group, Uckfield. Die-cut reproduction of one painting on the cover. Contents: paintings, drawings, and collages 2018–2023 and five sculptures 2007–2025 color plates and installation photography.

title: Gary Schneider: Portraits
contributors: Deborah Martin Kao (Author of text and interview with the artist)
description:
The first major study of Gary Schneider (b. 1954), the South African-born New York photographer whose long-exposure, flashlight-drawn portraits reimagine photographic likeness as a record of time and collaboration.

Written by Deborah Martin Kao, the Richard L. Menschel Curator of Photography at Harvard's Fogg Art Museum, the catalogue traces two decades of Schneider's portrait work: his re-presentations of nineteenth-century studio negatives, his life-size handprint photograms, and his fragmented face portraits, made by moving a light pen across a sitter's features during exposures that can last more than an hour. Kao also examines the scientific collaborations behind his images of blood, DNA, and hair, and closes with an extended interview with the artist. Yale University Press published it in association with the Harvard University Art Museums to accompany the retrospective at the Arthur M. Sackler Museum (28 February to 23 May 2004). Paperback, 122 pages, with 103 color and 49 black-and-white plates.

Schneider trained at the Michaelis School of Fine Art in Cape Town and at Pratt Institute, and has lived in New York since 1977, where in 1981 he co-founded the master printing lab Schneider/Erdman. His Genetic Self-Portrait (1998) and ongoing Nudes series pushed portraiture toward science and abstraction, and his work is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and the Art Institute of Chicago. He printed for many photographers, among them Peter Hujar, whose negatives are the subject of his 2024 memoir Peter Hujar: Behind the Camera and In the Darkroom.

title: Index
editor: Willem de Rooij, Axel Wieder, Susanne Gaensheimer
description:
An inquiry into the iconography of protest by the Dutch conceptual artist Willem de Rooij (b. 1969), Index compiles some 500 newspaper images of protest marches and collective mourning collected between 1999 and 2002.

The photographs, cut from daily newspapers over three years, were first organized in 2002 into eighteen framed panels arranged chronologically as Index: Riots, Protest, Mourning and Commemoration (as represented in newspapers, January 2000–July 2002). This 508-page artist's book reorganizes the complete series for the printed page, returning the images to the mass-circulation form in which they first appeared and documenting a way of working — clipping from print — that the shift to online image culture has made obsolete. It was published with essays by Sven Lütticken and Pablo Martínez on the occasion of exhibitions at Arnolfini, Bristol (2014–15) and MMK Museum für Moderne Kunst, Frankfurt (2016–17), co-published by the two institutions with Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König, Cologne.

De Rooij studied at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie and the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam and worked collaboratively with Jeroen de Rijke as De Rijke/De Rooij from 1994 to 2006, representing the Netherlands at the 2005 Venice Biennale. Professor of fine art at Frankfurt's Städelschule since 2006, he works across film, installation, and textile, and is represented by Petzel Gallery, New York, and Regen Projects, Los Angeles.

title: Ray Johnson
description:
A monograph on the collagist and mail-art pioneer Ray Johnson (1927–1995), presenting 42 collages made between 1966 and 1994, most never previously exhibited or published, with a new essay by the writer and biographer Brad Gooch.

Published by Matthew Marks Gallery in 2017, the clothbound volume reproduces Johnson's most expansive work in 87 plates: layered compositions of magazine clippings, photographs, and hand-worked elements that merge art history with celebrity, word with image, and the personal with the universal. Gooch's essay traces a practice delivering, in his words, "surprise and joy, excitement and entertainment," likening the collages to jokes sublimely told by a tortured stand-up comedian.

A Black Mountain College alumnus who turned from painting to collage after moving to New York in 1949, Johnson became a seminal Pop artist, a proto-conceptualist, and the founder of the New York Correspondance School, distributing his work through the postal service. By 1965 he was known as "New York's most famous unknown artist." The library also holds Ray Johnson c/o, the Art Institute of Chicago's 2021 survey of his correspondence art.
tags: Art, Collage, Mail Art, Pop Art
notes: Clothbound with jacket. Second Ray Johnson title in the collection alongside Ray Johnson c/o (ID 552, Art Institute of Chicago, 2021) — different publication, not a duplicate copy. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: 1954 Drawings on a Bus, Sketchbook 23
description:
A facsimile of Sketchbook 23 by the American painter Ellsworth Kelly (1923–2015), reproducing the ink drawings of shifting shadow patterns he made riding New York City buses in the fall of 1954, weeks after returning from six years in Paris.

In Paris, Kelly had built paintings from window patterns and the shadows cast by Seine bridges back in New York he sketched the sunlight moving across bus seat backs and overhead bars, then reworked the sketches in the studio into abstractions stripped of their physical source. These drawings fed directly into his earliest American paintings, among them Atlantic (1956), the first of his works to enter a museum collection when the Whitney purchased it in 1957. The sketchbook itself has an unusual origin: a friend gave Kelly a blank publisher's dummy of Sigfried Giedion's 1928 Bauen in Frankreich, its cover designed by Moholy-Nagy, and the facsimile reproduces that cover. Co-published by Matthew Marks Gallery and Steidl in 2007 as a slipcased hardcover with a 2006 text by the artist, accompanying the gallery's exhibition of twenty drawings from the sketchbook.

Kelly stands among the defining figures of postwar American abstraction, his hard-edge shape and color paintings drawn from observed fragments of the world. His work is held by MoMA, the Whitney, and Tate, among others, and his estate is represented by Matthew Marks Gallery.
tags: Art, Drawing, Sketchbooks, Abstract Art, Facsimile
notes: Anastatic facsimile of Kelly's Sketchbook 23 — originally a blank publisher's dummy of Sigfried Giedion's Bauen in Frankreich (1928) with cover design by Moholy-Nagy, reproduced here. Out of print at Matthew Marks. Dimensions per publisher (25 × 19 cm) AbeBooks lists 25.5 × 18.5 cm. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Visible World
description:
An encyclopedic artist's book by the Zurich duo Peter Fischli (b. 1952) and David Weiss (1946–2012), Visible World compresses 2,848 color photographs taken over fifteen years of travel into 260 flexibound pages. The world is rendered as a deadpan, seemingly total inventory.

Conceived and designed by the artists and co-published by Matthew Marks Gallery and Buchhandlung Walther König in 2000, the book is the printed form of their long-running Sichtbare Welt project, which the duo also presented as photographs on light tables. Airports, beaches, gardens, mountains, and cities pass in tight grids without hierarchy or commentary, extending the taxonomic impulse of their 1982 publication Suddenly this Overview. The pictures court the generic (sunsets and tourist views done straight) so that the book reads at once as archive, travelogue, and gentle parody of both.

Working together from 1979 until Weiss's death in 2012, Fischli and Weiss built one of contemporary art's most influential collaborative bodies of work, spanning the film The Way Things Go (1987), the clay Suddenly this Overview sculptures, and the retrospective How to Work Better at the Guggenheim (2016). The library holds several of their other titles, including 800 Views of Airports and How to Work Better.
tags: Art, Photography, Conceptual Art, Travel Photography
notes: Conceived and designed by the artists. Book form of the Sichtbare Welt (Visible World) project, also shown as photographs on light tables. Out of print at Matthew Marks. Ninth Fischli & Weiss title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: On Any Given Day in Spring / Light Balances
description:
A quiet two-volume set of late photographs by Robert Adams (b. 1937), the central chronicler of the American West's transformation, published as paired paperbacks in a plain cardboard slipcase by Matthew Marks Gallery and Fraenkel Gallery in 2012.

On Any Given Day in Spring (32 pages, 30 plates) follows seabirds, sand, ocean, and sky at North Beach on Washington's coast — encounters Adams describes as "less an answer to our questions than a rephrasing of them," adding that "there is no certainty, on any given day in spring, that the birds will be there." Light Balances (48 pages, 57 plates) records light filtering through the foliage of a protected forest near the Columbia River estuary in Astoria, Oregon, where Adams has lived since 1997. Both books hold to his spare black-and-white attentiveness, here turned from the developed landscapes of his New Topographics years toward what remains intact.

Adams came to prominence in the 1975 New Topographics exhibition and received the Hasselblad Award in 2009 his retrospective The Place We Live toured internationally from Yale University Art Gallery. He is represented by Fraenkel Gallery and Matthew Marks Gallery. The library also holds his Gone? (Steidl, 2010).
tags: Photography, Landscape Photography, Black and White Photography, Pacific Northwest, Photobooks
notes: Two-volume set in cardboard slipcase: On Any Given Day in Spring (32 pp, 30 plates, ISBN 9781880146637) and Light Balances (48 pp, 57 plates, ISBN 9781880146620). Set cataloged under the first volume's ISBN. Out of print at Matthew Marks. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Mr. Remember
editor: Lærke Rydal Jørgensen, Mathias Ussing Seeberg, William Pym, Alex Da Corte
contributors: Poul Erik Tøjner (Foreword) Bruce Hainley (Essay) Delia Solomons (Essay) Sarah Nicole Prickett (Essay) Steven Zultanski (Essay) Derek McCormack (Essay)
description:
The comprehensive monograph on the Philadelphia-based installation artist Alex Da Corte (b. 1980), published for Mr. Remember, his major European retrospective at the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art (July 14, 2022 – January 8, 2023).

Documenting all of Da Corte's major works to date, the book matches his high-production, ultra-chromatic sensibility: a three-color cloth binding with silver foil on the cover, 200 color and 50 duotone plates, more than 100 pages of installation views, and a paperback volume sewn into the binding. The Louisiana retrospective staged his Day-Glo paintings, sculptures, videos, and scenographies (colored walls, neon, even scent) around works like Rubber Pencil Devil, the 57-part film in which the artist impersonates figures from American children's television. Edited by Lærke Rydal Jørgensen, Mathias Ussing Seeberg, William Pym, and the artist, with a foreword by Poul Erik Tøjner and texts by Bruce Hainley, Delia Solomons, Sarah Nicole Prickett, Steven Zultanski, Derek McCormack, and others.

Rooted in American popular culture (as a teenager he planned to animate for Disney), Da Corte builds seductive, uncanny worlds from consumer imagery, appearing in his own films as Popeye, the Statue of Liberty, Mister Rogers, or Eminem. His 2021 Met Roof Garden commission As Long as the Sun Lasts brought the work wide attention. The library holds six of his other titles, including Rubber Pencil Devil and Free Roses.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Installation Art, Video Art, Pop Culture, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Three-color cloth binding with silver foil paperback supplement sewn in. Danish publication December 2022 US trade release March 2023 via DAP. Seventh Alex Da Corte title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Ellsworth Kelly in San Francisco
publisher: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art / University of California Press
contributors: Madeleine Grynsztejn (Essay) Julian Myers (Essay) Neal Benezra (Foreword)
description:
The catalog for Ellsworth Kelly in San Francisco, SFMOMA's 2002–03 exhibition uniting the twenty-two works the museum acquired from the artist's personal collection in 1999 with its earlier holdings, together the most important grouping of Ellsworth Kelly's work in any museum. The 1999 acquisition included Cité (1951), Red Blue (1966), and Curve XXI (1978–80).

Spanning fifty years of paintings, sculptures, collages, drawings, and reliefs drawn from the museum and Bay Area private collections, the exhibition (July 13, 2002 – January 5, 2003) presented 58 works in all. The primary essay by Madeleine Grynsztejn, SFMOMA's Elise S. Haas Senior Curator of Painting and Sculpture and the show's organizer, follows the evolution of Kelly's art, his interest in the phenomenology of vision, and his chance-generated compositions Julian Myers contributes analyses of key works and groupings, from the early figural paintings to the shaped panels and reliefs, with a foreword by Neal Benezra. Co-published with University of California Press.

Kelly (1923–2015) was a defining figure of postwar American abstraction, his hard-edge shape and color paintings drawn from observed fragments of the world. The library also holds 1954 Drawings on a Bus, Sketchbook 23, the facsimile of the sketchbook behind his earliest American paintings.
tags: Art, Abstract Art, Painting, Sculpture, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Page count per SFMOMA (96) Amazon lists 104. Second Ellsworth Kelly title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Sarah Morris
publisher: EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art
editor: Pilvi Kalhama, Ari Karttunen, Milla Rissanen, Pernilla Wiik
description:
The catalog for the British-American artist Sarah Morris's (b. 1967) solo exhibition at EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art (June 21, 2017 – January 7, 2018), documenting the abstract paintings and films of an artist who treats the two media as one continuous practice.

The exhibition brought together three of Morris's films, a selection of her graphic, hard-color paintings, and Mäntyjä (Pines), a 30-meter site-specific wall painting created for EMMA's Aalto-influenced Tapiola setting. Since the mid-1990s Morris has traced the tension between social space, identity, and power, reading cities (Paris, Rio de Janeiro, Beijing) through their architectures, logos, and systems of control. The 175-page hardcover, edited by museum director Pilvi Kalhama with Ari Karttunen, Milla Rissanen, and Pernilla Wiik, includes color illustrations throughout and, unusually, music notation. Published by EMMA in 2019.

Morris lives and works in New York. Her paintings and films are held by MoMA, Tate, and the Centre Pompidou, and she is represented by White Cube, Capitain Petzel, and Air de Paris.
