title: Neue Malerei
contributors: Markus Bertsch (Essay) Simon Elson (Essay) Florian Illies (Essay)
description:
A conceptual inversion of the painting catalog by the German artist Christian Jankowski (b. 1968), Neue Malerei ("new painting") presents oil canvases of works by Picasso, Richter, Warhol, Dürer, and other icons of art history, painted by an artist who, by his own admission, cannot paint at all.

Jankowski collected photographs of tableaux vivants found on the internet (people restaging famous paintings) and sent them to his studio in Shenzhen, where Chinese copy painters rendered them in oil on canvas. The catalog, published for his March 2018 exhibition at the Berlin auction house Grisebach, plays the result straight, in linen-bound quarto with texts by Markus Bertsch, Simon Elson, and Florian Illies. As Illies writes, "Nothing is right on the (following) pages of this catalog. Everything is shaking — the optics, the habits of seeing, the certainties, the standards of quality." It is a book of new painting in which we only see works of old masters. In German distributed by Walther König.

Jankowski works in video, performance, and installation built on collaborations with non-art professionals (TV fortune tellers, magicians, weightlifters), probing how art passes through mass media. He curated Manifesta 11 in Zurich (2016), teaches at the Stuttgart Academy, and is represented by Petzel Gallery, New York.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Conceptual Art, Appropriation, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Text in German. Distributed by Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König. First Christian Jankowski title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Nude and Landscape
contributors: Elizabeth Manchester (Essay) Sid Sachs (Essay) William Horner (Interview)
description:
A catalog that reads the British collagist John Stezaker (b. 1949) against art-historical tradition (landscape painting and the nude) rather than the cinematic imagery his found-image work is best known for.

Centered on works from the 1980s onward, when Stezaker turned from the culture of the image to the nature of the image, the book presents his Bridge collages and the anatomical nudes of the Fall and Expulsion series, including many works never previously shown. Most telling is its inclusion of unaltered found images: postcards and plates so close to the finished collages that only the absence or presence of the artist's cut distinguishes them, laying the methodology bare. Published by Ridinghouse with the Rosenwald-Wolf Gallery for the exhibition curated by Sid Sachs at the University of the Arts, Philadelphia (October 13 – November 19, 2011), later restaged at Petzel Gallery, New York (2013). With texts by Elizabeth Manchester and Sachs, and a conversation between Stezaker and William Horner.

Stezaker came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York. The library also holds the Rubell Family Collection volume on his work.
tags: Art, Collage, Contemporary Art, Appropriation, Found Photography, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Published by Ridinghouse in association with Rosenwald-Wolf Gallery DAP lists March 2012 publication, some sources say 2013. Second John Stezaker title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Crease Folds
description:
A pocket-sized artist's book by the British-American painter and filmmaker Sarah Morris (b. 1967), Crease Folds chronicles, in reality and in fiction, the period in which she made the film Strange Magic (2014).

Strange Magic surveys the Louis Vuitton empire's production of luxury goods (fashion, fragrance, champagne, architecture) as the capital source behind the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton, deconstructing the mechanisms of that cultural currency and the fantasy inherent in luxury itself. For the book, Morris juxtaposed this making-of material with an invented counterpart: after meeting the Oscar-winning Pulp Fiction screenwriter Roger Avary at the 2012 Locarno Film Festival, where an homage to her films was presented, she asked him to write a fictional text about her. The 120-page softcover, edited by the artist and published by Ivorypress LiberArs, Madrid, in 2015, sets fiction and fantasy against the record of an artwork's production.

Morris's paintings and city films (Paris, Rio, Beijing) trace the codes of social space and power. Her work is held by MoMA, Tate, and the Centre Pompidou she is represented by White Cube, Capitain Petzel, and Air de Paris. The library also holds the EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art catalog of her 2017–18 retrospective.
tags: Art, Film, Contemporary Art, Luxury, Fiction
notes: Fictional text by Roger Avary commissioned after meeting at the 2012 Locarno Film Festival. Second Sarah Morris title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Silkscreens
description:
The first comprehensive gathering of the silkscreens of John Stezaker (b. 1949), a side of the British collagist little known next to his small, intimate collages of film stills and postcards.

Spanning 1977 to 1994, the mid- to large-scale silkscreens work Stezaker's found imagery at the scale of painting: manipulated kissing couples, disembodied men and women, floating baby-heads, and film stills, estranged through enlargement and repetition. Caoimhín Mac Giolla Léith's essay is the first text to consider the silkscreens as a whole body of work. The 144-page volume, with 85 color illustrations, was published by Ridinghouse with Galerie Gisela Capitain, Cologne Friedrich Petzel Gallery, New York and The Approach, London, on the occasion of John Stezaker: Silkscreens at Capitain Petzel, Berlin (September 18 – October 30, 2010).

Stezaker came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach and Petzel Gallery. This is the third Stezaker title in the library, alongside Nude and Landscape and the Rubell Family Collection volume.
tags: Art, Silkscreen, Printmaking, Contemporary Art, Appropriation, Found Photography, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Co-published by Ridinghouse with Galerie Gisela Capitain, Cologne Friedrich Petzel Gallery, New York and The Approach, London. Ridinghouse lists softback 144 pp The Approach lists hardback 142 pp. Third John Stezaker title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: One on One
publisher: Ridinghouse / Tel Aviv Museum of Art
contributors: Irith Hadar (Essay) Dalit Matatyahu (Essay) Suzanne Landau (Foreword) Christophe Gallois (Interview) Daniel F. Herrmann (Interview)
description:
The catalog for One on One, John Stezaker's (b. 1949) 2013 exhibition at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art: a set of previously unseen collages made over the preceding two years, the British artist's found images spliced with his signature single cut.

The clothbound volume reproduces 63 color plates, including ten images from The 3rd Person Archive (1976–present), Stezaker's decades-long collection of tiny incidental figures clipped from illustrated books. Published by Ridinghouse in association with the museum for the exhibition (January 18 – May 18, 2013), it carries a foreword by director Suzanne Landau, Irith Hadar's essay "Arresting Resistance," Dalit Matatyahu's "Tabula Rasa," and "The Third Meaning," a conversation between Stezaker, Christophe Gallois, and Daniel F. Herrmann.

Stezaker came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York. This is the fourth Stezaker title in the library, alongside Silkscreens, Nude and Landscape, and the Rubell Family Collection volume.
tags: Art, Collage, Contemporary Art, Appropriation, Found Photography, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Ridinghouse ISBN 9781905464715 Tel Aviv Museum of Art edition also carries ISBN 9789655390537. Fourth John Stezaker title in the collection. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Révélations: Iconographie de la Salpêtrière, Paris 1875–1918
contributors: Gonzalo Golpe (design), Carlos Chiclana Actis y Cía, Javier Rodríguez Martínez, Priscilla Echeverría Alvarado (texts)
description:
Révélations presents one of the earliest and most significant photographic archives in the history of clinical psychiatry.

Compiled and edited by contemporary photographer and designer Javier Viver, this publication draws from over 4,000 photographs and thirty-two volumes that were systematically produced between 1875 and 1918 at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris. Under the direction of Jean-Martin Charcot—founder of modern neurology—and financed by the French government, the hospital's archive represented an unprecedented effort to document and categorize patients through innovative photographic-documentary techniques.

The archive reveals the complex intersection of medical science and public spectacle. Tuesday sessions at the Salpêtrière became celebrated events for Paris's cultural elite, where Charcot conducted demonstrations involving hypnosis-induced displays of patients. The photographic record reveals how emerging medical understanding became entangled with theatrical presentation.
tags: disaster, psychiatry, medical photography, archive, hysteria, Charcot, 19th century, Paris, institutional photography, Photography
notes: Winner of the Spanish Ministry of Culture First Prize for The Best Book of Art 2015 and the Ars Libris Barcelona award. Nominated for Best Photobook at the 2016 Fotobookfestival Kassel and the 2016 PhotoEspaña Prize for Best Book of Photography. Acquired by MACBA and the PhotoIreland Collection. Currently out of print. Restored 2026-07-23 from git history (original id 1581, row destroyed in commit 929ba691a (2025-11-29)).

title: Script of Demolition
binding: Thread-sewn brochure with loose gatefold cover
description:
"Script of Demolition" documents the visual methodology behind controlled industrial demolitions through an examination of the Fink family demolition company's 60-year archive.

The project reveals how blast specialists prepare for structural destruction: technicians create complex technical drawings predicting collapse sequences before detonation, multiple cameras record the actual implosion from various angles, and these drawings are then superimposed over photographs for verification and refinement.

The book compiles diverse imaging media—including 8mm film and digital photography—presenting movement sequences of collapsing chimneys, TV towers, and buildings documented according to technical rather than aesthetic criteria. By appropriating and recontextualizing these utilitarian industrial archives, Schmuch examines the relationship between visual documentation, planning, and reality.
tags: disaster, demolition, architecture, collapse, industrial photography, archive, Germany, Photography
notes: Alina Schmuch (born 1987 in Münster) is a German artist who uses photography, film, and artist's books to investigate how visual media influences and shapes reality. Selected for the best Photo-book selection at Fotobookfestival, Kassel, Germany in 2015. Restored 2026-07-23 from git history (original id 1582, row destroyed in commit 929ba691a (2025-11-29)).

title: 101 Tragedies of Enrique Metinides
description:
"101 Tragedies" represents Enrique Metinides's personal selection of 101 key images from over 50 years spent documenting crime scenes, accidents, and catastrophes throughout Mexico City.

Edited by filmmaker and curator Trisha Ziff, this is the first comprehensive overview of Metinides's work in many years and the only monograph comprised entirely of images chosen by the photographer himself. The book features extended captions authored by Metinides that provide his firsthand account of each photograph's subject matter: the street characters, criminals, heroism of emergency workers, and bereaved families he encountered.

Thirty of the selected photographs are paired with their original newsprint tearsheets from Mexico's "nota roja" crime press, which inspired the book's typography and design. This integration of archival material creates a hybrid document that contextualizes Metinides's work within its original journalistic form. Ziff contributes an interpretive essay exploring Metinides's life, artistic vision, and significance within Mexican photojournalism.
tags: disaster, accident, photojournalism, Mexico, nota roja, crime photography, Mexico City, Photography
notes: Enrique Metinides (February 12, 1934 – May 10, 2022) began his photographic career at age twelve. He worked professionally from 1948 through his retirement in 1997, earning recognition from Mexico's government, journalists' associations, and rescue organizations. In 1997, he received the Espejo de Luz (Mirror of Light) Prize, the highest award given to photographers in Mexico. His work has been exhibited at the Museum of Modern Art and Anton Kern Gallery in New York, the Photographers' Gallery in London, and toured Europe and the Americas from 2011 to 2013 as the "101 Tragedies" exhibition. author_full_name: Sandra S. Phillips Mark Haworth-Booth Carol Squiers
title: Police Pictures: The Photograph as Evidence
publisher: Chronicle Books in association with SFMOMA
editor: Sandra S. Phillips, Mark Haworth-Booth, Carol Squiers
description:
A landmark 1997 exhibition catalog accompanying the first major museum exhibition to examine historical and contemporary photographs taken as evidence in law enforcement contexts.

The work surveys more than 120 images from public and private sources—ranging from Civil War era Lincoln conspiracy photographs to mid-20th century crime scenes and contemporary forensic documentation—that question the conjunction of photography and enforcement while challenging the assumption that images represent unvarnished truth.

The three-part catalog features essays by the three editors: Sandra S. Phillips' essay examines mug shot photography and anthropometry Mark Haworth-Booth explores the photographer's role in crime documentation and Carol Squiers analyzes how press photography served as both evidence and propaganda during the FBI's expanded powers under J. Edgar Hoover. The book explores the evolution of surveillance from wartime reconnaissance to contemporary security monitoring.
tags: disaster, forensic photography, policing, crime scene, Surveillance, evidence, mug shots, Weegee, Photography
notes: The exhibition opened at SFMOMA October 17, 1997–January 20, 1998, and traveled to the Grey Art Gallery and Study Center at New York University (May 19–July 18, 1998). Sandra S. Phillips was Curator of SFMOMA Photography department Mark Haworth-Booth was photography curator at the Victoria & Albert Museum, London Carol Squiers is an independent photo curator and critic. This was the first comprehensive museum exhibition of its kind to treat police and forensic photography as cultural artifacts worthy of serious art historical examination. title: The Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death
binding: Hardcover with black cloth boards and black pictorial dust jacket
description:
"The Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death" documents the remarkable career and legacy of Frances Glessner Lee, a pioneering forensic scientist and philanthropist who revolutionized crime scene investigation training.

Published in 2004 with 225 pages of lush color photography and specially prepared line drawings, Corinne May Botz's book presents an extraordinary visual and narrative exploration of Lee's eighteen miniature crime-scene dioramas created in the 1940s and 1950s.

Built at a precise scale of 1:12 (one inch to one foot), these hyperrealistic dollhouse-sized models display meticulous attention to forensic detail: working doors and windows, carefully placed clues such as overturned ashtrays and bullet holes in walls, ligature marks painted on doll figures, and decomposition effects rendered with scientific accuracy. Each diorama cost between $3,000-$4,500 to construct and represents a composite based on actual case files. Botz's accompanying essay, drawing from archival research and interviews with Lee's family and police colleagues, provides biographical context.
tags: disaster, unexplained death, forensic, dioramas, Frances Glessner Lee, miniatures, crime scene, investigation training, Photography
notes: Frances Glessner Lee (1878-1962) was the first female police captain in the United States and is known as the "mother of forensic science." In 1931, she helped establish Harvard's Department of Legal Medicine—the only such forensic program existing in North America at that time—and in 1936 she endowed the department with a substantial gift of $250,000. Lee's Nutshell Studies are now housed at the Maryland Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Baltimore, where they continue to serve as active educational tools in annual forensic investigation seminars. The dioramas were designed to teach homicide investigators to "convict the guilty, clear the innocent, and find the truth in a nutshell." Exhibited by the Renwick Gallery of the Smithsonian American Art Museum from October 2017 to January 2018. Restored 2026-07-23 from git history (original id 1585, row destroyed in commit 929ba691a (2025-11-29)).

author_full_name: Sarah Pickering text by Karen Irvine
title: Explosions, Fires, and Public Order
description:
Sarah Pickering's "Explosions, Fires, and Public Order" documents four interconnected photographic series exploring the secretive spaces where civil defense and emergency preparedness training takes place.

The work begins with "Public Order," which examines the Metropolitan Police Public Order Training Centre near London, a simulated urban environment where officers rehearse responses to scenarios of civic unrest. This series reveals the carefully constructed infrastructure designed to prepare specialist officers for terrorism threats and civil disturbances.

The "Explosions" series captures controlled military detonations used to add realistic stress to training exercises, some created by pyrotechnic manufacturers who also work on James Bond films. Pickering's "Fire Series" and "Incident" were produced during her artist-in-residence at the UK Fire Training College, where she photographed both active training fires set inside meticulously constructed home interiors and the stark, charred remnants after blazes were extinguished.
tags: disaster, fire, explosion, public order, simulation, UK, training, emergency preparedness, civil defense, Photography
notes: Published by Aperture and the Museum of Contemporary Photography in 2010. Made possible in part by the Lannan Foundation. The book accompanied the exhibition "Sarah Pickering: Incident Control" at MoCP (Museum of Contemporary Photography) at Columbia College Chicago from April 9 through June 20, 2010. Sarah Pickering completed her MA in photography at the Royal College of Art, London, in 2005 and has received numerous awards including the Photographers' Gallery Graduate Award and a Jerwood Award. Her work was part of the "How We Are: Photographing Britain" exhibition at Tate Britain. Restored 2026-07-23 from git history (original id 1586, row destroyed in commit 929ba691a (2025-11-29)).

author_full_name: Arnold Odermatt text by Urs Odermatt
title: Karambolage
description:
Arnold Odermatt spent over four decades as a Swiss police photographer in the canton of Nidwalden, documenting automobile accidents from 1948 to 1990.

Working with his Rolleiflex camera, he initially photographed crashes to supplement written accident reports and provide evidence for court cases and insurance investigations. Unlike typical documentary police photography, Odermatt's images reveal a sophisticated artistic sensibility, combining clinical attention to detail with an aesthetic appreciation for composition and landscape.

His photographs transform scenes of destruction into unexpectedly haunting and sometimes surreal visual narratives, capturing damaged vehicles as sculptural objects arranged in the Alpine landscape. The work captures consequences of excessive speed, impaired driving, and traffic violations across four decades, presenting melancholic, sometimes darkly comedic, and always atmospheric moments that explore themes of human fragility and societal risk.

title: Slanted Magazine #46—Cairo
description:
Slanted Magazine #46—Cairo is a visual journey into the vibrant heart of Egypt's creative scene.

This issue showcases outstanding projects across graphic design, typography, visual communication, architecture, and product design that are shaping the cultural present and future of the region. It includes in-depth essays and articles on cultural, social, and creative topics related to Cairo and Egypt. The design features radiant sandy hues and bright pink accents with classic yet modern pyramid motifs finished with hot foil embossing.

title: NYC Manhole Covers
description:
Documentation of Lawrence Weiner's Public Art Fund project NYC Manhole Covers (2000) consisting of nineteen manhole covers designed by Weiner and installed in various Manhattan neighborhoods.

Features Weiner's plans for the covers and black-and-white photographs depicting their integration into the city's landscape. Covers inscribed with the phrase 'in direct line with another and the next' referencing Manhattan's street grid. Produced in collaboration with Con Edison and Roman Stone. Offset printed.

title: Selected Collages
description:
Published on the occasion of Thomas Eggerer's 2022 survey at 15 Orient, Selected Collages, 2002 to 2022 gathers two decades of the collage practice that runs beneath the painter's better-known canvases, where his figures in public space first take shape.

The softcover volume, produced with Brooklyn's Inpatient Press, reproduces collages built from Eggerer's archive of found printed matter: high-gloss 1980s university yearbooks, illustrated fitness manuals, self-help guides, nature books, and a favored 1982 Italian volume on the Milan subway. Cut-out photographs, he writes, rest in a box "until I feel more interested in them, which can sometimes take years" the source has to be "almost normal, not too sensational." An essay by art historian David Joselit accompanies the plates across 90 pages. The exhibition ran at 15 Orient, Brooklyn, from September 7 to October 8, 2022.

Eggerer (b. 1963, Munich) trained as a painter at the Art Academy in Munich and moved to New York in 1994, where he joined the collective Group Material. Represented by Petzel Gallery and Galerie Buchholz, he has exhibited at the Frans Hals Museum, Kunstverein Braunschweig, and the Wadsworth Atheneum, and his work is held by the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum, SFMOMA, and the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam.

notes: Exhibition catalogue published without ISBN by Inpatient Press with 15 Orient, Brooklyn softcover, 90 pages text by David Joselit. Sold directly through the gallery no WorldCat record or ISBN registration found. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Chapter 5
description:
Chapter 5 is the fifth installment in the long-running collaborative book series by Rita Ackermann and Andro Wekua, published by Nieves, Zurich, in 2026, its photocopy-style cover collaging the numerals 2, 3, and 5 so the title reads as Chapter 235.

The Chapter books began after the two artists met in 2002, unfolding as a correspondence in print: part visual diary, part exchange of drawings, collages, and fragments of text that drift between figuration and abstraction. The series moved from a self-published Chapter 1 to Nieves editions of Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 (both 2004), then to Chapter 4 (Fergus McCaffrey and Case Publishing, 2021). This volume returns the series to Nieves as 64 pages of black-and-white offset imagery without text, accumulating impressions of memory and distance rather than resolving into fixed narrative.

Rita Ackermann (b. 1968, Budapest) is a Hungarian-American painter, represented by Hauser & Wirth, whose process-driven canvases layer painting, drawing, and collage. Andro Wekua (b. 1977, Sokhumi, Georgia), represented by Gladstone and Sprüth Magers, works across painting, sculpture, film, and installation, with exhibitions at Kunsthalle Basel, Museo Tamayo, and the Venice Biennale.
tags: Art, Zines, Collage, Drawing, Collaboration, Nieves
notes: Identified as Nieves' Chapter 5 (First Edition 2026): no publication titled 'Chapter 235' exists the cover typography collages a struck-through 2, a 3, and a large 5 under 'Chapter', which reads as 'Chapter 235'. Cover also carries the hand-lettered phrase 'Shepherdess Trees'. Library already holds Chapter 4 (Fergus McCaffrey / Case Publishing, 2021) as catalog id 9 — this is a different, non-duplicate volume in the same series. Earlier Nieves chapters: Chapter 2 (2004, b/w photocopy, 60 copies, out of print) and Chapter 3 (2004, color/b&w offset, out of print). Illustrations: Black-and-white offset reproductions of drawings and collages throughout no text. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: David Weiss: Works, 1968–1979
contributors: Hans Ulrich Obrist (Text) Urs Lüthi (Text) Douglas Fogle (Essay)
description:
Before Fischli/Weiss there was a decade of David Weiss working alone, filling notebooks and sheets of paper with drawings that stayed hidden for more than thirty years.

Published by the Swiss Institute with Karma in 2016, this compact hardcover gathers the works on paper Weiss made between 1968 and 1979: cartoon imagery, ethereal abstractions and electric cityscapes, together with previously unpublished writings. Edited by Karen Marta and Simon Castets, the book pairs intimate recollections from Weiss's friends Urs Lüthi and Hans Ulrich Obrist with an essay by curator Douglas Fogle tracing the influences on the early work, from Robert Walser to Bugs Bunny. It follows the exhibitions at the Bündner Kunstmuseum in Chur (2014) and Swiss Institute, New York (2014–15), made possible only because Weiss, in the months before his death, began organizing the notebooks and early drawings he had set aside when the collaboration began.

Weiss (1946–2012) joined Peter Fischli in 1979 to form Fischli/Weiss, the duo behind Der Lauf der Dinge and one of contemporary art's most inventive bodies of work, honored with a Guggenheim retrospective in 2016. This volume restores the solo artist behind the partnership, and it sits alongside the many Fischli & Weiss titles held in this library.
tags: Art, Drawing, Works on Paper, Swiss Art, Fischli Weiss, Swiss Institute
notes: Solo David Weiss monograph, distinct from the library's Fischli & Weiss duo titles and from the 2014 Bündner Kunstmuseum catalogue David Weiss: Werke/Works 1968–1979 (ISBN 9783905240665). Out of stock indefinitely at D.A.P. Illustrations: 182 color, 70 b&w illustrations. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-23.

title: Jack Pierson
binding: Pocket-size edition cover carries only the artist's name and title, no other markings binding unverified
description:
A pocket-sized book on Jack Pierson published by Photology, the Milan photography gallery that has represented his photographs since 1999, on the occasion of his solo exhibition there in the spring of 2001. Barely bigger than a postcard, it carries nothing on its cover but the artist's name and the title, and nothing else anywhere: no ISBN or barcode, and none of the usual publishing apparatus. The gallery's own later listing describes it simply as its pocket size edition.

The artist's official bibliography credits the volume with a text by the poet Eileen Myles, Pierson's longtime friend and interpreter. The intimate scale suits his registers: longing, faded glamour, male beauty and out-of-focus American light. Photology returned to the artist around 2008 with a larger ISBN'd hardcover surveying some sixty works across media this small, early volume is its predecessor.

Pierson (b. 1960, Plymouth, Massachusetts) emerged from the Boston School alongside Nan Goldin, David Armstrong and Mark Morrisroe, and is best known for photographs steeped in longing and faded Americana and for the word sculptures, begun in 1991, that he assembles from salvaged signage letters. His Self-Portrait series appeared in the 2004 Whitney Biennial long represented by Cheim & Read, he now shows with Lisson Gallery.

title: Fotografías
description:
A darkened carnival cosmos, photographed at the edge of legibility.

Fotografías gathers 92 black-and-white photographs of the garish fantasy scenes Peter Fischli and David Weiss found painted on fairground attractions: shooting galleries, ghost trains, carousel panels and motorcycle fuel tanks, collected over years of travel through Switzerland and abroad. Shot on black-and-white slide film deliberately underexposed by two to three stops and printed at snapshot size, the pictures subdue their kitsch sources into murky, haunting nocturnes. Romantic sunsets, mystical mountains, wild boars, clowns and doe-eyed girls become small, dark, emotionally charged icons. The book, published by Walther König to accompany the 2005 exhibition at Galerie Eva Presenhuber, Zurich, carries no text beyond its title page, letting the sequence of images do all the work.

Fischli and Weiss collaborated from 1979 until Weiss's death in 2012, building a body of work, from the film The Way Things Go to the encyclopedic Visible World, that dignifies the overlooked and levels the distinction between high and low art, a project surveyed in the Guggenheim's 2016 retrospective How to Work Better. Fotografías is among their most distilled statements: vernacular painting remade as fine art through nothing more than exposure and scale.

title: The New York Times Paintings: November – December 2015
description:
A catalog for the exhibition that turned the daily front page of record into painting.

Published by Petzel to accompany The New York Times Paintings: November – December 2015 (November 10, 2016 – January 14, 2017), the book documents a body of work made from screenshots of the nytimes.com homepage captured over two months in late 2015. Guyton fed the files through an Epson 9900 large-format printer in UltraChrome HDR ink on linen, producing 84-by-69-inch canvases where headlines about terror, climate, and the coming election sit beside sidebar ads and navigation bars, complete with the glitches, streaks, and misregistrations the printer introduces. Edited by Jessica Li and designed by Joseph Logan, the 80-page volume pairs plates of the paintings with installation views of Petzel's uptown townhouse galleries the show opened, pointedly, two days after the 2016 presidential election.

Wade Guyton (b. 1972, Hammond, Indiana) has made paintings since the early 2000s by dragging folded linen through inkjet printers, letting the machine's errors stand as the work's mark-making. The Whitney Museum surveyed the work in Wade Guyton OS in 2012 long affiliated with Petzel and Galerie Gisela Capitain, he now shows with Matthew Marks Gallery and Galerie Chantal Crousel.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Digital Art, Exhibition Catalogs, New York, Media
notes: Cover is nearly blank white with a small block of cyan text listing artist, title, exhibition dates, and gallery address design by Joseph Logan. Library already holds 11 other Guyton titles (ids 464-474) this volume is not among them. Illustrations: Installation views and reproductions of the paintings. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. title: Life with P.
description:
Life with P.: Journals, 1966–1976 presents the previously unpublished journals of poet and painter Musa McKim Guston, an intimate decade-long record of daily life with her husband Philip Guston ("P." in her private shorthand), kept during the most consequential turn of his career.

Spanning 1966 to 1976, the entries move between the couple's home in Woodstock, visits to New York, artist residencies and travels to Mexico and Italy, tracing the years in which Guston abandoned abstraction for the cartoon-inflected figuration of his late work. Edited by Sara Harrison and Musa Mayer, the 432-page hardback interleaves McKim's journals and poems with 230 color illustrations of artworks and archival photographs, framed by an introduction and contextual notes by Mayer.

McKim (1908–1992) was an artist in her own right: a painting student at the Otis Art Institute when she met Guston, a collaborator on his WPA-era murals, and later a poet whose verses he embellished in their joint "Poem Pictures." Mayer, the couple's daughter and president of The Guston Foundation, extends the account begun in her 1988 memoir Night Studio. The book appeared alongside the Hauser & Wirth New York exhibition "Life With P. – Philip Guston: Paintings and Drawings 1964–1978."

Publication timeline: gallery book launch April 23, 2026, publication date May 19, 2026 per The Guston Foundation, US D.A.P. distribution June 16, 2026. Praised by Max Hollein, Director and CEO of The Metropolitan Museum of Art, as "a beautiful mosaic of a book." Illustrations: 230 color illustrations. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. title: Time Travel
description:
Time travel, in this catalog, is less a conceit than a method: hang a Canaletto near a Cindy Sherman and watch four centuries collapse into a single conversation.

Published on the occasion of the two-part exhibition at Petzel's Upper East Side townhouse (November 15, 2023 through February 10, 2024), the catalog records an unusual collaboration between the New York contemporary gallery and DYS 44 Lampronti Gallery, the London dealership in Italian Old Masters. The parlor floor held works from the sixteenth through nineteenth centuries, among them Artemisia Gentileschi's Bathsheba at her bath, Canaletto's The Prisons of St Mark, Domenico Remps's trompe-l'oeil Cabinet of Curiosities, and canvases by Guercino, Ribera, and Cagnacci, while the third floor gathered contemporary responses from John Currin, Cindy Sherman, Jeff Koons, Jutta Koether, Roe Ethridge, Emily Mae Smith, and Emma Webster.

The pairings argue that the Baroque's cinematic drama, its oscillation between sacred and profane, remains a living vocabulary. Koons's Gazing Ball and Sherman's history-portrait photography read here not as quotation but as continuation, mapping the masters' stylized theatricality onto the present moment.

title: How to See Like a Machine: Images After AI
description:
In How to See Like a Machine: Images After AI, the artist and geographer Trevor Paglen argues that photography’s basic terms have flipped: images are now made by machines, for machines, and the picture that once waited to be seen has started looking back.

Collecting essays written over roughly fifteen years, the book tracks the shift from human to machine vision: the training-image economy laid bare in Paglen’s Excavating AI research, and generative models now producing pictures indistinguishable from photographs. Chapters range from psyops and UFO photography to stage magic and public relations, arguing these seemingly alien systems are stranger, and more human, than they appear. Published by Verso in May 2026 as a 192-page hardback, it is Paglen’s sixth book.

Paglen (b. 1974, Camp Springs, Maryland) trained as a geographer at UC Berkeley and has spent two decades making the hidden infrastructures of surveillance and machine perception visible through photography, sculpture, and investigative research. A 2017 MacArthur Fellow, he showed for years with San Francisco’s Altman Siegel (closed 2025) and is now represented by Pace Gallery his work is held by SFMOMA, the Metropolitan Museum, and the Smithsonian American Art Museum, which surveyed his career in the 2018 retrospective Sites Unseen.

title: Adversarially Evolved Hallucinations
description:
Trevor Paglen’s Adversarially Evolved Hallucinations (2017–ongoing) treats machine hallucination not as a glitch but as the defining condition of AI-made images—and this slim critical reader, volume four in Sternberg Press’s Research/Practice series, unpacks what that means.

Edited by Anthony Downey, the book pairs a conversation between Paglen and Downey with Downey’s essay “The Return of the Uncanny: Artificial Intelligence and Estranged Futures.” Paglen describes training neural networks on invented corpora, then prompting a second network to hallucinate images from what it has learned to “see,” yielding uncanny prints like Vampire (Corpus: Monsters of Capitalism). Downey argues AI’s lack of embodied experience means it can only produce estranged, allegorical pictures of the world.

Paglen (b. 1974, Camp Springs, Maryland) is an American artist and geographer whose work exposes the infrastructures of state secrecy, surveillance, and machine vision. A 2017 MacArthur Fellow, he has shown at the Smithsonian American Art Museum and the Barbican, with work held by MoMA and the Whitney. The volume extends an inquiry into AI classification running from ImageNet Roulette (2019, with Kate Crawford) to his 2026 book How to See Like a Machine: Images After AI.

title: I Could Tell You But Then You Would Have to Be Destroyed By Me: Emblems from the Pentagon's Black World
edition_printrun: Updated paperback edition, with new information and additional patches
description:
Trevor Paglen's I Could Tell You But Then You Would Have to Be Destroyed by Me collects more than seventy insignia patches worn on classified U.S. military and intelligence programs, reading their cartoonish, occult imagery as an accidental portrait of the government's secret world.

Assembled through Freedom of Information Act requests and tips from current and former operators, the book reproduces each patch in full color with Paglen's decoding of its symbolism: a grey alien captioned "to serve man," six-pointed stars standing in for Area 51, red stars marking Nevada test ranges, and mottoes too obscene to print. This 2010 Melville House paperback updates Paglen's 2008 hardcover with new patches and research.

Paglen (b. 1974), an American artist and geographer trained at UC Berkeley and the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, makes the classified infrastructure of surveillance and military power visible through photography, sculpture, and investigation. This book followed Torture Taxi and preceded Blank Spots on the Map he later filmed for Citizenfour, won a MacArthur Fellowship in 2017, and had the survey Sights Unseen at the Smithsonian American Art Museum in 2018.

title: From the Archives of Peter Merlin, Aviation Archaeologist
description:
Trevor Paglen’s From the Archives of Peter Merlin, Aviation Archaeologist is a stark photographic inventory of fifty-nine objects (challenge coins, patches, models, and other classified-program ephemera) drawn from the private archive of Peter Merlin, the country’s foremost historian of secret aircraft.

Merlin, a former NASA archivist, has spent decades collecting flight wreckage, dossiers, and memorabilia from bases such as Area 51 and Edwards Air Force Base and their surrounding crash sites, often the only surviving trace of programs the government never officially acknowledged. Working from Merlin’s conviction that “something always remains,” Paglen photographed fifty-nine pieces, from the atomic age to today’s drone wreckage, in flat, deadpan close-up, paired with his own captions and an essay on secrecy and military symbology. Primary Information published the book: 150 pages, paperback, edited by Miriam Katzeff, designed by David Schoerner.

Trevor Paglen (b. 1974) is an American artist and geographer who took a PhD in geography at UC Berkeley in 2008. His photography, sculpture, and investigative research have examined surveillance and state secrecy since the early 2000s, from long-lens images of black-budget military sites to Mylar satellites launched into orbit. A MacArthur Fellow (2017) and winner of the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize (2016), he is represented by Pace Gallery, with work held by the Guggenheim, Tate, MoMA, and the Whitney.

title: Helter Skelter
contributors: Miuccia Prada (Introduction) Jöel Tettamanti (Photography) Aria Dean (Essay) Ashley James (Essay) Amy Taubin (Essay) Ashon Crawley (Essay) Jack Halberstam (Essay) Peter Watts (Essay) Randy Kennedy (Essay) Ernest Hardy (Essay) Martin Lund (Essay) Greil Marcus (Essay) Dorian Lynskey (Essay) Beth Coleman (Essay)
description:
The catalogue for Helter Skelter, Fondazione Prada's two-person exhibition setting the American artists Arthur Jafa (b. 1960) and Richard Prince (b. 1949) in dialogue at its Venice venue, Ca' Corner della Regina (9 May – 23 November 2026).

Edited by Nancy Spector with an introduction by Miuccia Prada, it gathers visual essays by both artists, a Jafa–Prince conversation, and Spector's curatorial essay The American Vernacular: Unpolished Truths, alongside commissioned texts by Aria Dean, Ashley James, and Amy Taubin and nine short essays on contemporary American culture by writers including Greil Marcus, Jack Halberstam, Dorian Lynskey, and Beth Coleman, plus plates and the exhibition checklist. The graphic concept is by Peter Saville with design by Graphic Thought Facility the Venice and Ca' Corner della Regina photographs are by Jöel Tettamanti. The title borrows the Beatles song long entangled with American myths of apocalyptic violence.

Jafa, a cinematographer (Daughters of the Dust) turned artist, won the Golden Lion at the 2019 Venice Biennale and is known for Love Is the Message, the Message Is Death (2016). Prince, a foundational appropriation artist from Untitled (Cowboy) to the Nurse paintings and New Portraits, is already held in depth in the library's collection. A black-and-white reader reprint, Helter Skelter (Dispensa) (Fondazione Prada, 2026), accompanies this catalogue.

title: Afro-Mingei
contributors: Mami Kataoka (Interview) Hirokazu Tokuyama (Essay) Coco Fusco (Essay) Chelsea Foxwell (Essay)
description:
The catalogue for Theaster Gates: Afro-Mingei, the American artist's first solo exhibition in Japan, held at the Mori Art Museum, Tokyo, in 2024.

Published by torch press and edited by the Mori Art Museum, the 272-page, Japanese/English bilingual volume documents Gates's coinage "Afro-Mingei," a fusion of the Japanese Mingei (folk-craft) movement with African American culture. Trained as a sculptor and urban planner, Gates first travelled to Japan in 2004 to study ceramics in Tokoname the book threads installation views with interlocking timelines (Tokoname pottery, the Mingei movement, the fictional potter Shoji Yamaguchi, Black American history, and Gates's own biography) alongside his architectural projects, three essays, and an interview with the artist by museum director Mami Kataoka. Texts by Hirokazu Tokuyama, Coco Fusco, and Chelsea Foxwell.

Theaster Gates (b. 1973, Chicago) is a social-practice artist, ceramist, and urban planner whose work spans object-making, performance, and the revival of Chicago's South Side through his Rebuild Foundation and the Stony Island Arts Bank. He has exhibited widely at major international institutions and is represented by Gagosian and White Cube.

title: The Complete Works of Toshiko Okanoue
publisher: Kawade Shobo Shinsha (河出書房新社)
description:
Okanoue Toshiko Zensakuhin (岡上淑子全作品) is the definitive catalogue raisonne of Toshiko Okanoue, the elusive Japanese photomontage artist whose brief, singular body of work reshaped postwar Japanese surrealism.

Published by Kawade Shobo Shinsha in January 2018 as the official catalogue for Okanoue's first major retrospective, "A Long Journey," at the Museum of Art, Kochi, this B5 hardcover assembles all 150 works known to survive: 128 collages and 22 photographs, cut from discarded Allied-occupation-era LIFE and Vogue magazines into uncanny, theatrical tableaux. It includes a complete work list, an inventory of lost pieces, the artist's own writings, a chronology, exhibition history, and an essay by art historian Hiroko Ikegami.

Okanoue (b. 1928, Kochi) studied design at Bunka Gakuin and, over roughly seven years in the 1950s, made collages largely in isolation. Discovered by surrealist critic Shuzo Takiguchi, she exhibited at Takemiya Gallery alongside the VOU poetry circle before marriage led her to set the work aside for four decades. Rediscovered in the late 1990s by historian Ryuichi Kaneko, she now has work held by MoMA, the National Museum of Modern Art Tokyo, and M+ Hong Kong.

title: Los dos amigos
publisher: A&R Press / Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Oaxaca (distributed by Turner Publicaciones)
description:
Los dos amigos documents an eighteen-year collaboration between the Mexican artists Abraham Cruzvillegas and Dr. Lakra, assembled less as a conventional exhibition catalog than as a shared scrapbook of two overlapping creative lives.

Published in 2006 by A&R Press with the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Oaxaca, the hardcover volume accompanied the artists' first public two-person exhibition, held at MACO in May 2005. Its pages reproduce raw material pulled directly from both artists' source files: magazine clippings, snapshots, posters, fanzines, flyers, found street objects, packaging, correspondence, and personal diaries, tracing an exchange of images built up over two decades rather than presenting finished works in isolation.

Cruzvillegas (b. 1968, Mexico City) works across sculpture and installation under the banner of autoconstrucción, an improvisational building logic drawn from his childhood neighborhood his work has appeared at Tate Modern, dOCUMENTA (13), and the Venice Biennale. Dr. Lakra (Jerónimo López Ramírez, b. 1972) trained alongside him in Gabriel Orozco's Taller de los Viernes workshop and built a tattoo-derived collage and painting practice mining ethnographic photography and pulp ephemera. The two have kept collaborating as Los dos amigos since, including a mezcal-bottle series shown at kurimanzutto.

title: Black Mirrors
publisher: Galerie du Jour – agnès b./Shelter Press
contributors: agnès b. (Text (Foreword, handwritten letter)) Sinziana Ravini (Text) Peter Sutherland (Text)
description:
Black Mirrors is the first monograph devoted to Julien Langendorff (b. 1982), gathering the Paris-based artist's early collage, drawing, and painting practice into a single fabric-bound artist's book.

Co-published in 2012 by Galerie du Jour – agnès b. (Paris) and Shelter Press (Brussels), the book accompanied Langendorff's solo exhibition Goddess Fuzz Fantasy at agnès b. gallery, New York. Across 64 unpaginated, bilingual French/English pages it gathers pen-and-ink drawings, paper cut-outs of 1970s erotic imagery, and abstract, saturated paintings floating dark, dreamlike forms against black grounds — drawing on gothic and hippie counterculture, Black Sabbath, and spiritism. Bound in thick cardboard wrapped in gray fabric, it includes texts by Langendorff, a handwritten letter from agnès b., Sinziana Ravini, and Peter Sutherland.

Langendorff studied at the École Duperré in Paris and has exhibited in New York, Tokyo, and Berlin since 2005 he met agnès b. in 2009, leading to his representation by Galerie du Jour. He also performs in the doom-psychedelic band Pillars of Fire and records solo as Skate Witches. Black Mirrors captures an early, painting-forward moment that later gave way to the denser, collage-driven work of his subsequent books and zines.

title: Cutting Edges: Contemporary Collage
editor: Robert Klanten, Hendrik Hellige, James Gallagher
description:
Cutting Edges surveys the early-2010s resurgence of collage as a contemporary art and design practice, gathering the work of dozens of international artists and illustrators who cut, layer, and reassemble found photographs, prints, and ephemera into new compositions.

Published by Gestalten in Berlin in 2011 and edited by Robert Klanten, Hendrik Hellige, and James Gallagher, the 215-page hardcover volume opens with an essay tracing collage's roots in Dada, Surrealism, and Constructivism, the movements that established the technique through artists such as Hannah Höch, John Heartfield, and El Lissitzky, before turning to full-color spreads of contemporary work. Most pieces are made by hand from cut paper and found material rather than digital montage, with several contributors treating the omission of source imagery as deliberately as its addition.

Klanten, Gestalten's founder, has shaped numerous surveys of contemporary visual culture for the publisher, with Hellige co-editing alongside him. James Gallagher, who also wrote the preface, is a New York collage artist trained at the School of Visual Arts he has since curated international collage exhibitions and, in 2013, founded the art magazine Secret Behavior. Cutting Edges arrived early in a broader wave of surveys cataloguing collage's parallel analog and digital revival.

title: The Age of Collage: Contemporary Collage in Modern Art
description:
The Age of Collage: Contemporary Collage in Modern Art gathers the cut-and-paste practices of dozens of contemporary artists into the first volume of Gestalten's ongoing collage anthology, documenting the medium's resurgence in the early 2010s.

Structured as a survey rather than a monograph, the book opens with a foreword by curator and art historian Silke Krohn tracing collage's lineage from Cubism, Merz, Futurism, Dada, and Surrealism through Pop Art and the combine paintings that followed, before profiling the artists who inherited that vocabulary. The artists collected here mine found photographs, scientific imagery, pop-cultural ephemera, and vintage erotica, favoring an interdisciplinary, cross-media approach that treats destruction and construction as a single gesture.

The volume was edited by Bremen-based artist Dennis Busch (b. 1971) with Gestalten founder Robert Klanten and designer Hendrik Hellige. Busch, who has cut and reassembled vintage imagery since the late 1980s as a self-described image butcher, became the throughline of the series he helped launch: The Age of Collage Vol. 2 followed in 2016, with Vol. 3 continuing the project and expanding its roster of contemporary collage artists.

title: The Age of Collage 2: Contemporary Collage in Modern Art
description:
The second installment in Gestalten's survey of contemporary collage, this anthology gathers work by more than seventy international artists to track how a century-old cut-and-paste technique has expanded into gallery-scale assemblage and digitally assembled composition alike.

Published in 2016, the volume builds on its 2013 predecessor, moving from handmade, analog cut-and-paste toward work produced digitally, and from small-format collage toward large-scale installation and public commission. Artists represented range from established figures such as John Baldessari and Richard Prince to younger practitioners including Lola Dupre, chosen to show collage's reach across fine art, illustration, and design.

The book was edited by Dennis Busch (b. 1971), a Hamburg-based collage artist who originated the Age of Collage project with Gestalten in 2013, together with Gestalten founder Robert Klanten. Busch's own hand-cut, analog practice, built from vintage found imagery, informed the volume's curatorial eye. It is the middle title in a three-part series, preceded by the original Age of Collage (2013, edited by Busch) and followed by The Age of Collage 3 (2020, edited by Klanten and Lincoln Dexter).

title: The Age of Collage 3: Contemporary Collage in Modern Art
description:
The third and concluding volume in Gestalten's Age of Collage series surveys collage as it stood in 2020, tracking a medium defined by juxtaposition, appropriation, and the recombination of found imagery into new, often uncanny, wholes.

Edited by Dennis Busch and Francesca Gavin, the book gathers work by more than sixty international artists, presented as visual portfolios interspersed with short statements on process, materials, and intent. Contributors range from artists working strictly by hand, cutting and pasting found photographs, magazines, and ephemera, to others who build their compositions digitally, and the book treats both as continuous with a single lineage. Published in a full-color, stitch-bound hardcover with a cloth cover, it runs to 320 pages.

Busch, a German collage artist known for hand-cut work built from vintage photography, originated the series with the first volume in 2013 and has edited all three installments Gavin, a London-based curator and critic and art editor at Twin magazine, joins as co-editor for this closing volume. Together the three books trace collage's shift from a niche craft revival into a widely practiced contemporary medium.
tags: Collage, Art, Design, Contemporary Art, Anthology, Found Imagery

title: One and One Is Four: The Bauhaus Photocollages of Josef Albers
description:
Published by The Museum of Modern Art in 2016, this volume is the first publication to reproduce, in full, the photocollages Josef Albers (1888-1976) made from photographs he shot at the Bauhaus between 1928 and 1932, a body of work unknown until after the artist's death.

Edited by MoMA curator Sarah Hermanson Meister with essays by Elizabeth Otto and Lee Ann Daffner, the book presents roughly seventy collages built from Albers's own snapshots of stadium crowds and scaffolding, regridded into serial arrangements that anticipate the adjacency, repetition, and handcraft-versus-mechanical concerns of his later painting. It accompanied a 2016-17 MoMA installation drawn largely from a 2015 acquisition of ten photocollages, making the Museum's holdings the most extensive outside the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation. 128 pages, 100 illustrations, hardcover.

Albers is best known as a teacher and theorist, at the Bauhaus and later Black Mountain College and Yale, where his treatise Interaction of Color and ongoing Homage to the Square series made him central to postwar geometric abstraction. These photocollages complicate that legacy, showing a more improvisatory, vernacular eye behind the systematic colorist and situating Albers within the Bauhaus's wider culture of experimental photography.

title: John Stezaker: Crossing Over
description:
John Stezaker: Crossing Over gathers a decade of the British collagist's (b. 1949) work with vintage postcards &mdash sixty-five image fragments, incidental details lifted from the edges of found photographs, reprinted at full scale for the first time.

Made between 2005 and 2013 and building on Stezaker's long-running 3rd Person Archive, the fragments trace postcard production from the Victorian era into the postwar period, moving from black-and-white to colour. Stezaker isolates figures at a picture's margin &mdash a passerby, a conversation on a bench &mdash reading these incidental presences as records of time and memory rather than documentary content. Ridinghouse published the 114-page clothbound volume in 2014.

Stezaker studied at the Slade School of Fine Art in the 1960s and taught for decades at Central Saint Martins, Goldsmiths College, and the Royal College of Art. He shaped a generation of collage and appropriation artists after him &mdash a pedagogical presence as consequential, in its way, as his own practice of cutting and crossing found pictures. He received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective, and is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York. The library holds four other Stezaker titles: Nude and Landscape, Silkscreens, One on One, and the Rubell Family Collection volume.

title: John Stezaker: Double Shadow
publisher: Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König / Ridinghouse
description:
John Stezaker: Double Shadow presents the British collagist's (b. 1949) recent series of paired, doubled silhouettes &mdash an uncanny turn in a five-decade practice built from found photographs.

Cutting figures from 1950s Hollywood publicity portraits and laying the remaining silhouettes as dark shapes against black grounds, Stezaker splits and superimposes two profiles into single hybrid forms &mdash doppelgängers, hermaphrodites, faces that blur masculine and feminine. The seventy-one collages mark what Stezaker has called a rediscovery of 'the pleasures of drawing,' worked entirely in cut paper. Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König published the 128-page softcover volume with Ridinghouse, following Stezaker's exhibition at The Approach, London (24 February &ndash 26 March 2022), with an essay by Margaret Iversen, 'John Stezaker: Doubles and Shadows.'

The doubling technique extends a method Stezaker has worked for decades: the single, precise cut that joins two found images into one, and the related 3rd Person Archive (1976&ndashpresent), his ongoing collection of incidental figures clipped from illustrated books. Stezaker came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York &mdash the fifth Stezaker title in the library's collection.

title: John Stezaker: Film Still
description:
John Stezaker: Film Still is the first comprehensive survey of the body of work the British collagist (b. 1949) is best known for &mdash collages built from vintage publicity stills clipped from classic-era Hollywood and B-pictures.

Stezaker began cutting into film stills in 1979, a shift away from the text-based conceptualism of his earlier work, and the series has run continuously since. The 144-page volume traces its evolution: an early reliance on Hitchcock's American-period stills gives way to the anonymous mass of low-budget 1940s and early 1950s studio product, as Stezaker's excisions and superimpositions turn found publicity photography into images of estrangement and doubling. Ridinghouse published the softcover survey in 2011 with a critical essay by David Campany and a recorded conversation between Campany and the artist.

The library's other Stezaker catalog, Nude and Landscape, reads the artist against art-historical tradition specifically to move away from 'the cinematic imagery his found-image work is best known for' &mdash this volume returns directly to that imagery, the source material Stezaker has mined longest. He came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York.

title: John Stezaker: Lost World
contributors: Geoffrey Batchen (Essay) David Campany (Essay) Robert Leonard (Essay)
description:
John Stezaker: Lost World catalogs a touring survey of the British collagist's (b. 1949) work, built on his account of collage as 'a yearning for a lost world' &mdash images from an archive of out-of-date film stills, actor headshots, and postcards that have lost their immediate relationship to the world they depicted.

Alongside the collages, the book documents Stezaker's found-object sculptures &mdash antique mannequin hands arranged as a repertoire of gestures &mdash and Crowd, a film work presenting hundreds of film-still crowd scenes for a single frame each. Ridinghouse published the 88-page softcover catalog in 2017 with essays by Geoffrey Batchen, David Campany, and curator Robert Leonard, for the exhibition Leonard organized at City Gallery Wellington (26 August &ndash 19 November 2017), which toured to the Govett-Brewster Art Gallery, New Plymouth Christchurch Art Gallery and the Centre for Contemporary Photography, Melbourne, through late 2018.

The tour across four New Zealand and Australian venues reflects how far Stezaker's reputation now extends beyond Britain: his work sits in the collections of MoMA, Tate, and the Art Gallery of New South Wales. He came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York &mdash the library's fifth Stezaker title.

title: John Stezaker
publisher: Ridinghouse, in association with Whitechapel Gallery, Mudam Luxembourg, and Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum
contributors: Dawn Ades (Essay) Michael Bracewell (Essay) Daniel F. Herrmann (Interview) Christophe Gallois (Interview)
description:
John Stezaker is the largest monographic survey yet published on the British collagist (b. 1949), the catalog for his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective &mdash the exhibition that established Stezaker, after four decades of work, as a defining figure in photographic appropriation.

The 220-page volume gathers found images, collages, and image fragments made from the 1970s onward, including a selection from The 3rd Person Archive, Stezaker's ongoing collection of incidental figures clipped from illustrated books, in over 120 illustrations. Essays by Dawn Ades and Michael Bracewell place the work in art-historical context, alongside a conversation between Stezaker and curators Daniel F. Herrmann and Christophe Gallois. Ridinghouse published the softcover volume with Whitechapel Gallery, Mudam Luxembourg, and the Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum, which hosted the exhibition on its tour.

The Whitechapel retrospective this catalog accompanies proved a turning point in Stezaker's reception: it led directly to his winning the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, a notable choice for an artist who has never taken a photograph. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York. This is the definitive survey among the library's Stezaker holdings, alongside Nude and Landscape, Silkscreens, One on One, the Rubell Family Collection volume, and the batch added with it: Crossing Over, Double Shadow, Film Still, and Lost World.

title: When I Was a Boy
description:
When I Was a Boy (2018) is Katrien De Blauwer's contribution to Libraryman's Seasons Series, a compact monograph built from found photographs the Belgian artist (b. 1969) cuts, layers, and reassembles into image without ever touching a camera.

The book gathers 27 color plates drawn from De Blauwer's practice of collecting vintage magazine and studio photography, then cutting each image down to a single ambiguous gesture &mdash a shoulder, a collar, a half-obscured face &mdash so that presence and erasure sit on the same page. Bound as a color offset hardcover with linen thread binding, a brown headband, and white foil-stamped cover typography, the 32-page volume was released in an edition of 500, with a signed 25-copy special edition in a screenprinted slipcase. It was shortlisted for the Author Book Award at Les Rencontres d'Arles in 2018.

De Blauwer, who studied painting in Ghent before abandoning fashion studies at Antwerp's Royal Academy, calls herself a "photographer without a camera": her collages work by subtraction and accumulation, the cut standing in for the frame. She is represented by Galerie Les Filles du Calvaire in Paris and Gallery Fifty One in Antwerp, and shows regularly at Paris Photo and Art Brussels When I Was a Boy inaugurated a run of Libraryman monographs that continued with Why I Hate Cars (2019) and You Could at Least Pretend to Like Yellow (2020).
tags: Collage, Photography, Artist Books, Belgian Art, Contemporary Art
notes: Second volume (Summer) in Libraryman's Seasons Series. Shortlisted for the Author Book Award, Les Rencontres d'Arles 2018.

title: Why I Hate Cars
description:
Why I Hate Cars (2019) follows Katrien De Blauwer's When I Was a Boy with a darker, more painterly turn: the Belgian artist begins layering paint and crayon directly over her cut photographic fragments, adding a second register of mark-making to a practice she still calls "photography without a camera."

The 72-page hardcover gathers 64 color plates built from collected magazine and newspaper imagery &mdash car interiors, rear windows, half-visible passengers &mdash overpainted in flat bands of red and black that block as much as they reveal. An excerpt from the artist's notebooks runs through the volume, and the book accompanied De Blauwer's 2019 Paris exhibition "Love me Tender" at Galerie Les Filles du Calvaire. Libraryman printed it in an edition of 1,000, offset and linen thread bound with a red headband and tipped-in cover images, alongside a 50-copy special edition with a hand-drawn signed print.

De Blauwer (b. 1969, Ronse) works by cutting rather than combining, treating the edge of the photograph as the meaningful gesture rather than the picture inside it. Why I Hate Cars sits at the midpoint of her ongoing Libraryman series, between the quieter When I Was a Boy and the more chromatic You Could at Least Pretend to Like Yellow, from a period in which her collages moved from art-fair presentations at Paris Photo and Art Brussels into gallery solo shows at Les Filles du Calvaire and Gallery Fifty One.
tags: Collage, Photography, Artist Books, Belgian Art, Contemporary Art
notes: Accompanied De Blauwer's 2019 Paris exhibition "Love me Tender" at Galerie Les Filles du Calvaire exact exhibition dates not confirmed from sources checked.

title: You Could at Least Pretend to Like Yellow
description:
You Could at Least Pretend to Like Yellow (2020) is the eighth book by Belgian collage artist Katrien De Blauwer, and the first in her Libraryman series to organize an entire monograph around a single color rather than a single subject.

De Blauwer built the book around a chance discovery: a companion volume to Vilgot Sjöman's 1967 film I Am Curious (Yellow), found in an antique shop before she had seen the film itself &mdash "pretending to like yellow" while she waited. The 40-page hardcover reproduces 40 works in color, each printed at its actual individual size and paired, unusually, with the verso of the cut photograph as well as its front, giving equal weight to the residue of the source image and the collage made from it. Libraryman produced it as a linen-thread-bound, color offset hardcover with a yellow headband and printed endpapers, in an edition of 450 with 250 signed copies.

The book extends what Libraryman calls De Blauwer's practice of "cut" rather than collage &mdash recovering discarded photographs and giving them a second, private narrative rather than fusing them into new composite scenes. Since her first collage books in the early 1990s, De Blauwer has shown at Paris Photo and Art Brussels and is represented by Galerie Les Filles du Calvaire, Gallery Fifty One, and Rosegallery Yellow followed Why I Hate Cars and When I Was a Boy as the third of her Libraryman monographs built around memory by accumulation rather than subtraction.

title: Cosmic Surgery
description:
Cosmic Surgery (2016) imagines cosmetic surgery rerouted through geometry: British-based photographer Alma Haser (b. 1989) folds her own portrait sitters into faceted origami masks built from photographs of their own features, so that eyes, lips, and cheekbones multiply across the folded planes of a paper polyhedron fixed to the face.

The self-published hardcover collects portraits from a project Haser began in 2013, photographing each sitter twice &mdash once straight, once concealed beneath a folded paper construction printed with details from the same shoot &mdash so that cubist multiplication stands in for the "cosmetic" transformation the title puns on (Haser, who is dyslexic, coined it by misspeaking "cosmetic surgery"). This second edition, funded through a 2016 Kickstarter and designed by Emily Macaulay of Stanley/Barker, runs 60 pages plus inserted booklets of speculative pseudo-medical text by science writer Piers Bizony describing the procedure's features and benefits the hardcover is foil-embossed on cover, spine, and back, in a signed edition of 600.

Haser studied photography at Nottingham Trent University, where she also took up origami, graduating in 2010 she works across analogue paper-folding, collage, and rephotography to push flat portraiture toward sculpture. Cosmic Surgery won the Magenta Foundation's Bright Spark Award and remains her best-known monograph, anchoring a body of work that continued with the twin-portrait jigsaws of Within 15 Minutes and the paper-and-plant hybrids of her ongoing Plant series.

title: Linder
description:
Published by Ridinghouse in 2015, Linder is the most comprehensive printed survey to date of work by the British artist Linder (b. Linder Sterling, 1954, Liverpool), gathering four decades of photomontage that splice advertising, pornography, and domestic imagery into a sustained feminist critique of gender and consumer culture.

The volume gathers over 240 works, interweaving Linder's recurring series rather than a single chronology. Die-cut pages and paper-stock shifts, developed with the artist's input, echo the images' own collage logic. 255 illustrations accompany a conversation between Linder and the art historian Dawn Adès, situating her work within photomontage's wider history, from Dada through punk-era graphic design.

Linder emerged from Manchester's punk scene, designing the Buzzcocks' "Orgasm Addict" sleeve (1977) and, with Morrissey, the fanzine The Secret Public. Her signature technique — fusing fashion imagery, pornography, and domestic appliances — critiques manufactured femininity, later extended into performance as frontwoman of Ludus. Surveys at Tate St Ives, the Hepworth Wakefield, MoMA PS1, and the Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris affirm her place as a central figure in feminist photomontage.

title: Linderism
publisher: Kettle's Yard, University of Cambridge / Koenig Books
contributors: James Boaden (Essay) Alyce Mahon (Essay) Sarah Victoria Turner (Essay) Andrew Nairne (Preface)
description:
Linderism is the catalogue for the first UK museum survey of the British artist Linder (b. 1954), published by Kettle's Yard, University of Cambridge, and Koenig Books to accompany her 2020 Cambridge retrospective.

The volume reproduces work spanning Linder's career, from the punk-era photomontages she began exhibiting in Manchester fanzines through her later photographic and performance work, alongside working drawings and research images. Four essays, by James Boaden, Alyce Mahon, Amy Tobin and Sarah Victoria Turner, address her methods of image-making and her turn toward spirituality and the occult, edited by Amy Tobin with Alina Khakoo. Designed by Julie Peeters, the paperback runs 128 pages with 50 color and 50 black-and-white reproductions.

Curated by Amy Tobin, the exhibition was the first UK survey to trace the full breadth of Linder's practice, positioning her within a longer history of British feminist art rather than only the post-punk milieu that first brought her attention. It drew on Linder's decades-long collaboration with Morrissey, her design commissions for fashion houses including Richard Nicoll, and new site-specific performances staged across Kettle's Yard, reassessing her legacy within British feminist art history.

title: Linder: Femme/Objet
contributors: Fabrice Hergott (Essay) Emmanuelle de l'Ecotais (Curator / Essay) Morrissey (Interview)
description:
Linder: Femme/Objet is the catalogue for the first full retrospective of the British artist Linder (Linder Sterling, b. 1954), staged by the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris / ARC in 2013 and tracing four decades of photomontage.

Structured like a magazine, the 112-page volume accompanies an exhibition of nearly 200 works (photographs, photomontages, light boxes, costumes, and performance documentation) curated by Emmanuelle de l'Ecotais and shown at the ARC from 1 February to 21 April 2013. Co-published by Paris Musées and Walther König, it reproduces roughly eighty works alongside essays by museum director Fabrice Hergott and de l'Ecotais, plus an interview between Linder and Morrissey.

Linder's photomontage splices pornography, fashion advertising, and appliance catalogues into one image. It extends a lineage of political collage running through John Heartfield and, most directly, Hannah Höch's Weimar-era critiques of the “New Woman.” The title Femme/Objet names that critique: cut faces and catalogue bodies stage the female figure as commodity, carrying Dada and Surrealist concerns into a punk and post-punk register. The retrospective marked a major European institutional endorsement of that work Linder continues to exhibit internationally, represented by Modern Art, London.

title: John Heartfield: Fotografie plus Dynamit
description:
John Heartfield: Fotografie plus Dynamit is the catalog for a major Akademie der Künste retrospective on John Heartfield (1891-1968), the Berlin Dada artist who turned photomontage into a weapon against fascism and war.

Co-published by the Akademie der Künste and Hirmer Verlag and edited by Angela Lammert, Anna Schultz, and Rosa von der Schulenburg, the 311-page volume draws on the Academy's own Heartfield Archive to survey his career across 250 color reproductions, from his Berlin Dada beginnings through his AIZ covers attacking Hitler and the Nazi regime to his postwar design work in East Germany. The exhibition opened at the Akademie der Künste in March 2020 before traveling to Museum de Fundatie in Zwolle and the Royal Academy of Arts in London.

Heartfield co-founded Berlin Dada with George Grosz and his brother, the writer Wieland Herzfelde, pairing found photographs with blunt captions to devastating satirical effect. His AIZ covers of the 1930s remain touchstones of anti-fascist visual culture and a foundational reference for later photomontage and collage artists working in political protest.

title: Negative Space
description:
Negative Space is a hand-bound artist's book by the San Francisco collage artist Matt Borruso, assembling found imagery into a strange, self-contained world of swamp creatures, mushroom-crowned cavemen, and exoskeletal beings.

Working from stacks of found photographs, magazines, and printed ephemera, Borruso collages source images into scenes of ritual and mutation, building a spectral, paranormal realm of evolutionary defects and hybrid bodies. Published under the artist's own imprint, Visible Publications, San Francisco, in a hand-bound edition of 50 hardcover copies with a one-color hand-screened cover and hand-sewn binding a softcover second edition of 100 followed in 2017. The book runs 44 pages in full color, at 10.25 x 7.5 inches (26 x 19 cm).

Borruso received his MFA from Yale University (2004) and BFA from the San Francisco Art Institute (2002), and has shown solo at Steven Wolf Fine Arts, 2nd Floor Projects, and Et al. in San Francisco, and Black Ball Projects in Brooklyn. Under Visible Publications, he has made collage-based artist's books since 2010 — including IMAGE File and Cave Life — held in the library collections of MoMA, the Whitney Museum, SFMOMA, and the International Center of Photography.
tags: Collage, Art, San Francisco, Appropriation, Found Imagery, Self-Published, Hand-Bound
notes: Both the artist's official site (mattborruso.org) and the publisher imprint site (visiblepublications.com) return HTTP 200 over plain http:// but fail entirely over https:// (TLS certificate mismatch — the served cert covers an unrelated domain, monongahelaareachamber.org looks like a shared-hosting/SNI misconfiguration, not evidence of a compromised site — content matches the artist's verified CV and his gallery's bio verbatim). Used http:// URLs for authors[0].url and publisher.url. Negative Space exists in two editions: a hardcover first edition (2010, hand-screened cover, hand-sewn binding, edition of 50) and a softcover second edition (2017, same page count/trim size, edition of 100). This record catalogs the first (2010) hardcover edition, matching the sourced front-cover image (a 2010-dated upload on mattborruso.org showing a cloth hardcover binding). No ISBN exists for either edition — confirmed absent via Printed Matter's catalog record and Google Books. The library holds two copies.

title: DATA
description:
DATA is a hand-screened artist's book by the San Francisco collage artist Matt Borruso, pairing flat bands of color with high-contrast, halftone-screened photographs to build an ambiguous, quasi-mechanical body language out of appropriated imagery.

Self-published in 2019 under Borruso's own imprint, Visible Publications, the book runs 56 pages in black and white, bound in a two-color, hand-screened softcover printed in an edition of 60. Each copy was pulled in one of two colorways, orange or pink, over a shared cover image of a gloved hand gripping a length of pipe. Borruso builds each spread from cropped, rescreened photographs and ephemera, coarsening found pictures into heavy halftone dots until figures dissolve into pattern and texture. Hand-sewn binding and hand-screening tie the book to the small-run, DIY tradition of West Coast zine and print culture.

Borruso received his MFA from Yale (2004) and BFA from the San Francisco Art Institute (2002), and has shown solo at Steven Wolf Fine Arts, Et al., and Black Ball Projects. Since founding Visible Publications in 2010, he has released a steady run of collage-based artist's books, among them Negative Space and Cave Life, held in the library collections of MoMA, the Whitney Museum, SFMOMA, and the ICP DATA sits within that same body of self-published work.
tags: Collage, Art, San Francisco, Appropriation, Found Imagery, Self-Published, Hand-Bound, Screen Print
notes: IMPORTANT CORRECTION: this research pass was originally requested as 'Christian Holstad — Data.' No book titled 'Data'/'DATA' could be verified anywhere in Christian Holstad's documented bibliography (checked his own site, his primary gallery Andrew Kreps's publications page, and AbeBooks' full title listing for him — none match). Instead, 'DATA' is a real, well-documented 2019 artist's book self-published by Matt Borruso (the same artist behind two other titles in this research batch, 'Negative Space' and the mis-titled 'Visible') under his own imprint, Visible Publications — confirmed via his official site's own chronological works archive (mattborruso.org) and a dedicated book page (mattborruso.org/data/) giving exact specs (56pp, softcover, B&W interior, two hand-screened cover colorways, hand-sewn, 11 x 8.25in, edition of 60). This record catalogs that confirmed Borruso book, NOT a Christian Holstad title.
