title: Frank Peter John Dick
description:
Frank Peter John Dick (2011) is the debut publication of American artist K8 Hardy, collecting photo collages she assembled privately, over several years, from magazines, advertisements, and found photographs as working research for her performance and photographic practice.

The book reproduces the collages largely as made: cut-and-glued fragments of fashion editorials, newsprint headlines, darkroom test strips, and junk-store snapshots, layered into studies of representation, style, and queer identity. Its cover assembles broken male first names — Frank, Peter, John, Richard, Steve, Gary, Robert — literalizing the title as found-text collage. Never made for exhibition, the material became a book only after studio visitors urged Hardy to publish it Capricious released it as 52 full-color, perfect-bound pages, with an essay by Eileen Myles and endnotes by the artist identifying her sources.

Hardy (b. 1977, Fort Worth, Texas) co-founded the queer feminist collective and journal LTTR in 2002 and holds an MFA from Bard College (2008). This collage practice underlies the photography, sculpture, and performance for which she is better known, including the Position Series photographs and her 2012 Whitney Biennial runway performance her work is held in the Whitney, Guggenheim, and MoMA collections, and she is represented by Reena Spaulings Fine Art.
tags: Collage, Photography, Fashion, Queer Culture, Feminist Art, Appropriation, Artist Books
notes: PUBLISHER CORRECTION: the task brief supplied 'Galerie Aurel Scheibler' as the publisher this was verified and found to be incorrect. Galerie Aurel Scheibler's own 'artists represented' page does not list K8 Hardy, and no source (Wikipedia, OpenLibrary, Archive.org, Printed Matter, Art Metropole, Quimby's, Antenne Books, Good Press, Blackwell's, Waterstones, Amazon) connects the gallery to this title. All independent sources agree the actual publisher is Capricious (New York small press/arts foundation, now operating as Capricious Foundation), 2011. Title spelling/word order confirmed as 'Frank Peter John Dick' (not 'Frank Peter Dick John', which appears as an apparent typo in one caption on capriciousfoundation.org's own press page, contradicted by the BOMB Magazine article it links to and by every retailer/library source). Page count listed as 52 by most retailers and 51 by Art Metropole used 52 as the majority figure. K8 Hardy has no dedicated portfolio site beyond a small Hostinger-built shop site (k8hardy.com) selling a 'studio dress' and linking to her film, LTTR, and museum pages — used as authors[0].url since it is genuinely hers (verified via linked works/collective/YouTube channel), but it is thin as a bio resource. No dimensions in cm given as height x width by any source height_cm/width_cm inferred from cover image aspect ratio (448x600 px, ratio 0.747) matched against the stated 23 x 30 cm sheet size (ratio 0.767), giving width_cm=23, height_cm=30 (portrait).

title: Woman with the Good Meat Removed
edition_printrun: First edition, signed and numbered, edition of 600
description:
Woman with the Good Meat Removed collects the erotic collage practice of Detroit-based artist Zoë Ligon, whose cut-paper reconstructions of vintage pornographic photography turn appropriated bodies into abstracted, self-possessed figures.

Published by Aint-Bad Editions (Savannah, GA) in 2016 with an introduction by Katy Ruth Ashcraft, the 96-page hardcover gathers collages Ligon built from vintage pin-up and pornographic magazines. She cuts each model's likeness into interlocking shapes of color and pattern, discards the surrounding studio context, and reassembles the fragments — often against invented natural backdrops — into compositions where her own framing replaces the original photographer's. The edition of 600 is signed, numbered, offset-printed in color, with sewn cloth binding.

Ligon (b. Detroit) began collaging as a teenager, later turning from her father's National Geographic archive to pin-up and adult magazines as source material. Her collage work has shown at Superchief Gallery, Brooklyn (2016), and been covered in Vice and Refinery29. She is also known publicly as a sex educator and founder of the online retailer Spectrum Boutique, a separate strand of her public profile from the studio practice gathered here.
tags: Collage, Art, Contemporary Art, Found Imagery, Appropriation Art, Erotic Art
notes: No ISBN gap here, but this is a small self-distributed art-press book with several sourcing caveats: (1) authors[0].url left null — no dedicated official artist website was found. Older interviews (e.g. nakid.io, Dec 2023) link to zoolioncomplete.com as her site, but that domain now resolves to a parked/squatted page (fingerprinting redirect script, no content) — it is NOT used anywhere in this record. Her only current verified web presences are the Big Cartel shop, Instagram (@thongria), and the separate Spectrum Boutique commerce site. (2) Binding conflict: Printed Matter's catalog (detailed bibliographic listing) gives Cover=Hardback-Cloth, Binding=Sewn Bound, Process=Offset Printed/Color, confirmed by two independent web searches her own Big Cartel shop listing text said 'Perfect Bound', which is inconsistent with a cloth hardcover. Printed Matter's cataloging was treated as authoritative for physical construction. (3) Publisher URL: Aint-Bad's specific product page for this title (https://aint-bad.com/product/books/zoe-ligon/, found via a working link on nakid.io) now 404s live a June 2023 Wayback Machine snapshot confirms the URL existed and belonged to Aint-Bad, but the archived page is JS-rendered and did not yield extractable text — the book appears to be delisted/out of print from the publisher's own site. publisher.url is set to the live Aint-Bad root domain instead. title: Stereosophic Conjunctions
editor: Frank van der Stok and Paul Bogaers
description:
Stereosophic Conjunctions (2016) gathers twenty-seven photographic pairings by Dutch artist Paul Bogaers, in which found snapshots, postcards, and magazine clippings collide with his own photographs into surreal, associative collisions.

Printed originally as black-and-white gelatin silver prints and reproduced here in duotone, the pairings set unrelated images — an amateur snapshot, a postcard, a torn magazine page — against each other in what Bogaers calls ‘gedachtenfotografie,’ or thought-photography: a medium built to describe the visible world turned toward picturing an inner one. The title puns on stereoscopy, echoed by the paired viewfinders on its orange cover. Published 2016 by Timmer Art Books, an imprint of Lecturis (Eindhoven), as a 48-page, cahier-stitched softcover designed by Rob van Hoesel and edited by Frank van der Stok and the artist.

Paul Bogaers (b. 1961, Tilburg) has worked since the 1980s across photography, collage, and sculptural assemblage, drawing on a growing archive of found and self-made images recombined into associative sequences rather than documentary series. Stereosophic Conjunctions isolates that collecting-and-pairing method, also central to Les Vacances de M. Rorschach, as a subject on its own.
tags: Collage, Photography, Found Photography, Dutch Art, Appropriation Art
language: English (colophon only the book is largely wordless/image-based)
notes: ISBN corrected from publisher listing: Lecturis's product page prints the ISBN as '987-94-6226-186-0' (invalid prefix, ISBNs start 978/979) — verified via ISBN-13 checksum that '978-94-6226-186-0' (9789462261860) is the valid form, a simple digit-swap typo on the publisher's site. Standard-edition print run not stated a signed/numbered special edition of 100 copies (each with a loose photographic print, 202 x 254 mm) was also issued — this record describes the standard trade edition. Cover image is Lecturis's clean flat product scan (467x600px), already tightly cropped to the cover, no further cropping performed.

title: Man Ray
description:
This TASCHEN monograph surveys Man Ray (1890–1976), the American-born photographer, painter, and filmmaker whose rayographs, solarizations, and Surrealist portraits redefined what a camera could do.

Issued in TASCHEN's compact Icons format, the 192-page hardcover moves from Man Ray's early New York experiments through his central Paris years, pairing reproductions with text by photography curator Katherine Ware and editorial direction by Manfred Heiting. It surveys his still lifes, fashion work, portraiture, and nude studies alongside the camera-less "rayographs" and solarized prints he pioneered, reproducing signature images including Noire et blanche and Le Violon d’Ingres.

Born Emmanuel Radnitzky in Philadelphia, Man Ray moved to Paris in 1921 and became a central figure of Dada and Surrealism, working across painting, film, sculpture, and object-making as fluently as photography, and photographing the Parisian avant-garde—Duchamp, Breton, Kiki de Montparnasse—along the way. TASCHEN has kept a Man Ray title in print in several forms since 2000 this compact edition is the publisher’s current standard survey of his work.
tags: Photography, Surrealism, Dada, Collage, Rayography, Portraiture
notes: PRIMARY EDITION CHOICE: taschen.com currently lists exactly one active Man Ray product (SKU 44037, /en/books/photography/44037/man-ray/): 'Man Ray' in the Icons collection, ISBN 978-3-8365-9399-1, hardcover, 192pp, 14 x 19.5 cm, 0.44 kg, text by Katherine Ware, ed. Manfred Heiting, in stock since 2023-11-22 (per the page's own Product JSON-LD). This is the only Man Ray title Taschen currently sells and is a genuine career-spanning survey (New York beginnings through Paris avant-garde, rayographs/solarization, portraiture/fashion/nude work) rather than a narrow niche title, so it was chosen as the primary catalog record. OTHER TASCHEN MAN RAY EDITIONS FOUND (not cataloged as separate records): (1) 'Man Ray, 1890–1976' — essay by Emmanuelle de l'Ecotais with a personal portrait by André Breton, ed. Manfred Heiting, TASCHEN Icons series, June 2001, ISBN 978-3-8228-5556-0 (3822855561), softcover, ~190pp, same compact ~14x19.5cm trim, multilingual English/German/French — the direct predecessor of the current title, different essayist. (2) 'Man Ray' (subtitle 'Photobook', per OpenLibrary/OCLC 44463344), TASCHEN, May 2000, ISBN 978-3-8228-7185-0 (3822871850), large-format hardcover, 252pp, ~33 x 27 cm, ~2.4kg — an earlier, much larger illustrated survey monograph bibliographic data sourced only from OpenLibrary/WorldCat (not cross-checked against a live Taschen listing since it appears discontinued), so treat page count/trim as medium-confidence. (3) 'Man Ray' paperback reissue under the Ware/Heiting text, TASCHEN, 21 Jul 2017, ISBN 978-3-8365-6449-6 (3836564491), 252pp, softcover — an intermediate printing between the 2001 essay edition and the current 2023 mini-hardcover OpenLibrary lists it at 252pp versus the current hardcover's 192pp, a discrepancy I could not resolve from secondary sources alone (flagged as unresolved). ARTIST LINK FALLBACK RATIONALE: Man Ray died in 1976, so there is no official living-artist website. Checked manraytrust.com (Man Ray Trust): the HTTPS certificate has been expired since ~2009 (confirmed via curl — TLS handshake fails outright), and the plain-HTTP version returns 200 but serves a stale ~512-byte placeholder page with a Last-Modified date of 2009 — the domain is effectively dormant/abandoned, so it was rejected as an authoritative source. Used the Guggenheim Museum's Man Ray artist/collection page instead (https://www.guggenheim.org/artwork/artist/man-ray), confirmed via curl to return HTTP 200 with page <title>Man Ray  The Guggenheim Museums and Foundation</title>. title: XAMAX
description:
XAMAX is an artist's book by the Swiss artist Fabian Boschung (b. 1983) that borrows its title and graphic identity, bold red-and-black stripes, from Neuchâtel Xamax, the football club of the city where he lives and works, turning a local sporting emblem into a study in pattern and appropriation.

Published in 2017 by TSAR Éditions in Vevey, Switzerland, the 48-page paperback carries the club's stripe motif and wordmark across its cover in place of any imagery of the team, treating the crest and colorway as a found visual system to be isolated, repeated, and re-staged as abstract composition, characteristic of Boschung's broader practice of appropriating forms and iconography from official emblems and vernacular material alike.

Boschung trained in graphic design in La Chaux-de-Fonds before studying visual art at HEAD Genève. He works across sculpture, painting, neon, and photography, has exhibited at CAN Centre d'art Neuchâtel and elsewhere since 2010, and is represented by Galerie Lange + Pult in Zurich. Xamax is the second of his two artist's books, following Feeling (2013), his first monograph, and shares its deadpan, design-forward approach to found imagery.
tags: Collage, Swiss Art, Appropriation, Contemporary Art
notes: Disambiguation check: 'Xamax' is also the name of the Neuchâtel Xamax football club this record is for Fabian Boschung's 2017 artist's book, which deliberately appropriates the club's red-and-black stripe branding as its subject (confirmed via Printed Matter catalog #50127, Motto Distribution's TSAR Éditions publisher listing, and exposition-format.ch artist bio). Boschung's official site, fabianboschung.com, is listed as his personal website by multiple independent sources (CAN Centre d'art Neuchâtel, fromnewithlove.ch) but currently returns HTTP 503 from a domain-parking service (gname.net) rather than a live site as of 2026-07-27, so it could not be used as the verified authors[0].url the CAN Centre d'art Neuchâtel institutional artist profile was used instead per the no-live-official-site fallback rule. Sources gave conflicting graduation years for his HEAD Genève degree (2009 vs. 2012) the exact year was omitted from the description rather than asserted. Printed Matter's product metadata lists 'Julien Fischer' as an associated credit (data-product-brand field) with an unconfirmed role, possibly the cover photographer not included as a contributor without confirmation. Language marked French per the publisher's home market and the book's Swiss-French (Vevey/Neuchâtel) context the book is largely visual/title-text with minimal running text, so this is a light inference, not confirmed against an inside page.

title: FIN?
description:
FIN? is a zine of killed, rejected, and forgotten studio work by the Manchester design duo DR.ME (Ryan Doyle and Mark Edwards), a running archive of the ideas that didn't survive the brief.

Launched as a monthly, free-to-download PDF &mdash a "Print It Yourself" release built from client and personal-project offcuts that would otherwise sit unused in plan chests and hard drives &mdash FIN? gathered its best material every six months into a printed compilation. Across its run DR.ME produced 29 P.I.Y. digital issues and 5 printed issues, some 540 artworks in total, before the studio stopped making new issues in 2019. The library holds that 2019 printed issue, by the duo's own account the series' final year. Its cover is built from the same raw collage vocabulary &mdash cut barcodes, crossed-out file names, sticker-sheet fragments &mdash that runs through the interior pages.

DR.ME is the studio name of Ryan Doyle and Mark Edwards, a Manchester, UK design partnership working across branding, illustration, and collage-driven art direction. FIN? sits outside that commercial practice: a self-published side project the pair used to keep rejected work in circulation and to push themselves toward constantly making something new.
tags: Collage, Zines, Graphic Design, Self-Published, British Design
notes: Self-published by DR.ME with no ISBN by design (small self-distributed studio zine, never assigned one). FIN? ran as monthly free-to-download PDF issues ("P.I.Y." / Print It Yourself) from roughly 2016-2019, with a printed "greatest hits" compilation about every 6 months DR.ME's own account (via The Weird Show interview, June 2020) says they stopped producing new issues in 2019, after which the full back catalogue (29 digital + 5 printed issues, ~540 artworks) was released free via Dropbox during the pandemic. The library's copy is the 2019 printed issue source article shows distinct cover art labeled by year (2017 vs. 2019), and the cover used here is the one explicitly labeled "PHYSICAL_COVER_2019" -- but it is not independently confirmed to be THE final printed issue vs. simply A 2019 printed issue, since exact print/issue numbering wasn't published. No page count, trim dimensions, weight, or print run were found for this specific issue in any source checked. Official studio site dr-me.com is live (verified 200 via curl with a browser user-agent) and matches the studio's current description ("Daring and disruptive design studio") however, the WebFetch tool itself received a 503 from dr-me.com on repeated attempts, apparently anti-bot blocking on the Cargo.site host rather than the site being down -- confirmed live independently via direct curl. The site is a single-page Cargo.site portfolio (sitemap.xml lists only the homepage) with no dedicated FIN? shop/product page, so no page count or dimensions could be sourced there. DR.ME's Twitter (twitter.com/drme_studio) and Instagram (instagram.com/drme_studio) were found linked from an associated DR.ME Cargo project page (waitingroom.press, contact email info@dr-me.com matches dr-me.com) but were not used as authors[0].url since the official site itself resolves Instagram content is login-walled and no FIN?-specific post could be verified.

title: The Luxury of Rigor
description:
The Luxury of Rigor (2013) is an early zine from Matt Borruso's San Francisco imprint Visible Publications, built entirely from appropriated photography run through screen-printed color and half-tone texture.

Printed in full color across 54 softcover pages in an open edition, the book cuts between glossy shelter-magazine interiors, close-up geological studies of salt and mineral crystal, a horror-film still, and the printer's own registration bars and color-swatch keys - treating the tools of commercial reproduction as material for the collage itself. The title's dry pairing of "luxury" and "rigor" frames the method: found images of aspirational excess are handled with the same deadpan, process-driven attention as the production marks that interrupt them.

Borruso has run Visible Publications since 2010, self-publishing close to twenty small-run, hand-assembled books that mine found imagery, screen printing, and appropriation. Hudson Street Library also holds his Negative Space (2010), DATA (2019), and Wax House of Wax (2016), all produced under the same imprint.
tags: Collage, Art, San Francisco, Appropriation, Found Imagery, Self-Published
notes: Out of print. The library holds the open-edition handmade artist book.

title: Lounge of Psychedelia
description:
Lounge of Psychedelia (2020) is a large-format art book by the Tokyo graphic artist Keiji Ito (b. 1958), built around an invented record shop of the same name that anchors his collage-driven, psychedelic visual world.

Published by G/P+abp as part of the Fuji Xerox-supported NEOTOKYOZINE (NTZ) series, the softcover volume unfolds Ito's fictional "Lounge of Psychedelia Records" - a shop perched beneath a smoking volcano, its porch lined with lounge chairs and houseplants - through the dense, hand-drawn collage of pattern, line, and pop iconography that runs through both his commercial and gallery work. At 31.8 x 23.6 cm, the book gives that imagery room to read as much like poster art as illustration.

Ito founded the Tokyo studio UFG (Unidentified Flying Graphics) and teaches at Kyoto University of the Arts. His art direction and collage-based illustration run through the 2005 Aichi Expo's official poster, NHK title sequences, and campaigns for Coca-Cola, SoftBank, and Converse (Tokyo ADC Award, 2001), alongside a 1999 New York ADC Gold Medal and CD-jacket work for Japanese musicians including Bonnie Pink and Orange Pekoe.
tags: Collage, Illustration, Graphic Design, Japanese Art, Psychedelia, Artist Book
notes: Artist identity confirmed by the user from the physical copy as Keiji Ito (not Keiichi Tanaami). Page count and ISBN are not listed on either the G/P+abp product page or Ito's own site (site-ufg.com) and are treated as unresolved rather than guessed. A related 2024 item, 'HEAVENLY GIFT' (gpabp.official.ec/items/94233841), is described by the publisher as a re-edited version of this same book released for a GINZA SIX Christmas promotion - noted here for disambiguation only it is a distinct product, not the title catalogued.

title: Targets
description:
A pointed artist's book by the New York artist Anne Doran, Targets holds two vocabularies of the aimed-at body in a single frame: vintage pornography stills seamlessly collaged with the human-silhouette practice targets of the shooting range.

Across forty-eight digitally printed color pages, the black target silhouettes — their scoring numbers and manufacturer's imprint left legible — are cut into and overlaid with anonymous nudes, so that zones of desire and zones of aim coincide. Published in New York by Ratstar Press in 2018 as a perfect-bound paperback, the book presents one collage per page, plate-style, and examines, in the publisher's phrasing, how the body can be a target for action and a catalyst for power.

Doran's appropriation-based photo-collage practice dates to New York in the mid-1980s her Photo-works (1985–1991), revisited in a later gallery survey, drew on the same found-image economy of advertising, pornography, and print ephemera that Targets distills to its starkest pairing.
tags: Collage, Appropriation, Found Photography, New York
notes: The library holds two copies.

title: Paper Assemblage 1
description: A paper assemblage work by William Alexander Shum, produced in 2015 and held in the library's Collage collection. Cataloged from the physical copy.
notes: Cataloged from the physical copy no published documentation of this title exists online. cover to be photographed from the physical copy

title: Paper Tales
description:
A compact hardcover of collages by Peter Dowker, Paper Tales gathers work developed over several years in which the faded pastels of the past form blocks of color over the broken lines and torn edges of vintage cuttings and ephemera.

Published in 2020 by Redfoxpress of Achill Island, County Mayo, in a numbered edition of 150 copies, the 44-page volume presents each collage as a single frame of an unseen storyboard, hinting at a larger narrative held between the found fragments — mid-century advertising, typography, and photographic scrap reassembled into quiet, cinematic stills.

Redfoxpress, the Achill Island press known for its handmade dada, mail-art, and visual-poetry editions issued in small numbered runs, publishes collage books as intimate, hand-made objects Paper Tales sits squarely in that lineage.

title: The First March of Gentlemen
description:
A fictitious narration composed of authentic stories, Rafał Milach's The First March of Gentlemen collages 1950s photographs of the townspeople of Września into bright constructivist tableaux that weigh protest against the mechanisms of discipline.

The source material — portraits by local photographer Ryszard Szczepaniak of communist-era Września — is cut loose and marshaled across fields of red and blue, echoing the town's history as the site of the celebrated early twentieth-century children's strikes. Across 72 pages with 48 illustrations, designed by Milach with Ania Nałęcka-Milach, the figures assemble, march, and disperse like players in a drill the book never quite names. First published in 2017 by Muzeum Dzieci Wrzesińskich / OUT OF PRINT this record follows the GOST Books second edition of 2018.

Milach (b. 1978), a member of Magnum Photos and co-founder of the Archive of Public Protests, has built a body of work on power, propaganda, and civic resistance in Central and Eastern Europe, including 7 Rooms and The Winners The First March of Gentlemen distills those concerns into the collage book at its most pointed.
tags: Collage, Photography, Archival Photography, Protest, Poland
notes: First edition published 2017 by Muzeum Dzieci Wrzesińskich / OUT OF PRINT in an edition of 650 this record follows the GOST Books second edition.

title: Stellungen
description:
A staple-bound booklet by the Danish artist Jesper Fabricius, Stellungen collages vintage pornographic imagery until explicitness collapses into pure composition.

Published in Leipzig in 2011 by the artist with Lubok Verlag in an offset edition of 500, the booklet pastes snippets of images — genitalia and other erogenous fragments — over full-page sex scenes, bombarding the reader with raw, frenetically positioned imagery. The chopped and reassembled pictures have the odd effect of removing shock or titillation altogether, breaking the sexual act down into component parts and harmless pixels. It precedes his related 2012 book Porno Kommunistisk.

Fabricius (b. 1957) is a central figure in Danish artists' publishing, co-founder of the long-running journal Pist Protta and the imprint Space Poetry, with a decades-long practice of cutting found printed matter into small, serial artist books.

title: Why I Hustle to Feed My Pimp
description:
A staple-bound volume of collages by the Brazilian artist Caco Neves, Why I Hustle to Feed My Pimp turns images appropriated from digital photographic archives into pointed visual reflections on human rights, militarism, and sexuality.

Printed in Colombia by Calipso Press in 2016 as part of the 'More is More' collection, in a first edition of 300 copies, the book works by cutout and juxtaposition: found images are resignified through severing and recombination, opening new possibilities of reading — as on the cover, where two mid-century heads lean back from facing chairs into an open scream.

Neves's research-driven collage practice sits within a wider South American small-press current, and Calipso Press of Cali has become one of its notable engines, printing artists' editions that move between graphic design, protest, and the found image.
tags: Collage, Appropriation, Found Photography, Zines, Brazil

title: What to Want: Collages
description:
Published by Ampersand Editions with Zieher's 2014 exhibition at Ampersand in Oregon, What to Want collects collages the artist describes as loose but sculptural, uncouth and unkempt, improvised yet controlled.

Zieher's raw materials are the paper sediment of small-town American life — salesmanship, office supplies, jazz, baseball, taverns, bowling, magazines, race forms, postcards — worked into compositions that stay close to the scavenged page. The publication appeared in four companion forms: Poems, Collages, a combined Poems & Collages, and a deluxe edition the collages share the book with the concerns of his fourth poetry collection, whose 39 poems circle invented memories of a dead father and the loneliness and loss of small-town Americana.

Zieher (b. 1965, Waukesha, Wisconsin) took his MFA in poetry at Columbia and co-founded the New York gallery ZieherSmith his collage and poetry practices have run in parallel for decades, each feeding the other's economy of salvage.
notes: Published in four variants: Poems Collages Poems & Collages deluxe edition. cover to be photographed from the physical copy

title: Aaron Curry: Boxxes
edition_printrun: Reprint edition (April 28, 2015). Part of a series
description:
A book built on deliberate loss: for Boxxes, the Los Angeles artist Aaron Curry created 160 unique works of art and then destroyed them, photographing each beforehand so that the book stands as both their only record and a new singular work assembled from their remains.

Published by Koenig Books in 2015 and edited by Karen Marta with the designer Brian Roettinger, the 144-page paperback grew out of UCCA's 'The Los Angeles Project' in Beijing. Curry's painted and collaged box constructions — checkerboards, torn figures, gestural blacks — pass through the camera into sequence, the page becoming the only place the work now exists.

Curry (b. 1972) is known for sculpture that pushes biomorphic modernism into cartoon and collage registers Boxxes extends the conceptual lineage of John Baldessari's cremated paintings and Ed Ruscha's bookworks, where destruction and documentation trade places.
tags: Collage, Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, Sculpture

title: John Stezaker: Fumetti
contributors: Barry Schwabsky (Essay) David Lillington (Essay) William Horner (Interview)
description:
Fumetti is the catalog for a 2008 exhibition of the same name by the British collagist John Stezaker (b. 1949), in which vintage film-annual publicity portraits are grafted into monstrous double-faced hybrids.

Rather than the aged bromides of his best-known film-still series, Stezaker works here from glossy 1950s and '60s film-annual star portraits, splicing their perfected hair and makeup into uncanny composite faces. Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König published the 112-page hardcover in 2009 for the exhibition at GAK Gesellschaft für Aktuelle Kunst, Bremen (30 August – 9 November 2008), with essays by Barry Schwabsky and David Lillington. The book reproduces the Fumetti series alongside excerpts from twelve further Stezaker series its title borrows the Italian fumetti tradition of comics built from photographs rather than drawings.

Stezaker came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York, and the library holds several other Stezaker titles, including Tabula Rasa and Film Still.
tags: Collage, Found Photography, Appropriation, Film Stills, Exhibition Catalog

title: John Stezaker: Tabula Rasa
description:
Tabula Rasa gathers three decades of John Stezaker's (b. 1949) central methods, the silkscreen and the single exacting cut, around a 2010 exhibition at The Approach, London, that reads his practice through voids and apertures rather than doubled images.

The book unites silkscreens on canvas from the early 1990s with film-still collages made between the 1990s and 2009, illustrated in full color with installation photographs from the London gallery. Ridinghouse published the 40-page softcover in 2010 for the exhibition (29 January – 21 March 2010), with an essay by Michael Bracewell tracing "tabula rasa" as a term Stezaker first applied in the mid-1980s to collages with rhomboid holes cut into landscape photographs and film stills, an aperture that, in the newer work, opens onto another image entirely.

Stezaker came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York, and the library holds several other Stezaker titles, including Fumetti and One on One.

title: The Cast
description:
The Cast (2017) collects Ruth van Beek's (b. 1977) sculptural collages built from an archive of found photographs, botanical and craft images clipped from vintage books and magazines, physically reworked into biomorphic, almost animate forms.

Van Beek cuts, folds, and layers her source images, adding painted paper and cast shadow to turn flat found pictures into what read as small sculptures, actors staged rather than depicted, borrowing photography's own conventions of shadow, pedestal, and gesture to lend invented objects an unearned authority. New Documents, the Los Angeles art-book publisher, released this 40-page softcover-with-jacket first edition in 2017.

Van Beek studied photography at the Gerrit Rietveld Academy in Amsterdam, where she has taught since 2014, and works from her home in Koog aan de Zaan, near Amsterdam. Her books include The Arrangement (2013) and The Oldest Thing (2023), both shortlisted for the Aperture Photobook of the Year Award her work has appeared in The New Yorker, Vogue, and Foam Magazine, and she is represented by The Ravestijn Gallery, Amsterdam.
notes: Publisher confirmed as New Documents (Los Angeles), not Art Paper Editions or RVB Books as initially guessed in the assignment brief — van Beek's own site (ruthvanbeek.com) lists The Cast under New Documents, matching the publisher's own product page and Printed Matter's listing. No exhibition ties to this title it reads as a standalone artist book, so classification is set to Individual Artist Monographs. Both New Documents (per book page framing) and Printed Matter list the title as sold out/unavailable, so distributor availability is marked false throughout. Existing books.csv row id 1204 for 'Ruth Van Beek' is a different, sparsely-populated title (Houseplants Covered With Snow & Houseplants) and not a duplicate of this record. title: Young Ideas
description:
Young Ideas assembles five years of imagery by the American filmmaker Eddie O'Keefe (stills from his films and music videos alongside photographs of the Southwest) into a numbered artist-book edition that reads as one continuous, uneasy travelogue of the American West.

Compiled over five years, the book interleaves location shots and stills from O'Keefe's short films and music videos with photographs taken around the American Southwest: gun-toting figures, hooded beauty-contest contestants, and blood-soaked ravers alongside laundromats, Disneyland topiary, and bleached-out street scenes. Bywater Bros. Editions published it in 2015 as a numbered edition of 500: 88 pages, softcover, 17.8 × 14 cm, designed by Roger Bywater and O'Keefe.

O'Keefe, born 1988 in Elmhurst, Illinois, is a photographer, writer, and director who studied at Columbia College Chicago and the American Film Institute. Known for music videos for The Orwells and Springtime Carnivore and for the short films Sun Sessions (2008) and The Ghosts (2011), he later directed the feature Shangri-La Suite (2016). Young Ideas was his second book, first in an ongoing investigation of the American psyche continued in Patriotic Pavement.
notes: Cover downloaded from the publisher's product page (small, 253x315px source image — no larger version found on bywaterbros.com). Third-book sibling 'Patriotic Pavement' (Bywater Bros., 2017) confirms this is the second installment in an ongoing series not treated as a required field. title: Ficciones
description:
Ficciones is Chinese artist Sun Yanchu's altered-photograph project, which won the inaugural Gucang Dummy Book Award, selected by Martin Parr, in 2015.

The book gathers anonymous photographs Sun found in antique markets across China: snapshots of family gatherings, travel, and daily life from the 1970s and 1980s. Working directly on the found prints with collage, drawing, gold leaf, and paint, he obscures faces and layers in fragments of contemporary news, blurring the line between the photographs' original documentary content and his own invented narratives. Published by Jiazazhi Press in Ningbo in August 2016, the book is hardcover and spiral-bound, 112 pages, 18 × 23 × 3 cm, in a first edition of 500 copies, with text in Chinese and English.

Sun Yanchu (b. 1978, Zhoukou, Henan Province) lives and works in Zhengzhou, working by hand on found and self-made photographs. His awards include the Lianzhou International Photo Festival New Photography Award (2011) and the Jinan International Photo Biennale Best Photographer Award (2012) a related series, Developer Paintings, applies darkroom chemistry and brushwork directly to photographic paper. Ficciones followed Obsessed, Sun's 2011 debut with Jiazazhi Press.

title: The New World
description:
Collage and visual poetry from the German mail artist Horst Hahn, whose The New World layers wartime aircraft photography, road signage, and cut typography into a dense artist's book issued as volume 137 in Redfoxpress's C'est mon Dada series.

Published in December 2019, the 40-page hardcover is thread-and-quarter-cloth bound and laser-printed on ivory paper, in the A6 format (10.5 × 15 cm) standard to the series. Hahn builds each spread from salvaged ephemera &mdash maps, product labels, comic lettering, a photograph of a WWII-era bomber &mdash layering found text and image in the collage tradition Kurt Schwitters established with Merz.

Hahn (b. 1937, Bergisch Gladbach) spent decades as a professional restorer, working from 1968 to 1996 on Joseph Beuys's works in the van der Grinten collection at Museum Schloß Moyland, while corresponding through mail-art networks since the early 1970s. He has issued the graphic edition Zufall since 1974 and pursues travel photography of Africa with his wife Barbara. The New World extends that same instinct for reassembling found material into book form.

title: Papeles Pegados
description:
Collage and mail art converge in Papeles Pegados ("Glued Papers"), the Barcelona artist Pere Sousa's contribution to Redfoxpress's C'est mon Dada series, its cover pairing old-master portraiture with a photograph of a technician adjusting a measuring apparatus.

Published in February 2020 as volume 141, the 44-page hardcover follows the series' standard A6 format (10.5 × 15 cm), thread-and-quarter-cloth bound and laser-printed on ivory paper. Sousa's spreads glue together salvaged prints, portrait photography, and diagrams of scientific instruments, working in the cut-and-paste tradition &mdash text combined with found image &mdash that defines the series.

Sousa (1955&ndash2023) was a central figure in Spanish mail art: born in Pont de Suert, Catalonia, he studied sculpture at the University of Barcelona before turning to postal art in 1992. He edited P.O.BOX and Artstrike from 1994 to 2000, founded the Factoria Merz Mail archive, organized artist-stamp and mail-art exhibitions across Spain, and was recognized as one of the country's foremost sound poets for his interpretations of Kurt Schwitters.

title: Mind Machines
description:
Vintage mechanical imagery collides with hand-cut typography in Mind Machines, the German collage artist Sabine Remy's entry in Redfoxpress's C'est mon Dada series, its cover built around blueprint-style renderings of viewing apparatuses under a hand-lettered title.

Issued in January 2020 as volume 140, the 40-page hardcover follows the series' standard A6 format (10.5 × 15 cm), thread-and-quarter-cloth bound and laser-printed on ivory paper. Remy assembles her collages from salvaged books and printed ephemera dating largely from the 1950s and earlier, pairing technical diagrams with fragments of vintage advertising and instructional graphics.

Remy is a German analogue collage artist who has kept the blog Miriskum.de since 2012, posting over a thousand works and building an international network of collaborators. She favors old paper "because they are often a little bizarre ... full of lived life," summarizing her method as "I cut, therefore I am." Her work has appeared in Collage &ndash Contemporary European Perspectives at the Neue Sächsische Galerie, Chemnitz, and the Retroavangarda anthology Modern Collage.

title: Pictorial Atlas of a Girl Who Cut a Library into Pieces
description:
Pictorial Atlas of a Girl Who Cut a Library into Pieces is a two-volume artist's book by the Czech artist Eva Koťátková (b. 1982), staging roughly 300 collages as an imagined 1980s schoolbook from her Prague childhood under Communist rule.

Co-published in 2016 by JRPEditions and tranzit.cz — the twelfth volume in tranzit's series on Central and Eastern European artists — the book gathers collages and drawings made 2013–2015: children at play or bound into diagrams, spliced with anatomical fragments and puppet-like armatures, in scenes with the psychological unease of Kafka. A companion volume, Institutional, Operational and Organisational Rules and Regulations 1961–1989, reprints twenty-two sets of real Czechoslovak bureaucratic regulations, pairing Koťátková's invented pedagogy with the actual machinery of state control it echoes.

Koťátková studied at the San Francisco Art Institute and the Academy of Fine Arts in Prague, and works across collage, sculpture, and performance to examine how institutions discipline the body and imagination of children. Her work has appeared in the 2013 and 2024 Venice Biennales and documenta fifteen she is represented by Hunt Kastner (Prague) and Meyer Riegger (Berlin/Karlsruhe).
notes: Page count conflicts across sources: co-publisher tranzit.cz lists 712 pp for the two-volume set, JRPEditions' own product page lists 703 pp, and DAP/artbook.com lists 400 pp (likely counting a single volume). Publication year also varies (JRP: January 2016 tranzit.cz: 2015) used JRP's 2016, matching the internationally distributed ISBN 9783037643617. title: Collages 2020-2022
description:
Collages 2020-2022 gathers three years of collage work by the South African artist Nico Krijno (b. 1981), published by Art Paper Editions as the fullest survey yet of a practice that treats photography as raw material for cutting, layering, and reassembly.

Designed and edited by APE founder Jurgen Maelfeyt, the 448-page paperback compiles images made between 2020 and 2022, presented without captions or narrative sequence, an accumulation rather than a chronology. Studio setups, still lifes, and staged figures are sliced, taped, folded, and rephotographed, producing work the publisher calls "disorientating and fantastical, and at times almost absurd, but wondrous nevertheless." The book was issued in an edition of 1,000 in December 2022.

Krijno moved into visual art around 2008 after working in filmmaking and experimental theatre he now works across photography, collage, painting, sculpture, and performance, mixing analogue and digital tools. Based in South Africa, he has exhibited across Europe, Asia, and the United States and collaborated with Givenchy and Loewe. Collages 2020-2022 is his most extensive book to date with Art Paper Editions, the Ghent publisher known for treating the book as an exhibition space.

title: Jamais je ne t'oublierai
description:
Jamais je ne t'oublierai is a 2019 artist's book by the French-Moroccan photographer Carolle Bénitah (1965–2024), in which anonymous flea-market photographs are reworked with gold leaf into a meditation on inherited memory and its gaps.

Published by L'Artiere Edizioni, curated by Laura Serani and designed by Teresa Piardi, the 56-page volume replaces Bénitah's own family archive — subject of her earlier book Photos Souvenirs — with photographs of strangers bought at flea markets. Faces are partly obscured under applied gold leaf, a surface that both erases and reflects, multiplying the identities of people whose names are lost. Bound in Japanese spiral stitching, it appeared in an edition of 1,000 and won the 2020 Prix HiP photography award.

Born in Casablanca in 1965, Bénitah trained at the École de la Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne and spent ten years as a fashion designer before turning to photography in 2001, graduating with distinction from the École Nationale Supérieure de la Photographie in Arles. Represented by Galerie Clémentine de la Féronnière, she used embroidery, beading, and gold leaf on found and family photographs to work through memory and loss. She died in Marseille in 2024.

title: Stills
contributors: Danny Clay (Music/Composition) Taylor Deupree (Mastering) Paula Karolak (Viola)
description:
Stills is a call-and-response between the Belgian collage artist Katrien De Blauwer and the American composer Danny Clay, issued in 2016 as IIKKI 001, the debut release of the French label IIKKI, which pairs a visual artist with a musician for each of its book-and-vinyl editions.

Working independently over several months in 2016 from a shared set of prompts, De Blauwer and Clay never saw or heard each other's work in progress. Her 75 collages and his piano, voice, harmonium, and viola composition (with Paula Karolak, mastered by Taylor Deupree) converge on a shared mood of memory and disappearance. The collages splice figures, torn interiors, and sepia fragments recut from old magazines. The 112-page hardcover, designed by Sprflxgrfzm on Munken white stock with an embossed circle and slot, appeared in a first edition of 500 copies alongside a matching 500-copy LP, meant to be viewed and heard separately and together.

De Blauwer (b. 1969, Ronse, Belgium) calls herself a "photographer without a camera," building every image from cut and recombined found photographs. Stills was nominated for the Revelation Book Awards at La Maison Rouge, Paris, and stands among the clearest translations of her collage practice into collaborative, cross-media form.
notes: IIKKI 001 is a combined book+vinyl project this record catalogs the book component. Listed weight (0.83 kg) is from the publisher spec sheet and may reflect the book alone. Cover image cropped from a publisher product photo showing the book and matching vinyl sleeve side by side used image is the book's front cover only. Sold out at publisher as of research date. title: Dirty Scenes
edition_printrun: First edition, 400 numbered and signed copies
description:
Dirty Scenes gathers twenty collage plates by the Belgian artist Katrien De Blauwer, published by the Stockholm press Libraryman in 2019 as a first edition of 400 numbered and signed copies.

The images began as an accident during work on De Blauwer's companion book Why I Hate Cars and grew into a detached supplement in their own right: anonymous figures, their faces cut away or obscured, set against paint strokes, cardboard scraps, and pencil marks layered over vintage photographic sources. Edited and designed by Tony Cederteg, the 40-page softcover is saddle-stitched and housed in a grey paperboard slipcase with black foil-stamped typography, browsed Japanese-style from left to right. The book accompanied De Blauwer's exhibition Love Me Tender at Galerie Les Filles du Calvaire, Paris, May 18–June 15, 2019.

De Blauwer (b. 1969, Ronse, Belgium) calls herself "a photographer without a camera," building her collages entirely from found and recut printed images rather than original photography. Dirty Scenes sits alongside her other Libraryman titles — Why I Hate Cars, When I Was a Boy, You Could at Least Pretend to Like Yellow — as part of a body of work centered on memory, anonymity, and appropriated photography.
notes: Edition is numbered and signed as a feature of the print run (400 copies) whether HSL's specific copy is physically signed/numbered was not verified. Out of print at publisher as of research date. Collage collection archiving, July 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-29.

title: Sub Rosa
description:
Sub Rosa gathers a private practice of collage that runs alongside Ron Nagle's better-known career as a ceramic sculptor, revealing an artist who has spent decades merging vintage postcards with photo-booth self-portraits into small, uncanny tableaux.

Published on the occasion of two exhibitions (Euphoric Recall at Fridericianum, Kassel, and a solo show at Secession, Vienna, both in 2019), the hardcover volume reproduces the collages alongside a text by Nagle and a conversation with curator Massimiliano Gioni. Nagle describes taking hundreds of photographs of himself at a novelty photo booth on San Francisco's 24th Street, then splicing the results into found postcards until a convincing tableau emerged, letting him, in his words, "insinuate myself into a scene from someone else's experience."

Nagle (b. 1939, San Francisco) began as a studio assistant to Peter Voulkos and became a central figure of the California Clay Movement, developing the small-scale, jewel-colored ceramic sculptures for which he is best known he is represented by Matthew Marks Gallery. Sub Rosa documents the parallel, largely unseen collage practice running alongside that sculptural work.

title: Chambre Sauvage
description:
Chambre Sauvage collects the staged photographic tableaux of Swiss photographer Nadin Maria Rüfenacht (b. 1980), where taxidermied animals, costumed figures, and painted stage flats combine into theatrical, faintly unsettling still lifes.

Published by Lubok Verlag, Leipzig, in 2013 on the occasion of the exhibition of the same name at Galerie Kleindienst, the hardcover catalog reproduces 53 images in four-color offset, designed by Toni Schönbuchner. Rüfenacht builds her scenes from inherited props (furniture, tools, and tableware once belonging to a woman named Johanna), reconstructing an imagined circus of hybrid creatures the volume pairs the photographs with texts by theater director Sebastian Hartmann and critic Markus Stegmann.

Rüfenacht trained under Timm Rautert at the Academy of Visual Arts Leipzig, earning her photography diploma in 2005 and completing Meisterschüler studies there in 2008. She lives and works in Leipzig (sharing a studio with her husband, painter Tilo Baumgärtel, at the Leipzig Cotton Mill) and in her native Grosshöchstetten and Bern she is represented by Galerie Kleindienst. Her photography returns to the friction between the organic and the artificial.

title: Fragrance of Kogiku: Early Pop Collages
description:
Fragrance of Kogiku: Early Pop Collages assembles more than 200 collages by Japanese pop artist Keiichi Tanaami (1936–2024), made in the late 1960s and early 1970s — works never intended for exhibition, rediscovered in 2012 among an uncle's inherited warehouse materials.

Cut from pre-war movie magazines, 1960s American comics, and pin-up magazines, the collages layer weaponry, superheroes, and movie stars into dense, hallucinatory sheets anticipating Tanaami's better-known paintings and prints. First published in Japan by P-Vine's ele-king books in 2016, the volume appeared internationally in 2018 through Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König, Köln, as a 272-page hardcover with 238 color reproductions and text by Tanaami.

Tanaami studied at Musashino Art University, worked as a graphic designer and illustrator, and became the first art director of the Japanese edition of Playboy in 1975. A 1968 meeting with Andy Warhol pushed him toward the posters, prints, and animation that made him a forerunner of Japanese Pop art. His work entered the collections of MoMA and the Walker Art Center, and was the subject of the 2024 retrospective Adventures in Memory at Tokyo's National Art Center, the year of his death.

title: Stereotypes Vol. 005
description:
A volume in the Lebanese-American artist Lucien Samaha's self-published ftA (from the Archive) series, Stereotypes Vol. 005 collects collages that splice the swaggering leading men and starlets of vintage Arabic-language movie magazines into pointed, funny recombinations.

Issued in New York in 2022 as a signed first-edition softcover, the zine draws on Samaha's collage practice rooted in his long engagement with Arab visual culture. He was an early member of the Arab Image Foundation, and his cut-and-paste works recirculate the printed ephemera of mid-century Beirut and Cairo pop cinema, probing the stock characters its title names.

Samaha (b. Beirut) is best known as a pioneer of digital photography (while at Kodak he shot among the first digital photographs ever taken) and as an obsessive archivist of his own life: three decades of images from airline galleys, New York nightclubs, and the Windows on the World DJ booth, sequenced into ongoing self-published series like FLM and ftA.
notes: Series: ftA (from the Archive), no. 005. No ISBN (self-published). Sold as signed first edition at Dashwood Books. Collage collection archiving, July 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-29.

title: John Stezaker: Unassisted Readymade
description:
Its title borrowed from Duchamp, Unassisted Readymade is a large-format monograph that frames the British artist John Stezaker's collage practice as the act of choosing an image rather than making one: the found photograph as readymade.

Across 144 oversize pages, publicity stills of golden-era Hollywood icons are spliced, inverted, and overlapped into uncanny hybrid stars, alongside works that examine the photograph's competing roles as document of truth, purveyor of memory, and emblem of modern culture. Edited by Jürg Trösch and Markus Bosshard and co-published by JRPRingier and Codax Publisher, Zurich, the volume carries an essay by the writer and curator David Campany, who reads Stezaker's method as returning seemingly banal imagery to its essential freedom.

Stezaker (b. 1949) has worked with found images from books, magazines, and postcards since the early 1970s, well represented in this collection by titles including Fumetti, Tabula Rasa, Film Still, and Lost World he won the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012 for a practice built entirely on photographs he never took.
tags: Collage, Found Photography, Appropriation, Film Stills
notes: Two copies held. Collage collection archiving, July 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-29.

title: Terry Winters: Red Yellow Green Blue
description:
A catalog documenting the American painter Terry Winters's Red Yellow Green Blue, the third exhibition of the 2014 season at 'T' Space, the architect Steven Holl's gallery in the woods outside Rhinebeck, New York.

The exhibition, which opened August 30, 2014 to a crowd that included Jasper Johns and Brice and Helen Marden, installed Winters's work on the gallery's largest interior wall. The catalog's cover reproduces a layered collage of red, yellow, green, and blue transparencies — taped, hole-punched, and overlapped into an off-register color wheel — and carries the theorist Sanford Kwinter's essay 'The Temperature of Things,' which takes the work as a starting point for a speculative exploration of the logic embedded in form. Issued by the gallery without an ISBN, in the modest format of its exhibition-catalog series.

Winters (b. 1949, Brooklyn) makes paintings, drawings, and prints that filter natural systems, crystallography, and information graphics through gestural abstraction he is represented by Matthew Marks Gallery, and his layered, diagrammatic image-building gives his printed matter a natural kinship with collage.
tags: Collage, Abstract Art, Exhibition Catalog, Contemporary Art
notes: No ISBN (small gallery publication). Essay: Sanford Kwinter, 'The Temperature of Things.' Collage collection archiving, July 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-29.

title: Paradise Found
description:
An artist's book by the Los Angeles artist Devin Troy Strother with the designer Yuri Ogita, Paradise Found answers a found book with an act of reauthorship, examining who owns an image and who gets pictured in it.

The book responds to Lost Paradise, by the artist Žiga Kariž and designer Vasja Cenčič, which compiled preexisting images without text or context. Strother and Ogita abstract those pages into new ones: unpeopled images are digitally filtered and painted over, some annotated with Strother's humor images of white figures have their hands and arms painted black and their faces superimposed with scans of hand-painted stickers from Strother's studio practice. The publisher describes this faux diversification as the artist — a Black man then living in Germany among a majority-white population — regaining a sense of ownership and altering a nameless book into something significant. Perfect-bound and digitally printed by Coloured Publishing, 2019, 138 pages.

Strother (b. 1986, West Covina, CA) works across painting, collage, sculpture, neon, and installation, citing Joseph Cornell and Matisse among his touchstones his work is held by LACMA, the Santa Barbara Museum of Art, and the Studio Museum in Harlem, and he co-runs Coloured Publishing, the imprint behind this volume.
notes: Response to Lost Paradise by Žiga Kariž and Vasja Cenčič. No ISBN (small-press artist book). Collage collection archiving, July 2026. Accessioned 2026-07-29.

title: John Stezaker: At the Edge of Pictures
description:
At the Edge of Pictures is the first monographic study of the British collagist John Stezaker (b. 1949). The Oxford scholar Yuval Etgar takes the eventful decades of the 1970s and 1980s as the prism for a historical account of the artist's life and work, and a mapping of collage and image appropriation in that pivotal period.

Amid the post-conceptual crisis of the 1970s, Etgar argues, Stezaker pursued neither the agitprop-inspired photomontage of his British contemporaries nor full alignment with the Pictures Generation across the Atlantic, instead treating mechanically reproduced imagery (studio portraits, film stills, landscape postcards) as an outmoded visual currency to be recombined with minimal, exacting cuts. Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König published the 176-page Otabind softcover in 2020 with Luxembourg + Co., on the occasion of the first exhibition devoted to Stezaker's early output of 1975–1990, gathering rarely seen collages, readymades and silkscreens in 82 color and 15 black-and-white illustrations.

Stezaker came to prominence among the British conceptualists of the 1970s and received the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2012, following his 2011 Whitechapel Gallery retrospective. He is represented by The Approach, London, and Petzel Gallery, New York. As the first historical study of the practice, this volume complements the library's Stezaker survey catalogs, among them the 2010 Whitechapel monograph and Film Still.

title: 30 Years of Being Cut Up
description:
The catalog for the acclaimed 2009 retrospective at Invisible-Exports, New York, 30 Years of Being Cut Up surveys three decades of collage by Genesis Breyer P-Orridge (1950–2020) — photomontage, Expanded Polaroids, and early mail art, much of it published here for the first time.

Drawn largely from the artist's own archive, the Lower East Side gallery's fall survey (through October 18, 2009) showed works previously seen only in P-Orridge's home, the same year Tate acquired h/er papers. The work extends the cut-up method of Brion Gysin and William S. Burroughs from the page to the photograph — and, in the pandrogyny project undertaken with h/er late wife Lady Jaye Breyer P-Orridge, to the body itself, pursued through matching plastic surgeries as a single merged identity. The unpaginated 128-page first edition, bound in boards patterned with the diamond-lattice photomontages, includes a folding color poster and two loose color postcards.

Before being recognized as a visual artist, P-Orridge founded the COUM Transmissions collective and the pioneering industrial band Throbbing Gristle in 1970s Britain, later fronting Psychic TV museum recognition followed with S/he is Her/e at the Andy Warhol Museum, Pittsburgh (2013) and Try to Altar Everything at the Rubin Museum, New York (2016). This is the library's first P-Orridge title, joining the collage holdings alongside Stezaker, Linder, and the cut-up tradition the collection traces.

title: Unusual View of Unknown Subjects
description:
Unusual View of Unknown Subjects is the first book by the Swiss artist Simon Rimaz (b. 1987), winner of the Unseen Dummy Award in 2014. It excavates American press-photo archives by cutting away exactly what was published, leaving only the discarded margins of each picture.

Working from press prints gathered in United States newspaper archives, Rimaz follows the stigmata of publication (grease-pencil crop marks, strike-outs, stamps and index annotations) and excises the portion of the photograph the public actually saw. What remains is the picture's unseen perimeter: an inversion that turns editorial cropping into a cutting tool and asks what a photograph's claim to depict "that-which-has-been" still amounts to once its subject is removed. Lecturis, Eindhoven published the 144-page, 24 × 30 cm paperback in 2015, the year after the dummy won at Unseen Amsterdam the design, by Pierre Girardin with the artist, wraps the book in the black marker kill-marks of the archive itself.

Rimaz lives and works in Lausanne, trained at the Vevey School of Photography (CEPV), and works across photography, sculpture, installation and video. He has had solo exhibitions at Photoforum PasquArt, Biel, and Galerie Forma, Lausanne, and his work is held by Photo Elysée, Lausanne. In the collage collection his surgical excisions of found photographs sit naturally beside John Stezaker's cut film stills, the same act of removal doing the work of picturing.

title: Ada: A Series of Collages
description:
Ada: A Series of Collages is the announcement card for Jack Walls's 2008 exhibition at Fuse Gallery in the East Village. Mounted at fifty, it was the Chicago-born artist's fine-art solo debut: collages cut from imagery sourced from Robert Mapplethorpe, whose partner and muse Walls had been through the 1980s.

The 4 × 6 inch card fronts one of the Ada works: a black-and-white studio portrait of a young man sliced into rhythmic crescent cuts and remounted on a pale painted ground, the figure surfacing between the blades. The reverse carries the particulars: February 23 through March 22, 2008 at 93 Second Avenue, the gallery in the back room of Lit Lounge, with an opening reception on the 23rd and a video installation by Zachary Stuart-Pontier. The card comes from Gallery 98, the online archive of downtown New York art ephemera.

Walls met Mapplethorpe in the early 1980s and remained his partner and muse until the photographer's death in 1989, then built a practice of his own across writing, painting, and collage, and became an elder to the downtown generation of Ryan McGinley, Dan Colen, and Dash Snow. He lives and works in Hudson, New York. This is the first Jack Walls item in the library, filed with the collage collection's ephemera.

title: Collected Works. Study Edition, Volume 2: 1947–1963
editor: Peter W. Kunhardt, Jr., Paul Roth
contributors: Henry Louis Gates, Jr. (Text), Deborah Willis (Text), Maurice Berger (Text), Barbara Baker Burrows (Text)
description:
The second volume of Gordon Parks’s Collected Works, spanning the years on the staff of Life that made him the best known photographer at the magazine.

The volume covers 1947 to 1963, overlapping the close of Volume 1 and the opening of Volume 3. Its span takes in the assignments and extended picture stories on crime, poverty and the politics of race and class that Parks reported through the 1950s, and his fashion and portrait work of the same decade.

Peter W. Kunhardt, Jr. and Paul Roth edited the Study Edition, a smaller-format reissue of the 2012 Collected Works. It runs to 1,084 pages across five clothbound volumes, arranged chronologically. The printed cardboard box they ship in is part of the design, not packaging. Texts across the set are by Henry Louis Gates, Jr., Deborah Willis, Maurice Berger, Barbara Baker Burrows, Paul Roth and Parks himself. The library holds Volumes 1 to 3.

title: Gordon Parks: Stokely Carmichael and Black Power
publisher: Steidl / The Gordon Parks Foundation / Museum of Fine Arts, Houston
contributors: Cedric Johnson (Essay) Stokely Carmichael (Text (reprint of "What We Want," 1966))
description:
A landmark reappraisal of Gordon Parks's 1967 Life magazine essay "Whip of Black Power," his nuanced profile of Stokely Carmichael at the moment the young SNCC chairman's call for Black Power made him the most controversial figure in the civil rights movement.

On contract with Life, Parks shadowed Carmichael from fall 1966 through spring 1967 as he gave speeches and built the movement, capturing his intelligence and humor in equal measure and revealing both the man behind the headlines and Parks's own sympathy for Black Power's message of self-determination. This clothbound volume gathers the essay and surrounding photographs with texts by curator Lisa Volpe and scholar Cedric Johnson, plus a full reprint of Carmichael's 1966 manifesto "What We Want." It accompanied the exhibition organized by the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, with The Gordon Parks Foundation (October 2022–January 2023).

Parks (1912–2006), the first Black staff photographer at Life and later a novelist, composer, and director of Shaft, documented American life from segregation-era Alabama to Harlem's streets. The book continues the Steidl/Gordon Parks Foundation series devoted to his major bodies of work, alongside The Atmosphere of Crime, 1957, Segregation Story, and Muhammad Ali.

title: Segregation Story: Expanded Edition
edition_printrun: Expanded edition, 2022 (2nd printing January 2023) original edition Steidl, 2014
contributors: Dawoud Bey (Essay) Maurice Berger (Essay) Charlayne Hunter-Gault (Essay)
description:
The expanded edition of Gordon Parks’ Segregation Story, the definitive presentation of his 1956 color photographs of an African American family living under Jim Crow segregation in Alabama, images that became, in Parks’ words, a “weapon of choice” against racism.

On assignment for Life, Parks spent weeks with the extended Thornton family near Mobile and Shady Grove, Alabama, photographing daily life (churchgoing, farm work, shopping beneath “White Only” signs) in saturated color. Twenty-six images ran in the September 24, 1956 issue as “The Restraints: Open and Hidden” the bulk of the assignment was thought lost until The Gordon Parks Foundation recovered more than 70 transparencies in 2011. Revising Steidl’s 2014 edition, this 2022 volume adds some 30 previously unpublished photographs and enhanced reproductions from the original transparencies, with a new essay by Dawoud Bey joining first-edition texts by Maurice Berger and Charlayne Hunter-Gault.

Parks (1912–2006), the first African American staff photographer at Life and later the director of The Learning Tree and Shaft, documented American life from the 1940s into the 2000s Steidl and the Foundation continue to publish his archive, including Invisible Man with Ralph Ellison.

title: American Gothic: Gordon Parks and Ella Watson
publisher: Steidl / The Gordon Parks Foundation / Minneapolis Institute of Art
contributors: Melanee C. Harvey (Text) Hank Willis Thomas (Text) Salamishah Tillet (Text) Deborah Willis (Text)
description:
A definitive study of one of the most celebrated photographs of the twentieth century: Gordon Parks's 1942 portrait of Ella Watson, a Black government charwoman posed with broom and mop before an American flag, restaging Grant Wood's American Gothic as a visual reckoning with racially segregated Washington, D.C.

The book surveys the full series Parks made with Watson during his Farm Security Administration fellowship under Roy Stryker, gathering more than 50 photographs, some never before published, alongside archival material. Parks followed Watson from her work routines to family meals and the church where she served as deaconess, composing an intimate collaborative portrait of Black life in the wartime capital. With texts by Philip Brookman, Melanee C. Harvey, Hank Willis Thomas, Salamishah Tillet and Deborah Willis, the clothbound volume accompanied the exhibition organized by the Minneapolis Institute of Art (January 6–June 23, 2024), later presented at the Gordon Parks Foundation Gallery.

Gordon Parks (1912–2006) was the first Black staff photographer at Life magazine and a novelist, composer and filmmaker (Shaft, 1971). This volume joins the Steidl/Gordon Parks Foundation series devoted to his archive, alongside Segregation Story and The Atmosphere of Crime, 1957.

title: Born Black: A Personal Report on the Decade of Black Revolt 1960–1970
edition_printrun: First Steidl edition, March 2024 (expanded edition of the 1971 original)
description:
The expanded Steidl edition of Gordon Parks's 1971 Born Black, the first book to unite his photography and his writing in a firsthand account of the civil rights and Black Power movements of the 1960s.

The book gathers the nine series Parks produced for Life between 1963 and 1970: a rare look inside San Quentin State Prison, extensive documentation of the Black Muslim movement and the Black Panthers, reflections on the deaths of Malcolm X and Martin Luther King, Jr., portraits of Stokely Carmichael, Muhammad Ali and Eldridge Cleaver, and the daily life of Harlem's Fontenelle family. Co-published with The Gordon Parks Foundation and edited by Peter W. Kunhardt, Jr. and Michal Raz-Russo, this clothbound, 304-page edition expands the 1971 Lippincott original with additional photographs from each series, spreads from the first edition, early correspondence, reproductions of the related Life articles, and new essays by Jelani Cobb and Nicole R. Fleetwood.

Parks (1912–2006), the first Black staff photographer at Life and also a novelist, composer and filmmaker (Shaft), left an unmatched record of American life centered on race, poverty and the struggle for justice. Born Black is a cornerstone of that legacy and joins Steidl and the Foundation's ongoing series of his books, among them Segregation Story.

title: Thomas Demand
description:
An essential catalog documenting German artist Thomas Demand's (b. 1964) exhibition at the Serpentine Gallery, London, from June to August 2006, published jointly by Serpentine Gallery and Schirmer/Mosel in a limited edition of 1,000 copies.

The publication centers on Demand's distinctive process: he meticulously reconstructs spaces—kitchens, parking garages, elevators, bureaucratic interiors—at full scale using only paper and cardboard, photographs the constructed environments with exacting precision, then destroys the models. The resulting images oscillate between documentary authenticity and uncanny artifice, their subjects often drawn from mass-media images of politically or historically charged sites. Beatriz Colomina's accompanying essay, "Media as Modern Architecture," examines how contemporary architecture relies on mass-media imagery, while an interview between Demand and filmmaker Alexander Kluge explores the conceptual implications of the artist's three-dimensional to two-dimensional transformation process. Designed by Supermarket/Naomi Mizusaki, the catalog includes wallpaper swatches from the exhibition installation.

Thomas Demand came to international prominence in the 1990s as a key figure in German contemporary photography alongside Andreas Gursky, Thomas Struth, and Candida Höfer. His work is held in major collections including MoMA, Tate, and the Guggenheim, and he is represented by Sprüth Magers, Matthew Marks Gallery, and Esther Schipper. The Serpentine exhibition marked a significant mid-career survey of his photographic oeuvre, examining how his meticulously crafted paper reconstructions interrogate the relationship between image, memory, and truth.
tags: Photography, Conceptual Art, German Art, Installation Art, Contemporary Photography
notes: Limited edition of 1,000 copies. Catalog design by Supermarket/Naomi Mizusaki. Includes wallpaper swatches from the exhibition. Also published in a German edition by Schirmer/Mosel (ISBN 9783829602495). Summer acquisitions 2026.

title: Rarely Seen Bas Jan Ader Film
description:
A layered work of appropriation and myth-making by the California conceptual artist David Horvitz (b. 1978), published as the nineteenth title in 2nd Cannons Publications' artist book series in 2009, in an edition of 500 copies.

The flipbook comprises 152 sequential stills extracted from a brief black-and-white film uploaded to YouTube in 2007 under the title "Rarely Seen Bas Jan Ader Film." The video depicted a figure biking into the ocean and claimed to be footage discovered in Dutch conceptual artist Bas Jan Ader's locker at UC Irvine following his mysterious disappearance at sea in 1975 during a solo transatlantic sailing voyage. YouTube removed the video after a third-party copyright complaint, rendering Horvitz's flipbook a significant archival trace of this contested footage. Each copy originally included a two-sided newsprint produced for Horvitz's exhibition at the 2nd Cannons project space. The work operates in the ambiguous terrain between documentation and fabrication, raising questions about authenticity, artist mythology, and the circulation of images in the digital age.

David Horvitz is known for conceptual projects that explore time, geography, distribution, and participation across photography, performance, digital media, and artist books. His practice often involves unconventional sites of presentation (billboards, airports, public spaces) and ephemeral or networked actions. This flipbook engages directly with the legacy of Bas Jan Ader (1942–1975), whose disappearance while attempting to sail from Massachusetts to England solidified his status as a legendary figure in conceptual art, and whose final work In Search of the Miraculous remains one of art history's most poignant unfinished pieces.
tags: Conceptual Art, Photography, Artists' Books, Flipbooks, Appropriation Art, Internet Art, Art
notes: 2nd Cannons Publications #019. Each copy originally included a two-sided newsprint produced for the exhibition. The original YouTube video was removed following a copyright infringement complaint. Summer acquisitions 2026.

title: Communist Guide to New York City
description:
An archival photographic guide documenting the hidden topography of American communist history in New York City, published by common books in 2008 in an edition of 500 copies with support from the Graham Foundation for Advanced Studies in the Fine Arts.

The 180-page book comprises 76 photographs of buildings, public places, and sites throughout New York that are connected to the history of the Communist Party USA: former party headquarters, residences of communist leaders, sites of strikes and demonstrations, and courthouses where communist figures stood trial. Each location is accompanied by explanatory captions and neighborhood maps that situate the sites within the city's geography, creating a parallel history of New York legible only through Fiks's lens. Designed by Geoffrey Han and edited by common room, the book includes essays by Olga Kopenkina, Kim Förster, and Fiks himself, examining the relationship between place, political memory, and the erasure of radical history from public consciousness. The monochrome offset-printed guide, glue and sewn bound with a green cover emblazoned with hammer-and-sickle dollar signs, functions both as artist's book and activist cartography.

Yevgeniy Fiks is a New York-based artist whose work explores intersections of Soviet history, American communist movements, LGBTQ+ politics, and Jewish identity through archival investigation, institutional critique, and photographic documentation. His practice examines how ideological histories are encoded in urban space and cultural memory, often focusing on suppressed or marginalized political narratives. Other projects include Lenin for Your Library! (2012–ongoing), which placed Lenin's writings in public libraries, and Dictionary of the Queer International (2021), documenting LGBTQ+ terms across communist and post-communist contexts.
tags: Photography, Political Art, Documentary Photography, Artists' Books, Urban History, Communism, New York
notes: Funded by the Graham Foundation for Advanced Studies in the Fine Arts. Distributed through multiple independent bookstores and cultural venues in New York, Berlin, Chicago, Montreal, Moscow, and Paris. Monochrome offset printed. Stock ID: 110514 D. Summer acquisitions 2026.

title: Pier Groups: Art and Sex Along the New York Waterfront
description:
A landmark study of the abandoned Hudson River piers of 1970s Manhattan, where avant-garde art-making and a newly liberated queer sexual culture converged in the same fire-ravaged structures, written by the painter and art historian Jonathan Weinberg as part art history, part memoir.

Weaving interviews, documentary photographs, literary texts, artworks, and film stills, Weinberg reconstructs how the derelict piers, at the center of the world's busiest shipping port only two decades earlier, became simultaneously makeshift studios and exhibition spaces (Pier 34) and what Delmas Howe called an "arena for sexual theater" (Pier 46) in the years after Stonewall. The book gathers one hundred exemplary works by artists as varied as Vito Acconci, Alvin Baltrop, Gordon Matta-Clark, Shelley Seccombe, and David Wojnarowicz, examining the relationship of avant-garde practice to resistant subcultures and radical sexuality. Published by Penn State University Press in 2019, with 34 color and 66 black-and-white illustrations.

Weinberg is a painter, art historian, and curator of the Maurice Sendak Foundation who teaches at the Yale School of Art and RISD. The author of Male Desire: The Homoerotic in American Art and Ambition and Love in Modern American Art, he was lead curator of the touring exhibition Art After Stonewall, 1969-1989, organized by the Columbus Museum of Art for the fiftieth anniversary of the Stonewall riots his paintings are held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Montclair Art Museum.

title: The Shabbiness of Beauty
description:
A cross-generational visual dialogue between the New York photographer and writer Moyra Davey (b. 1958) and Peter Hujar (1934–1987), in which Davey mines Hujar's archive for little-known images and answers them with photographs of her own.

Drawing mainly on scarcely seen pictures from the Hujar archive, Davey pairs his work with her own responses across an idiosyncratic set of shared subjects: nudes, animals, water, babies, and city streets. The sequence is spiritually anchored in New York even as it ranges out to rural Quebec and Pennsylvania, crystallising tensions between city and country, human and animal, and between Davey's postmodern sensibility and Hujar's humanist one. The book follows the exhibition Davey curated at Galerie Buchholz in spring 2020 and includes a new text by Eileen Myles, Davey's text for that show, and a note by Stephen Koch on a Hujar letter reproduced in the book. Debossed printed hardback, 128 pages, published by MACK in 2021.

Davey, known for works such as the Copperhead series and her essay-films, pairs photography with language throughout her practice Hujar, a central figure of downtown New York's queer artistic circles, left an archive whose portraits, nudes, and animal studies have shaped contemporary photography. The volume joins the library's other Hujar holdings, including Peter Hujar: A Retrospective and Hujar:Contact.
