title: The My Comrade Anthology
description:
The My Comrade Anthology gathers the campy, radical heart of Les (Linda) Simpson's legendary New York drag zine into a 256-page newsprint volume, published by Boo-Hooray in 2022 for the magazine's 35th anniversary.

Selected by Simpson from past issues, the anthology surveys a zine that set itself apart from the deluge of Xeroxed titles in late-1980s New York: through parody of both mainstream tabloids and the self-serious gay press, an ironic sensibility, and radical-left sloganeering, My Comrade captured the zeitgeist of the gay downtown scene. Eleven issues appeared between 1987 and 1994, several flipped with the lesbian companion magazine Sister!, with covers and features starring RuPaul, Lady Bunny, Tabboo!, and the Pyramid Club orbit. Printed offset on newsprint in illustrated wraps, the volume was published on the occasion of the exhibition My Comrade Magazine: Happy 35th Gay Anniversary at Howl! Happening, which also prompted a new issue.

Simpson, a pioneering drag performer, publisher, and photographer, has become a de facto historian of queer downtown New York: her slideshow and photo archive The Drag Explosion documents the scene from the late 1980s through the 1990s, the My Comrade archives were acquired by Harvard's Houghton Library in 2021, and the zine featured in the Brooklyn Museum's Copy Machine Manifestos: Artists Who Make Zines.

title: The Piers
publisher: Szaransky Print Co. and Kapp Kapp
description:
The first book devoted solely to Stanley Stellar's photographs of Manhattan's West Side piers, an essential document of the ruined waterfront that served as daylight sanctuary, cruising ground, and open-air studio for New York's queer community in the decade before AIDS and demolition erased it.

Drawn from Stellar's vast archive, the book presents more than 70 color and black-and-white documentary, portrait, and street photographs made at the piers from the late 1970s through the late 1980s, when the structures were officially torn down. Among the subjects is photographer Peter Hujar, seen in Peter at the Door (1981). The volume opens with a new essay by art historian Desiree Mitton and includes an extensive interview with Stellar by artist Gabriel Martinez. Edited by Sam and Daniel Kapp with clothbound design by Honza Zamojski, it was produced on the occasion of Stanley Stellar: The Piers, the inaugural exhibition at Kapp Kapp's Tribeca gallery (January 15 – February 19, 2022) and the first survey of this body of work.

Stellar (b. 1945, Brooklyn) has photographed gay life in New York since the years following Stonewall, from Christopher Street to his Tribeca studio, building one of the most sustained visual records of the city's gay community. His work is held in the collections of the Museum of Modern Art, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, Harvard Art Museums, and Yale University Art Gallery, and this volume joins earlier publications including Stellar Men (1992).

title: 63 E 9th Street: NYC Polaroids 1975-1983
description:
A charged, intimate portrait of gay New York in the years before AIDS, Tom Bianchi's 63 E 9th Street gathers the Polaroids he made in his East Village apartment between 1975 and 1983.

Bianchi moved to New York in 1975 to work as in-house counsel at Columbia Pictures, which gave him the Polaroid SX-70 he carried to Fire Island on summer weekends those beach pictures became the 2013 book Fire Island Pines: Polaroids 1975-1983. Published by Damiani some forty-four years after they were taken, the 262 images collected here are that book's interior counterpart. Where Fire Island offered a communal experience under huge open skies, the apartment at 63 E 9th Street was, in Bianchi's words, an intimate, track-lit den, a safe stage where he and his friends played out erotic night games. The New York Times called the work "a compelling, charged portrait of gay men in New York, depicted in their sexual prime in the golden years before the major devastation of AIDS."

Bianchi (b. 1945, Chicago) left corporate law in the 1980s to work full-time as an artist, and over three decades of monographs, from Out of the Studio to the Fire Island Polaroids, has built one of the most sustained photographic records of American gay life. 63 E 9th Street is the essential companion volume to Fire Island Pines and an important document of urban gay culture.

title: Physique
description:
A major visual archive of the clandestine golden age of American physique photography, drawn entirely from the private collection of Vince Aletti, the New York critic and curator who has spent five decades assembling one of the most significant holdings of this once-underground material.

Physique reproduces more than 250 rare photographic prints by pioneering studios and photographers including Bob Mizer's Athletic Model Guild, Bruce Bellas (Bruce of Los Angeles), and Don Whitman's Western Photography Guild. Sold discreetly through mail-order catalogues and physique magazines that posed as fitness publications, these images of posed male bodies constituted a coded homoerotic visual culture made largely by and for gay men under legal threat, in which photographic prints offered connection, solace, and an emergent queer visibility. A personal essay by Aletti traces the historical and political significance of the pictures and celebrates the artistry of the photographers, models, and studios behind them. Designed by Bruce Usher as a debossed flexibound volume, the book carries back-cover tributes from Nan Goldin, Collier Schorr, and Ryan McGinley, and appeared alongside a 2025 exhibition of prints from the collection at Dashwood Projects, New York.

Aletti (b. 1945), longtime photography critic for the Village Voice and The New Yorker and the first journalist to write about disco, is among the most influential chroniclers of photography's printed forms. Physique is his second collaboration with SPBH Editions, following The Drawer (2022), and extends the collection-based books Male (2008) and Issues: A History of Photography in Fashion Magazines (Phaidon, 2019).

title: Bill Jacobson: 1989-1997
edition_printrun: First edition, printed by EBS, Verona
description:
A survey of the nine years in which Bill Jacobson (b. 1955) made his signature out-of-focus photographs, images conceived amid the AIDS crisis as meditations on desire, loss, and photography's role as a vehicle for remembrance.

Published by Twin Palms in 1998, the book gathers 49 tritone plates spanning the bodies of work Jacobson produced between 1989 and 1997: the pale, spectral Interim portraits, figures, couples, and landscapes the darker Song of Sentient Beings series, in which defocused figures emerge from deep black grounds and the nearly monochromatic Thought Series linking the human figure to nature. Deliberately unresolved, the pictures function, in Jacobson's words, as metaphors for the way the mind works, collecting some images while letting others go, fading as memories and photographs themselves fade. The volume includes "Lost Profile," a short story written for the book by the critic and curator Klaus Kertess, and was printed in tritone on heavy coated stock by EBS in Verona.

Born in Norwich, Connecticut, and trained at Brown University and the San Francisco Art Institute, Jacobson began blurring his lens in 1989 as the epidemic's losses mounted, and this volume remains the definitive record of that first decade. His photographs are held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, SFMOMA, the Museum of Fine Arts Boston, and the Victoria and Albert Museum, and his later series, from New Year's Day to A Series of Human Decisions and Lines in My Eyes, turned the same searching attention toward color, place, and focus itself.

title: Alphabet
description:
An intimate abecedarium of the male body by Peter McGough (b. 1958), one half of the duo McDermott & McGough, who posed nude models into each letter of the alphabet and rendered the results as 26 spectral, deeply queer cyanotypes.

The staged photographs were made in a single day in McGough's Canal Street studio around 2008, then set aside for fifteen years before being printed with the cameraless, UV-exposed cyanotype process, whose inky Prussian-blue tonality gives the images their painterly cast. The poses draw on Hellenistic sculpture and queer photographic histories, recalling Baron Wilhelm von Gloeden's tableaux vivants. Karma published this 56-page clothbound volume to accompany Alphabet at its 172 East 2nd Street gallery in New York, November 1&ndashDecember 21, 2024, where the prints hung in alphabetical rows modeled on Alfred Stieglitz's 291 gallery.

Since 1980 McGough has collaborated with David McDermott as McDermott & McGough, the downtown New York dandies whose Victorian-era time experiment extended to working in antiquated processes such as cyanotype, platinum, and salt printing. Creators of the Oscar Wilde Temple (2017), the duo's work is held by Tate Modern, the Whitney, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art McGough is also the author of the memoir I've Seen the Future and I'm Not Going (2019).

A psychedelic meditation on masculinity, the second volume of Jack Pierson's (b. 1960) Tomorrow's Man series doubles down on the collision of vintage beefcake and contemporary art that made the inaugural Lynn Valley volume a cult object.

Published by Bywater Bros. Editions in 2014, edited and designed by Pierson with publisher Roger Bywater, the 112-page softcover splices imagery appropriated from the 1950s-60s bodybuilding magazine that lends the series its name into contributions from fifteen artists working in wildly different registers — among them illustrator Mel Odom, painters Jeff Elrod, Paulo Monteiro and Richard Tinkler, conceptualist Alejandro Cesarco, ceramicist Dan McCarthy and photographer Evan Whale — with a short story by Veralyn Behenna rounding out the volume. Pierson, who emerged from the Boston School alongside Nan Goldin and Mark Morrisroe, has made the artist's book a central strand of a practice spanning photography, collage and found-letter word sculptures his work is held by the Metropolitan Museum, the Whitney and the Guggenheim. title: The Hungry Years
description:
A tender, unguarded chronicle of American youth in the shadow of the AIDS era, The Hungry Years gathers Jack Pierson's (b. 1960) early photographs of the 1980s, the images that made his name as a member of the Boston School and that have only grown in stature since they were first editioned in 1990.

Shot among friends and lovers in bedrooms, motels and along the roadsides of an itinerant decade, the photographs are inherently autobiographical, trading in traditional Americana motifs whose bright, distanced surfaces reveal the uncanny running beneath the quotidian. Melancholy and introspective yet buoyed by homoeroticism, seduction and glamour, they frame what Pierson has called his ultimate subject: hope. The 104-page clothbound volume, published by Damiani in 2017 with a tipped-in cover image, opens with an introduction by the poet Eileen Myles and a foreword by photographer Stephen Shore.

Pierson emerged from the Boston School alongside Nan Goldin, David Armstrong, Philip-Lorca diCorcia and Mark Morrisroe, and has spent more than three decades moving across photography, drawing, painting and his signature found-letter word sculptures to examine the intimate and emotional registers of everyday life. His work is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art and the Guggenheim, among others the collection also holds his Photology monograph Jack Pierson.

title: Jesus and Nazimova
description:
A slate-blue softcover catalogue for Jack Pierson's 2012 exhibition at Xavier Hufkens, Brussels, a melancholic hymn to fame, desire, and the passage of time built around two emblematic 'gods of love': the crucified Christ of Velázquez's Prado masterpiece and the silent-film idol Rudolph Valentino.

Published to accompany Pierson's third exhibition with the Brussels gallery (7 September – 13 October 2012), the 56-page volume carries an essay by the art historian and critic Elisabeth Lebovici. It documents word sculptures assembled from found sign letters (Nazimova, Fame, Symbolism, Souvenirs, Last Century) alongside a life-size photograph of Velázquez's crucifixion, folded pigment prints, automatic drawings, and an actual door salvaged from Falcon Lair, Valentino's Hollywood estate. The Nazimova of the title is Alla Nazimova (1879–1945), the Russian-born actress and queer Hollywood icon whose circle included Valentino's wife, the designer Natacha Rambova.

Pierson (b. 1960, Plymouth, Massachusetts) emerged from the Boston School alongside Nan Goldin, David Armstrong, and Mark Morrisroe, and is best known for the found-letter word sculptures and photographs that thread longing, glamour, and gay desire through American vernacular culture. His work is held by MoMA, the Whitney, and the Guggenheim, and this catalogue sits alongside Andre, Array (Miami Beach), and the Photology monograph in the collection.

title: Chi Chi LaRue's Live and Raw
edition_printrun: First edition (a signed hardcover edition of 750 was also issued paperback reissue 2005, ISBN 9783861879510)
description:
A pink-spined artifact of gay adult entertainment's print era: Chi Chi LaRue's Live and Raw gathers erotic photographs of the performers of LaRue's films, published in 2004 by Berlin's Bruno Gmünder, then the leading gay publishing house in Europe.

Across 80 pages, the hardcover presents the models who starred in LaRue's productions in the director's signature high-gloss studio style — tattooed, denim-clad pin-ups shot against saturated club-lit backdrops, the book functioning as both portfolio and promotional object for her video empire. A signed hardcover edition of 750 copies was also issued, and a paperback reissue followed in 2005 the title has been out of print since Gmünder's closure in 2017.

Chi Chi LaRue is the drag persona of Larry David Paciotti (b. 1959, Hibbing, Minnesota), among the most prolific and influential directors in gay adult film, with nearly 500 director credits, five GayVN Best Director awards, and a place on Out magazine's list of the 50 most influential people in LGBT+ culture. This book is one of the few print monuments to a career built almost entirely on screen.

title: The Wild Ones: The Erotic Photography of Mel Roberts
edition_printrun: First edition, limited to 3,000 casebound copies
description:
A defiant anthology by Mel Roberts (1923-2007), the Los Angeles photographer whose sun-saturated color images of California youth, twice seized by the LAPD, became a touchstone of pre-liberation queer visual culture.

The second of FotoFactory Press's two Roberts anthologies, carrying the series banner California Boys on its cover, The Wild Ones gathers roughly 200 color photographs of young men made between 1956 and 1980, among them images confiscated by the Los Angeles Police Department in the late 1970s and reproduced here from surviving prints and from negatives and transparencies Roberts processed himself, since commercial labs of the era refused to develop male nudes. Edited by David Sprigle with Roberts, the first edition was limited to 3,000 casebound copies and published in conjunction with an exhibition at the David Aden Gallery, Venice Beach.

Born in Toledo, Ohio, Roberts served as a combat cameraman in the South Pacific, took a film degree at USC, and worked in Hollywood, including as music editor on the blacklisted Salt of the Earth, before turning his Rolleiflex on the tanned, boy-next-door models of the physique press. Living openly as a gay man and active in the early Mattachine Society, he amassed some 50,000 photographs of nearly 200 models before LAPD raids in 1977 and 1979 ended his career by 1981. His estate is represented by CLAMP, New York the companion volume is California Boys: Photographs from the 1960s and 1970s (FotoFactory Press, 2000).

title: Legends: Men of Falcon
description:
A high-gloss anthology from Berlin's Bruno Gmünder Verlag drawing on the photographic archive of Falcon Studios, the San Francisco company that, more than any other, manufactured the commercial image of American gay erotica in the closing decades of the twentieth century.

Promoted at publication as the first and only photo book of Falcon photographs, Legends collects 136 color images across 133 pages: studio promotional stills and set photography of the company's marquee models, among them Ken Ryker, Mike Branson, Jeremy Penn, Joey Stefano and Trent Black. The pictures codify the Falcon house style: athletic, all-American physique photography staged with locker-room and workwear props, the cover model posed with a football helmet and jockstrap. First issued in 1999, the book returned in this Berlin softcover edition of 2004, bound in navy pictorial wraps.

Falcon Studios was founded in San Francisco in 1971 by Chuck Holmes, who built it into the largest producer of gay adult film and whose philanthropy later put his name on the city's LGBT Community Center. Bruno Gmünder Verlag, the Berlin house founded in 1981, was for decades Europe's leading gay publisher, and its photo-book program (of which the Falcon titles, including the companion Young Men of Falcon, were a fixture) circulated this imagery well beyond the video-store context that produced it.

title: Love... Hate... Nature.
edition_printrun: Limited edition of 150 numbered copies plus 25 artist's proofs each copy includes a signed original inkjet print tipped in at the last page
description:
The first book by New York photographer Jeremy Kost (b. 1977, Corpus Christi, Texas), Love... Hate... Nature. is an intimate Polaroid study of the model Max Emerson, published by the International Center of Photography in 2009 in a signed, numbered edition of just 150 copies.

Across 62 color plates printed recto only, Kost follows Emerson and a stuffed tiger through a voyeuristic, erotically charged romp, embracing the technical restrictions of the obsolescent Polaroid camera — uneven luminosity, fuzzy contours, and the disarming promise of an immediately tangible picture. The softbound volume, issued in conjunction with Dress Codes, the Third ICP Triennial of Photography and Video (2009–2010), carries a tipped-in original inkjet print in Polaroid format, signed by the artist, in each of its 150 numbered copies and 25 artist's proofs.

Kost is known as New York's Polaroid artist, extending the instant-film portrait tradition of Warhol and Hockney into the city's queer nightlife with images of drag performers, go-go boys, and downtown personalities. This debut anticipates the later monographs It's Always Darkest Before Dawn, Fractured, and Isolated but Not Alone, in which single frames give way to sprawling Polaroid composites.

title: Toscana
description:
The opening volume of Matthias Herrmann's Toscana series, a limited-edition artist's book of erotic self-portraits staged in the olive groves and woodland around the photographer's home in rural Tuscany, published by Printed Matter, New York, in 2005 in an edition of 500.

In this unpaginated softcover, Herrmann turns the pastoral landscape near Riparbella into a stage for queer self-presentation, photographing himself amid the trees and grasses in one-man tableaux that shift between the idyllic and the explicit. The book carries a text by the Australian painter Peter Maloney and, in a characteristically playful credit, "selected underwear" by the Toronto artist and queer-scene organizer Will Munro. It launched a sustained series continued in Toscana 2 (2008, with texts by AA Bronson, Gregg Bordowitz, Christophe Chemin, and John Giorno), Toscana 3 (2009), and Toscana Dance (2010), all published by Printed Matter.

Herrmann (b. Munich, 1963) danced with the Vienna State Opera Ballet before studying at the University of Applied Arts Vienna, and has made the artist's book the primary carrier of a photographic practice centered on identity, the male body, and homosexual desire. President of the Vienna Secession from 1999 to 2006 and professor of art and photography at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna, he has also published extensively with FOTOHOF edition, Salzburg, including 8x10, A-Z, and Mantua Mantua.

title: Portfolio
description:
A late-life, artist-authorized collection of drawings by REX (1943–2024), the famously secretive American illustrator whose pointillist pen-and-ink images of leathermen, hustlers, and rough trade defined the graphic idiom of gay S&M culture alongside Tom of Finland and Etienne.

Portfolio was issued under REX's own imprint, REX Publications, whose web storefront at rexbooks.press offered a small program of print-on-demand editions in 2022–2023 — Rough Trade, Leather Cult, Posters and Portraits, and reissues of the bound portfolios Männespielen and ICONS among them. Listed in the imprint's "standard edition collection," this US-letter-format paperback compiles images from the unbound 8-by-10-inch portfolios (Rexwerk, Uncut, Undercover, Armageddon, Scorpio, Rexland, Legends) that REX sold by mail order for four decades through his business Drawings by REX. The cover carries his winged-figure drawing beneath a red title band the spine reads rexbooks.press.

REX began drawing in mid-1960s New York, when explicit photography was still illegal but drawing was protected speech, and his work ran in Drummer, Straight to Hell, and Honcho his posters for the Mineshaft, the notorious New York sex club, sold in the tens of thousands and appeared in the film Cruising. He influenced Robert Mapplethorpe, published the hardcover Rexwerk (Paris, 1986) and the retrospective Verboten (Bruno Gmünder, 2012), was inducted into the Leather Hall of Fame in 2022, and died in Amsterdam, his home since 2010, in March 2024.

title: Cruis'n: Uncovering Gay Design History Through Collecting
description:
A collector's archive turned work of visual storytelling, Cruis'n is graphic designer Rick Heffner's 312-page excavation of postwar gay print culture: the physique magazines, pulp paperbacks, pamphlets, protest buttons, and posters through which gay men found identity, community, and each other in an analog world.

Built from Heffner's own collection of historical gay memorabilia, the book reproduces the material at full scale in dense, collaged spreads: Athletic Model Guild and Physique Pictorial imagery, RAM-10 pulp series covers, hanky codes and other secret languages of sex and survival, and the activist graphics of figures like Frank Kameny, Marsha P. Johnson, Sylvia Rivera, Harvey Milk, and ACT UP. Decades before the internet and hookup apps, Heffner argues, it was print culture (easy to disseminate, difficult to track) that let gay men find their compatriots the book aims to be an accessible archive that preserves that history. Developed as Heffner's MFA in Graphic Design thesis at Vermont College of Fine Arts, it was self-published in 2023 under his HEFF Publishing imprint in Alexandria, Virginia, as a large-format (30.5 × 22.9 cm) digitally printed paperback, and distributed through Printed Matter.

Heffner is a graphic design professor at George Mason University School of Art and creative director of the Alexandria studio Fuszion, whose clients have included the Smithsonian Institution and National Geographic. Named a fellow of Writing Space's Design Writing Fellowship, he is developing Cruis'n into an expanded trade book on gay design history.

title: Salvation
description:
A meditation on loss, death, and nothingness, Salvation is the final artist's book of East Village photographer Jimmy De Sana (1949-1990), conceived as he was dying of AIDS-related illness and published for the first time in 2024 by Primary Information, more than three decades after his death.

The book presents 44 of De Sana's late photographic abstractions: relics, body parts, flowers, and fruit transformed through collage and darkroom manipulation into images at once intimate and otherworldly. Variations of many of the works first appeared in his last exhibition at Pat Hearn Gallery in 1988 shortly afterward he began assembling a maquette for the book, using black-and-white images as placeholders for the color works he intended for the final layout. On his deathbed he dictated completion instructions to his longtime friend, the artist Laurie Simmons, whose studio matched extant slides to his sequence and selected color gels from his archive to realize each image. The result is a quiet, sophisticated counterpoint to the bold political statements that dominated art made in response to the HIV/AIDS crisis.

De Sana was a central figure of New York's downtown scene of the 1970s and 80s, moving through mail art, punk, and No Wave circles and producing a body of photography known for saturated color, concealed figures, and surreal stagings of suburbia and queer fetish subculture, most famously in Submission (1980), made with writer Terence Sellers with an introduction by William S. Burroughs. His estate, overseen by Simmons and represented by P·P·O·W, New York, was the subject of the retrospective Jimmy DeSana: Submission at the Brooklyn Museum in 2022-23.

title: Fire Island Art: 100 Years
contributors: Sam Ashby (Essay) AA Bronson (Essay) Michael Bullock (Essay) Fabio Cherstich (Essay) Marc Christensen (Essay) Andrew Durbin (Essay) Jarrett Earnest (Essay) Philip Gefter (Essay) Carl Little (Essay) Richard Meyer (Essay) Jack Parlett (Essay) Ksenia M. Soboleva (Essay) Lola Flash (Interview) Pamela Sneed (Interview) Wolfgang Tillmans (Interview)
description:
The first book to survey a century of art made on Fire Island, edited by historian John Dempsey: a richly illustrated account of the slender barrier island's outsized role as a haven and engine of queer artmaking from the 1930s to the present.

Published by Monacelli in 2026, the 304-page volume unfolds in fifteen chapters, each written by a leading art writer and centered on a group of friends and collaborators. Historic figures (Paul Cadmus, David Hockney, Peter Hujar, Robert Mapplethorpe, Paul Thek, Andy Warhol) share the pages with the explosion of art-making on the island over the past fifteen years, represented by TM Davy, Nicole Eisenman, Lola Flash, K8 Hardy, Lyle Ashton Harris, Doron Langberg, Wolfgang Tillmans, and Salman Toor. Essays by Sam Ashby, AA Bronson, Michael Bullock, Andrew Durbin, Jarrett Earnest, Philip Gefter, Richard Meyer, Jack Parlett, Ksenia M. Soboleva, and others sit alongside interviews with Flash, Pamela Sneed, and Tillmans, drawing on archival materials, some never before published.

Dempsey, a technology executive and historian who serves as president of the Fire Island Pines Historical Society, built the book out of the Society's living archive in 2025 he also helped return the cult classic The Butch Manual to print. Kirkus awarded the book a starred review, calling it "a lush survey that makes a powerful case for Fire Island as a wellspring of queer art."

title: Donovan
contributors: Bruce LaBruce (Contributor) Daniel Riera (Contributor) Paco y Manolo (Contributor) Roberta Marrero (Contributor) Felix d'Eon (Contributor) Pol Anglada (Contributor) Luis Venegas (Contributor) Alberto de las Heras (Contributor) Leo Adef (Contributor) Ismael Alvarez (Contributor)
description:
A self-published queer zine from Barcelona, Donovan is filmmaker, writer, and activist Elio's love letter to pre-digital gay print culture, splicing homoerotic vintage imagery from the 1950s through the 1980s with new work by contemporary artists.

Each issue, its cover flagged simply "gay X rated," pairs archival physique-era photography and period graphic design with commissioned drawings, collages, and photographs from an international roster that has included Bruce LaBruce, Daniel Riera, Paco y Manolo, Roberta Marrero, Felix d'Eon, Pol Anglada, and Luis Venegas. The zine launched in December 2019 with a party at Bar Candy Darling in Barcelona organized with the LGBTQ+ bookshop Llibreria Antinous, and has run for at least five issues through 2023, circulating through queer bookshops such as Antinous (Barcelona) and Berkana (Madrid).

Elio, credited on bookseller listings as Elio Colen Mirete, edits and publishes Donovan as an independent project dedicated to the photographic culture and design of the 1950s-1980s seen from an LGBTI perspective, keeping the look and feel of the vintage gay magazines it draws on while placing them in dialogue with current queer image-makers.

title: (pôr'nə-graf'ik)
edition_printrun: First edition of 4,000 copies (a deluxe clamshell edition of 50 signed and numbered copies with an original print was also issued, ISBN 9780944092538)
description:
A deadpan behind-the-scenes document of California's adult-film industry by San Francisco photographer Ken Probst, its title printed on the black cover as a dictionary phonetic spelling — (pôr'nə-graf'ik) — that turns the loaded word into a specimen for examination.

Probst was hired to shoot publicity stills and video-box covers on pornographic film sets, and once inside began photographing everything the product shots leave out: elaborate sexual set-ups and actors waiting between takes, crew, lights, and longueurs, all given the same unblinking weight. The 48 duotone plates, by turns comic and unsettling, observe what the publisher calls the banality of manufacturing desire. A short story by the novelist A.M. Homes, "Ballad for the Beautiful Boy, or Why I Like Photography," accompanies the pictures. Twin Palms published the landscape-format hardcover in December 1998 in a first edition of 4,000 copies, alongside a deluxe clamshell edition of 50 signed and numbered copies containing an original print.

Probst (1952-2010) worked largely within the gay adult industry, and the book sits alongside the queer documentary photography of its decade long out of print, it is now a landmark of 1990s erotic photobook publishing, in the company of Twin Palms' other transgressive titles.

title: Jack Pierson: It's Not Dark Yet (Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac)
description:
An elegant gallery catalogue in black textured wraps stamped in gold Art Deco capitals, It's Not Dark Yet documents Jack Pierson's summer 2010 exhibition at Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac in Paris, an elegiac meditation on beauty, memory and loss carried almost entirely in drawing.

Published by the gallery to accompany Pierson's fifth solo show at its Paris Marais space (6 July – 6 September 2010), the 40-page volume reproduces the exhibition's nine ink drawings of Antinous (the drowned lover the Emperor Hadrian deified and memorialized across the ancient world) alongside large-format drawings of the silent-film star Pola Negri, pencil renderings of earlier word-pieces such as Glory and My sin, and the letter-sculpture Golden Years. An essay by Zoe Stillpass reads the show as Pierson at 'the edge of night, where memories, like nearly faded stars, still glisten.' The cover carries no title at all, only the artist's and gallery's names in gold foil on black.

Pierson (b. 1960, Plymouth, Massachusetts) emerged from the Boston School alongside Nan Goldin, David Armstrong and Mark Morrisroe, and moves across photography, drawing, installation and his signature found-letter word sculptures his work is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney and the Guggenheim. This slim Ropac catalogue sits with the collection's other Pierson volumes, including the Photology monograph Jack Pierson and The Hungry Years.

title: The Young and Evil: Queer Modernism in New York, 1930–1955
contributors: Ann Reynolds (Text) Kenneth E. Silver (Text) Michael Schreiber (Interview)
description:
The catalogue of Jarrett Earnest's acclaimed 2019 exhibition at David Zwirner, recovering a circle of queer artists and writers (Paul Cadmus, Pavel Tchelitchew, George Platt Lynes, Jared French, Margaret Hoening French, Fidelma Cadmus Kirstein, Bernard Perlin, George Tooker, Charles Henri Ford and their intimates) who pursued a figurative, body-driven modernism in New York between 1930 and 1955, when homosexuality was as transgressive for American culture as figuration was for modernist painting.

Taking its title from Ford and Parker Tyler's 1933 novel, the book documents the exhibition held at 533 West 19th Street (February 21 – April 13, 2019), gathering never-before-exhibited photographs, sculptures, drawings, and ephemera, including erotic material from the Kinsey Institute, alongside rarely seen major paintings such as Cadmus's Shore Leave (1933). New scholarship by art historians Ann Reynolds and Kenneth E. Silver and an interview with Alexander Jensen Yow by Michael Schreiber frame these interwoven lives 162 color illustrations are set in a kraft-board binding designed by McCall Associates.

Earnest, a New York critic and writer, is the author of What It Means to Write About Art (2018), editor of Peter Schjeldahl's Hot, Cold, Heavy, Light (2019), and host of the New York Review of Books podcast Private Life this catalogue remains his defining curatorial statement on queer modernism.

title: Treasures of Gay Art from the Leslie/Lohman Gay Art Foundation
edition_printrun: First trade edition (after a special limited edition of 100 copies)
contributors: Charles Leslie (Prefatory Note) Fritz Lohman (Prefatory Note) James M. Saslow (Mission Statement) Allen Ellenzweig (Essay)
description:
The first book-length survey of the collection of the Leslie/Lohman Gay Art Foundation, the pioneering New York institution — now the Leslie-Lohman Museum of Art — founded by Charles Leslie and Fritz Lohman to preserve gay art that much of the art world once refused to show or sought to destroy.

Edited and introduced by the Austrian curator Peter Weiermair, the volume presents nearly three hundred pages of works from the Foundation's holdings, organized by medium: paintings, drawings and prints, photographs, and sculpture and objects, with images by Paul Cadmus, Patrick Angus, Andy Warhol, and dozens of less familiar figures of gay erotic art. A prefatory note by Leslie and Lohman, a mission statement by art historian James M. Saslow, and Allen Ellenzweig's essay Pictures at an Exhibition frame the plates, and alphabetically arranged artist biographies and bibliographies close the book. This first trade edition followed a special limited edition of 100 copies.

The Foundation grew from a 1968 exhibition of gay erotic art that Leslie and Lohman staged in their SoHo loft chartered in 1990, it was accredited in 2016 as the Leslie-Lohman Museum of Art, the first museum devoted to LGBTQ+ art. Weiermair (1944–2021), longtime director of the Frankfurter Kunstverein, edited numerous surveys of the male nude in art and photography, and this catalog sits squarely within that body of curatorial work.

title: Physique (Naughty Edition)
edition_printrun: Naughty Edition: website-exclusive, 250 signed and numbered copies
description:
A major visual archive of the clandestine golden age of American physique photography, drawn entirely from the private collection of Vince Aletti, the New York critic and curator who has spent five decades assembling one of the most significant holdings of this once-underground material.

Physique reproduces more than 250 rare photographic prints by pioneering studios and photographers including Bob Mizer's Athletic Model Guild, Bruce Bellas (Bruce of Los Angeles), and Don Whitman's Western Photography Guild. Sold discreetly through mail-order catalogues and physique magazines that posed as fitness publications, these images of posed male bodies constituted a coded homoerotic visual culture made largely by and for gay men under legal threat, in which photographic prints offered connection, solace, and an emergent queer visibility. A personal essay by Aletti traces the historical and political significance of the pictures and celebrates the artistry of the photographers, models, and studios behind them. Designed by Bruce Usher as a debossed flexibound volume, the book carries back-cover tributes from Nan Goldin, Collier Schorr, and Ryan McGinley, and appeared alongside a 2025 exhibition of prints from the collection at Dashwood Projects, New York.

Aletti (b. 1945), longtime photography critic for the Village Voice and The New Yorker and the first journalist to write about disco, is among the most influential chroniclers of photography's printed forms. Physique is his second collaboration with SPBH Editions, following The Drawer (2022), and extends the collection-based books Male (2008) and Issues: A History of Photography in Fashion Magazines (Phaidon, 2019).
tags: Photography, Queer Culture, Physique Photography, Male Nudes, Vernacular Photography, Collections, SPBH Editions
notes: Naughty Edition of Aletti's Physique (SPBH Editions, 2025): website-exclusive edition of 250 signed and numbered copies with an alternative erotic cover and a signed image plate glued into the inside back cover. Standard edition catalogued separately (ISBN 9781915743879). Accessioned 2026-06-21, catalogued 2026-08-05 (Queer Culture collection).

title: 930 Vol 02: Concealed Identity 02: Transfiguration
binding: Paperback, perfect bound two-volume set with folded poster
description:
A two-volume artist book and poster set from Melbourne artist and publisher Tim Coghlan, continuing his Concealed Identity series, a catalogue of masked and hidden faces drawn from the 930 Archive, the image collection he has amassed daily from the internet since 2017.

Subtitled Transfiguration, this second volume sequences hundreds of found black-and-white images of concealment (ceremonial masks, surgical theatre, riot gear, costume and disguise) in dense grids across 364 pages. Coghlan frames the work in combative terms: "this book is a lethal weapon," the publisher's note begins, positioning the collection as a talisman against those who would intrude on a life. Published as Knowledge Editions Book No. 47 in an edition of 50, the set comprises two perfect-bound volumes and a folded poster.

Coghlan is a graphic designer who founded the Knowledge Editions imprint in 2012, building an output of zines and books that catalogue found imagery. The first volume, 930 Vol 01: Concealed Identity (2024), collected 779 mask images sourced over five years, its design a nod to Hans-Peter Feldmann's Voyeur the exhibition Hidden Fortress at the Tokyo gallery commune surveyed twenty years of his notebooks.
tags: Art, Found Photography, Appropriation Art, Archives, Masks, Australian Artists
notes: Knowledge Editions Book No. 47. Two-volume set with folded poster, black-and-white throughout, edition of 50.

title: Satura
contributors: Giorgio Di Domenico (Text); Filippo Bosco (Text); Chiara Portesine (Text); Michele Bertolino (Text)
description:
The first institutional monograph of the American painter Louis Fratino (b. 1993), published with the Centro per l'arte contemporanea Luigi Pecci, Prato: a decade of paintings, drawings, etchings, and sculpture keyed to the artist's relationship with Italy.

Produced for Fratino's exhibition at the Centro Pecci (September 26, 2024 to February 2, 2025) and expanded in this updated edition with the new works made for the show, the volume gathers 96 color and 20 black-and-white plates plus a folded poster, with texts by curator Stefano Collicelli Cagol, Giorgio Di Domenico, Filippo Bosco, Chiara Portesine, and Michele Bertolino. The title draws on the Latin lanx satura, the ritual dish heaped with first fruits, and the Italian sense of "saturated": an apt description of paintings that compress landscape, still life, and the male body into dense, erotically charged interiors.

Fratino, born in Annapolis, Maryland, and based in Brooklyn, has become one of the most closely watched figurative painters of his generation, folding the lessons of Italian modernism into scenes of queer domestic life. His work appeared in the 60th Venice Biennale in 2024 and is held by the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Baltimore Museum of Art, and the Hammer Museum, among others.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Queer Culture, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026. Accessioned 2026-08-07.

title: Tuskegee airmen
binding: Softcover, staple bound; photocopy, monochrome on colored paper
description:
A photocopied zine from Yusuf Hassan's BlackMass Publishing that turns the archive of the Tuskegee Airmen, the first Black aviators of the U.S. Army Air Corps, into a spare, material meditation on Black service and public memory.

Staple-bound and photocopied in monochrome on colored paper, the zine works in BlackMass's signature reductive idiom: its kraft cover carries a single archival photograph of airmen lined up beside their aircraft over a typewritten caption. The publisher's note recounts the history the images carry: civilian training programs opened to Black pilots in 1939, the segregated units of 1941, and the squadrons trained at Tuskegee, Alabama. Those were the 99th Fighter Squadron and 332nd Fighter Group, which flew combat missions from North Africa and Italy, and the 477th Bombardment Group.

Hassan (b. 1987, New York) founded BlackMass Publishing in 2019 to publish books and zines by Black artists, combining archival photographs and found print material with poetry and jazz in what he calls the collective improvisation of African diasporic culture. BlackMass took part in Greater New York at MoMA PS1 (2021), and its publications are held in the collections of the MoMA Library, the Schomburg Center, the Whitney Museum Library, and Tate.
tags: Art, Zines, Black Artists, Photography, Archives, History
notes: Photocopy zine; monochrome on colored paper. Tuskegee Airmen, Inc., the airmen's official heritage organization: https://tuskegeeairmen.org/

title: Painted Time: (2020–2024)
contributors: Christopher J. Brownawell (Text); Anne Collins Goodyear (Text); Jaime DeSimone (Conversation)
description:
A survey catalogue of five years of Ann Craven's serial painting (the moons, birds, trees, and flowers she calls her "icons"), published for her 2025 exhibition at Maine's Farnsworth Art Museum.

Published on the occasion of Ann Craven: Painted Time (2020–2024), curated by Jaime DeSimone in collaboration with the artist (Farnsworth Art Museum, Rockland, Maine, May 3, 2025 – January 4, 2026), the catalogue traces a practice in which repetition becomes a way of capturing time: moons painted from observation on successive nights, birds and flowers returned to again and again, each canvas dated and archived. Across 128 pages it pairs a contribution from Farnsworth director Christopher J. Brownawell with a new essay by Anne Collins Goodyear, co-director of the Bowdoin College Museum of Art, and a conversation between DeSimone and Craven.

Craven, who divides her time between New York and Cushing, Maine, has built three decades of formally innovative, conceptually loaded work on seriality and memory, including the Time stripe paintings made from the palettes of her finished canvases. She is represented by Karma, New York; a companion presentation, Painted Time: Moons (Laboratory), was mounted at the Bowdoin College Museum of Art in 2025.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Maine
notes: Published on the occasion of the Farnsworth Art Museum exhibition, May 3, 2025 - January 4, 2026; curated by Jaime DeSimone in collaboration with the artist.

title: Writing a Letter: Akerman Ballet, Act 1
description:
Six years in the making, Writing a Letter is Collier Schorr's translation of Chantal Akerman's 1974 film Je tu il elle into a ballet, and her argument that queer histories survive through adoration, adaptation and repetition.

Schorr directed the piece as a sequence of videotaped dances and cast herself in it, learning to dance for the work rather than staying behind the camera. Following Akerman's themes of transparency, sexuality, shame and love, the ballet questions the age, gender and racial norms that classical dance has historically enforced, telling a story about power, desire and compulsion. This first volume gathers 180 black-and-white film stills pulled from Act 1, printed at a hand-sized 5.5 × 7.5 inches across 240 pages, with an introduction by the performance scholar Peggy Phelan. Published by The Song Cave, it stands as a document of one artist working closely inside another's film.

Schorr (b. 1963, New York) studied at the School of Visual Arts and built a four-decade practice around portraiture that sits between document and fiction, most familiarly in Jens F., in which a German teenager restages Andrew Wyeth's Helga pictures, and in Neighbors/Nachbarn, 8 Women and Paul's Book. Her work was included in the 2002 Whitney Biennial and is held by MoMA, the Whitney and the Walker Art Center; she has taught photography at Yale since 2003 and shoots regularly for fashion houses and magazines.
tags: Photography, Queer Culture, Film Stills, Film, Performance, Dance, Artist Book
notes: Act 1 of a projected multi-part publication of Schorr's Akerman ballet. No LOC or WorldCat record at time of cataloguing (August 2026); bibliographic data from the publisher and ARTBOOK | D.A.P. Artist's official site is HTTP-only (no TLS).

title: Late Paintings
description:
Encompassing more than twenty-five paintings that Francis Bacon made in London and Paris during the last two decades of his life, this book serves as a companion to the 2015 exhibition at Gagosian Gallery, New York, and is the first in-depth exploration of the innovations of the artist’s late work.

In his late paintings, Francis Bacon refined themes that had long obsessed him. He quoted reflexively from his oeuvre, reworking subjects to strip them to the bare essentials. This stunning new book features over 150 color illustrations of the artist’s work and related materials, including reproductions of ephemera from Bacon’s Hugh Lane studio.
notes: One of two copies in the collection.

title: Glass Life
description:
Cwynar’s research-driven and visually complex images constitute the hallmarks of contemporary post–Pictures Generation work―in which photography is pursued in relation to film, sculpture, digital culture, and the cultural and technological history of image-making.

Cwynar’s work revolves around her interest in subjective notions of beauty through images the fetishization of consumer objects and colors and the exploration of the informal image archives that have emerged around the industrialization and capitalization of these ideas.

As part of her core practice, Cwynar collects, arranges, and archives her eBay purchases and creates studio studies of these consumer objects, exploring how images circulate online and how the lives and purposes of both physical objects and their likenesses change over time. Sara Cwynar: Glass Life is a must-have sourcebook for understanding the multilayered practice of this celebrated, multidisciplinary artist.
notes: One of two copies in the collection.

title: Cityscapes
edition_printrun: Second edition, 2008. First published December 2006 for the Miami exhibition.
contributors: Manon Slome (text), Michael Betancourt (text), Stefan Ruiz (cover photograph)
description:
José Parlá’s first book, published for Cityscapes, his Miami solo debut, staged by Spoonfed during Art Basel Miami Beach in December 2006.

Some 150 pages of paintings and photographs follow Parlá’s calligraphic, layered surfaces back to the walls that inform them: weathered posters, scrawled tags and the palimpsest of the street, recorded in his own photographs and reworked in paint. An introduction by the exhibition’s curator Manon Slome and an essay by the theorist Michael Betancourt place the work between graffiti, abstraction and urban archaeology. Designed by Chris Rubino with the artist; cover photograph by Stefan Ruiz.

Parlá (b. 1973, Miami) grew up writing graffiti in Miami and Puerto Rico and has since produced large-scale public commissions, including murals for One World Trade Center and the Barclays Center. Cityscapes precedes the Hatje Cantz survey Walls, Diaries, and Paintings, also in the collection.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Street Art, Graffiti
notes: One of two copies in the collection. Edition to be verified against the copy (first edition 2006 / second edition 2008). Record filled from empty stub.

title: Here She Comes Now
description:
The catalogue of Elizabeth Peyton’s 2013 exhibition at the Staatliche Kunsthalle Baden-Baden, the first to gather her portraits of musicians as a body of work in their own right.

Rock performers such as David Bowie, Kurt Cobain, Jarvis Cocker, Pete Doherty, the Gallagher brothers, John Lydon and Keith Richards appear alongside opera singers including Jessye Norman, Jonas Kaufmann and Ludwig Schnorr von Carolsfeld, shown not in formal poses but in performance. The source snapshots and archival photographs are reproduced en face with the finished oils and works on paper, surveying twenty years of painting and drawing and making visible how Peyton edits a found image into a portrait. Texts by curator Johan Holten and Dodie Kazanjian; 64 colour plates, in English and German.

Peyton (b. 1965) came to prominence in the 1990s with small, jewel-toned portraits of friends, musicians and historical figures, and her painting has since been the subject of surveys at the New Museum, the Whitechapel Gallery and the National Portrait Gallery, London. Here She Comes Now sits alongside the collection’s other Peyton titles, including Aire and Angels and the Hatje Cantz monograph.
tags: Art, Painting, Portraiture, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Music
notes: One of two copies in the collection. Record filled from empty stub.

title: Neo Rauch: At the Well
notes: One of two copies in the collection. One of the two copies is signed.

title: Georg Baselitz: Springtime
description:
Springtime documents the moment an eighty-three-year-old Baselitz let collage into his painting for the first time, gluing pairs of nylon stockings onto canvas and working over and around their diaphanous forms in white, black, and gold.

The book was published for the exhibition of the same name at Gagosian, 555 West 24th Street, New York, May 4–June 12, 2021, whose title was meant to herald a reawakening from the constraints of the pandemic much as Dada emerged from the First World War. Across 106 pages it reproduces the new paintings alongside photography of the works in progress in the artist's German studio, with texts by Baselitz himself and the French art historian Eric Darragon. In some canvases the stocking-figures stand distinct from their grounds; in others the hosiery is gone and only its printed impression remains. The volume was designed by Purtill Family Business, Los Angeles.

Baselitz (born 1938 in Deutschbaselitz, Saxony) has inverted his motifs since 1969 as a way of forcing attention onto paint rather than subject, and his Heroes, Fracture paintings, and carved wood sculpture have shaped postwar German art for six decades. The New York show coincided with an exhibition of new work at the Museo di Palazzo Grimani, Venice.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, German Art

title: Saul Bass: A Life in Film and Design
description:
The first substantial book on Saul Bass, and still the reference: 428 pages and more than 1,400 illustrations, most of them drawn from the Bass archive and many never published before.

Design historian Pat Kirkham, who knew Bass, wrote the text; Jennifer Bass, his daughter and a graphic designer, selected and designed the material, building on the picture research Bass himself had assembled for a memoir he never finished. Martin Scorsese, whose Goodfellas, Cape Fear, and Casino titles Bass made late in his career, contributes a foreword. The book runs from the Los Angeles studio's earliest advertising through the title sequences that redefined the form — The Man with the Golden Arm, Vertigo, Anatomy of a Murder, Psycho, Spartacus — to the corporate identities for AT&T, Quaker Oats, United Airlines, Continental, and Minolta, and the short films, among them the Oscar-winning Why Man Creates.

Bass (1920–1996) trained at Brooklyn College under Gyorgy Kepes and moved to Los Angeles in 1946. From the late 1950s he worked in partnership with his wife Elaine Bass, a collaboration the book documents in detail and one that had long been under-credited.
tags: Design, Graphic Design, Film, Posters, Typography

title: Cecily Brown: The Lady and the Swan
description:
Eight variations on a single borrowed image: Cecily Brown's Lady and the Swan cycle takes Franz Marc's 1907 sketchbook grisaille of Leda and the swan and works it into a sequence in which the mythological seduction dissolves into paint.

The catalogue accompanies Brown's exhibition at the Staatliche Graphische Sammlung München in the Pinakothek der Moderne, and the project began in the collection's own study room, where Brown examined Marc's tempera and chalk double-page from Sketchbook II in September 2021. It runs 88 pages with 35 colour plates, in German and English, and was issued in a limited edition with a four-colour screenprint on a Contesse silk-linen cover; a signed edition was also produced. The paintings and works on paper reproduced here were shown in Munich and again in Brown's exhibition The Spell at Contemporary Fine Arts, Berlin, in autumn 2022.

Brown (born 1969, London) has painted for three decades in the difficult territory between abstraction and figuration, repeatedly returning to art history (Rubens, Goya, Hogarth, Bruegel) not as quotation but as raw material to be pulled apart. Her survey Death and the Maid opened at The Metropolitan Museum of Art the following year.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: Cecily Brown: The Triumph of Death
contributors: Sylvain Bellenger (Introduction); Catherine Foulkrod (Text); Sergio Risaliti (Text)
description:
A book built around one painting: Cecily Brown's colossal multi-panel Triumph of Death, in which Death rides roughshod over a town and its inhabitants, answering a fresco of 1446 in the Palazzo Abatellis, Palermo.

Published on the occasion of the painting's exhibition at the Museo e Real Bosco di Capodimonte, Naples, the clothbound volume runs 104 pages with 50 colour plates at 10 by 11.5 inches, in English and Italian. Gavin Delahunty edits and contributes the principal text, with an introduction by Capodimonte's director Sylvain Bellenger and essays by Catherine Foulkrod and Sergio Risaliti. Alongside details of the painting it publishes a group of previously unseen preparatory drawings, tracing how the composition was assembled and how a preoccupation with mortality that has run through Brown's work for decades arrived at this scale.

Brown (born 1969, London) moved to New York in the mid-1990s and has since built a body of painting that holds abstraction and figuration in unresolved tension. The Old Master borrowings that drive this work — Bruegel, Goya, Rubens — recur across her practice and were surveyed in Death and the Maid at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2023.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Drawing

title: Cecily Brown: Death and the Maid
contributors: Ian Alteveer (Text); Adam Eaker (Conversation with the artist)
description:
The catalogue of Cecily Brown's first full museum survey in the city she has painted in for thirty years, and an argument for reading her work through the vanitas rather than through gesture alone.

Published for the exhibition at The Met Fifth Avenue, April 4 to December 3, 2023, the book gathers 21 paintings and 26 works on paper (drawings, watercolours, sketchbooks, and monotypes) across 140 pages and 81 colour plates, including recently finished and never-before-published works. Ian Alteveer, who organised the exhibition, contributes the essay, and Adam Eaker of the museum's European Paintings department is in conversation with the artist. The title alters Schubert's Der Tod und das Mädchen from maiden to maid, and the selection follows that shift through still life, memento mori, and the mirror.

Brown (born 1969, London) trained at the Slade and moved to New York in 1994. The book situates her between the modern painters she absorbed early (de Kooning, Guston, Mitchell) and the Old Masters she keeps returning to, among them Goya, Hogarth, Manet, and Rubens.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Drawing

title: Reynold Brown: A Life in Pictures
description:
The first full account of Reynold Brown, whose paintings for Attack of the 50 Foot Woman, Creature from the Black Lagoon, and Cat on a Hot Tin Roof are among the most reproduced American images of the 1950s and are almost never credited to him.

Daniel Zimmer and David J. Hornung assembled the book from original paintings, drawings, photographs, and printed ephemera, running 224 pages at 12.25 by 9.75 inches with more than 500 colour illustrations, many reproduced full page. It follows Brown's whole working life rather than the poster years alone: the Tailspin Tommy newspaper strip he drew as a teenager, the cutaway technical drawings he developed for North American Aviation during the war, early paperback covers and magazine illustration, and then the roughly 300 film posters. A first printing of 1,000 copies was issued, with a deluxe edition of 100 signed by the artist's widow and both authors; an expanded version followed from the same press in 2017.

Reynold Brown (1917–1991) worked almost entirely to commission and to deadline, and studios rarely put his name on the results. He taught at Art Center in Los Angeles late in life, and a stroke in 1976 ended his painting career.
tags: Illustration, Design, Film, Posters, American Art

title: Chris Burden
contributors: Lisa Le Feuvre (Text); Paul Schimmel (Text); Kristine Stiles (Text); Robert Storr (Text)
description:
For twenty years there was no serious book on Chris Burden; this 416-page volume, edited in close collaboration with the artist, is the one that fixed his work in print.

Coordinated by curator Fred Hoffman in association with Gagosian Gallery, it is arranged thematically rather than chronologically, so that the early performances sit beside the later sculpture and reveal the conceptual argument running between them. There are 377 illustrations, 244 in colour, many carrying commentary by Burden himself, together with a catalogue of projects and publications from 1971 to 2005 and documentation of numerous works he never realised. Essays come from Lisa Le Feuvre on Ghost Ship, Paul Schimmel on the works on paper, Kristine Stiles on light, and Robert Storr, with Hoffman on the early years. Designed by Mark Thomson and printed in Florence.

Burden (1946–2015) made his name with the endurance and risk pieces of the early 1970s — Shoot, Trans-Fixed, Five Day Locker Piece — then spent four decades building machines, bridges, and city-scale sculptures that test power, engineering, and belief. Urban Light at LACMA is the best known.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Sculpture, Performance Art, Installation

title: The Art of Nancy Ekholm Burkert
edition_printrun: Original Peacock Press/Bantam edition, issued simultaneously with the Harper & Row hardcover
description:
Nancy Ekholm Burkert drew slowly and published rarely, and this slim 1977 volume remains the only real gathering of her work — forty colour plates of an illustrator who treated children's books with the deliberation of a Renaissance draughtsman.

Edited by David Larkin for the Peacock Press imprint and issued as an original Peacock Press/Bantam paperback alongside a Harper & Row hardcover of the same year, it reproduces plates from Roald Dahl's James and the Giant Peach (1961), her first commission, the jacket for John Updike's A Child's Calendar (1965), Andersen's The Nightingale (1965) and The Fir Tree (1970), Edward Lear's The Scroobious Pip (1968), and the Caldecott Honor Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1972). Portraits for which she used her own children as models are included, among them a brush-and-coloured-ink profile of her daughter Claire. Michael Danoff, then a curator at the Milwaukee Art Museum, contributes a long introduction describing her working method in detail.

Burkert (born 1933, Sterling, Colorado) studied at the University of Wisconsin and worked from Wisconsin for most of her career, producing only a handful of illustrated books over five decades, a body of work whose scarcity is inseparable from its finish.
tags: Illustration, Drawing, Art, Children's Books, Watercolor
notes: No trustworthy cover image found online — cover to be photographed from the physical copy.

title: Tom Burr: Torrington Project
contributors: George Baker (Text); Jordan Carter (Text); Aria Dean (Text); Jody Graf (Text); Renée Green (Text); David Joselit (Text); Christine Messineo (Text); Humberto Moro (Text)
description:
Between 2021 and 2024 Tom Burr took over a disused nineteenth-century factory in Torrington, Connecticut, and turned it into what he called a living archive; this 400-page book is the project's last element and a deliberately subversive take on the catalogue raisonné.

Neither exhibition nor studio, the building held more than ninety works from across Burr's career, restaged and in some cases restored, while Gordon Hall, Maria Hassabi, and Nick Mauss staged performances in the space and a shifting cast of writers, curators, and friends passed through. Edited by Blake Oetting, the book carries 345 colour and 15 black-and-white images documenting the build-out and the works in situ, Burr's diaristic writing on his stewardship of the building, and archival ephemera, with essays by George Baker, Aria Dean, Renée Green, David Joselit, and others. Dia hosted the launch in September 2025.

Burr (born 1963, New Haven) came out of the Whitney Independent Study Program and American Fine Arts, Co., and belongs to the generation that rebuilt institutional critique and minimalism around questions of identity and public space. His earlier extra-institutional work includes Body/Building, a year-long residency in Marcel Breuer's Pirelli Tire Building in New Haven.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Sculpture, Installation, Architecture, Institutional Critique

title: Bisa Butler: Portraits
publisher: The Art Institute of Chicago / Yale University Press
contributors: Jordan Carter (Text); Michèle Wije (Text); Isabella Ko (Catalogue entries); Bisa Butler (Catalogue entries)
description:
Bisa Butler builds portraits entirely from cloth — cut, layered, and stitched printed cottons standing in for skin, light, and shadow — and this catalogue for her first solo museum exhibition makes the case for reading them as painting's equal rather than as craft.

Published for Bisa Butler: Portraits, co-organised by the Katonah Museum of Art, where it opened in March 2020, and the Art Institute of Chicago, where it ran from November 2020 to September 2021. The 96-page volume carries 37 colour and 3 black-and-white plates with essays by Erica Warren, associate curator of textiles at the Art Institute, on Butler's portraits and art-historical discourse; by Michèle Wije on the relation between photography and quiltmaking, since Butler works from historical photographs, many of them anonymous; and by Jordan Carter setting her alongside Faith Ringgold. Catalogue entries are by Butler, Carter, Isabella Ko, Warren, and Wije.

Butler (born 1973, Orange, New Jersey) came to quilting through a fibre arts class at Howard University and made her first quilt for her dying grandmother, with whom she had spent childhood afternoons over black-and-white family photographs. She taught high school art in New Jersey for a decade before working full time as an artist.
tags: Art, Textiles, Quilts, Portraiture, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: Cahiers d'Art: Calder in France: La Revue No. 1, 2015 (39th Year)
editor: Staffan Ahrenberg, Sam Keller, Hans Ulrich Obrist, Anya Bondell
contributors: Alexander S. C. Rower (Introduction); Susan Braeuer Dam (Text); Alfred Pacquement (Text); Raphaël Bouvier (Text); Robert Rubin (Text); Georges Mounin (Text); Joan Simon (Interview); Ugo Mulas (Photography); Agnès Varda (Photography)
description:
Cahiers d'Art resumed publication in 2012 after a half-century silence, and this 2015 number turns the revue's own archive back on one of its subjects: Alexander Calder's French decades, told through the studios he worked in.

Produced with the Calder Foundation to mark twenty-five years of the Atelier Calder residency, the issue follows Calder from his Paris years of 1926–33 through his return in 1946, Aix-en-Provence in 1953, and finally Saché in the Loire valley, where he designed his last monumental studio in 1963. Archival documentation reconstructs each workplace, and reprinted essays from the revue's earlier run recover Calder's relationship with the founding publisher Christian Zervos, alongside photographs by Ugo Mulas and Agnès Varda and an interview by Joan Simon. A second half attends to the fifty artists who have since worked in the Saché studio, with interviews with Tadashi Kawamata, Abraham Cruzvillegas and Rachel Harrison and a portfolio of sculpture models by the 2014 resident Monika Sosnowska.

Calder (1898–1976) invented the mobile inside the Paris avant-garde of the late 1920s, and France remained his second working base for the rest of his life. Edited by Staffan Ahrenberg, Sam Keller, Hans Ulrich Obrist and Anya Bondell, with an introduction by the artist's grandson Alexander S. C. Rower, the issue runs 194 pages with 143 color plates in the revue's large format; a limited edition adds a signed work by Darren Bader.
tags: Art, Sculpture, Modern Art, Artist Interviews

title: Caravaggio
description:
Taschen's Basic Art volume on Caravaggio is a primer rather than a scholarly monograph, and it does the one thing that format does well: it puts more than fifty paintings in front of the reader in sequence and lets the argument for the early Baroque make itself.

Gilles Lambert sets the work against a short and violent biography — gambling, debt, brawls and a murder charge — and traces the theatrical naturalism, the models drawn from the street and the handling of light that made the pictures both scandalous and unignorable in their own moment. Like every title in the series, it carries a chronological summary of the artist's life and oeuvre, a concise biography, and captioned color plates throughout; Gilles Néret edited the volume for the Basic Art line, which Taschen began in 1985.

Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio (1571–1610) was largely written out of the canon after his death and recovered only at the end of the nineteenth century. He is now read as the pivot of the early Baroque, with a line of influence running through Ribera, Zurbarán, Velázquez, Georges de La Tour and Vermeer, and further on to Rembrandt, Delacroix, Courbet and Manet.
tags: Art, Painting, Art History, Baroque, Old Masters

title: If You Don't Belong, Don't Be Long
contributors: Richard Price (Foreword); Justin Theroux (Foreword); Al Moran (Text); Terry Richardson (Photography)
description:
Scott Campbell's first book takes its title from a 2010 OHWOW gallery show and refuses the usual separation between the tattoo shop and the gallery, treating both as one continuous body of work.

Published by Rizzoli with the gallery and imprint OHWOW, the volume gathers tattoos alongside the objects Campbell makes from them: dollar bills lasered into lace-like lattices and cursive phrases, drawings, burnt tortillas, granite tombstones, enamel holograms and graphite on ostrich eggshells, including work that came out of a visit to Mexico's Santa Marta prison, where he tattooed inmates. The book is built as a physical object in its own right, with an embossed flock cover and sections divided by black-and-white flash and transfer sheets printed on tracing paper against high-gloss color plates. Forewords come from the novelist Richard Price, OHWOW's Al Moran and Justin Theroux, with photography by Terry Richardson.

Campbell, born in Louisiana and based in Brooklyn, runs the Williamsburg studio Saved Tattoo and draws on nineteenth-century hand-lettering, kitsch and classic American flash. He carries that vocabulary intact into sculpture and works on paper. His tattoo clients have included Heath Ledger and Marc Jacobs.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Tattoo, Drawing, Works on Paper

title: Shelf Life
description:
Mathew Cerletty paints ordinary things — a Diet Coke logo, a bottle of ZzzQuil, a fish, a planet — with a flatness and precision that makes recognition itself feel slightly off, and this is the first book to take the full measure of that method.

Published by Karma in an edition of 1,000 to coincide with the artist's Shelf Life exhibition at the gallery's East 2nd Street space in spring 2018, the 232-page volume gathers roughly 160 color reproductions of paintings and drawings together with the artist's working notes. Nicole Rudick's essay traces the development: representational painting encouraged and abstraction discouraged at Boston University, early portraits of friends and of models found in magazines, and then the encounter with Lisa Yuskavage, John Currin and Richard Phillips that gave him permission to bring color, patterning and a deliberate ridiculousness into the work.

Cerletty was born in 1980 and lives and works in New York. Karma has continued to publish him since, including True Believer in 2023 with a text by Catherine Lacey.

title: Forking at Perfection
contributors: Raphael Gygax (Text); Franziska Bigger (Text); Ian Cheng (Text)
description:
Ian Cheng's live simulations are video works that nobody, including the artist, can watch to the end: virtual ecosystems seeded with a few programmed properties and then left to evolve without authorial control, endlessly and without resolution. This is the first book to treat them as a body of work.

Published by JRP|Ringier with the Migros Museum für Gegenwartskunst for Cheng's exhibition there in spring 2016, the volume covers the simulations he had made to that point, with essays by the curator Raphael Gygax and by Franziska Bigger alongside a selection of the artist's own writing. The 140-page book carries 64 color plates and was designed by Studio Marie Lusa. Cheng's touchstones surface throughout — video game design, improvisational theater, Darwinian brutality, and Julian Jaynes's 1976 argument about the bicameral origins of consciousness — as does his own description of the simulations as a "neurological gym," a place to practice the confusion and cognitive dissonance that unrelenting change produces.

Cheng, born in Los Angeles in 1984, studied cognitive science before turning to art, and went on to make the Emissaries trilogy (2015–17) and the artificial lifeform BOB, shown at the Serpentine in 2018.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Media Art, Video Art

title: Emissaries Guide to Worlding
publisher: Koenig Books, with Serpentine Galleries and Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo
editor: Joseph Constable, Rebecca Lewin, Veronica So
contributors: Nora Khan (Text); Hans Ulrich Obrist (Text); Ben Vickers (Text); Yana Peel (Foreword); Patrizia Sandretto Re Rebaudengo (Foreword)
description:
Part exhibition book, part instruction manual, Emissaries Guide to Worlding is Ian Cheng's attempt to write down what making a world actually requires. It reads less like a catalogue than like a working method handed over for others to use.

Published by Koenig Books with the Serpentine Galleries and the Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo on the occasion of Cheng's 2018 Serpentine exhibition, the 320-page volume derives its argument from Emissaries (2015–17), his trilogy of live simulations, each built around a figure caught between an unraveling reality and a strange emerging one. Cheng proposes four masks a maker must be able to wear in turn (the Director, the Cartoonist, the Hacker and the Emissary) and treats worlding as a whole-brain discipline for holding attention and agency inside conditions that will not stay still. Edited by Joseph Constable, Rebecca Lewin and Veronica So, with texts by Nora Khan, Hans Ulrich Obrist and Ben Vickers.

Cheng, born in Los Angeles in 1984, has since extended the same line of thinking into BOB (Bag of Beliefs) and the Life After BOB anime. He kept revising the guide after the book appeared: version 1.0, retitled Emissary's Guide To Worlding, was released digitally by Metis Suns in November 2018.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Artist Writings, Media Art, Exhibition Catalog
notes: The printed edition is titled "Emissaries Guide to Worlding"; the revised digital version 1.0 (Metis Suns, 2018, ISBN 9781949902006) is titled "Emissary's Guide To Worlding."

title: In/Out Studio
publisher: D.A.P./Distributed Art Publishers, with Verlag Kettler
contributors: Matthias Koddenberg (Text); Wolfgang Volz (Photography); Ugo Mulas (Photography); Peter Doherty (Translation)
description:
Christo and Jeanne-Claude's projects are remembered as public spectacles, but this book is about the decades of labor behind them: the studio, the drawings sold to fund the work, and the crews on the ground.

Edited with text by Matthias Koddenberg and published by D.A.P. with Verlag Kettler, the 320-page volume assembles more than 250 largely unpublished photographs, many of them from the artists' private archives, alongside reproductions of drawings, collages and objects. Every major project is documented: Wrapped Coast (1968–69), Valley Curtain (1970–72), Running Fence (1972–76), Surrounded Islands (1980–83), The Pont Neuf Wrapped (1975–85), The Umbrellas (1984–91), Wrapped Reichstag (1971–95) and The Gates (1979–2005), together with early drawings from Christo's Bulgarian years, temporary sculptures, and works since lost or unknown. Photographs come from Wolfgang Volz, Ugo Mulas and others who followed the projects over decades.

Christo Javacheff (1935–2020) and Jeanne-Claude Denat de Guillebon (1935–2009) were born on the same day and worked jointly from 1961, financing everything themselves through the sale of preparatory studies. A revised edition of this book appeared in 2021, ahead of the posthumous wrapping of the Arc de Triomphe.
tags: Art, Sculpture, Installation, Land Art, Photography

title: The Most Special Day of My Life: Works by Rob Clayton & Christian Clayton
publisher: La Luz de Jesus Press / Last Gasp
contributors: Michael Criley (Text); Jeff Kling (Text); Long Gone John (Text)
description:
Rob and Christian Clayton make paintings the way a conversation gets made: one brother starts a canvas, hands it to the other, and the second redirects or overwrites what the first put down until neither can claim it. This first book is the record of that method.

Published in 2003 by La Luz de Jesus Press with Last Gasp of San Francisco, the volume runs to 184 pages of color and duotone plates and holds individual paintings by each brother alongside the collaborations, with essays by Michael Criley, Jeff Kling, Long Gone John and the artists. Their subjects are narrative and autobiographical, drawn from memories of suburban decay, and the book documents installations as well as pictures — among them Tim House, a six-by-eight-by-thirteen-foot church-schoolhouse hung inside with portraits of people real and imagined. Designed by Mark Murphy, it is built to be sampled rather than read straight through.

Rob Clayton (b. 1963) and Christian Clayton (b. 1967) both graduated from Art Center College of Design in Pasadena, where they went on to teach illustration, and began collaborating in the mid-1990s. Their work sits alongside the lowbrow and pop-surrealist artists who came out of La Luz de Jesus in Los Angeles, and has extended into film, music video and print campaigns.
tags: Art, Painting, Drawing, Collage, Contemporary Art

title: Writings/Interviews
contributors: Douglas Crimp (Interview); David Sylvester (Interview); Peter Eisenman (Interview); Alan Colquhoun (Interview)
description:
Serra was the rare sculptor who argued his own case in print, and this collection is where the arguments live: on what site specificity obliges, on why a work cannot be moved without being destroyed, and on the difference between sculpture and decoration.

Published by the University of Chicago Press in 1994, the 286-page volume gathers essays, statements and interviews spanning roughly three decades, with 32 halftones. The interlocutors include the critics Douglas Crimp and David Sylvester, who press him on specific installations, and the architects Peter Eisenman and Alan Colquhoun on what sculpture and architecture owe each other. Longer pieces include "Extended Notes from Sight Point Road" and Serra's sustained account of the removal of Tilted Arc from Federal Plaza in New York, a dispute that turned a commissioned public sculpture into a legal argument about authorship and public space.

Richard Serra (1938–2024) came out of the Process Art milieu of the late 1960s — lead thrown molten against a wall, propped plates held up by gravity alone — and spent the following decades on weathering steel works whose scale and curvature reorganize the ground a viewer walks on. His later dialogues with Hal Foster were collected as Conversations about Sculpture in 2018.
tags: Art, Sculpture, Artist Writings, Minimalism, Contemporary Art

title: Cindy Sherman
publisher: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
contributors: Eva Respini (Text); Johanna Burton (Text); John Waters (Interview)
description:
MoMA's 2012 survey was the first major American account of Cindy Sherman's work in nearly fifteen years, and its catalogue does what the exhibition did: it puts thirty-five years of self-staged photographs in one sequence and lets the accumulation make the case.

Published by the Museum of Modern Art for the exhibition of 26 February to 11 June 2012, organized by Eva Respini with Lucy Gallun, the 264-page volume reproduces roughly 180 photographs from the mid-1970s onward, including work made for the show and not previously published. Every major body of work is represented — the Untitled Film Stills (1977–80), the centerfolds (1981), the history portraits (1989–90), the head shots (2000–2002) and the later series on aging and social display. Respini's essay reads the reception of the work across three decades rather than narrating a career; Johanna Burton reconsiders the recent series, and a conversation between Sherman and John Waters gets at her working method. The exhibition travelled to SFMOMA, the Walker Art Center and the Dallas Museum of Art.

Sherman, born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey in 1954 and formed in the artist-run scene around Hallwalls in Buffalo, has used herself as the sole model for almost the entire body of work without producing a single self-portrait. The subject is always the type, the costume and the picture convention rather than the person.
tags: Art, Photography, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: Anne Collier: Photographic
designer: Doug Lloyd, Lloyd & Co, New York
description:
Anne Collier's first solo museum exhibitions in Europe produced a deliberately spare book: forty-two plates that show how thoroughly a found photograph can be made to give up its emotional programming.
