Published by Hartmann Books for the exhibition organized by Stefan Gronert at the Sprengel Museum Hannover in 2018 and by Nadine Wietlisbach at the Fotomuseum Winterthur the following year, the large-format softcover covers eleven years of work and carries texts by both curators, in a design by Doug Lloyd. The selection runs across Collier's recurring motifs — eyes, mouths, clouds, waves, record sleeves, magazine pages — rephotographed against neutral studio grounds so that the source image is quoted rather than absorbed.

Collier (b. Los Angeles, 1970; lives in New York) has worked since the early 2000s with the printed residue of 1970s and 1980s popular culture: self-help LPs, camera advertising, paperback covers, film stills. The long-running series Women With Cameras and Women Crying set women as makers of images against women as material for them. Her American survey, organized by the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago with essays by Michael Darling, Chrissie Iles and Kate Zambreno, appeared in 2014.
tags: Photography, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Appropriation
notes: Published on the occasion of the exhibition Anne Collier: Photographic, Sprengel Museum Hannover, 2018, and Fotomuseum Winterthur, 2019.

title: Anne Collier
contributors: Madeleine Grynsztejn (Foreword); Michael Darling (Text); Chrissie Iles (Text); Kate Zambreno (Text)
description:
The catalogue for Anne Collier's first major American museum survey, and still the fullest account of how her studio photographs turn found pictures into instruments for looking at looking.

Published by the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago in 2014 for the exhibition curated by Michael Darling, the ten-inch-square hardcover carries fifty-five colour plates drawn from 2002 onward. Madeleine Grynsztejn provides the foreword; Darling traces the influences and thematic threads of a decade's work; Chrissie Iles, of the Whitney Museum of American Art, places Collier within photographic and cinematic history; the novelist Kate Zambreno writes on self-portraiture, collecting and obsession. Recurring subjects include pop psychology, the conventions of commercial photography, autobiography and the act of seeing. The exhibition travelled to the Hessel Museum of Art at CCS Bard.

Collier (b. Los Angeles, 1970; lives in New York) photographs album sleeves, paperbacks, posters and magazine pages on plain studio backdrops, so that each source keeps its era and its sales pitch while losing its authority. Later projects include the slide work and book Women With Cameras (Anonymous) and the European survey Photographic (Hartmann Books, 2018).
tags: Photography, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Appropriation
notes: Published for the exhibition Anne Collier, Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago, 2014; travelled to the Hessel Museum of Art, CCS Bard. Distributed by D.A.P.

title: John Currin: The Dogwood Thieves
description:
A painter's account of failure held in public: thirty-nine destroyed states of one canvas that John Currin worked, scraped back and overpainted across six years.

Published by A.S.A.P. in 2012, the clothbound book grows out of a lecture Currin gave at the Acadia Summer Arts Program in August 2010 and keeps that talk's conversational register. Forty colour reproductions follow the painting from its first prompt — a photograph in a magazine advertisement — through iteration after iteration, none previously published and none still extant, since each version was buried under the next. The result is closer to a working diary than a monograph: an artist known for finish showing the accumulated wrong turns underneath it.

Currin (b. Boulder, Colorado, 1962) has built a career on the friction between old-master technique and deliberately awkward contemporary subject matter, from the yearbook-derived portraits of 1989 through the middle-aged women, the elongated nudes and the later explicit paintings. His tone here is characteristically self-deflating: he offers the book partly to show what a painting costs to make, and partly to discourage anyone from spending six years on one.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Artist Writings
notes: Based on a lecture given at the Acadia Summer Arts Program, August 2010.

title: John Currin: Œuvres / Works 1989–1995
description:
The first substantial catalogue of John Currin's painting, issued at the moment his work crossed from downtown notoriety to European institutional attention.

Produced by the Fonds Régional d'Art Contemporain Limousin in Limoges for Currin's 1995 exhibition there, the bilingual French and English paperback covers six years of work: the yearbook-derived portraits of 1989, the middle-aged women that first made his reputation, and the early elongated nudes. Frédéric Paul and Keith Seward supply the texts (Seward's essay is titled 'Boomerang') alongside thirty-two colour plates, a list of illustrations, a list of works and a bio-bibliography. The show was reviewed by Jean-Yves Jouannais in Art Press.

Currin (b. Boulder, Colorado, 1962) began showing with Andrea Rosen Gallery in New York in 1992, and 1995 brought exhibitions at the Institute of Contemporary Arts in London and at Donald Young and Jack Hanley on the American west coast alongside the Limoges presentation. The technical polish and provocations that followed (the Gagosian years, the explicit paintings of the 2000s) are already visible here in outline.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Published for the exhibition at the FRAC Limousin, Limoges, 1995. Texts in French and English. Some records date the edition 1996.

title: Faux Pas: Selected Writings and Drawings
editor: Charlotte Houette, François Lancien-Guilberteau, Benjamin Thorel
description:
Amy Sillman writes about painting the way she paints: fast, funny, impatient with the pieties that have settled over abstraction. Faux Pas is the book that made her one of the few artists whose prose is read for its own sake.

Published in Paris by After 8 Books and edited by Charlotte Houette, François Lancien-Guilberteau and Benjamin Thorel, with a foreword by Lynne Tillman, the collection gathers essays, reviews and lectures alongside drawings made specially for the volume, which run with the texts rather than illustrating them. This expanded edition adds four pieces (on Cézanne, Carolee Schneemann, Elizabeth Murray and Louise Fishman) plus a previously unpublished lecture on drawing and new work from 2020–22, including drawings from her installation for The Milk of Dreams at the 59th Venice Biennale. Sillman rereads Abstract Expressionism through a queer lens, argues for awkwardness and the body as working method, and takes up colour and shape as problems rather than properties.

Sillman (b. Detroit, 1955; lives in New York) has moved between painting, drawing, zines and animation since the 1980s, and her subjects here run from Delacroix to Maria Lassnig and Laura Owens. Faux Pas first appeared in 2020.
tags: Art, Painting, Drawing, Artist Writings, Contemporary Art
notes: First published 2020; this is the expanded edition, with four additional texts and drawings from 2020–22.

title: Hugh Steers: The Complete Paintings, 1983–1994
contributors: Cynthia Carr (Text); Dale Peck (Text); James Smalls (Text)
description:
The complete paintings of an artist who died at thirty-two, and the record of a figurative practice that insisted on tenderness at the height of the AIDS crisis.

Published by Visual AIDS in 2015 and compiled by Wheelock Whitney, the volume reproduces every painting Hugh Steers made between 1983 and 1994 alongside an account of his life, with texts by the journalist Cynthia Carr, the novelist Dale Peck and the art historian James Smalls, in a design by Bethany Johns. The chronology carries him from student work at Yale to the allegorical hospital rooms, bathtubs, slanted artificial light and paired male figures of the late 1980s and early 1990s — pictures made when representational painting was thoroughly unfashionable and the subject matter more so.

Steers (1962–1995) graduated cum laude from Yale in 1985 and studied at the Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture; he was diagnosed with HIV in 1987 and died of AIDS-related illness at thirty-two. Caregiving between men is his recurring subject, handled without either sentiment or protest-poster directness. Visual AIDS, which maintains the archive of artists lost to AIDS and supports HIV-positive artists, published the book; the Yale University Art Gallery holds three of his paintings.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Queer, AIDS, Catalogue Raisonné
notes: Catalogue raisonné compiled by Wheelock Whitney.

title: Slow Graffiti
contributors: Bruce Hainley (Conversation with the artist); Bob Nickas (Photographic comic strip, Sorcery); Jeanette Pacher (Curator)
description:
Slow Graffiti is less a catalogue than a second staging of the exhibition it accompanies, a two-volume object that carries Alex Da Corte's Vienna installation into print with the same appetite for saturated, slightly sinister surfaces.

Published by the Secession with Revolver Publishing in an edition of 400, the work arrives as two staple-bound volumes of 132 and 84 pages with a sticker sheet, designed by Studio Claus Due. The first gathers photographs alongside a conversation between the artist and the critic Bruce Hainley; the second carries Sorcery, a photographic comic strip by Bob Nickas. The exhibition, curated by Jeanette Pacher and shown from 6 July to 3 September 2017, filled the 600-square-metre main hall with a broken urban landscape of neon, velvet-lined walls and patchwork flooring, built around Da Corte's shot-for-shot remake of Jorgen Leth's film The Perfect Human (1967), with the artist as Boris Karloff playing Frankenstein's monster.

Da Corte (b. 1980, Camden, New Jersey) works in Philadelphia, assembling immersive environments from consumer materials, borrowed film language and the iconography of household products. His other publications include A Man Full of Trouble, C-A-T Spells Murder and Marigolds with Karma, Free Roses with MASS MoCA, and TRUE LIFE with Walther Konig.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Installation, Exhibition Catalog, Video Art

title: A Man Full of Trouble
description:
A Man Full of Trouble takes its title from a pre-Revolutionary tavern still standing in Philadelphia's historic district, and turns an archaeological hole in the ground into a method for making a book.

Published by Karma, New York, in an edition of 750, the volume runs to 328 pages at 11 by 8 1/4 inches and is carried almost entirely by colour images. Da Corte uses the tavern's privy, the excavated pit where three centuries of discarded objects settled together, as the organising conceit: a portal in which memories, props, past and present aggregate and reconstitute. The result reads as an inventory of the artist's working vocabulary, the household goods, prosthetics, fluorescent surfaces and film-set fragments that recur across his installations, photographed and sequenced rather than explained. Karma also issued a special edition alongside the trade printing.

Da Corte (b. 1980, Camden, New Jersey) lives and works in Philadelphia, and his practice runs from video and neon-lit environments to sculpture assembled from consumer packaging. His other books include Slow Graffiti for the Vienna Secession, C-A-T Spells Murder and Marigolds with Karma, and Free Roses with MASS MoCA.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Photography, Installation, Artist Book

title: The Gorgeous Nothings: Emily Dickinson's Envelope Poems
description:
The Gorgeous Nothings makes the case that Emily Dickinson's late writing cannot be separated from the scraps she wrote it on, and it does so by reproducing those scraps rather than describing them.

Published in 2013 by New Directions and Christine Burgin in association with Granary Books, the large-format volume presents all fifty-two of Dickinson's envelope writings in full colour and at life size, front and back, each facing a transcription that preserves line breaks, angles and variant words. Marta Werner and Jen Bervin edited the book and supply the scholarly and visual apparatus, with a preface by Susan Howe; Bervin's design lets the torn flaps, folds and pencil marks read as compositional decisions. The trade edition follows a limited artist's-book edition issued by Granary Books, and it remains the standard reference for the envelope poems.

Dickinson (1830-1886) wrote most of these fragments in her final years, on envelopes cut, split and turned inside out. The facsimile approach has since been influential well beyond Dickinson studies; New Directions later drew a compact selection from it as Envelope Poems, and Bervin and Werner's editorial method is regularly cited in discussions of manuscript, materiality and visual poetics.
tags: Poetry, Manuscripts, Facsimile, Book Design, Literature

title: Otto Dix
contributors: Dietrich Schubert (Text); Karsten Muller (Text); James van Dyke (Text); Ernst Kallai (Text); Willi Wolfradt (Text)
description:
No German painter did more to fix the popular image of the Weimar Republic than Otto Dix, and this catalogue is the first serious attempt to put that reputation before a North American audience.

Published by Prestel with the Neue Galerie New York in 2010, the 258-page volume accompanied the exhibition shown at the Neue Galerie from March to August 2010 and at the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts from September 2010 to January 2011. Olaf Peters edited the book and opens with an essay on Dix's intransigent realism between the wars; texts by Dietrich Schubert, Karsten Muller and James van Dyke sit alongside period criticism by Ernst Kallai and Willi Wolfradt, so the 1920s reception runs next to current scholarship. The plates track the trajectory from the trench drawings and the Der Krieg print cycle to the cold, technically archaic portraits of the Neue Sachlichkeit years.

Dix (1891-1969) volunteered in 1914, served four years at the front, and spent the following decade converting that experience into some of the most unsparing images in twentieth-century painting. Declared degenerate and dismissed from his Dresden professorship in 1933, he retreated to painting landscapes and allegories on Lake Constance. The Neue Galerie has continued this line of enquiry in later publications including Neue Sachlichkeit / New Objectivity.
tags: Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, German Art

title: Marcel Duchamp: Étant donnés
publisher: Philadelphia Museum of Art / Yale University Press
contributors: Michael R. Taylor (Author and curator); Andrew Lins (Text); Melissa S. Meighan (Text); Beth A. Price (Text); Ken Sutherland (Text); Scott Homolka (Text); Elena Torok (Text); Claire Howard (Bibliography)
description:
For twenty years Marcel Duchamp let the art world believe he had given up art for chess while he built Étant donnés in secret, and this is the book that finally opens the door on how he did it.

Published in 2009 by the Philadelphia Museum of Art with Yale University Press for the exhibition marking the fortieth anniversary of the work's unveiling, Michael R. Taylor's volume runs to 448 pages with 343 colour and 117 black-and-white illustrations. It reconstructs the making of the tableau between 1946 and 1966 across two New York studios, reproducing Duchamp's Polaroids and the colour photographs from the First Manual of Instructions, Denise Browne Hare's 1968 portfolio and the letters to Maria Martins. Conservation essays by Andrew Lins, Melissa S. Meighan and colleagues report on the materials, and a closing section traces the work's afterlife in art by Les Levine, Hannah Wilke, Robert Gober and Marcel Dzama. The catalogue received the 2009 George Wittenborn Memorial Book Award.

Duchamp (1887-1968) spent his last two decades apparently at leisure, and Étant donnés was revealed as a permanent installation in Philadelphia in July 1969, the year after his death. Its peep-hole voyeurism and trompe-l'oeil realism reversed the conceptual austerity his admirers had assumed was final.
tags: Art, Sculpture, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Conceptual Art, Dada

title: Duchamp: 1887-1968, Art as Anti-Art
description:
Taschen's Basic Art volumes exist to get an artist's whole argument into ninety-six pages, and Duchamp is the hardest possible test of that format: an artist whose most consequential works were bought rather than made.

Janis Mink's text, first issued in the series in 1995 as number 35, moves chronologically from the early Cubist-adjacent paintings and Nude Descending a Staircase through the Large Glass, the readymades and the Rrose Selavy alter ego, to the chess years and the posthumously revealed Étant donnés. Chapters carry titles drawn from the work itself, among them Why not sneeze?, A young man in spring and Breaking free. As with the rest of the series, the book pairs roughly a hundred colour illustrations and captions with a chronological summary of the life and a short biography, making it a compact reference rather than an argument.

Mink studied art history at Smith College and the University of Hamburg, where she took her doctorate under Martin Warnke, and works as a writer and curator. Duchamp (1887-1968) remains the pivot on which most accounts of conceptual art turn; more specialised treatments in this collection include Michael R. Taylor's Philadelphia Museum of Art study of Étant donnés.
tags: Art, Dada, Conceptual Art, Modern Art, Painting

title: Carroll Dunham: Drawings 1974–2024
contributors: Susan Tallman (Essay, The Ropemaker's Coil: Following Carroll Dunham's Line); Robert Storr (Text); Makayla Bava (Text)
description:
Carroll Dunham has spent fifty years drawing every day and archiving the results, and this is the first museum publication to treat that daily habit as the centre of his work rather than a supply line to the paintings.

Published by the Art Institute of Chicago in 2026 and distributed to the trade by Yale University Press, the 168-page volume carries 175 colour illustrations, many of them drawings never previously published. Edited by Thea Liberty Nichols, who also curated the accompanying exhibition, it includes Susan Tallman's essay The Ropemaker's Coil: Following Carroll Dunham's Line, with further contributions by Robert Storr and Makayla Bava. The selection follows Dunham from the abstract work of the 1970s and 1980s, made against the grain of ascendant Expressionism, through the decades in which his biomorphic forms hardened into outright figuration, producing the hypersexualised, cartoon-derived characters that connect him to underground comix, West Coast Funk and Chicago Imagism.

Dunham (b. 1949, New Haven) works in painting, printmaking and occasional sculpture, and the exhibition ran at the Art Institute of Chicago from 31 January to 1 June 2026. His gallery publications include In the Flowers, The Beach, produced with Karma and Galerie Eva Presenhuber.
tags: Art, Drawing, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: Carroll Dunham: In the Flowers, The Beach
description:
By 2014 Carroll Dunham's nudes had been running for the better part of a decade, and this slim volume catches the point where the figure stops being isolated and gets pushed into a landscape.

Co-published by Karma, New York, and Galerie Eva Presenhuber, Zurich, in an edition of 750, the 96-page hardcover documents two bodies of work. In the Flowers is a set of seven paintings of cropped nudes surrounded by blossom; The Beach is a single large canvas in which a tree trunk, flowers and a full-bodied nude share the same shallow, hard-edged space. George Pendle supplies the text. The book was produced alongside the gallery's presentation of the work, and preparatory drawings for The Beach, dated 2013, have circulated separately through Presenhuber.

Dunham (b. 1949, New Haven) came out of a 1980s abstraction that gradually turned figurative, and his bathers, wrestlers and tree-and-flower settings have since become his most recognisable subject. The Art Institute of Chicago's Drawings 1974-2024 traces the drawing practice underlying these paintings.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Drawing, Exhibition Catalog

title: Marcel Dzama: Puppets, Pawns, and Prophets
description:
Marcel Dzama took over an eighteenth-century Georgian townhouse and filled it with a chess game played by masked dancers, and Puppets, Pawns, and Prophets is the record of what that looked like from inside the building.

Published in 2013 by David Zwirner with Hatje Cantz and made in close collaboration with the artist, the 184-page hardcover carries 154 colour reproductions across a nine-and-a-quarter by eleven inch page, designed by David Chickey with a text by Deborah Solomon. It documents the London exhibition in which Dzama hung puppets from the skylight above the central spiral staircase and set video monitors into the street-facing windows so the films could be watched from the pavement, alongside the drawings, collages, dioramas, paintings, masks and sculptures that surrounded them.

Dzama (b. 1974, Winnipeg) works in New York, and his ink-and-watercolour vocabulary of polka-dotted figures, bat-headed dancers and armed women has extended into film, costume and stage design, including a ballet with Justin Peck for New York City Ballet. Related publications include the Abrams monograph Sower of Discord and Crossing the Line with David Zwirner Books.
tags: Art, Drawing, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Video Art

title: Marcel Dzama: Sower of Discord
contributors: Raymond Pettibon (Foreword); Dave Eggers (Short stories); Bradley Bailey (Essay); Spike Jonze (Interview)
description:
Sower of Discord is the book that gathers fifteen years of Marcel Dzama's output in one place, and it is assembled less like an art-historical survey than like a company of the artist's own collaborators.

Published by Abrams in November 2013, the 288-page volume carries more than five hundred colour images covering work from the late 1990s to the early 2010s: the root-beer-tinted ink drawings, the dioramas, the polka-dotted and bat-headed figures, the sculptures and the films. Raymond Pettibon contributes the foreword, Dave Eggers three short stories written in response to the drawings, the art historian Bradley Bailey a critical essay, and Spike Jonze an interview with the artist. The mix is deliberate, treating Dzama's work as something that has circulated through music videos, album art and theatre as readily as through galleries.

Dzama (b. 1974, Winnipeg) emerged from the Royal Art Lodge collective in Manitoba and now works in New York. His other publications include The Berlin Years with McSweeney's, Puppets, Pawns, and Prophets with David Zwirner and Hatje Cantz, and The Book of Ballet, made around his collaboration with the choreographer Justin Peck.
tags: Art, Drawing, Contemporary Art, Sculpture, Collage

title: Martin Eder: Der blasse Tanz / The Pale Dance
description:
Martin Eder paints the things a serious painter is not supposed to want, kittens and nude girls rendered with Old Master competence, and the watercolours gathered here are where that provocation is at its most unguarded.

Published by Prestel in 2010 in a German and English edition, Der blasse Tanz / The Pale Dance runs to roughly 320 pages and reproduces 152 works at full page in colour, drawn from a decade of watercolour painting between 2001 and 2010. Most are studies of naked young women, interspersed with portraits and the cats that recur throughout Eder's work; the wash technique leaves the paper visible and the figures half-dissolved, which pulls the pictures away from the airbrushed finish of his oils. Isabelle Azoulay, who writes on feminism and erotic art, contributes the accompanying essay.

Eder (b. 1968, Augsburg) trained in Munich and Dresden and lives in Berlin, where he has also worked in music and performance. His painting deliberately borrows from Botticelli, Cranach, Renoir and Manet while keeping one foot in kitsch, and the resulting tension between technical seriousness and disreputable subject matter is the argument his work keeps making.
tags: Art, Painting, Drawing, Contemporary Art, German Art

author_full_name: Barry McGee, Stephen Powers, Todd James
title: Street Market: Barry McGee, Stephen Powers, Todd James
description:
Street Market is the book record of one of the defining street-art installations of its moment: the salvage-yard bodega that Barry McGee, Stephen Powers and Todd James built, wrecked and rebuilt inside the gallery, transposing a whole block of storefront vernacular into an art space.

Published by Little More in Tokyo in 2000 and edited by Taka Kawachi, with photographs by Cheryl Dunn, the 144-page volume documents the fabricated shopfronts, hand-lettered signage, overturned delivery truck and shelves of invented product packaging that made up the installation, alongside the drawings, spray work and painted panels the three artists produced around it. The project originated at Deitch Projects in New York and was remade in different configurations for later venues including the Venice Biennale, so the book reads less as a catalogue of objects than as a portrait of a temporary, collapsible street.

McGee (b. 1966, San Francisco) came out of Bay Area graffiti writing as Twist and trained at the San Francisco Art Institute, becoming a central figure of the Mission School; Powers wrote as ESPO before turning to hand-painted sign work; James wrote as REAS and works between comics, graffiti and painting.
tags: Art, Street Art, Graffiti, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Installation

title: Fuzz Gathering
edition_printrun: Second printing, with new front and back cover designs by the artist
description:
Fuzz Gathering is Barry McGee at zine scale: a pocket-sized, cloth-spined fanzine that returns his photographs, collages and drawings to the cheap, hand-assembled format his work came out of in the first place.

Published by Perrotin on the occasion of the exhibition Fuzz Gathering at Perrotin Paris, 16 October to 18 December 2021, the book runs 144 pages at 15.5 x 10.5 cm, offset printed and sewn bound. It gathers McGee's own source photographs alongside the geometric pattern panels, clustered drawings and recurring glum faces that structure his installations, sequenced so the visual language reads as a single accumulating system rather than a set of discrete works. The second print run recorded here carries new front and back cover designs by the artist.

McGee (b. 1966, San Francisco) came up through Bay Area graffiti writing as Twist and studied painting and printmaking at the San Francisco Art Institute. Photography has run underneath the whole practice as raw material for the paintings, installations and zines, an archive first surveyed at length in Barry McGee: Reproduction (Aperture, 2022).
tags: Art, Zine, Street Art, Contemporary Art, Drawing, Collage

title: Les Enfantillages Pittoresques
contributors: Michel Poivert (Text); Arthur Kopel (Text); Christine Besson (Text)
description:
Les Enfantillages Pittoresques is the fullest account of Laurent Millet's method, in which the photograph is the final justification for everything built, propped and abandoned before it, and it took the 2014 Prix Nadar for photography book of the year.

Published by Filigranes in May 2014 as a co-production with the Musées d'Angers, the 352-page hardcover carries some 200 colour and black-and-white photographs with texts by Michel Poivert, Arthur Kopel and Christine Besson, in French and English. It accompanied the retrospective at the Musée des Beaux-Arts d'Angers, which brought more than 200 works together for the first time, and traces roughly seventeen years of Millet's serial projects: hybrid contraptions assembled from traditional, scientific and architectural objects, set in the studio or in the estuary landscape and then photographed. He calls them poetic machineries, and works, by his own account, from an erudition of clumsiness rather than from skill.

Millet (b. 1968) has worked in photography since the early 1990s and lives on the Gironde estuary, which supplies most of his settings. Filigranes had already published two of his books: the six-metre leporello La méthode (2002) and Petites machines à images.
tags: Photography, Contemporary Art, Sculpture, French Photography, Exhibition Catalog

title: All Systems Fail
contributors: Bettina Funcke (Text); Asad Raza (Text); Christopher Bollen (Interview)
description:
All Systems Fail is the first book to treat Sarah Morris's paintings and films as one practice rather than two, tracking how the gridded surfaces of corporate glass and the moving image feed each other in an art of urban psychology.

Published by Hatje Cantz in 2023 and edited by Dirk Luckow, the 320-page bilingual German and English volume carries 508 illustrations across more than fifty paintings, documentation of the installations, drawings, film posters and sculpture, and Morris's complete cinematic output. New essays by Bettina Funcke and Asad Raza are joined by an interview with Christopher Bollen; the design is by Scott King and Tom Etherington. It accompanied the retrospective of the same name at Deichtorhallen Hamburg, organised with the Kunstmuseen Krefeld, the Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern and the Kunstmuseum Stuttgart, which brought together over 180 works.

Morris (b. 1967, Sevenoaks) lives and works in New York. Since the late 1990s she has built a body of high-gloss household-paint abstractions keyed to specific cities and power structures, running in parallel with films including Midtown, Capital, Los Angeles, Beijing, Rio and Finite and Infinite Games.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Film

title: Nguva na Nyoka
description:
Nguva na Nyoka records the moment Wangechi Mutu left Mylar behind, and with it the translucent, floating look her collages had been known for, in favour of vinyl and linoleum grounds dense enough to carry soil, tea and hair.

Published by Victoria Miro in 2014 for the gallery's second Mutu exhibition, held at 16 Wharf Road, London, from 14 October to 19 December, the black cloth hardcover carries a text by the Kenyan writer Binyavanga Wainaina and an essay by Adrienne Edwards. The title translates from Kiswahili as sirens and serpents, and the works reproduced draw on East African coastal mythologies of the nguva, or water woman, alongside gender and racial politics, Western popular culture and autobiography. Painterly passages sit against Mutu's cut-and-collaged figures, with batik fabric, synthetic hair, Kenyan soil, feathers and sand worked into the surfaces; the show also included video and sculpture.

Mutu (b. 1972, Nairobi) works between Nairobi and New York. Her hybrid female figures have since scaled up into bronze, most publicly the seated sentinels installed in the façade niches of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2019.
tags: Art, Collage, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Sculpture, African Art

title: The Soul of a Tree: A Woodworker's Reflections
description:
The Soul of a Tree is the rare furniture book written from inside the workshop rather than about it: part memoir, part working method, part argument that the maker's job is to find the one right use for a particular board.

Published by Kodansha International in 1981 with an introduction by the Nobel laureate George Wald, the volume runs to some 221 pages of colour and black-and-white photographs, drawings and shop renderings of the tables, desks, chairs and cabinets produced at Nakashima's farm compound outside New Hope, Pennsylvania. He sets the free-edge slabs, butterfly joints and rare timber against the biography that produced them: an architecture degree from MIT, years in Paris and Tokyo, work in Antonin Raymond's office, the design of Golconda at the Sri Aurobindo Ashram in Pondicherry, and internment at Camp Minidoka, where he learned traditional Japanese joinery from Gentaro Hikogawa.

Nakashima (1905-1990) remains the reference point for the American studio furniture movement, and the workshop has continued under his daughter Mira Nakashima. The book has stayed in print through successive Kodansha editions since its first appearance.
tags: Design, Furniture, Craft, Woodworking, Artist Writings

title: Georgia O'Keeffe: Art and Letters
contributors: Sarah Greenough (Letters selected and annotated); J. Carter Brown (Foreword)
description:
Art and Letters is the book that let Georgia O'Keeffe speak for herself at scale, setting a full colour survey of the paintings beside 125 of her letters and, in doing so, replacing a good deal of the mythology that had accumulated around her.

Published by the National Gallery of Art in Washington in 1987 with the New York Graphic Society and Little, Brown, the 306-page volume was the catalogue of the artist's centennial exhibition, which travelled to the Art Institute of Chicago, the Dallas Museum of Art and the Metropolitan Museum of Art between 1987 and 1989. It reproduces the 120 works shown, from early charcoals and pencil drawings through watercolours, pastels and the oils on canvas that make up the bulk of the selection. The letters were chosen and annotated by Sarah Greenough, then curator of photographs at the Gallery, and are grouped into four periods: the teaching years in Virginia, South Carolina and Texas; the New York years with Alfred Stieglitz; the turn toward the Southwest; and the New Mexico decades after his death. Jack Cowart and Juan Hamilton edited the volume, with a foreword by J. Carter Brown.

O'Keeffe (1887-1986) had died the year before the show opened, and this remains one of the primary published sources for her correspondence.
tags: Art, Painting, Artist Writings, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, American Art

title: Georgia O'Keeffe: The Poetry of Things
contributors: Elizabeth Hutton Turner (Text); Marjorie P. Balge-Crozier (Essay); Elsa Smithgall (Chronology)
description:
The Poetry of Things makes the case that Georgia O'Keeffe's real subject was the object, and that her apples, shells, bones and doors amount to a reinvention of still life rather than a sideline to the flowers and the landscapes.

Published in 1999 by The Phillips Collection with Yale University Press, the 160-page volume carries 80 colour and 69 black-and-white illustrations. Elizabeth Hutton Turner's essay traces the formative influence of Arthur Wesley Dow and the meeting of Eastern and Western thought in O'Keeffe's handling of things; Marjorie P. Balge-Crozier sets her inventions against the academic and traditional models of Western still life; Elsa Smithgall supplies an illustrated chronology. Full-page plates are interleaved with photographs of the artist's studios and collections, so the objects she kept can be read against the objects she painted. The exhibition opened at the Phillips in April 1999 and travelled to the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe, the Dallas Museum of Art and the Legion of Honor in San Francisco.

The Phillips has a particular claim on this material: in 1926 it became the first museum to buy a work by O'Keeffe, and had been showing her since 1927. The book took the Border Regional Library Association's Southwest Book Award.
tags: Art, Painting, Still Life, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, American Art

title: Nam June Paik: The Late Style
contributors: John G. Hanhardt (Curator); John G. Hanhardt (Text)
description:
A sustained look at the decade of Nam June Paik's work that scholarship had largely stopped watching for, when the founder of video art was still building battered television cabinets, laser projections and toy robots into a recognisably late idiom.

Published on the occasion of Nam June Paik: The Late Style at Gagosian Hong Kong, 17 September to 7 November 2015. It was the first exhibition of Paik's work in the city, and the first mounted after the gallery took on the representation of his estate. John G. Hanhardt, who organised Paik surveys at the Whitney Museum of American Art and the Smithsonian American Art Museum, supplies the catalogue essay. The bilingual English and Chinese volume reproduces video sculptures, paintings and drawings from Paik's final years, many never previously exhibited, alongside anchoring works from the 1960s through the 1980s, and closes with an exhibition history, a bibliography and a facsimile of one of the artist's notebooks from 1984. Designed by Goto Design, New York.

Paik (1932–2006) was born in Seoul, trained in music and aesthetics in Tokyo and Germany, and made his name in the Fluxus circle before turning the television set into an artist's material. His work runs from the prepared-TV experiments of the 1960s to the satellite broadcasts Good Morning, Mr. Orwell and Wrap Around the World.
tags: Art, Video Art, Media Art, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Fluxus

title: Paik's Virtual Archive: Time, Change, and Materiality in Media Art
description:
A conservator-turned-historian's argument that Nam June Paik's television works are less objects to be frozen than scores to be re-performed, and that the archive holding them has to change shape accordingly.

Hanna B. Hölling trained and worked as a conservator before taking a doctorate in art history, and the book draws on both careers. Close studies of works including Zen for Film, TV Buddha and Sistine Chapel trace how cathode-ray tubes fail, formats fall out of manufacture and installations are rebuilt, then ask what identity a work retains across those substitutions. Published by the University of California Press in 2017 in 264 pages with colour and black-and-white illustrations, it develops out of Hölling's dissertation on time, changeability and identity in the conservation of Paik's multimedia installations, and sits alongside her earlier Revisions — Zen for Film (Bard Graduate Center, 2015).

Paik (1932–2006) left behind an unusually fragile body of work: hundreds of installations dependent on broadcast equipment, magnetic tape and analogue synthesis, much of it now held in the Nam June Paik Archive at the Smithsonian American Art Museum, which acquired it from the estate in 2009.
tags: Art, Media Art, Video Art, Conservation, Art History, Contemporary Art

title: Nam June Paik
contributors: Leontine Coelewij (Text); Grace Deveney (Text); Rachel Jans (Text); Susanne Neuburger (Text); Andrea Nitsche-Krupp (Text); Valentina Ravaglia (Text); David Toop (Text)
description:
The catalogue for the first full-scale reassessment of Nam June Paik in a generation, and the book that recast him not as a technologist but as a transnational artist whose Eurasian imagination anticipated the borders and networks we now argue about.

Published for the retrospective organised by Tate Modern and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which opened at Tate Modern in October 2019 and travelled to the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam, SFMOMA and National Gallery Singapore. Edited by Sook-Kyung Lee and Rudolf Frieling, who curated the exhibition with Andrea Nitsche-Krupp, the 176-page volume gathers essays by curators from the four venues alongside a text by the musician and writer David Toop, roughly 150 illustrations, archival material and excerpts from Paik's own writings. The exhibition assembled over two hundred works across five decades — early Fluxus performance scores, prepared televisions, robots, room-scale video walls and satellite broadcasts — and the essays read his concepts of "Eurasia" and the "Electronic Superhighway" through transnationalism rather than through the history of technology.

Paik (1932–2006) worked between Seoul, Tokyo, Cologne and New York, and collaborated across his career with John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Joseph Beuys and the cellist Charlotte Moorman.
tags: Art, Video Art, Media Art, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Fluxus

title: Nam June Paik: Global Groove 2004
contributors: John G. Hanhardt (Text); Caitlin Jones (Text); Anja Osswald (Text); Nam June Paik (Text)
description:
Thirty years after Global Groove was broadcast on New York public television, Nam June Paik went back to it — and the book that records the return is also the best account in print of what he thought television was for.

Published for Nam June Paik: Global Groove 2004 at the Deutsche Guggenheim, Berlin, 17 April to 9 July 2004, where the artist filled a single room with some sixty-five monitors and projections in an installation made for the space. The 144-page volume carries "Paik for TV and Video: Global Groove 2004" by John G. Hanhardt, "Escape from Videoland" by Caitlin Jones and a shot-by-shot analysis of the original tape by Anja Osswald, together with 111 colour and 96 black-and-white illustrations, selections from Paik's writings on the future of television, and material on the Paik-Abe video synthesiser and the tapes Suite 212, Guadalcanal Requiem and Lake Placid '80. It also reprints, in facsimile, the 1974 Everson Museum of Art catalogue Videa 'n' Videology: Nam June Paik 1959–1973.

The original Global Groove, made with John Godfrey and aired on WNET Channel 13 in 1974, remains Paik's most cited tape: a thirty-minute collage of Korean drummers, tap dancers, Allen Ginsberg and Charlotte Moorman that proposed a television schedule drawn from everywhere at once.
tags: Art, Video Art, Media Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Fluxus

title: We Are in Open Circuits: Writings by Nam June Paik
editor: John G. Hanhardt, Gregory Zinman, Edith Decker-Phillips
description:
A large illustrated volume about the most famous video artist of the century that contains almost none of the famous images — no television walls, no Buddha watching himself — and is the better for it: this is Paik thinking on paper, in four languages and a typewriter's worth of visual puns.

Edited by John G. Hanhardt, Gregory Zinman and Edith Decker-Phillips for the MIT Press series Writing Art, the 464-page book assembles long out-of-print essays such as "Global Groove and Video Common Market" with unpublished texts on Paik's partnership with the cellist Charlotte Moorman and on the role of public television, a substantial part of his compilation "Scrutable Chinese", and detailed plans for the satellite broadcasts Good Morning, Mr. Orwell (1984), Bye Bye Kipling (1986) and Wrap Around the World (1988). Nearly 150 pages reproduce Paik's original typed and handwritten sheets, with 37 colour and 116 black-and-white illustrations; much of the material comes from the Nam June Paik Archive at the Smithsonian American Art Museum.

Paik (1932–2006) trained in music history and aesthetics, wrote steadily from the late 1950s to the mid-1990s, and treated the essay, the score and the press release as continuous with the work.
tags: Art, Artist Writings, Video Art, Media Art, Fluxus, Contemporary Art

title: Nam June Paik: Global Visionary
publisher: Smithsonian American Art Museum / D Giles Limited
contributors: John G. Hanhardt (Curator); John G. Hanhardt (Text); Ken Hakuta (Text); Elizabeth Broun (Foreword)
description:
The first exhibition to open Nam June Paik's studio drawers to the public, and a book that argues his working method (hoarding, wiring, rewiring) matters as much as the finished walls of televisions.

Published for Nam June Paik: Global Visionary at the Smithsonian American Art Museum, 13 December 2012 to 11 August 2013, which brought together 67 artworks and more than 140 items from the Nam June Paik Archive, acquired from the estate in 2009. John G. Hanhardt, the museum's consulting senior curator for film and media arts and the organiser of Paik surveys at the Whitney and the Guggenheim, contributes the central essay "Nam June Paik: From Avant-Garde to Post-Video Art"; the artist's nephew and estate executor Ken Hakuta writes "My Uncle Nam June Paik", with a foreword by Elizabeth Broun. Loans came from the Museum Moderner Kunst in Vienna, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum and the Hessel Museum of Art at Bard College. Alongside the plates the 208-page volume reproduces televisions, radios, antiques, toys, cameras, announcements and correspondence from the archive.

Hanhardt frames the book around a question of identity (Korean-born artist, video artist, Fluxus artist, performer, composer, German artist, American artist) and concludes that Paik (1932–2006) was all of them at once.
tags: Art, Video Art, Media Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Fluxus

title: Giulio Paolini
contributors: Maddalena Disch (Catalogue entries); Gabriele Guercio (Text); Barry Schwabsky (Text); Ilaria Bernardi (Text); Giulio Paolini (Text)
description:
Giulio Paolini has spent sixty years making work about the moment before a work begins: the blank canvas, the stretcher, the artist's own absence. This bilingual volume is the clearest recent account of how that programme reads across half a century.

Published by Quodlibet in 2014 to document two linked exhibitions: at MACRO in Rome, curated by Bartolomeo Pietromarchi, and at the Whitechapel Gallery in London, curated by Daniel F. Herrmann. The shows brought together 23 works spanning 1965 to 2013, including a piece conceived for the occasion; each is catalogued in an entry by Maddalena Disch, keeper of the artist's catalogue raisonné. Critical texts come from the two curators and from Gabriele Guercio, Barry Schwabsky and Ilaria Bernardi, with a contribution by Paolini himself, who states the position plainly: the artist does not wish to speak or to communicate directly, but to listen, to catch an echo. 168 pages, softcover with flaps, 240 × 280 mm, in Italian and English.

Paolini, born in Genoa in 1940 and long resident in Turin, is usually filed with Arte Povera but works closer to conceptual practice, building from citation, duplication and fragmentation: plaster casts of antique heads, doubled photographs, canvases turned to face the wall.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Conceptual Art, Arte Povera, Italian Art

title: George Tooker
editor: Robert Cozzolino, Marshall N. Price, M. Melissa Wolfe
contributors: Robert Cozzolino (Text); Marshall N. Price (Text); M. Melissa Wolfe (Text); Anna C. Chave (Text); Thomas H. Garver (Text); Jonathan Weinberg (Text)
description:
George Tooker painted the twentieth-century American crowd as a place where nobody meets anybody — subway corridors, waiting rooms, government offices — and this retrospective volume, the first in thirty years, finally treats him as a serious formal painter rather than an illustrator of alienation.

Published by Merrell in 2008 for George Tooker: A Retrospective, organised by the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and shown there, at the National Academy Museum in New York and at the Columbus Museum of Art. Edited by Robert Cozzolino, Marshall N. Price and M. Melissa Wolfe, the 192-page volume reproduces more than eighty works in colour and carries new essays by the three editors with Anna C. Chave, Thomas H. Garver and Jonathan Weinberg, addressing Tooker's obsessive approach to composition, his Catholicism and the question of identity that runs beneath the paintings. A chronology, exhibition history, bibliography, checklist and index complete the book, issued in silver-stamped boards.

Tooker (1920–2011) worked almost exclusively in egg tempera, a slow medium he learned from Paul Cadmus, producing only a few paintings a year across a career of six decades; The Subway (1950) and Government Bureau (1956) are the pictures by which most people know him.
tags: Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog, American Art, Figurative Painting, Museum Publication

title: Salman Toor: No Ordinary Love
publisher: Gregory R. Miller & Co. / Baltimore Museum of Art
contributors: Asma Naeem (Curator); Asma Naeem (Text); Evan Moffitt (Text); Hanya Yanagihara (Short story); Christopher Bedford (Foreword)
description:
Salman Toor paints young brown queer men in green-lit apartments and airport queues with the compositional manners of Van Dyck and Watteau, and the effect is deliberately unstable: an old-master intimacy applied to lives European painting never had any intention of holding.

Published by Gregory R. Miller & Co. with the Baltimore Museum of Art in 2022 for Salman Toor: No Ordinary Love, curated by Asma Naeem, then the BMA's chief curator and now its director. The exhibition gathered more than forty-five recent paintings and works on paper, several made for the show in response to seventeenth- to nineteenth-century European pictures in the museum's collection, among them Anthony van Dyck's Rinaldo and Armida of 1629, together with drawings and notebooks. The 144-page volume carries 76 colour plates, essays by Naeem and the critic Evan Moffitt on Toor's formal sources and his handling of desire, family and history, and an original short story by Hanya Yanagihara illustrated with his paintings. Designed by Topos Graphics; the exhibition travelled to the Tampa Museum of Art, the Honolulu Museum of Art and the Rose Art Museum at Brandeis.

Toor, born in Lahore in 1983 and based in New York, works between the two cities in his subject matter as much as his biography.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Queer, Museum Publication

title: Men in the Cities: Photographs 1976-1982
description:
Before Robert Longo drew them at mural scale, the contorted figures of Men in the Cities were friends on a Manhattan rooftop, pelted with objects while he shot roll after roll. This book is that source archive, published as photographs in their own right.

Schirmer/Mosel's 2009 volume gathers ninety-four photographs made between 1976 and 1982, the raw material from which Longo built the charcoal and graphite drawings that came to stand for the anxious affluence of the Reagan years. The models were his downtown circle, among them Cindy Sherman, Gretchen Bender, Glenn Branca, Brooke Alexander and Larry Gagosian, roped and toppled on the roof of his loft. Sherman contributes a personal foreword, and the book reprints Richard Price's 1987 interview with the artist, in which Longo traces the series to a still from Fassbinder's The American Soldier. Texts run in English and German.

Longo (b. 1953) came out of the Pictures Generation by way of Hallwalls, the artist-run space he co-founded in Buffalo, and has worked since across drawing, sculpture, film and music. His later charcoal series have taken up sharks, waves, nuclear tests and news photographs at the same punishing scale.
tags: Art, Photography, Contemporary Art, Drawing, Pictures Generation

title: Mural with Blue Brushstroke
contributors: Calvin Tomkins (Essay); Bob Adelman (Photographs and Interview); Pari Stave (Text)
description:
In 1986 Roy Lichtenstein finished a five-storey painting on the lobby wall of the Equitable Center in Midtown Manhattan, and this book is the record of how it got there, from first maquette to the last taped outline.

Calvin Tomkins's essay sets Mural with Blue Brushstroke against the long life of the Brushstroke motif in Lichtenstein's work, while Bob Adelman's photographs and interview follow the commission through the studio and onto the site: the design drawings begun in autumn 1984, the projection of the maquette onto plaster, and the six weeks of execution completed by assistants in January 1986. Pari Stave writes on the collaboration between artist and patron. Abrams produced the volume as a square nine-inch book carrying some 142 illustrations, 130 of them in colour, so that details of the finished wall can be read against the process shots.

The mural folds a compressed history of twentieth-century art into cartoon shorthand, quoting Léger, Matisse and Lichtenstein's own earlier paintings alongside a blast symbol, a sponge and a wedge of Swiss cheese. Lichtenstein (1923-1997) had been working at architectural scale since the late 1970s, and at roughly 20 by 10 metres this remained the largest painting he made.
tags: Art, Painting, Pop Art, Contemporary Art, Public Art

title: Roy Lichtenstein 1970-1980
description:
The 1970s are the decade of Lichtenstein most accounts skip past, and Jack Cowart's 1981 survey remains the book that argues them back into the centre of the work, tracking the move out of Pop sources and into Cubism, Surrealism and the studio itself.

Published by Hudson Hills Press with The Saint Louis Art Museum for the survey Cowart organised there, the catalogue covers paintings, sculpture and drawings made between 1970 and 1980: the Mirrors, the Entablatures, the Artist's Studios, the Cubist and Futurist paraphrases and the Surrealist canvases of the decade's end. Sixty-seven colour plates, five of them gatefolds, are set against a hundred black-and-white illustrations. Cowart describes these compositions as a rich dialogue of forms, all intuitively modified and released from their nominal sources, a formulation the Roy Lichtenstein Foundation still quotes.

Lichtenstein (1923-1997) had by then moved his main studio to Southampton on Long Island, and most of the work here was made there. German and Italian editions followed in 1982, and a limited issue was bound in red cloth with a slipcase and signed by artist and author.
tags: Art, Painting, Pop Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: Roy Lichtenstein: A Retrospective
publisher: Yale University Press in association with The Art Institute of Chicago
contributors: Clare Bell (Chronology); Yve-Alain Bois (Text); Iria Candela (Text); Harry Cooper (Text); Sara Doris (Text); Chrissie Iles (Text); James Lawrence (Text); Stephen Little (Text)
description:
Assembled for the first full retrospective since Lichtenstein's death, this catalogue runs the work from 1950 to 1997 and gives as much attention to the abstractions, the landscapes in the Chinese style and the late nudes as to the war and romance panels.

The exhibition, organised by James Rondeau for the Art Institute of Chicago and Sheena Wagstaff for Tate Modern, brought together more than 130 paintings and sculptures with some thirty drawings and collages, many of them rarely or never shown, and travelled to the National Gallery of Art, Tate Modern and the Centre Pompidou across 2012 and 2013. Nine essays follow the editors' introduction, among them Harry Cooper's 'On the Dot', Iria Candela's 'Picasso in Two Acts' and Sara Doris's 'Missing Modernism', with further texts by Yve-Alain Bois, Chrissie Iles, James Lawrence and Stephen Little. Clare Bell of the Lichtenstein Foundation supplies a full chronology. 368 pages, 172 colour plates and a further 99 figures in the essays.

Lichtenstein (1923-1997) worked for close to fifty years, and the retrospective's argument is that the sources never stopped shifting: comics and advertising first, then Monet, Cubism, Futurism, German Expressionism, Chinese scroll painting and finally his own back catalogue.
tags: Art, Painting, Pop Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: Lichtenstein
description:
Taschen's Basic Art volume on Lichtenstein is the kind of introduction the series does well: ninety-six pages, a chronological run through the career, the key paintings reproduced large and the apparatus kept short.

Janis Hendrickson traces Lichtenstein from Look, Mickey of 1961, the painting he made after his sons dared him to draw a comic character, through Drowning Girl and Whaam! to the Brushstrokes, the Mirrors and the later art-historical paraphrases, explaining the Ben-Day dot and the enlarged commercial-printing vocabulary that became his signature. A chronology of the artist's life closes the book. Taschen first issued the title in 1988 and has revised it repeatedly; it now appears in the hardcover Basic Art Series 2.0 format.

Lichtenstein (1923-1997) came to Pop in his late thirties after years of Cubist-inflected figuration, and spent the rest of his career testing how much of art history could survive translation into dots, flat colour and printed line. This volume sits on the shelf alongside the fuller monographs as an entry point.
tags: Art, Painting, Pop Art, Contemporary Art

title: Biscuits
publisher: MACK / The Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles
contributors: Ali Subotnick (Conversation with the artist); Rebecca Lowery (Text); Maggie Nelson (Text); Evan Calder Williams (Text)
description:
Tala Madani's paintings of bald men behaving badly, lit from within by projectors, torchbeams and their own excretions, get their first full North American accounting in this catalogue for MOCA's 2022 survey.

Published by MACK with The Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, for the exhibition at The Geffen Contemporary from September 2022 to February 2023, the book gathers roughly eighty plates covering fifteen years of paintings and animations from 2005 onward, along with forty previously unpublished sketchbook drawings. Ali Subotnick, who guest-curated the show, is in conversation with the artist, and new essays by Rebecca Lowery, Maggie Nelson and Evan Calder Williams take up motherhood, sexual politics and the projection logic that runs through the animations. 224 pages, OTA-bound paperback with flaps.

Madani (b. 1981, Tehran) moved to the United States as a teenager and has worked in Los Angeles since studying at UCLA. The Shit Moms, Corner Projections and Manual Man series turn slapstick and scatology on the figure of male authority; the animations, built frame by frame from repainted canvases, extend the same logic into time.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Animation

title: Allen Ruppersberg Sourcebook: Reanimating the 20th Century
description:
The second volume in ICI's Sourcebook series turns four decades of Allen Ruppersberg's collected texts, images, films, records and ephemera into a working portrait of how a conceptual artist's work actually gets made.

Edited by Ruppersberg from archives split between his family home in Cleveland and his Los Angeles studio, the book is built around nine projects from 1978 to 2012 — among them his 1995 commission for the fiftieth anniversary of the United Nations, his 1997 guidebook for the Münster Sculpture Project, and No Time Left to Start Again/The B and D of R 'n' R (2012), dedicated to the American vernacular of recorded music. Reproduced alongside them are the clippings, advertisements, photographs and printed matter he treats as raw material. Foreword by Kate Fowle, introduction by Constance M. Lewallen, design by General Working Group; 284 pages, full color, softcover with French-fold jacket.

Ruppersberg (b. 1944) belongs to the first generation of American conceptual artists, working across installation, photography, prints and books, and has collected American popular print matter and educational films of 1931–1967 for most of his career. ICI launched the Sourcebook series in 2011; each volume is edited by an artist from their own archive.
tags: Art, Conceptual Art, Artist Writings, Archive, Popular Culture

title: Paintings
edition_printrun: Published on the occasion of Ed Ruscha: Paintings, Gagosian, Rome, 20 November 2014 – 10 February 2015
description:
Ten paintings in which Ruscha's road-trip iconography is given the light, finish and atmosphere of old master painting, the American landscape rendered as something already ruined.

Published for Ed Ruscha: Paintings at Gagosian, Rome (20 November 2014 – 10 February 2015), the bilingual English/Italian catalogue reproduces all ten works in color together with installation photography, an essay by Alex Kitnick and an interview with the artist by Bob Monk. Among the paintings are Gators (2014), meticulously rendered shredded tires floating against a blank white ground, and Bliss Bucket (2014), a mattress with rumpled bedding lying beneath a giant musical bar and treble clef foreshortened for depth. Hardcover, 56 pages, designed by McCall Associates, New York.

Ruscha (b. 1937) has traced the decline of the American landscape across decades of painting, from Course of Empire (his 2005 project for the United States pavilion at the Venice Biennale, built on Thomas Cole's five-painting sequence of a landscape passing from wilderness to development to desolation) through the elegiac Psycho Spaghetti Westerns of 2011, to which these works form a coda.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Los Angeles
notes: Published on the occasion of Ed Ruscha: Paintings, Gagosian, Rome, 20 November 2014 – 10 February 2015. Text in English and Italian.

title: The Twofold Commitment
contributors: Erika Balsom (Interview); Patricia Alvarez Astacio (Interview); Benjamín Schultz-Figueroa (Interview); Lucie Kim-Chi Mercier (Interview); Stefan Östersjö (Interview)
description:
A film turned back into a book: Trinh T. Minh-ha's script for Forgetting Vietnam printed alongside its images and a decade of conversation about what the work was trying to hold.

The 2015 feature at the center of the volume marks the fortieth anniversary of the end of the war in Vietnam and takes its structure from the creation myth of two dragons whose intertwined bodies fell into the South China Sea to form the country's S-shaped coast, a legend the film uses to stage an ongoing conversation between land and water as a third space for historical and cultural re-memory. The book reproduces the film's lyrical script with stills distributed rhythmically through the text, then gathers conversations conducted between 2016 and 2022 with film and sound scholars including Erika Balsom, Patricia Alvarez Astacio and Benjamín Schultz-Figueroa, Lucie Kim-Chi Mercier and Stefan Östersjö, closing with an index of key concepts. 208 pages, paperback, published by Primary Information in 2023.

Born in Vietnam and long based in California, Trinh (b. 1952) is a filmmaker, writer and composer whose films include Reassemblage (1982) and Surname Viet Given Name Nam (1989), and the author of twelve books, among them Woman, Native, Other: Writing Postcoloniality and Feminism (1989), D-Passage: The Digital Way (2013) and Lovecidal: Walking with the Disappeared (2016).
tags: Art, Film, Artist Writings, Interviews, Vietnam

title: The House
edition_printrun: The Los Angeles Project, UCCA Beijing
description:
Kaari Upson's first artist's book turns years of source material, automatic drawings and sketches into something closer to a psychosexual graphic novel than a catalogue of works.

Organized through successive combinations and ordering systems rather than chronology, the book runs 224 pages with 130 color and 65 black-and-white reproductions, and remains the fullest published account of Upson's drawing practice. It was commissioned by UCCA for The Los Angeles Project in Beijing, a group of individual artist's books made in the tradition of John Baldessari and Edward Ruscha; the companion volumes were by Kathryn Andrews, Aaron Curry, Alex Israel, Matthew Monahan, Sterling Ruby and Ryan Trecartin. Edited by Karen Marta, designed by Brian Roettinger, and published by Koenig Books with UCCA.

Upson, who died in 2021, built much of a decade's work from the Larry Project, an obsessive reconstruction of a stranger's life assembled from papers and belongings left behind in an abandoned house near her childhood home in San Bernardino — material that fed a practice spanning drawing, sculpture, cast rubber and video, and that surfaces throughout this book.
tags: Art, Drawing, Contemporary Art, Artist Book, Los Angeles
notes: Companion volume to Aaron Curry's Boxxes in UCCA's The Los Angeles Project series.

title: Oil Studies
edition_printrun: Published on the occasion of Neil Welliver: Oil Studies, Alexandre Gallery, New York, 1 May – 18 June 2004
description:
The small paintings Neil Welliver made outdoors (standing in streams, inside the woods, in snow) collected in a square catalogue that treats the studies as finished pictures rather than preparation.

Published by Alexandre Gallery for the exhibition of 1 May – 18 June 2004, the book reproduces thirty studies in color across 48 pages at 8 × 8 inches, with texts by the poet Mark Strand and the curator Robert M. Doty and a checklist at the back. The studies were painted on the spot in the Maine woods and then carried back to the studio, where Welliver translated them, without preliminary sketching, into canvases as large as eight feet square, so the small panels record both the observed motif and the compositional decisions the big paintings would inherit.

Welliver (1929–2005) trained at Yale under Josef Albers and taught for two decades at the University of Pennsylvania before settling in Lincolnville, Maine, where the surrounding forest, streams and quarries became his only subject. Alexandre Gallery began representing him in 1998 and continues to represent the estate.
tags: Art, Painting, Landscape, Exhibition Catalog, Maine

title: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
publisher: Whitney Museum of American Art / Yale University Press
contributors: Chrissie Iles (Curator, Essay); Meg Onli (Curator, Essay); Eva Hayward (Essay); Amber Jamilla Musser (Essay)
description:
The 2024 Whitney Biennial took the instability of the real as its subject — bodies, identities and images at a moment when artificial intelligence and legislated definitions of personhood were making "authenticity" a live political question.

Curated by Chrissie Iles and Meg Onli, the catalogue opens with a thematically organized image section drawn from the exhibition rather than an artist-by-artist march, then follows with individual entries on each participating artist. The curators contribute essays on the exhibition's premises, joined by texts from Eva Hayward and Amber Jamilla Musser that take up specific currents in the show. 256 pages with 175 color illustrations, paperback, published by the Whitney Museum of American Art and distributed by Yale University Press.

The Biennial has surveyed developments in American art since 1932 and remains the museum's principal statement about the present; this eighty-first edition extended across the Whitney's Meatpacking District galleries with an accompanying program of film, performance and sound.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, American Art

author_full_name: Linda Goode Bryant, Marcy S. Philips
title: Contextures
edition_printrun: Facsimile edition of the 1978 Just Above Midtown publication
description:
A 1978 argument for Black abstraction and conceptual art, written against a canon that had no place for either, and out of print for four decades until this facsimile.

Linda Goode Bryant — founder of the Harlem-born, 57th Street gallery Just Above Midtown — wrote the book with Marcy S. Philips and published it through JAM in 1978. It traces Black artists working in abstraction from 1945 to 1978 and the conceptual practices then emerging around them, combining extended critical writing with interviews and documentation of work by twenty-five artists across 58 black-and-white and 16 color images. The 2024 edition reproduces the original in full color at 112 pages and adds a newly commissioned afterword by Thomas (T. Jean) Lax, curator at the Museum of Modern Art; co-published by Pacific and Primary Information.

Just Above Midtown opened in 1974 as one of the few commercial galleries in New York to show Black artists as a matter of course, giving early platforms to David Hammons, Senga Nengudi, Howardena Pindell, Lorraine O'Grady and others, and was the subject of MoMA's 2022 exhibition Just Above Midtown: Changing Spaces. Contextures is the gallery's own theoretical statement, and the clearest surviving account of what it thought it was doing.
tags: Art, Abstraction, Conceptual Art, African American Art, Art History, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Facsimile of the 1978 Just Above Midtown edition, co-published by Pacific and Primary Information in September 2024, with a new afterword by Thomas (T. Jean) Lax.

title: Erik Parker: Colorful Resistance
edition_printrun: Published in association with The Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum, Ridgefield, Connecticut
contributors: Mónica Ramírez-Montagut (Text); Peter Saul (Foreword); Angela Stief (Text); KAWS (Interview)
description:
The first survey of Erik Parker's painting, Colorful Resistance makes the case for his dense, hallucinatory canvases as a form of dissent — comic-book line and psychedelic colour turned against inherited authority and received ideology.

Published by Skira Rizzoli with The Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum, the book gathers roughly two decades of work: the early diagrammatic word maps that chart cultural hierarchies and name-check their sources, the viscera-like organic forms, and the animated portrait heads that became Parker's signature. Curator Mónica Ramírez-Montagut contributes the principal essay, the painter Peter Saul a foreword, Angela Stief of the Kunsthalle Wien a critical text, and KAWS an interview with the artist.

Parker was born in Stuttgart in 1968, grew up in San Antonio and studied under Saul at the University of Texas at Austin before moving to New York in the mid-1990s. His painting draws openly on alternative comics, hand-lettered flyers, graffiti and record-sleeve design, holding those underground graphic traditions in tension with the museum context this volume documents.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: José Parlá: Walls, Diaries, and Paintings
contributors: Isolde Brielmaier (Text); Greg Tate (Text); Michael Betancourt (Text)
description:
Parlá's paintings read as walls: layered, scarred, written over and washed out, and this monograph is the first full account of how a private script came to carry the memory of whole cities.

Published by Hatje Cantz in 2011 to accompany the exhibition of the same title at Bryce Wolkowitz Gallery, New York, the volume surveys two decades of work in some 131 illustrations. Parlá builds his surfaces from plaster, collaged posters, homemade inks, acrylic, oil and enamel spray paint, using fresco techniques to age them, then cuts them with a looping calligraphy that stops short of legibility. Essays by Isolde Brielmaier, Greg Tate and Michael Betancourt situate the work between painting, graffiti and documentary; the book was designed by Jutta Herden.

Born in Miami in 1973 to Cuban parents, Parlá began in the graffiti culture of the 1980s and has since drawn material from Havana, London, Istanbul, Hong Kong, Tokyo and Brooklyn, where he lives and works. He acts as a historical transcriber as much as a painter, and his later large-scale commissions extend the same argument about how cities record themselves.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Street Art

title: Elizabeth Peyton
description:
The catalogue for Peyton's 2001 Deichtorhallen Hamburg exhibition, this was the first substantial European survey of a painter who had made intimacy — and the small canvas — central to contemporary portraiture.

Published by Hatje Cantz with the Deichtorhallen, the bilingual German and English volume brings together some seventy paintings, drawings, photographs and prints. Zdenek Felix, who edited the book, and Ronald Jones examine Peyton's method of working from two kinds of source: public images lifted from print media and private snapshots she takes herself, a distinction that lets Princess Diana sit beside friends and lovers without a change of register. Her titles usually give only a first name. The exhibition ran from 28 September 2001 to 13 January 2002.

Peyton was born in Danbury, Connecticut in 1965 and studied at the School of Visual Arts in New York. Her later books include the print survey Ghost and the National Portrait Gallery's Aire and Angels; this early catalogue records the moment her work moved from downtown New York attention to museum scale.
tags: Art, Painting, Portraiture, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: Elizabeth Peyton: Aire and Angels
contributors: Lucy Dahlsen (Text); Nicholas Cullinan (Text); Thomas Crow (Text)
description:
Made in close collaboration with the artist, Aire and Angels sets Peyton's luminous portraits against four centuries of the genre and argues that her subject was never celebrity but the wish to hold time still.

Published by the National Portrait Gallery, London for the 2019 exhibition, the book surveys Peyton's work with particular attention to the decade after 2009, when her repertoire widened to take in figures such as Isa Genzken alongside longstanding subjects like Kurt Cobain. Texts by the curator Lucy Dahlsen, the Gallery's director Nicholas Cullinan and the art historian Thomas Crow trace the range of her technique — oil, pencil, pastel, watercolour and printmaking — and the exhibition hung her paintings among historic portraits from the collection, including work by and after Van Dyck. The show travelled to Frederiksborg Castle in Denmark and UCCA in Beijing, with around 100 colour plates in the book.

Peyton, born in Danbury, Connecticut in 1965, has been central to the return of figurative painting since the early 1990s. This was her first UK museum survey in a decade.
tags: Art, Painting, Portraiture, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: Elizabeth Peyton: Portrait of an Artist
description:
Peyton's first photography book is a quieter companion to the paintings: sixty-two portraits of friends and fellow artists, made across two decades and never intended as finished work.

Published by Damiani in 2009 following the exhibition at The Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum, the volume was edited by Richard Klein with a text by Rirkrit Tiravanija. The pictures were shot on 35mm, Polaroid and latterly digital cameras, and the book keeps their accidents intact — over- and underexposure, subjects drifting out of focus. Sitters include Marc Jacobs, Matthew Barney, Chloë Sevigny, Jake Chapman, Urs Fischer, Olafur Eliasson, Jonathan Horowitz, Spencer Sweeney and her gallerist Gavin Brown, along with a self-portrait.

Peyton does not describe herself as a photographer, but photographs have been the origin of her paintings from the beginning, and the book reads as the working substrate of that practice rather than a parallel career. She was born in Danbury, Connecticut in 1965 and lives and works in New York.
tags: Art, Photography, Portraiture, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog

title: Pablo Picasso: 1881–1973
edition_printrun: Originally issued in two volumes: I. The Works 1890–1936; II. The Works 1937–1973. Reprinted by Taschen in single-volume form.
description:
Carsten-Peter Warncke's Taschen survey remains the standard single-shelf account of Picasso: a chronological reading of the whole career, from the Barcelona years to the last paintings, at a scale most monographs cannot afford.

Edited by Ingo F. Walther and running to some 740 pages, the book was first issued in two volumes — The Works 1890–1936 and The Works 1937–1973 — and later reprinted by Taschen in single-volume form. Warncke moves period by period through the Blue and Rose paintings, the invention of Cubism with Braque, the neoclassical work of the 1920s, Guernica and the political pictures, the ceramics and sculpture, and the late variations on Velázquez, Delacroix and Manet, with biography and documentary photographs set alongside the plates.

Picasso (1881–1973) worked across painting, sculpture, printmaking, ceramics and stage design over seven decades, and the sheer spread of that output is what the book is built to accommodate. Warncke is a German art historian who has written on modern art extensively for the same publisher.
tags: Art, Painting, Modern Art, Cubism, Sculpture
notes: Taschen reissued this text repeatedly (two-volume 1991, one-volume hardcover, 2002 paperback, 2007 anniversary edition); the printing recorded here should be confirmed against the copy’s colophon. No clean cover image found online — cover to be photographed from the physical copy.

title: Secret Images: Picasso and the Japanese Erotic Print
edition_printrun: Published in association with Museu Picasso, Barcelona
contributors: Ricard Bru (Text); Malén Gual (Text); Hayakawa Monta (Text); Diana Widmaier Picasso (Text)
description:
A genuinely new argument about Picasso: that the shunga prints he kept privately all his life shaped the erotic drawing of his youth and returned, transformed, in the work of his last decade.

Published by Thames & Hudson with the Museu Picasso, Barcelona, the book reproduces more than twenty previously unpublished Japanese erotic prints from Picasso's own collection and sets them beside his drawings and paintings. Essays by Ricard Bru, Malén Gual, Hayakawa Monta and Diana Widmaier Picasso cover the ukiyo-e and shunga traditions, the spread of japonisme through the young Picasso's Barcelona and Paris circles, the provenance of his collection and its passage through that of Philippe Berthelot, and the specific line that runs from Hokusai's octopus to Picasso's own tentacular figures.

The volume accompanied the Museu Picasso exhibition of the same name and remains the fullest published account of Picasso's Japanese holdings, a part of his collecting largely absent from the standard literature. Irreverent drawings of his youth are followed through to the mature images of a man cast as both participant and voyeur.
tags: Art, Modern Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Japanese Prints, Erotica

title: Sigmar Polke: Die Editionen 1963-2000: Catalogue Raisonné
editor: Jürgen Becker, Claus von der Osten
description:
The first complete accounting of the editions Sigmar Polke made across four decades, and the book that established them as central to his practice rather than a sideline to the paintings.

Jürgen Becker and Claus von der Osten had been gathering Polke's editioned work since the early 1970s; here they catalogue more than 140 of them, from the first efforts of 1963 through 2000 - prints, editioned drawings and photographs, objects, catalogue inserts, artist's books and posters. The volume runs to 424 pages with 388 illustrations, 238 in colour, and carries an essay by Martin Hentschel alongside cataloguing notes by Hubertus Butin. Hatje Cantz issued it in parallel German and English editions in August 2000, the English titled The Editions 1963-2000 (ISBN 978-3-7757-0957-6). Reference apparatus and picture book at once, it tracks the wit, the mockery and the constant technical improvisation that run through the editions.

Sigmar Polke (1941-2010) was born in Oels, Silesia, and studied at the Düsseldorf academy under Karl Otto Götz and Gerhard Hoehme, where he founded Capitalist Realism with Gerhard Richter and Konrad Lueg in 1963. He received the Goslar Kaiserring in November 2000, the year this catalogue appeared.
tags: Art, Painting, Printmaking, Contemporary Art, Catalogue Raisonné

title: Jackson Pollock
publisher: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
contributors: Kirk Varnedoe (Text); Pepe Karmel (Text); Glenn D. Lowry (Foreword)
description:
The catalogue for MoMA's 1998 Pollock retrospective, the exhibition that reset the terms of Pollock scholarship for a generation and the first survey of his work in New York since 1967.

Kirk Varnedoe's long essay, "Comet: Jackson Pollock's Life and Work," carries the biographical and critical argument; Pepe Karmel's "Pollock at Work: The Films and Photographs of Hans Namuth" reconstructs how the poured paintings were actually built, using a computer-assisted reading of Namuth's 1950 films and stills and some sixty documentary photographs. Glenn D. Lowry supplies the foreword. The oblong volume runs 344 pages with more than 400 illustrations.
