The exhibition ran at MoMA from 1 November 1998 to 2 February 1999 and travelled to the Tate Gallery, London, in 1999; MoMA followed it with two companion readers, Jackson Pollock: New Approaches and Jackson Pollock: Interviews, Articles, and Reviews.

Jackson Pollock (1912-1956) worked under Thomas Hart Benton before arriving at the poured and dripped canvases of 1947-50 that made him the pivotal figure of Abstract Expressionism. MoMA holds the deepest institutional collection of his work, including the copper plates and unique proofs from his printmaking.
tags: Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Abstract Expressionism

title: Fairfield Porter: Raw: The Creative Process of an American Master
publisher: GILES, in association with the Parrish Art Museum
description:
An exhibition that hung Fairfield Porter's paintings unframed, unstretched and often unfinished, and a book that argues the unfinished quality was never an accident but the condition of the work.

Klaus Ottmann, then Robert Lehman Curator at the Parrish Art Museum, selects some forty paintings and works on paper from the museum's Porter collection, given by the artist's widow after his death in 1975. Alongside completed canvases the Parrish holds a rare concentration of half-finished ones, painted on Masonite, cardboard, aluminium sheet and other salvage, and the installation left them bare - stretchers unframed, boards leaning on picture rails - so the support was as visible as the image. The volume includes a sketchbook facsimile and Ottmann's essay "An Unfinished Quality: Fairfield Porter's Creative Process." It accompanied the exhibition at the Parrish in Southampton, New York, 11 April to 13 June 2010, which travelled to the Middlebury College Museum of Art in 2011.

Fairfield Porter (1907-1975) painted the interiors, gardens and family life of Southampton and Great Spruce Head Island while working as a critic for ARTnews and The Nation, holding to representation through the years when American painting was expected to abandon it.
tags: Art, Painting, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: Man Ray | Lee Miller: Partners in Surrealism
publisher: Merrell, in association with the Peabody Essex Museum
contributors: Phillip Prodger (Text); Lynda Roscoe Hartigan (Text); Antony Penrose (Text)
description:
The first exhibition to treat Man Ray and Lee Miller as collaborators rather than master and pupil, and to ask what each of them actually took from the other.

Phillip Prodger, then Curator of Photography at the Peabody Essex Museum, assembles roughly 115 photographs, paintings, drawings and manuscripts across 160 pages and some 100 plates, following the pair from Miller's arrival in Man Ray's Paris studio in 1929 through the solarisation experiments they made together and the decades of exchange that outlasted the affair. Lynda Roscoe Hartigan, the museum's chief curator, and Antony Penrose, director of the Lee Miller Archives and Miller's son, contribute further texts. Merrell published the volume with the Peabody Essex Museum in 2011; the exhibition opened in Salem that June and travelled to the Montclair Art Museum and to the Legion of Honor, San Francisco, in 2012.

Man Ray (1890-1976) moved from New York Dada to Paris in 1921 and made the rayographs and solarised portraits that carried Surrealism into photography. Lee Miller (1907-1977), a Vogue model turned photographer, went on to shoot for British Vogue as a war correspondent, reporting from the liberation of Paris, Dachau and Hitler's Munich apartment.
tags: Photography, Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication, Surrealism

title: Pop Touched Me: The Art of Rob Pruitt
contributors: Jeffrey Deitch (Text); Bob Nickas (Text); Glenn O'Brien (Text); Domenick Ammirati (Text); Jennifer Bornstein (Text)
description:
The first full survey of Rob Pruitt, an artist who built a career out of testing how much bad taste, sincerity and self-sabotage the art world could absorb.

Two hundred and twenty-four pages and some 250 colour plates track twenty years: the fast rise and faster fall of Pruitt & Early in the early 1990s, the exile that followed, and the return through work that refused to stay conceptual - the Cocaine Buffet, 101 Art Ideas You Can Do Yourself, the flea-market pieces, the glitter pandas, and the excursions into painting, drawing, sculpture, textile and industrial design. Jeffrey Deitch, Bob Nickas, Glenn O'Brien, Domenick Ammirati and Jennifer Bornstein contribute essays, and short statements from artists, dealers and friends including Jeff Koons, Marc Jacobs and John Waters fill out the picture. Abrams published it in 2010, edited by Eva Prinz, who according to Pruitt commissioned the book after meeting him on the street while he was casting cement into blue jeans.

Rob Pruitt (b. 1964, Washington, DC) works in New York and remains best known outside the gallery world for the Rob Pruitt Art Awards, the annual prize-giving he staged as both tribute to and parody of the art establishment.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Sculpture, Pop Art

title: Jon Rafman
contributors: Kevin McGarry (Text); Maitreyi Maheshwari (Text); Ana Teixeira Pinto (Text); Tom McCarthy (Interview)
description:
The catalogue for Jon Rafman's first major solo exhibition in Britain, and a compact reader on an artist whose raw material is the residue the internet leaves behind.

Produced for the show at the Zabludowicz Collection, London, 8 October to 20 December 2015, the 132-page paperback carries 59 colour plates, texts by Kevin McGarry, Maitreyi Maheshwari and Ana Teixeira Pinto, and an interview between Rafman and the novelist Tom McCarthy. Maheshwari edited it, Mark Holt and Malcolm Southward designed it, and it was printed in an edition of 1,000. The exhibition, staged as the Zabludowicz Collection Annual Commission, turned the galleries into a sequence of enveloping video and sculptural installations built around desire and its simulation, and premiered Sticky Drama, Rafman's first live-action film, made with Daniel Lopatin, co-produced by Warp Records and cast largely with children.

Jon Rafman (b. 1981, Montreal) came to notice with Nine Eyes of Google Street View, the ongoing archive of images harvested from Google's camera cars, and has since worked through Second Life, virtual reality, 3D animation and found online video in projects including Kool-Aid Man in Second Life and Brand New Paint Job.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Video Art, Exhibition Catalog, Media Art
notes: Published in an edition of 1,000 for the Zabludowicz Collection Annual Commission, London, 8 October – 20 December 2015. Cover to be photographed from the physical copy.

title: Robert Rauschenberg: Sympathy for Abandoned Objects
description:
The first survey of Robert Rauschenberg's sculpture in three decades, published for his centennial and organised around a single constraint: everything in it is scaled to the human body.

Gladstone Gallery mounted the exhibition at 530 West 21st Street in New York, 1 May to 14 June 2025, with the Robert Rauschenberg Foundation, gathering more than thirty small floor and pedestal works made between the 1950s and the late 1990s from the Scatole Personali, the Elemental Sculptures, the Combines, the Kabal American Zephyr, the Gluts and ROCI, all of them assembled from found matter. The 168-page Swiss-bound volume, designed by Chris Svensson, carries an essay by Lisa Le Feuvre of the Holt/Smithson Foundation, entries on each series and detailed exhibition histories. The title is Rauschenberg's own phrase for the impulse that made him carry things home from the street.

Robert Rauschenberg (1925-2008) is remembered first for the Combines, which broke the line between painting and object in the mid-1950s, but he worked continuously in three dimensions from the Scatole Personali of 1952 onward; the last exhibition to treat that work on its own terms was at the Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth in 1995.
tags: Art, Sculpture, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Assemblage

title: Daniel Richter: Paintings Then and Now
contributors: Eva Meyer-Hermann (Text); Verena Dengler (Text); Max Hollein (Text); Roberto Ohrt (Text); Cord Riechelmann (Text)
description:
The first chronological account of Daniel Richter's painting, and one that treats his swings between abstraction and figuration as a continuous argument rather than a run of abrupt reversals.

Eva Meyer-Hermann edits and writes the book, following more than 200 works across 464 pages and some 400 plates. Her reading is that the turns critics have described as breaks look, up close, like consequences - deliberate moves by a painter working out how to be modern in a medium long written off as old-fashioned. Where postwar German painting mostly took the past as its subject, Richter positions himself in the present, making pictures that make demands on the viewer without offering a moral. Verena Dengler, Max Hollein, Roberto Ohrt and Cord Riechelmann contribute further texts; Yvonne Quirmbach designed the volume, which Hatje Cantz published in May 2023 in parallel English and German editions.

Daniel Richter (b. 1962, Eutin) came out of the autonomous left-wing scene of the 1980s, designing record sleeves and posters before studying under Werner Büttner in Hamburg. He has taught in Berlin and at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna, and has been among the most visible painters of his generation for more than twenty years.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, German Art

title: Gerhard Richter: 100 Abstract Pictures
description:
Less a book about works than a work in book form: one hundred photographs of enamel poured on glass, chosen by Gerhard Richter and set against passages of randomly generated letters.

Richter made the images by pouring coloured enamel onto a glass plate and letting the paints run into one another, then photographing the shapes at the moment before they settled or dissolved. From that pool he selected a hundred and fixed them in sequence across 208 pages, each plate faced by text that is abstract in the same way the pictures are - letter combinations generated at random, legible as type but not as language. David Zwirner Books published the volume in 2023 in a small hardcover format, 23 by 16 centimetres, with all 100 images in colour. Nothing here is documentation of paintings held elsewhere; the pictures exist for and as the book.

Gerhard Richter (b. 1932, Dresden) has worked for more than sixty years across photo-painting, colour charts, grey monochromes, glass and the squeegee abstractions, and has used the book as a medium in its own right in projects such as Patterns and War Cut, where a single image is subdivided and re-sequenced until the printed sequence becomes the work.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Artist Book

title: Jean-Michel Basquiat
description:
The Gagosian survey is the volume that reads Basquiat's paintings through the Afro-Atlantic visual traditions they draw on, and sets that scholarship beside a first-hand memoir by the critic who put him in front of an art audience.

Published by Gagosian with Rizzoli in 2015 at 10 1/4 x 12 inches, the book gathers some sixty colour plates with foldouts, candid photographs of the artist at work, and full-page installation views. Robert Farris Thompson, the Yale historian of Kongo and Yoruba art, situates the major paintings within both twentieth-century art history and the Atlantic diaspora sources Basquiat drew on. Rene Ricard, whose 1981 Artforum essay "The Radiant Child" first placed Basquiat before an art readership, contributes a close account of their friendship from 1981 until the artist's death in 1988.

Basquiat (1960-1988) moved from the SAMO(c) tags he wrote with Al Diaz on downtown Manhattan walls to the canvases, drawings and Warhol collaborations of a career that lasted barely eight years. His work is held by the Whitney, MoMA, the Broad and the Fondation Louis Vuitton, and has been the subject of retrospectives at the Whitney, the Brooklyn Museum, the Fondation Beyeler and the Barbican.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Neo-Expressionism

title: Jean-Michel Basquiat: 1960-1988
description:
Taschen's Basic Art volume is the primer version of Basquiat: ninety-six pages that carry the whole arc of the work in a format designed to put it in as many hands as possible.

Published in 2003 and written by the German art historian Leonhard Emmerling, the book follows the chronology from the SAMO(c) graffiti Basquiat wrote with Al Diaz on SoHo walls, through the breakout group show "New York/New Wave" at P.S.1 in 1981, to the Warhol collaborations and the late paintings. Colour plates of the major canvases are set against a biographical chronology and short readings of individual works. Basic Art is the format Taschen has used since 1985 for single-artist introductions, and this remains the most widely circulated Basquiat title in print.

Basquiat (1960-1988) was the first Black American painter to reach that scale of international attention in his own lifetime, showing at Documenta 7 at twenty-one and in the 1983 Whitney Biennial. Emmerling has written similar volumes on Jackson Pollock for the same series.

title: Jennifer Packer: Tenderheaded
publisher: The Renaissance Society at the University of Chicago
contributors: Kerry James Marshall (Conversation); Jessica Bell Brown (Text); April Freely (Text); Safiya Sinclair (Poem); Solveig Ovstebo (Introduction)
description:
Packer's first monograph is the book that introduced her painting to a wider readership: portraits and funerary bouquets held in thin, searching washes of colour, made at a moment when the question of how Black bodies are seen and mourned had become unavoidable.

Published by the Renaissance Society at the University of Chicago in 2018, the hardcover documents "Tenderheaded," Packer's autumn 2017 exhibition there. Alongside full documentation of the paintings and works on paper it carries a conversation between Packer and Kerry James Marshall, essays by Jessica Bell Brown and April Freely, a poem by Safiya Sinclair, and an introduction by the curator Solveig Ovstebo. The design is by Hyo Kwon. The volume argues for Packer's rigorous engagement with the history of painting as inseparable from her highly personal response to the present political landscape.

Packer (b. 1984, Philadelphia) studied at Tyler School of Art and Yale, and has since had solo presentations at the Serpentine in London and the Whitney Museum of American Art. Her flower paintings, made as elegies for people killed by police violence, are among the works this book first published.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Portraiture

title: Jean-Michel Basquiat
publisher: Whitney Museum of American Art / Harry N. Abrams
description:
This is the catalogue that made Basquiat a museum artist: the record of the first full retrospective of his work, organised by Richard Marshall for the Whitney Museum of American Art four years after the artist's death.

Published in 1992 by the Whitney with Harry N. Abrams, the 272-page volume documents the exhibition that travelled from New York to the Menil Collection in Houston, the Des Moines Art Center and the Montgomery Museum of Fine Arts. Marshall's catalogue assembles the paintings, drawings and painted objects alongside a detailed chronology, exhibition history and bibliography, and it established the framework - the SAMO(c) years, the downtown scene, the Warhol collaborations, the recurring vocabulary of crowns, anatomy and erased words - that later scholarship has argued with and built on.

Basquiat (1960-1988) produced roughly a thousand paintings and two thousand drawings in eight years. Marshall, then a curator at the Whitney, had earlier organised its "New Image Painting" and "Fifty Years of Collecting" surveys; his Basquiat catalogue remains the point of departure for the Brooklyn Museum, Fondation Beyeler and Barbican projects that followed.
tags: Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication

title: Streetlamps
contributors: Russell Ferguson (Text); Christopher Bedford (Text); George Roberts (Text); Michael Govan (Text); Ari Marcopoulos (Photographs)
description:
Gagosian's five-hundredth book takes the measure of the one Chris Burden project a mass audience knows by heart: the antique cast-iron streetlamps he stripped, restored and massed into forests of light, of which LACMA's Urban Light is only the most famous.

Published in September 2018, three years after Burden's death, the volume follows the streetlamps he began amassing in the early 2000s. Two hundred and two of them, restored from 1920s Los Angeles stock, became Urban Light (2008) at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art; four further streetlamp sculptures were realized for public and private sites. Each is documented across 172 pages from conception through restoration to installation, with texts by Russell Ferguson, Christopher Bedford and George Roberts, a contribution from LACMA director Michael Govan, and photographs by Ari Marcopoulos.

Chris Burden (1946–2015) built his reputation in the early 1970s on performances that put his own body at risk, among them Shoot and Trans-Fixed, then spent four decades converting that appetite for physical consequence into engineering: Erector-set bridges, Meccano skyscrapers, the thousand-car freeway of Metropolis II. The streetlamps belong to the same instinct for accumulation and civic scale, and are the works through which most people now meet him.
tags: Art, Sculpture, Contemporary Art, Installation, Public Art, Los Angeles

title: Drawings 1958–64
description:
A 640-page brick of a book that finally gives Lee Lozano's drawings the scale her paintings have long enjoyed: six years of graphite and crayon in which hammers, screwdrivers and light switches are drawn as bodies, and bodies as tools.

Published by Karma in September 2021, the volume gathers 568 color reproductions of work made between 1958 and 1964, the period in which Lozano moved from raw figurative sketches to the anthropomorphized tool drawings that remain her most confrontational work. Genitals are rendered as machine parts, plugs and sockets are read for exactly what they suggest, and the human figure is attacked outright as a design failure. Two essays commissioned for the book, by Helen Molesworth and Tamar Garb, take the drawings on their own terms rather than as a prologue to the later conceptual pieces. Molesworth: “For Lozano, connection is fraught and hairy. Connection is dangerous.” Bound in orange cloth at 9 by 7 1/4 inches.

Lee Lozano (1930–99) trained in Chicago, arrived in New York in 1960, made the large Wave paintings, and then in 1971 withdrew from the art world altogether, treating the withdrawal as her final work and extending it into a decades-long refusal to speak to women. Karma has published her steadily, issuing the Private Book notebooks in facsimile alongside Lozano c. 1962.
tags: Art, Drawing, Conceptual Art, Contemporary Art, Feminist Art, American Art

title: Bildrausch: Drawings 1966–2018
description:
Bildrausch is the book that shows the other Walter Pfeiffer: not the photographer of Swiss youth and beauty but the draughtsman who came first and never stopped drawing.

Running to 492 pages and 380 colour plates, it gathers half a century of graphic work. The early 1970s brought large-scale hyper-realist pencil drawings that served as working models for the photographs, a manner that carried into his posters for the Zurich Filmpodium, magazine illustration and commissioned portraits. From the 1980s and through the 1990s, when he set photography aside for a time, Pfeiffer worked in China ink, coloured pencil and watercolour: portraits of beautiful boys and of the women friends around him, still lifes and flowers, drawn with a line that alternates between graphic reduction and a taste for ornament. Designed by Marietta Eugster with texts by Martin Jaeggi, it was named one of the Most Beautiful Swiss Books of 2018.

Pfeiffer (b. 1946, Beggingen) trained as a window dresser and a graphic designer before turning to photography, self-taught, around 1972. Shown from 1974 in Transformer at the Kunstmuseum Luzern, he stayed an artist's artist until Welcome Aboard (2001) reached a wider public and led to work for i-D and Vogue. Edition Patrick Frey has published most of his books, among them Cherchez la femme!, Scrapbooks 1969–1985 and Chez Walti.
tags: Art, Drawing, Photography, Contemporary Art, Swiss Art

title: Notebook #41, 1977
description:
A facsimile of a single composition book kept by Paul Thek (1933–1988) in 1977, published on the artist's own terms: Thek counted the more than one hundred notebooks he left at his death as artworks in themselves, not as preparation for them.

Reproduced page for page in color across 144 pages, the notebook holds watercolors, diary entries, poetry, correspondence, lists, scribbles and sketches, alongside the long, meticulous transcriptions of philosophers and theologians that Thek copied out by hand. The binding reproduces the marbled green Mead cover and its Square Deal / Composition label at close to the original 9¾ × 7½ inches, banded in kraft paper. The edition behaves less like a monograph than like the object it copies, and it records the daily texture of a practice that otherwise survives largely in fragments.

Thek was a central and famously uncommercial figure of the post-1960s New York generation, known for the wax-and-Plexiglas Technological Reliquaries, the effigy The Tomb, and the large collaborative environments he built across Europe through the 1970s. Much of that installation work was dispersed or destroyed, and his reputation was rebuilt largely posthumously, above all by the 2010 Whitney retrospective Diver. The notebooks are the most continuous surviving body of his work, which gives an edition like this unusual weight in the literature.
tags: Art, Drawing, Artist Notebooks, Facsimile, Diaries, Watercolor
notes: Facsimile of Thek's 1977 composition notebook, one of over 100 he left at his death. Extent cataloged at 144 pages / 144 color plates, per the Pace shop listing and confirmed independently by the ARTBOOK/D.A.P. trade record (Hbk, 7.5 x 9.75 in.); the 148 pages given in Pace's journal feature is an outlier. Cover taken from Pace's flat front-cover plate and cropped from the 16:9 press image.

title: Nothing But Time: Paul Thek Revisited 1964–1987
description:
A slim staple-bound catalogue that compresses Paul Thek's entire working life into 72 pages, made for the 2013 Pace London exhibition that carried his posthumous reappraisal out of the museum and into the gallery.

Curated by Kenny Schachter, Nothing But Time: Paul Thek Revisited 1964–1987 gathered a focused selection across every medium Thek worked in — the early paintings made on newspaper, the wax-and-Plexiglas Technological Reliquaries, and the late watercolors painted in the years before his death in 1988 — with an introduction by Schachter. Thirty color and two black-and-white plates run across an oblong 8½ × 9½ inch page. The object itself is deliberately modest: flecked grey board, blue type, three staples through the spine, no jacket and no scholarly apparatus, closer to a gallery handout than to a monograph.

Thek (1933–1988) was among the most influential and least commercial figures of his New York generation, known for the Technological Reliquaries, the effigy The Tomb, and the large collaborative environments he built across Europe through the 1970s, most of which were dispersed or destroyed. His reputation was rebuilt almost entirely after his death from an AIDS-related illness, above all by the Whitney's 2010 retrospective Diver; this catalogue belongs to the wave of gallery exhibitions that followed it. Long out of print.
tags: Art, Exhibition Catalog, Sculpture, Painting, Watercolor, New York Art, American Artists, 1960s-1970s
notes: Published for Nothing But Time: Paul Thek Revisited 1964-1987, Pace London, 2013, curated by Kenny Schachter, who also contributes the introduction. Saddle-stitched with three staples; 30 color and 2 black-and-white plates. Out of print, listed as sold out by Pace. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-17.

title: Untitled Sketchbook
description:
A facsimile of the 1969 sketchbook in which Paul Thek drew himself over and over again, issued by American Art Catalogues in an edition of 1,000 — thirty-one pencil drawings, none of which had been shown publicly before this edition.

The original is a Dutch WIREO Schetsboek, oblong and wire-bound, and the facsimile reproduces it as an object rather than as a book about one: the same 9½ × 12½ inch leaf, the same spiral, the stationer's stamp still sitting in the corner of the cover, the whole thing housed flat in a grey board tray printed in red with the drawing's own credit line. What fills it is mostly self-portraiture, faces worked and reworked and probably drawn in a mirror. “No one has ever interested me quite as much as myself,” Thek once wrote. Nearby leaves carry a Christ in a crown of thorns and a run of strange still lifes: a crucifix laid beside an empty ashtray, a mushroom growing what looks like a corkscrew tail.

Thek (1933–1988) was among the first artists to work at the scale of a whole environment, and he spent much of the 1970s in Europe building theatrical installations with collaborators, nearly all of which were dispersed or destroyed. That loss is what gives the notebooks their weight: they are the most continuous surviving record of a practice otherwise known through photographs and reconstruction. He has since been the subject of exhibitions at the Whitney Museum, the Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, ZKM Karlsruhe, Sammlung Falckenberg and the ICA Philadelphia, and his estate is represented by Pace Gallery, Galerie Buchholz and Mai 36 Galerie.
tags: Art, Drawing, Facsimile, Artist Notebooks, Self-Portraits, New York Art, American Artists
notes: Facsimile of Untitled (Sketchbook), c. 1969, pencil on 31 leaves, 9 1/2 x 12 1/2 inches. The original is a Dutch WIREO Schetsboek; the facsimile reproduces the wire binding and sits flat in a grey board tray printed in red. First printing December 2024, edition of 1,000. No ISBN issued. The publisher states 31 leaves and gives no page count, so page_count is left empty. Cover cropped from the publisher's photograph of the open tray. Summer acquisitions and archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-17.

title: Deaf Material
description:
A sweeping visual archive by the Berlin-based American sound artist Christine Sun Kim (b. 1980), Deaf Material collects over 600 vernacular photographs and images documenting deaf representation in mainstream culture from the late 19th century to the present.

The 384-page publication unfolds across 24 thematic categories (including Airports, Celebrity ASL, Call and Wait, Deaf Power, Deaf/death, Parking Lots, and Trash), each carrying Kim's expanded captions that provide historical context and commentary on deaf experiences and aesthetics. Drawing from pop culture imagery, memes, advertisements, disability signage, artworks, personal ephemera, and archival material from Gallaudet University, the book employs a Tumblr-style aesthetic that mirrors how visual culture circulates and accumulates meaning online. Kim's approach transforms these everyday encounters with deaf representation into a critical taxonomy of visibility and misrepresentation.

Christine Sun Kim is a sound artist whose practice employs drawing, video, performance, American Sign Language, and closed-captioning to explore how sound operates in society while advocating for Deaf community visibility. Deaf since birth, Kim challenges hearing-world power structures through works that interrogate "hearing etiquette" and institutional barriers. Her major works include Degrees of Deaf Rage (mathematical angle drawings depicting emotional intensity), The Sound of Temperature Rising (2019, ASL-based climate change drawings), and her Super Bowl LIV ASL interpretation. She holds MFAs from School of Visual Arts (2006) and Bard College (2013), and is represented by François Ghebaly (Los Angeles), Gallery Hyundai (Seoul), and White Space (Beijing).
tags: Photography, Artists' Books, Deaf Culture, Visual Culture, American Sign Language, Archives
notes: Publication date: September 15, 2026 (forthcoming). Features archival photographs with expanded captions exploring deaf imagery and cultural representation, incorporating musical notation, body language, and American Sign Language. Kim sourced materials from her daily life, books, online resources, and the archives at Gallaudet University.

title: E Pluribus Venom: The Art of Shepard Fairey
edition_printrun: First edition, trade state; out of print. Patterned paper over boards, quarter-bound in green cloth, no dust jacket as issued.
description:
The book of Shepard Fairey's 2007 exhibition E Pluribus Venom at Jonathan LeVine Gallery in New York, in which the OBEY artist turned the graphic language of American currency and mid-century advertising against the institutions they represent.

The title, "out of many, poison," reworks the national motto E Pluribus Unum printed on U.S. coins and bills. The works reproduced here borrow engraved banknote ornament and a Norman Rockwell register to question the symbols and methods of the American machine, while a second strand, drawing on Art Nouveau, hippie poster art and revolutionary propaganda, celebrates figures who opposed blind nationalism and war. More than an exhibition catalogue, the volume expands on the themes of the show, with essays by Sarah Jaye Williams and gallerist Jonathan LeVine and an introduction by the artist.

Fairey (b. 1970) began the Andre the Giant sticker campaign as a Rhode Island School of Design student in 1989; it grew into the OBEY Giant project and a body of stencilled, screen-printed and collaged work that has moved between the street, the gallery and political campaigning. E Pluribus Venom sits between the 2006 survey Supply & Demand and the 2008 Obama Hope poster that made him widely known.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Street Art, Graphic Design, Exhibition Catalog, Pop Culture
notes: Published to accompany the 2007 exhibition at Jonathan LeVine Gallery, New York. Issued without dust jacket. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Mayday: The Art of Shepard Fairey
edition_printrun: First edition; out of print. Flag-motif pictorial boards with gilt-stamped black cloth spine, no dust jacket as issued.
description:
The book of Mayday, Shepard Fairey's 2010 exhibition that closed Deitch Projects in New York, a distress call and a celebration of the renewal that revolutionary movements promise.

The collection is built around portraits of advocates for the working class and the oppressed. Fairey argues that artists, musicians and writers such as Joe Strummer, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Woody Guthrie and Cornel West all have a part in stirring a response to injustice, and the works layer his stencil and collage vocabulary of stars, stripes and printed ephemera over these figures. Essays by writer and filmmaker Antonino D'Ambrosio and gallerist Jeffrey Deitch accompany 134 colour illustrations. The book is bound in flag-patterned pictorial boards with a gilt-stamped black cloth spine and was issued without a jacket.

Fairey (b. 1970) founded the OBEY Giant campaign in 1989 and by 2010 had moved from street stickers to museum retrospectives, following the Obama Hope poster and the 2009 ICA Boston survey. Mayday is the third Gingko Press volume on his work, after Supply & Demand and E Pluribus Venom.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Street Art, Graphic Design, Exhibition Catalog, Pop Culture
notes: Published to accompany the May 2010 exhibition at Deitch Projects, New York, the gallery's final show. Issued without dust jacket. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Obey: Supply & Demand: The Art of Shepard Fairey, 20th Anniversary Edition
edition_printrun: 20th Anniversary Edition, 2009 (expanded from the 2006 first edition, ISBN 9781584232445). Cloth spine over silver-embossed black boards; issued with a folded poster. Out of print.
contributors: Carlo McCormick (Essay); Steven Heller (Essay); Henry Rollins (Essay); Rob Walker (Essay); Roger Gastman (Essay)
description:
The expanded 20th-anniversary edition of Supply & Demand, the survey of Shepard Fairey's work from the first OBEY Giant sticker in 1989 to the Obama Hope poster, published with Obey Giant to coincide with his 2009 retrospective at the ICA Boston.

The volume adds 100 pages of illustrations and text to the 2006 first edition, bringing the record of the OBEY street campaign, Fairey's design practice and his gallery exhibitions up to the 2008 presidential campaign. It reproduces versions of the Obama image alongside the letter from the President-elect thanking Fairey for his support. Essays by Carlo McCormick, Steven Heller, Henry Rollins, Rob Walker and Roger Gastman frame the work in relation to propaganda, punk and skate graphics and contemporary art. The book is bound in black boards embossed in silver with a cloth spine, and was issued with a folded poster; 780 colour illustrations.

Fairey (b. 1970) started the Andre the Giant Has a Posse sticker as a Rhode Island School of Design student; the campaign became the OBEY Giant project and, by 2009, a body of screen-prints, stencils and murals shown in museums. This is the reference volume for the first two decades, later followed by the exhibition books E Pluribus Venom and Mayday.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Street Art, Graphic Design, Pop Culture, Punk
notes: 20th Anniversary Edition (2009), expanded by 100 pages from the 2006 first edition (ISBN 9781584232445); the publisher's site no longer lists either edition, so the anniversary edition is recorded here. Issued with a folded poster. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Stencil Graffiti
edition_printrun: First edition, 2002 (Street Graphics / Street Art series). Out of stock at the publisher.
description:
Tristan Manco's 2002 survey of stencil graffiti, the first book devoted to the medium and the first to profile Banksy, published by Thames & Hudson at the start of its Street Graphics / Street Art series.

Manco traces the history of the cut stencil from political sloganeering to the spray-can street work of the late 1990s and gathers more than 400 examples from cities around the world, with subjects ranging from the political to the poetic. Featured artists include Blek le Rat, Miss.Tic, Nemo, Western Cell Division, Gerardo Yepiz, Swifty, Bonehead, Dave Kinsey, Atelier Populaire and Shepard Fairey, who describes the stencilled image as "integrated with the texture of the street." The book also follows the medium off the wall onto canvas, clothing and metal, and into style magazines and new media. Compact, square-format paperback with flaps, 405 illustrations.

Manco, a Bristol-based designer and writer, began the project in 1999; it was his first book and was followed by Street Logos, Graffiti Brasil, Street Sketchbook and, in 2020, The Stencil Graffiti Handbook. He also edited Nicholas Ganz's Graffiti World.
tags: Art, Street Art, Graffiti, Stencil, Graphic Design, Design
notes: Street Graphics / Street Art series. First book on stencil graffiti and the first to profile Banksy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Art of Rebellion: World of Streetart
edition_printrun: First edition, Publikat, 2003; issued with 50 stickers and an audio CD mixed by Florian Keller (Compost Records). A simultaneous US co-edition appeared from Gingko Press (ISBN 9781584231578). Out of print.
description:
The first volume of The Art of Rebellion, the series edited by Munich designer and writer Christian Hundertmark (C100), and one of the earliest books devoted to street art as distinct from letter-based graffiti.

Published by Publikat, the house behind the graffiti magazine Stylefile, the book presents around 130 artists from Australia, Asia, Europe and the Americas working with stickers, posters, stencils, sculptural pieces and hybrids in between. Space Invader, Above, Lefunk, Milk, Fume, Hoernchen and East Eric are among those shown, each documented with photographs, quotes and short interviews, with a foreword by D*Face. The compact hardcover was issued with a sheet of 50 stickers and an audio CD of thirteen tracks mixed by Florian Keller of Compost Records; the cover, a photograph of a Munich traffic signal marked "place your stickers here, please," invites the reader to join in.

Hundertmark began painting graffiti in 1989 and turned to street art in 2000; he runs the Munich studio C100 Purple Haze, working for clients in sports and music. The series continued with The Art of Rebellion 2 (2006), 3 (2010) and 4 (2016) and became one of the most widely circulated street-art surveys.
tags: Art, Street Art, Graffiti, Stencil, Graphic Design, Ephemera
notes: Volume 1 of the series. First edition issued with 50 stickers and an audio CD; a Gingko Press co-edition (ISBN 9781584231578) was published for the US market the same year, and a 2005 Gingko paperback (ISBN 9781584232094) followed. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Killer Joe's Early Times 1965-73
contributors: Nils Olsen (Text); Fredi Fischli (Text); Yuji Yamashita (Text)
description:
A catalogue raisonné of Keiichi Tanaami's early work, 1965 to 1973, the years in which the Tokyo designer turned the language of American Pop, psychedelia and underground comics into an art of his own.

Named after the Tokyo discotheque for which Tanaami produced graphics in the late 1960s, the volume gathers collage, painting, silkscreen prints and animation: his illustrations for the magazine Shosetsu Gendai, drawings and collages for Art Journal, album covers for the Monkees and Jefferson Airplane, stills from the animation series made for the film festival at Sogetsu Art Center, anti-Vietnam War silkscreens and the painting series of Hollywood actresses. Much of the material was rediscovered in the artist's own storage after decades. Edited by Momoko Fukurama and Shinji Nanzuka with texts by Nils Olsen, Fredi Fischli and Yuji Yamashita, it is a large-format hardcover with 250 colour plates and an obi.

Tanaami (1936–2024) was a protagonist of Japan's postwar avant-garde and one of the first Japanese artists to work across art and commerce; his work appeared in advertising and magazines from 1962, and a 1968 trip to New York and a meeting with Andy Warhol set him on parallel paths of poster design, happenings, prints and record sleeves.
tags: Art, Collage, Pop Art, Psychedelia, Japanese Art, Illustration, Animation
notes: Catalogue raisonné of the years 1965 to 1973, produced with Nanzuka, Tokyo. Full title on the title page: Keiichi Tanaami: Killer Joe's Early Times 1965-73. The cover carries the short title Killer Joe's with a printed obi. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Unfiltered: The Complete Ralph Bakshi: The Force Behind Fritz the Cat, Mighty Mouse, Cool World, and The Lord of the Rings
description:
The first book to chronicle the full career of Ralph Bakshi, the animator who took the medium into X-rated, adult territory with Fritz the Cat in 1972 and kept it there through Heavy Traffic, Coonskin, Wizards and The Lord of the Rings.

Jon M. Gibson and Chris McDonnell follow Bakshi from his Brownsville childhood and his apprenticeship at Terrytoons through each film, television series and unrealised project, drawing on more than thirty years of material from the director's own archive: hundreds of pieces of pre-production art, animation cels, rough sketches, line drawings and doodles never previously published. Interviews and anecdotes from John Kricfalusi, Albert Ruddy, Bruce Timm, Peter Chung, John Sparey, Tom Minton and Frank Frazetta place his work among the animators he influenced. Quentin Tarantino contributes the foreword and Bakshi the afterword. The book was launched at Comic-Con International in San Diego in July 2008 and is now out of print.

Gibson is a screenwriter, journalist and curator; McDonnell is an artist and designer and the publisher of the comics anthology Meathaus. Bakshi (b. 1938) continued to paint and make short films from his studio in New Mexico.
tags: Art, Animation, Film, Illustration, Drawing, Comics, Pop Culture
notes: First edition, Universe Publishing, 2008. Foreword by Quentin Tarantino, afterword by Ralph Bakshi. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Graffiti World: Street Art from Five Continents
edition_printrun: First edition, Abrams, October 2004 (UK co-edition Thames & Hudson, ISBN 9780500511701). Jacket folds out into a poster; three 8-page gatefolds and one 4-page foldout. An updated edition followed in 2009 (ISBN 9780810980495).
description:
Nicholas Ganz's 2004 survey of graffiti and street art across five continents, at the time the most comprehensive book on the subject and a fixture of the wave of street-art publishing that followed.

The book traces the movement from anonymous New York spray-can writing of the late 1960s to a global practice taking in stickers, stencils, posters and murals. Arranged first by continent and then by the artists' noms de plume, it presents more than 2,000 illustrations by over 150 artists, among them Banksy and Os Gêmeos, with interviews and statements from many of them; each continent also gets a foldout of local work. Edited by Tristan Manco, author of Stencil Graffiti, and produced as an oversized hardcover with three 8-page gatefolds, a 4-page foldout and a jacket that opens into a poster.

Ganz, who paints as Keinom, is a graffiti artist based in Essen, Germany, and travelled widely to gather the material. He followed this volume with Graffiti Women: Street Art from Five Continents (Abrams, 2006), and an updated edition of Graffiti World appeared in 2009.
tags: Art, Street Art, Graffiti, Stencil, Graphic Design, Culture
notes: First edition, Abrams, 2004; the jacket folds out into a poster. Dimensions taken from the Thames & Hudson UK co-edition. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Disposable: A History of Skateboard Art
edition_printrun: Gingko Press edition (first Gingko printing, 2007); first published 2004
description:
Sean Cliver's Disposable is the standard visual history of skateboard graphics, gathering more than 1,000 deck designs from the early 1980s to the start of the 2000s.

Cliver, who drew boards for Powell-Peralta from 1989 and later for World Industries and its offshoots, arranges the graphics chronologically and pairs them with first-hand recollections from the artists and skaters who made and rode them, among them Andy Howell, Barry McGee, Ed Templeton, Steve Caballero and Tony Hawk. The result is an insider's account of a commercial art form built to be destroyed: decks were printed in short runs, sold, skated and scrapped, and their imagery, from Vernon Courtlandt Johnson's Powell-Peralta skulls to the deliberately crude parodies of the early 1990s, survived mostly in memory and in collectors' garages.

First published in 2004, the book was reissued by Gingko Press in 2007 and again in 2014, and was followed by Cliver's companion volume The Disposable Skateboard Bible (2009). Together they remain the primary reference for a graphic tradition that fed directly into street art, illustration and independent publishing.
tags: Art, Skateboarding, Illustration, Graphic Design, Pop Culture, Design History
notes: Gingko Press edition. First published in 2004; Gingko Press issued a softcover edition in 2007 (ISBN 9781584232643) and a hardcover edition in 2014 (ISBN 9781584233787), both 237 pages with the same cover. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Techniques for Drawing Female Manga Characters
edition_printrun: How to Draw Manga, volume 20 (English-language edition)
contributors: Society for the Study of Manga Techniques (Series)
description:
A volume from Graphic-sha's How to Draw Manga series, this instructional manual by Hikaru Hayashi sets out the conventions for drawing female figures in Japanese comics.

Published in Tokyo in 2000 as volume 20 of the English-language series, the book moves from proportion, posture and facial construction to clothing, hair and expression, each lesson built from clean line drawings intended to be copied and adapted. Hayashi frames manga sketching as a matter of selecting and controlling information: deciding what a figure needs to communicate and how much detail carries it. The examples reproduce the bishōjo idiom of late-1990s commercial manga, with its large eyes, simplified anatomy and exaggerated poses.

The How to Draw Manga series, produced by Graphic-sha with the Society for the Study of Manga Techniques, was the first sustained attempt to export Japanese comics pedagogy to English-speaking readers, and its volumes circulated widely among Western art students and fan artists in the years before manga became a mainstream publishing category. The book is held here as a document of that transmission and of the visual codes it standardised.
tags: Art, Manga, Comics, Drawing, Illustration, Pop Culture
notes: Volume 20 of the English-language How to Draw Manga series; also listed under the series title How to Draw Manga: Female Characters. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Bat-Manga!: The Secret History of Batman in Japan
edition_printrun: First edition, softcover; issued 28 October 2008 alongside a limited hardcover edition
contributors: Geoff Spear (Photography); Saul Ferris (Collection); Jiro Kuwata (Artist)
description:
Chip Kidd's Bat-Manga! recovers the Batman comics that Jiro Kuwata drew for the Japanese weekly Shōnen King in 1966 and 1967, stories never collected in Japan and never previously translated.

Licensed at the height of the television-driven Batman craze, Kuwata's serials pit Batman and Robin against mutant dinosaurs, alien invaders and atomic-age villains in a brisk, brush-drawn style that owes as much to Osamu Tezuka as to Bob Kane. Kidd reproduces the stories from the original printed pages, yellowed paper and halftone included, and surrounds them with Geoff Spear's photographs of Saul Ferris's collection of Japanese Batman toys, trading cards and ephemera. An interview with Kuwata closes the volume. The book is issued as an oversized softcover with French flaps and a wraparound band, designed by Kidd in the manner of a period Japanese magazine.

Kidd, associate art director at Alfred A. Knopf and the designer of jackets for Michael Crichton's Jurassic Park and Cormac McCarthy's novels, has built a parallel body of work on comics history, including Batman Collected (1996), Peanuts: The Art of Charles M. Schulz (2001) and Mythology: The DC Comics Art of Alex Ross (2003).
tags: Art, Comics, Manga, Graphic Design, Pop Culture, Illustration
notes: Copy carries an obi band. A limited hardcover edition (ISBN 9780375425455, 384 pages, with a different cover and an additional Kuwata story) was published simultaneously. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Art of Getting Over: Graffiti at the Millennium
description:
Written by the graffiti writer ESPO, Stephen Powers's The Art of Getting Over is a history of graffiti from inside the culture, published as the form reached the end of its first three decades.

Powers combines a general history with extended interviews with the writers who shaped it, from the New York subway generation to the crews active in Philadelphia, Los Angeles and San Francisco in the late 1990s, and illustrates the account in colour with pieces, throw-ups, sketches and blackbook pages. The title turns on the writers' own term for succeeding by any means, and the book's argument, that graffiti had become ubiquitous without being understood, is made through the voices of practitioners rather than critics. The black cover carries Powers's hand-lettered title in silver.

Powers (b. 1968) began writing in Philadelphia, published the graffiti magazine On the Go from 1988 to 1998, and moved to New York in 1994. His later work moved from walls to painted signs and public murals: A Love Letter for You (Philadelphia, 2009), commissions for the Brooklyn Museum and Coney Island, and the ESPO's Art World studio and sign shop in Brooklyn. This is his first book.
tags: Art, Graffiti, Street Art, Culture, Pop Culture, Typography
notes: First edition, St. Martin's Press, 1999. Out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Bauhaus 1919–1933: Workshops for Modernity
contributors: Benjamin H. D. Buchloh (Essay); Brigid Doherty (Essay); Hal Foster (Essay)
description:
The catalogue of MoMA's 2009 Bauhaus exhibition, the first comprehensive survey of the school in New York since the museum's own 1938 show, edited by curators Barry Bergdoll and Leah Dickerman.

Organised with the three German Bauhaus collections in Berlin, Weimar and Dessau, the exhibition brought together some 400 works across the school's fourteen years: furniture, textiles, ceramics, metalwork, typography, photography, theatre design, architecture, painting and sculpture. The book reproduces them in 510 colour images and sets them against essays by Bergdoll and Dickerman on the school's history and pedagogy, with shorter texts by Benjamin H. D. Buchloh, Brigid Doherty, Hal Foster and fourteen other scholars, each devoted to a single key object. A chronology and documentary section follow.

The exhibition Bauhaus 1919–1933: Workshops for Modernity was on view at The Museum of Modern Art, New York, from 8 November 2009 to 25 January 2010. It marked the school's ninetieth anniversary. The clothbound catalogue is out of print.
tags: Art, Bauhaus, Modernism, Design, Architecture, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication
notes: Catalogue of the exhibition at The Museum of Modern Art, New York, 8 November 2009 – 25 January 2010, organised with the Bauhaus-Archiv Berlin, the Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau and the Klassik Stiftung Weimar. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: VU: The Story of a Magazine
edition_printrun: First English edition (US title); the UK issue carries the title VU: The Story of a Magazine that Made an Era under the same ISBN
description:
Michel Frizot and Cédric de Veigy's VU is the first full study of the Paris illustrated weekly that, between 1928 and 1940, set the pattern for the modern photo magazine.

Founded and directed by Lucien Vogel, VU ran for 638 issues under the motto 'the text explains, the photograph proves', conceived as an ongoing film that would bring the whole of life within range of the eye. Its pages were built from photographs by André Kertész, Germaine Krull and Robert Capa, among many others, laid out with photomontage covers by Alexander Liberman and his colleagues, and its special issues on the Soviet Union, Germany and the Spanish Civil War shaped the political photo-essay. The book reproduces covers, pages and spreads from across the run, with commentary on the magazine's editorial methods, its layouts and its photographers.

Frizot, research director at the CNRS in Paris and editor of A New History of Photography (1998), and de Veigy, a writer on photography and film, draw on the complete run. The English edition, translated by Ruth Sharman, was published by Thames & Hudson in London (as VU: The Story of a Magazine that Made an Era) and in New York under this title.
tags: Photography, Magazines, Photojournalism, Graphic Design, Design History, Modernism, Photomontage
notes: US issue of the Thames & Hudson edition; the UK issue is titled VU: The Story of a Magazine that Made an Era, with a different jacket and the same ISBN. Translated from the French by Ruth Sharman. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: László Moholy-Nagy
edition_printrun: English trade edition; German edition ISBN 9783791350011
contributors: Ulrike Gärtner (Essay); Kai-Uwe Hemken (Essay); Gerald Köhler (Essay); Herbert Molderings (Essay); Joyce Tsai (Essay)
description:
Catalogue of the Schirn Kunsthalle's 2009 retrospective, the first comprehensive survey of László Moholy-Nagy in nearly two decades, covering painting, photography, film, sculpture, stage design and typography from every phase of his career.

Edited by Ingrid Pfeiffer and Max Hollein, the book presents around 170 works in 220 illustrations, with essays by Ulrike Gärtner, Kai-Uwe Hemken, Gerald Köhler, Herbert Molderings, Pfeiffer and Joyce Tsai on the artist's Bauhaus years, his advertising graphics and the debate over 'Bauhaus typography', his photograms and photosculptures, and the late paintings on plastics. A section documents the reconstruction of the Raum der Gegenwart (Room of the Present), the multimedia room Moholy-Nagy designed in 1930 for the Provinzialmuseum Hannover but never built, realised in 2009 for the exhibition.

Moholy-Nagy (1895–1946), Hungarian-born painter, photographer and theorist, taught the preliminary course and the metal workshop at the Bauhaus from 1923 to 1928, worked in Berlin and London, and founded the New Bauhaus in Chicago in 1937. The exhibition was shown at the Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt from 8 October 2009 to 7 February 2010; Prestel issued the catalogue in English and German editions.
tags: Art, Bauhaus, Modernism, Photography, Painting, Photomontage, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Prestel edition. Catalogue of the retrospective at the Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt, 8 October 2009 – 7 February 2010; a German-language edition (ISBN 9783791350011) was issued in parallel. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Merz to Emigre and Beyond: Avant-Garde Magazine Design of the Twentieth Century
edition_printrun: First edition, hardcover; a paperback edition (ISBN 9780714865942) followed
description:
Steven Heller's Merz to Emigre and Beyond surveys the avant-garde magazine across the twentieth century, from Kurt Schwitters's Merz to Rudy VanderLans and Zuzana Licko's Emigre, as the form in which new art, politics and typography first reached print.

Arranged chronologically, the book follows the little magazine and the underground press through Futurism, Dada, De Stijl and the Bauhaus, the Surrealist View and VVV of the 1940s, the East Village Other and the 1960s underground papers, Punk, Raw and the desktop-published titles of the 1980s and 1990s. Some 350 reproductions of covers and spreads carry the argument: that the magazine, cheap, periodic and disposable, was where designers tested ideas before they hardened into style.

Heller (b. 1950), art director of The New York Times Book Review for over thirty years and co-founder of the MFA Design programme at the School of Visual Arts, has written more than 100 books on graphic design history, among them Design Literacy and Graphic Style. This hardcover first edition was published by Phaidon in 2003; a paperback edition followed.
tags: Art, Graphic Design, Magazines, Design History, Typography, Modernism, Design
notes: First edition, hardcover, Phaidon 2003. Bibliography and index. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: László Moholy-Nagy: The Art of Light
edition_printrun: First English edition; out of print
contributors: Oliva María Rubio (Curator and essay); Vincenzo Vitiello (Essay); Hubertus von Amelunxen (Essay); Frans Peterse (Essay); Oliver A. I. Botar (Essay); Jeanpaul Goergen (Essay)
description:
Catalogue of the touring exhibition László Moholy-Nagy: The Art of Light, organised by PHotoEspaña and curated by Oliva María Rubio, which presented the artist's work across media as a single sustained investigation of light.

More than 200 works from 1922 to 1946 are reproduced: photographs, photograms, photoplastics, paintings and works on paper, stage and graphic design, and films, with a commented filmography for 1921–1934 and a list of works. Essays by Rubio, Vincenzo Vitiello, Hubertus von Amelunxen, Frans Peterse, Oliver A. I. Botar, Jeanpaul Goergen and the artist's daughter Hattula Moholy-Nagy, who edited the volume, trace the passage from the Constructivist paintings of the Berlin years through the Bauhaus photograms and the Light Prop for an Electric Stage to the late Plexiglas sculptures and the pedagogy of the Institute of Design in Chicago.

The exhibition opened at the Círculo de Bellas Artes, Madrid, during PHotoEspaña 2010 (9 June – 25 July) and travelled to the Martin-Gropius-Bau, Berlin (November 2010 – January 2011) and the Gemeentemuseum, The Hague (February – April 2011). La Fábrica published the English edition clothbound with a dust jacket; it is out of print.
tags: Art, Photography, Bauhaus, Modernism, Photomontage, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Catalogue of the exhibition organised by PHotoEspaña: Círculo de Bellas Artes, Madrid, 9 June – 25 July 2010; Martin-Gropius-Bau, Berlin, November 2010 – January 2011; Gemeentemuseum, The Hague, February – April 2011. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Berlin: The Twenties
edition_printrun: First US edition; English edition of Berlin: Die Zwanzigerjahre (Christian Brandstätter Verlag, Vienna)
description:
An illustrated cultural history of Weimar Berlin by the Austrian art historian Rainer Metzger, assembling some 400 photographs, paintings, posters and pieces of printed ephemera from the years between the November Revolution of 1918 and the Nazi seizure of power in 1933.

The book moves through the period year by year, setting the work of Grosz, Dix, Höch, Schwitters, Brecht, Piscator and the Bauhaus circle against the street photography, cabaret programmes, film stills, magazine covers and advertising that made the city the emblem of the modern metropolis. Expressionism, Dada, Neue Sachlichkeit and the building programmes of the late 1920s appear alongside inflation, unemployment and the political violence of the closing years. The picture editing is by the Viennese publisher Christian Brandstätter, whose firm issued the original German edition, Berlin: Die Zwanzigerjahre; Abrams published this English edition in New York in 2007.

Metzger (b. 1961) is professor of art history at the Karlsruhe Academy of Fine Arts and has written extensively on Van Gogh, Klimt and Viennese modernism.
tags: Art, Design, Photography, Weimar, Culture, Modernism, Design History
notes: Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Mythology: The DC Comics Art of Alex Ross
edition_printrun: First edition, 2003. An expanded edition with 32 additional pages followed in 2005 (ISBN 9780375423833).
contributors: Chip Kidd (Text); Geoff Spear (Photography); M. Night Shyamalan (Introduction); Paul Dini (Text)
description:
A designed monograph on the painter Alex Ross and his DC Comics work, assembled by Chip Kidd with photography by Geoff Spear and published by Pantheon in 2003.

The book gathers Ross's painted treatments of Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, the Flash, Aquaman, Green Lantern and the Justice League, and sets the finished work beside its working material: pencil sketches, the photographs of costumed models Ross paints from, limited-edition prints and prototype sculptures. Vintage DC panels are cut in as reference points, so the reader can follow how Ross reworks the source imagery. Kidd's layout treats the paintings at full scale and the studio material at close range. The volume also carries an original Superman-Batman story written by Kidd and painted by Ross, a new Robin origin by Paul Dini, and an introduction by M. Night Shyamalan.

Ross (b. 1970) came to prominence with Marvels (1994) and Kingdom Come (1996), bringing a gouache-based realism to superhero comics. Kidd, the Knopf book designer, has produced a run of books on comics and their material culture, including Batman Collected and Peanuts: The Art of Charles M. Schulz; Mythology is among the most widely circulated of them, and it received an Eisner Award.
tags: Comics, Illustration, Painting, Pop Culture, Graphic Design, Design
notes: Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Another Science Fiction: Advertising the Space Race 1957–1962
description:
A study of the advertising the American aerospace industry ran in its own trade journals between Sputnik and the Apollo commitment, assembled by the historian Megan Prelinger from the pages of Aviation Week and Missiles and Rockets.

Nearly 200 advertisements from Lockheed, Douglas, Convair, Republic, North American and smaller subcontractors are reproduced and read as a visual record of the early Space Race. Aimed at recruiting engineers and at the military and government buyers who funded the work, the ads promised orbital stations, lunar bases and crewed flights to Mars in an idiom borrowed from science-fiction illustration. Prelinger organises the material thematically, in chapters on satellites, the body in space, spacecraft form, the landscape of space and mid-century modern design, and traces the shift in tone from speculative imagery to sober systems engineering by 1962.

Prelinger is co-founder, with Rick Prelinger, of the Prelinger Library in San Francisco, an independent research collection of periodicals, ephemera and government documents; this book draws on its holdings. A companion volume, Inside the Machine: Art and Invention in the Electronic Age (2015), extends the same method to electronics advertising.
tags: Design, Graphic Design, Illustration, Science Fiction, Design History, Advertising, Pop Culture
notes: Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Russian Avant-Garde Book 1910–1934
edition_printrun: First edition, 2002; second printing 2003. Also issued by Abrams under ISBN 0810962241. Out of print.
contributors: Jared Ash (Essay); Nina Gurianova (Essay); Gerald Janecek (Essay); Glenn D. Lowry (Foreword)
description:
The catalogue of the Museum of Modern Art's 2002 exhibition of Russian avant-garde books, the first full account of the Judith Rothschild Foundation gift of some 1,200 books, journals and related printed works that made MoMA's holdings in the field the largest outside Russia.

The volume follows the book from the Futurist lithographed pamphlets of 1910 to 1916, in which Kruchenykh, Khlebnikov, Goncharova, Larionov, Rozanova and Malevich set handwritten and rubber-stamped text against coarse paper and collaged covers, through the Suprematist and Constructivist typography of Lissitzky and Rodchenko after 1917, to the photomontage propaganda albums and children's books of the early Stalin years. Essays by Margit Rowell, Deborah Wye, Nina Gurianova, Gerald Janecek and Jared Ash cover the poets' collaborations, the transrational language of zaum, the printed word as a Constructivist object and the political turn of the late 1920s. The exhibition ran at MoMA from 28 March to 21 May 2002, organised by Wye, then chief curator of prints and illustrated books, with Rowell as guest curator.

The catalogue is out of print. It sits with the library's other Russian avant-garde holdings, including Lodder's Russian Constructivism and MoMA's Stenberg Brothers.
tags: Art, Russian Avant-Garde, Constructivism, Typography, Graphic Design, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication
notes: Out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Russian Constructivism
edition_printrun: First edition, 1983. Paperback issued under ISBN 9780300034066; reprinted several times.
description:
Christina Lodder's history of Russian Constructivism, published by Yale in 1983 and still the standard English-language account of the movement.

Working from Soviet archives and from interviews with surviving participants, Lodder traces the movement from the non-utilitarian constructions of Tatlin, Rodchenko, the Stenbergs and Medunetsky in 1919 to 1921, through the theoretical turn that fused formal research with utilitarian purpose, into the Vkhutemas workshops where the programme was taught, and out to the designed object, the Constructivist interior, photomontage and the organic construction of Tatlin's Letatlin glider. A postscript follows the movement's reception in Germany and the West. The book is illustrated throughout with reproductions of works, documents and workshop photographs, and carries a substantial bibliography.

Lodder (b. 1948) is a historian of the Russian avant-garde who has taught at St Andrews and Kent and edited Malevich's writings; her later books include Constructive Strands in Russian Art 1914-1937. The volume anchors the library's Constructivism shelf alongside MoMA's Russian Avant-Garde Book and Stenberg Brothers catalogues and the Tate's Rodchenko & Popova.
tags: Art, Constructivism, Russian Avant-Garde, Soviet Design, Design History, Modernism
notes: Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Rodchenko & Popova: Defining Constructivism
contributors: Christina Kiaer (Essay); Vicente Todolí (Foreword); Alexander Rodchenko (Artist); Liubov Popova (Artist)
description:
The catalogue of the Tate Modern exhibition that set Alexander Rodchenko and Liubov Popova side by side as the two artists who defined Constructivism between the October Revolution and Popova's death in 1924.

Edited by Margarita Tupitsyn, the book follows both artists from abstract painting through the 5x5=25 exhibition of 1921, where Rodchenko showed the three monochromes Pure Red, Pure Yellow and Pure Blue and Popova her Space-Force Constructions, into the work in production that followed: Rodchenko's posters, advertising with Mayakovsky, book covers and the Workers' Club of 1925; Popova's textile designs for the First State Cotton-Printing Factory, theatre sets for Meyerhold and typography. More than 200 works are reproduced. Tupitsyn's essay reads the Constructivist code of production, and Christina Kiaer's "His and Hers Constructivism" takes up the question of gender in the movement. Texts by Rodchenko and Popova, including Rodchenko's "The Line", are reprinted. The exhibition ran at Tate Modern from 12 February to 17 May 2009.

Tupitsyn is a curator and historian of Russian avant-garde art and photography, author of Malevich and Film; Kiaer teaches at Northwestern and wrote Imagine No Possessions on Constructivist objects.
tags: Art, Constructivism, Russian Avant-Garde, Graphic Design, Posters, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication
notes: Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Shooting Stalin: The 'Wonderful' Years of Photographer James Abbe
editor: Bodo von Dewitz and Brooks Johnson
description:
The retrospective catalogue of the American photojournalist James Abbe (1883-1973), published by Steidl for the Museum Ludwig, Cologne, and built around the 1932 Kremlin sitting in which Abbe became the only foreign photographer permitted to portray Stalin.

Edited by Bodo von Dewitz and Brooks Johnson, the book reproduces more than 300 photographs in tritone. It opens with Abbe's theatre and film portraiture of the 1920s, when he photographed Rudolph Valentino, Charlie Chaplin, Josephine Baker and the Ziegfeld chorus, and follows him to Europe: the studios of Sergei Eisenstein and the Moscow theatre, the last years of the Weimar Republic in Berlin, the coming of the Nazis, and the battlefields of the Spanish Civil War. Abbe made a specialty of photographing leaders, Hitler, Mussolini and Franco among them, and the Stalin pictures, with the dictator at his desk under a portrait of Marx, are reproduced with the illustrated reportages in which they first appeared. Terence Pepper contributes an essay on the portrait work. Texts are in English and German.

The book accompanied the exhibition at the Museum Ludwig from 2 October 2004 to 9 January 2005 and received the Deutscher Fotobuchpreis. It is now out of print.
tags: Photography, Photojournalism, Portraiture, Weimar, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication
notes: Out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Stenberg Brothers: Constructing a Revolution in Soviet Design
edition_printrun: First edition, 1997. Also distributed by Abrams under ISBN 9780810961739. Out of print.
contributors: Peter Kenez (Essay); Vladimir Stenberg (Artist); Georgii Stenberg (Artist)
description:
The catalogue of the Museum of Modern Art's 1997 exhibition of Vladimir (1899-1982) and Georgii (1900-1933) Stenberg, the first critical survey of the brothers whose film posters carried Constructivist montage onto the Soviet street.

Organised by Christopher Mount of MoMA's Department of Architecture and Design, the show drew on the Ruki Matsumoto collection in Tokyo and brought together around 100 works, including 65 film and political posters. The book reproduces the posters at full page in colour: the Stenbergs' designs for Battleship Potemkin, The Man with the Movie Camera, Symphony of a Big City and dozens of imported Hollywood and German features, in which faces are cut, tilted and enlarged, lettering runs on diagonals and photographic fragments are redrawn by hand to simulate the effects of montage. Mount's essay sets the posters against the brothers' earlier work as sculptors of spatial constructions in the Obmokhu group and as stage designers for Tairov's Kamerny Theatre; Peter Kenez contributes an essay on the film culture of the early Soviet years. A chronology closes the volume.

The exhibition ran at MoMA from 10 June to 2 September 1997. The catalogue is out of print and remains the principal English-language reference on the Stenbergs.
tags: Graphic Design, Posters, Constructivism, Soviet Design, Film, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication
notes: Out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Postmodernism: Style and Subversion 1970–1990
edition_printrun: First edition, 2011; distributed in North America by Abrams. Out of print.
contributors: Paola Antonelli (Essay); Charles Jencks (Essay); Paul Greenhalgh (Essay); David Byrne (Essay); Arindam Dutta (Essay); Victor Buchli (Essay)
description:
The catalogue of the Victoria and Albert Museum's 2011 exhibition, the first large museum survey to treat postmodernism as a design movement with a beginning and an end rather than as a condition of contemporary culture.

Edited by Glenn Adamson and Jane Pavitt, the book runs from the anti-modernist positions of Venturi, Scott Brown and Hans Hollein around 1970, through the Italian radical groups, Alchimia and Memphis, to the moment in the mid-1980s when the style was absorbed by advertising, corporate architecture and the music industry, and ends with its collapse into commercial mannerism by 1990. Forty-one short essays by the editors and by Paola Antonelli, Charles Jencks, Paul Greenhalgh, David Byrne, Arindam Dutta and others cover architecture, furniture, product and graphic design, fashion, film, television and video. The 250 colour plates include Sottsass's Carlton bookcase, Jean-Paul Goude's images of Grace Jones, Peter Saville's record sleeves and Charles Moore's Piazza d'Italia. The exhibition ran at the V&A from 24 September 2011 to 15 January 2012.

Adamson, then head of research at the V&A, has since written Thinking Through Craft and Fewer, Better Things; Pavitt curated the V&A's Cold War Modern (2008). The book is out of print.
tags: Design, Postmodernism, Architecture, Graphic Design, Design History, Exhibition Catalog, Museum Publication
notes: Out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Red Star Over Russia: A Visual History of the Soviet Union from the Revolution to the Death of Stalin
edition_printrun: Abrams first edition, September 2009. Out of print in this edition.
description:
A visual history of the Soviet Union from the October Revolution to the death of Stalin, drawn entirely from the London designer David King's archive of Soviet graphic material.

More than 550 posters, photographs, paintings, magazine covers, book jackets, advertisements and pieces of street ephemera are reproduced in sequence, carrying King's account of the revolution, the civil war, the constructivist years, the purges and the personality cult. Photomontage by Klutsis and Rodchenko sits beside anonymous agitprop, doctored official photographs and pages from illustrated magazines such as USSR in Construction. King designed the book himself, in the dense red-and-black manner of his earlier Soviet titles.

David King (1943–2016) was art editor of the Sunday Times Magazine from 1965 to 1975 and spent four decades building what became one of the largest private collections of Soviet visual culture, now held by Tate. His related books include The Commissar Vanishes (1997), on the falsification of photographs under Stalin, and Ordinary Citizens (2003). Red Star Over Russia was published simultaneously by Abrams in New York and Tate in London; the Abrams edition carries the subtitle recorded here.
tags: Design, Graphic Design, Soviet Design, Posters, Photomontage, Culture
notes: Abrams first edition. Published the same year by Tate Publishing in London under the subtitle 'A Visual History of the Soviet Union from 1917 to the Death of Stalin'. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: VALIE EXPORT: Zeit und Gegenzeit / Time and Countertime
contributors: Sabeth Buchmann (Text); Yilmaz Dziewior (Text); Elke Krasny (Text); Toby Axelrod (Translation)
description:
The catalogue of the two-city retrospective that the Belvedere in Vienna and the Lentos Kunstmuseum in Linz mounted for VALIE EXPORT in 2010, and the most comprehensive single volume on the artist's work.

Published for Zeit und Gegenzeit / Time and Countertime (16 October 2010 – 30 January 2011), the book centres on recent and new work while setting it against a concentrated selection of the early actions, expanded-cinema pieces and video works. The title derives from a 1973 video-sculpture concept by the artist. Edited by Agnes Husslein-Arco and Stella Rollig, with texts by Sabeth Buchmann, Yilmaz Dziewior and Elke Krasny; German and English run in parallel throughout. Large format, 304 pages, extensively illustrated.

VALIE EXPORT (b. Linz, 1940) adopted her name in 1967 and became a central figure of the Viennese avant-garde with works such as Tapp und Tastkino (1968), Aktionshose: Genitalpanik (1969) and the film Unsichtbare Gegner (1977). Her practice moves across performance, photography, film, video, installation and writing, and has been the subject of retrospectives in Vienna, Paris and Linz, where the VALIE EXPORT Center opened in 2017.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Performance Art, Video Art, Conceptual Art, Photography, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Bilingual German/English. Published for the Belvedere and Lentos exhibitions, 2010–11. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Fashion at the Time of Fascism: Italian Modernist Lifestyle 1922–1943
description:
The first visual history of Italian fashion during the two decades of Fascist rule, tracing how a modernist industry negotiated between international couture and the dictates of the regime.

Edited by Mario Lupano and Alessandra Vaccari, the book draws on extensive archival research in period magazines, photographs, advertising and design publications, presenting around 700 images in a running sequence of picture and text. The material is arranged under four themes, Measurements, Model, Brand and Parade, that follow the rhythms and rituals of the Italian day, from the standardised body and the autarkic textile to the branded label and the mass spectacle. Thematic maps, cross-references, an iconographic index and a full bibliography support both reading and scholarly use. Published by Damiani in 2009 in a 400-page hardcover.

Mario Lupano is an architectural historian and Alessandra Vaccari a fashion historian, both teaching at the Università Iuav di Venezia. The book belongs with the library's holdings on graphic design and photography of the interwar period, in which the same rationalist typography and photomontage seen here served advertising, propaganda and the illustrated press.
tags: Fashion, Design, Graphic Design, Photography, Fascism, Culture, Art
notes: Cover credits 'Edited by Mario Lupano, Alessandra Vaccari'. Retailer listings give the subtitle as 'Italian Modernist Lifestyle Between 1922 and 1943'. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: H.N. Werkman
edition_printrun: Monographics series. Co-published by Laurence King, London (ISBN 9781856693899) and Yale University Press, New Haven. Out of print.
description:
The first English-language monograph on Hendrik Nicolaas Werkman (1882–1945), the Groningen jobbing printer who turned the letterpress shop into an instrument for abstract picture-making.

Written by Alston W. Purvis for the Monographics series edited by Rick Poynor, the book follows Werkman from his commercial printing business through the experimental druksels he began around 1923, the nine issues of his periodical The Next Call (1923–26), the stencilled and hand-inked prints of the 1930s and the clandestine publications of De Blauwe Schuit during the German occupation, among them the Chassidische Legenden suite. Werkman was arrested by the Sicherheitsdienst and shot on 10 April 1945, three days before Groningen was liberated; much of his work was destroyed in the fire that followed. 132 illustrations, 123 in colour, with a bibliography. 112 pages, paperback.

Purvis, professor of graphic design at Boston University and co-author with Philip B. Meggs of Meggs' History of Graphic Design, had earlier surveyed the same ground in Dutch Graphic Design 1918–1945 (1992). The book sits alongside the library's holdings on Dutch modernism, typography and the printed page as an artist's medium.
tags: Art, Graphic Design, Typography, Design, Printmaking
notes: Yale University Press edition of the Laurence King Monographics title (series editor Rick Poynor); the same book was also issued in London under ISBN 9781856693899. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The New Infinity: Visuelle Kunst und Musik in Planetarien / Visual Art and Music in Planetariums
contributors: Ulrike Bergermann (Text); Michaela French (Text); Metahaven (Text); David OReilly (Text)
description:
A record of The New Infinity, the Berliner Festspiele programme that treated the planetarium dome as a gallery for contemporary art and commissioned new fulldome works for it.

Conceived by Thomas Oberender within the Festspiele's Immersion strand and produced with Planetarium Hamburg, the series opened the projection and sound infrastructure of planetariums to artists of the digital age. This publication reflects on the history of the planetarium and its possibilities as an exhibition space and documents the commissioned works, among them pieces by Agnieszka Polska, Robert Lippok & Lucas Gutierrez and the collective Metahaven. Texts by Ulrike Bergermann, Michaela French, Metahaven, Thomas Oberender and David OReilly run in German and English. Designed by the Berlin studio Eps51 and published by Walther König in 2019; 88 pages in a tall paperback format.

Oberender directed the Berliner Festspiele from 2012 to 2021 and built its Immersion programme around virtual reality, 360-degree film and dome projection. The book belongs with the library's holdings on media art and on the exhibition formats that lie outside the white cube.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Media Art, Video Art, Sound Art, Exhibition Catalog
