notes: Bilingual German/English. Some dealer records give 83 numbered pages; the trade listing is 88. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: H.o.Me.: Heim für obsolete Medien / Home for Obsolete Media
contributors: Amulets (Text); Kristen Gallerneaux (Text); Doris Gassert (Text); Hannes Grassegger (Text); Martina Haidvogl (Text); Eva-Maria Knüsel (Text); Peter Kraut (Text); Yves Niederhäuser (Text); The Mutha_Ship Landing (Text)
description:
A bilingual survey of obsolete audiovisual media and of the artists who keep them running, published for the exhibition H.o.Me. – Home for Obsolete Media at Kunsthaus Langenthal.

Edited by curator Raffael Dörig and the Swiss artist and engineer Flo Kaufmann, the book takes objects from Kaufmann's collection, magnetic tape, vinyl, audio cassette, Super 8, as points of departure for short technological and cultural histories of each format. Works by Flo Kaufmann, Christian Marclay, !Mediengruppe Bitnik, Alexandra Navratil, Strotter Inst. and others show what can be made from discarded machines, and specialists in conservation, music and media offer practical advice on keeping analogue material playable. Texts by Kristen Gallerneaux, Doris Gassert, Hannes Grassegger, Martina Haidvogl, Peter Kraut and others. 208 pages with 96 illustrations, issued in a slipcase modelled on a VHS cassette box.

Kaufmann, known for his work rescuing vinyl-cutting technology, and Dörig, director of Kunsthaus Langenthal, place the book between media archaeology and artists' practice. It joins the library's holdings on sound art, media art and the material culture of recording.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Media Art, Obsolete Media, Sound Art, Exhibition Catalog, Culture
notes: Bilingual German/English. Cover styling of the title is 'H.o.Me.'; the slipcase imitates a VHS box. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Portrait Machine Project
description:
A portrait series made with a machine that claims to photograph what a psychic would see, and a first monograph by the New Zealand-born, Brooklyn-based photographer Carlo Van de Roer (b. 1975).

Van de Roer works with an AuraCam, a modified Polaroid Land camera developed in the 1970s. Sitters place their hands on sensors; the device converts their biofeedback into washes of colour laid over the instant print, and issues a typed description and diagram of the character it has read. Friends, family and public figures, among them Miranda July, Terence Koh, Aurel Schmidt and James Frey, are shown in the resulting Polaroids together with the machine's printouts, so that the reader can weigh the readings against the faces. Text by Val Williams. 40 plates, 88 pages, clothbound, published by Damiani in 2013.

The project asks what a viewer expects a portrait to disclose and how far the apparatus, rather than the photographer, shapes the answer. Van de Roer later founded Satellite Lab, a research studio for camera and lighting technology, through the New Museum's NEW INC programme, and works as a director and cinematographer. He is represented by Danziger Gallery, New York.
tags: Photography, Portraiture, Contemporary Art, Conceptual Art, Polaroid
notes: Clothbound. Sold out at the publisher. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Book of Stamps
description:
An album of artists' postage stamps issued by Cabinet magazine, continuing a lineage of artist-made philately that runs from Fluxus and Ray Johnson's mail-art circle to the present.

Edited by Sina Najafi and Jeffrey Kastner, the clothbound volume holds fifteen full-page sheets of limited-edition stamps, perforated, gummed and bound to be torn out and used. The contributing artists are Walead Beshty, Melissa Brown, Melissa Dubbin & Aaron S. Davidson, Spencer Finch, Carl Michael von Hausswolff & Leif Elggren, Jonathan Herder, Mikhail Iliatov, Emily Jacir, Julia Jacquette, Vandana Jain, Sandra Eula Lee, Line Up, Frank Magnotta, Michael Oatman and David Shrigley. An essay by the writer George Pendle sets out the history of the artist's stamp and its ambiguous relation to state postal authority. 76 pages, published by Cabinet Books, Brooklyn, in 2008.

Cabinet, the quarterly founded by Najafi in 2000, has published a small run of books and multiples extending the magazine's interest in classification, bureaucracy and the overlooked object. The volume joins the library's holdings on artists' multiples, ephemera and the printed edition as a work in its own right.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Postage Stamps, Artist Multiples, Ephemera, Mail Art
notes: Fifteen detachable sheets of perforated, gummed artist stamps. Sold out at the publisher. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: The Stampographer
description:
The first English-language introduction to Vincent Sardon (b. 1970), the Paris artist who designs, casts and sells rubber stamps under the name le Tampographe, and uses a bureaucratic tool to refuse authority rather than assert it.

Edited by Lisa Pearson and Richard Kraft for Siglio, the book gathers around 200 impressions from Sardon's output: insult sets in a dozen languages, skeletons and organs, obscene hands, sport and pornography, and the defacement of art-historical monuments, printed in the colours of the stamp pad. An interview with the artist by the editors, translated by Philippe Aronson, sets out the workshop economy behind the work; Sardon makes everything himself and sells it directly from his shop at 4 rue du Repos beside Père Lachaise, outside galleries and the art market. 100 pages, hardcover, published in 2017.

Sardon drew for Libération for a decade before turning to stamps full time. His blog chronicles were collected as Le Tampographe Sardon (L'Association, 2012), and a further volume, Le Tampographe, followed from Flammarion. Dada and pataphysics are the nearest reference points; the library's holdings on rubber stamps, mail art and artists' multiples are the nearest shelves.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Rubber Stamps, Printmaking, Drawing, Culture
notes: Library holds two copies. Publisher lists 100 pages; the distributor lists 108. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Pose: Couple's Therapy
edition_printrun: Edition of 1,500, with a hand-pulled one-colour screen print signed by the artist. Co-published with Rock Enterprises. Out of print.
description:
The first collected works of POSE (Jordan Nickel), the Chicago graffiti writer whose paintings splice comic-strip faces and lettering into shattered, layered compositions.

Couple's Therapy follows the work through every stage: illegal walls and freight pieces, large murals in Chicago, Los Angeles and Detroit, gallery paintings and sculpture, and the studio process behind them, with more than fifty paintings and sculptures reproduced. The title names the tension the book keeps returning to, between the street and the studio, and between love, loss and triumph as the recurring subjects of the images. Text by Roger Gastman. Published by Gingko Press with Rock Enterprises in 2016 as a hardcover in its own slipcase, printed in part on neon paper, in an edition of 1,500 copies, each with a hand-pulled one-colour Color Study screen print signed by the artist.

POSE began writing graffiti in Chicago in 1992, took a degree at the Kansas City Art Institute in 2004 and is a member of the Mad Society Kings (MSK) and The Seventh Letter collectives. His later work has moved further into painting and sculpture, but the fractured pop vocabulary set out here remains its base.
tags: Art, Graffiti, Street Art, Painting, Contemporary Art, Limited Edition, Pop Culture
notes: Edition of 1,500. Hardcover in slipcase with a hand-pulled one-colour screen print signed by the artist. Co-published with Rock Enterprises. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Skinner: Every Man Is My Enemy
description:
Three years of work by the self-taught Sacramento artist Skinner, whose murals and paintings run 1980s toy and cartoon culture, Dungeons & Dragons, heavy metal and religious painting together into a single overloaded surface.

Every Man Is My Enemy reproduces murals, wall-to-wall gallery installations, canvases, drawings, skateboard decks and commissioned illustration, photographed in situ and as flat works, in colour and black and white. The compositions borrow the crowded frames of rococo altarpieces and the flat colour of playing cards and cel animation, and fill them with horned deities, skull mounds and lightning-veined giants. Published by Gingko Press in 2012 after Skinner had appeared in the press's Juxtapoz anthologies; 172 pages, hardcover.

Skinner has shown at the Graphic Design Museum, Breda, the Illustrative festival in Berlin, and galleries in Japan, France and the United States, and has appeared regularly in Juxtapoz and Hi-Fructose. He painted the cover of Mastodon's 2014 album Once More 'Round the Sun, and in 2012 founded Critical Hit, the label through which he issues prints, toys and zines.
tags: Art, Illustration, Painting, Skateboarding, Pop Culture, Contemporary Art
notes: First monograph; out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Scrawl Too: More Dirt
description:
The second volume of Scrawl, the Booth-Clibborn survey that in 1999 first gathered the artists who had come up through graffiti, comics and club flyers and were reshaping commercial graphics from outside the design profession.

More Dirt widens the field geographically, with work from Vancouver, Osaka, Rio de Janeiro, Melbourne and the European cities of the first book, and follows each artist across surfaces: record sleeves, self-published zines, painted walls, canvases and screen work. The editors frame the material as public art of the early twenty-first century, drawing on graffiti's rebellion and tribal identity, the hand-drawn revival in comics, and the rhythms of hip-hop and beat-based music. Roughly 176 unpaginated pages, illustrated in colour throughout, paperback, published in London in 2001. Phil Ashcroft and the other Scrawl Collective artists who went on to paint live at Tate Modern's Turbine Hall appear here early in their careers.

Ric Blackshaw ran the Scrawl Collective and the associated gallery projects; Liz Farrelly is a design writer and editor whose Booth-Clibborn titles documented British graphic subcultures through the 1990s and 2000s.
tags: Art, Graffiti, Street Art, Graphic Design, Illustration, Design, Zines
notes: Sequel to Scrawl: Dirty Graphics and Strange Characters (1999). Out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Stickers: Stuck-Up Piece of Crap: From Punk Rock to Contemporary Art
edition_printrun: First edition (paperback issue; a numbered deluxe clamshell edition of 300 was issued in parallel). Out of print.
description:
The first book-length history of the sticker as an art form, assembled by the DJ and collector DB Burkeman from thousands of examples spanning punk rock, skateboarding, graffiti and contemporary art.

Arranged by scene rather than chronology, Stickers moves from band and label logos of the late 1970s through skate-company graphics, hardcore and hip-hop flyers, and the hand-drawn and printed slaps of graffiti writers, to the sticker campaigns of Shepard Fairey and others that carried street work into museums. Introductions by Shepard Fairey and Carlo McCormick set the medium in the context of cheap reproduction and public space. Bound into the 300-page paperback are eight sheets of removable stickers, most of them original works commissioned for the book from artists including Barry McGee, Ryan McGinness and José Parlá. The cover's own "Stuck-Up Piece of Crap" sticker is the book's alternative subtitle. Published by Rizzoli's Universe imprint in 2010.

Burkeman came to stickers through skateboarding and punk before a career as a DJ and A&R man in London and New York. A second volume, Stickers Vol. 2 (aka More Stuck-Up Crap), followed from Rizzoli in 2019.
tags: Art, Stickers, Punk, Street Art, Graffiti, Skateboarding, Graphic Design
notes: Includes eight sheets of removable stickers. Cover sticker reads "Stuck-Up Piece of Crap", the book's alternative subtitle. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

author_full_name: Philip Aarons, Emma Reeves, Mark Gonzales
title: Non Stop Poetry: The Zines of Mark Gonzales
contributors: Kim Gordon (Introduction); Rita Ackermann (Text); Maurizio Cattelan (Text); Cameron Jamie (Text); Harmony Korine (Text); Aaron Rose (Text); Steven Salardino (Text); Tom Sachs (Text); Jocko Weyland (Text)
description:
A catalogue raisonné of the zines of Mark Gonzales (b. 1968), the skateboarder whose hand-drawn, collaged and typed pamphlets form one of the largest bodies of artist-made publications of the past three decades.

Compiled over years of searching by Philip Aarons and Emma Reeves, Non Stop Poetry presents every zine the editors could locate, made from 1992 to 2014, including collaborations with Harmony Korine and Cameron Jamie, each with its available publishing details and reproduced through cover and interior scans. Gonzales kept no records; the count passes 145. The zines were run off in tiny numbers and given away or mailed to friends, in the manner of Wallace Berman's Semina, and rarely reached even Printed Matter or Colette. Kim Gordon introduces; Rita Ackermann, Maurizio Cattelan, Aaron Rose, Tom Sachs, Jocko Weyland and others contribute. Launched at the NY Art Book Fair at MoMA PS1 in September 2014; 416 pages, sewn paperback, offset in colour, edition of 2,000.

The book places Gonzales's scribbled poems and portraits in the line of artist publications from Ed Ruscha to Raymond Pettibon, and a companion website, markgonzaleszines.com, continues the census of zines found since publication.
tags: Art, Zines, Skateboarding, Drawing, Poetry, Artists' Books, Contemporary Art
notes: Edition of 2,000. Introduction by Kim Gordon. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Arabic Graffiti
edition_printrun: First printing, hardcover, 2011. A revised third edition in paperback (2013) added a chapter on the Arab uprisings.
description:
The first book to survey the meeting of Arabic script with graffiti writing and street art, edited by the German graffiti writer and publisher Don Karl and the Lebanese type designer Pascal Zoghbi.

Arabic Graffiti sets out without regional borders: its artists, writers and typographers work in Beirut, Bahrain, Palestine and Cairo, and in Paris, Berlin and Los Angeles, and approach the script from calligraphy, from Latin-alphabet graffiti styles, and from type design. Chapters cover classical and contemporary calligraphy, Arabic typography, the painted lettering of Lebanese freight trucks, political graffiti on the walls of Palestine, and the crossover into Western cities, with essays by practitioners and writers in the field. Two hundred pages, hardcover, illustrated throughout, published in Berlin by From Here to Fame in 2011. This is the first printing; a revised third edition in paperback followed in 2013 with a new chapter on graffiti of the Arab uprisings.

Don "Stone" Karl began writing graffiti in 1983 and published his first book on train writing in 1986; he runs From Here to Fame and the Common Ground gallery in Berlin. Pascal Zoghbi founded 29Letters, the Arabic type foundry in Beirut.
tags: Art, Graffiti, Street Art, Typography, Calligraphy, Middle East, Design
notes: First printing. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

author_full_name: Robert Klanten, Hendrik Hellige, Michael Mischler
title: Trigger
editor: Robert Klanten, Hendrik Hellige, Michael Mischler
description:
A snapshot of late-1990s graphic design from Berlin's Die Gestalten Verlag, gathered from the studios the publisher met while researching its club-flyer survey Flyermania.

Trigger collects logos, corporate identities, flyers and print typefaces rather than finished campaigns, and presents them as a working reference for designers handling fast-changing visual codes. The contributors map the scene the publisher grew out of: The Designers Republic, eBoy, km7, DED Associates, Stylorouge, Stefan Sagmeister, Kim Hiorthøy, Marok, Büro Destruct, François Chalet, Dextro, Eike König, Dirk Rudolph, Stefan Gandl, Sweden Graphics, Surface, Function, Maia Gusberti and Peter Christopherson among them, with the full list printed down the cover. Two hundred pages, softcover, English, published in 1999 and edited by Robert Klanten with Hendrik Hellige and Michael Mischler.

Klanten co-founded Die Gestalten in 1995 with Markus Hollmann-Loges and Andreas Peyerl after designing flyers, posters and record sleeves for the Berlin techno scene and the Love Parade; the publisher's early compilations, Trigger among them, set the format its later design surveys followed.
tags: Graphic Design, Design, Typography, Illustration, Pop Culture, Ephemera
notes: Companion to Die Gestalten Verlag's Flyermania (1998). Out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: L'Image Obscène / The Obscene Image: Parisian Hospital Break Room Graffiti
description:
A photographic record of the painted salles de garde of Paris, the hospital break rooms whose walls carry generations of obscene murals made by the medical staff who eat and rest in them.

Gilles Tondini photographed the frescoes in a dozen hospitals of greater Paris, from the Hôtel-Dieu and La Pitié-Salpêtrière to Paul-Brousse and Gustave-Roussy in Villejuif and André-Mignot in Versailles, several of them rarely documented before. The imagery is sexual by rule, but its sources run from the Last Judgement and chivalric romance to comic-book heroes and villains. Marie L. Bouchon's introduction traces the custom from the barber-surgeons of the medieval period into the hospital buildings of the eighteenth century onward, and explains the codes that govern who may paint and what. Bilingual French and English throughout, translated by Jake Davis; 160 pages, hardcover, published in New York by Mark Batty Publisher in 2010, with Libération giving the book a feature on release.

Tondini, a photographer based in France, had documented the city's catacombs and tunnels for the same publisher in Paris Underground; here he applies the same access to a subculture closed even to most Parisians.
tags: Photography, Erotica, Graffiti, Culture, Drawing, France
notes: Bilingual French and English edition. Out of print. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Magic City: Die Kunst der Strasse: The Art of the Street
description:
The bilingual catalogue for Magic City: Die Kunst der Strasse, the touring street-art exhibition curated by the New York critic Carlo McCormick that opened in Dresden in October 2016 and travelled on to Munich and Stockholm.

Produced by Semmel Concerts Exhibitions and staged first in the Kultur-Quartier Zeitenströmung in Dresden (1 October 2016 to 12 March 2017), then in the Kleine Olympiahalle in Munich (13 April to 3 September 2017), the show took the city itself as subject and canvas, with more than 40 artists from some 20 countries painting, spraying, pasting and building work in situ. The catalogue, published in German and English by From Here To Fame in 2017, documents the first staging with installation photography and artist profiles alongside McCormick's curatorial text, which frames the exhibition as a celebration of the universal character of cities and their diversity.

Participants ranged from Banksy and Shepard Fairey to the graffiti photographer Martha Cooper and the installation artist Brad Downey, with the works changing from city to city as the show travelled. Edited by Don Karl and Amber Grünhäuser, the volume belongs to From Here To Fame's programme of graffiti and urban-art publishing.
tags: Street Art, Graffiti, Exhibition Catalog, Contemporary Art, Art
notes: Bilingual German/English text. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Modern Artifacts
contributors: Mary Ellen Carroll (Artist project); Rhea Karam (Artist project); Mary Lum (Artist project); Clifford Owens (Artist project); Michael Rakowitz (Artist project); Paul Ramirez Jonas (Artist project)
description:
A compilation of the Modern Artifacts series that Esopus magazine ran with the Museum of Modern Art Archives from 2006 to 2019, reproducing documents from the museum's institutional record in facsimile.

Edited by Esopus founder Tod Lippy with Michelle Elligott, MoMA's Chief of Archives, Library, and Research Collections, the volume gathers all eighteen instalments of the series. Its contents run from planning documents for exhibitions that were never staged to pages from the museum's first guest book, each introduced by Elligott. Six artists, Mary Ellen Carroll, Rhea Karam, Mary Lum, Clifford Owens, Michael Rakowitz and Paul Ramirez Jonas, contributed new projects responding to particular holdings, many taking the form of removable inserts in keeping with the magazine's tactile approach to print. An introductory essay by Elligott and a foreword by Lippy open the book.

Esopus, founded by Lippy in 2003, published artists' projects, essays, fiction, interviews and music, each contribution produced in a format of its maker's choosing. Published by Esopus Books in 2020, Modern Artifacts was named among the best art books of the year by the New York Times.
tags: Art, Museum Publication, Archives, Contemporary Art, Ephemera, Design
notes: 235 colour illustrations; removable inserts. Out of print at the publisher. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Sex Magazine #1–10: 2012–2015
description:
The first print edition of Sex, the free, web-native culture magazine founded in New York by the artist Asher Penn, collecting its first ten issues from 2012 to 2015.

Conceived for the browser and distributed at no cost, Sex took its cue from the independent magazine renaissance of the turn of the millennium, titles such as Index, Butt and Made in USA, and channelled the lo-fi, digital-native aesthetic of a still largely unregulated internet. Almost entirely interview-based, its stories gave direct, non-academic voice to artists, designers, musicians, photographers and writers of the post-internet moment. Contributors across the ten issues include Maggie Lee, Brendan Fowler, Jordan Wolfson, Petra Cortright, Amalia Ulman, Eckhaus Latta, Venus X, Bill Strobeck, Laurie Spiegel, Korakrit Arunanondchai, Ratking and Cali Thornhill DeWitt.

Published by powerHouse Books in 2016, the edition functions as a yearbook of a scene that otherwise existed only online and as a record of art and culture at the coming of age of the new millennium. Penn, a New York artist, has also written for Artforum, Interview and Art in America.
tags: Magazines, Periodical, Contemporary Art, Culture, Fashion, Photography
notes: Boxed set of issues 1–10. Distributor listings describe the powerHouse edition as a single 360-page softcover. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Dr. Lakra
contributors: Gabriel Orozco (Conversation); Eduardo Abaroa (Text); Pedro Alonzo (Text)
description:
The principal monograph on the Oaxaca-based artist and tattooist Dr. Lakra (Jerónimo López Ramírez, b. 1972), whose drawings overlay vintage printed matter with the iconography of tattoo, folk ritual and the underworld.

Published by Editorial RM in 2010, the book reproduces some 120 works in colour: mid-century Mexican magazine covers, pin-up advertisements, calendar prints and Japanese woodblock images on which Lakra has inked gang tattoos, skulls and bones, Aztec warrior heads, spider webs, serpents and demons, so that the polished commercial surface and its dark, funerary underlayer share one sheet. Sculptural pieces and modified objects extend the same logic into three dimensions. Texts in English and Spanish include a conversation with Gabriel Orozco and essays by Eduardo Abaroa and Pedro Alonzo.

Lakra, the son of the painter Francisco Toledo and the poet Elisa Ramírez, began as a tattooist and built his drawing practice from that trade's vocabulary. He is represented by kurimanzutto in Mexico City, and the year of this book also brought his first US museum survey, at the ICA Boston, curated by Alonzo. The library also holds Los dos amigos, his 2006 collaboration with Abraham Cruzvillegas.
tags: Art, Contemporary Art, Tattoo, Drawing, Collage, Mexico
notes: Trade edition. Bilingual English/Spanish text; 120 colour plates. Also issued under Mexican ISBN 9786077515548. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: FAILE: Works on Wood: Process, Paintings and Sculpture
description:
A survey of the Brooklyn duo FAILE's decade-long work in wood, from salvaged window-frame paintings to carved prayer wheels and large-scale installations, published by Gestalten in 2014.

Edited by the curator and critic Ian Bourland, the book is organised as a visual timeline of the medium in FAILE's practice: early paintings on found lumber and doors, the stacked and painted blocks of their puzzle-box works, the carved and stencilled Prayer Wheels, and commissions including their 2013 installation for the New York City Ballet. Large photographs are paired with captions and process essays written by the artists themselves, and Bourland's text places their blend of digital design and analog assemblage in a line from Rauschenberg and Johns. The book was released to coincide with an exhibition at Allouche Gallery, New York, in November 2014.

Patrick McNeil and Patrick Miller formed FAILE in 1999, moving from wheat-pasted street work in New York to gallery painting, sculpture and public projects, and were early in fusing pop, pulp and comic-book sources with fine-art technique. The volume follows Gestalten's earlier FAILE: Prints + Originals 1999–2009 and FAILE Temple.
tags: Street Art, Contemporary Art, Painting, Sculpture, Art
notes: Out of print at the publisher. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: FAILE Temple
description:
FAILE's documentation of Temple, the full-scale ruin of a chapel that the Brooklyn duo built on Lisbon's Praça dos Restauradores for the Portugal Arte 10 festival in 2010.

Modelled on the remains of a Baroque chapel, the temporary structure carried frescoes, tiled surfaces and sculptural figures drawn from FAILE's own vocabulary of pulp heroines and hand-lettered slogans, translated into carved stone, painted plaster and azulejo-style ceramic tile. The book, designed by the artists and published by Gestalten in 2012, records the finished installation in detail and traces its making, from the historical ornament and devotional imagery that fed the design through construction and installation on site. An essay by the critic W. Ian Bourland reads the project against the duo's wider work. The linen-bound cover reproduces the temple's blue-and-white tile pattern.

Patrick McNeil and Patrick Miller have worked together as FAILE since 1999, moving between street interventions, painting, sculpture and immersive environments. Temple was their most ambitious public project to that date; the book sits between Gestalten's FAILE: Prints + Originals 1999–2009 and FAILE: Works on Wood.
tags: Street Art, Contemporary Art, Installation, Sculpture, Art
notes: Trade edition. A signed studio edition with a ceramic tile from the installation was also issued. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: FAILE: Prints + Originals 1999–2009
description:
The first comprehensive collection of FAILE's works on paper, gathering a decade of screenprints, stencils and collaged originals by the Brooklyn duo from their street beginnings in 1999 to 2009.

Published by Gestalten in 2010, the book reproduces at full page the prints and unique works through which Patrick McNeil and Patrick Miller built their visual language: pulp-novel covers, comic panels, advertising type and wheat-paste fragments recombined in layered, over-printed compositions that carry the wear of the wall into the print shop. A closing reference section reproduces in thumbnail the complete works on paper the duo released through their website between March 2006 and May 2010, making the volume a working catalogue of their editions. Text by Matt Barber accompanies the plates.

FAILE began as a street-art collaboration in New York and by 2010 had shown with Lazarides in London and in institutional contexts while continuing to paste work in cities worldwide. This was the first of three Gestalten volumes on the duo, followed by FAILE Temple (2012) and FAILE: Works on Wood (2014).
tags: Street Art, Contemporary Art, Printmaking, Pop Culture, Art
notes: Trade edition. A signed and stamped studio edition of 600 in screenprinted packaging was also issued. Edition state to be verified from the physical copy. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Fafi: The Carmine Vault
description:
The first graphic novel by the Toulouse-born street artist Fafi, following the character Birtak and his ambition to join the Paris Opéra Ballet through the artist's world of Fafinettes.

Drawn, coloured, lettered and laid out entirely by Fafi, The Carmine Vault carries her wall-painted figures into sequential narrative for the first time, in a hardcover art-book format that closes with ten additional full-page drawings of Fafinettes. The project began as a ten-page sketch that Rizzoli editor Ian Luna saw through the Paris concept store colette, which hosted the launch signing in April 2012. Published by Rizzoli's Universe imprint in 2012, the book is printed in the artist's saturated palette, with a lounging, cocktail-holding Fafinette on the cover.

Fafi began painting in the streets of Toulouse in the mid-1990s and became known for the Fafinettes, exaggerated, sexualised female figures that play on and against stereotypes of girlhood. Her work has since moved across walls, toys, fashion collaborations and magazine illustration; an earlier book, Love and Fafiness, collected her drawings and paintings.
tags: Street Art, Graffiti, Illustration, Comics, Art
notes: Graphic novel; closes with ten additional full-page Fafinette drawings. Summer archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-08-27.

title: Covert to Overt: The Under/Overground Art of Shepard Fairey
contributors: Pedro Alonzo (Text); Russell Brand (Text); D*Face (Text); Dennis Morris (Text); Sean Bonner (Text); Mark Sloan (Text)
description:
A monograph on the American street artist and graphic designer Shepard Fairey (b. 1970) covering 2010 to 2015, the years in which the author of the OBEY Giant campaign moved from paper onto murals, installations and cross-cultural collaborations.

Published by Rizzoli in 2015, the book is organised year by year, each section opened by a text from Fairey or a collaborator, among them the curator Pedro Alonzo, Russell Brand, D*Face, the photographer Dennis Morris, Sean Bonner and Mark Sloan of the Halsey Institute. It documents large-scale murals on several continents, mixed-media installations, silkscreens and music-and-art events, alongside work for the OBEY clothing line, much of it previously unpublished. The cover reproduces the Andre the Giant face that Fairey first stickered as a Rhode Island School of Design student in 1989.

Fairey's 2008 Hope poster for Barack Obama brought him wide public recognition; his work is held by the Smithsonian, LACMA, MoMA and the V&A. Covert to Overt follows Supply and Demand, the 2006 Gingko Press survey of his first two decades, and was edited by Simon Steinhardt.

title: Board: Surf/Skate/Snow Graphics
edition_printrun: Expanded edition, 2003. First published as Bored: Surf/Skate/Snow Graphics (Laurence King, 1997; US edition Watson-Guptill, 1998).
description:
A survey of the graphic art of surfing, skateboarding and snowboarding, gathering more than four hundred board designs from rare archival material to the work of contemporary studios.

First published in 1997 as Bored, the book treats the board as a printed surface with its own history: hand-painted longboards, the screen-printed skate decks of the 1980s and the digitally produced snowboard graphics of the 1990s. Artists and art directors including Jim Phillips, Erik Brunetti, Todd Francis, Marc McKee and Scott Clum discuss the subcultures that produced the work and its exchanges with music, fashion and graphic design. This expanded 2003 edition adds a section of recent board graphics to the original survey.

Jeremy Leslie is a magazine designer and the author of Issues: New Magazine Design and magCulture; Patrick Burgoyne is the editor of Creative Review and co-author of the Browser series on internet design. Published by Laurence King in the UK and distributed in North America under the Harper Design imprint.

title: Astro Noise: A Survival Guide for Living Under Total Surveillance
contributors: Jay Sanders (Curator/Introduction); Ai Weiwei (Contributor); Lakhdar Boumediene (Contributor); Kate Crawford (Contributor); Cory Doctorow (Contributor); Dave Eggers (Contributor); Jill Magid (Contributor); Trevor Paglen (Contributor); Hito Steyerl (Contributor); Edward Snowden (Contributor)
description:
Astro Noise: A Survival Guide for Living Under Total Surveillance is the catalogue for filmmaker and artist Laura Poitras's first major museum exhibition, staged at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 2016, and doubles as a guide to living under mass surveillance.

Poitras invited a wide range of contributors, including artists, novelists, technologists, and former detainees, to respond to material she gathered while working with the National Security Agency documents leaked by Edward Snowden. Contributions include writing and imagery from Ai Weiwei, Lakhdar Boumediene, Kate Crawford, Cory Doctorow, Dave Eggers, Jill Magid, Trevor Paglen, and Hito Steyerl, alongside an introduction by Whitney curator Jay Sanders. The book reproduces material connected to the exhibition's installations, which placed viewers inside classified surveillance footage and declassified government documents.

Poitras is best known for her post-9/11 documentary trilogy, which culminated in Citizenfour (2014), winner of the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature and a chronicle of her work with Snowden. Astro Noise marked her move from film into gallery-based installation, and the book was published by the Whitney to coincide with the exhibition's run from February to May 2016.

title: Beautified
description:
Beautified is artist Tom B. Aicrag's digest-format study of the Mehadrin filter, a content-blocking technology built to censor what employees at certain organizations can view on a browser.

The book compiles undated, unattributed screenshots gathered from unnamed sources, each altered by the filter: skin tones blackened, faces and bodies blocked out entirely, image data replaced with dense black patches. Aicrag sets the politics of the technology aside and instead treats these glitches as found abstraction, presenting the filter's errors and overreaches as a body of accidental images. Published by Open Projects Press in an edition of 100, the book is a small, perfect-bound paperback printed in digital color.

title: Blinds
description:
Blinds is the first of three risograph-printed pamphlets by Philip Tomaru that read the interior of a Mies van der Rohe apartment building through its architecture of privacy.

Photographed at Baltimore's Highfield House between 2001 and 2015, the series works through blinds, walls, and windows in turn (Blinds first, followed by Walls and Windows), each volume printed with a different reproduction method tied to its subject. The book is a bound, staple-stitched pamphlet of sixteen unnumbered leaves, its title taken from the colophon rather than a printed cover.

Tomaru lived in Highfield House, one of Mies van der Rohe's last residential commissions, and the trilogy works through the building's modernist logic of transparency and enclosure as lived experience rather than architectural history. Arts & Sciences Projects published the series alongside public programming, including an event at Printed Matter timed to Mies van der Rohe's 130th birthday.

title: Dark Rooms
description:
Dark Rooms gathers five interlocking series of photographs by British photographer Nigel Shafran, all built around domestic scenes and the routines of ordinary life.

The photographs move between the overt, such as supermarket checkout lines and underground escalators, and the quietly charged, including a sequence Shafran made while going through the contents of his late mother's house. Across the sequences, everyday clutter, from till receipts to shop displays to waiting rooms, becomes a study of transition: what people accumulate, discard, and leave behind as time moves forward. The book is designed by Mevis & Van Deursen, co-edited by Liz Jobey, and includes essays by David Chandler and Paul Elliman.

Shafran worked as a photographer for The Face and i-D before turning his camera toward domestic and mundane subjects in books including Ruth on the Phone (2012). Dark Rooms was published by MACK in 2016 and was named among the year's best photobooks by several photography publications.

title: Data Rush
description:
Data Rush is the catalogue for the 2015 Noorderlicht International Photofestival, gathering fifty photographers and multimedia artists working on the tension between personal data and digital control.

Curated by Wim Melis, the festival took data traffic itself as its subject, asking how photographers could make visible something with no fixed physical form. The catalogue reproduces work from the festival's Groningen exhibition, held in the city's former Sugar Factory, alongside supporting texts on the show's central question: how much control people retain over the data their lives generate online and off.

Noorderlicht, founded in 1991, has run its international photofestival annually since and operates its own publishing arm through Aurora Borealis. Data Rush appeared the same year the WikiLeaks and NSA disclosures were reshaping public debate about mass data collection, a context the festival's programming addressed directly.

notes: Group-show catalogue with roughly 50 contributing photographers; authorship credited to festival curator Wim Melis, per the book's own credit line. title: Negative Publicity: Artefacts of Extraordinary Rendition
description:
Negative Publicity: Artefacts of Extraordinary Rendition documents the CIA's secret prisoner-transport program through photographs and the paper trail left by the businesses that made it possible.

Photographer Edmund Clark and counterterrorism investigator Crofton Black spent years tracing invoices, incorporation papers, and billing records connected to extraordinary rendition, the CIA's post-9/11 practice of transferring detainees between secret prisons without legal process. Clark's photographs of empty rooms, aircraft, and administrative buildings sit alongside reproductions of the documents Black uncovered, building a paper trail for a program designed to leave none. The book includes a text by Eyal Weizman and is printed spiral-bound with a cloth spine, a format that lets photographs and documents interleave directly.

Clark's earlier work, including Guantanamo: If the Light Goes Out (2010) and Control Order House (2012), examines state control and incarceration through the physical traces institutions leave behind. Negative Publicity extends that project into the financial and bureaucratic infrastructure of rendition and was copublished by Aperture and the Magnum Foundation, whose Emergency Fund supported the research.

title: Peepers Patterns
description:
Peepers Patterns pairs photographs of people caught looking out of their windows with images of pattern and repetition, published under the pseudonym Cuss This.

A man leans out in a tank top; a woman looks over a balcony ledge. These voyeuristic glimpses are interspersed with photographs of unrelated patterns, some flat and graphic, some built from three-dimensional shapes and shadow. The pairing sets the isolation of the window-watcher against the visual noise of pattern and line, running a dry, understated humor through the sequencing.

Peepers Patterns was published by the Swedish micro-press Modes Vu in February 2015 as a small-format trade paperback.

title: Foam Magazine #43: Freedom of Expression under Surveillance
description: Foam Magazine #43, 'Freedom of Expression under Surveillance,' was produced in close collaboration with Chinese artist and activist Ai Weiwei, who served as guest editor for the issue. Having lived under constant government surveillance for years, Weiwei uses the issue to turn the camera back on the watchers, presenting images from his own Instagram feed and stills from the 24-hour 'WeiWeiCam' he trained on himself. The issue is organized into four sections, 'Sousveillance,' 'Self Surveillance,' 'Urban Surveillance,' and 'Art and Surveillance,' and includes an interview with the artist alongside his own commentary. Published by Foam in Amsterdam in December 2015, it marked the magazine's first issue built entirely around a single guest editor's practice and its first dedicated feature on Ai Weiwei.

title: Dear Erin Hart
description: In 2009, artist Jessamyn Lovell's wallet was stolen from San Francisco Camerawork, and her identity was subsequently used by a woman named Erin Hart. Rather than pursue the case only through police and courts, Lovell hired a private investigator and spent nearly two years tracking, following, and photographing Hart, compiling a grainy, evidentiary archive that mirrors the surveillance culture used against her. The resulting photographs are stylistically anxious, often blurred and off-kilter, conveying the unsettled tension of both photographer and subject. First shown as an exhibition at SF Camerawork in 2014, the project was published as a book in 2015 with an introduction by Heather Snider and an essay by curator Renny Pritikin. Lovell occupies the roles of victim, investigator, artist, and vigilante simultaneously, using photography as a tool of personal justice.

title: Inside Embassies
description: Inside Embassies presents Elisabeth Ida Mulyani's photographs of meeting rooms, waiting areas, and anonymous corridors inside a dozen embassies around the world. Working in a restrained, objective style, Mulyani examines the embassy as a physical stand-in for a nation abroad, a site meant to embody transnational relations and diplomacy, and, just as often, an ordinary workplace of drab offices and mismatched furnishings under the watchful gaze of a state portrait. The photographs register the small, deliberate gestures architecture and interior design make toward national identity and hospitality, gestures that read as gauche as often as they read as elegant. Published by Art Paper Editions (Ghent, Belgium) in 2015 as a first edition of 500 softcover copies, the book was Mulyani's first monograph, following her training in fine art photography at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Belgium.

title: Framing Bodies
description: Framing Bodies draws on the Hasselblad Foundation's collection to present photographs by fifteen photographers, among them Walker Evans, Nan Goldin, Ernest Cole, Annika von Hausswolff, and Adriana Lestido, spanning from the late nineteenth century to the present. Edited by Dragana Vujanović and Louise Wolthers and published by Art and Theory Publishing in Stockholm in 2015, the book considers how photographs of the body in private and public space register surveillance, transgression, labor conditions, and racial discrimination. Wolthers contributes a bilingual English/Swedish essay, 'Surveilling Bodies: Photography as Control, Critique and Concern,' situating the selected images within histories of photographic control and resistance. The publication followed an earlier Hasselblad Foundation collection exhibition series that included Still Life / Work Life (2013), and anticipated the Foundation's later surveillance-focused title Drone Vision: Warfare Surveillance Protest (2022).

title: Lovers
description: Lovers is a limited-edition zine by Corey Presha, drawn from a larger body of work titled Night Shift. The images are pulled from security-camera footage recorded in the elevators of unidentified New York City hotels during the overnight shift, showing anonymous couples in unguarded, intimate moments. Produced by S_U_N (SUN Editions) for Printed Matter's 2013 NY Art Book Fair, the zine repurposes surveillance footage as a found-photography source, proposing that people are most themselves, and most intimate, when they believe they are unobserved. It sits alongside Presha's other zine-based work, including 100 Girls I Don't Know, in S_U_N's publications catalog.

title: Figur I, Figur II
description: Figur I, Figur II collects two related series of black-and-white portraits: in Figur I, a young woman is photographed against a neutral background in a shifting range of poses and clothing that resist a fixed reading of gender; in Figur II, a second figure stands before a lamella curtain trying on a tube cowl, subject to the same ambiguity. Steinbach draws on the gestural vocabulary of fashion photography, repeatedly undercutting it to strip away the roles it typically assigns its subjects. The book, designed by Steinbach with HIT and published by Spector Books in Leipzig, accompanied an exhibition at the Sprengel Museum Hannover, on view June 9 through October 25, 2015. Spector Books also issued limited-edition signed prints from the two series alongside the book.

title: Letzte Generation Ost
description: Letzte Generation Ost focuses on the last generation born in the German Democratic Republic, centered on a housing complex in Hagenow, East Germany, where photographer Kristin Trüb herself grew up. Trüb interviewed nine of her peers who came of age there, combining their portraits with landscape photographs of the housing blocks and, crucially, surveillance records kept on their families by the East German state without their knowledge at the time. Presented alongside maps and individual dossiers for each family, the book pieces together how state surveillance shaped identities its subjects only later learned had been recorded. Published by Éditions Bessard in Paris in 2015 in an edition of 500, the book takes the form of a hardcover housed in a printed box, with a small portfolio of photographs riveted onto the cover and nine loose information-sheet dossiers, one per family.

title: Fear of Disappearance
description: Fear of Disappearance began as Mariya Ustymenko's exploration of one's connection to a particular space, developed during a 2015 Arts Council-funded residency with bookRoom under the guidance of Akina in London. Working across black-and-white and color photography, Ustymenko photographed in the streets of London to examine how identity is shaped and eroded by continuous urban change and redevelopment. The zine edition, sequenced and printed by Akina Factory, presents 31 images across 52 pages in a soft cover of laminated Pergamenata Fedrigoni paper, issued in a hand-numbered edition of 100. The project also produced a companion artist-book edition and a standalone sculptural object in concrete, steel, and laser-engraved perspex, extending the work's interest in permanence and disappearance into physical, architectural materials.

title: Hide
edition_printrun: First edition, limited to 400 numbered copies
description: Hide is Jason Vaughn's first monograph, a photographic typology of deer stands built by hunters across Wisconsin, the state he adopted as his home. Inspired by conversations with hunters who described their stands as structures meant to be passed down to the next generation, Vaughn began the project while anticipating the birth of his own son. The work took on additional weight when Vaughn was diagnosed with leukemia in 2011, at age 32, with a three-month-old at home; the deer stands came to stand less for hunting and death than for permanence, inheritance, and time spent in nature with family. Published by Trema Förlag (Stockholm) in 2015 in a first edition of 400 numbered hardcover copies with 40 four-color plates, the book also appeared in a limited boxset edition with two signed prints, produced in partnership with TBW Books. Vaughn writes: 'hide became my reflection on legacies and family, my homage to the state that has become my home, and a narrative about accepting change.'

title: Podmoskovye
description:
Podmoskovye gathers still images pulled from surveillance-camera footage of Moscow's suburbs, printed full-bleed and offered without captions or explanation.

Pascal Anders built the book around an epigraph from Michel Foucault's Discipline and Punish, using its account of disciplinary power to frame eighty-four images that give the viewer nothing to interpret them by beyond the fact of having been recorded by a camera never meant to produce pictures for anyone. Self-published in Paris in 2015 as a 144-page softcover in an edition of 100, the book was distributed free to anyone who requested a copy, a gesture Anders described as restitution for images that surveillance cameras take from people without their knowledge every day.

Anders is a French photographer whose later self-published books, including CCTV (2016) and Common Street Views (2019), return repeatedly to surveillance footage and appropriated street imagery as material.

title: Married Man
description:
Married Man is Natasha Caruana's record of eighty dates she arranged with married men through websites built for people seeking affairs, each meeting documented on a disposable camera.

Between 2008 and 2009 Caruana met more than fifty men, some days three or four in a row, and instead of faces she photographed what was in front of her: a soiled coffee cup, a rain-soaked umbrella, hands signing a credit-card receipt or clasping hers across a table. The men rarely appear directly; the book reads through gesture and the debris of a staged date instead. Here Press published the book in an edition of 500, bound in faux black leather with a blind-embossed title, pairing the photographs with transcriptions of Caruana's conversations. Many of the men, she has said, were driven less by desire than by loneliness, and turned the dates into confession as often as flirtation.

Caruana, born in 1983 and based in London, works across photography, moving image, and installation on themes of love, betrayal, and fantasy. She holds an MA in Photography from the Royal College of Art and is a Senior Lecturer in Photography at the University for the Creative Arts, Farnham. The original photographs were also shown as part of "Invisible Adversaries" at the Northern Gallery for Contemporary Art in 2010.

title: Predator
description:
Predator gathers anonymous amateur photographs from the 1920s through the 1970s that share one incongruous detail: the photographer's own shadow, falling across the frame, always wearing a hat.

Jean-Marie Donat, a collector who has spent more than twenty-five years assembling an archive of some 10,000 vernacular photographs, pulled these two hundred images from that collection on the strength of a single coincidence repeated across decades and countries. Stripped of any other context, the recurring silhouette turns from an accident of amateur technique into something closer to a stalking presence, the same hatted figure seeming to loom over unrelated subjects in unrelated decades. Innocences published the book in an edition of 500, printed and bound in Italy, with a postface by the aesthetics scholar Jacinto Lageira.

Donat has produced several other books from the same archive, each organized around a single visual coincidence isolated across thousands of found photographs rather than around a single named photographer.

title: Pictures of People Taking Pictures
description:
Pictures of People Taking Pictures is Cheryl Dunn's argument that the compulsion to photograph everything did not start with the iPhone, built from her own pictures of other people mid-shot.

Dunn, a street photographer and documentary filmmaker who has spent decades working New York's streets, gathers photographers caught in the act across different eras and settings; changes in wardrobe and, more tellingly, in the cameras being used, from press bodies to point-and-shoots to phones, run through the book as a rough timeline. Heavy Time, the Melbourne imprint run by Rob Cordiner, Ed Davis, and Todd Jordan, published the book in 2015 in an edition of 100.

Dunn is best known for the photo books Bicycle Gangs of New York (2005) and Some Kinda Vocation (2007), and for directing the documentary Everybody Street (2013), which profiles a generation of New York street photographers including Martha Cooper and Jill Freedman.

title: Modern Monsters: Death and Life of Fiction
editor: Anselm Franke and Brian Kuan Wood
contributors: David Der-Wei Wang (Essay); Nabil Ahmed (Essay); Chen Chieh-Jen (Essay); Reza Negarestani (Essay); Jow Jiun Gong (Essay); Joachim Koester (Essay); James T. Hong (Essay); Jei Li (Essay); Bavand Behpoor (Essay); Sophie Wahnich (Essay); Ian Svenonius (Essay); Eric Baudelaire (Essay); Masao Matsuda (Essay); Mark Fisher (Essay); Alberto Toscano (Essay); Hu Fang (Essay); Chihiro Minato (Essay); Natasha Ginwala (Essay)
description:
Modern Monsters: Death and Life of Fiction is the reader that followed the Taipei Biennial 2012, gathering the essays, images, and source texts that shaped the exhibition Anselm Franke curated under the same title.

The biennial took its starting point from the Taowu, a monster from Chinese mythology that the literary historian David Der-Wei Wang reads as a stand-in for history itself, a figure said to foresee and thwart human intention, later invoked by writers to describe the violence buried inside China's project of modernity. Franke and co-editor Brian Kuan Wood built the 300-page volume around that figure, pairing scholarly essays with artists' texts and images from contributors to the biennial's exhibition and its six "mini-museums," including Chen Chieh-Jen, Joachim Koester, Eric Baudelaire, and Mark Fisher. The book is thread-sewn, illustrated with roughly one hundred black-and-white images, and published by Spector Books in Leipzig.

Franke, a curator and writer based in Berlin, is Head of Visual Art and Film at Haus der Kulturen der Welt; his research addresses the relation between subjectivity, animism, and biopolitics in art and architecture, and he later served as chief curator of the 10th Shanghai Biennale. Wood is a writer and editor associated with e-flux journal.

title: Photourist
description:
Photourist collects Andy Gershon's photographs of tourists and museumgoers photographing what is in front of them, each picture built around the glowing rectangle of a phone screen held between the viewer and the view.

Working in the vein of Thomas Struth's Museum Photographs but with a phone screen instead of a crowd as the subject, Gershon frames tourist attractions and artworks so they are visible only in fragments around or through the device a visitor is using to record them, adding his own camera as a third party to the exchange between viewer and object. The self-published book, credited to Gershon's imprint Daniel 13, gathers images shot at museums and monuments; a related body of the work was shown as a group exhibition at Weinberger Gallery in Kansas City in May 2015.

Gershon, a former music-industry executive who signed artists including Moby and The White Stripes before turning to photography, is based in New York.

title: Private Rooms
description:
Private Rooms collects stills Fred Hüning pulled from video clips uploaded to Youporn by private users, cropped down to the domestic space around the subject rather than the subject itself.

Hüning's crops move past the point the clips were made for, isolating a bedspread, a shelf of belongings, a doorframe, so that what remains reads as a study of ordinary rooms rather than the acts recorded in them; the people who appear register more through their unguarded domestic surroundings than through explicit content, an effect the book's text connects to the quiet vulnerability of Sophie Calle's The Sleepers. Peperoni Books published the seventeen-image book in an edition of 150 numbered and signed copies, a thread-stitched softcover with accompanying text by Hüning.

Hüning is a German photographer whose work frequently returns to appropriated and found imagery sourced from the internet; Private Rooms extends that interest to material never intended to be seen as photography at all.

title: Robber Queen's Favorites
description:
Robber Queen's Favorites reprints, in full color, every photograph a single Flickr user favorited under the handle Robber Queen, organized by subject from the mundane to the violent.

Nathaniel Matthews compiled the book from one person's accumulated "favorites," the images a Flickr account marks rather than posts, treating that quieter layer of activity as a kind of self-portrait. The range runs wide, banal snapshots alongside darker and more violent material, with no editorializing beyond the sequence itself; a digital identity, the book suggests, is built as much from what an account favorites or stars as from what it posts. Matthews produced the book through 8 Ball Zines, part of the 8-Ball Community collective built around the zine fairs run out of Grand Billiards in East Williamsburg, Brooklyn.

Matthews is a Brooklyn-based artist whose practice draws on self-publishing and zine subcultures; his other publications include The Count's Lounge and The Players.

title: NTSOTWBH (Never Take Shortcuts On The Way Back Home)
description:
NTSOTWBH: Never Take Shortcuts On The Way Back Home works from the Interpol missing-persons database, the only public international registry of its kind, to ask what a photograph does once it is disconnected from the person it depicts.

Benedetta Pomini drew on a snapshot of the database from July 2014, when it listed 832 open cases across ninety countries, 129 of them without a photograph at all; Jamaica, Colombia, and Honduras returned the highest numbers. The book sets these images and their case data side by side, treating the database's mix of ID photos, snapshots, and blank entries as a study of how an image is asked to stand in for a person who is absent, legally presumed dead in most countries after seven years and in Italy only after ten. Pomini designed the 196-page book herself; it was published by Skinnerboox, the Jesi-based Italian photobook press, in September 2015, digitally offset-printed with PUR binding.
