notes: Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Type 42: Fame Is the Name of the Game: Photographs by Anonymous
description:
A selection of 120 black-and-white Type 42 Polaroids of Hollywood actresses photographed off a television screen by an unidentified photographer, discovered in 2012 by artist Jason Brinkerhoff and introduced here by Cindy Sherman.

In 2012, Brinkerhoff came across a collection of roughly 950 Polaroids made on Type 42 film, a stock introduced in 1955 and discontinued in 1992, each shot of a close-up on a television screen catching an actress mid-broadcast: Brigitte Bardot, Doris Day, Catherine Deneuve, Jane Fonda, Sophia Loren, Barbra Streisand, Elizabeth Taylor, and others. Many prints carry the actress's name and sometimes a film title, inked along the border in the same distinctive hand, the photographer's only trace. Edited by Nicole Delmes and Susanne Zander of the Delmes & Zander gallery, which first exhibited the archive in Berlin in late 2014, the book reproduces 120 of the images.

Cindy Sherman's introductory essay reads the anonymous, obsessive body of work as, in her words, \"an exhaustive study of what it is to be a woman,\" and considers the ambiguity of an author whose gender and motive cannot be recovered from the archive alone. The book's title borrows a phrase attributed to the anonymous maker, found scrawled among the Polaroids.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Found Photography, Polaroid, Anonymous
notes: The photographer of the original archive is unidentified; author credit follows the book's own framing ("Photographs by Anonymous"). Not an anthology of multiple artists. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Suite Vénitienne
edition_printrun: First English-language definitive edition, designed in collaboration with Calle
contributors: Dany Barash (Translator); Danny Hatfield (Translator); Charles Penwarden (Translator)
description:
Sophie Calle's first artist's book, chronicling her two-week covert surveillance of a stranger she followed from Paris to Venice in 1980, reissued by Siglio in a definitive English-language edition designed in collaboration with the artist.

After following strangers through Paris for months, photographing them and logging their movements, Calle happened to meet one of her subjects, a man she calls Henri B., at a gallery opening. Learning he was about to leave for Venice, she decided to follow him there. Over nearly two weeks, wearing a wig as a disguise, she tracked his movements through the city in time-stamped entries, combining methodical investigation (calling every hotel, visiting the police) with arbitrary chance (following strangers, like a flower delivery boy, hoping they might lead her back to him).

First published in 1988 and long out of print, this edition presents Calle's photographs and diary-like text as originally conceived, printed on Japanese paper with a die-cut cover and gilded edges. The book established the investigatory, rule-bound method Calle has used across four decades of work spanning photography, writing, and installation, and that made her one of the defining figures of conceptual art's engagement with surveillance and the ethics of looking.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Artist Book, Surveillance, Conceptual Art
notes: Reissue of the 1988 first edition; this Siglio edition is the definitive English-language version, designed with the artist. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: The Encyclopedia of Kurt Caviezel
description:
Kurt Caviezel's first monograph gathers screenshots taken over fifteen years of watching roughly 15,000 publicly accessible webcams around the world, sorted into a taxonomy of recurring human behavior.

Working from his studio, Caviezel captured whatever caught his eye across an archive that grew to more than three million images, then grouped the results by subject and gesture rather than by location: bathers, weddings, photographers at work, stolen kisses, and the reflexive poses people strike for a camera they know is there, the wave, the thumbs-up, the bike raised overhead. The book prints more than 2,000 of these images alongside a foreword by German artist Joachim Schmid, who argues that the sheer quantity is the point, that a single frame is banal but a sequence of kindred ones becomes evidence of pattern. The dust jacket lists all 15,000 web addresses Caviezel used to build the archive.

A selection from the project was shown in the 2016 exhibition Public, Private, Secret at the International Center for Photography in New York, part of a wider body of critical work on the ambient, consent-free photography produced by networked cameras.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Surveillance, Appropriation, Photobook
notes: A selection from this archive was included in the Public, Private, Secret exhibition at the International Center for Photography, New York. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Visibility Machines: Harun Farocki and Trevor Paglen
publisher: CADVC (Center for Art, Design and Visual Culture, UMBC)
contributors: Jimena Canales (Essay); Jonathan Kahana (Essay); Hilde Van Gelder (Essay)
description:
A catalogue pairing filmmaker Harun Farocki and artist Trevor Paglen, both close observers of surveillance, espionage, and military image-making, with newly commissioned scholarly essays and visual essays drawn from a dialogue between their work.

Edited by curator Niels Van Tomme for the Center for Art, Design and Visual Culture at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, the book accompanies an exhibition examining how both artists interrogate the ways military and intelligence operations transform, and complicate, our relationship to images and the realities they claim to represent. Farocki's essay films and Paglen's photographs of classified installations and reconnaissance satellites approach the same terrain, the machinery by which the state renders some things visible and others deliberately obscure, from different generations and different media. The volume includes texts by both artists alongside commissioned essays by Jimena Canales, Jonathan Kahana, and Hilde Van Gelder, plus three visual essays built around themes that emerge from putting the two bodies of work in conversation.

The accompanying exhibition opened at CADVC in 2014 and toured to the Akademie der Künste, Berlin; Gallery 400 at the University of Illinois Chicago; and Be-Part, Waregem, Belgium, through early 2016.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Surveillance, Exhibition Catalog, Contemporary Art
notes: Catalogue authorship is shared between the two featured artists (Farocki, Paglen) and editor/curator Niels Van Tomme; the seed record's photographer credit reflects the editor. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: The Watchers
description:
Haley Morris-Cafiero's first monograph gathers self-portraits from her viral Wait Watchers series, in which she photographed herself in public settings while capturing the passing judgmental glances of strangers, alongside a sample of the thousands of hostile anonymous comments the images drew online.

The project began in 2010, when Morris-Cafiero set up a camera to make a self-portrait in Times Square and later noticed a man in the frame sneering at her, a fraction-of-a-second expression the camera happened to catch. She began staging further self-portraits in public and mining them for these unguarded reactions from strangers. After the Wait Watchers images circulated online starting in 2013, they drew a readership estimated in the hundreds of millions along with a flood of anonymous, often cruel, comments about her body, which the book reproduces alongside the photographs, turning the work into a study of both being watched and being judged.

Published by The Magenta Foundation with an introduction by Amanda de Cadenet and a foreword by curator Marvin Heiferman, the book was released in a regular trade edition alongside boxed and deluxe special editions.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Surveillance, Self-Portraiture, Body Image
notes: Released in a regular trade edition, a boxed special edition, and a deluxe special edition with a print. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Wealth Management
edition_printrun: Edition of 1000 copies, also released as a collector's edition
description:
Carlos Spottorno's artist's book poses as a sales brochure for the fictitious WTF Bank, using black-and-white images of polo matches, ski trips, and glass-walled offices to picture the one-percent lifestyle that private wealth management quietly protects.

Wealth management, in banking terms, is the practice of helping the already rich get richer through tax strategy, legal planning, and financial advice bundled for a fee, often through offshore structures that keep both the money and its movements out of public view. Spottorno's 33 black-and-white photographs, captioned like a glossy prospectus and finished with gold embossing, adopt the visual language of private banking marketing to make that invisibility legible: polo, skiing, boardrooms, and the discreet infrastructure of a class whose wealth compounds largely unseen. The project grew out of a fictional Ferrari advertisement for the same imaginary WTF Bank that appeared on the back cover of Spottorno's earlier Economist-styled photobook The Pigs.

Published jointly by Editorial RM and PHREE in an edition of 1,000, with a separate collector's edition, the book extends Spottorno's documentary practice of using the format and design language of financial and news media against itself.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Artist Book, Photobook, Economics
notes: Grew out of a fictional WTF Bank advertisement that first appeared in Spottorno's earlier photobook The Pigs. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: The Neighbors
description:
Arne Svenson's clothbound monograph collects the photographs of unwitting neighbors he made with an inherited telephoto lens from his Tribeca studio window, a series that provoked national debate over surveillance and privacy when it was first exhibited in 2013.

After inheriting a telephoto bird-watching lens, Svenson began photographing residents of the glass-walled apartment building across the street, catching them, unstaged and unaware, framed by their own windows: napping, eating breakfast, talking on the phone. The compositions have been compared to Vermeer interiors and Edward Hopper's isolated figures, tender in tone but frankly voyeuristic in method. Following an August 2013 exhibition, the series drew extensive press coverage and a lawsuit from photographed residents, arriving at a moment of heightened public anxiety over surveillance and the boundary between public and private space.

This first book collection of the project, published by Julie Saul Gallery and distributed by D.A.P./Artbook, prints 42 full-color plates with an accompanying text by critic David Ebony.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Surveillance, Photobook, New York City
notes: The photographed series first exhibited in August 2013 and drew legal action from subjects photographed without consent; this book, published in 2015, is the first collected edition. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Un universo pequeño
edition_printrun: Edition of 800 copies, plus a special edition of 10
description:
Spanish photographer Antonio M. Xoubanova's second book compresses images shot along ten meters of a single street into what he describes as a 2.5-second film of his own imagined universe.

Xoubanova has described the project in his own words: "Un universo pequeño representa mi imaginario del universo en 2,5 segundos y 10 metros lineales de calle." It compresses his imagined universe into a brief span of time and a short stretch of pavement. The 464-page book sequences roughly 250 color images touching on technology, religion, love, matter, and the everyday texture of a city block, treating the street as a site where the largest human questions surface in passing, unremarkable moments. It follows Xoubanova's first book, Casa de Campo, and was co-published by the Barcelona press Ca l'Isidret Edicions and the Japanese imprint Rondade in an edition of 800 copies, with a special edition of 10 boxed copies including a signed print and a text by Iván del Rey.

The project accompanied Xoubanova's first solo exhibition with Ángeles Baños Gallery in 2015 and was later shown at Photoforum Pasquart.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Street Photography, Photobook, Spain
notes: Co-published by Ca l'Isidret Edicions (Barcelona) and Rondade (Japan). Book text is in Spanish. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: A Treatise on the Camera Obscured
description: A Treatise on the Camera Obscured documents an odd, low-tech act of resistance to post-9/11 photography restrictions: rather than photograph banks, transit hubs, and communications infrastructure outright, Bush built a portable camera obscura from a magnifying glass, a mirror, and plywood, then used it as a drawing aid at sites where photography was informally or formally discouraged. The book interleaves an account of London's post-9/11 security apparatus with a short history of the camera obscura, a step-by-step record of building the device, and the drawings produced with it. A slim, text-heavy, Blurb-format paperback with black-and-white reproductions, it treats the camera obscura as a way to sidestep, and quietly comment on, the arbitrary policing of who is allowed to look at what. Bush is a British photographer, writer, and researcher whose broader practice examines forms of invisible institutional power, and this project sits alongside his other self-published work on surveillance and state authority.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Surveillance, Self-Published
notes: No ISBN found; self-published print-on-demand edition. Page count and print details not published. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Identity Zine
description: Identity Zine #1 is a self-published photo zine of portraits by Los Angeles photographer Dave Naz, documenting people across the transgender and genderqueer spectrum. The project grew out of an earlier book, Genderqueer: And Other Gender Identities, using images Naz shot for that project but didn't include, and it developed into an ongoing series of zines pairing portraits with subjects' own words. A later issue, Identity Zine #2, ran to 60 pages in black-and-white offset in an edition of 300, hand-stamped, and included essays such as "Loving a Trans Person" and "The Gender Inspector" alongside portraits of named subjects from the community. Naz's zine work eventually formed the basis of a full-length book, Identity: In & Beyond the Binary, published in 2017.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Zine, Self-Published, Queer
notes: No ISBN; self-published zine. Page count for issue #1 not published (a later issue, #2, ran 60 pages). Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Kim Jong Il Looking At Things
description: Kim Jong Il Looking At Things collects and republishes photographs appropriated from the North Korean Central News Agency, all showing the country's late leader in the act of inspecting something, usually flanked by an entourage of military officers and advisers who appear alternately fawning and anxious. João Rocha, an advertising art director in Lisbon, began posting the images to a Tumblr blog in October 2010 under flat, matter-of-fact captions such as "looking at blue rods" or "looking at a DVD labeling machine," and the blog became one of the most shared and imitated single-subject Tumblrs of its era. This book gathers the images into a bilingual English/French hardcover, published in Jean Boîte Éditions' Follow Me: Collecting Images Today collection, which treats online image-collecting itself as a curatorial practice. It includes an essay by visual-culture writer Marco Bohr, "Looking at Kim Jong-Il Looking at Things," which examines how the project's refusal to editorialize, its captions withhold judgment and don't try to be funny, is exactly what let the images spread and take on a life as internet memes.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Surveillance, Propaganda
notes: Compiled from officially released North Korean state photographs; no single photographer is credited. Attributed here to editor João Rocha, who created and curated the source project. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Miklós Klaus Rózsa
description: Miklós Klaus Rózsa was kept under surveillance for nearly two decades by the Swiss Federal Office of Police, the cantonal police, and the Zurich municipal police, who compiled a State Protection file on him between 1971 and 1989. This book, conceived and designed by Christof Nüssli and Christoph Oeschger, juxtaposes Rózsa's own photographs, taken from within the Zurich youth movement he documented and took part in, against the bureaucratic language and images of the police files that tracked him. The collage that results sets the immediacy of a participant's images against the flat, often uncomprehending distance of institutional observation, producing a document of a politically volatile period in Swiss history built entirely from the friction between watcher and watched. Published in cooperation with cpress, Zurich, the 624-page book includes roughly 400 black-and-white illustrations and text by Nüssli, Oeschger, historian Peter Kamber, and Rózsa himself, bound as a thread-sewn, lay-flat brochure with flaps.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Surveillance, Archive
notes: Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Disguise and Deception
edition_printrun: First edition, with a hardcover collector's edition limited to the first 40 copies
description: Disguise and Deception takes its title from the German army division "Tarnen und Täuschen," a special unit that researches and fabricates camouflage technology and decoy weaponry, from inflatable tanks and vehicles to imitation land mines. The unit descends from a comparable division of the East German National People's Army that continued its work after German reunification. Schwarzlose photographs this world of manufactured deception and turns it into a meditation on the image itself, on the relationship between originals and copies, and on the overlap between military and artistic strategies of illusion. The book, designed by Gael Paccard with 20 gatefold pages, includes an essay by Johan Frederik Hartle situating the photographs against the aesthetics-ideology relationship the unit's own work embodies. It was Schwarzlose's first publication with Kodoji Press and was accompanied by a related exhibition and symposium at Foam, Amsterdam.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Surveillance, Military, Camouflage
notes: Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Vienna MMIX–10008/7000: Surveillance Panorama Project No. 4—The Vienna Opera Ball
binding: Hardcover and softcover volumes with text booklet in slipcase
description: Vienna MMIX–10008/7000 is the fourth work in Jules Spinatsch's Surveillance Panorama Project, a series begun in 2003 that uses networked surveillance-camera systems to record public events and expose the gap between social performance and social reality. For the 2009 Vienna Opera Ball, the Vienna State Opera ceded control of part of its own surveillance system to Spinatsch, who set two computer-controlled cameras rotating continuously in a grid, photographing the room roughly every three to four seconds from the moment the 7,000 guests entered at 20:32 until the ball ended at 05:10. The publication reproduces the resulting 10,008 images across a hardcover volume presenting them in chronological order, one minute of the ball per page, and a companion softcover volume of selected single frames, accompanied by a text booklet, all housed together in a slipcase, in an edition of 600 numbered copies. The British Journal of Photography described the resulting document as "an anthropological study in class constructed," reading the accumulated frames as a study of Viennese high society under its own cameras.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Surveillance
notes: Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: H. said he loved us
description: H. said he loved us grew out of three years of travel and research into the former German Democratic Republic and the Ministry for State Security, the Stasi. Tanini mixes documentary photographs, found images, and literary references into a fictional narrative that follows the stories of five people who lived under Stasi surveillance, presented as a patchwork of collected documents, autobiographical notes, and anonymous portraits. The images are deliberately stripped of names and specific places, giving the book a timeless, placeless quality that pushes the work toward psychological rather than documentary territory: a study of the dread and oppression particular to living inside a state built on suspicion. Designed and published by Discipula, the collective Tanini co-founded, the book was printed on Tatami paper in an edition of 800 with a soft cover and Swiss binding. It won the Author Book Award at Les Rencontres d'Arles in 2015, the 2014 Premio Pesaresi for Contemporary Photography, and was shortlisted for the 2015 Anamorphosis Prize.

notes: No ISBN published for this title. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: North Warning System
description: North Warning System is the third and final book in Donovan Wylie's Tower series, a body of work concerned with the relationship between vision and power in military architecture. Here Wylie photographs a radar installation just inside the Canadian Arctic, part of the network of short- and long-range stations built jointly by Canada and the United States in the 1950s as the Distant Early Warning Line, after long-range bombers and missiles made the Arctic frontier a vulnerable point of approach. Renamed the North Warning System in the 1990s and upgraded as northern maritime traffic increased, the station appears in Wylie's 17 photographs as an isolated, largely unmanned structure set against a bleached, near-white landscape, its automated detection apparatus standing in for the human observer entirely. The book completes a project that began with Maze/Long Kesh and Watchtowers, tracing surveillance architecture from the overtly staffed to the fully automated.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Surveillance, Military
notes: Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Temps Mort
description:
Temps Mort gathers eight months of exchanges between the French-Algerian artist Mohamed Bourouissa and his friend Al, an inmate, conducted entirely by SMS and MMS on a phone smuggled into the prison where Al was held.

Bourouissa gave Al framing and shooting instructions by text, and Al photographed his surroundings on the phone's low-resolution camera and sent the results back, alongside ordinary text messages that trace the two men's evolving dialogue. The phone was Al's only tie to the world outside. The book collects 21 of these images and message exchanges, punctuated by blank pages marked only with dates, stretching the reader's sense of time the way incarceration stretches it for the person living inside it. It retraces the origin of Bourouissa's better-known 2009 video and photo project of the same name (its title borrowed from a track by the rapper Booba, and first developed as a film during his studies at Le Fresnoy), reconstructing the earlier, image-and-text collaboration the later project grew from. Études Studio published the book with the kamel mennour gallery in Paris in January 2014: a 140-page, full-color offset softcover in an edition of 1000, with text by Magali Jauffret, in English and French.

Bourouissa (b. 1978, Blida, Algeria; based in Paris) is known for staged and collaborative photographic and video projects that examine social marginalization, incarceration, and the built environments of the French banlieues, including the series Périphérique. Temps Mort's remote, improvised, camera-smuggled method extends that interest into a direct collaboration with someone the state had physically removed from view, using surveillance-grade image quality to document a life the prison system otherwise keeps unseen.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Artist Book, Incarceration, Collaborative Art
notes: Cover sourced from the Surveillance Index CDN at 2400px width. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Periscope
binding: Softcover with clear plastic protective cover
description:
Over eight years, José Diniz traced the Brazilian coastline from Maranhão to Rio Grande do Sul and into Uruguay, photographing people, buildings, and the horizon always from the same low, water-level vantage: face-on, beneath, or above the waves.

Periscope collects 54 black-and-white images from that project across 74 pages. Despite the title, Diniz never used an actual periscope; as he has put it, the name is "just a metaphor for the way of observing I chose — it's as if my eyes weren't enough to see and photograph under those conditions." Working with the camera held below the horizon line, waves reading as moving mountains and the water itself bending the optics into new readings of the scene, Diniz built a body of work that treats the shoreline as a threshold rather than a backdrop. Editor Iatã Cannabrava describes the sequence as a narrative told by an innocent periscope that surfaces from the depths to find humanity endangering the planet itself, closing on an image of water symbolically flooding Rio de Janeiro's Copacabana Palace.

Published by Editora Madalena with Editora Terceiro Nome in a signed edition of 900 softcover copies wrapped in a clear plastic cover, designed by Ekaterina Kholmogorova and printed in Brazil by IPSIS, Periscope was Diniz's first book. It launched in São Paulo in September 2014, at the Museu de Arte Contemporânea in Niterói that November, and again at Paris Photo's Grand Palais signing program the same year. Diniz (b. 1954, Niterói) is the grandson of a founder of the Sociedade Fluminense de Fotografia and the son of painter José Maria Nogueira Diniz, from whom he inherited both his fascination with marine imagery and his path toward studying at Rio's Museu de Arte Moderna.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Brazilian Photography, Landscape
notes: Two publisher credits appear across sources: Editora Madalena and Editora Terceiro Nome (the seed data's 'Terceiro' is the shortened form of Terceiro Nome). Cover sourced from the Surveillance Index CDN at 2400px width. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Rear Window
description:
Rear Window turns Dutch photographer Jordi Huisman's camera on the backs of buildings across European capitals, the unplanned, patched-together architecture that faces courtyards and alleys rather than the street.

Where a building's front is designed and presented, its rear tends to accumulate balconies, satellite dishes, extensions, and repairs added piecemeal over decades by whoever lived there at the time; Huisman found that this informal accretion produced an oddly consistent visual language across cities that otherwise share little architectural history. The idea traces back to a bedroom window in The Hague, where Huisman studied photography at the KABK art academy: the chaotic view of houses across the courtyard, evidently built at different times and glued together over the years, stayed with him until, living in Amsterdam five years later, he began deliberately photographing the same phenomenon at friends' and acquaintances' homes. The Velvet Cell published the project in London in January 2014 as a saddle-stitched, 24-page softcover limited to 300 copies.

Huisman (b. 1982, Almere, the Netherlands) trained first in engineering before switching to photography at KABK, and has worked as a freelance photographer since 2005. Rear Window's voyeuristic vantage on the private, unshowcased side of urban buildings fits a broader interest, across his work, in what architecture and the built environment reveal when nobody is arranging it for a camera.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Architecture, Urban Landscape
notes: Cover sourced from the Surveillance Index CDN at 2400px width. Image counts (color/bw split) not found in the sources checked. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Taxi Dirty Book
description:
Yoshinori Mizutani's first book pairs two bodies of pictures made in Tokyo: taxi drivers photographed frontally from the back seat, and books and magazines, some of them pornographic, abandoned on the street.

The two series sit against each other without text or captions, proposing distinct ways of experiencing the city and, by extension, distinct ways of looking: one an enclosed, face-to-face encounter with a stranger doing his job, the other a glance down at discarded printed matter that once circulated its own images of looking and desire. Published by the Geneva imprint Boabooks in November 2014 as a 48-page softcover with 33 color illustrations, the book carries no text, letting the two series' juxtaposition make its own argument about the layered, sometimes furtive ways a city gets seen.

Mizutani (b. 1987, Fukui) studied at the Tokyo College of Photography after a degree in economics, and the same year Taxi Dirty Book appeared he was named to the LensCulture Emerging Talents Top 50, selected for Foam Talent Amsterdam, and included in the Kiyosato Museum of Photographic Arts' Young Portfolio. His subsequent books, including Tokyo Parrots, Colors, and Hanon, continued to find unnoticed intersections between Tokyo's built and animal life; the library holds several of these later titles alongside this early, image-only debut.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Japanese Photography, Street Photography
notes: Fourth Mizutani title in the collection, alongside Colors, Hanon, and Tokyo Parrots. Dimensions given as 8.2 x 11.6 in / 20.8 x 29.5 cm per the seed data and Les presses du réel's listing; the artist's own site lists a smaller 140 x 180 mm figure for the same ISBN, which appears to be an error or refers to a different printing — the larger figure is corroborated by two independent sources. Out of print. Cover sourced from the Surveillance Index CDN at 2400px width. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: N.A.
description:
Doug Rickard's N.A. gathers still frames pulled from YouTube videos uploaded by ordinary Americans, assembling a jittery, unauthorized portrait of the country's urban underbelly.

Over roughly three years, Rickard combed through amateur cellphone footage, pausing and advancing frame by frame to extract images from what he has described as hijacking other people's own devices to give him "very special views and intimate situations" — scenes ranging from petty crime and comic mishap to moments of unguarded intimacy, none of it staged or consented to as photography. The 128-page hardcover, published by D.A.P. with Verlag Kettler in 2014 (following a smaller 2013 edition from Cologne's White Press), reproduces 96 color images alongside text by Z. Redman and a poem by Ann Garlid. The title deliberately resists a single reading: Rickard has said it stands variously for "National Anthem," the bureaucratic "Not Applicable," or simply "North America."

N.A. extends the found-image, appropriation-based method Rickard developed in A New American Picture (2010), his acclaimed series built from Google Street View captures, into an even more intimate and unstable source: footage its subjects filmed and posted themselves, then repurposed without their knowledge into a document of race, technology, and a culture under constant, casual self-surveillance.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Found Photography, Surveillance, Appropriation
notes: The library separately holds Doug Rickard's Tom (Little Big Man Books, 2013, id 964), a different title assembled from a found archive of vintage street photographs; N.A. is a distinct work built from appropriated YouTube stills, first issued by White Press (Cologne) in 2013 in a small edition, then released more widely by D.A.P./Verlag Kettler in 2014 (the edition catalogued here). Cover sourced from the Surveillance Index CDN at 2400px width. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: One Picture Book #83: Witness
edition_printrun: Limited edition of 500 numbered copies, each including an original signed photograph
description:
Dan Solomon's Witness radically crops stills from the Zapruder film and the Moorman Polaroid, isolating the bystanders who watched the Kennedy assassination unfold rather than the event itself.

By decontextualizing individual and grouped figures from Dealey Plaza's most examined footage, Solomon turns two of the most scrutinized images in American photographic history into a study of witnessing itself: how memory dims, how an eyewitness account slips, and how a camera's claim to record objective fact erodes the more closely its frames are parsed. The book is #83 in Nazraeli Press's One Picture Book series, a run of uniform, casebound 5.5 x 7.25 inch volumes, each built around a single artist's cohesive body of work across 16 pages. This edition is limited to 500 numbered copies, each bound with 7 four-color plates and accompanied by one original signed photograph by the artist.

Dan Solomon (b. 1957) is better known as a photography collector and curator than as a working photographer: his personal collection of roughly 250 prints, spanning early photography to contemporary practice, is now held by the National Gallery of Art, and he has curated historical and contemporary exhibitions including surveys of Muybridge, Stieglitz, and Atget. Witness is a rare instance of Solomon working as an artist rather than a collector, using his connoisseur's eye for archival material to interrogate the reliability of the photographic record.

title: Ramya
description:
Petra Stavast moved into her landlady Ramya's Amsterdam home in 2001, and the camera became the two women's shared language over the fourteen years that followed.

The resulting photographs are quiet and domestic: the house, its rooms, and Ramya herself, gathered slowly enough that the changes in a life only show up in hindsight. Ramya died in 2012, and rather than closing the project, her death sent Stavast deeper into it — she went through her former landlady's private archive and located photographs a neighbor had taken over the years, assembling a fuller biography than the original portrait project had set out to make. That research surfaced an unexpected history: Ramya had belonged to the Rajneeshpuram commune, the Oregon settlement founded in 1981 by followers of the Bhagwan (Osho), and a later video shows her back in Amsterdam attending a workshop with a different guru. Stavast weaves these photographic and archival threads, along with video stills, into a 224-page hardcover designed by Hans Gremmen, published by Fw:Books with Roma Publications in Amsterdam in 2014.

The book was widely recognized on its release, named to De Volkskrant's 15 Best Dutch Photobooks of 2014, Photo-eye's Best Books of 2014, and the Kassel Fotobookfestival's year-end selections. It stands as one of Stavast's best-known long-form documentary projects, built on the kind of sustained, cohabiting proximity to a subject that only fourteen years of shared address could produce.

title: Tabula Rasa Magazine, Volume I: Identity
description:
The inaugural issue of Tabula Rasa, a New York- and Copenhagen-based magazine treating fashion photography as an independent, advertisement-free medium, gathers eighteen photographers' takes on a single theme: Identity.

Each contributor, drawn from varied backgrounds and working in distinct styles, produced an exclusive series responding to the issue's brief, turning the fashion image toward the photographers' own identities and the concept of identity more broadly. Under editor in chief Sabrina Banta, the magazine positions itself deliberately between magazine and art book, free of advertising and unbound by seasonal or trend-driven constraints, aiming instead for a plurality of outlooks rather than a single house style. Banta has described the title's premise directly: as children we don't yet know the limits of our imagination, curiosity alone sets the boundaries, and the magazine takes its name from that unmarked, fearless state.

Volume I launched in 2014 alongside a companion website, and the issue was carried by galleries and bookstores including Artbook at MoMA PS1, Gagosian, McNally Jackson Books, and International Playground in New York, Wood Wood in Copenhagen, and Daikanyama T-Site in Tokyo. The magazine describes itself as a non-profit platform for photographers, stylists, and writers to collaborate outside a producer-consumer relationship; more recent social media activity suggests the publication has been on extended hiatus since its early issues.

title: The Epilogue
description: The Epilogue reconstructs the life of Cammy Robinson, a 26-year-old who died from complications of bulimia, through testimonies, family photographs, letters, medical records, and other archival ephemera gathered in close collaboration with her family. Laia Abril combines her own color photographs with these found documents, using multiple inserts and in-page gatefolds to interleave the family's private materials with her own observational images of the spaces and objects Cammy left behind. Rather than centering the disorder itself, the book follows its aftermath, the grief, guilt, and altered family dynamics of those who survive a loved one's death from an eating disorder, extending Abril's visibility to the indirect victims usually left out of the clinical narrative. The book is presented as the concluding chapter of Abril's long-running investigation into eating disorders and the visual culture surrounding them, a project she began in 2010 with earlier multimedia work addressing bulimia and pro-anorexia imagery online. The Epilogue was shortlisted for the 2014 Paris Photo–Aperture Foundation First PhotoBook Award and named a best photobook of the year by numerous critics.

title: The Blue Hour
description: The Blue Hour documents Uri Gershuni's virtual return to Lacock, the English village where William Henry Fox Talbot pioneered photography, walked entirely through Google Street View. Where his first visit to Lacock was made in person, this second journey unfolds from a computer screen: 255 black-and-white images captured from the online map-image database, presented one to a page. Gershuni converts the borrowed screen captures into a classical, uniform photographic aesthetic, so the visible seams of the digital source, compression artifacts, stitching errors, oddly cropped views, sit against the stately reserve of the presentation. The project treats Google's surveillance-scale mapping infrastructure as a found camera, using the birthplace of photography as its test subject to ask what has and hasn't changed in the medium's relationship to place and looking. The book was designed by Gila Kaplan and published by The Green Box Kunstedition in Berlin.

title: Source Code
description: Source Code is Mishka Henner's print-on-demand archive of the raw HTML source code behind the home pages of U.S. intelligence agencies, harvested on a single day, 24 June 2013. The United States Intelligence Community, the network of agencies established under Executive Order 12333 to conduct research, produce intelligence, and support espionage and military planning, presents a public face online; Henner's book strips that presentation down to the code underneath it, the invisible scaffolding a browser normally renders and hides. The book was made as a contribution to Kenneth Goldsmith's Printing Out the Internet, a crowdsourced exhibition at LABOR gallery in Mexico City (26 July–30 August 2013) that asked participants worldwide to print out and submit pages from the internet, ultimately filling the gallery with roughly ten tons of paper. Henner's submission turns an act of bureaucratic transparency-theater into raw material, using print-on-demand publishing, a recurring method in his practice for bypassing traditional gatekeeping, to make the agencies' own code physically legible as an object.

title: The Looking Game
description: The Looking Game pairs the once-secret photographic archive of serial killer Rodney Alcala with writing by art critic John Berger, whose name Alcala took as an alias while a fugitive in New York in 1968. Alcala, an amateur photographer active through the late 1960s and 70s, left behind more than a thousand photographs that police discovered in a storage locker only in 2010; roughly 120 were released publicly in hopes the public could help identify the people pictured. Mirko Smerdel and M.F.G. Paltrinieri set that archive against extracts of Berger's writing, most pointedly Ways of Seeing, building a structure of five sections, intro, biography, statement, main body of work, and appendix, that asks whether Alcala's choice of alias was coincidence or a knowing appropriation of a critic concerned with exactly the ethics of looking Alcala's own photographs raise. The project drew criticism on publication for aestheticizing the case: reviewers questioned whether obscuring victims' faces for artistic effect sits uneasily alongside claims of investigative or identificatory purpose. The Looking Game is the first installment of The Subnarratives, an ongoing series of case studies by Smerdel and Paltrinieri examining photography's status as documentary evidence.

title: You See Me, I See You
description: Audrey Tan's first photobook and solo exhibition catalog, made to mark her return to Singapore after years in London, uses portraiture and self-portraiture to trace connection, isolation, and belonging. The images, made over roughly seven years, function as a personal record of her time abroad and double as a study of the self under observation, portraits and self-portraits that turn the camera into both witness and mirror. Tan frames the work as an examination of self-surveillance within a metropolitan setting, the quiet visibility and invisibility of a person moving through a crowded city, hiding, as the book's own framing has it, in plain sight. It was published in a limited edition of 200 copies to accompany her first solo exhibition in Singapore. Tan's related work in this period was also recognized by the International Photography Awards.

title: Privacy Settings
description: Privacy Settings is a sequence of black-and-white photographs of Erik van der Weijde's sleeping son, the boy cast about the bed in different positions across the book, occasionally joined by his sleeping mother. The premise, a parent obsessively photographing a child in sleep, courts unease, but the images themselves read as light and tender: a boy cuddling a bear, cocooned in a blanket, growing progressively more off-kilter as the sequence continues. The son is never named, yet the photographs place the viewer intimately inside his private, unconscious world, invoking the same domesticity and vulnerability found in Sophie Calle's The Sleepers and Fred Hüning's Private Rooms. Sleep recurs across van der Weijde's practice, appearing in titles such as This is Not My Wife and This is Not My Son, and later a series photographing his sleeping dog, Nina; Privacy Settings sits in the middle of that thread. Bound in cloth, sewn, and offset printed, the book was published by 4478zine in an edition of 700.

title: XY XX
description: XY XX is Fosi Vegue's first photobook, a voyeuristic sequence shot through a window facing a row of rooms where sex workers meet clients, its digital noise pushed to the point of abstraction rather than erased. Where most photographers try to eliminate sensor noise, Vegue amplifies it, letting the exaggerated grain blur and distort the scenes into something closer to afterimage than document, a visual analogue for the subconscious operating beneath the transaction he's watching. Critics have compared the project to Merry Alpern's Dirty Windows, though Vegue frames the act of looking explicitly as a study of control: prostitution and pornography become social problems only when a system decides they should be, and the photographer's own stolen vantage point replicates that same structure of surveillance and permission. The book was edited by Vegue and Eloi Gimeno, designed by Gimeno, and published by Dalpine in 108 softcover pages. It received attention in Voices of Photography (Taiwan), IMA Magazine (Tokyo), and L'Oeil de la Photographie (Paris) following its 2014 release.

title: Getting to Know My Neighbors
description: A zine built from Joseph Wilcox's personal collection of anonymous ATM receipts, gathered without any initial intent to make art from them. "I want to know what people buy at the store, how much they have or don't have, how they keep themselves afloat, and how close they are to drowning," Wilcox has written of the project. The receipts, most pulled from shared ATMs, are stripped of any identifying context beyond the numbers themselves, balances, withdrawals, purchases, yet those numbers sketch a picture of the strangers who left them behind. Wilcox has described his zine-making as a deliberately low-effort practice, treating the accumulation of everyday ephemera (receipts here, rejection emails in a companion project) as material that becomes a zine once enough of it piles up, an art practice folded into ordinary life rather than set apart from it. The work poses a direct question: who are the people sharing a bank machine with you, and what does the money passing through it reveal about how close, or distant, that connection really is.

title: World of Details
description:
Binschtok worked in two stages: she selected New York street scenes from Google's archive while in her Berlin studio, then traveled to each location to photograph it again with her own camera. The Street View source images are grayscale, distant, and mechanically framed. Binschtok's photographs, made later and in color, close in on the same scenes: a diner booth, a stack of newspapers, a painted wall, the kind of detail the automated camera passed over without registering.

The book presents both sets of images side by side across 136 pages, roughly 60 photographs split between the archival black-and-white references and Binschtok's color work, sequenced to trace this back-and-forth rather than resolve it. Matthias Harder's accompanying essay situates the project within a broader body of work in which Binschtok examines how images circulate and get remade as they pass between digital systems and physical places.

Binschtok, born in Moscow in 1972 and based in Berlin since the 1980s, studied under Timm Rautert at the Academy of Visual Arts Leipzig. Her other series include Globen, built from globes bought at online auction alongside the listing photos that sold them, and Cluster and Networked Images, which trace visual echoes between her own photographs and images returned by reverse image search. World of Details extends that same interest in the space between a networked, automated view of the world and a photographer's deliberate one.

notes: Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Dutch Landscapes
description:
Mishka Henner built Dutch Landscapes from a quirk of Google Earth's satellite coverage: the Dutch government, unlike most, chose not to blur or pixelate sensitive sites but to cover them with bold, brightly colored polygons, an intervention meant to obscure that instead reads as a deliberate visual mark. Henner gathered these polygon-covered views of military bases, ammunition depots, NATO storage annexes, and royal palaces and presented them as found landscape images, framing state censorship as an unlikely continuation of Dutch landscape painting.

The book is a softcover, print-on-demand edition, 25 x 20 cm, 106 pages, self-published by Henner in Manchester; some archives list a 2013 printing of the same open edition. The related images were also produced as a series of twelve archival pigment prints and shown in group exhibitions including "From Here On" at Les Rencontres d'Arles (2011), Centre Pompidou-Metz (2013), and the Metropolitan Museum of Art (2014).

Dutch Landscapes helped establish Henner's reputation for work built from appropriated satellite and aerial imagery. He went on to win the Kleine Hans Award in 2011, was shortlisted for the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2013, and received the ICP Infinity Award for Art the same year.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Self-Published, Surveillance, Landscape Photography

title: No Man's Land
description:
No Man's Land collects fifty-nine images of isolated women on the margins of southern European roadsides, all sourced entirely from Google Street View.

Henner found the coordinates on online forums where men trade information about the location of sex workers, then used Street View to see whether Google's mapping car had captured a woman waiting there; the resulting figures, faces pixelated by Google's own privacy blurring, appear as small, distant shapes against expansive fertile landscape. The book was self-published in Manchester as an open-edition, print-on-demand softcover.

The work was shown in the group exhibition "From Here On" at Les Rencontres d'Arles in 2011 and was shortlisted for the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize in 2013. Critical response has centered on the ethics of the appropriation: reviewers have noted the tension between exposing a form of surveillance and reproducing it, since the book identifies its subjects, however anonymously, as sex workers without their knowledge or consent. No Man's Land belongs to Henner's broader practice of mining automated and institutional image archives, alongside works built from satellite imagery and CCTV.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Self-Published, Surveillance, Appropriated Imagery

title: Top Secret: Bilder aus den Archiven der Staatssicherheit
description: Simon Menner mined the archives of the Stasi, East Germany's secret police, to surface formerly classified photographs of officers and employees putting on professional uniforms, gluing on fake beards, and signaling to each other with their hands. The Stasi's archive held roughly 1.4 million photographs from a force of nearly 300,000 employees, a workforce per capita larger than that of the CIA or KGB, and Menner drew from that material to build the book's sequence. One recurring section documents disguise training, images taken during seminars where personnel practiced blending into public life unnoticed. Hatje Cantz published the book in 2013 as a 128-page bilingual German/English softcover with 166 illustrations. The photographs carry the weight of a surveillance-state document while reading, decades later, as comic and absurd; the New York Times Book Review noted it as the first visual study of the Stasi's activities, and LensCulture called it a well-researched, historically grounded selection with contemporary relevance to present-day surveillance debates.

title: The Nine Eyes of Google Street View
description:
The Nine Eyes of Google Street View collects hundreds of found images from Rafman's ongoing project, begun in 2008, in which he combs Google's Street View archive for scenes its roving cameras caught by accident: car crashes, animals in odd postures, masked figures, landscapes lit like paintings. The book, published by Jean Boîte Éditions in a bilingual English/French edition of 160 color pages, was the first monograph devoted to the project and pairs Rafman's selections with a critical text by architect and artist Guillaume Aubry.

Rafman is a Canadian artist, born 1981 in Montreal, whose work across video, digital media, and photography examines how internet culture reshapes identity and desire. Nine Eyes established him as a central figure in post-internet art and has been shown and collected internationally, including at MoMA, the Stedelijk Museum, and the National Gallery of Canada, alongside later works such as Kool-Aid Man in Second Life and Dream Journal.

title: Cruising
description:
Chad States's first monograph documents two years spent photographing the parks, public restrooms, and roadside wooded groves that gay men across the United States have used as cruising sites, gathering 80 color plates from locations nationwide.

States composites elements from multiple sites into single, lush landscape compositions; the men who appear read as small, partial figures folded into dense foliage and shadow rather than posed as portrait subjects, and the book moves gradually from empty clearings toward these more populated scenes. The approach invites comparison to Kohei Yoshiyuki's The Park, though critic Vince Aletti observed that States's subjects read as more solitary than furtive, and the pictures stop short of sensationalism. The volume includes texts by geographer Gordon Brent Ingram and photographer Alec Soth, and it was shortlisted for the Aperture Foundation/Paris Photo First PhotoBook Award in 2012.

The book was States's debut monograph, published by powerHouse Books in 2011. Its inclusion in Surveillance Index Edition One (2016) follows the anthology's own logic, gathering photographs built from scanning open landscape for hidden, half-concealed human activity.

title: Behind the Curtains
description:
Over seven years, photojournalist Tomas van Houtryve secured unprecedented access to seven countries where the Communist Party still holds power: North Korea, Cuba, China, Nepal, Vietnam, Laos, and Moldova. The resulting photographs move past ideology to record a secretive world of revolutionaries, spies, opposition fighters, and ordinary workers, tracing the gap between communism's founding ideals and its present-day reality.

Published by Editions Intervalles in 2012 as van Houtryve's first monograph, the 288-page hardcover book carries a foreword by philosopher and historian Tzvetan Todorov. Van Houtryve began the project after working as an Associated Press photographer covering Latin America and Guantánamo Bay before leaving to pursue long-form documentary work, starting with the Maoist rebellion in Nepal that led him toward this broader survey of communism's twenty-first-century holdouts.

The related photo series won the 2012 POYi World Understanding Award. Van Houtryve, a Belgian-American photographer and emeritus member of VII Photo Agency, went on to produce Blue Sky Days, a drone's-eye view of American life that won the 2015 ICP Infinity Award; his work is held in the permanent collections of the International Center of Photography, the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, and the Museum of Contemporary Photography in Chicago.

title: Privat/Privacy
contributors: Boris Groys (Essay); Christian Heller (Essay); Jan Verwoert (Essay); Lisa Beißwanger (Essay)
description:
The catalog for "Privat/Privacy," a 2012 group exhibition at Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt that surveyed how contemporary art has tracked the collapse of the boundary between private life and public display.

Curated by Martina Weinhart and shown at the Schirn from November 2012 to February 2013, the exhibition gathered roughly thirty artists working across photography, film, and installation to examine domestic scenes, personal secrets, and surveillance-adjacent looking. The book reproduces work by Merry Alpern, Richard Billingham, Sophie Calle, Tracey Emin, Hans-Peter Feldmann, Nan Goldin, Birgit Jürgenssen, Leigh Ledare, Christian Marclay, Ryan McGinley, Laurel Nakadate, Peter Piller, Martha Rosler, Dash Snow, Fiona Tan, Kohei Yoshiyuki, and Akram Zaatari, among others, alongside essays by Boris Groys, Christian Heller, and Jan Verwoert and interviews Weinhart conducted with Ledare, Nakadate, and Piller.

The 240-page, German/English bilingual volume was published by Distanz Verlag, Berlin, with a foreword by then-Schirn director Max Hollein. It is included in Surveillance Index Edition One as an example of art-world engagement with covert and voyeuristic looking, from Yoshiyuki's photographs of couples observed on Tokyo beaches at night to Alpern's images shot through a rear window onto strangers' private encounters.

title: Woman With a Camera (35mm)
description:
Woman With a Camera (35mm) is a 2009 artist's book by Anne Collier, published by the New York imprint Hassla Books, built from a sequence of found and appropriated photographs.

Each image in the book shows a woman photographed in the act of photographing: a 35mm camera raised to her eye, her own gaze hidden behind the viewfinder. Drawn from vernacular and commercial sources rather than shot by Collier herself, the sequence turns a single, repeated gesture into a study of who gets to hold the camera and who is pictured holding it, folding the photographer's own instrument back into the frame as its subject.

The book sits within a body of work in which Collier has repeatedly rephotographed and recontextualized found imagery of cameras, eyes, and other tools of looking, including related bodies of work such as Women With Cameras (Anonymous) and Women With Cameras (Self-Portrait) and her exhibited series Anne Collier: Photographic, in which the mechanics and history of photography itself become her recurring subject.

title: The Thirty-Two Inch Ruler / Map of Babylon
description:
The Thirty-Two Inch Ruler / Map of Babylon pairs two color photographic essays by John Gossage, his first books shot in color, issued as companion volumes with neither taking precedence over the other.

The Thirty-Two Inch Ruler documents the Washington, D.C. neighborhood where Gossage lives, a district of ambassadors' residences, embassies, and the private homes of the capital's power elite, begun the year a new neighbor, Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld, moved in nearby. Photographed across a full cycle of seasons, the images of streets, cars, houses, and yards favor days of clear blue sky and full foliage, an almost too-perfect calm that reads as the visual manner of privilege itself.

Steidl has published several of Gossage's later books, including The Thirty-Two Inch Ruler (2010), Looking Up Ben James: A Fable (2018), and Should Nature Change (2019); this edition also carries the imprint of the International Center of Photography, New York.

title: Fifty-One US Military Outposts
description:
Fifty-One US Military Outposts is Mishka Henner's first book to use satellite imagery as both research tool and creative medium, a project that replaces the photographer's camera with the reconnaissance apparatus already deployed by states and institutions.

Working only from material already in the public domain — official US military and veterans' websites and forums, domestic and international news reports, and both official and leaked government documents — Henner located and compiled aerial views of fifty-one American military outposts, overt and covert, spread across countries including Germany, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Djibouti, and the United Kingdom. The book takes the plain form of a print-on-demand softcover, its bureaucratic presentation matching the source material it repurposes.

Henner began the project in the years following the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, prompted by a wish to understand the scale of US military engagement abroad; a related portfolio of prints from the series has been exhibited at Carroll/Fletcher in London, the Grundy Art Gallery in Blackpool, and Örebro Kunsthall in Sweden. It marks the start of Henner's long-running use of satellite imagery and open-source data as a documentary method.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Surveillance, Self-Published, Conceptual Art
notes: No ISBN was assigned to this print-on-demand open edition; the seed data's publisher URL (a Lewis Bush storefront) did not match this book and was not used. Dimensions and page count sourced from Henner's own site and the V&A Museum collection record, which agree. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Cell
description:
Cell collects Taiji Matsue's experiments in what he calls "super trimming" — extracting and radically enlarging a single fragment from within a larger photograph — turning found scenes into ambiguous, at times abstract images.

Working from color photographs, many of them casual scenes of leisure such as a hotel pool deck, Matsue isolates a small portion of the frame, the "cell," and blows it up many times over until grain, color, and gesture overtake legible content. The results shift between disorienting, comic, and abstract, echoing the way Antonioni's Blow-Up treats magnification as a route to new, unstable meaning rather than to clarity. The book, published in Tokyo by Akaaka in 2008, includes an interview with Matsue by the photography critic Minoru Shimizu.

Cell extends Matsue's longer-running interest in photographing landscape and terrain from unusual vantage points, testing how far an image can be cropped before it stops describing its subject and starts describing only itself; he later adapted the same idea for tablet screens in the interactive work CCcell.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Japanese Photography, Abstraction
notes: Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Exposed: Voyeurism, Surveillance, and the Camera Since 1870
contributors: Philip Brookman (Essay); Marta Gili (Essay); Carol Squiers (Essay); Richard B. Woodward (Essay); Neal Benezra (Foreword); Vicente Todolí (Foreword)
description:
Exposed: Voyeurism, Surveillance, and the Camera Since 1870 is the catalogue for a survey exhibition co-organized by Sandra S. Phillips, senior curator of photography at SFMOMA, and Simon Baker of Tate Modern, tracing the point at which the impulse to look becomes an urge to spy.

The book is organized across five sections: The Unseen Photographer, Voyeurism and Desire, Celebrity and the Public Gaze, Witnessing Violence, and Surveillance. It gathers work by both named and anonymous photographers, moving from hidden-camera street pictures and paparazzi shots to erotic photography and images produced by state and military surveillance apparatus. Artists represented include Sophie Calle, Henri Cartier-Bresson, Walker Evans, Harun Farocki, Nan Goldin, Robert Mapplethorpe, Helmut Newton, Andy Warhol, and Weegee, among many others.

The plates are accompanied by essays from Phillips, Baker, Philip Brookman, Marta Gili, Carol Squiers, and Richard B. Woodward, with a foreword by Neal Benezra and Vicente Todolí. The exhibition opened at Tate Modern in May 2010 before traveling to SFMOMA and the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Surveillance, Voyeurism, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Multi-photographer exhibition catalogue; the primary curator/editor (Sandra S. Phillips) is used as the catalogue author per house convention for named-editor anthologies (cf. id 1845, Police Pictures, same curator). Toured Tate Modern (2010), SFMOMA (2010–11), and Walker Art Center (2011). Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Könnte Sein
description:
Könnte Sein, German for "Could Be," is a 2008 photobook by Katja Stuke, published by the Swiss imprint Kodoji Press in Baden.

The title's conditional, unresolved phrasing runs through Stuke's broader practice, which frequently works with photographs whose origin and authorship are uncertain: surveillance-like street pictures, appropriated news imagery, and self-made photographs treated with the same evidentiary distance, so that the viewer is left to judge what a given image could or might be showing.

Stuke, based in Düsseldorf, has worked in long-term collaboration with the photographer Oliver Sieber, with whom she founded the publishing and exhibition platform ANT!FOTO in 2010; her work, made independently and with Sieber, repeatedly returns to questions of surveillance, identity, and control in the image.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, German Photography, Surveillance

title: Jurkjes en Jason: 27 Views On Terrorism Today
description:
Jurkjes en Jason: 27 Views On Terrorism Today collects short image- and text-based contributions from twenty-seven different makers, each responding in a page or two to the same brief: how terrorism appears, circulates, and is represented in contemporary visual culture.

Published by the Eindhoven imprint Onomatopee in 2008, the book takes its Dutch title — roughly "little dresses and Jason" — from the tonal range of the contributions inside, which move between the domestic and the horror-film register the reference implies. Rather than a single authored essay or portfolio, the book is structured as an anthology of brief, plural takes, closer in form to a group survey or a class project than a monograph.

As a multi-contributor project with no single named editor credited on the cover, it is catalogued here under the library's Various Artists convention; individual contributors are not itemized in the source record consulted.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Terrorism, Anthology, Dutch Photography
notes: No single credited editor or artist was found for this multi-contributor Onomatopee anthology, so it is catalogued under the library's NA VA (Various Artists) convention. Page count conflicts between sources consulted (60 vs. 64); 64 used per the more frequently cited figure, flagged here as unresolved.
