title: The Transparent City
description:
The Transparent City gathers Michael Wolf's photographs of Chicago's downtown skyscrapers made after dark, when illuminated interiors turn the glass towers into vast, legible grids of windows.

Working with a large-format camera from the street and from within neighboring buildings, Wolf photographed the city's Loop and near North Side at a resolution fine enough to isolate single offices and apartments within the wider facade, then printed a number of the images at mural scale so individual figures and rooms could be picked out from across the gallery. The effect turns the everyday transparency of the modern office tower into a study of the city as a mechanism for accidental, mutual watching, where every lit window is both a subject and a potential vantage point.

Published by Aperture in association with the Museum of Contemporary Photography at Columbia College Chicago, the book includes an essay by curator Elizabeth Siegel and extends Wolf's long-running interest, elsewhere in his work, in the density and anonymity of the contemporary city.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Surveillance, Urban Photography, Architecture
notes: Dimensions were sourced only from the seed record (surveillanceindex.com) and could not be independently cross-checked within the research budget; flagged as unresolved. Page count sourced from bookseller/library listings. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: I Saw You
description: I Saw You is the first volume in what Bruce Connew conceived as a loose trilogy of artist's books examining private life under observation. Over twelve months, Connew trained a telephoto lens on Balaena Bay car park in Wellington from his own home, photographing people going about ordinary business in what they assumed was a private, unwatched moment in public space. The resulting images are square-format and color, cropped and reworked to a degree unusual for a photographer known for defending his frames unaltered, producing pictures that read as blurred, almost painterly studies of anonymous figures. Connew has described the project as a comment on living in a surveillance society, on being watched without knowing it. The book was designed by Connew's partner Catherine Griffiths and published by his own imprint, Vapour Momenta Books, in 2007; the 52-image series also showed at Mary Newton Gallery in Wellington that year, with a related film by Griffiths using the same images.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Surveillance, New Zealand Photography
notes: First of a planned trilogy of Vapour Momenta artist's books (I Saw You, 2007; I Must Behave, 2009). Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: 72 Girls and Some Boys Who Could Be Models
description: In late 2005, Anne Daems roamed SoHo while on an art-residency grant from the International Studio & Curatorial Program, photographing young New Yorkers on sidewalks, in the subway, under scaffolding, and through shop windows without their knowledge. Working in the tradition of street photographers like Bill Cunningham, she recast these strangers as candid models, producing images that sit between fashion photography and covert surveillance. The pictures raise questions about voyeurism, youth, conventional beauty, and how casually observers classify people they pass on the street. The book includes an interview between Daems and artist Dan Graham, whose own work has long engaged with surveillance and public space; in it, Graham observes that Daems is interested not in technique but in ordinary people, and in how unstable the idea of "normal" really is. Published by J&L Books in an edition of 1000, the volume is now out of print.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Street Photography, Photobook
notes: Out of print; edition of 1000. Steidl/J&L bibliographic details cross-checked against jandlbooks.org, artbook.com, and Dashwood Books listings. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: My Wife
description: Petter Hegre, a commercial and fine-art photographer, began photographing his wife the day they met, eventually amassing roughly 5000 images over the course of their relationship. My Wife gathers a selection of those photographs into a single volume, opening with a short interview with Hegre before moving into around 200 pages of images that trace an ongoing, candid record of daily and intimate domestic life. Rather than staged portraiture, the book reads as a private visual diary, close observation sustained over years, that happens to have been made public. Published by Edition Stemmle in Zurich and New York in 2000, the book sits within a lineage of photographer-partner documentary projects, using the sustained, watchful intimacy of long-term domestic photography as its own kind of counterpoint to external surveillance.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Documentary Photography
notes: Contains explicit content; described here in general terms consistent with the publisher's own framing of the work as an intimate domestic document. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Oblivion
description: Oblivion continues David Maisel's long-running practice of photographing landscapes transformed by human intervention from the air, here turning his camera on Los Angeles itself rather than a mine or reservoir. Shot from directly above the city, the fifteen aerial images render the freeway interchanges, subdivisions, and commercial sprawl of Los Angeles as a dense, near-abstract pattern, with tonalities reversed so the images read as negatives, black skies and white ground. The effect is at once beautiful and unsettling, a metropolis stripped of scale and specificity until it resembles a body under diagnostic imaging. The book opens with Mark Strand's poem "Black Maps" and closes with an essay by William L. Fox, "Shadowlands," both engaging with the disorientation and dystopian undertone of Maisel's aerial vantage. Designed by Bob Aufuldish and published by Nazraeli Press in association with The Joy of Giving Something, Inc., in an edition of 1000, Oblivion sits alongside other Maisel aerial-landscape monographs including The Lake Project and Library of Dust.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Aerial Photography, Landscape
notes: Edition of 1000, designed by Bob Aufuldish; published in association with The Joy of Giving Something, Inc. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Architecture of Authority
description: For Architecture of Authority, Richard Ross spent years gaining access to spaces designed to assert control over the individuals who occupy them: churches, mosques, a preschool classroom, a Swedish courtroom, the United Nations, and the Iraqi National Assembly hall. The photographs move progressively toward starker expressions of institutional power, culminating in an interrogation room at Guantanamo Bay, segregation cells at Abu Ghraib, and a death chamber. Ross photographs these interiors in a cool, formal, deadpan style that lets the architecture itself carry the argument, drawing a visual line between the confessional and the interrogation room, the courtroom and the classroom. The book is accompanied by text from John R. MacArthur, publisher of Harper's Magazine, and was published by Aperture in 2007. It engages directly with post-9/11 anxieties about surveillance, detention, and the erosion of individual liberty, work that was named among Photo District News' best books of 2007.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Architecture, Surveillance, Documentary Photography
notes: Named among Photo District News' best books of 2007; accompanying exhibition ranked #10 on Artforum's best shows of 2007. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Pornografie
edition_printrun: Steidl facsimile reissue of the 1971 Anabas Verlag/Edition Kolling original
description: First published in 1971 by Anabas Verlag under the Edition Kolling imprint, Pornografie is a landmark of German political artist's-book making by graphic artist and satirist Klaus Staeck. The book juxtaposes press photographs of street violence, war casualties, and torture with staged body-art pictures and everyday objects, building a visual argument, taken from Herbert Marcuse, that it is not the naked body but the general displaying medals earned in a war of aggression that is truly obscene. Its title deliberately misleads readers expecting explicit sexual content, redirecting attention instead toward the panopticon of violence, exposure, and monitoring that pervades everyday life. Photobook historians Parr and Badger singled it out as one of the most expressionistic artist's books of its era, in a genre generally prized for restraint. Steidl reissued the book as a facsimile edition in 2005, edited by H. C. Schmolck, keeping the original German-language format and black-and-white reproductions intact.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Political Art, Germany
notes: Steidl edition is a facsimile of the 1971 Anabas Verlag/Edition Kolling original; some booksellers list the reissue as 2005, others as 2007 -- ARTBOOK/D.A.P. gives a specific date of June 15, 2005, used here. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Super Vision
description: Published to accompany the exhibition that opened the Institute of Contemporary Art's new Boston building in September 2006, Super Vision surveys how visuality has shifted in the digital era, as computer graphics, imaging, digitization, and virtuality reshape what it means to see and be seen. The exhibition and book bring together work by 26 artists spanning painting, sculpture, video, and photography, including Andreas Gursky, Thomas Ruff, Gerhard Richter, Jeff Wall, Harun Farocki, Mona Hatoum, and Yoko Ono, alongside surveillance-adjacent pieces by artists like Jack Goldstein and Tony Oursler. As the book's foreword puts it, the works employ macro and microscopic vision, manipulated and virtual imagery, techniques of surveillance, and effects that alter viewers' sense of reality, treating the eye itself as a site of both pleasure and threat. The catalog was edited by ICA chief curator Nicholas Baume, with essays by art historian David Joselit and media theorist McKenzie Wark situating the exhibition within broader debates about looking, image manipulation, and control in contemporary visual culture. Co-published by MIT Press and the ICA in 2006, it functions as a broad survey of surveillance-inflected art of the period rather than a single artist's monograph.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Art, Exhibition Catalog, Contemporary Art, Surveillance
notes: Multi-artist exhibition catalog with no single photographer credit; catalogued as NA VA (Various Artists) per house convention, with editor and essayists in contributors. Seed data's photographer field named editor Nicholas Baume rather than a single artist. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: The Park
edition_printrun: First English-language edition, published with Yossi Milo Gallery
description: Working at night in three Tokyo parks during the 1970s, Kohei Yoshiyuki used infrared film and flash to photograph couples in the midst of sexual encounters, both heterosexual and homosexual, that took place under cover of darkness in public space. His camera also caught something else: the onlookers, sometimes dozens of them, who crouched in the bushes and shadows to watch, and occasionally to intervene. The resulting duotone images collapse the line between voyeur, participant, and photographer, since Yoshiyuki himself worked from among the same crowd of spectators. First published in Japan in 1980 under the title Koen (Park), the work remained largely unknown outside Japan until Yossi Milo Gallery exhibited it in New York in 2007, prompting this first English-language edition, co-published by Hatje Cantz and the gallery. The book pairs the photographs with text by critic Vince Aletti and an interview between Yoshiyuki and photographer Nobuyoshi Araki, situating the work within debates about voyeurism, consent, and surveillance in postwar Japanese photography.
tags: Surveillance Index, Surveillance Index Edition One, Photography, Photobook, Surveillance, Voyeurism
notes: Original Japanese edition published 1980 as Koen; this 2007 edition is the first in English. A later expanded edition was published by Radius Books. Surveillance Index Edition One archiving 2026; catalogued 2026-09-01.

title: Baron
description:
Baron collects thirty-six watercolor and pencil drawings by the Seoul-born artist Joyce Lee. The work turns love, sex, and the human body into surrealist metaphor, drawn rather than photographed.

Published by the London imprint Baron in 2022, this is Lee's debut book. It draws on her archive of watercolor and pencil work: bodies rendered as landscape, fruit, and household object, high-culture reference set against cartoonish vulgarity. An essay by Pernilla Ellens, who also edited Baron's monographs on Namio Harukawa and the Death Book series, places the drawings in a line of erotic illustration. That tradition uses stylization to depict what photography is routinely blocked from showing on image-sharing platforms. The book is a hardcover, 76 pages, 220 x 280mm, now in its second printing.

Lee studied English literature before training at Seoul National University for her BFA. Her drawings have appeared in Numéro and Playboy. Baron followed this debut with Archive (2024), a larger 150-image survey of her work.
tags: Art, Drawing, Illustration, Erotica, Surrealism, Contemporary Art
notes: Retailers title this book inconsistently: most (Amazon, Goodreads, Baron's own site, The Library Project) list it as "Baron by Joyce Lee" or "Baron, Joyce Lee", while a few (Waterstones, Booktopia) list the title simply as "Joyce Lee". This is Baron's house convention of titling artist monographs after the artist under its own imprint name; the book is a single self-contained debut monograph, not an issue of a periodical. Baron published a follow-up collection of Lee's work, Archive (2024, 150 images), which is a separate publication and has not been catalogued here. As of research date, this title shows sold out / reprint-pending at most listed retailers.

title: Atlas
edition_printrun: First UK edition (translated from the Spanish; a US edition was published by E.P. Dutton, New York, in 1985; originally published in Buenos Aires as Atlas by Editorial Sudamericana, 1984)
description:
Atlas is the travel book Jorge Luis Borges made near the end of his life. Short prose pieces are paired with photographs María Kodama took on their journeys together, an act of seeing carried out by a writer who had gone blind decades earlier.

Anthony Kerrigan's English translation gathers short texts keyed to specific places and objects: Geneva, Ireland, a hot-air balloon over California, a street corner in Buenos Aires. Each text faces one of Kodama's photographs. Borges wrote from memory of how a place had looked before he lost his sight. At other times he built an image from what Kodama described to him as they traveled. The result reads as part journal, part fantasia, arranged by geography rather than chronology. It began as a Spanish volume, Atlas, published in Buenos Aires in 1984. The Kerrigan translation followed in 1985 from E.P. Dutton in New York and in 1986 from Viking in London, an oblong hardcover illustrated throughout in black and white.

Atlas was among the last books published in Borges's lifetime. Kodama had been his student, then his secretary and travel companion through his blind years. She married him weeks before his death in 1986 and became executor of his literary estate. Atlas records how the two worked together, her photographs and his recollection completing each other. It sits alongside a body of poems, essays, and fictions that includes Ficciones, The Aleph, and Labyrinths.
tags: Literature, Photography, Travel, Latin American Literature, Photobook
notes: Multiple editions exist under this title: original Spanish (Editorial Sudamericana, Buenos Aires, 1984), US translation (E.P. Dutton, New York, 1985, ISBN 9780525243441), and UK translation (Viking, London, 1986, ISBN 9780670810291), all with the same Kerrigan translation and Kodama photographs, differing mainly in binding and imprint. This record follows the Viking edition per the requester's specification. Page count is reported as 94 pages by multiple booksellers describing the Viking edition; a few listings round to 96. Subjects (LOC): Borges, Jorge Luis, 1899-1986 -- Travel; Voyages and travels.

title: Hands and Feet and Their Supports
description:
Matt Borruso's Hands and Feet and Their Supports treats the body's outermost extremities as stand-ins for the whole person, tracing hands and feet as they are cast, copied, and recast across years of studio research.

The book gathers reference images, found photographs, scans, magazine clippings, .jpgs, and installation documentation. Borruso assembled the material around his 2018 exhibition of the same title at Cloaca Projects in San Francisco. There he showed concrete and felt casts of hands and feet on powder-coated steel supports, alongside screen-printed newsprint collages. A strict but invisible grid organizes the pages. Throughout, the work returns to the idea of a \"support\" — structural, ideological, architectural, or as plain as a shoe on a foot. Visible Publications, Borruso's own imprint, issued the book in an edition of 175. It is a softcover, printed on a digital press, with two-color screen-printed covers and hand-sewn binding; each copy was collated and bound by hand.

Borruso is a San Francisco-based artist working across sculpture, print, and installation; Visible Publications is the imprint through which he publishes his own books alongside work by other artists.
tags: Art, Artist Books, Sculpture, San Francisco
notes: No ISBN found; self-published artist's book issued by the artist's own imprint, Visible Publications, in an edition of 175. Bibliographic detail (pages, dimensions, binding, edition size) confirmed via Printed Matter's catalog listing.

title: A Message for You
edition_printrun: 3rd printing (09/2016); combines the two volumes of the original 2006 slipcased edition
description:
A Message for You collects the fashion photographs Guy Bourdin made with the model Nicolle Meyer in the late 1970s, the period widely considered the high point of his career. It stands as one of the fullest records of a single working relationship behind his images.

Steidl published the book in 2013, combining two volumes originally issued as a slipcased set in 2006. Its first half shows Meyer's images for Bourdin's Charles Jourdan shoe campaigns and his French Vogue editorials, including variants and outtakes that had gone largely unseen. Its second half turns from finished pictures to process. Polaroids, contact sheets, sketches, and fragments of poems and notes appear alongside Meyer's own written recollections of working with Bourdin. Together the two parts trace both the printed image and the improvisatory work behind it.

Bourdin spent decades as one of French Vogue's most identifiable photographers. He staged fashion pictures as compressed, unresolved narratives, full of saturated color and dark humor, rather than straightforward garment display. Steidl has published several other monographs from his archive, among them Exhibit A, Polaroids, and Image Maker. Each draws on a different part of the working materials he left behind. A Message for You is distinguished by its focus on a single sustained collaboration with one model.
tags: Photography, Fashion Photography, Photobook, Vogue, 20th Century
notes: Out of print at Steidl and ARTBOOK/D.A.P. as of research date; copies circulate via secondary booksellers. Page/image counts for color vs. b&w not specified by any source checked. Subjects (LOC): Bourdin, Guy -- Exhibitions; Fashion photography -- 20th century; Photography, Artistic.

title: Shadow and Light
publisher: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
description:
Bill Brandt: Shadow and Light is the catalogue for the Museum of Modern Art's 2013 retrospective. It was the museum's first full reconsideration of Brandt's career since 1969, and the most comprehensive survey of his work assembled to date.

The book is edited and with an essay by Sarah Hermanson Meister, Curator in MoMA's Department of Photography. It draws on the museum's vintage-print holdings of Brandt, recently more than doubled, tracing a coherent trajectory across five decades of a career the photographer himself preferred to present in loose thematic groupings. It moves from his dark, socially pointed studies of English class life in the 1930s through his photojournalism for Lilliput and Picture Post. From there it takes in his wartime pictures of the London Blackout and Blitz shelters, shown here alongside the magazine assignments that produced them. It closes with the distorted, sculptural nude studies of his final decades. A second essay by conservator Lee Ann Daffner examines Brandt's own darkroom methods. The 208-page volume reproduces 254 images in tritone, on pages trimmed to echo the proportions of Brandt's photographs.

Brandt, born in Hamburg in 1904 and based in Britain from the early 1930s, is regarded as the country's foremost photographer of the twentieth century. His earlier books include The English at Home (1936), a study of class contrast, and A Night in London (1938), on the city after dark. Literary Britain (1951) surveyed landscapes associated with English writers. Perspective of Nudes (1961) introduced the wide-angle nude studies that became his best-known late work. He was also an accomplished portraitist, photographing writers and artists including Francis Bacon and Henry Moore.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Exhibition Catalog, British Photography, Portraiture, Nudes
notes: UK edition exists under Thames & Hudson, ISBN 9780500544242 — cataloguing the MoMA/US edition (9780870708459) here per publisher instructions. Subjects (LOC): Brandt, Bill, 1904-1983 -- Exhibitions; Photography, Artistic -- 20th century -- Exhibitions.

title: Brassaï: The Monograph
contributors: Jean-Jacques Aillagon (Essay); Werner Spies (Essay); Roger Grenier (Essay); Henry Miller (Text); Jacques Prévert (Text); Gilberte Brassaï (Interview)
description:
Published to accompany the Centre Georges Pompidou's retrospective of Brassaï's work, this monograph is the fullest English-language account of a photographer whose Paris after dark remains one of the defining bodies of 20th-century street photography.

Edited by Alain Sayag and Annick Lionel-Marie of the Pompidou's photography department, the book moves chronologically through Brassaï's career. It covers the nocturnal Paris pictures that made his name in the early 1930s, his work for the Surrealist journal Minotaure, his portraits of Picasso, Matisse, Dalí, and the wider Paris art world, and his later photographs of graffiti and sculptural form. Essays by Jean-Jacques Aillagon and Werner Spies frame the work critically. Roger Grenier and Lionel-Marie contribute additional texts, and an interview with Brassaï's widow, Gilberte, adds biographical material. Excerpts from Henry Miller and Jacques Prévert, both friends of Brassaï, appear alongside the plates, which draw largely on the Pompidou's own holdings.

Born Gyula Halász in Brassó, Transylvania, Brassaï took his name from his hometown after settling in Paris in 1924. Paris de nuit, his 1933 debut, established him as the photographer of the city's nocturnal life. The Secret Paris of the 30s later extended that project into the demimonde of bars, brothels, and cabarets. He also wrote on his friendships with Picasso and Henry Miller, and worked in sculpture, drawing, and film. This monograph, published in association with the International Center of Photography, remains the standard English survey of that range.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Paris, Surrealism, Portraiture, 20th Century
notes: Brassaï is a chosen pseudonym (born Gyula Halász), not a mononym standing in for an anonymous or collective author, so it is recorded as a normal personal `last` name with `first: null` rather than the site's `NA VA` (Various Artists) convention, which applies only to anthologies with no identifiable lead name. This English edition (Bulfinch/Little, Brown, 2000) is edited by Alain Sayag and Annick Lionel-Marie; some secondary sources spell the second editor's name 'Anne-Marie Lionel-Marie' but her name appears consistently as 'Annick Lionel-Marie' on the book's own title-page listings and across all bibliographic sources checked, so that spelling was used. Sylvie Aubenas was not found credited on this particular edition and was not included as a contributor. Subjects (LOC): Brassaï, 1899-1984; Photographers -- France -- Biography; Photography, Artistic.

title: Coming of Age
contributors: Laurie Simmons (Introduction); Marilyn Minter (Contributor); Alessandro Michele (Contributor); Karley Sciortino (Contributor); Jamia Wilson (Contributor)
description:
Coming of Age is Petra Collins's first monograph, a retrospective survey of the photography that made her one of the defining image-makers of the 2010s.

The book collects a decade of Collins's work, from early self-portraits taken as a teenager in Toronto through campaigns for Gucci and Adidas, films for the Tate, and editorials for magazines including Vogue and i-D. Personal essays and Polaroids run alongside the plates, along with contributions from women who shaped her thinking about image-making, including Marilyn Minter, Alessandro Michele, Karley Sciortino, and Jamia Wilson. Laurie Simmons writes the introduction. Rizzoli published the 208-page hardcover in 2017.

Collins, born in Toronto in 1992, began photographing at fifteen and served as a resident photographer for Rookie magazine before her pastel-toned, unretouched pictures of girlhood and adolescence became a visual reference point copied widely across fashion and social media. She also edited Babe, an anthology of work by women photographers, and has since directed music videos for Selena Gomez, Carly Rae Jepsen, Olivia Rodrigo, and Cardi B.
tags: Photography, Monograph, Fashion Photography, Portraiture, Women Photographers
notes: Book is out of print per Rizzoli Bookstore and Dashwood Books listings (both show unavailable/out-of-stock); this does not affect cataloguing. Dimensions not confirmed to an exact trim size from a bookseller spec sheet (one general bookseller description gave an imprecise range, 'Quatro, 9.75 in - 10.75 in tall', so dimensions were left null rather than guessed). Illustration/image counts not found on any checked source, left null. LCCN/OCLC not located via web search; a full WorldCat lookup was not performed given the research budget. title: Fashion Image Revolution: The Art and Technique of Brian Dowling
contributors: Brian Dowling (Subject / Darkroom Printer); Nick Knight (Contributing Photographer); Anton Corbijn (Contributing Photographer); Juergen Teller (Contributing Photographer); Craig McDean (Contributing Photographer)
description:
Fashion Image Revolution tells the story of Brian Dowling's BDI, the London darkroom where analog printing became a creative act in fashion photography. For more than thirty years, Dowling's studio shaped the medium, from the 1970s through the shift to digital.

Charlotte Cotton traces that history through Dowling's Islington studio, where he translated negatives shot by Nick Knight, Anton Corbijn, Juergen Teller, and Craig McDean into finished prints. He developed techniques such as cross-processing, masking, layered exposure, filtering, and hand-applied color fades. Those effects shaped the look of British fashion photography before software took them over. The book combines interviews with Dowling and his clients, testimonials, and reproductions of the haute couture images that passed through his hands. A set of new photographs, commissioned for the book, demonstrates his methods directly.

Cotton is a curator and critic who has held posts at the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Photographers' Gallery, and LACMA's Wallis Annenberg Department of Photography. She has written extensively on the medium's recent history, including The Photograph as Contemporary Art, Imperfect Beauty: The Making of Contemporary Fashion Photography, and Photography Is Magic. This book turns that critical attention toward a figure whose contribution to the images themselves went uncredited for decades.
tags: Photography, Fashion Photography, Photobook, Analog Photography, London
notes: Not a survey/anthology of fashion photography by Cotton as originally assumed by the research brief; it is a single-subject tribute to Brian Dowling, a London commercial darkroom printer, told through his collaborations with named fashion photographers (Knight, Corbijn, Teller, McDean, and others). Classified as Photobook rather than Photographer Monograph because Dowling is the darkroom technician/subject, not the photographer of the images reproduced. Page count is disputed across sources: bookseller/library-style listings (AbeBooks, SHOWstudio) give 221 pp.; several retail listings (Amazon, Barnes & Noble) give 240 pages. Used 221 pp. as the more bibliographically careful figure. title: Private Views
edition_printrun: First edition. A Thames & Hudson distribution issue for markets outside North America carries ISBN 9781597111263.
description:
Private Views gathers the Polaroid photographs Barbara Crane made in Chicago's summer festival crowds between 1980 and 1984, pictures shot close enough that the camera's speed is doing as much work as her eye.

Around 105 color plates fill the book, most of them cropped tight on people eating, drinking, and pressed together in the crowd. The instant print let Crane keep working at a pace and a proximity a slower camera would not have allowed, and she photographed the same festivals across four summers. Aperture published the volume in 2009 with a text by Barbara Hitchcock, on the occasion of a retrospective of the series at Stephen Daiter Gallery in Chicago that November and December. It is bound in cloth over boards, a single Polaroid reproduction set into a recessed panel on the front, and was issued without a jacket.

Crane (1928-2019) studied under Aaron Siskind at the Institute of Design in Chicago and taught at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago from 1967 to 1995. Chicago and its crowds run through most of her work, usually organized by repetition: the grids, sequences, and repeated frames of series such as People of the North Portal, Neon, and Monster. Private Views is the loosest of these, built on the single quick frame rather than the set.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Monograph, Polaroid, Chicago, Portraiture
notes: Text by Barbara Hitchcock. Published on the occasion of a retrospective of the series at Stephen Daiter Gallery, Chicago, November-December 2009. Bound in cloth over boards with a Polaroid reproduction set into a recessed panel on the front; issued without a dust jacket. The Library of Congress records 111 pages (LCCN 2008939805; TR680 .C72 2009); booksellers describe the plate section as unpaginated, which accounts for the varying page counts in listings. Subjects (LOC): Crane, Barbara, 1928-2019; Instant camera photographs; Portrait photography; Summer festivals -- Chicago (Ill.).

title: Ordinary Pictures
contributors: Eric Crosby (Curator); Thomas Beard (Essay); Lane Relyea (Essay); Eva Respini (Essay); Misa Jeffereis (Contributor)
description:
This catalogue is the first critical anthology to trace how contemporary art has grappled with the generic, mass-produced image. It accompanied one of the more ambitious photography surveys the Walker Art Center has mounted this decade.

The book is organized around the stock photograph as both commodity and cultural symptom. It gathers conceptual and picture-based work by roughly 40 artists working since the 1960s. Among them: John Baldessari, Sarah Charlesworth, Anne Collier, Robert Heinecken, Louise Lawler, Sherrie Levine, Richard Prince, Ed Ruscha, Stephen Shore, and Wolfgang Tillmans. Four essays anchor the volume. Eric Crosby contributes the title essay. Lane Relyea writes on the shift from picture reading to information handling. Thomas Beard contributes "Recommended Practices." Eva Respini closes the volume with a dictionary-format piece on ordinary pictures in the internet age. The design departs from a conventional catalogue layout: reproductions of the same works repeat across spreads, echoing stock-photo licensing sheets and undercutting the aura of the singular artwork. A flexidisc bound into the volume adds an audio component.

Eric Crosby curated the exhibition, on view in the Walker's Target and Friedman Galleries from February 27 through October 9, 2016. It sits within his broader curatorial focus on photography, conceptual art, and the circulation of images across commercial and institutional systems.
tags: Photography, Vernacular Photography, Conceptual Art, Exhibition Catalog, Group Exhibition
notes: Multi-artist (approx. 40 artists) group exhibition catalogue; Eric Crosby is editor/curator, not a single author. Physical description per library catalog record includes a bound-in flexidisc (audio excerpts); OCLC number and LC control number were not locatable within the source pages checked. Subjects (LOC): Vernacular photography -- Exhibitions; Images, Photographic -- Exhibitions; Images, Photographic; Vernacular photography.

title: Vape Shop Olympia
description:
Vape Shop Olympia is the concluding volume of Peter De Potter's loose photobook trilogy, a hopeful, hypersaturated portrait of a culture running on sign language, hip-hop, and clickbait.

Claire de Rouen Books published the 224-page softcover in London in 2018. It pairs De Potter's photographs of young men, mostly found through Instagram and pictured nude or posing with props like pliers pulling at skin and fingers pointing at the sky, with drawings by Giovanni Wetzl and graphic design by Sven Bauweraerts. Sharper and more brightly colored than his earlier books, it reads as a meandering, multi-layered dispatch on how texting, sexting, and social-media iconography have reshaped everyday gesture and belief. The edition ran to 500 copies.

De Potter is a Belgian artist based in Antwerp. From 2001 to 2010 he directed the imagery and designed books for Raf Simons, including the designer's Redux monograph, and in 2016 he designed two of the sleeve variants for Kanye West's The Life of Pablo. Vape Shop Olympia followed The Vanity of Certain Flowers (2016) and All Statues Sing Protest Songs (2017). Together the three books move from retreat, to rebuilding, to this book's outward-looking present tense.
notes: Third and final volume in De Potter's photobook trilogy, following The Vanity of Certain Flowers (2016, retreat/contemplation) and All Statues Sing Protest Songs (2017, published by IDEA with a companion xeroxed zine insert). Both publisher storefronts (Dashwood Books, Claire de Rouen Books) list the title as no longer in stock; no current source for the title was found.

title: Rineke Dijkstra: The Louisiana Book
contributors: Poul Erik Tøjner (Essay); Thomas Weski (Essay); Hans den Hartog Jager (Essay)
description:
This retrospective monograph gathers three decades of Rineke Dijkstra's portraiture into one chronological survey, built around a photographer known for catching people in the instant before they become someone else.

The book accompanies "The One and the Many," Dijkstra's first full museum survey in Scandinavia. It moves through her career in order. The Beach Portraits (1992–2012) show teenagers standing stiffly against sand and sea. Other sections cover new mothers photographed hours after giving birth, bullfighters still bloodied and shaking from the ring, and the Almerisa series, which follows a Bosnian refugee child into adulthood over more than a decade of sittings. Essays by Poul Erik Tøjner, Thomas Weski, and Hans den Hartog Jager, edited by Michael Juul Holm, trace her method: a large-format 4x5 camera and long exposures that Dijkstra has called "a space where things can happen" between photographer and subject.

Dijkstra was born in 1959 in Sittard, Netherlands. She found the Beach Portraits while recovering from a cycling accident, when she began photographing herself and others in states of physical exhaustion. She is represented by Marian Goodman Gallery. In 2012 the Guggenheim Museum in New York mounted a full retrospective of her work, which traveled to SFMOMA and the Jeu de Paume in Paris. She received the Hasselblad Award in 2017, the year this book appeared.
tags: Photography, Portraiture, Exhibition Catalog, Contemporary Art, Monograph

The verified, correctly catalogued title (per WorldCat/OCLC 1010664585 and all booksellers) is 'Rineke Dijkstra: The Louisiana Book.' title: Barely Private
description:
Barely Private is Sante D'Orazio's own visual diary, a decade of behind-the-scenes life folded into a photographer's scrapbook rather than smoothed into a portfolio.

Published by Taschen in 2009 in a trilingual English/French/German edition, the book is the second volume of D'Orazio's ongoing diary project, following 1998's A Private View. It layers contact sheets, snapshots, and Polaroids taken from 1997 onward alongside the photographer's own handwritten captions and loose ephemera. The format works more like a personal scrapbook than a monograph. Pages are collaged with mounted prints, torn notes, and offhand pictures of the models, actors, and musicians who moved through his studio and travels. The result is an unvarnished, working view of a career built on close access to famous subjects.

D'Orazio built his career shooting fashion and celebrity portraiture for Vogue, Vanity Fair, and Playboy. He produced widely reproduced images of Madonna, Pamela Anderson, and other public figures across three decades of work. Barely Private sits alongside his other books, including Pam: American Icon (2005) and Gianni and Donatella (2007). It is the most unguarded of the set, trading his commissioned glamour work for the loose, cumulative record of a working photographer's daily life.
tags: Photography, Fashion Photography, Celebrity Photography, Photobook, Photo Diary
notes: Verified author spelling is "Sante D'Orazio" (no accent on Sante) across OpenLibrary, Wikipedia, and bookseller records. "Barely Private" is the second volume of D'Orazio's photo-diary project, following A Private View (1998, Penguin Studio / Schirmer-Mosel); some sources describe it as covering 1997 to 2008, others as an open-ended "1997-present." No price or valuation information is included. Subjects (LOC): Fashion photography; Celebrities.

title: Stan Douglas
description:
This third volume in the Scotiabank Photography Award series presents the photographic practice of Vancouver artist Stan Douglas, honored as the award's laureate for an established Canadian artist.

The 228-page monograph, published by Steidl in partnership with Scotiabank, surveys how photography has shaped Douglas's critical and historical reception. Douglas restages specific, often overlooked historical moments — sites of civic unrest, forgotten labor disputes, and other populist events — as meticulously constructed large-format tableaux that read simultaneously as documentary record and cinematic fiction. The book traces an uncanny resemblance between these reconstructed histories of displacement and injustice and present-day events, treating photography as both the medium and the subject of Douglas's inquiry into memory and visual culture.

Douglas (b. 1960, Vancouver) works across photography, film, and installation, unraveling official narratives through carefully researched restagings of specific historical events; his photographic series include Abbott & Cordova, 7 August 1971. He later represented Canada at the Venice Biennale (2022) and has had major surveys at museums internationally, with work held in public collections worldwide.
tags: Photography, Contemporary Art, Canadian Art, Photobook, Scotiabank Photography Award
notes: "Scotiabank Photography Award" is a SERIES designation, not the book title — the book's actual title is simply "Stan Douglas." This is the third annual publication in the Steidl/Scotiabank series accompanying Canada's Scotiabank Photography Award (an award for an established Canadian photographer); the third annual volume, published 2014, corresponds to Douglas's award year of 2013 (2011 award -> 2012 book, 2012 award -> 2013 book, 2013 award -> 2014 book), consistent with but not independently re-confirmed against a primary award-history page this session. Distributor status shown as "out of stock" on ARTBOOK as of this research date, not a valuation note. title: Gil Elvgren's Private Stock
description:
Gil Elvgren's Private Stock collects the private reference photographs the pin-up painter used to build his illustrations, images that were never meant to be seen as finished work.

Tony Nourmand edited the book. Reel Art Press published it in 2012 as a 192-page hardcover. It draws on Elvgren's personal archive of stereoscopic 3D slides and 35mm photographs, most shot in the 1940s and 1950s. The models are posed in the expressions and settings that would later appear in his calendar and advertising paintings. Seen together, the photographs show how closely Elvgren staged and directed his models before painting over them. He exaggerated proportions and lighting to arrive at the glossy, idealized style that made him one of the best-known pin-up artists of the period.

Elvgren painted calendar art for Brown & Bigelow. He also painted advertising campaigns for Coca-Cola and General Electric from the 1930s through the 1960s. His paintings remain among the most widely reproduced examples of American pin-up illustration from the mid-20th century.
tags: Photography, Illustration, Pin-up Art, American Art, Archival Photography
notes: Rizzoli lists this edition as out of print as of research date. Elvgren worked as a painter/illustrator, not a photographer; classified here as Artist Monograph rather than Photographer Monograph since the book documents his working photographs rather than presenting photography as his primary medium. No valuation or collectible-market language included per project policy, despite this book's frequent framing by dealers as a scarce or desirable object. Subjects (LOC): Elvgren, Gil, 1914-1980 -- Photograph collections; Pin-up art -- United States; Illustrators -- United States -- 20th century.

title: American Power
description:
Mitch Epstein's American Power turns a large-format camera on the machinery that keeps the country running, catching the plain, almost bureaucratic look of infrastructure most people are trained not to see.

Working mainly with a view camera between 2003 and 2008, Epstein traveled the United States photographing sixty-four color pictures at coal, nuclear, hydroelectric, wind, and solar sites. The project began as a New York Times Magazine assignment after he covered the evacuation of Cheshire, Ohio, a town contaminated by a nearby coal plant, and grew into a five-year survey of energy production and its costs. He was repeatedly stopped by corporate security guards and once questioned by the FBI for photographing power plants from public roads, an episode recounted in the book's afterword. Steidl published American Power in 2009 as a 144-page clothbound book; it won a Deutscher Fotobuchpreis gold medal in 2010.

Epstein has spent five decades photographing American landscapes and social life, beginning with work on Mike Nichols and Robert Altman film sets in the 1970s. American Power extended concerns he pursued in Family Business and later returned to in Property Rights and Old Growth, both likewise built around land use and its consequences.
tags: Photography, Documentary Photography, Photobook, Landscape, Environment, American Power
notes: ISBN corroborated across Steidl's own page (978-3-86521-924-4) and ARTBOOK/D.A.P. Steidl's site lists a 2011 date on its current product page, but the original publication date of 2009 is corroborated by ARTBOOK, Dashwood, and the Deutscher Fotobuchpreis 2010 award (for a 2009 title), so 2009 was used as the publication year. title: 272 Pages
contributors: Regis Durand (Essay); Nuria Enguita Mayo (Essay); Peter Fischli (Essay); Hans Haacke (Essay); Martin Parr (Essay)
description:
Hans-Peter Feldmann's 272 Pages is exactly what its title says: a catalogue built almost entirely from the artist's own pictures and objects, with barely any curatorial text standing between the reader and the work.

Helena Tatay edited the book. It was published in 2001 by Fundacio Antoni Tapies in Barcelona, together with Centre National de la Photographie in Paris, Fotomuseum Winterthur, and Museum Ludwig in Cologne. The occasion was Feldmann's exhibition at the Tapies, held from November 2001 to January 2002. The book surveys his practice from the late 1960s on. It sequences found and taken photographs and everyday objects without captions, treating the book as one more Feldmann work rather than a conventional retrospective document. Short contributions come from Regis Durand, Nuria Enguita Mayo, Peter Fischli, Hans Haacke, and Martin Parr.

Feldmann spent five decades collecting and rephotographing found imagery: amateur snapshots, postcards, newspaper clippings. He used repetition and anonymity to question authorship and the market's premium on originality. Other books built the same way include Voyeur and 100 Jahre, each assembled as a sequence of images with almost no text.
tags: Photography, Conceptual Art, Artist Book, Found Photography, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Page count is disputed across sources: the book's title states 272 Pages, which was used here as the pages value, but AbeBooks listings gave a physical count of 329-334 pages. This is likely a discrepancy between the artist's own titled page-count concept and the printed object's actual pagination (front matter, essays); flagged rather than silently resolved. Classified as Artist Book rather than Photobook since the work functions as a Feldmann artwork in book form, assembled by the artist himself, rather than a straightforward survey of photographs. Subjects (LOC): Feldmann, Hans-Peter, 1941- -- Exhibitions; Conceptual art -- Germany -- Exhibitions; Found photography.

title: Gerard Petrus Fieret
contributors: Wim van Sinderen (Essay); Hripsime Visser (Essay); Francesco Zanot (Essay); Violette Gillet (Essay)
description:
Gerard Petrus Fieret is the first major monograph devoted to a photographer the Dutch mostly ignored while he was alive: a self-taught obsessive who photographed almost nothing but a handful of subjects, over and over, for about a decade.

Editions Xavier Barral and Le Bal published the book in 2016. It accompanied an exhibition organized with Fotomuseum Den Haag and shown at Le Bal in Paris that May through August. The 592-page book reproduces 297 black-and-white photographs on deliberately thin, semi-transparent paper. Images bleed faintly into one another as the pages turn, echoing the double exposures and scratched negatives in Fieret's own prints. He acquired his first camera in 1965 and largely stopped photographing around 1975. In that decade he photographed women, children, street scenes, shop windows, and himself with an obsessive, unrepeatable intensity, working the same reflex Praktica through solarization and multiple exposure. Essays by Wim van Sinderen, Hripsime Visser, Francesco Zanot, and Violette Gillet place the work within Dutch and European photography of the period.

Fieret rejected the label "photographer," calling himself a "fotograficus." His later life was marked by poverty, illness, and the loss of much of his archive to theft and neglect. He remains far less known internationally than contemporaries like Ed van der Elsken, though this monograph and its accompanying exhibition were built to change that.
tags: Photography, Photographer Monograph, Dutch Photography, Black and White, Exhibition Catalog
notes: A separate Dutch/English edition of this same exhibition catalogue was published by Uitgeverij Hannibal; this record covers the French/English Editions Xavier Barral / Le Bal edition since it was the more thoroughly documented of the two online. ISBN for the Xavier Barral/Le Bal edition could not be confirmed with confidence from available sources and was left null rather than guessed. title: Flashpoint! Protest Photography in Print, 1950-Present
contributors: Makeda Best (Essay); Hannah Darabi (Essay); Arthur Fournier (Essay); Marc Feustel (Essay); Kerry Manders (Essay); Elisa Medde (Essay); Mark Sealy (Essay); Pauline Vermare (Essay)
description:
Flashpoint! surveys how photography has printed protest, not just photographed it, from mimeographed strike handbills to museum-shelf photobooks, treating cheap, hand-distributed print as seriously as fine bindings.

Russet Lederman and Olga Yatskevich edited the book. 10x10 Photobooks published it in November 2024 as a 576-page anthology. It gathers 760 images from photobooks, zines, posters, pamphlets, independent journals, and alternative newspapers documenting protest and resistance from 1950 to the present, drawn from more than twenty countries. Seven chapters organize the material: Anti, Gender, Displacement, Race and Class, Environment, Political, and War and Violence. The book moves between canonical photobooks and ephemeral material like strike posters and underground newspapers. Its argument is that photobooks belong back among the everyday objects of protest they were often made to be, not treated only as precious objects. Essays come from Makeda Best, Hannah Darabi, Arthur Fournier, Marc Feustel, Kerry Manders, Elisa Medde, Mark Sealy, and Pauline Vermare.

It is the sixth thematic anthology from 10x10 Photobooks, a nonprofit founded in 2012 to build public engagement with photobooks. Earlier surveys covered Latin American, African, Japanese, Chinese, and Middle Eastern photobook traditions.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Protest, Photojournalism, Zines, Anthology
notes: No single author; catalogued with both editors as primary authors per the book's own credit. Subjects (LOC): Protest movements -- Pictorial works; Photojournalism -- History; Photobooks -- History.

title: Robert Frank: Books and Films, 1947-2019
contributors: Robert Enright (Essay); Meeka Walsh (Essay); Fritz Gottler (Essay); John Farrel (Essay); Monte Packham (Essay)
description:
Robert Frank: Books and Films, 1947-2019 is Steidl's own account of a publishing partnership that ran for three decades and reshaped how Frank's work reached readers.

Gerhard Steidl edited the book, published in 2020 as a 120-page hardcover. It walks through more than thirty books Frank published with Steidl, reproducing spreads alongside explanatory texts, interviews, and documentary photographs of Frank at the print works in Gottingen. The relationship began in 1989, when publisher Walter Keller asked Steidl to print The Lines of My Hand for his Scalo imprint. After Scalo closed in 2004, Steidl began publishing Frank directly. That work eventually covered reprints of early books, previously unseen projects, newly conceived volumes, and a complete DVD collection of Frank's films.

Frank worked with Steidl on that footing until his death in 2019. He treated the printing process, and his habit of personally signing off every printed sheet, as part of the work rather than production overhead. Steidl offers this volume as the place to start when approaching the full range of Frank's photobooks.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Bibliography, Publishing History, American Photography
notes: A distinct, differently formatted publication also exists under a near-identical title, 'Robert Frank: Books and Films, 1947-2016,' an unconventional newsprint-format catalogue (64pp) published as a special edition of the Sueddeutsche Zeitung newspaper for a separate exhibition; it is not the book described in this record. This record covers the 2020 Steidl hardcover overview, ISBN 9783958293069, which several dealers list under the title 'Robert Frank: Books and Films, 1947-2019' and others as '...Published by Steidl'; Steidl's own product page omits the date range from the title. title: Looking In: Robert Frank's The Americans
edition_printrun: Expanded edition; first edition Feb 2009, third edition July 2015
contributors: Jeff L. Rosenheim (Essay); Anne Wilkes Tucker (Essay); Stuart Alexander (Essay); Martin Gasser (Essay); Michel Frizot (Essay); Luc Sante (Essay); Philip Brookman (Essay)
description:
Looking In: Robert Frank's The Americans is the catalogue built for the exhibition marking the fiftieth anniversary of The Americans, and it is as much about how Frank made the book as about the pictures themselves.

Sarah Greenough, senior curator of photographs at the National Gallery of Art, edited the book. The National Gallery of Art and Steidl published it in 2009 as a 528-page expanded hardcover. It reproduces the original eighty-three photographs from The Americans alongside contact sheets, work prints, and correspondence from Frank's 1955-56 Guggenheim-funded road trip. Together they trace how he selected and sequenced the book from thousands of exposures. Essays by Greenough, Jeff L. Rosenheim, Anne Wilkes Tucker, Stuart Alexander, Martin Gasser, Michel Frizot, Luc Sante, and Philip Brookman examine Frank's early career as a magazine photographer. They also cover his relationships with Walker Evans and Edward Steichen, and the roots of the book in earlier European and American photobooks. The accompanying exhibition traveled from the National Gallery of Art to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2009 and 2010.

The Americans was first published in France in 1958 and in the United States in 1959. It remains one of the most influential photobooks of the twentieth century. Looking In won the Association of Art Museum Curators' award for Outstanding Museum Catalogue and the International Center of Photography's Infinity Award for Publications.
tags: Photography, Documentary Photography, Photobook, American Photography, Exhibition Catalog
notes: Robert Frank is listed as primary author/photographer since the book's content is his photographic work, with Sarah Greenough credited as editor; a softcover first edition (396pp, ISBN differs) also exists, but this record describes the 528-page expanded hardcover, which is the more widely held library edition per WorldCat/library catalog data. title: Drone Vision: Warfare, Surveillance, Protest
contributors: Ignacio Acosta (Artist / Text); Behjat Omer Abdulla (Artist); Mhairi Sutherland (Artist / Text); Wajahat Saeed (Text); Ran Slavin (Text); Daniel Jewesbury (Text); Stelios Kallinikou (Text); Sajid Khan (Text); Salman Khan (Text); Efi Savvides (Text); Vicky Pericleous (Text); Kathrin Maurer (Text); Yiannis Toumazis (Text); Ellada Evangelou (Text); Imran Qureshi (Text); Sehr Jalil (Text); Markus Miessen (Text)
description:
Drone Vision: Warfare, Surveillance, Protest gathers artists, curators, and scholars around one premise. The drone's eye has reorganized who gets to see and who is seen. That asymmetry now runs through war, protest, and daily life alike.

The book is the outcome of a two-year research project led by HDK-Valand, University of Gothenburg, with the Hasselblad Foundation. It is built around a triptych of exhibitions staged in Gothenburg, Nicosia, and Lahore. Commissioned artists Ignacio Acosta, Behjat Omer Abdulla, and Mhairi Sutherland respond to drone use in specific settings. Among them: Sami resistance to mining exploration in northern Sweden, and aerial bombing recounted by a Syrian refugee. Across 352 pages, essays and artist projects trace how verticality and visibility play out differently in Sweden, Cyprus, and Pakistan.

Sarah Tuck, a curator and researcher at Valand Academy, directed the research project. She co-edited the volume with Louise Wolthers of the Hasselblad Foundation. Contributors include Kathrin Maurer, Imran Qureshi, Wajahat Saeed, Daniel Jewesbury, and Markus Miessen, with design by Karl Stefan Andersson.

No OCLC/LOC record was located in the sources checked. Cover image sourced from the publisher's own product page. title: Leon of Juda
description:
The seventh in Robert Frank's private, book-length visual diaries, pairing images from across his career with the photographs he was still making in his eighties.

Leon of Juda interleaves still lifes shot inside Frank's Bleecker Street apartment in New York and landscapes around his house in Mabou, Nova Scotia. Informal portraits of friends and collaborators, his wife June Leaf, and found vintage postcards run alongside them. There is no caption or narrative thread; Frank's loose, non-chronological sequencing gives the fifty-two page book the texture of a personal scrapbook rather than a survey. Steidl published it in October 2017 as a softcover volume housed in a slipcase, continuing the diaristic, hand-assembled form Frank had been developing with the press since the early 2000s.

Frank (1924-2019) was the Swiss-born photographer whose The Americans reshaped postwar documentary photography. He spent his final decades working almost entirely in this album format, treating the book itself as the site of the work rather than a record of it. Leon of Juda sits alongside other late Steidl diaries such as Household Inventory Record and Tal Uf, Tal Ab. The same domestic and Nova Scotia material recurs across them, reworked and re-sequenced from one volume to the next.
notes: Subjects (LOC): Frank, Robert, 1924-2019 -- Photograph collections; Photography, Artistic.

title: Gas Stop
binding: Four hardcover volumes in slipcase (boxed set)
description:
A four-volume boxed set gathering David Freund's survey of the American gas station, photographed between 1978 and 1981 across more than forty states.

Freund drove the country with a handheld 35mm camera, photographing customers and attendants going about the ordinary business of gassing up. Alongside them he recorded the corporate and vernacular signage, pump architecture, and regional landscaping that framed each stop. The 574 black-and-white images, selected from roughly two thousand negatives, are divided across four separately bound hardcover volumes titled Midwest, West, East, and South. They are housed together in a single slipcase and total more than 700 pages, and each volume closes with a short essay by Freund. Steidl published the set in 2017; Freund describes the gas station of that era as "a nation-sized fountain from which gasoline flowed to all on equal terms," a democratic roadside commons largely erased by the self-service convenience store.

Freund worked within the social-landscape tradition associated with photographers like Stephen Shore and Lewis Baltz, but brought to it a large-format clarity of composition despite shooting handheld: horizontal bands of land and sky, the geometry of pumps and canopies, and a careful eye for incidental human detail. Gas Stop is his major photobook and the fullest public presentation of this body of work. It sat largely unpublished for over three decades before Steidl's Gerhard Steidl agreed to produce it.
notes: Catalogued as a single boxed set (one ISBN, one Steidl product) comprising four separately bound volumes: Midwest, West, East, and South. Subjects (LOC): Gas stations -- United States -- Pictorial works; Photography, Artistic; Automobiles -- Social aspects -- United States.

title: Hotel Oracle
description:
A visual meditation on the cosmos, superstition, and the sacred, threading photographs made across twelve countries into a loose meditation on belief.

Hotel Oracle opens on the line "My neighbor June believes in Zeus" and proceeds from there as a sequence of pictures searching out the prophetic and the numinous inside ordinary, even banal, settings. A 99-cent store, in this method, stands as plausibly for the cosmos as any temple. The photographs, edited by Lorenzo de Rita, were made in the United States, Canada, Italy, Greece, the Czech Republic, Poland, South Korea, Japan, Hungary, India, Bermuda, and Germany. They are sequenced without captions so that coincidence and pattern do the work of narrative. The Soon Institute published the 144-page hardcover in 2013 in an edition of 1,000 copies.

Fulford, a photographer and co-founder of the press J&L Books, built his reputation on this kind of open-ended, associative sequencing rather than single iconic images. Hotel Oracle followed earlier books including Sunbird, Crushed, Raising Frogs for $$$, and The Mushroom Collector, and preceded his later MACK title The Heart Is a Sandwich, which extends the same method into prose-inflected short stories.
notes: Subjects (LOC): Photography, Artistic; Religion and photography; Signs and symbols -- Pictorial works.

title: The Heart Is a Sandwich
description:
A novel-sized paperback of twelve short, photograph-driven stories drawn from a decade of Jason Fulford's encounters in Italy.

Designed to look and feel like an ordinary paperback novel, complete with title page, dedication, and colophon in their expected places, the book gathers loosely linked episodes: a meeting with a ball-breaking baker, an exploding museum cellar, Aldo Rossi's notes on happiness, a visit to Guido Guidi's garage, and a trip to the geographic center of the Earth. Photographs and short prose passages are cut together with Fulford's characteristic editorial rhythm, where a picture's meaning shifts depending on what sits beside it. MACK published the 320-page book in April 2023 as an embossed softcover with flaps.

Fulford is known as much for his editing and sequencing as for his own photographs; he co-founded the independent press J&L Books and co-edited The Photographer's Playbook, a widely used collection of assignments from working photographers. His other titles include Raising Frogs for $$$ and Hotel Oracle, both built, like this one, around oblique narrative and visual pun rather than straightforward documentary sequence.
notes: Subjects (LOC): Fulford, Jason -- Travel -- Italy; Photography, Artistic; Italy -- Pictorial works.

title: Rivages
description:
Lara Gasparotto's first monograph, gathering years of unposed photographs of her friends as they grew up together in Belgium.

Gasparotto began photographing her circle of friends as a teenager and kept at it into her twenties, building a body of pictures shot on the fly rather than staged: swimming holes, bedrooms, cigarettes, bruises, skin, and the ordinary drift of adolescence into early adulthood. Rivages (French for "shores") sequences these images without captions or chronology, favoring chance and intimacy over a polished or curated narrative arc. Lannoo published the 140-page hardcover in 2014, designed in close collaboration with the photographer, bilingual in Dutch and English.

Gasparotto (b. 1989) studied photography at the School of Photography of Saint-Luc in Liège and has since exhibited in Berlin, Paris, Brussels, Antwerp, Arles, and Beijing, and is represented by Stieglitz19 gallery in Antwerp. Rivages established the loose, diaristic documentary style — young bodies, found intimacy, muted color and grain — that has carried through her later editorial and gallery work.
notes: Subjects (LOC): Photography, Artistic; Youth -- Belgium -- Pictorial works; Portrait photography.

title: Sex-Theater
description:
André Gelpke's 1970s documentary series on the performers of Hamburg's St. Pauli sex theaters, reissued in an expanded edition with new texts.

Working inside Hamburg's Reeperbahn sex clubs over several years, Gelpke photographed the performers between and during acts. He treated them less as spectacle than as individuals negotiating a public trade in private fantasy. As he put it, his fascination came "from the personality of the individual, from the performer who was prepared to realize in public the secret sexual fantasies of an inhibited society, simply in exchange for a fee." The series first appeared as a book in 1981 and sold out quickly. This 2015 edition, co-published by Spector Books and cpress, expands the original selection to 170 black-and-white duotone plates over 216 pages. New contextual essays accompany the plates. They frame a milieu, and its subsequent decline, that has since largely disappeared.

Gelpke (b. 1947) studied under Otto Steinert at the Folkwang School in Essen. He co-founded the Visum photo agency before turning to independent artistic work in the late 1970s. He became, alongside Heinrich Riebesehl and Michael Schmidt, one of the central figures of West German art photography of the period. From 1990 to 2012 he headed the photography program at Zurich University of the Arts. His work has been shown at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam, the Museum Folkwang, and the Centre Pompidou. Sex-Theater remains one of his most widely referenced bodies of work.
notes: Cover image contains full nudity (the book's real trade-edition front cover, showing a performer from the series); flagging for the human reviewer before publishing to the site, per usual editorial review of adult subject matter. Subjects (LOC): Erotic photography; Sex-oriented businesses -- Germany -- Hamburg -- Pictorial works; Photography, Artistic.

title: Nude
description:
A career-spanning survey of Ralph Gibson's nude photography, collecting his best-known images of the female form alongside more recent work.

Gibson's nudes work through tight cropping, hard-edged black-and-white contrast, and a fragmentary framing of the body that turns skin, shadow, and gesture into near-abstraction. The approach is in dialogue with the history of the nude in painting and sculpture as much as with photography's own erotic tradition. TASCHEN's volume gathers this body of work across five decades into a single 352-page hardcover, printed in tritone. It includes a newly commissioned interview between Gibson and painter Eric Fischl on the nude as a subject each has returned to throughout his career. The book was first issued in a limited collector's edition in 2009 before this expanded, trade edition followed.

Gibson (b. 1939) apprenticed with Dorothea Lange and worked as an assistant to Robert Frank. In 1970 he published The Somnambulist, a book that helped define the modern photobook as an authored, sequenced object rather than a portfolio. His prolific output since, including the geometric, high-contrast black-and-white work collected in One Picture Book and, more recently, Unfiltered, has made him one of the most widely exhibited American photographers of his generation. Nude sits alongside that body of work as his sustained study of a single subject.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Nude, Black and White
notes: Library already holds two other Ralph Gibson titles (One Picture Book, Unfiltered/Bakshi); confirmed via research that Nude is a distinct TASCHEN title with its own ISBN and content, not a duplicate or reissue of either. Subjects (LOC): Nude photography; Photography, Artistic; Gibson, Ralph, 1939-.

title: This Will Not End Well
contributors: Vince Aletti (Text); Thomas Beard (Text); Guido Costa (Text); Marvin Heiferman (Text); Roni Horn (Text); Patrick Radden Keefe (Text); Caitlín R. Kiernan (Text); Gabor Maté (Text); Eileen Myles (Text); Cookie Mueller (Text); Alfred Pacquement (Text); Darryl Pinckney (Text); Rene Ricard (Text); Lucy Sante (Text); Sarah Schulman (Text); Anne Swärd (Text); Hala Wardé (Text and drawings); David Wojnarowicz (Text); Andrea Lissoni (Interview)
description:
The first comprehensive book on Nan Goldin's filmmaking practice, reconstructing nearly a dozen of her slideshows and moving-image works on the page.

Moderna Museet, Stockholm organized the retrospective the book was published to accompany. It translates works assembled from thousands of photographs, film sequences, audio tapes, and music tracks into a sequence of 374 images printed on black backgrounds. It follows the pacing of the original slideshow and film installations rather than reformatting them as a conventional photo survey. The material spans the full arc of Goldin's practice: the bohemian and queer communities of her early Ballad of Sexual Dependency years, family trauma, the AIDS crisis, and, in later work, her own addiction and recovery. Twenty newly commissioned texts accompany the images. Contributors include critics, novelists, poets, and collaborators such as Eileen Myles, Lucy Sante, Sarah Schulman, Vince Aletti, and Patrick Radden Keefe, alongside earlier writing by David Wojnarowicz and Cookie Mueller. Steidl and Moderna Museet co-published the 216-page clothbound hardcover in 2022; it has since gone through further printings.

Goldin (b. 1953) is among the most influential photographers of her generation, known for a diaristic, unguarded style that first reached wide audiences through The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1986). She has continued through decades of slideshow and film work exploring intimacy, loss, and dependency. This Will Not End Well is the fullest account yet published of that moving-image practice, which has often been overshadowed by her still photography.
notes: Subjects (LOC): Goldin, Nan, 1953- -- Exhibitions; Slide shows -- Exhibitions; Video art -- Exhibitions; Photography, Artistic.

title: Nan Goldin: I'll Be Your Mirror
editor: Nan Goldin, David Armstrong, Hans Werner Holzwarth
contributors: Elisabeth Sussman (Curator, Essay); Luc Sante (Essay); Marvin Heiferman (Essay); David Wojnarowicz (Contribution); J. Hoberman (Interview); James Fenton (Essay); Darryl Pinckney (Essay); Joachim Sartorius (Essay); Cookie Mueller (Contribution); Walter Keller (Interview)
description:
Nan Goldin: I'll Be Your Mirror accompanied the photographer's 1996 mid-career retrospective at the Whitney Museum of American Art. It was the first museum survey to present two decades of her work as a continuous visual diary.

The book gathers photographs from Goldin's years in Boston in the 1970s through her move to downtown New York. It includes images from The Ballad of Sexual Dependency, self-portraits made during and after an abusive relationship, portraits of the transvestite and transgender friends who appear in The Other Side, and pictures documenting the toll of AIDS on her circle, among them the death of Cookie Mueller. Elisabeth Sussman curated the exhibition with David Armstrong. The 491-page volume reproduces hundreds of images with essays and interviews by Luc Sante, Marvin Heiferman, David Wojnarowicz, and J. Hoberman, and was co-published by the Whitney Museum and Scalo, Zürich.

Goldin (b. 1953) began photographing friends and lovers in Boston's queer subculture before moving to New York's Bowery in the late 1970s. Her style is unposed and confessional, treating the camera as a form of memory. I'll Be Your Mirror followed The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1986) as the fullest institutional account of her practice. Its title, taken from the Velvet Underground song, has stayed attached to the intimate portraiture running through her later books and exhibitions.
tags: Photography, Portrait Photography, Exhibition Catalog, Documentary Photography, LGBTQ, AIDS
notes: Multiple editions exist under different ISBNs: this record uses the Scalo (Zürich/Berlin/New York) hardcover, ISBN 9783931141332, October 1996 — the edition matching the requested publisher/year. A co-issued Whitney Museum of American Art edition (ISBN 9780874271027, March 1997) carries the same content and pagination and holds the LC/OCLC record used here for loc_data, since no separate LOC record was found under the Scalo ISBN. Cover sourced from OpenLibrary (348x475px); no higher-resolution front-cover scan was found within the research budget. title: Avec le Coeur
edition_printrun: 2nd edition, 2014 (1st edition 2013, numbered edition of 460 copies)
description:
Avec le Coeur collects Théo Gosselin's photographs of a 2012 road trip from Harlem to Venice Beach, taken when he was in his early twenties and still a student at Amiens' Arts Déco.

Gosselin funded and navigated the trip largely through social media. He posted images as he traveled and relied on followers for places to stay and eat along the way. The 96-page book gathers the color photographs that resulted: mostly informal portraits of the friends and strangers he met en route, with almost no accompanying text. Éditions du LIC first published it in 2013, in a numbered edition of 460 copies that sold out quickly, then reissued it in 2014 as a second edition of 1,000 copies with 75 color plates in a hot-foil-embossed hardcover.

Gosselin, born in Normandy in 1990, has named Ryan McGinley and Nan Goldin as reference points for this early work. His subjects, though, are his own friends rather than models or constructed scenes. Avec le Coeur established him as a photographer working in that lineage of loose, socially embedded portraiture. He has since published Sans Limites, also with Éditions du LIC, and Roll with Fisheye Éditions.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Color Photography, Contemporary Photography
notes: Publisher name given in the brief ('Éditions du Lic') is correct; verified proper capitalization is 'Éditions du LIC' via the publisher's own site (editionsdulic.com). This record documents the 2nd edition (2014, ISBN 9788293341055, 1,000 copies); the original 2013 first edition (460 numbered copies) predates ISBN assignment on most retailer listings and is noted here rather than catalogued separately.

title: Neü Sex
description:
Neü Sex (2010) is a photography monograph by the actor and adult-film performer Sasha Grey, published by Vice and distributed by powerHouse Books.

The book gathers around 150 color photographs taken during Grey's work in the adult film industry. Most were shot by Grey herself, with additional images by the photographer Ian P. Cinnamon. Grey has described the project as self-documentation rather than a professional portfolio: a way of recording film sets and the private moments around them on her own terms. She has cited Cindy Sherman and Nan Goldin as reference points for that kind of image-making. The hardcover volume runs 192 pages at 6.7 x 9 inches.

Grey was born in 1988 in Sacramento, California. She worked in adult film from 2006, then moved into mainstream acting, including a lead role in Steven Soderbergh's The Girlfriend Experience (2009). She has since worked as a musician, DJ, and novelist, writing The Juliette Society trilogy. Neü Sex is her only photography book. It stands apart from that later work as a record made from inside the industry she was documenting, not about it from the outside.
notes: US edition (Vice, distributed by powerHouse Books, ISBN 9781576875568) is the record described here. A separate UK edition was issued by Vice Books, London, under ISBN 9780955801532; treated as an alternate edition, not a duplicate. Publisher category tags: Celebrity / Erotica / Verite. Page count: publisher's own product page (via Wayback Machine, archived 2014-12-30) gives 192 pages; OpenLibrary's MARC-derived record gives 191 p. — 192 used as the publisher-stated figure. Subjects (LOC): Actresses; Photography of women; Erotic photography; Portraits; Photography of the nude.

title: Color Correction
description:
Color Correction gathers color photography Ernst Haas made but never printed or exhibited in his lifetime. It stands apart from the images that built his reputation as the pioneering color photojournalist of the 1950s.

Edited by William A. Ewing, with additional text by Phillip Prodger, the book collects 163 color images shot between 1952 and 1986. Most are street and studio work Haas set aside rather than published; they were found in his archive and appear here for the first time. Steidl's cloth-bound edition was designed by Thomas Lenthal and Mathieu Perroud. Ewing's title answers the reception Haas got in his lifetime: magazines prized his color work for its vibrancy, but curators later dismissed it as too accessible next to the cooler, more conceptual color of William Eggleston, Stephen Shore, and Joel Meyerowitz.

Haas (1921-1986) joined Magnum Photos in 1949. Through Life and Look assignments, and the bestselling 1971 book The Creation, he became one of the most widely published photographers of the twentieth century. He received the Hasselblad Award in 1986, the year he died. Color Correction, published 25 years later, opens the private side of an archive long read only through its public commissions.
tags: Photography, Color Photography, Photojournalism, Magnum Photos, Photobook
notes: Steidl's product page lists this as the 1st edition (June 2011); a 2nd edition was released September 2016 (also cited under ISBN 9783958291546 in some listings) — this record uses the 1st-edition ISBN (9783958290563) confirmed directly on steidl.de. Currently listed out of print by the publisher.

title: You an Orchestra You a Bomb
description:
You an Orchestra You a Bomb is Cig Harvey's third monograph. She made these color photographs after a personal accident left her newly alert to how briefly anything lasts.

Schilt Publishing released the book in 2017. It pairs Harvey's large-format color images, domestic interiors, flowers, self-portraits, scenes from her rural life in Maine, with her own short poems and prose. The pictures work in the register Harvey has built across her career. She applies heightened, saturated color to ordinary rooms and objects until they read as charged or momentarily strange, drawing on a private set of subjects she returns to rather than a documentary world outside herself.

Harvey is a British-born photographer based in Maine. This book followed the widely noticed You Look at Me Like an Emergency (2012) and Gardening at Night (2015), continuing her long-running project on attention, domestic life, and sensory experience. Later titles, including Blue Violet and Emerald Drifters, extend the same project into further color studies.
tags: Photography, Color Photography, Photobook, Contemporary Photography
notes: Page count and dimensions were not published on the sources checked (Schilt, Setanta Books, ARTBOOK 404'd); left null rather than estimated. Publisher confirms 2017 release and 'third monograph' status.

title: Irene
edition_printrun: 2nd edition, 2021 (1st edition 2011; originally published as Liebes Leben, 1978)
description:
Irene is Roswitha Hecke's portrait of a Zurich sex worker known as Lady Shiva, made over three weeks in the late 1970s and first published in 1978 as Liebes Leben.

Hecke met Irene through the director Werner Schroeter and photographed her daily routine in Zurich before accompanying her to Rome, where Irene celebrated her birthday each year. The resulting black-and-white images, a mix of staged and documentary frames, follow Irene through apartments, streets, and hotel rooms with a directness that made the original book both a cult object and, on reissue, an international success.
