This Edition Patrick Frey edition, first released in 2011 and revised again in 2021, reprints 107 images including a number never published in the earlier editions, alongside texts by Hecke, Irene, and Baudelaire.

Hecke (b. 1944) trained as a photographer before working as the house photographer for the theater director Peter Zadek. Her other books include Menschen-Orte-Fäuste, made while traveling the United States with the writer Wolf Wondratschek, and Pigalle, on the transvestite scene in Paris. Irene remains her best known work, republished repeatedly since 1978 for a portrait that treats its subject with unusual directness for its time.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Portraiture, Zurich, Black and White Photography
notes: Subject matter (sex work) handled in strictly documentary/curatorial terms per publisher and reviewer sources; no valuation or sensational language included. Publisher page lists a 2nd edition (2021); the record uses that year and the shared ISBN 9783905509960 that AbeBooks/AbeBooks-linked retailers list across editions.

title: Czech and Slovak Photo Publications 1918-1989
contributors: Vojtech Lahoda (Text); Amanda Maddox (Text); Petr Roubal (Text); James Steerman (Text); Thomas Wiegand (Text)
description:
Czech and Slovak Photo Publications 1918-1989 is a reference survey of the photobooks and printed photography that came out of Czechoslovakia across seven decades of independence, occupation, and Communist rule.

Compiled by the photobook historian Manfred Heiting to mark the hundredth anniversary of the Czechoslovak Republic's founding in 1918, the book surveys more than 800 publications across nine chapters, with contributions from Vojtech Lahoda, Amanda Maddox, Petr Roubal, James Steerman, and Thomas Wiegand. It covers the work of over 250 photographers and graphic artists, from the interwar avant-garde of Jaroslav Rössler, Jindrich Štyrský, and Karel Teige through Josef Sudek, František Drtikol, and Josef Koudelka, tracing how book design and photographic publishing carried the country's visual culture through Nazi annexation and forty years of Communist control. The 516-page hardback reproduces more than 2,800 images from the books themselves.

Heiting is a photobook collector and historian whose Steidl series, Collection Manfred Heiting, has produced comparable national surveys of the photobook in other countries. This volume extends that project to a region whose publishing history, shaped as much by censorship as by design innovation, is otherwise thinly documented outside specialist collections.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Czechoslovakia, Book History, Reference
notes: Given task title used the date range '1918-1989' as supplied; this was verified as correct against steidl.de and multiple independent sources (Brooklyn Rail, PhotoBite, Amazon, ARTBOOK) — no discrepancy found. Classification set to Photobook since this is an editorial survey of photobooks/publications rather than a single photographer's monograph.

title: Beaton: Photographs
description:
Beaton: Photographs surveys six decades of work by Cecil Beaton (1904-1980). The English photographer's portraits and stage-managed tableaux shaped the visual language of British society, fashion and celebrity from the 1920s through the 1970s.

Edited by Mark Holborn, with an introductory appreciation by Annie Leibovitz, the book draws together Beaton's portraits of figures including Pablo Picasso, Gertrude Stein, Greta Garbo, Audrey Hepburn, Lucian Freud, Francis Bacon, David Hockney and Mick Jagger. It sets these alongside his coverage of royal ceremonies, his wartime photography for the British Ministry of Information, Hollywood glamour portraiture and the pop culture of 1960s London. Abrams published this US edition in 2015, following Jonathan Cape's UK edition of the same material; both draw on the Cecil Beaton Studio Archive.

Beaton worked simultaneously as a society and fashion photographer for Vogue and Vanity Fair, an official war photographer, and a stage and costume designer for theatre and film. He won Academy Awards for his costume and set design on Gigi and My Fair Lady. Holborn, a longtime editor of photography books, also edited Beaton's Theatre of War for Jonathan Cape and the Imperial War Museums, drawing on the same archive of Beaton's wartime negatives.
notes: Cecil Beaton is credited as authors[0]/Photographer for cataloguing purposes since the book is a monograph of his photographs; Mark Holborn (editor) and Annie Leibovitz (introduction) are listed as contributors per the actual title-page credit on the Abrams/Jonathan Cape editions. Two closely related editions exist: this Abrams US edition (9781419717833, 2015) and an earlier/parallel Jonathan Cape UK edition (9780224101806) with the same editorial credits; the task specified Abrams, so that edition is used here. Page count (354) and dimensions are from dealer listings, not the publisher's own product page (Abrams product page was not directly fetched); treat as approximate. Subjects (LOC): Beaton, Cecil, 1904-1980; Photography, Artistic; Portrait photography -- Great Britain.

title: Jungle Check
description:
Jungle Check is a collaborative project between Cristina de Middel and Kalev Erickson, published by RM in 2018. It turns a critical eye on the studio-backdrop and postcard conventions long used to picture the tropics in vernacular and commercial photography.

The two photographers work with the recurring device of the painted or printed jungle backdrop, a stock prop of colonial-era and mid-century studio portraiture. They trace how a generic image of dense foliage came to stand in for entire regions and peoples in the popular imagination. The 120-page softcover, with an accompanying text by photo-historian Luce Lebart, sets new photographs alongside appropriated studio and postcard imagery to expose the artifice behind the genre.

De Middel, a Spanish photographer best known for The Afronauts (2012), works consistently at the boundary between documentary and fiction, using staged and appropriated imagery to question photography's authority as evidence. Erickson's practice similarly moves between found and constructed images. Jungle Check extends both photographers' shared interest in the visual tropes that photography inherits and repeats without questioning.
notes: Cover image URL is a best-effort publisher-CDN guess reconstructed from RM's site structure and was NOT independently confirmed to return 200 at write time (RM's own product page for this title returned inconsistent results during research); the locally saved file jungle_check.jpg was downloaded and visually verified as a genuine flat front cover before this record was written, so the artifact itself is confirmed even though this specific URL string may not resolve — treat cover_image.url as approximate provenance, not a guaranteed live link. Project description drawn from RM/dealer publisher-blurb framing of the book's theme (studio jungle-backdrop convention); no direct access to a full page-by-page description, so classify confidence as medium.

title: In the Studio: Paintings/Photographs
description:
In the Studio: Paintings/Photographs is a two-volume exhibition catalogue examining how painters and photographers have depicted the artist's own workplace, from the sixteenth century to the late twentieth.

The Paintings volume, with an essay and catalogue entries by John Elderfield, brings together more than fifty paintings and works on paper by nearly forty artists spanning four centuries. The companion Photographs volume, organized by Peter Galassi, traces photography's own engagement with the studio as subject. Gagosian published the slipcased two-volume set with Phaidon in 2015 to accompany simultaneous exhibitions, one of paintings and one of photographs, held at Gagosian's New York galleries from February 17 to April 18, 2015. The set was designed by Goto Design and printed by Shapco Printing.

Elderfield is Chief Curator Emeritus of Painting and Sculpture at the Museum of Modern Art, where he organized retrospectives of Henri Matisse and Willem de Kooning among others. Galassi spent three decades at MoMA, twenty of them as Chief Curator of Photography, mounting exhibitions on Henri Cartier-Bresson, Walker Evans, Lee Friedlander and Andreas Gursky. Their pairing of volumes treats the studio not as a single tradition but as a subject each medium has returned to on its own terms.
tags: Photography, Painting, Exhibition Catalog, Art History
notes: Group/thematic exhibition catalogue with no single artist subject; authors[0]/[1] are the two curator-editors (Elderfield for the Paintings volume, Galassi for Photographs), which is how the title page and distributor listings credit the set. Classified as Photobook rather than Artist Book/Monograph since it is a multi-artist survey rather than one artist's own project or career; flagging this as a judgment call. Pages reflects combined total of the two volumes (180 + 188 per one bibliographic source); other listings round to ~368. Subjects (LOC): Artists' studios in art -- Exhibitions; Painting -- Exhibitions; Photography, Artistic -- Exhibitions.

title: Noki
description:
Noki gathers more than a decade of photographic collaboration between Axel Hoedt and JJ Hudson, the London-based designer and performance artist who works under the name Noki. The project is built almost entirely around the improvised masks Hudson wears in place of a face.

Hudson constructs each mask from textile collage and salvaged garment fragments, working against the uniformity of mass-produced fashion and corporate branding. Hoedt photographs the results as portraits, treating the masks as studies in otherness, refusal, belonging and isolation rather than as costume. Art Paper Editions published the 52-page softcover in 2018 in an edition of 1,000 copies.

Hoedt was born in Freiburg in 1966 and has been based in London since 1999. His portraiture and documentary work returns often to disguise, ritual and performed identity, including his earlier book on the masked carnival traditions of the Alps, Once a Year (Dewi Lewis, 2011). Noki extends that interest in the mask as a social and psychological device from folk custom into the language of contemporary fashion and subculture.
notes: JJ Hudson (Noki) is the subject/collaborator whose masks are photographed, not a separate credited author on the title page; no contributor entry added since sources do not credit him as a book author.

title: The Light of Coincidence: The Photographs of Kenneth Josephson
description:
The Light of Coincidence is the first career-spanning monograph on Kenneth Josephson (b. 1932), one of the pioneers of conceptual photography in postwar America.

The book gathers work across Josephson's major series, including his best-known Images within Images photographs. It also includes his studies of chance, illusion and the photograph as a made object rather than a passive record. Text by Lynne Warren traces his development from his early studies under Aaron Siskind and Harry Callahan at Chicago's Institute of Design through his own long teaching career. A foreword by Gerry Badger situates the work within the wider history of conceptual photography. The University of Texas Press published the 344-page hardcover in 2016.

Josephson taught at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago from 1967 to 1997 and was a founding member of the Society for Photographic Education. Since the early 1960s, when documentary photography dominated institutional taste, he treated the photograph itself as subject matter. He built images that fold copies, mirrors and multiple exposures into the frame to question what a photograph actually shows. That body of work made him a formative influence on later generations of conceptually minded photographers.
notes: Page count taken from the University of Texas Press's own product page (344); a dealer listing separately gives 'x, 331 pp.' for the same edition — kept the publisher figure as primary and noted the discrepancy. Subjects (LOC): Josephson, Kenneth, 1932- -- Criticism and interpretation; Conceptual photography -- United States.

title: The Japanese Photobook, 1912-1990
description:
The Japanese Photobook, 1912-1990 is a 576-page survey of Japanese photographic book publishing, compiled from the Manfred Heiting Collection. Kaneko Ryuichi, one of the foremost historians of the Japanese photobook, edited it together with Heiting himself.

The book documents several hundred titles across nearly eight decades, from early twentieth-century amateur and Pictorialist annuals through wartime propaganda publications and postwar reconstruction-era photography. It closes with the radical are-bure-boke (grainy, blurred, out-of-focus) publications of Provoke-era photographers including Daido Moriyama and Nobuyoshi Araki. Steidl published this English-language edition in 2017, extending the pair's ongoing project of documenting Japan's photobook history for a Western readership.

Kaneko, formerly a curator at the Japan Foundation and Tokyo Metropolitan Museum of Photography, has been a central authority on Japanese photobook history since the 1990s. Heiting, a designer, photo-historian and collector, has built one of the most extensive private archives of Japanese and international photobooks and has co-edited numerous Steidl surveys drawing on that collection, including The Book of 101 Books.
notes: The publisher's own cover typography reads '1912/1980' in one small corner detail, but every catalogue record, dealer listing and Steidl's own title metadata give 1912-1990 as the correct span; treating the cover detail as a printing/design anomaly rather than the true date range. Direct steidl.de product page returned 404 for two guessed URL variants; bibliographic data assembled from AbeBooks/dealer listings and secondary sourcing instead. Dimensions not confirmed from any source and left null rather than guessed. Subjects (LOC): Photograph collections -- Japan -- Catalogs; Photography, Artistic -- Japan -- History.

title: Die Bücher
description:
Die Bücher ("The Books") is a single-subject photographic project by the German artist Annette Kelm. In it, books themselves, photographed straight-on against neutral grounds, become the sole subject of the series.

Kelm's project extends her long-running method of isolating everyday and printed objects, from textiles to flags to found ephemera. She photographs them with a deadpan, studio-lit directness that treats surface, cover design, typography and material wear as historical evidence. Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther König published the 148-page hardcover in German in 2022. It presents the book-as-object as both a formal still life and a document of design and printing history across the volumes she selects.

Kelm studied at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf and Städelschule Frankfurt. She has exhibited widely at institutions including the Kunsthalle Basel, the Institute of Contemporary Arts London and the Museum of Modern Art, New York. Her practice consistently treats photography's descriptive neutrality as a tool for close observation of the manufactured object. Die Bücher, focused entirely on books as things rather than texts, is a direct extension of that practice.
tags: Photography, Artist Book, Conceptual Art, Still Life
notes: Publisher's direct product page (buchhandlung-walther-koenig.de) returned 404 for the guessed product URL; bibliographic details assembled from dealer/secondary listings instead, so cover_image.url should be treated as unverified for live-200 status even though the locally saved file was downloaded and visually confirmed as the genuine front cover. Classified as Artist Book (parallel to the Fathi/Wolfgang precedent in the existing catalogue) since it is a single artist's own conceptual project rather than a career-survey monograph.

title: Lee Miller in Fashion
description:
Lee Miller in Fashion, by the historian Becky E. Conekin, traces Lee Miller's path through the fashion industry that shaped and was shaped by her: model, muse, and eventually photographer in her own right.

Miller began as a Condé Nast model in 1920s New York. She then moved to Paris, entered Man Ray's circle, and became a central figure of Surrealism both in front of the camera and behind it. Conekin follows her into her own fashion photography for Vogue, and through the years when that same eye turned to war reportage. The 224-page book draws on archival fashion photographs, contact sheets, studio memos, and Miller's own published illustrations, many reproduced here for the first time. It traces a career usually remembered for its war photography back to its roots in fashion and Surrealist image-making.

Lee Miller (1907–1977) worked across modeling, Surrealist photography, fashion photography, and war correspondence for British Vogue. She covered the liberation of Paris, the concentration camp at Dachau, and Hitler's abandoned Munich apartment. Conekin is a cultural historian who has also written on postwar British fashion and consumption. This book followed her 2006 essay collection on Miller and drew on the Lee Miller Archives, run by Miller's son Antony Penrose.
tags: Photography, Fashion Photography, Surrealism, 20th Century Photography, Biography
notes: Two co-published editions exist: Monacelli Press (US, ISBN 9781580933766) and Thames & Hudson (UK, ISBN 9780500516911). This record uses the Monacelli/US edition. Subjects (LOC): Miller, Lee, 1907-1977; Fashion photography -- History -- 20th century.

title: Life Here Is Serious
edition_printrun: Sketchbook Series no. 02, limited edition of 750 numbered copies
description:
Life Here Is Serious is a small numbered volume from Rob Hornstra and Arnold van Bruggen's Sochi Project, gathering Rob Hornstra's color portraits of boys and young men training as wrestlers in the North Caucasus.

The book collects 28 photographs across 48 pages, including one fold-out spread. It was issued as the second title in the project's self-published Sketchbook Series. That series released material from Hornstra and van Bruggen's long-term field research between larger publications. Wrestling runs deep in the region's culture. It is prized there as both sport and a route out of poverty. Hornstra photographs his subjects plainly, straight-on, against bare gymnasium walls. The marked and worn training clothes carry as much of the story as the faces do. The edition was limited to 750 numbered, hand-bound copies with blue cloth boards and a printed title bookplate.

Hornstra and van Bruggen worked together for years as the Sochi Project. They documented the North Caucasus and the Russian Black Sea coast in the run-up to the 2014 Winter Olympics. The project produced dispatches, sketchbooks, and the large-format Sochi Project: An Atlas of War and Tourism in the Caucasus. Hornstra is the photographer. Van Bruggen, a writer and filmmaker, provided the text and reporting.
tags: Photography, Documentary Photography, Russia, Color Photography, Portraiture
notes: No ISBN found across 8 dealer listings checked; this is a small self-published, numbered limited edition (750 copies) rather than a trade-distributed book, consistent with the absence of an ISBN. The dealer photograph used for the cover shows this specific copy numbered 494. One of the four listings found credits Hornstra alone; the other three credit both Hornstra and van Bruggen, which this record follows.

title: André Kertész
description:
André Kertész, published by Éditions Hazan with the Jeu de Paume in 2010, surveys the full seventy-year career of the Hungarian-born photographer widely credited as a founding figure of modernist photography.

Compiled by Michel Frizot and Annie-Laure Wanaverbecq to accompany the Jeu de Paume's 2010 retrospective, the book reproduces roughly 500 images, including 18 color Polaroids, drawn from rare vintage and period prints. The 360-page volume covers three periods of Kertész's working life: Budapest from 1914 to 1925, Paris from 1925 to 1936, and New York from 1936 to 1985. Each section pairs an illustrated historical essay with a portfolio of the work and notes on his approach to composition, cropping, and the handheld Leica.

Kertész (1894–1985) began photographing as a largely self-taught amateur in Hungary. He settled in Paris in 1925, moved among Mondrian, Chagall, and the emerging Surrealist circle, and produced the geometric studies and Distortions nudes that shaped a generation of European photographers, Brassaï among them. He emigrated to New York in 1936 and worked for years in commercial photojournalism. Recognition as a major artist came late: John Szarkowski's 1964 Museum of Modern Art retrospective revived interest in his early European work.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Exhibition Catalog, Modernism, 20th Century Photography
notes: Subjects (LOC): Kertész, André, 1894-1985 -- Exhibitions; Photography, Artistic -- 20th century -- Exhibitions.

author_full_name: Erik Kessels, Thomas Sauvin, Karel de Mulder
title: Incomplete Encyclopedia of Touch
description:
Incomplete Encyclopedia of Touch, published by RVB Books, is a visual taxonomy built from thousands of found family photographs. Its subject is one recurring gesture: a hand placed on something, to claim it, measure it, or simply pose beside it.

Assembled by Erik Kessels with Thomas Sauvin and Karel de Mulder from more than 15,000 vernacular albums, the book sorts roughly 1,919 anonymous snapshots into alphabetical entries named for the object touched. Airplanes and animals fall under A, fences and fireplaces under F, and gravestones sit alongside cars, trees, and other people. The 496-page paperback reads as a dictionary of an unspoken human habit. Its categories are deadpan and its images unposed. Every page raises the same question: are these people asserting ownership, seeking contact, or measuring themselves against the world around them?

Kessels is a Dutch artist and co-founder of the advertising agency KesselsKramer. For two decades he has built projects from vernacular and appropriated photography, including In Almost Every Picture and 24HRS in Photos. Sauvin is known for Beijing Silvermine, his archive of negatives recovered from a Beijing recycling plant, and de Mulder is a longtime collector of amateur photography. The book continues Kessels' recurring method of turning anonymous snapshots into encyclopedic structures.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Vernacular Photography, Found Photography, Appropriation Art
notes: The RVB Books product page currently lists a September 2025 second edition; the first edition is dated 2024 by other sources (OpenLibrary, PhMuseum review). Year set to 2024 for the first edition; flagged as unresolved.

title: Barricade
description:
Barricade, published by Harper's Books in 2012, brings together previously unpublished photographs Kazuo Kitai made inside the student barricades of 1968 Tokyo, at the height of Japan's protest movement.

John Gossage designed the book as the launch title of Harper's Books' publishing imprint. The 80-page hardcover pairs the Barricade pictures with scanned pages from Kitai's first book, Resistance (1965), which documented protests near the American naval base at Yokosuka. Kitai's own essay, translated by Hiroshi Masaki, describes an approach built against the era's photographic conventions: blurred, off-kilter frames shot from inside the crowd rather than composed from a safe distance. The book accompanied Kitai's first American exhibition, held at Harper's Books, East Hampton, from August 18 to October 1, 2012. It was issued in a first edition of 1,000 copies alongside a signed deluxe edition of 36.

Kitai (b. 1944) began photographing in 1965 at age twenty-two. His student protest work is often cited as a precursor to Provoke, the short-lived magazine and movement that overturned Japanese photography's conventions of clarity and distance. He went on to document rural depopulation and construction labor across Japan. That later work was gathered in retrospectives, including a 2014 survey at the Aichi Prefectural Museum of Art.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Protest, Japanese Photography, Provoke Era

title: Underworld
description:
Underworld, published by Alfred A. Knopf in 1995, is Kelly Klein's anthology of the body in underclothing. It draws 154 photographs from a century of picture-making, running from the 1880s to the 1990s.

Klein assembled work by more than eighty photographers into a single visual argument about intimacy and exposure. Jacques-Henri Lartigue, Imogen Cunningham, Louise Dahl-Wolfe, André Kertész, Brassaï, Man Ray, Richard Avedon, Helmut Newton, and Robert Mapplethorpe all appear alongside contemporary fashion and portrait photographers. Anne Rice contributes the introduction, framing the corset, slip, and undergarment as a threshold between the private body and the camera. Sam Shahid designed the large-format hardcover, and Klein directed all proceeds from the book to the CFDA Foundation Fund for AIDS.

Klein is a former fashion editor at Calvin Klein and Anne Klein who built a career editing large-format photography anthologies organized around a single object or subject. Underworld followed Pools (1992) and preceded Horses (2000) and Mane (2007), each assembling historical and contemporary photographers around one recurring theme rather than presenting a single photographer's body of work.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Fashion Photography, Anthology, Nude Photography
notes: Confirmed this is Kelly Klein (fashion editor, editor of Pools/Underworld/Horses/Mane), not William Klein, the street photographer already catalogued in this library. Different person, different publisher history, verified via AbeBooks, OpenLibrary, and LensCulture.

title: Vlastimil Kula
description:
Vlastimil Kula, published by Taschen, is a monograph of the Czech photographer's staged black-and-white images of the body, made in explicit opposition to what he called the boredom of pornography.

The 280-page hardcover collects Kula's shadowy, theatrical compositions built around sex, taboo, love, passion, and rebellion. Figures emerge from darkness in tight interiors, often doubled by mirrors or obscured by props. The effect favors mystery over explicitness, closer to staged tableau than documentary nude photography. Taschen has published several monographs on photographers working at the edges of erotic imagery, and Kula's sits near Jan Saudek's in that list; both are Czech, and both built staged, theatrical nudes out of the same postwar photographic culture.

Kula was born in Czechoslovakia in 1950 and studied art photography at the Prague Academy of Arts. He traveled to England, Canada, and the United States before the Soviet invasion of 1968 forced his return, and he has lived and worked in his hometown of Cheb since. His photography carries the imprint of that history. Picturing sexuality and the body openly was, for him, a form of resistance to a state that policed both.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Erotic Photography, Czech Photography
notes: Verified as a real, findable book before writing this record, per the task briefing's caution: Vlastimil Kula is confirmed via AbeBooks (multiple listings, ISBN 9783822822586) and OpenLibrary as a genuine Taschen monograph. Publication year is uncertain between a 2001 first edition (a related multilingual ISBN 9783822832264 is dated 2001) and a 2004 printing that OpenLibrary and one AbeBooks listing carry under the same ISBN 9783822822586; used 2001 and flagged the conflict.

title: Baldwin Lee
description:
Baldwin Lee, published by Hunters Point Press in 2022, is the first monograph of a body of work Lee made across the American South in the 1980s. It gathers 88 black-and-white photographs from that project.

Between 1983 and 1989, Lee drove through Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana on repeated trips from his teaching post in Tennessee, photographing Black families and neighbors in yards, homes, and streets. The project produced nearly 10,000 negatives, from which editor Barney Kulok selected the 88 images in this book. Jessica Bell Brown interviews Lee, and Casey Gerald contributes an essay. Together they frame the pictures within American documentary photography and within the specific circumstances, personal and racial, under which a Chinese American photographer came to make this work in the South.

Lee (b. 1951) studied under Walker Evans and Minor White at Yale before joining the faculty of the University of Tennessee, where he taught photography for over four decades. The work went largely unpublished and unexhibited for decades. This monograph has since brought gallery shows and renewed critical attention to it as a major, long-overlooked document of the South. This is a different photographer from H. Lee, whose Grassland (Kehrer Verlag) is also in this collection.
tags: Photography, Photobook, American South, Documentary Photography, Black and White Photography
notes: Confirmed this is Baldwin Lee (b. 1951, Chinese American photographer, Yale-trained, University of Tennessee faculty), photographer of the 1980s American South project published by Hunters Point Press. He is a different person from H. Lee, whose Grassland (Kehrer Verlag) is already in this library's catalogue. A second ISBN (9798218088484) also circulates under the Hunters Point Press imprint, listed by some dealers as "Baldwin Lee" and by one as "Southern Photographs"; it may be a later printing or repackaging with the same Kulok/Bell Brown/Gerald credits. This record uses the earlier, more widely cited ISBN 9780578315034 and flags the alternate edition as unresolved.

title: Emergence
description:
Emergence is a 1977 portrait book by the photographer Cynthia MacAdams, gathering women who defined American feminism, art, and culture in the decade after the women's movement took hold. Four decades later it became the visual source for the 2018 Netflix documentary Feminists: What Were They Thinking?

Chelsea House published the book with an introduction by Kate Millett. It collects more than 100 black-and-white portraits, many shot in natural or infrared light, of writers, artists, actors, and activists including Patti Smith, Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin, Judy Chicago, Meredith Monk, Alice Neel, Marisol, and Shelley Winters. MacAdams worked without studio lighting or elaborate sets. She photographed each sitter plainly and at close range, so the picture rests on the subject's own bearing rather than on staging.

MacAdams (b. 1939) came to photography from acting. She had appeared in Robert Frank's Me and My Brother and worked with Dennis Hopper before turning her camera on the women around her. Emergence remained her best-known project; she went on to photograph portraiture, the Bowery, and sacred architecture in black-and-white and infrared for decades afterward, working between Los Angeles and New York.
notes: Also issued the same year in a Dutton paperback edition (introduction by Kate Millett, no ISBN located); this record follows the Chelsea House hardcover per the research brief. No official artist website found; MacAdams's biographical record is thin outside press coverage tied to the 2018 documentary Feminists: What Were They Thinking?, which used the book's portraits.

title: Vivian Maier: A Photographer Found
description:
Vivian Maier: A Photographer Found is John Maloof's fuller 2014 account of the archive he discovered at a Chicago storage-locker auction. It expands well past the black-and-white Chicago-New York street pictures that made Maier's name in his first book.

The volume presents more than 235 photographs, most published here for the first time, including the initial substantial showing of Maier's color work from the 1970s onward alongside her earlier black-and-white negatives. Maloof writes as author, working with text by Marvin Heiferman and an edit by the dealer Howard Greenberg, whose gallery represents Maier's estate. A foreword comes from the novelist Laura Lippman. Reproductions of contact sheets, cameras, and personal effects recovered from Maier's boxes sit alongside the photographs, filling in more of the biography that her first book left largely implicit.

Maier (1926-2009) spent four decades working as a nanny in the Chicago area while photographing constantly and privately. Her archive of over 100,000 negatives only surfaced after her death. Hudson Street Library also holds Maier's Street Photographer (2011), Maloof's first book from the find, and Out of the Shadows (2012), Richard Cahan and Michael Williams's independent, interview-based account of her life.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Color Photography, Chicago, New York
notes: Second of three Maier titles in this batch — confirmed distinct from Street Photographer (2011, same editor, earlier and narrower book) and from Out of the Shadows (2012, different authors/publisher). Page count reported inconsistently across dealer listings (285-288); 288 used here as the most frequently cited figure.

title: Vivian Maier: Out of the Shadows
description:
Out of the Shadows is Richard Cahan and Michael Williams's 2012 book on Vivian Maier. It is built around more than 300 previously unseen duotone photographs and interviews with the families who employed her and the people who knew her, and it was the first attempt to set her photography inside a documented biography rather than the mystique of its discovery.

Where the Maloof-edited volumes work from inside the found archive itself, Cahan and Williams approached Maier as a subject for reporting. The two are Chicago writers and historians who published the book through their own CityFiles Press, tracking down former employers and their children, corroborating dates and addresses, and setting her photographs of Chicago's North Shore and downtown streets against an account of the life she led while making them. The book runs to nearly 300 pages, printed at roughly square 9.5-inch format to match the printing of the negatives themselves.

Maier (1926-2009) worked as a nanny in the Chicago area for four decades while photographing constantly and privately. Her archive of over 100,000 negatives surfaced only after her death, when John Maloof bought a storage locker at auction. Hudson Street Library also holds Maloof's own Street Photographer (2011) and A Photographer Found (2014), the two books drawn directly from his side of the archive.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Black-and-White Photography, Chicago, Biography
notes: Third of three Maier titles in this batch, confirmed distinct from the two Maloof-edited books: different authors (Cahan and Williams) and a different publisher (CityFiles Press). Page count reported as 287-289 across dealer listings; 288 used here.

title: Vivian Maier: Street Photographer
description:
Vivian Maier: Street Photographer is the 2011 book that introduced Vivian Maier to the public. Its duotone black-and-white pictures come from a Chicago nanny's secret archive of more than 100,000 negatives. John Maloof found the archive two years after her death; no one had known of it during her lifetime.

Maloof edited the book, and Geoff Dyer wrote the foreword. Between them they gathered over 100 images shot in Chicago and New York from the 1950s through the 1960s: children, storefronts, self-portraits caught in shop windows, strangers observed at close range. The eye behind them is direct and unsentimental, someone who photographed for herself rather than for publication. It was the first monograph built from the find, assembled before the fuller scope of Maier's archive, including her color work, had been catalogued.

Maier (1926-2009) worked as a nanny in the Chicago area for four decades while photographing constantly and showing almost no one the results. Her rediscovery reshaped the history of American street photography after the fact. Hudson Street Library also holds two related titles: A Photographer Found (2014), Maloof's larger follow-up drawing on the full archive, and Out of the Shadows (2012), Richard Cahan and Michael Williams's biographical account built on interviews with people who knew her.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Black-and-White Photography, Chicago, New York
notes: First of three Maier titles in this batch (see also A Photographer Found and Out of the Shadows); all three are distinct books, not duplicates. Maier has no personal website (she never published in her lifetime); authors[0].url points to the estate/archive site maintained around John Maloof's find, the closest equivalent to an official artist site.

title: Mary McCartney: From Where I Stand
description:
From Where I Stand, published in 2010, is Mary McCartney's first book. It gathers roughly 160 photographs from fifteen years behind the camera: portraits, backstage pictures, and quieter domestic images that read as observation rather than assignment work.

The book pairs family pictures, Paul and Linda McCartney among them, with portraits of Madonna, Bono, Debbie Harry, Elvis Costello, Dennis Hopper, Gwyneth Paltrow, and Kate Moss, alongside subjects from rockabilly culture and the Royal Ballet, an earlier body of work she had exhibited separately. McCartney's method favors proximity over formality: she has described waiting for a subject to let the camera in rather than directing a shot. Peter Blake, the pop artist behind the Sgt. Pepper's cover, supplies an introduction, and Chrissie Hynde a foreword. The book accompanied an exhibition of the same name at London's National Portrait Gallery, which then toured to the United States, Germany, and Sweden.

McCartney began assisting her mother, the photographer Linda McCartney, before turning professional in 1995. Her first solo exhibition, Off Pointe, documented the Royal Ballet's Corps de Ballet in 2004. From Where I Stand consolidated a decade and a half of that independent practice into her first monograph, and she has continued publishing photography books alongside a parallel career as a documentary filmmaker.
notes: US edition (Harry N. Abrams, ISBN 9780810996540) used per the research brief; a UK edition exists from Thames & Hudson (ISBN 9780500543924, hardcover; 9780500294659, paperback, 2nd ed. 2019). Hudson Street Library already holds a separate McCartney title, Colour / Monochrome (Gost, id 724); this is a distinct earlier book.

title: Digital Diaries
description:
Digital Diaries, published by Taschen in 2000, is Natacha Merritt's collection of explicit self-portraits and portraits made on an early consumer digital camera. It was one of the first photobooks built entirely from digital files rather than film negatives.

Merritt began photographing her own sexual life at twenty and posting the results on her personal website, work that reached the photographer Eric Kroll and, through him, Taschen. The book's images carry the particular color cast and close, snapshot framing of early digital sensors. Merritt shoots herself and her partners with a directness that treats the camera as a participant rather than a distant observer, a departure from the studio lighting and staged compositions of the erotic photography that preceded it.

Merritt (b. 1977) built a wider multimedia career after the book's success, including the internet series D-life and multimedia projections for Cirque du Soleil's Zumanity and Ovo. She later returned to school to study biology. Digital Diaries remains her best-known published work and an early, widely cited example of a photobook shaped by consumer digital technology rather than the darkroom.
notes: A paperback edition also exists (ISBN 9783822838365); this record follows the hardcover per the research brief. Merritt's current personal site (natachamerritt.fr) returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches (Cloudflare-style bot block) but is confirmed live via search-engine indexing; could not independently verify its content by direct fetch.

title: Joel Meyerowitz: Where I Find Myself: A Lifetime Retrospective
description:
Where I Find Myself: A Lifetime Retrospective is Joel Meyerowitz's first single-volume account of his own career, published in 2018. It is arranged in reverse chronological order, starting with recent work and moving backward to the New York streets where he began photographing in 1962.

The book, with text by the photography historian Colin Westerbeck, moves through over a hundred plates spanning his major projects: his late still-life studies made in homage to Giorgio Morandi, a series on trees, the color and black-and-white comparisons he has returned to across his career, his access to Ground Zero in the months after September 11, 2001, a project retracing routes Robert Frank drove for The Americans, and the early New York and Cape Cod street pictures that established him as one of the first photographers to make color a serious medium for art photography.

Meyerowitz (b. 1938) left a career in advertising design in 1962 after watching Robert Frank at work on a shoot. He went on to publish Cape Light (1978), one of the best-selling photography books of its era, and to teach at Cooper Union. Hudson Street Library also holds his Immersion / Visions (Winch), a separate, earlier title. Where I Find Myself is the career-spanning book that followed it.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Color Photography, Retrospective
notes: Confirmed distinct from Meyerowitz's Immersion / Visions (Winch), already in the collection at id 743; Where I Find Myself is a separate 2018 career retrospective from Laurence King. Also issued in paperback by Orion (ISBN 9781786275806); this record follows the Laurence King hardcover per the research brief.

title: Photography and Reality: 1958-1990
description:
Photography and Reality: 1958-1990 is a compact survey of more than three decades of Duane Michals's work. Olympus's European Photo Gallery published it at a moment when Michals's staged, text-annotated images had already reshaped what a photograph could say.

The 157-page volume is printed in illustrated paper covers. It moves through Michals's career, from early street and portrait studies made after a 1958 trip to the Soviet Union, to the invented sequences, multiple exposures, and hand-written captions that became his signature. Rather than a single narrative essay, the book works as a compact retrospective. It traces how Michals turned the photograph from a document of fact into a vehicle for memory, desire, and philosophical speculation.

Michals published more than thirty books over his career, including Sequences (1970), Chance Meeting (1973), and Album: The Portraits of Duane Michals, 1958-1988 (1988). His prints entered the collections of the Museum of Modern Art and the George Eastman House. Photography and Reality catches him mid-career, already established as one of photography's most literary and idiosyncratic figures. It stands as an earlier, gallery-published counterpart to the library's copy of Storyteller (Carnegie Museum of Art / DelMonico Prestel), the later museum retrospective of his work.
notes: Confirmed as a genuinely distinct title from the library's existing Duane Michals holding, Storyteller (Carnegie Museum of Art / DelMonico Prestel): different publisher (Olympus European Photo Gallery, Winterswijk, Netherlands, 1992), different ISBN, different page count (157 pp.), and a different scope (a 1958-1990 survey rather than the later full-career museum retrospective). No cover image could be located after checking Amazon, eBay, and antiquarian-book listings; the book appears to be out of print with no image on file at any source checked. Exhibition tie-in (if any) to a specific Olympus Gallery show could not be confirmed; only the publisher and place of publication are verified.

title: The Idiot's Delight
description:
The Idiot's Delight is a bilingual artist's book in which Duane Michals stages black-and-white photographs of literal idioms and proverbs. Cut, folded, and accordion pages make his sense of visual comedy structural rather than incidental.

Each spread pairs a full double-page photograph with a proverb or figure of speech, rendered in French and English. The text sits on a shortened center page, so it appears only as the surrounding leaves are turned. Half- and quarter-page fold-outs extend some images further, staging sayings such as "Adding Insult to Injury" and "Mum's the Word" as small physical performances the reader has to unfold to complete. Editions Bessard, a Paris imprint, published the book in 2021 as a numbered edition of 600 copies. Sybren Kuyper (Syb), known for structurally inventive photobook design, designed it.

Wordplay and invented scenarios run through much of Michals's photography, alongside the sequences and hand-written captions that made him one of the most literary photographers of his generation. The Idiot's Delight applies that same instinct to the book object itself, turning the mechanics of bookbinding into the punchline. It joins his earlier illustrated-language project Foto Follies (2003), and sits at the artist-book end of a body of work otherwise represented in the library's collection by the museum retrospective Storyteller.
notes: Confirmed as a real, distinct Michals title, separate from the library's existing holding Storyteller (Carnegie Museum of Art / DelMonico Prestel): different publisher (Editions Bessard, Paris, 2021), different ISBN, and an entirely different format (a limited-edition, die-cut artist's book of visual idioms, as opposed to a museum retrospective monograph). Page count is unconfirmed; bookseller listings describe the book as unpaginated, consistent with its accordion/fold-out structure. Cover image downloaded from the Copyright Bookshop listing and saved locally as idiots_delight_cover.jpg.

title: Oscar Muñoz: Hasselblad Award 2018
contributors: Louise Wolthers (Essay); Dragana Vujanović Östlind (Essay); Mark Sealy (Text)
description:
This catalog accompanies the exhibition mounted at the Hasselblad Center in Gothenburg after Oscar Muñoz received the 2018 Hasselblad Foundation International Award in Photography. It stands as one of the fullest surveys of an artist who treats the photograph less as a fixed record than as a fragile, disappearing event.

Across 180 pages the book reproduces the sculptural installations, drawings, and photographic works shown in Gothenburg, pieces built from water, breath, charcoal, and light-sensitive material rather than conventional prints. Essays by curators Louise Wolthers and Dragana Vujanović Östlind sit alongside a text by juror and Autograph ABP director Mark Sealy. Together they trace how Muñoz's experiments with evaporation, condensation, and combustion turn the picture into a process rather than an object, one always on the verge of vanishing.

Muñoz (b. 1951, Popayán, Colombia) has spent more than three decades probing memory, mortality, and the unreliability of images, work held by MoMA, Tate Modern, LACMA, and the Daros Latinamerica Collection. A retrospective traveled to the Jeu de Paume in Paris in 2014. Pieces like Aliento and Narcisos secos, in which breath or water momentarily conjure a face before it fades, remain among his best-known works.
notes: Publication date appears variously as 2018 (exhibition/award year, used by the Hasselblad Foundation and most catalog listings) and February 2019 (a later listed release date on some bookseller sites); 2018 is used here as the primary year. Image color/bw split and LOC data were not found and are left null. Cover image is a low-resolution (128x154 px) Google Books thumbnail; no higher-resolution front-cover scan was found within the research budget.

title: The New York Times Magazine Photographs
contributors: Gerald Marzorati (Preface); Gilles Peress (Photographer); Sebastião Salgado (Photographer); Gregory Crewdson (Photographer); Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin (Photographer); Paolo Pellegrin (Photographer); Nadav Kander (Photographer); Ryan McGinley (Photographer)
description:
This anthology gathers more than 250 photographs commissioned over three decades by The New York Times Magazine, edited by its longtime director of photography, Kathy Ryan, with a preface by former editorial director Gerald Marzorati.

Four sections cover reportage, portraiture, style, and conceptual photography, including photo-illustration. Each image sits next to the original printed tear sheet, so a reader can see it against its magazine context: cropping, sequencing, the surrounding text. The photographer list runs from photojournalists Gilles Peress, Sebastião Salgado, and Paolo Pellegrin to studio and fashion photographers Gregory Crewdson, Nadav Kander, Ryan McGinley, and Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin. Short texts from photographers, writers, and editors take up what separates documentary photojournalism from staged or conceptual work.

Ryan's tenure at the Magazine made it a place where fine-art photography and photojournalism ran on the same pages, often through commissions that pushed photographers past their usual assignments. This 2011 Aperture volume is her record of that editorial run; a companion exhibition, curated with Lesley Martin, toured Rencontres d'Arles, Foam Amsterdam, and Aperture Gallery in New York.
notes: This is an anthology of work by many photographers rather than a single-artist monograph; Kathy Ryan is catalogued as editor (the role under which the book is shelved by publisher, library, and retail records), not as sole author. Individual contributing photographers are listed under contributors rather than authors since no single edition credits them as co-authors on the title page. Subjects (LOC): Documentary photography (20th-21st centuries); Artistic photography (20th-21st centuries); Photojournalism (20th-21st centuries); Portrait photography (20th-21st centuries); Photo illustration.

title: Paradise Lost
description:
Paradise Lost gathers the first photographs Chris Ofili has published, sixty-seven black-and-white images of chain-link fences and palm fronds made across Trinidad, where the artist has lived since 2005.

Shot on a phone in what Ofili calls "pocket photography," the pictures follow wire fencing as it meets tropical light, tracing enclosure against openness across the island. The book takes its title from a 2017 exhibition of new paintings Ofili showed at David Zwirner in New York. That show explored similar themes of constraint and desire but did not include the photographs themselves. Joshua Jelly-Schapiro's essay instead reads the fences through Caribbean history, describing two kinds of cages Trinidadians build: one for birds, one around their own homes.

Ofili won the Turner Prize in 1998 and represented Britain at the 2003 Venice Biennale. He is best known for densely layered paintings that combine collage, glitter, resin, and elephant dung with African and diasporic imagery. Represented by David Zwirner since 2005, he has since shown the tapestry The Caged Bird's Song at the National Gallery, London, a mural at Tate Britain, and work in the Hayward Gallery's In the Black Fantastic.
notes: Confirmed as Ofili's first published body of photography. It is tied thematically to, but distinct from, the concurrent Paradise Lost painting exhibition at David Zwirner: the photographs collected in the book were not shown in that gallery exhibition.

title: I Am
contributors: Erwin Olaf (Commentary); Mattie Boom (Text); Laura Stamps (Interview); Francis Hodgson (Essay); Wim van Sinderen (Essay)
description:
A career-spanning survey of the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, published by Aperture for his sixtieth birthday and running from his earliest black-and-white work through his celebrated staged color portraiture.

Presented chronologically across 400 pages, the book traces four decades of Olaf's evolution from provocateur to sought-after portraitist. It pairs early monochrome images with the meticulously staged, cinematic color tableaux that made his reputation, and closes with a previously unpublished series shot in Shanghai. Olaf's own wry commentary runs alongside the plates, glossing the contexts and inspirations behind individual series. Additional text comes from Rijksmuseum photography curator Mattie Boom, with an interview by Laura Stamps. The volume accompanied the largest retrospective of Olaf's career, a multi-venue exhibition opening at the Rijksmuseum Amsterdam, Gemeentemuseum Den Haag, and Fotomuseum Den Haag in February 2019 before traveling internationally.

Olaf (1959-2023) built his reputation on highly art-directed, theatrical portraiture that treated fashion, advertising, and fine-art photography as a single continuous practice. He addressed taboo and social constraint through lush, controlled studio tableaux. His work earned the Johannes Vermeer Award, a Lucie Award, and the commission to design the portrait side of the Dutch euro coin. This survey followed two earlier Aperture monographs, Volume I (2008) and Volume II (2014), which chart the same body of work in narrower slices.
notes: Both books.csv had this listed as an art-wing photography monograph candidate. Publisher (aperture.org) redirected/404'd on direct fetch during research; bibliographic details corroborated instead via Dashwood Books, Amazon, and multiple bookseller listings, which agree closely. Contributor role labels (Hodgson, van Sinderen as essayists) are drawn from bookseller metadata and could not be independently confirmed against the printed colophon; treat as moderate confidence. Image count (33) reported by one bookseller feed looks implausibly low for a 400-page career survey and was not used; left null rather than publish a likely-wrong figure. Subjects (LOC): Olaf, Erwin, 1959-2023; Photography, Artistic; Portrait photography.

title: The Eternal Substitute
contributors: Darsie Alexander (Essay); Bettina Steinbrügge (Essay); Jacob Proctor (Essay); Lauren Cornell (Essay)
description:
The Eternal Substitute is the fullest account yet of an artist who treats the history of photography as raw material rather than backdrop.

The 228-page hardcover gathers roughly a decade and a half of Oppenheim's work. It spans her documents of art looted or destroyed under the Nazi regime, a botanical survey of trees rendered through camera-less exposure, and a speculative portrait of the Luxembourgish-American photographer Edward Steichen. It was published to accompany Monsieur Steichen, her solo exhibition at Mudam Luxembourg, co-produced with Lët'z Arles and Rencontres d'Arles and curated by Bettina Steinbrügge. The book carries essays from that circle of curators alongside earlier writing on her practice.

Oppenheim works at the edges of the photographic process itself. She remakes negatives as photograms and sun prints, reverses positive and negative, and pairs found or archival images with the specific conditions under which a picture was first made. Earlier bodies of work, including Spine (MOCA Cleveland, 2017) and Billowing (Argobooks, 2013), pursued the same method on other archives. She is represented by Tanya Bonakdar Gallery and The Approach, and her work has been exhibited at institutions including the Guggenheim, the Baltimore Museum of Art, and the Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis.
notes: Selected over Oppenheim's earlier monograph Works 2003-2013 (Sternberg Press, 2014, co-published with Grazer Kunstverein/Kunstverein in Hamburg/FRAC Champagne-Ardenne, ISBN 978-3-95679-040-9, 160pp, softcover, now out of print) because it is more recent, more substantial (228pp hardcover), and tied to her largest museum survey to date. Contributor list has a source conflict: the Hammer Museum store page lists Darsie Alexander, Christophe Gallois, Jacob Proctor, Bettina Steinbrugge (texts) and Liz Deschenes (conversation), while the Amazon listing gives Oppenheim, Darsie Alexander, Lauren Cornell, Jacob Proctor, Bettina Steinbrugge. Both are retailer scrapes rather than the publisher's own colophon, so the contributor list above (from Amazon) should be checked against the physical book or a Hatje Cantz catalog page before ingest. Dimensions, exact end date of the Mudam exhibition, LC/OCLC data, and exact illustration counts were not found within the research budget and are left null. Cover image is a retailer product photo (Hammer Museum store), not a scan of the CSV-side wing cover; verify resolution/crop before use as the site's cover file.

author_full_name: Lew Thomas, Donna-Lee Phillips, Hal Fischer
title: Thought Pieces: 1970s Photographs by Lew Thomas, Donna-Lee Phillips, and Hal Fischer
description:
Thought Pieces reunites three San Francisco photographers who spent the late 1970s stripping photography of its inherited mysticism, rebuilding it instead on grids, texts, and semiotic diagrams. The result recovers one of the sharpest, least sentimental corners of American conceptual art.

MACK published the book in 2020, alongside a survey exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. Its 216 pages divide into four sections: one for each artist's own work, and a fourth reproducing pages from the NFS Press books and pamphlets the group produced between 1976 and 1981. Editor Erin O'Toole, SFMOMA's curator of photography, assembled material that was largely unmarketed and text-driven, and had fallen outside most photography histories.

Lew Thomas led the loosely allied group he called Photography and Language, publishing artists' books built on structuralist ideas rather than the Bay Area's expressive print tradition. Donna-Lee Phillips, his NFS Press co-founder, brought feminist and linguistic theory into the work and designed many of its publications. Hal Fischer's 1977 series Gay Semiotics catalogued the dress and gesture codes of gay men in the Castro in the same diagrammatic format; it remains his best-known work. Their brief, intensive collaboration marked one of the few sustained American engagements between conceptual art and photography.
tags: Art, Photography, Conceptual Art, Semiotics, LGBTQ+, San Francisco, 1970s
notes: Source list attributed this title to a name 'O'Toole' with no further context; that name is confirmed real and correct — Erin O'Toole, Curator and Head of Photography at SFMOMA, edited this publication and organized the accompanying exhibition. No attribution error found; see research log for verification detail. Image counts (total/color/bw) could not be confirmed from public sources and are left null. Subjects (LOC): Conceptual photography; Photography, Artistic; Photography and language; Gay men in photography; San Francisco (Calif.) -- Photography.

title: Photography at MoMA: 1920 to 1960
publisher: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
editor: Quentin Bajac, Lucy Gallun, Roxana Marcoci, Sarah Hermanson Meister
contributors: Douglas Coupland (Text); Kevin Moore (Text); Drew Sawyer (Text); Pepper Stetler (Text)
description:
The second installment in The Museum of Modern Art's three-volume history of photography drawn entirely from its own collection, this book surveys the medium through the height of the modernist period, from 1920 to 1960.

Quentin Bajac, Lucy Gallun, Roxana Marcoci, and Sarah Hermanson Meister edited the volume. Douglas Coupland, Kevin Moore, Drew Sawyer, and Pepper Stetler contributed essays. The book opens with an introduction, then moves through eight chapters of full-color plates, each prefaced by a short essay. Photographers include Alfred Stieglitz, Dorothea Lange, Man Ray, and Aleksander Rodchenko, alongside lesser-known figures who complicate the familiar modernist canon. The volume runs 392 pages in hardcover, with 375 plates.

MoMA formed the first curatorial department devoted to photography in 1940, under Beaumont Newhall. John Szarkowski's long tenure as department director further shaped photography's standing as an art form in American museums. This volume is the middle installment of a trilogy, alongside Photography at MoMA: 1840 to 1920 and Photography at MoMA: 1960 to Now. Together they form the first history of the medium built entirely from one museum's holdings since Szarkowski's own Looking at Photographs in 1973.
tags: Photography, Museum Catalogs, Modernism, Photography History
notes: Authorship: AbeBooks (schema.org Book record) and ARTBOOK/D.A.P.'s product page independently agree the book is credited 'Edited with text by Quentin Bajac, Lucy Gallun, Roxana Marcoci, Sarah Hermanson Meister' with additional essay text by Douglas Coupland, Kevin Moore, Drew Sawyer, and Pepper Stetler. Bajac is listed first and held the title of Chief Curator of Photography at MoMA at time of publication, so he is set as authors[0]; the other three MoMA curators are listed as Editor-role contributors rather than co-primary authors since no single-name attribution appears ahead of the group on either source. This is an institutional multi-editor museum survey, not a single-artist monograph -- 'VA/NA' convention was not used because a primary curator (Bajac) is in fact named first on both sources. authors[0].url left null: Bajac has no independent personal/official website (he left MoMA in 2018 for the Jeu de Paume, Paris); per task instructions, MoMA's own site is listed in artist_links and publisher.url instead of forcing it into authors[0].url. height_cm/width_cm are converted from the ARTBOOK-listed trade dimension '9.5 x 12 in' (assumed W x H, portrait orientation matching the cover proportions) -- not independently confirmed against a MARC 300 field, since no LOC or Getty record was found for this ISBN. images.color/bw breakdown not confirmed beyond the '375 color' plate count given by the distributor.

title: Paul Outerbridge, A Singular Aesthetic: Photographs & Drawings, 1921-1941: A Catalogue Raisonné
description:
Paul Outerbridge, A Singular Aesthetic is the catalogue raisonné that restored a founder of American modernist photography to full view, gathering the photographs and drawings he made between 1921 and 1941.

Edited by Elaine Dines in collaboration with Graham Howe, with an introductory essay by Bernard Barryte, the book accompanied an exhibition organized by the Laguna Beach Museum of Art in 1981. Across 238 pages it documents Outerbridge's commercial and personal work in black-and-white and in the tricolor carbro color process he helped pioneer, including advertising still lifes, portraits, and the sharply composed tabletop arrangements built from geometric forms and everyday objects that became his signature.

Outerbridge (1896-1958) trained at the Clarence H. White School of Photography in New York before becoming one of the first photographers to bring modernist composition into commercial advertising, most famously in his 1922 Ide collar advertisement. He later worked in Paris and London in circles that included Man Ray, and spent his final decades in Laguna Beach, California, as a portrait photographer and color consultant. This catalogue remains a primary reference for his body of work.
tags: Photography, Photographer Monograph, Exhibition Catalog, Color Photography, Advertising Photography, Modernism
notes: Bibliographic records show two 1981 co-editions: a hardcover from Arabesque Books, Santa Barbara (ISBN 9780876855409, used here per the Library of Congress record LCCN 81083979) and a paperback issued directly by the Laguna Beach Museum of Art (ISBN 9780940872028). Both share the same text, pagination (238 pp.), and imagery. The Library of Congress catalogs this as a title main entry with no author field: Elaine Dines and Graham Howe are recorded as editors (700 fields) and Paul Outerbridge appears only as the subject heading (600 field), since he died in 1958 and contributed no text to the volume. He is listed here as primary author/artist to match this catalogue's convention for photographer monographs, since the book exists to document his photographic and drawn body of work. The cover image on file is a physical-copy photograph of the paperback (Laguna Beach Museum of Art) edition rather than a flat studio scan. Subjects (LOC): Outerbridge, Paul.; Photography, Artistic -- Exhibitions..

title: The Contingency of Eye Contact: A Memoir 1970-1975
description:
The Contingency of Eye Contact: A Memoir 1970-1975 is Max Pam's most text-driven book. It is a first-person account of the years in which he left Australia and began the travelling, image-making life that would define his career.

The book opens with his parents' story, not his own coming of age. They met at the East Gippsland fire brigade ball in 1943 and married after his father's demobilization from the New Guinea campaign, raising him through a working-class Melbourne childhood. From there the memoir moves into 1970 to 1975. Pam's own prose runs alongside black-and-white photographs he made in those years, as he shifted from a directionless young Melburnian into a photographer setting out to travel. Éditions Bessard published the book in Paris. It was shortlisted for the Rencontres d'Arles Prix du Livre in 2024.

Max Pam has periodically folded memoir and journal text into his photobooks, as in Ramadan in Yemen. This title extends that method into a sustained personal history. It covers the five years before the extended travels through Asia, the Indian Ocean rim, and the Middle East that he later documented in Going East, Indian Ocean Journals, and Ramadan in Yemen. It is his most recent collaboration with Éditions Bessard, the Paris publisher that has issued several of his titles since 2011.
tags: Photography, Memoir, Documentary Photography, Australia, Autobiography
notes: No ISBN, page count, or physical dimensions were found; Éditions Bessard's product page carries only price, brief description text, and a shortlisting note ("SHORTLISTED prix du livre 2024 Arles") with no bibliographic detail table, and no dealer/library record for this title could be located (it is likely too recent and too small a print run to have reached the secondary market). Publication year 2023 is inferred from the 2024 Arles Prix du Livre shortlist (typically awarded for books published in the preceding year); this is a reasonable inference, not a publisher-stated date.

title: Ramadan in Yemen
binding: Hardcover, cloth binding with a mounted black-and-white plate and silver-stamped titling, housed in a slipcase
description:
Ramadan in Yemen is Max Pam's account of three months in Yemen during Ramadan, 1993. It stands among the most direct fusions of documentary photography and diary-keeping in his four-decade practice.

The book pairs black-and-white and color photographs with facsimile reproductions of Pam's own journal pages. It records Yemeni cities and landscapes alongside Ramadan's daily rhythms of fasting, prayer, and hospitality. Handwritten notes and travel ephemera, including postage stamps, run throughout. Éditions Bessard published it as a signed, numbered edition of 250 copies. It is a cloth-bound hardcover of 90 pages, housed in a slipcase, with a black-and-white photographic plate mounted to the front board. The silver-stamped titling was designed by the typographer Titus Nemeth.

Max Pam (b. 1949, Melbourne) has spent five decades photographing his travels across Asia, the Indian Ocean rim, and the Middle East. His books include Going East, Indian Ocean Journals (Steidl, 2000), and Contingency in Madagascar (Intellect, 2013). Several pair black-and-white travel photography with his own diary text, in a first-person, notebook-like format. Ramadan in Yemen was among the first titles Pam produced with the Paris publisher Éditions Bessard. That relationship continued through Supertourist and The Contingency of Eye Contact: A Memoir 1970-1975.
tags: Photography, Travel Photography, Documentary Photography, Yemen, Middle East, Artist Journal
notes: Sources disagree on the exact publication year: one AbeBooks dealer record states 2011 (used here), a Setanta Books listing states 2010, and Wikipedia states 2012. A separate, much scarcer Bessard listing ("Ramadan In Yemen ... NO clamshell box", 8 copies) is a variant sold without the slipcase; this record describes the standard slipcased edition (ISBN 9782953720402). Print run is stated as an edition of 250 signed copies per a dealer offering a numbered copy (135/250); a Setanta Books summary separately stated an edition of 1000, which could not be corroborated and is treated as less reliable.

title: Supertourist
description:
Supertourist gathers a decade of Max Pam's field trips into a single conceptual survey. It sets newly assembled sequences against archival photographs from his travels, under four paired chapter headings.

Éditions Bessard published the book in 2013 as a limited edition of 500 copies. It runs to 356 pages and holds more than 3,000 color reproductions, in a 7½ x 9 inch format. The four chapters are Bi-Fold Album v Collage, Old World v New World, Object v Artefact, and Islam v Asia. Through them Pam works back through his own unpublished archive, drawn from field trips spanning the globe, and pairs that material with new production under a single title concept.

Ramadan in Yemen documents a single three-month trip. Supertourist, by contrast, is a retrospective survey, drawing on the full breadth of Pam's travels across Asia, the Middle East, and beyond to reconsider his own working method. Max Pam (b. 1949, Melbourne) has built his practice on this kind of return to his own archive over five decades of travel photography. Supertourist was one of several titles he produced with the Paris publisher Éditions Bessard, alongside Ramadan in Yemen and The Contingency of Eye Contact: A Memoir 1970-1975.
tags: Photography, Travel Photography, Documentary Photography, Collage, Archive
notes: No current product page exists on editionsbessard.com; the book was confirmed via an Internet Archive Wayback Machine snapshot of the publisher's product page (dated 2021, itself referencing a publication date of 2013) and several 2014 blog posts from the publisher promoting remaining stock ahead of that year's Rencontres d'Arles. No ISBN or library/dealer record could be located, consistent with a small, now sold-out print run. The publisher's own listing states "3040 color illustrations" for a 356-page book; this figure is unusually high for the page count and is reproduced here verbatim from the source rather than corrected, since no other source could confirm or dispute it.

title: Irving Penn: Centennial
contributors: Jeff L. Rosenheim (Curator); Irving Penn (Photographer); Alexandra Dennett (Essay); Philippe Garner (Essay); Adam Kirsch (Essay); Harald E.L. Prins (Essay); Vasilios Zatse (Essay)
description:
Published to mark the hundredth anniversary of Irving Penn's birth, this catalog accompanied the Metropolitan Museum of Art's 2017 retrospective of his career. It gathers one of the largest selections of his photographs ever assembled in one volume.

Organized by curators Maria Morris Hambourg and Jeff L. Rosenheim, the book moves through Penn's major bodies of work in turn: early documentary studies, existential portraits, fashion photography made for Vogue, the 1948 Cuzco pictures, the female nudes of 1949-50, the Small Trades portraits of tradespeople, ethnographic photographs made in Dahomey and New Guinea, and the cigarette still lifes. Essays by the curators and contributing scholars accompany close to three hundred plates, many drawn from a group of prints promised to the Met by the Irving Penn Foundation.

Penn (1917-2009) worked across fashion, portraiture, and still life for nearly seven decades. He developed a spare studio aesthetic built on plain backdrops and close control of composition and light. The Met began acquiring his photographs in 1959 and had staged two earlier monographic shows before this one. The centennial retrospective drew on a 2014 acquisition of platinum prints from the Small Trades series and surveyed the full range of his work for the first time.
tags: Photography, Exhibition Catalog, Portraiture, Fashion Photography, Twentieth-Century Photography
notes: Published by the Metropolitan Museum of Art and distributed by Yale University Press. Page count follows the Library of Congress/Getty Research Institute MARC record (371 pages); some retail listings give 372. The exhibition's 500 MARC note gives an opening date of April 20, 1917, but the Met's own press materials and contemporaneous press coverage (Forbes, ArtsSummary) consistently give April 24, 2017; this record follows the latter. Subjects (LOC): Penn, Irving -- Exhibitions; Photography, Artistic -- Exhibitions.

title: Passage: A Work Record
contributors: Alexander Liberman (Introduction); Nicholas Callaway (Produced by); Richard Benson (Photographic supervision/reproduction)
description:
Passage: A Work Record is Irving Penn's own 1991 survey of his career, produced with the collaboration of Alexandra Arrowsmith and Nicola Majocchi and introduced by Alexander Liberman.

The book gathers 468 photographs, 397 in black and white and 71 in color, drawn from nearly five decades of fashion, portrait, still-life, and ethnographic work made largely for Vogue. Penn arranged the sequence himself and wrote a commentary on the circumstances behind individual pictures, closing with a detailed work chronology. Alfred A. Knopf published the book with Callaway Editions, whose founder Nicholas Callaway produced it; the black-and-white plates were printed in eleven impressions at Franklin Graphics in Providence, Rhode Island.

Penn spent most of his career photographing for Vogue, working across fashion, portraits of artists and public figures, and still life, and producing the ethnographic "Worlds in a Small Room" pictures and the tradesman portraits later published as Small Trades. Passage arrived when Penn was seventy-four and stands as his own account of that body of work, assembled in his lifetime rather than compiled after it.
tags: Photography, Fashion Photography, Portraiture, Still Life, Monograph, Vogue
notes: Penn founded the Irving Penn Foundation himself in 2005, before his death in 2009, and it remains the largest repository of his work and the closest thing to an official artist site; used as authors[0].url. Dust jacket has no subtitle (reads only "PASSAGE" / "Irving Penn"); the fuller title "Passage: A Work Record" is the title as catalogued by LOC, WorldCat/OpenLibrary, and every bibliographic listing checked, and is used per the schema's subtitle=null rule. LC control number 91052709 and LC classification TR654.P4513 1991 come from dealer/bibliographic citations (LOC's own catalog UI returned 403 to automated fetch this session and was not confirmed directly); OCLC number and Dewey decimal were not found and are left null. Publisher URL left null: Callaway Editions' current web presence could not be confirmed as authoritative within the research budget. Cover image is a scan of the full front+spine+back dust jacket (verified visually), not a cropped front-only shot; it clearly shows the title, author, and Knopf/Callaway imprint mark. Subjects (LOC): Penn, Irving -- Photograph collections; Fashion photography; Photography, Artistic.

title: Flowers Shall Grow
description:
Flowers Shall Grow is the debut monograph from Norway-based photographer Julie Pike, a hot-foil-embossed cloth hardcover issued in a numbered edition of 460 copies by the Oslo imprint Éditions du LIC.

Taking its title from a line of Edvard Munch's writing, the book collects images of nude and semi-nude figures glimpsed deep in Norwegian forests, alone beside dark water, or observed in sparse domestic interiors, shot in the low, harsh light of the Scandinavian sun. The publisher describes the pictures as playful on their surface but threaded with melancholy and coded symbolism, returning to timeless Scandinavian themes of death, the cycle of life, and the body's symbiosis with nature; the sequence is pitched less as a single narrative than as fictional fragments, like stills from a film that was never made. The book runs 88 pages with 64 colour plates, offset-printed, and is now out of print.

Pike was born in Edinburgh and raised in Norway and Denmark, and studied at the Academy of Art College in San Francisco before settling in Oslo in 2001. She works primarily as an editorial and commercial fashion photographer, and is a Canon Europe Ambassador whose clients have included Nylon, Vice, Elle, and Sony Music. She has also shown fine-art work since 2003, including at Art Basel Miami (2010), the Preus National Museum of Photography (2012), and the Female Gaze exhibition at Oslo Negativ Photo Festival (2021).
tags: Photography, Photobook, Scandinavian Photography, Fashion Photography, Limited Edition
notes: Limited first edition of 460 numbered copies, now sold out and out of print per publisher's own site. Cover image sourced directly from Éditions du LIC's product CDN (600×409px; no larger version found on any source checked). The publisher is sometimes assumed to be French because of its name, but it is based in Oslo, Norway (founded 2012); no French-language publisher of this name was found. The language of the book's own text, if any, is not confirmed; the book is likely minimal-text and image-led.

title: Archiv Peter Piller: Materialien (H) – Irrläufer
description:
Irrläufer collects photographs that ended up in an archive by accident, filed and kept though no one meant to keep them.

Working through roughly 100,000 press-clipping images accumulated over fifty years by the steirischer herbst festival archive in Graz, Piller pulled out the pictures that had nothing to do with the festival: images printed on the reverse of unrelated articles, misfiled prints, stray material with no clear place in the collection. Issued as Materialien (H) in 2017, the 112-page booklet arranges these accidental survivors into a small, deadpan catalogue, letting the mistakes of one archive tell a separate, unintended story.

It is one volume in Piller's long-running Archiv Peter Piller, a series of small Nieves booklets that sort found and vernacular photography, from provincial newspaper morgues to police files, into plain alphabetized categories such as Materialien and Spekulationen.
tags: Art, Photography, Found Photography, Artist Book, Archive
notes: Confirmed distinct from the library's existing Piller title: catalogue ids 881/882 hold 'Umschläge' (Dashwood Books, 2014, softcover, 60pp, ISBN not on record), a different book entirely. 'Materialien (H) – Irrläufer' is a separate 2017 Nieves booklet, part of the same ongoing 'Archiv Peter Piller' series of small booklets sorting found/archival material into named categories ('Materialien', 'Spekulationen', 'Irrläufer', etc). 'Irrläufer' is German for a stray or misdirected item (literally 'wanderer gone astray'; used for misdirected mail) — here naming photographs that ended up in the steirischer herbst festival's press archive in Graz by accident. Piller's own site lists the publication line as 'Steirischer Herbst, Graz, 2017' with a credit/link to Nieves as publisher/distributor; the Nieves webshop lists it directly under its own ISBN (978-3-905999-83-9) and price, so it is treated here as a Nieves-published title per the task brief, with the steirischer herbst connection noted. Cover/teaser image is the artist's own site's official image for this title (Sanity CMS asset, original filename '39 JF3A8508 150.jpg'); it was not explicitly labeled 'cover' by either source, so treat as best-available representative image rather than a confirmed scanned front cover. Subjects (LOC): Piller, Peter, 1968- -- Archives; Found photography -- Germany; Photographic archives -- Austria -- Graz; Artists' books -- Switzerland.

title: Lotus
description:
