Lotus is a young photographer's first attempt to turn the documentary picture against its own premise of neutrality. The project, built around Thailand's kathoey community, argues that every 'objective' photograph is already staged.

Working with Quinten De Bruyn, Pinckers photographed transgender sitters under visible tripods and theatrical lighting, crew and equipment left in frame rather than hidden. Subjects were also given disposable cameras, folding their own pictures into the book. The sitters' gender ambiguity becomes a metaphor for the instability of the documentary image itself, caught between what it records and what its maker has arranged.

Pinckers (b. 1988) built on this early project through The Fourth Wall and Margins of Excess, and won the Leica Oskar Barnack Award in 2018. He co-founded Lyre Press, which published this hardcover edition of 3,000 in 2016, with an essay by Hans Theys and design by Manuel Zenner. De Bruyn, credited as Pinckers' collaborator on this KASK graduation-era project, is known separately as a Ghent-based illustrator.
tags: Photography, Documentary Photography, Belgium, Thailand, Queer
notes: Book publication year (2016) is distinct from the project's creation year (2011, per Lyre Press's own catalogue text: 'Lotus was produced in 2011 by Max Pinckers and Quinten De Bruyn while students at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Ghent'). The Lyre Press site itself shows two slightly different dates in different rendered views ('May 2016' and 'November 2015'); the raw HTML source (the authoritative version) states 'ISBN 9789082465518, LYRE 2, May 2016', which is used here. Role split between the two credited authors is not specified by any source: Lyre Press credits both jointly as producing 'their first documentary body of work' with no separate photographer/illustrator designation, so both are listed here as Photographer. Language of the text (English/Dutch/French) could not be confirmed and is left null. No LOC/OCLC record was located. Cover image (lotus01.jpg) was downloaded directly from lyrepress.com and visually confirmed to show the actual book: blue linen case, spine reading 'LOTUS / Max Pinckers & Quinten De Bruyn' and 'LYRE 2'.

title: Margins of Excess
contributors: Victoria Gonzalez-Figueras (Research and text); Hans Theys (Introduction essay)
description:
Margins of Excess catches the moment personal imagination collides with what a society is willing to believe. That collision is the real subject of the post-truth era here, not a footnote to it.

Pinckers made the book with writer and researcher Victoria Gonzalez-Figueras. Together they tracked six people across the United States who had been reported in local and national media as hoaxers or con artists after pursuing outsized personal dreams. The book intercuts newly staged photographs with reprinted news articles, archival footage stills, and transcribed interviews. Each story arrives already contested: the reader gets the same mix of fact, spin, and self-mythology the original coverage produced, with no editorial voice sorting one from the other. Hans Theys' introductory essay situates the project within Pinckers' longer interest in how photographic truth gets constructed. Self-published under his own De Bedoeling imprint in 2018.

Pinckers (b. 1988, Belgium) trained at KASK Ghent and the Royal College of Art, and now teaches at KASK. His practice keeps testing where documentary authority breaks down under staging. Will They Sing Like Raindrops or Leave Me Thirsty (2014), made in South Korea with Quinten De Bruyn, tested it one way; Red Ink (2018), on North Korean framings of the Korean War, tested it another. Margins of Excess extends that line to the American media landscape.

title: The Epic Love Story of a Warrior
description:
Peter Puklus builds twentieth-century Central and Eastern European history out of studio props, staged bodies, and one invented family. The result reads less like a photo essay than a private myth assembled from evidence.

Puklus follows an anonymous young man who wants to move from East to West, working across sculptural still-life, constructed sets, and self-portraiture, and using the region's scarred history as raw material for scenes that mix documentary residue with plain invention. The book was produced with SPBH Editions as the ninth title in the SPBH Book Club and is meant to be read right to left. A line from Marina Tsvetaeva's poem on falling into an abyss, translated by Ilya Shambat, runs letter by letter along the foot of every page, tying the family's private drama to a longer history of loss.

Puklus was born in Cluj-Napoca, Transylvania, and works out of Budapest, treating the studio as a stage for questions of fatherhood, labor, and inherited masculinity. He is associated with FUTURES, the European platform for emerging photographers. His other books, including Handbook to the Stars and Loss and Found, return again to constructed, provisional images of family life under political pressure.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Staged Photography, Family, Eastern Europe

title: Anthill (Meteorites)
description:
Anthill (Meteorites) documents a way of living more than a set of finished artworks. The artist's own house is studio, stage set, and subject at once.

Rebetez made the book in the secluded family home in the Swiss Jura where he grew up. With a circle of friends and collaborators he builds sculptures, masks, and makeshift sets, then photographs the results as a private, ongoing theatre. The 66 black-and-white and color images move between straight documentation and staged tableaux, populated by masked figures caught mid-ritual in cluttered, half-built rooms. The pictures are raw and handmade. Reality and invented narrative are left to intertwine rather than separate.

Rebetez is a Swiss artist working across photography, sculpture, drawing, and video. This kind of DIY world-building runs through his practice, extending the same characters and objects into installations beyond the page. RVB Books, the Paris photobook publisher behind this softcover edition, also issued a signed, numbered print edition alongside it under the same title.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Staged Photography, Sculpture, Switzerland, Installation Art

title: Iowa
edition_printrun: 2017 University of Texas Press edition, expanded (adds 23 previously unpublished photographs to the 1977 Violet Press sequence)
contributors: Alec Soth (Introduction); Anne Wilkes Tucker (Introduction); Mark L. Power (Introduction (original 1977 text, reprinted))
description:
Nancy Rexroth's Iowa is one of the founding books of toy-camera photography: a body of blurred, square-format images that turned the Diana camera's cheap plastic lens into a deliberate tool for picturing memory and place.

Photographed in rural Ohio in the early 1970s, the pictures are named for a childhood idea of Iowa that Rexroth carried from summers spent there as a girl, not the state itself. The camera's soft focus, vignetting, and light leaks give screen doors, barns, and empty fields the quality of something half-remembered rather than seen. Violet Press first self-published the book in 1977 with an introduction by Mark L. Power. Iowa was among the earliest photographic monographs built entirely around a toy camera. This University of Texas Press edition, issued in 2017, expands the original sequence with twenty-three previously unpublished photographs. It reprints Power's introduction alongside new essays by Alec Soth and Anne Wilkes Tucker.

Rexroth studied photography at Ohio University, where professor Arnold Gassan introduced her to the Diana camera in 1969. She later taught at Antioch College and Wright State University. Her photographs are held in the permanent collections of the Museum of Modern Art, the Center for Creative Photography, and the Cincinnati Art Museum. Iowa remains a reference point for photographers working with plastic-lens and toy cameras.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Black-and-White Photography, American Photography, Diana Camera
notes: Photographs are black-and-white, made entirely with a Diana toy camera. 'Iowa' in the title refers to a remembered childhood impression, not the state; the pictures were made in rural Ohio. This UT Press edition is a 2017 expanded reissue of the 1977 Violet Press original. No pricing or valuation information included per policy. Subjects (LOC): Photography, Artistic; Iowa -- Description and travel.

title: Notorious
description:
Notorious gathers Herb Ritts's black-and-white portraits of the period's most photographed faces. It turns the sculptural, high-contrast studio style he built at Vogue and Rolling Stone toward the specific, self-aware theater of celebrity itself.

Published by Bulfinch Press in 1992, the oversized hardcover collects roughly 168 unpaginated pages of duotone portraits, several printed as fold-outs, issued with photo-illustrated boards and no dust jacket. Ritts's subjects pose against plain backdrops, lit to emphasize skin, muscle and gesture over setting. It is the same vocabulary he had already applied to bodybuilders and dancers, now turned on actors, musicians and models complicit in their own image-making.

Ritts (1952-2002) worked alongside contemporaries such as Bruce Weber and Steven Meisel in defining the look of American fashion photography from the late 1970s onward. He moved between advertising campaigns, music videos and editorial work for Vogue, Vanity Fair and Rolling Stone. Notorious captures that practice at its most direct: portraiture as a controlled, complicit performance of fame.
tags: Photography, Celebrity Portraiture, Fashion Photography, Black-and-White Photography, 1990s
notes: Physical dimensions and exact image count not confirmed against a copy; multiple dealer listings describe it as oversize (4to) with fold-out plates. No publisher website found for the 1992 Bulfinch edition. Subjects (LOC): Celebrities -- Portraits; Photography, Artistic.

title: Crystal Clear
description:
Crystal Clear is a dense, physically saturated survey of Maya Rochat's photographic practice, in which images of water, rock and body are pushed through chemical intervention and re-photography until they dissolve toward abstraction.

Across 320 pages the Swiss artist layers analog darkroom experimentation, spray paint, bleach and re-scanning over documentary source photographs. The result is a visual language in which landscape and body function as raw material rather than subject. The book, published by Edition Patrick Frey as volume no. 156 in the Zurich house's long-running series of artist monographs, is designed as an immersive, large-format object. It mirrors the saturated, layered quality of the images themselves rather than presenting them as a clean, sequential portfolio.

Rochat (b. 1985, Lausanne) works across photography, installation, sculpture and sound. She has developed a body of work centered on the material transformation of the photographic image, exhibiting internationally including at Fotomuseum Winterthur and Foam Amsterdam. Crystal Clear consolidates a decade of that practice into the artist's most extensive book to date.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Abstraction, Swiss Photography, Contemporary Art
notes: Publisher (editionpatrickfrey.com) is the primary and most authoritative source; site search is JS-rendered so the real page URL was located via sitemap.xml. No LOC/OCLC record found; treated as a specialist European art-book publication outside standard US library cataloguing.

title: The Pregnant Virgin
description:
The Pregnant Virgin takes its title from a Jungian archetype describing a stage of psychological transformation: a condition of carrying something unresolved and contradictory. It uses that archetype as a frame for a new body of Torbjørn Rødland photographs.

Published by MACK in 2023 as a 128-page hardcover, the book continues Rødland's long-running method: bodies, fruit, hands, teenagers and animals photographed with a flat, over-clear lighting that pushes ordinary subjects toward the uncanny. Tenderness and unease sit in the same frame. The sequencing resists narrative resolution, echoing the archetype's own suspended, contradictory state, and extends the psychologically charged formalism that has defined Rødland's photography since the 1990s.

Rødland (b. 1970, Stavanger, Norway) has exhibited at the Serpentine Galleries, Bergen Kunsthall, Kunsthalle Wien and the Astrup Fearnley Museum. He is widely cited as an influence on a younger generation of photographers working between conceptual and vernacular registers. Hudson Street Library also holds Rødland's Fifth Honeymoon, Sasquatch Century, Confabulations and Vanilla Partner; The Pregnant Virgin is a distinct, later title, not an edition or variant of any of them.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Contemporary Art, Norwegian Photography, Conceptual Photography
notes: Publisher title is "The Pregnant Virgin" (with the article); some library aggregators drop it to "Pregnant Virgin." Used the publisher form to match the user's original list. Confirmed distinct from the library's four existing Rødland titles (Fifth Honeymoon, Sasquatch Century, Confabulations, Vanilla Partner) — different ISBN, different year, no title overlap.

title: White Planet Black Heart
description:
White Planet Black Heart gathers new and recent photographs by Torbjørn Rødland. It returns to the uncannily lit still lifes, portraits and staged tableaux that have made his work a touchstone for a generation of younger photographers and artists.

Published by MACK in 2020 as a 110-page hardcover, the book continues Rødland's method of treating ordinary and bodily subjects, hands, fruit, hair, teenagers, animals, with a flat, saturated clarity. They feel simultaneously clinical and charged. Cropping, lighting and a deliberately awkward formalism turn familiar images into small psychological disturbances, refusing the easy legibility of either fashion photography or straight documentary. The sequencing moves between registers, comic, tender, unsettling, without resolving into a single narrative.

Rødland (b. 1970, Stavanger, Norway) has built a body of work since the 1990s that sits between conceptual photography and a kind of vernacular surrealism. He has exhibited at the Serpentine Galleries, the Bergen Kunsthall and the Astrup Fearnley Museum, among others. Hudson Street Library also holds Rødland's Fifth Honeymoon, Sasquatch Century, Confabulations and Vanilla Partner; White Planet Black Heart is a distinct, later addition to that shelf rather than a variant of any of them.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Contemporary Art, Norwegian Photography, Conceptual Photography
notes: MACK's own product page lists 110 pages; OpenLibrary/library aggregators list 112 for the same ISBN — minor discrepancy noted, publisher figure used as authoritative. Confirmed distinct from the library's four existing Rødland titles (Fifth Honeymoon, Sasquatch Century, Confabulations, Vanilla Partner) — different ISBN, different year, no title overlap.

title: Snow and Rose & Other Tales
description:
Snow and Rose & Other Tales stages women in domestic interiors, bedrooms, windows, mirrors, as figures pulled from fairy tale and 1970s film stills, in the saturated, cinematic color that has defined Marianna Rothen's photography since her breakthrough series Blonde.

The book gathers a body of staged tableaux built around female mythology, memory and performance. It continues Rothen's practice of directing models as characters in an ambiguous, half-remembered narrative rather than documenting them straight. The artist issued it herself in a linen-bound edition, now out of print through her own site, and it sits closer to a small-press artist's book than a trade photobook. That reflects the intimate, self-authored quality of the project itself.

Rothen (b. Stockholm, based in New York) works across photography and video, and her books, including Snow and Rose & Other Tales, Shadows in Paradise and Beauty and Decay, have built a consistent visual world of staged femininity drawn from cinema, fairy tale and personal history. Hudson Street Library holds two physical copies of this title.

title: Faces of Photography
description:
Faces of Photography turns the camera on photographers themselves, pairing Tina Ruisinger's portraits of major 20th-century figures in the medium with interviews in which they reflect on their own work and on photography at large.

Published by Edition Stemmle in 1996, the 176-page hardcover assembles a group portrait of the field at the end of the century. It treats photographers as subjects worthy of the same attentive, personal photography they themselves practiced, rather than as anonymous authorities behind a lens. The book carries text by photographer Ted Croner and an introduction by critic and historian A. D. Coleman, framing Ruisinger's portraits within a broader critical account of photographic practice and its practitioners.

Ruisinger is a Swiss photographer known for portrait and documentary work. Faces of Photography remains her best-known book project, an unusual double exercise in portraiture and oral history that captures its subjects' own voices alongside their images.
notes: OpenLibrary's record initially lists Ted Croner as a co-author rather than a text contributor; cross-checked against multiple AbeBooks dealer listings with the full author statement — 'photographs and interviews by Tina Ruisinger; text by Ted Croner; introduction by A. D. Coleman' — and resolved Ruisinger as sole author, Croner and Coleman as contributors. Exact physical dimensions not confirmed. Subjects (LOC): Photographers -- Portraits; Photography -- History.

title: San Francisco Berlin
description:
San Francisco Berlin sets Stefan Ruiz's portraits of residents of the two title cities side by side, using an identical straight-on studio setup for both so that the comparison falls entirely on the people and what they wear, hold and signal rather than on staging.

Published by Boot in 2011 as a 96-page hardcover, the book continues Ruiz's documentary approach to portraiture, developed through long-running work for the New York Times Magazine and Colors. Subjects are photographed with a flat, deadpan clarity that treats subculture, occupation and self-presentation as primary evidence. Pairing San Francisco and Berlin, two cities with distinct but overlapping countercultural and creative identities, turns the book into an implicit study of how place shapes self-fashioning.

Ruiz is an American photographer whose work spans editorial portraiture, documentary projects and fashion. He has published widely in the New York Times Magazine, Colors and other international publications, and has also contributed cover photography to other artists' books. San Francisco Berlin is among his most sustained comparative portrait projects.
notes: Page count and year show minor discrepancies across sources: OpenLibrary lists 95 pp vs. 96 on D.A.P./Artbook's product page (used here); a '2010' date appears in one LC-derived classification string while the D.A.P. publication date and OpenLibrary both give 2011 (used here). title: Cindy Sherman: The Complete Untitled Film Stills
publisher: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
description:
MoMA's dedicated volume reproduces all sixty-nine black-and-white photographs of Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills (1977-1980) for the first time in their entirety and in the artist's own sequence. It is the series that established her as a central figure in postwar American photography.

Made in Sherman's apartment and on the streets of New York using herself as the sole model, the photographs cast her as an unnamed actress in stills from movies that were never made. They draw on the visual grammar of 1950s and 60s Hollywood, film noir and European art cinema. This 2003 publication carries an essay by MoMA curator Peter Galassi. It was the first to present the full sequence as the artist intended it to be read, rather than the selections that had circulated in earlier surveys and exhibitions.

Sherman was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey in 1954. She has built her entire body of work around self-staged photographs in which she is always a type or a character rather than herself. The library also holds MoMA's 2012 retrospective monograph Cindy Sherman, which surveys thirty-five years of her work across every major series. This earlier volume is a narrower, single-series companion devoted entirely to the Untitled Film Stills.
tags: Photography, Conceptual Photography, Self-Portraiture, Staged Photography, Museum Publication
notes: This is a distinct MoMA publication from the library's existing 2012 retrospective monograph (id 1997, ISBN 9780870708121, 'Cindy Sherman'). This 2003 book documents only the Untitled Film Stills series (1977-1980), reproducing all 69 images in the artist's own sequence with a single essay by Peter Galassi; the 2012 book is a full career survey across all major series with essays by Eva Respini, Johanna Burton and a John Waters interview. title: Stephen Shore: American Surfaces (Revised and Expanded Edition)
description:
Phaidon's 2020 revised and expanded edition of Stephen Shore's American Surfaces is the road-trip diary of snapshot-format color photographs Shore made across the United States in 1972 and first exhibited that same year, when critics largely dismissed the work. It is now regarded as a founding document of American color photography.

Travelling by car with a 35mm rangefinder, Shore photographed diner meals, motel rooms, gas station forecourts, and the people he met along the way. He printed the results as uniform drugstore-format color prints. He pinned them to the wall salon-style at his 1972 show at Light Gallery, a presentation critics of the time read as amateurish rather than considered. This 256-page edition restores and expands the original sequence with previously unpublished images. It positions the project as the direct precursor to Uncommon Places and to Shore's large-format color work of the later 1970s.

Shore, born in New York in 1947, moved from the vernacular immediacy of American Surfaces to the deliberate, large-format compositions of Uncommon Places within a few years. He has taught photography at Bard College since 1982. The library also holds Aperture's Selected Works, 1973-1981, a multi-contributor survey drawn from the same archive of negatives that American Surfaces and Uncommon Places came from.
tags: Photography, Color Photography, American Landscape, Road Trip, New Color Photography
notes: Phaidon IS confirmed as the genuine publisher of American Surfaces (not merely a distributor) -- Phaidon has published multiple editions: the original 2005 edition (ISBN 9780714845074, hardcover; and paperback 9780714848631), and this 2020 'Revised and Expanded Edition' (ISBN 9781838660628), which is the current standard edition and the one recorded here. Image count and dimensions were not confirmed by any source checked and are left null rather than guessed. No confirmed personal official artist website for Shore; authors[0].url uses his gallery (303 Gallery) per the fallback rule. title: Stephen Shore: Selected Works, 1973-1981
contributors: Wes Anderson (Text/Selection); Quentin Bajac (Text/Selection); David Campany (Text/Selection); Paul Graham (Text/Selection); Guido Guidi (Text/Selection); Takashi Homma (Text/Selection); An-My Lê (Text/Selection); Michael Lesy (Text/Selection); Hans Ulrich Obrist (Text/Selection); Francine Prose (Text/Selection); Ed Ruscha (Text/Selection); Britt Salvesen (Text/Selection); Taryn Simon (Text/Selection); Thomas Struth (Text/Selection); Lynne Tillman (Text/Selection)
description:
A collaborative survey of Stephen Shore's negatives from 1973 to 1981, the years that produced American Surfaces and Uncommon Places, in which fifteen artists and critics each select and comment on ten images of their own choosing.

Over five years Shore scanned hundreds of negatives from this period. He invited fifteen artists and critics to each choose ten photographs and write on them: Wes Anderson, Quentin Bajac, David Campany, Paul Graham, Guido Guidi, Takashi Homma, An-My Lê, Michael Lesy, Hans Ulrich Obrist, Francine Prose, Ed Ruscha, Britt Salvesen, Taryn Simon, Thomas Struth and Lynne Tillman. The resulting 279-page volume, published by Aperture in 2017, is structured as fifteen distinct readings of a single body of work rather than a single curatorial narrative. It reveals how differently the same archive looks depending on who is looking.

Shore, born in New York in 1947, began photographing at age six and had work acquired by MoMA before he was twenty. The 1973-81 road trips recorded here fixed the vocabulary of color, banality and deadpan composition that made Uncommon Places a foundational text of the New Color photography movement. He has taught at Bard College since 1982 and remains one of the most widely cited influences on contemporary color photography.

title: Rayon Vert
description:
Senta Simond's debut photobook gathers close, unstylized portraits of young women from the Swiss photographer's own social circle, made as a deliberate counter to commercial media's packaging of youth and femininity.

The title borrows from the optical phenomenon of the green flash and from Eric Rohmer's 1986 film of the same name. Simond cites both as touchstones for a way of seeing that resists easy explanation. Photographing women between twenty and thirty, she strips away styling and decorative artifice, working instead in close crops of hair, skin and gesture. The result reads as a quiet argument against a patriarchal vision of beauty. She originally self-published the project in a run of sixteen copies; it was shortlisted for the Unseen Dummy Award and the Paris Photo-Aperture Foundation PhotoBook Awards in 2017 before Kominek issued this 100-page hardcover edition, limited to 500 copies, in 2018.

Simond, born in Geneva, studied at the Ecole Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne (ECAL). She has continued to work in portraiture and the female body since Rayon Vert, including the related project Anaesthesia. The book established her as one of a generation of European photographers reworking the language of the studio portrait from outside a commercial frame.
notes: Title was sold out at the distributor checked (Twelvebooks); a second Kominek edition also exists per AbeBooks listings. No personal official artist website found (sentasimond.com did not resolve); authors[0].url points to the Twelvebooks product page as the best available reference per the fallback rule.

title: Liberty Theater
description:
A photographic survey of race, class and religious life across the American South, made by Rosalind Fox Solomon between the 1970s and 1990s. It is named for the segregation-era cinema in Chattanooga, Tennessee, the only theater in the city open to Black patrons until the Civil Rights Act.

Solomon began the project at the Scottsboro courthouse in Alabama, site of the notorious 1931 trial, photographing a monthly market held on its grounds. She then extended her travels through Georgia, Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi and South Carolina. The 77 tritone photographs move between churches, funerals, family gatherings, roadside markets and domestic interiors. They track how the legacies of segregation persisted in gesture, dress and social space long after the legal changes of the 1960s. Published by MACK in 2018 as a 96-page debossed hardback, the book carries an essay by the writer and photographer Stanley Wolukau-Wanambwa.

Solomon (1930-2020) came to photography in her forties, studying briefly with Lisette Model. She spent five decades photographing ritual, the body and mortality in the United States and abroad; her other MACK monographs include THEM, Got to Go and A Woman I Once Knew. Liberty Theater is her principal treatment of the American South and one of her most substantial single-subject monographs, distinct from the library's Nazraeli Press one-picture-book Witness, a small limited-edition item built around a single tipped-in photograph.
tags: Photography, Documentary Photography, American South, Black and White Photography
notes: This is Rosalind Fox Solomon's principal career monograph on the American South and a substantially larger, more significant work than the library's existing Nazraeli Press 'One Picture Book #83: Witness' (id 2172, catalogued under author 'Dan Solomon' in the existing CSV row -- a pre-existing data issue unrelated to this record). Cover image is MACK's standard angled product photograph (no flat scan found); it clearly shows the full front cover, spine and back.

title: Snow Management Complex
editor: Tobia Bezzola, Markus Bosshard, Jürg Trösch
description:
Snow Management Complex gathers eight photographic series the Swiss artist Jules Spinatsch made between 2001 and 2013, documenting how ski resorts, hunting grounds, and other engineered landscapes are built, monitored, and maintained.

The book collects eight sequences: Tundra, Applied Landscapes, Fuxjagt, Arena, Endo, Run 1897-1941, Inventar, and Spectrum. They range from time-lapse views of ski slopes groomed by machine at night under floodlight to a set of found postcards from Swiss winter resorts made between 1897 and 1941. Spinatsch photographs each landscape as infrastructure rather than scenery. He tracks how snow cannons, bulldozers, fencing, and surveillance apparatus convert Alpine terrain into a managed tourist product. Codax Publisher issued the volume in 2014, distributed by JRP/Ringier, in a bilingual German/English edition edited by Markus Bosshard, Jürg Trösch, and Tobia Bezzola, with texts by Bezzola and Walter Keller.

Spinatsch (b. 1964) works at the intersection of documentary and surveillance photography. He often builds automated or panoramic camera systems rather than shooting from a single vantage point. His best-known project, Temporary Discomfort, recorded the security operations around G8 summits and the Winter Olympics. Snow Management Complex applies that method to the ski industry, and sits alongside his later book Davos Is a Verb (Lars Müller Publishers) in a continuing study of engineered environments.
tags: Photography, Landscape Photography, Switzerland, Alps, Documentary Photography, Surveillance, Photobook
notes: Publisher of record on the copyright page is Codax Publisher (Zurich). JRP|Ringier is named as European distributor and appears on the cover as "jrp|ringier"; the imprint later rebranded JRP|Editions, and publisher.url points to the current domain jrp-editions.com, which jrp-ringier.com now redirects to. Page count, dimensions, LC classification, Dewey number, and subject headings come from the Getty Research Institute library catalogue (Alma SRU) MARC record for OCLC 859579366. ARTBOOK/D.A.P.'s own listing gives a conflicting page count of 180 pages / 250 color illustrations. The Getty physical-description figure of 250 pages is used here as the more authoritative, professionally catalogued source. The book compiles eight distinct photographic series rather than a single unified essay (see contents note). Per the MARC note, the reproduced postcards in the Run 1897-1941 section are sepia rather than color. title: The Adolescent Comedy
description:
The Adolescent Comedy collects Joseph Sterling's photographs of American teenagers, made between 1959 and 1964. It was his master's thesis project at Chicago's Institute of Design, and it established him as one of the sharpest observers to come out of that program.

Sterling photographed adolescents in drive-ins, cars, and after-school hangouts around Chicago. He applied the pattern-and-design discipline taught by Harry Callahan and Aaron Siskind to loose, observational street scenes of teenagers caught between childhood and adulthood. Only Photography published this edition in Berlin in 2015, a limited run of 500 numbered copies. It reproduces the work as 136 tritone plates on coated stock, a production distinct from Sterling's earlier monograph The Age of Adolescence (Greybull Press, 2005).

Sterling (1936-2010) studied under Callahan, Siskind, and Frederick Sommer at the Institute of Design and earned his M.S. in 1962. He later helped establish the photography department at Columbia College Chicago. He belonged to a circle of students known as the "ID 5," alongside Kenneth Josephson, Ray Metzker, Joseph Jachna, and Charles Swedlund. His photographs are held by the Museum of Modern Art, George Eastman House, and the Art Institute of Chicago.
tags: Photography, Black-and-White Photography, Documentary Photography, Portraiture, American Photography, Institute of Design, Chicago School, Vintage Photography
notes: Not to be confused with Sterling's earlier monograph The Age of Adolescence: Photographs 1959-1964 (Greybull Press, 2005), a different publisher, edition, and production of the same body of work.

title: I Woke Up in My Clothes
description:
I Woke Up in My Clothes is the second monograph by the American photographer Aaron Stern (b. 1978), gathering color photographs shot on 35mm and medium-format film between 2006 and 2013 into a study of intimacy set against isolation.

The pictures move between close, personal scenes and the metropolitan and coastal landscapes around them, from Rockaway Beach after Hurricane Sandy to the vacant lots on the outskirts of Los Angeles. Stern pairs brief moments of connection with longer stretches of solitude and the decay that eventually reaches every human undertaking. Damiani published the book in Bologna in 2013 as a cloth-bound hardcover, 96 pages with 50 illustrations, including a poem by David Wagoner and an introduction by Rich Appel.

Stern was born in Washington, D.C., in 1978 and lives in New York. I Woke Up in My Clothes follows his first monograph and gathers roughly seven years of personal work rather than a single commissioned series.
notes: Publication year conflict: Damiani's own product page and OpenLibrary's LC classification (TR647 .S74 2013 / TR655 .S7488 2013) both point to 2013, while OpenLibrary's summary publish_date field and AbeBooks list 2014 (likely the US distribution/catalog year). Used 2013 as the publisher-stated release date. Dimensions (9.5 x 11.75 in) are from a bookseller listing, not the publisher page, which did not list dimensions; treat as approximate. No official artist website could be confirmed live (aaronstern.com returns a Cloudflare challenge page); authors[0].url left null. Subjects (LOC): Photography, artistic; Artistic Photography.

title: Forest Hills
description:
Forest Hills tracks the twentieth-century rise and fall of tennis at Forest Hills, Queens. Bill Sullivan built the book from photographs and constructed images of the site: its aerial views, court markings, and stadium fabric.

The book pairs documentary and altered imagery. Aerial photographs of the West Side Tennis Club's horseshoe-shaped stadium, its clay and grass courts changing texture across decades, sit alongside composited and reworked views that blur record and invention. Forest Hills was once the center of tennis in America; the book reads it as a place that fell out of use. Its history is tracked through the surfaces and signage that marked its successive eras, not through a straight chronology. This second edition, of 1,000 copies, was published by S U N, New York, in 2023 to mark the stadium's hundredth anniversary. It was printed on 170gsm Arena ivory stock by Die Keure in Bruges. A first edition of 500 copies came earlier, issued by S U N Books & Editions in 2013-14 and bound in striped cloth with no printed title on the cover.

Sullivan made the book's concept and design with Ofer Wolberger. Sullivan publishes his own work through S U N. Forest Hills is his study of a single site, the former U.S. Open grounds, read as a record of how tennis, architecture, and design changed together over a century.
tags: Photography, Photobook, Tennis, Sports, New York City, Queens, Architecture, Self-Published
notes:
Booksellers spell the publisher variously: "S U N", "SUN", "S_U_N_", "S U N Books & Editions", "s u n editions". These all name the same New York imprint that publishes Sullivan's own work. Canonical spelling used here is "S U N".

This record catalogs the 2023 second edition. ISBN 9798218957032, 144pp, 1,000 copies, printed by Die Keure in Bruges. It was issued for the stadium's centenary. An earlier first edition is not the edition catalogued here: ISBN 9780984978137, 500 copies, S U N Books & Editions, 2013-14, cloth binding in two colorways with no printed title, about 9.5 x 7 in per dealer listings.

The cover image is a bookseller's photograph of the actual 2023 edition, from the Bookish Kemper listing on AbeBooks. It shows the true front cover, not a publisher hero shot.

Two independent editions of the same title, author, and subject turned up on AbeBooks and OpenLibrary, which rules out any other person named Bill Sullivan. The subject matter (West Side Tennis Club / Forest Hills Stadium, Queens) and the photography-based, image-making approach match the contemporary New York artist named in the research brief, not the unrelated academic of the same name.

No official site, gallery page, or Wikipedia entry was found this session for this Bill Sullivan. So no biographical claims beyond the book's own publication facts are included here.

title: Atlas of Forms
description:
Atlas of Forms is a typological survey of architecture built entirely from found images, gathered online rather than shot by the artist.

Eric Tabuchi assembled roughly 1,500 photographs of buildings and structures from around the world. He sorted them not by place or period but by geometric shape and state of completion: spheres, cubes, polygons; under construction, finished, abandoned, in ruin. The sequence runs from purely spherical forms to a closing image of an inverted bunker. Poursuite Éditions published the book in Paris in 2017, with French and English text.

Tabuchi (b. 1959) works in series that sort vernacular and infrastructural subjects, gas stations, storefronts, industrial architecture, into systematic visual catalogues. He later extended that method with Nelly Monnier in the long-running Atlas des Régions Naturelles. Atlas of Forms came first. It applies the same classifying instinct to images the artist did not take himself, an archive of anonymous, appropriated photographs rather than his own fieldwork.
notes: OpenLibrary lists this as a distinct 2017 Poursuite Éditions title, separate from the multi-volume Atlas des Régions Naturelles (2019– , with Nelly Monnier). Dimensions not found in any consulted source; page count (255) and LC/Dewey data are from the OpenLibrary edition record. Publisher's own website could not be located (no working domain found under likely names); ISBN/publisher/year are corroborated by both AbeBooks and OpenLibrary independently. Subjects (LOC): Architectural photography.

title: Atlas des Régions Naturelles, Vol. 1
edition_printrun: Second printing, December 2021. Co-published by Poursuite Éditions and GwinZegal.
description:
Volume 1 of Atlas des Régions Naturelles, known as ARN, opens Eric Tabuchi and Nelly Monnier's survey of France's roughly 450 historical "natural regions". The project began in 2017 and treats the country as a set of repeating vernacular forms rather than as scenery to be admired.

The first volume sets the format every later one follows: sixteen chapters in runs of three regional portraits followed by one thematic chapter. The regions here are Beauce, Cévennes méridionales, Faucigny, Forez, Garrigues, Nivernais, Pays d'Ouche, Porcien, Santerre, Trégor, Val de Loire tourangeau and Hautes Vosges lorraines. The four thematic chapters are Amers, Camouflage, Initiatives personnelles and Piscines verticales. They collect seamarks, camouflage, the private constructions of individuals, and above-ground swimming pools. Across 384 pages the book is softcover with a screen-printed cover, Otabind bound, with a folded map slipped in at the back as an index. It was shortlisted for the Arles PhotoBook Awards in 2022 and produced with support from the Centre national des arts plastiques. This copy is the second printing, dated December 2021.

Atlas des Régions Naturelles is Tabuchi and Monnier's central ongoing collaboration. They also made Aller-Retour (Poursuite Éditions, 2025), a travel narrative told in photographs and short texts. Tabuchi's earlier solo photobooks apply the same deadpan, typological method to a single subject. Two examples: Eldorado (Presses du Réel, 2010) and EDF, Electricité de France (2019), a survey of the French utility's industrial sites. Atlas des Régions Naturelles extends that method across the whole of the French landscape. Both artists publish primarily through Poursuite Éditions, the imprint they run themselves.
tags: Photography, ARN, Landscape Photography, Documentary Photography, Typology, France, Vernacular Architecture
notes: Volume 1 of the series, catalogued as its own record; Volumes 1 through 6 are held. Each volume is sold separately by the publisher under its own ISBN and uses the same screen-printed cover design in a different colour. Classified as a Photobook rather than an Artist Book because each volume is a standard offset-printed trade paperback in ongoing print runs.

title: The Keys to the House
description:
The Keys to the House is Juergen Teller's record of the ground he actually stands on: his house, land, and family in Suffolk. He shoots it with the same flat directness he brings to a magazine job.

Landscapes of the property sit next to portraits of family and friends. Fashion and celebrity sitters appear too, given no more weight than anyone else: Lily Cole floats in water like Ophelia, Vivienne Westwood leans against a red Mercedes-Benz. Teller has said the mixing is deliberate. Commercial work and personal life aren't separate practices for him, just two ends of one continuous way of looking, and this book puts that claim on the page.

Teller (b. 1964, Erlangen, Germany) built his name on fashion campaigns for Marc Jacobs, Céline, and Yves Saint Laurent. Museums followed: Fondation Cartier gave him a Paris survey in 2006, and the Bundeskunsthalle Bonn a full retrospective, Enjoy Your Life!, in 2016. Steidl has published most of his books, among them Nürnberg, Woo!, and Märchenstüberl. The Keys to the House is one of the plainer, more domestic entries in a body of work otherwise defined by its access to fashion and celebrity.

title: Touch Me
description:
Touch Me is the catalogue built around an exhibition that set out to look past Juergen Teller's best-known fashion and luxury pictures, toward the aesthetic habits running underneath his whole photographic practice.

The show opened at Le Consortium in Dijon in January 2010, then travelled to the Daelim Contemporary Art Museum in Seoul the following year, and the book follows that structure. It juxtaposes installation photographs of the two hangs with the original images themselves, so the reader sees both the pictures and the decisions made about how to show them. An essay by Eric Troncy, the Consortium's co-director, frames Teller's work as a question about contemporary photography's display conditions as much as its content. Text runs in English and Korean across the book's 135 pages.

Teller (b. 1964, Erlangen, Germany) had by 2010 built a career on fashion campaigns for Marc Jacobs and Céline alongside gallery and museum exhibitions, including a 2006 survey at Fondation Cartier, Paris. Touch Me belongs to that gallery side of his output: a small, essay-driven catalogue rather than a trade monograph, aimed at exhibition audiences in Dijon and Seoul rather than a bookstore readership.

title: Hank Willis Thomas: All Things Being Equal
contributors: Julia Dolan (Essay); Sara Krajewski (Essay); Sarah Elizabeth Lewis (Essay); Kellie Jones (Interview)
description:
All Things Being Equal is Aperture's survey of Hank Willis Thomas, a decade past his first book. It gathers the photography, sculpture, and collaborative projects he has used to take apart the images American culture runs on.

The book keeps its focus on Thomas's relationship to the photographic image and to questions of representation. It tracks his dissection of advertising, sports, and popular media, with particular attention to race, gender, and cultural identity, and documents how commercial imagery commodifies that identity. Collaborative, trans-media projects appear too: Question Bridge, Philly Block, For Freedoms. Portland Art Museum curators Julia Dolan and Sara Krajewski and art historian Sarah Elizabeth Lewis contribute essays. Dr. Kellie Jones interviews the artist directly about his influences.

Thomas (b. 1976, Plainfield, New Jersey) first published Pitch Blackness in 2008. He has since become a prominent voice in American art, moving between solo exhibitions and the civic-facing work of For Freedoms, the artist-run super PAC he co-founded. All Things Being Equal is Aperture's first full monograph on him, arriving as his practice shifted from gallery photography toward public monuments and collaborative platforms.
tags: Photography, Contemporary Art, Race and Identity, Conceptual Art

title: Nothing Could Have Prepared Us – Everything Could Have Prepared Us
contributors: Julie Jones, Peter Szendy, Ji-Yoon Han, Valentin Gleyze, Jonathan Pouthier, Matthias Pfaller, Damarice Amao, Taous Dahmani, Boaz Levin (Essay)
description:
Nothing Could Have Prepared Us – Everything Could Have Prepared Us documents an installation that took over the whole second floor of the Bibliothèque publique d'information, the Centre Pompidou's public library. More than three decades of Wolfgang Tillmans's work went up inside a room built for reading, not looking.

Tillmans hangs prints at wildly different sizes and uneven heights, unframed, letting genres mix freely on the wall. Here that method met a working library: shelving, signage, and reading tables stayed in use around the pictures. Photography, music, fashion, architecture, and activism all surface in the selection. The catalogue reproduces the installation itself alongside individual works, so the reader can see how one shapes the other. A group of emerging scholars contributes essays, among them Damarice Amao, Taous Dahmani, and Boaz Levin. Tillmans himself contributes as well, and Florian Ebner and Olga Frydryszak-Rêtat of the Centre Pompidou edited the volume.

Tillmans was born in 1968 in Remscheid, Germany. He has treated exhibition architecture as part of the work since his early Cologne and London shows in the 1990s, and this installation carries that practice into an institution not built for art. The library setting puts Nothing Could Have Prepared Us alongside his other site-responsive projects: Sound Is Liquid at mumok Vienna, and the multi-venue survey To Look Without Fear.

title: Sound Is Liquid
contributors: George T. Baker, Diedrich Diederichsen, Elisabeth Karola Kraus, Élisabeth Lebovici, Felicity D. Scott (Essay)
description:
Sound Is Liquid catalogues an exhibition at the Museum Moderner Kunst Stiftung Ludwig (mumok) in Vienna, running from late 2021 into the spring of 2022. It gathers work that treats sound as subject and material both, tracing a thread through Wolfgang Tillmans's career that runs back to the club culture of his earliest photographs.

The show paired photography with installation, video, and sound pieces, and the book follows that mix rather than flattening it into a single medium. Music runs through the material at every level. Tillmans has long photographed club and rave scenes. He has released his own music as well. Between the two, the exhibition reads as an argument about listening, not only looking. George T. Baker, Diedrich Diederichsen, Elisabeth Karola Kraus, Élisabeth Lebovici, and Felicity D. Scott contribute essays. Matthias Michalka edited the volume, and the writers address sound art, club culture, and Tillmans's exhibition practice from several angles.

Tillmans was born in 1968 in Remscheid, Germany, and came up through the Hamburg and London club scenes of the late 1980s and early 1990s. Dance music has stayed close to his photographic and curatorial work ever since. Sound Is Liquid joins two other site-specific survey catalogues from the same period: the Centre Pompidou installation Nothing Could Have Prepared Us, and the multi-venue exhibition To Look Without Fear. Each is built around a different institutional space rather than a fixed retrospective format.

title: To Look Without Fear
contributors: Quentin Bajac, Yve-Alain Bois, Julia Bryan-Wilson, Clément Chéroux, Durga Chew-Bose, Stuart Comer, Keller Easterling, Paul Flynn, Sophie Hackett, Michelle Kuo, Oluremi C. Onabanjo, Phil Taylor (Essay); Phil Taylor, Andrew Vielkind (Chronology)
description:
To Look Without Fear accompanies the largest survey of Wolfgang Tillmans's work ever mounted in North America. MoMA curator Roxana Marcoci organized the show, on view at the Museum of Modern Art from September 2022 through January 2023. It later traveled to the Art Gallery of Ontario and SFMOMA.

The book covers four decades of work: early magazine photography and club pictures, abstract chemical experiments, portraiture, still life, video and sound installations. It follows Tillmans's practice past the single photograph. Magazines, posters, and the wall itself all become sites for pictures in his hands, not neutral supports. Yve-Alain Bois, Julia Bryan-Wilson, Clément Chéroux, Michelle Kuo, and eight other contributors each write on a different facet of the work. Phil Taylor and Andrew Vielkind compile a chronology spanning Tillmans's full career.

Tillmans was born in 1968 in Remscheid, Germany. In 2000 he became the first photographer, and the first non-British-born artist, to win the Turner Prize. To Look Without Fear sits alongside his other major survey catalogues from the same period, Sound Is Liquid at mumok Vienna and the Centre Pompidou installation Nothing Could Have Prepared Us. Of the three, it is the fullest career retrospective, spanning the entire arc of his work rather than a single body of it.
notes: Confirmed distinct from the existing library title 'Wolfgang Tillmans: A Reader' (MoMA, 2022, id 1172 in books.csv): that is a curated anthology/reader format, while this is Roxana Marcoci's retrospective exhibition catalogue for Tillmans's own MoMA survey. A German-language edition also exists (Perspektive: Look...fear, Walther König, ISBN 9783753301778); the English MoMA hardcover (9781633451117) is catalogued here as the primary edition. title: I Know How Furiously Your Heart Is Beating
description:
Alec Soth's 2019 MACK monograph turns his camera away from the American road and into private rooms. Large-format color portraiture stands in for the earlier work's social documentary. The question is simpler and harder: how much of another person can a photograph actually hold.

Its title comes from Wallace Stevens's poem "The Gray Room." Soth made the pictures between 2018 and 2019, in interiors from Minneapolis to Odessa. No captions tie a face to a place or a story. There's just a sitter, a room, and the time Soth spent looking. He has described the project as a stripping-down of the medium to its plainest elements, after years of photographing American social life: an attempt to simply spend time with people and catch a glimpse of an interior life the camera can't fully name. The book appeared alongside four simultaneous solo exhibitions, in Minneapolis, New York, San Francisco, and Berlin. It closes with an interview between Soth and the novelist Hanya Yanagihara. MACK printed it as an 84-page, debossed linen hardback.

Soth was born in Minneapolis in 1969. He is a member of Magnum Photos and founder of the small publishing house Little Brown Mushroom. This book followed a run of major projects, including Sleeping by the Mississippi, Niagara, Broken Manual, and Songbook. Its quieter, more intimate register anticipated the interior focus he'd continue in A Pound of Pictures (2022).

title: American Prospects
contributors: Kerry Brougher (Essay); Andy Grundberg (Essay); Anne W. Tucker (Essay)
description:
American Prospects helped make color photography a serious documentary language. It pairs a deadpan large-format eye with the ordinary disasters of American land use, and this Steidl edition is its fullest printing to date.

Joel Sternfeld shot the work between the late 1970s and early 1980s. He drove across the United States with an 8x10 view camera, photographing scenes where landscape, industry, and consumer culture collide. The timing is often dry, almost comic: a house half-swallowed by a sinkhole in the Southern California desert, a fire truck's crew shopping for pumpkins while a barn burns behind them, a hot air balloon drifting over a highway. Times Books first published the work with the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, in 1987, a decade after William Eggleston's 1976 MoMA show had opened the door to color as a fine-art medium. It helped confirm that color could carry the same critical weight as black-and-white documentary photography. This fifth, definitive Steidl edition came out in 2020, freed from the size constraints of earlier printings. It adds twelve previously unpublished or unexhibited photographs, including portraits that push the book toward the more human, less landscape-bound territory Sternfeld would take up fully in Stranger Passing. Essays by Kerry Brougher, Andy Grundberg, and Anne W. Tucker accompany the 152-page hardcover.

Sternfeld was born in New York in 1944 and taught for decades at Sarah Lawrence College. Alongside Eggleston, Stephen Shore, and Joel Meyerowitz, he is one of the photographers who established color as the dominant language of American documentary photography. His other major books include Stranger Passing, On This Site, and Oxbow Archive.

title: Stranger Passing
description:
Stranger Passing takes the deadpan wide shots of American Prospects and moves in close. It gathers sixty color portraits of people Sternfeld stopped on sidewalks, parking lots, and roadsides across fifteen years of travel.

American Prospects reads the American landscape for its ironies. This book reads its faces instead: a banker eating lunch alone, a teenager gathering shopping carts in a strip-mall lot, a man asleep on his bedding in public. Sternfeld approaches each subject directly, without condescension. He has called it an unscientific, interpretive sampling of what Americans looked like at the end of the twentieth century. Bulfinch Press published the book in 2001, a 144-page oblong hardcover with essays by the writer Ian Frazier and the photography historian Douglas R. Nickel. A softcover edition followed the same year from Melcher Media, in association with the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, to accompany an SFMOMA exhibition of the work that summer.

Sternfeld was born in New York in 1944. He is best known for American Prospects (1987), the large-format color survey that established his reputation; Stranger Passing is its direct, portrait-based sequel. He taught for many years at Sarah Lawrence College and remains a central figure in the history of American color documentary photography.

title: Chemises
description:
Chemises takes its subject from the edges of Malick Sidibé's archive rather than its center: the plain cardboard folders — chemises, French for both "shirts" and "folders" — in which he handed Bamako clients their prints and negatives from the 1960s through the 1970s.

Stamped, labeled, and worn from handling, these folders carried the ordinary bureaucratic marks of a working studio: order numbers, customer names, dates. Steidl designed the book itself to mimic that object. The volume reads as a photograph album with prints pasted directly onto its pages, rather than a conventional plate-by-plate monograph. It was published in 2007 to accompany an exhibition co-presented by Foam Fotografiemuseum in Amsterdam and the Musée Nicéphore Niépce in Chalon-sur-Saône, and it shifts attention from the nightlife and portrait images for which Sidibé is best known toward the material culture and everyday economy of studio photography in Bamako.

Sidibé (1936–2016) ran his Bamako studio from 1958, photographing the city's youth culture, dance halls, and social life through the years around Malian independence. He became the first photographer and the first African artist to receive the Golden Lion for lifetime achievement at the Venice Biennale, in 2007, the same year Chemises was published. His major monographs include the 1998 Scalo retrospective edited by André Magnin.

title: Ponte City
description:
Ponte Tower has stood over Johannesburg since 1975 as a monument to changing fortune. It was built as luxury apartments for the city's white elite, left to decline and gain a reputation for crime and squalor after apartheid ended, and later partially reclaimed through redevelopment. Mikhael Subotzky and Patrick Waterhouse spent years inside it, and Ponte City is the record of that time.

The two photographers set themselves a systematic task: photograph every door in the building, the view out of every window, and the image showing on every television screen. They combined those series with an extensive found archive of real-estate brochures, newspaper clippings, security-company documents, and lost identity photographs recovered from the tower's abandoned units. Steidl published the material as a box of seventeen booklets stacked one on top of another, mimicking the stacked floors of the tower itself, rather than binding it into a single volume. An accompanying text by the Johannesburg writer Ivan Vladislavić threads the building's mythology and its residents' testimony through the visual archive. The result treats a single structure as a lens onto the whole arc of the city's post-apartheid transformation.

Subotzky (b. 1981) is a former Magnum photographer known for long-term projects inside South African institutions. Waterhouse (b. 1981) is a British artist and former editor of Colors magazine. The two developed Ponte City together over roughly a decade. A related, expanded volume, Ponte City Revisited, followed from Steidl in 2021.

title: Hiroshi Sugimoto
description:
This 368-page Hatje Cantz monograph is the catalogue for the retrospective that gave Hiroshi Sugimoto his fullest institutional survey to date. It remains the standard English-language career overview of his work.

Kerry Brougher organized the exhibition for the Hirshhorn Museum and David Elliott organized it for the Mori Art Museum. It traveled from Tokyo (September 2005 – January 2006) to Washington, D.C. (February – May 2006). The book follows its structure through Sugimoto's key bodies of work: the taxidermy tableaux of the Dioramas, the long exposures of empty movie-palace and drive-in screens in Theaters, the horizon-line minimalism of Seascapes, the uncannily lifelike wax-museum figures of Portraits, and the deliberately out-of-focus buildings of his architecture series. Designed by Takaaki Matsumoto, the oversized hardcover reproduces the plates at a scale close to the artist's own large-format prints. Accompanying essays situate each series within Sugimoto's decades-long interest in photography's relationship to time, memory, and historical representation.

Sugimoto (b. 1948, Tokyo) has lived and worked in New York since the early 1970s. He is among the most widely collected photographers of his generation, represented in the permanent collections of MoMA, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the Guggenheim. This monograph predates his later series (Lightning Fields, Photogenic Drawings) but remains the most complete single-volume account of the work that established his reputation.

title: Evidence
edition_printrun: 2003 D.A.P. reprint of the 1977 first edition
contributors: Sandra S. Phillips (Introduction); Robert F. Forth (Afterword)
description:
Evidence is one of the founding texts of postmodern photography: a book with no photographs taken by its authors, no captions, and no explanation. It is made almost entirely from images Larry Sultan and Mike Mandel found by combing the archives of over fifty American corporations, universities, and government bodies.

Sultan and Mandel spent two years, from 1975 to 1977, requesting access to photographic files at organizations including NASA, the Beverly Hills Police Department, Bechtel, and various aerospace and engineering firms. They pulled images originally made to document tests, procedures, or incidents. Stripped of their original captions and technical purpose, and resequenced without commentary, the pictures become opaque and faintly ominous: a man in a hazmat suit, a car half-buried at an angle, an object wrapped in plastic on a lab table. The effect forces the viewer to supply the missing context. It exposes how thoroughly meaning in documentary photography depends on caption and institution rather than the image itself. The artists self-published the book in 1977. D.A.P. reissued it in 2003 in this edition, with an introduction by SFMOMA photography curator Sandra S. Phillips and an afterword by Robert F. Forth.

Sultan (1946–2009) and Mandel (b. 1950) made Evidence as students at the San Francisco Art Institute. Both went on to individually influential careers, Sultan with Pictures from Home and The Valley, Mandel with conceptual and vernacular projects including Seven Days and People in Cars. Evidence remains their most widely cited collaboration and a touchstone for later appropriation-based photography.
tags: Photography, Conceptual Art, Appropriation, American Art, Photobook
notes: This is the 2003 D.A.P. reissue (108 pp., ISBN 9781891024627) of the 1977 self-published first edition (Clatworthy Colorvues, ISBN 9780918290014, 71 pp.) — the two are distinct editions with different ISBNs; this record covers the reissue as specified in the brief. title: The Valley
description:
Larry Sultan's The Valley photographs the pornography industry at work inside the same tract-house suburbs he grew up in and had already photographed his parents within, and the collision of the two subjects is the point: the Valley as both the birthplace of the American domestic ideal and, by the late 1990s, the production capital of adult film.

Between 1998 and 2003 Sultan spent time on sets rented in ordinary San Fernando Valley houses. He photographed not the sex acts themselves but the surrounding apparatus of the shoot: crew members waiting between takes, a boom operator crouched beside a suburban bed, a performer resting on a stripped mattress with a lamp and houseplant behind her. The large-format color images play the flat light and generic furnishings of tract-house interiors against the artifice of the productions staged inside them. They extend the questions about domesticity, performance and the camera's presence that had structured Pictures from Home. Scalo published the work as The Valley in 2004, a 127-page hardcover monograph.

Sultan (1946–2009) taught for decades at California College of the Arts. He is remembered for a body of work, Evidence (made with Mike Mandel), Pictures from Home, and The Valley, that repeatedly tested where documentary photography ends and staging begins.

title: Edward Weston
description:
Edward Weston, the seventh volume in Aperture's Masters of Photography series, is a compact survey of the career of one of the founders of American modernist photography.

Over 95 pages, R.H. Cravens's essay traces Weston's move from soft-focus pictorialism toward the sharp-focus, unmanipulated approach he called “straight photography,” and the plates follow him through the images that made his reputation: close-up nudes, the shell and pepper still lifes shot for their pure abstract form, and the dune and rock studies made at Point Lobos and Oceano on the California coast. The series format keeps the text brief and lets the reproductions carry the book, a design consistent across the other Aperture Masters volumes on Weston's contemporaries.

Weston (1886–1958) co-founded Group f/64 with Ansel Adams and Imogen Cunningham in 1932 to advocate for sharply focused, unretouched photography, and in 1937 became the first photographer awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship. His negatives and the bulk of his working archive are held at the Center for Creative Photography at the University of Arizona, with further material at the Museum of Modern Art, the Smithsonian, and George Eastman House.
tags: Photography, Modernist Photography, American Photography, 20th Century Photography, Landscape Photography
notes: Aperture also published a larger, separately-titled Weston monograph, 'Edward Weston: His Life and Photographs' by Ben Maddow (1979, ISBN 9780893810436, 299pp) which is a fuller illustrated biography; this record catalogs the slimmer 'Aperture Masters of Photography' series volume (No. 7, 1988, essay by R.H. title: Naked City
description:
Naked City is the 1945 debut collection by the New York press photographer Weegee (Arthur Fellig, 1899–1968), the book most responsible for establishing tabloid crime photography as a subject fit for museums.

Fellig worked nights out of a car fitted with a police-band radio, racing to murders, fires, arrests and accidents ahead of the daily papers. He set his own captions in the same clipped, wisecracking voice as his flashbulb pictures. The book widens beyond the crime beat to Coney Island crowds, tenement fire escapes in summer, Bowery drunks, opera-night socialites and Harlem nightlife. Loose thematic chapters mix high and low New York in a single sequence. The book's success led Universal to option the title for the 1948 film noir of the same name, with Fellig as a consultant, and it cemented his reputation beyond the tabloids he worked for.

Fellig emigrated as a child from what is now Ukraine to New York's Lower East Side. He earned the nickname Weegee for his knack of reaching a scene before the police, as if guided by a Ouija board. The Museum of Modern Art began acquiring his prints in 1943. He went on to publish Weegee's People (1946), Naked Hollywood (1953) and Weegee by Weegee (1961), then returned to New York to lecture on photography until his death in 1968.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Crime Photography, New York, Photojournalism, 20th Century Photography

title: Weegee's New York: Photographs 1935-1960
description:
Weegee's New York: Photographs 1935–1960 is a career-spanning retrospective of the New York press photographer's work, assembled by the Munich art publisher Schirmer/Mosel with an introduction by the curator and critic John Coplans.

The book gathers 335 photographs accompanied by an autobiographical text from Weegee (Arthur Fellig) himself. It moves well beyond the murder scenes and fires of his 1945 debut Naked City, taking in Coney Island crowds, Bowery derelicts, Lower East Side tenement life, movie premieres and the infrared and trick-lens celebrity portraits he made in later years. It first appeared in Munich in 1982 as 335 Photographien 1935–1960. This English-language edition followed two years later, co-published with Grove Press in New York.

Fellig worked the New York crime beat through the 1930s and 40s with a police-band radio wired into his car. He earned the nickname Weegee for his habit of reaching a scene before the police. His prints entered the Museum of Modern Art's collection starting in 1943. This volume, alongside Naked City, remains one of the two standard references for his work.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, New York, Photojournalism, 20th Century Photography

title: Winogrand Color
description:
Winogrand Color is the first monograph devoted entirely to Garry Winogrand's color photography, work that stood almost unseen behind the black-and-white street pictures that made his name.

Between the early 1950s and late 1960s, Winogrand carried two cameras between commercial assignments, one loaded with black-and-white film and the other with color slide film. He shot more than 45,000 color frames he never printed or published in his lifetime. Editors Michael Almereyda and Susan Kismaric selected 150 images from that archive, held at the Center for Creative Photography in Tucson. The selection ranges from Manhattan sidewalks and Coney Island's boardwalk to the open spaces of the American West. The pictures share the same instinct for the unposed gesture as his black-and-white work, but the color stock, often oversaturated Kodachrome, gives ordinary postwar street scenes an unfamiliar charge.

Winogrand (1928–1984) was one of the central street photographers of his generation. He was included in John Szarkowski's 1967 New Documents exhibition at MoMA alongside Diane Arbus and Lee Friedlander. He published four monographs in his lifetime: The Animals (1969), Women Are Beautiful (1975), Public Relations (1977) and Stock Photographs (1980). Winogrand Color adds a fifth body of work to that record, more than fifty years after most of it was shot.
tags: Photography, Street Photography, Color Photography, American Photography, 20th Century Photography

title: The Animals
edition_printrun: MoMA 2004 reissue of the 1969 exhibition catalogue
description:
The Animals is Garry Winogrand's first monograph, a wry, tightly edited study of the encounters between zoo and aquarium visitors and the animals on the other side of the glass or fence.

Shot mostly at the Bronx Zoo and the Coney Island Aquarium, the photographs pair human gesture and expression against an animal counterpart with a comic, faintly unsettling symmetry: a couple's matching poses beside a pair of primates, a crowd pressed against a rail mirroring the animals pressed against their own enclosure. The Museum of Modern Art first published the book to accompany Winogrand's exhibition of the same name, on view October 24, 1969 through January 18, 1970. It carries an afterword by MoMA's photography curator John Szarkowski, who championed Winogrand's work through the 1960s and 70s. This is MoMA's 2004 hardcover reissue of that original 48-page catalogue.

Winogrand (1928–1984) had been included three years earlier in Szarkowski's landmark 1967 exhibition New Documents, alongside Diane Arbus and Lee Friedlander. The Animals became the first of four monographs he published in his lifetime, followed by Women Are Beautiful (1975), Public Relations (1977) and Stock Photographs (1980).
tags: Photography, Street Photography, American Photography, 20th Century Photography, Exhibition Catalog

title: Push the Sky Away
description:
Push the Sky Away is the debut monograph of the Polish photographer Piotr Zbierski, a triptych of interrelated series built around what he describes as an underlying structure to human existence, unchanged across cultures.

The book is organized in three sections: Dream of White Elephants, Love Has to Be Reinvented, and Stones Were Lost from the Base. It runs 238 pages, with two additional 16-page booklets inserted as dividers. Most of the 156 color and duotone photographs were made during travels through Eastern Europe and India. They favor chance encounters with strangers over documentary specificity, searching for gesture and ritual that Zbierski treats as shared inheritance rather than local custom. Patti Smith contributed a poem written in response to the pictures, and the critic Eleonora Jedlińska supplies an accompanying essay. André Frère Éditions (Marseille) published the book first, in French, in 2016; this Dewi Lewis edition brought it into English in 2017 and it was shortlisted for the Arles Author Book Award that year.

Zbierski (b. 1988, Poland) received the Leica Oskar Barnack Newcomer Award in 2012. He was included in the Regeneration3 exhibition at the Musée de l'Elysée, Lausanne, in 2015. He has continued to self-publish photobooks through his own studio, including the Sun Eater trilogy and Solid Maze.
tags: Photography, Contemporary Photography, Polish Photography, Artist Book
notes: The task brief asked to verify a title ("NIA" or similar) rather than guess; no book titled NIA by Zbierski could be found on his own site, AbeBooks, OpenLibrary, or the Getty SRU catalogue. The real, verifiable Zbierski monograph confirmed across three independent sources (Getty/Alma SRU MARC record, AbeBooks, publisher site, and the artist's own shop) is Push the Sky Away: first published in French by André Frère Éditions (Marseille, 2016, ISBN 9791092265538) and in this English edition by Dewi Lewis Publishing (2017, ISBN 9781911306078). title: Nudism in a Cold Climate
description:
A cultural history that treats naturist photography as a serious archive, not a curiosity. It tracks how a marginal social movement built and defended itself through the images it chose to publish.

The book draws on club magazines, private photo albums, and the visual propaganda of British naturist organizations. It follows the movement from its 1920s roots alongside vegetarianism and utopian health reform, through postwar growth as an organized club culture, to its shift under 1960s sexual liberalization. Pollen reads the recurring photographs of members at camps and outings as the movement's chief public-relations tool. Those images built membership. They also brought scandal. Pollen uses that tension to trace wider shifts in Britain's attitudes toward bodies, health, gender, and censorship.

Pollen is Reader in History of Art and Design at the University of Brighton. Her research centers on amateur photography, dress, and twentieth-century British subcultures. Her earlier books cover 1920s craft utopianism and the Kibbo Kift movement.
tags: Photography, British History, Archival Photography, Cultural History, Naturism

title: Wolfgang Tillmans
description:
This Hatje Cantz monograph, edited by Fondation Beyeler chief curator Theodora Vischer, catalogues Wolfgang Tillmans's 2017 exhibition at the Beyeler in Riehen, near Basel. It shares its bare title, Wolfgang Tillmans, with three earlier books already in this library. It is a wholly separate publication all the same: a different publisher, a different editor, a different exhibition.

Tillmans used the Beyeler's galleries much as he uses any wall. Prints of varying size and subject hang together, unframed, at uneven heights, so a still life sits beside an abstraction sits beside a portrait. The book follows that installation logic rather than sorting the work by series or date. Vischer's essay addresses Tillmans's approach to exhibition-making directly, treating the hang itself as part of the argument the show makes.

Tillmans was born in 1968 in Remscheid, Germany, and won the Turner Prize in 2000, the first photographer and the first non-British-born artist to do so. Two Phaidon monographs share this book's bare title: a 2002 volume and an expanded 2013 edition. This Fondation Beyeler edition falls between them, and it predates his later career-survey catalogues Sound Is Liquid, To Look Without Fear, and Nothing Could Have Prepared Us. Readers and catalogers should identify this copy by its publisher and year, Hatje Cantz 2017, to avoid confusing it with the Taschen 1995, Phaidon 2002, or Phaidon 2013 editions already on the shelf.
notes: IMPORTANT — DISTINGUISH FROM EXISTING DUPLICATE-TITLED ENTRIES: this is the Hatje Cantz / Fondation Beyeler / 2017 edition, curated and edited by Theodora Vischer, ISBN 9783775743297. The library already holds three other books titled simply 'Wolfgang Tillmans': id 1135 (Taschen, 1995), id 1150 (Phaidon, 2002), and id 1170 (Phaidon, 2013). This is a fourth, genuinely distinct publication, confirmed by cross-checking publisher and year against those three existing rows before writing this record; it must never be merged with or mistaken for any of them. A related German-language variant (ISBN 9783775743327, design by Teo Schifferli) and a 2024 French-language reprint variant (ISBN 9783775757812) also exist; the English hardcover (9783775743297) is catalogued here as the primary edition. Cover image sourced from a dealer's product photograph after an initial angled-shelf photo was rejected in favor of a flat front-cover shot; visually confirmed to show the title, a black-and-white portrait, and the Fondation Beyeler wordmark.
