The book lays out the Directive's legal text and background, the tension between the Directive and information technologies then emerging, and policy recommendations meant to avert a transatlantic trade dispute over privacy.

Swire, then a law professor at Ohio State University, had already written on cryptography and internet regulation and later served as a privacy official in the Clinton and Obama administrations. Litan directed the Economic Studies program at the Brookings Institution, which published the book in 1998.

title: The War on the Bill of Rights and the Gathering Resistance
description:
The War on the Bill of Rights and the Gathering Resistance is Nat Hentoff's account of the expansion of government surveillance and detention power after September 11, 2001. He wrote it as the USA PATRIOT Act's provisions were being implemented and a second PATRIOT Act was under discussion in Washington.

Hentoff drew on interviews with reporters, defense attorneys, civil liberties lawyers, and administration officials. He documents surveillance programs including Carnivore and the Total Information Awareness system, the use of material-witness detention, and proposals that would have suspended habeas corpus or allowed revocation of citizenship. He pairs this with an account of the opposition the Act drew from an unusually broad range of critics, including conservative members of Congress. The book closes with suggestions for readers who want to push back against the measures it describes.

Hentoff wrote a syndicated column for decades and covered the First Amendment and the Bill of Rights for the Village Voice. At the time of this book, published by Seven Stories Press in 2003, he was also a senior fellow at the Cato Institute. It followed a long run of his writing on free speech and civil liberties, including Free Speech for Me But Not for Thee.

title: Spying with Maps: Surveillance Technologies and the Future of Privacy
edition_printrun: First edition (a paperback edition followed, ISBN 9780226534282)
description:
Spying with Maps surveys the geographic surveillance technologies, satellite imagery, GPS tracking, and geographic information systems, that had by 2002 moved location monitoring from military and intelligence use into law enforcement, market research, and traffic engineering.

Monmonier explains how each technology works and who uses it before turning to the privacy questions it raises, a subject he treats as a genuinely new problem for cartography rather than as an occasion for alarm; reviewers described the book's approach to what he calls "dataveillance" as even-handed rather than as a warning of an Orwellian future. The University of Chicago Press published the hardcover in 2002 and later issued it in paperback.

Monmonier is a Distinguished Professor of Geography at Syracuse University's Maxwell School and the author of How to Lie with Maps and Bushmanders and Bullwinkles. Spying with Maps extends his long-running attention to the political uses and consequences of mapmaking into the era of satellite and location tracking.
notes: "GPS" added as a new tag; nothing in the existing fixed vocabulary covers geospatial/location tracking specifically.

title: Cryptography & Liberty 1999: An International Survey of Encryption Policy
description:
A country-by-country survey of encryption law and policy compiled by the Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC) on behalf of the Global Internet Liberty Campaign (GILC), documenting the legal status of cryptography in seventy-six national and territorial jurisdictions as of 1999.

Most countries surveyed, industrial and developing alike, imposed no controls on the use, manufacture, or sale of cryptography. The report found a broad international trend toward relaxing what restrictions did exist. It also tracked a parallel rejection of key escrow and key recovery schemes, the approach then favored by the U.S. government. France had recently dropped its own escrow requirement, and other governments were declining to adopt one. Only a small number of countries, the report noted, kept strong domestic controls on cryptographic use. The survey updated an earlier 1998 report of the same title by Wayne Madsen, David L. Sobel, Marc Rotenberg, and David Banisar, published as a law-journal article. A further edition, Cryptography and Liberty 2000, followed it.

EPIC is a Washington, D.C. public-interest research organization focused on privacy and civil liberties in the information age, founded in 1994 by Marc Rotenberg and David Sobel. Through the late 1990s it was a leading participant in the U.S. cryptography-policy debate. It opposed the Clinton administration's Clipper Chip key-escrow initiative and export controls on strong encryption, and published this survey as part of its broader case against criminalizing encryption technology.
notes: Authored/edited by EPIC staff Wayne Madsen and David Banisar (per the earlier 1998 journal-article version's byline and secondary sources on the 2000 follow-up), but published and credited on the title page as an EPIC organizational report; catalogued here under EPIC as the organizational author per the title page. No LOC or WorldCat record was located; bibliographic data is from AbeBooks (schema.org Book record) and OpenLibrary. Dimensions not found in any source consulted.

title: The First Amendment and the Fourth Estate: Communications Law for Undergraduates
description:
The second edition of a communications-law textbook Marc A. Franklin wrote for undergraduate journalism students, not law students. It surveys First Amendment doctrine and the legal problems reporters and broadcasters meet gathering and publishing news.

The book opens by reviewing the philosophical justifications for freedom of expression and the structure of the American judicial system. It then works through the legal problems journalists face gathering information and publishing what they gather. Its final chapters turn to broadcasting: the technology and regulatory structure of the industry, the licensing of broadcasters, and the content restrictions that apply to broadcast but not to print. The preface says the book organizes these problems the way working journalists and editors encounter them, not the way a law-school casebook would, and assumes no legal training. This second edition, published in 1981, revises Franklin's 1977 first edition, written with Ruth Korzenik Franklin. Robert Trager assisted on the revision.

Franklin was the Frederick I. Richman Professor of Law at Stanford University. He is best known for his long-running torts casebook with Robert Rabin. This undergraduate text grew into a separate law-school casebook, The First Amendment and the Fourth Estate: The Law of Mass Media. Franklin developed it with T. Barton Carter and Jay B. Wright, and it has run through more than a dozen editions since.
notes: No cover photograph could be confirmed. AbeBooks' schema.org record for this ISBN gives title/subtitle/author as "The First Amendment and the fourth estate: Communications law for undergraduates" / Franklin, Marc A. (matching this record). A separate AbeBooks dealer listing for the same ISBN instead credits Carter, T. Barton; Franklin, Marc A.; Wright, Jay B. That is almost certainly bookseller cross-contamination. A similarly titled, separately numbered companion casebook, "The First Amendment and the Fourth Estate: The Law of Mass Media" (Carter/Franklin/Wright), launched its own first edition the same year, 1981. OpenLibrary's MARC-derived edition record for this ISBN (by_statement "by Marc A. Franklin, assisted by Robert Trager", edition "2nd ed.", 715 pages) is used here as the more authoritative source. One dealer describes the binding as red cloth with gilt titling. That matches the 1977 first edition's binding, confirmed directly from a scanned copy, but no photograph of this specific 2nd-edition printing was located.

title: Digital Evidence and Computer Crime: Forensic Science, Computers and the Internet
description:
The first edition of Eoghan Casey's foundational digital-forensics textbook, laying out how to locate, preserve, and interpret digital evidence. It covers how computer networks figure in crimes ranging from fraud and stalking to homicide and child exploitation.

Casey wrote the book to bridge four fields he saw as inseparable in practice: law, computer science, forensic science, and behavioral evidence analysis. Chapters cover the legal framework governing digital evidence, how computers and networks function well enough to locate and recover that evidence, and how to reconstruct events at a digital crime scene. Case examples, references to the specialized literature, and a glossary of terms run throughout. Susan W. Brenner and other contributors supplied material on the legal-issues chapters. Computer networks were becoming central to a widening range of offenses when the book appeared. It was among the first attempts to treat digital evidence with the same rigor as physical forensic evidence, rather than as a specialist add-on to traditional investigation.

Casey holds a Ph.D. in computer science from University College Dublin. He has moved between digital-forensics practice and research throughout his career: as information security officer at Yale University, lead cybersecurity engineer at MITRE, chief scientist at the Department of Defense Cyber Crime Center, and, later, professor of digital forensic science at the University of Lausanne. He has testified as an expert witness in criminal and civil cases and edited the journal Digital Investigation since 2004. This book's success led him to expand it substantially in later editions and to edit the companion Handbook of Computer Crime Investigation and Handbook of Digital Forensics and Investigation.
notes: A second ISBN, 9780121631048, appears in dealer and OpenLibrary records for what is described as the same 1st-edition text (Academic Press, 279pp.) without the subtitle displayed; this may be a concurrent US/UK issue of the same edition rather than a distinct printing, but that could not be confirmed. Description above reflects the 1st edition (2000, 279pp.) specifically; later editions (2nd ed. 2004, 3rd ed. 2011/2017) were substantially expanded to roughly 800 pages with a five-part structure and additional contributors, and their content should not be conflated with this edition's.

title: The Spy's Guide: Office Espionage - How to Bug a Meeting, Booby-Trap Your Briefcase, Infiltrate the Competition, and More
description:
A tongue-in-cheek office-espionage manual that repackages real intelligence-agency tradecraft, from bugging a conference room to reassembling shredded documents, as workplace tactics for getting ahead. H. Keith Melton and television producer Craig Piligian wrote it with Duane Swierczynski, with a foreword by retired KGB Major General Oleg Kalugin.

Its premise, stated in the publisher's copy, is that information is the currency of business, and no one gathers it more effectively than spies. Illustrated, step-by-step sections cover planting bugs, tapping phones, disguising your identity at a trade show, sending untraceable e-mail, photographing confidential documents, encrypting an address book, and piecing together shredded paperwork. Each section pairs the technique with a real anecdote of the CIA, the KGB, or a Fortune 500 company using it. The tone throughout stays closer to a novelty gift book than a security manual, part of the same Quirk Books line as its companion, The Action Hero's Handbook.

Melton is a historian of espionage technology, the author of Ultimate Spy, and a board member of the International Spy Museum in Washington, D.C. The Hudson Street Library also holds his The Secret History of KGB Spy Cameras, 1945-1995, co-written with Vladimir Alekseenko. Piligian is an Emmy-winning television producer who has made several documentaries on espionage tradecraft. Swierczynski, credited as a contributing writer here, later became a bestselling and twice Edgar-nominated crime novelist.
notes: Page count is reported as 180 by one OpenLibrary edition and 165 by several bookseller listings; 165 is used here as the more consistently repeated figure, but this is not fully resolved.

title: The Well: A Story of Love, Death & Real Life in the Seminal Online Community
description:
A social history of the WELL (Whole Earth 'Lectronic Link), the San Francisco Bay Area dial-up bulletin board founded in 1985. It grew into one of the first sustained online communities, a proving ground for what people would later call internet culture.

Stewart Brand and Larry Brilliant founded the WELL and modeled it loosely on the salon. It drew journalists, programmers, Deadheads, and other early adopters into public conferences. Over years online, its members came to know each other with real intimacy. Hafner traces that history from the WELL's founding through its 1999 sale to Salon.com, expanding on a 1997 Wired cover story she wrote on the same subject. She builds the book around the on- and offline relationship between two WELL members she calls Mandel and Nana. That relationship runs through breakdown, illness, and death, and Hafner uses it to show how the boundary between a person's public online self and private life could dissolve inside the community. The book covers the WELL's triumphs and losses alike, including births, reunions, and the deaths of several members whose final illnesses played out in public on the system's message boards.

Hafner is a longtime technology reporter for The New York Times. She also wrote Where Wizards Stay Up Late: The Origins of the Internet, a history of ARPANET, and has covered cybercrime and hacking. The WELL was eclipsed in scale by the networks that followed it. Its close-knit, high-intimacy culture is still widely credited as a founding model for online community. Later writers, notably Howard Rheingold in The Virtual Community, cite it as a benchmark rarely matched by the larger, more anonymous forums that came after it.

title: GPS Made Easy: Using Global Positioning Systems in the Outdoors
description:
A non-technical guide to using handheld GPS receivers outdoors. It was revised after the U.S. government turned off Selective Availability in May 2000. That change alone improved unaided civilian accuracy from roughly 100 meters to under 10.

The book explains how the GPS satellite constellation and signal work. It surveys the features common to handheld receivers of the period. And it works through practical field examples: setting waypoints, plotting routes, and using a receiver alongside a paper topographic map in rough or featureless terrain. This third edition, marketed as "SA Revised," added material on the first two editions covering GPS with maps for hiking, kayaking, and other backcountry travel.

Lawrence Letham is an electrical engineer by training. He wrote the book for the hikers, campers, and outdoor navigators he counted himself among. GPS Made Easy went through five editions between the mid-1990s and 2008, tracking each new generation of consumer GPS technology from the pre-SA era through WAAS-corrected receivers.
notes: AbeBooks' pictures.abebooks.com image for this ISBN (9780898868029) is mismatched: it actually shows the 5th-edition cover (co-authored with Alex Letham). The cover used here instead comes from OpenLibrary's cover API for this exact ISBN and correctly shows the third-edition, SA-revised cover.

title: The Essential Guide to Wireless Communications Applications: From Cellular Systems to Wi-Fi
description:
A nontechnical survey of consumer and business wireless technology, aimed at engineers, marketers, and investors. This second edition updates the book for 2002, past the WAP-and-m-commerce moment of the 2000 first edition.

Chapters cover wireless economics and industry structure, buying guidance for cellular phones and service plans, and setting up and securing wireless LANs. Others cover mobile commerce and payment systems, the leading handheld operating systems of the day (BlackBerry, Pocket PC, Palm, Tablet PC), and public concern over the health effects of wireless communications. The book arrived as 3G and 3.5G cellular networks, WLANs, and wireless optics were reaching a general business readership, not just engineers.

Andy Dornan was a senior editor covering wireless technology at Network Magazine in San Francisco. He has written on wireless and network security for Wired, Red Herring, and Dark Reading. This book followed his earlier Essential Guide to RF and Wireless.
notes: Page count varies by listing: OpenLibrary's edition record for this ISBN gives 448pp; an AbeBooks listing for the same ISBN gives 414pp. The first edition (2000, ISBN 9780130317162, subtitled "From Cellular Systems to WAP and M-Commerce") is a distinct, earlier edition from the one catalogued here.

title: Loose Lips
description:
A comic novel of CIA tradecraft training, published in 2003. It follows a young recruit through the agency's clandestine-service program at "the Farm."

Selena Keller is an unemployed New Yorker with a doctorate in Oriental studies and no clear career ahead of her. On a whim, she sends her resume to the CIA. An Agency recruiter asks her how she would feel about persuading another human being to commit treason. She passes the background investigation, the polygraph, and a battery of psychological aptitude tests, then begins an eighteen-month training program while living under cover as a government budget analyst. At the Farm she falls for a fellow trainee, Stan, a brilliant and increasingly paranoid classmate with presidential ambitions. The novel mixes satire, romance, and procedural detail on tradecraft and agency culture. On publication it was praised as an unusually candid, funny account of CIA training life, written from a woman's point of view.

Claire Berlinski is an American journalist and novelist educated at Balliol College, Oxford, where she took a doctorate in international relations. Loose Lips was her debut novel. She later published a second spy novel, Lion Eyes, alongside nonfiction political books including There Is No Alternative: Why Margaret Thatcher Matters and Menace in Europe.
notes: Berlinski has not held a CIA position herself; the novel draws on research and reporting rather than personal agency employment. A later paperback (Ballantine Books, ISBN 9780812967098) reissued the same text as "Loose Lips: A Novel."

title: Alvin's Secret Code
description:
The second Alvin Fernald novel, published in 1963 with line illustrations by Bill Sokol. Twelve-year-old Alvin and his friend Shoie turn a self-taught grounding in codes and ciphers into a full treasure hunt.

The two boys, calling themselves secret agents, intercept a coded message and cannot break it themselves. They seek out Mr. Link, a retired code expert, who teaches them cipher wheels, the scytale, and other classical methods. The arrival of a woman in distress and a mysterious stranger draws Alvin, Shoie, and Alvin's younger sister into a hundred-year-old town mystery and a scheme against a local orphanage. It ends in a hunt for buried treasure, which Alvin's "Magnificent Brain" resolves through his own improvised cipher. An appendix at the back lays out the codes, ciphers, and code wheel used in the story for readers to try themselves.

Clifford B. Hicks was a Popular Mechanics editor and a Silver Star-decorated Marine veteran of World War II. He introduced Alvin Fernald in 1960 with The Marvelous Inventions of Alvin Fernald. Alvin's Secret Code was the second of what grew into a long-running series, later adapted into two Disney television movies.
tags: Children's Books, Codes and Ciphers, Puzzles

title: The First Book of Codes and Ciphers
description:
An introductory primer on codes and ciphers for young readers, published in 1956 as part of Franklin Watts's "First Book" series, with drawings by Laszlo Roth. It opens by distinguishing the two methods of secret writing it covers throughout: a code, which substitutes symbols for whole words or phrases, and a cipher, which substitutes symbols for individual letters.

Short chapters move from a reader's first attempt at a simple substitution code through the Caesar cipher, a backward cipher, and a cipher the authors identify in the Bible. Later chapters cover number ciphers, the semaphore and Morse codes, the ogam script of the Celts, and the breaking of a Spanish king's cipher. Others take up the Rosetta Stone, invisible inks, business codes, and codes used in detective fiction. The book closes with an answer key and index. Contemporary listings describe it as issued in gray buckram boards with the title lettered on the spine and front board.

Sam and Beryl Epstein were a husband-and-wife writing team. From 1938 onward they published more than 120 children's nonfiction titles and biographies together, including many entries in Franklin Watts's First Book series. Under several joint pseudonyms they also wrote the Ken Holt mystery series.
tags: Children's Books, Codes and Ciphers, Puzzles
notes: No ISBN: pre-dates the ISBN system (introduced 1970). Page count is reported inconsistently across dealer listings (59 vs. 62 pages); 62 is used here per an AbeBooks listing citing an explicit page count. Full text is digitized at the Internet Archive (identifier codesciphers00seps_vt0), which is also the source of the cover image used here since no dealer listing for this title carried a usable cover photo.

title: The Clue in the Crossword Cipher
description:
Book forty-four in the Nancy Drew Mystery Stories series, first published in 1967. It sends Nancy to Peru to decode a cipher carved into an ancient wooden plaque, before a smuggling ring can reach the treasure it points to.

Carla Ponce, a young woman living in Peru, invites Nancy, Bess, and George to help solve her family's "monkey mystery." It centers on a wooden plaque bearing a crossword cipher that time has largely worn away. A gang led by a smuggler known as El Gato steals the plaque, so Nancy has to recover it before she can even begin decoding it. Her investigation carries her to the Incan ruins at Cuzco and Machu Picchu. There she and her friends help break up the smuggling ring and turn up an archaeological find of their own.

Carolyn Keene is the house pseudonym the Stratemeyer Syndicate, and later Grosset & Dunlap and Simon & Schuster, used across the entire Nancy Drew series. Individual volumes were written by a rotating set of ghostwriters under contract, beginning with Mildred Wirt Benson on the earliest titles. This catalogue follows its own convention for house pseudonyms and credits the byline as printed, not an individual ghostwriter.
tags: Children's Books, Codes and Ciphers, Puzzles
notes: Reported page counts vary by printing (177-192pp across dealer listings); 192 is used here per the publisher's own current listing. "Carolyn Keene" is a Stratemeyer Syndicate house pseudonym, not an individual person; per this catalogue's existing convention for house pseudonyms (e.g. "NA VA" for Various Artists), the printed byline is credited as-is rather than substituted with a ghostwriter's name.

author_full_name: Kenneth W. Dam, Herbert S. Lin
title: Cryptography's Role in Securing the Information Society
editor: Kenneth W. Dam, Herbert S. Lin
contributors: Committee to Study National Cryptography Policy (Committee); Computer Science and Telecommunications Board, National Research Council (Issuing body)
description:
Congress asked a committee with security clearances whether the United States should go on restricting cryptography. This is the book-length answer, and it came back no.

The 1994 defense authorization act mandated the study. The National Research Council's Computer Science and Telecommunications Board published it in 1996, edited by Kenneth W. Dam and Herbert S. Lin for the Committee to Study National Cryptography Policy. The members were cleared to read the classified material, then wrote an unclassified report. It runs to 720 pages. It explains how cryptography works, weighs what encryption would cost law enforcement and signals intelligence, and traces how export control had shaped what American companies could sell abroad. A long section reviews the Escrowed Encryption Standard, known outside government as the Clipper chip. The conclusions are blunt. Relax export controls, and pass no law restricting the domestic use of encryption.

Both recommendations were resisted and then largely adopted. Export rules loosened in 1996 and again at the end of the decade, and key escrow was abandoned. The report holds its value for how it argued: in the open, on the record, with the classified evidence in hand. Little else from the crypto wars can say the same.
notes: DOI 10.17226/5131. Committee to Study National Cryptography Policy, Computer Science and Telecommunications Board, National Research Council.

title: Cryptography: A Primer
description:
One of the first American textbooks to treat cryptography as ordinary applied mathematics rather than as a government subject.

Alan Konheim wrote it out of IBM Research, where the Data Encryption Standard had been developed a few years earlier, and Wiley published it in 1981. The book is more rigorous than its title suggests: probability and the statistics of language come first, then substitution and transposition systems worked through as mathematics rather than as puzzles, then rotor machines, then DES in detail, and finally the public-key work of the preceding five years. Exercises run through all 432 pages.

Konheim went on to teach computer science at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and returned to the material in Computer Security and Cryptography (2007). The primer belongs to the short shelf of books, with Kahn's history and Dorothy Denning's Cryptography and Data Security of 1982, that carried the subject into university teaching in the years when the open literature on it was still small enough to read.

title: Cryptography: The Science of Secret Writing
description:
The wartime primer that taught a generation of American amateurs to read and write ciphers, and stayed in print long enough to teach several more.

Norton published it in 1943, at a point when cryptography had a large civilian audience and almost no published literature to serve it. Smith works upward from concealment devices and simple substitution through Playfair, Vigenere and transposition systems to the mechanics of breaking them by frequency analysis, then sets problems and prints the answers at the back, which is what the jacket subtitle promises. 164 pages, grey cloth under a black and red jacket carrying a Polybius square.

Dover reprinted the book and kept it available for decades, which is how most readers met it; copies in the original Norton jacket are less common. On a shelf of this kind it sits beside Helen Fouche Gaines's Elementary Cryptanalysis of 1939 as one of the two self-teaching texts an interested amateur could actually get hold of before David Kahn's The Codebreakers opened the subject up in 1967.
tags: Codes and Ciphers, Cryptography, Cryptanalysis, Puzzles
notes: First edition. Cover image is a bookseller's photograph of another copy in the original jacket, not this copy.

title: The Principles of Mathematics
description:
Russell's first full argument that mathematics is logic, and the book in which he published the paradox that brought down Frege's system.

He wrote it between 1900 and 1902, and it was published in 1903. The case is made in prose rather than symbols: the whole of pure mathematics follows from a small number of logical premises. Appendix B states the contradiction of the class of all classes that are not members of themselves. That is Russell's paradox, and the same appendix sketches the theory of types he and Whitehead would later build out in Principia Mathematica. This is the second edition. George Allen & Unwin issued it in 1937 with a new introduction, in which Russell reconsiders the argument after thirty-five years and says how much of it he no longer holds. The copy here is the seventh impression.

Russell (1872-1970) wrote it before the Principia, before the Nobel and before the political work. He had lately read Peano and was rebuilding the subject from its premises. It is filed in this wing as the foundational end of a shelf that runs on into cipher manuals: the formal machinery that mathematical cryptography, and computing after it, was assembled from.
notes: Second edition (1937), seventh impression. Pre-ISBN.

title: Super Crunchers: Why Thinking-by-Numbers Is the New Way to Be Smart
description:
Ian Ayres's argument that large datasets and regression analysis now beat expert intuition at prediction, made just as statistical decision-making was moving out of the back office.

Ayres builds the case from worked examples. Orley Ashenfelter's weather equation prices Bordeaux vintages before anyone tastes them, and a formula for gestation length outperforms Naegele's rule. Other chapters take up sabermetric scouting, box-office forecasting, randomised A/B testing of advertisements, and the DISTAR teaching method. Two tools run through all of them, multiple regression and the randomised trial. Ayres treats these as the working method of the people he calls super crunchers. He also weighs the costs. An equation that overrules a specialist creates winners and losers, and the same techniques can be turned against the people they are meant to serve. Bantam published it in 2007. The Economist named it a book of the year, and the American Library Association listed it among its Notable Books.

Ayres is an economist and lawyer, the William K. Townsend Professor at Yale Law School and a professor at Yale's School of Management. He edited the Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization for seven years and was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2006. Super Crunchers is the best known of his ten books. It appeared two years after Freakonomics, whose co-author Steven D. Levitt supplied the endorsement printed across the jacket.
tags: Data, Statistics, Decision Making, Economics, Prediction
notes: Two distinct editions of the same text were published in 2007 under different subtitles. The US edition is this one, Bantam, Super Crunchers: Why Thinking-by-Numbers Is the New Way to Be Smart (hardcover 9780553805406; Bantam trade paperback 9780553384734 followed in 2008 with a different, red jacket). The UK edition came from John Murray as Super Crunchers: How Anything Can Be Predicted (hardcover 9780719564635, paperbacks 9780719564659 and 9780719564642). AbeBooks and OpenLibrary agree on that split. The US Bantam edition is catalogued here as instructed. The two jackets look nothing alike, so the copy on the shelf can be told apart by sight. Subjects (LOC): Statistics; Regression analysis; Sampling (Statistics); Human behavior -- Mathematical models; Decision making -- Methodology.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, January 1984
description:
The first year of 2600, twelve monthly issues beginning in January 1984, when the magazine was a few photocopied sheets of telephone network intelligence edited by Emmanuel Goldstein.

The debut carries "AHOY! - 2600 Debuts" alongside "FBI Goes After ADS Hackers" and "The Truth Behind Those 9999 Numbers." Across the year the newsletter prints a White House phone list, guides to Telenet, MCI and Telemail, MILNET host tables, CN/A and E-Com dialups, and "Arpanet Hopping: America's Newest Pastime." "ESS: Orwell's Prophecy" and "TRW: Big Business is Watching You" state the surveillance argument the magazine has made ever since. Hardware begins with "Introducing the Clear Box!"; "Some Thoughts on 'Garbage Picking'" and "More on Trashing" make dumpster diving a standing subject. Later issues add "The Hacker's Guide To An Area Code," "History of British Phreaking," "Vital Ingredients: Switching Centers and Operators" and "Fun With Fortress Fones."

AT&T's breakup took effect on 1 January 1984, the month 2600 began, and the volume reads as running commentary on it: "The Dark and Tragic Side of the Great Break-up," "Whose Strike Was That Anyway?" and "Be Nice To Your Telco." MCI's lawyers wrote to the magazine before the year was out, an exchange printed as "MCI Mail Targets 2600."
notes: The twelve 1984 issues are 2600's own reproduction of the first year, sold by the magazine at its HOPE conferences. They are not 1984 printings.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, January 1985
description:
The second year, in which 2600's own bulletin board was seized in a federal raid and the newsletter turned to defending the people it wrote for.

Early issues announce the 2600 Bulletin Board online. By mid-year the headline is "2600 Bulletin Board Seized in Raid on Hackers," printed beside "Sherwood Forest Shut Down by Secret Service" and "The Threat To Us All." Operating systems carry the technical run: "Interesting Things To Do on a DEC-20," a two-part guide to VMS, "RSTS: A Trick or Two" and "Surveying the COSMOS." "The Theory of Blue Boxing" and "What a White Box Can Do" cover the hardware. "The Cipher Disk" is the newsletter's first piece of cryptography, and "A Guide to the Israeli Phone System" starts the foreign-system series. Bill Landreth's Out of the Inner Circle is reviewed, and the year closes with a list of more than 1,500 BBS numbers.

"Some Words on Hacker Morality" and "And They Call US Crooks?" put the ethical case; "Some Important Questions To Ask" is practical advice for readers expecting a visit. "The Infinity Transmitter - An Old Bug" and "The Early Phreak Days" begin the newsletter's habit of writing its own prehistory.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, January 1986
description:
The third year, which opens with the Private Sector board coming back online and closes on cellular telephony, the technology that would occupy the magazine for the next decade.

"Private Sector Returning" leads the year, followed by "Divestiture: What Happened?" two years after the AT&T break-up. Construction and code run throughout: blue box programs, "An Overview of AUTOVON and Silver Boxes," "Mobile Phones - Theory & Construction," "Boxing on ITT" and "Cellular Telephones - How They Work." Systems coverage finishes the VMS series and adds "RSTS For Beginners," "Knowing UNIX," "How To Hack a Pick" and "Violating a Vax." The newsletter also prints "Exploits in Operator Hell," "A Story of Eavesdropping," "The Free Phones of Philly," "Death of a Pay Phone" and "Trashing: America's Source for Information," with number lists for Winnipeg, London and Britain's boards.

Two reviews record how the subject was being written about elsewhere, The Computer Underground and a computer crime review. "The Computel Scoop" opens a story the newsletter finished the following year, and "Things We're Not Supposed To Know About" closes the volume.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, January 1987
description:
The fourth and last monthly year, twelve issues that end with 2600 about to become the quarterly it has been ever since.

"TAP: The Legend is Dead" opens the volume with the end of the newsletter 2600 had succeeded. COSMOS gets a guide and a second article, and Telenet, TSPS and equal access get guides of their own. "Hacking PC Pursuit," "More Vax Tricks," "IBM's VM/CMS System" and "Capturing Passwords" carry the systems coverage. The telephone material widens well beyond North America: "Phoning From Europe," "English Dial-it Service," Saudi Arabian and South African BBS lists, and an AT&T submarine cable map. "The Ballad of Captain Crunch" and an interview with Hugo Cornwall fill out the year. "Cellular Fraud," "How Phreaks are Caught" and "FBI Revealed" run alongside "New York Telephone Exposed."

"Computel Put to Sleep" ends the story begun in 1986. From Spring 1988 the newsletter became a digest-sized quarterly magazine, and the monthly sheets of the first four volumes were never resumed.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1988
description:
The first volume published quarterly: four digest-sized issues in place of twelve monthly sheets, the format 2600 has kept for the thirty-eight years since.

Spring runs "Monitoring Phone Calls," "The Hacker Threat," "A ROLM Catastrophe," "Private Sector Scam Revisited" and AT&T/BOC routing codes. Summer prints "A Solution To Viruses" beside "How To Write a Virus," together with "Building a Red Box," "Allnet's Legal Problems" and a reply to Captain Zap. Autumn covers outside loop information, cellular phones, a map of the 516 area code and a red box program, and asks "Who Was Strowger?" Winter opens with "The Internet Worm Story," the magazine's account of the worm that had taken down much of the network that November, and adds a hacker's guide to UNIX, "Overhearing Phone Calls," "Soviet Operators," "Hardwiring Free Calls" and a report on the Chaos Computer Club.

Red boxes arrive in the catalogue here, with construction plans in Summer and a program in Autumn. The magazine returned to the subject for the next fifteen years, through "The Ten Dollar Red Box" in 1994 and "Why Redboxing Still Works (sorta)" in 2003.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1989
description:
The 1989 volume, which follows the arrest and prosecution of hackers on both sides of the Atlantic while continuing to document the network they worked in.

Spring opens with "Hackers in Jail" and runs "The Wonders of UNIX," "800 & 900 Exchanges" and "Payphones Explained." Summer prints the first half of a guide to PRIMOS, "Scanning For Calls," "Tips on Trashing," "A Sprint Story," "Spanish Phones" and "A Summer Worm," with reviews of the Pirate Radio Directory and the revived TAP. Autumn covers the NYNEX strike, "British Telecom's Guilty Conscience," "The Death of COSMOS?," "The Secrets of 4TEL," REMOBS, voice mail hacking and "Punching Payphones." Winter carries "The AT&T Story," NYNEX central office data, the second half of the PRIMOS guide and instructions for building a silver box.

Autumn's report on the Galactic Hacker Party, held in Amsterdam that August, is the magazine's first coverage of a large European hacker gathering, a connection it kept through the Dutch camps of the following decades.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Winter 1989-1990
description:

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1990
description:
The 1990 volume, published through the year of the E911 document prosecution and the founding of the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

Spring prints "The 911 Document," the file at the centre of the government's case, next to "How Blue Boxers Are Caught," "Facts About MIZAR," a touch tone decoder project and a review of Clifford Stoll's The Cuckoo's Egg. Summer covers "The Neidorf/Phrack Trial" with an interview with Craig Neidorf and an explanation of the new Electronic Frontier Foundation, under the editorial "A Bittersweet Victory." Autumn turns to Caller ID, with "Defeating Trap Tracing," "The Definitive ANAC Guide," a credit card algorithm and an interview with the cryptographer Dorothy Denning. Winter runs "A Political Hacking Scandal," "The Hacker Reading List," more leaked documents and an anatomy of the 1-900-STOPPER service.

"Fun at the 2600 Meeting" in the Spring issue is an early account of the monthly public meetings the magazine organises, a fixture of its back pages from this period onward.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1991
description:
The 1991 volume, whose Autumn issue printed "Simplex Locks: Illusion of Security," the article that put a mechanical lock among the magazine's cover subjects and drew replies for the next twenty years.

Spring reports the sentencing of Len Rose in "The Terminus of Len Rose," with an Atari virus, a Soviet BBS list, a UNIX password hacker, internet outdials and "The New LEC Order." Summer asks "Where Have All The Hackers Gone?" and covers magnetic stripes, MCIMAX, a tone tracer project, "More on the CLASS Struggle" and a review of Katie Hafner and John Markoff's Cyberpunk. Autumn adds "Dutch Hacker Intrusion," "Protecting Your SSN," "Postal Hacking," "Psychology in the Hacker World" and useful UNIX programs. Winter runs the crypt() source, class features, a COCOT column, mobile frequencies, "Gulf War Printer Virus," "Major Telco Privacy Hole" and "Human Database Centers."

The Simplex piece produced a Simplex and USPS update in the same volume and a full sequel two decades later, "Simplex Locks: Illusion of Security, Version 2.0," in the Winter 2011 issue.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1992
description:
The 1992 volume, in which viruses take up as much space as the telephone network and the magazine reviews both Sneakers and Bruce Sterling's The Hacker Crackdown.

Spring prints an MS-DOS virus, a batch virus, "Virus Scanners Revealed," "Hacking WWIV," "How To Take Apart a Payphone," "The Australian Phone System," "Catching Peepers" and a review of Steve Jackson's Hacker card game. Summer covers portable hacking, a hitchhiker's guide to boxing, a demon dialer review, "Defeating *69," "The View of a Fed" and voice mail hacking. Autumn adds "Hacking AmiExpress," "Defeating Callback Verification," a shopper's guide to COCOTs, a simple C virus and "Toll Fraud." Winter runs "Hackers in a World of Malls," "Cipher Fun," a beginner's guide to Minitel, vehicle identification numbers, a list of Secret Service sites and a letter from prison.

Steve Jackson Games had been raided by the Secret Service two years earlier, which is why a card game gets a technical review here. The Autumn review of The Hacker Crackdown covers the book written about that raid and the prosecutions around it.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1993
description:
The 1993 volume, published while the Secret Service was on trial over the Steve Jackson Games raid and the magazine's attention was moving to cellular telephony and cable.

Spring runs "Cellular Magic," "Trouble in the White House," beige box construction, "Descrambling Cable," "Secret Service on Trial," "A Study of Hackers" and "Getting Your File." Summer prints a guide to the 5ESS switch, "British Credit Holes," "High School Hacking," a DTMF decoder review, meeting advice and a toll fraud device. Autumn covers the Hacking at the End of the Universe camp, "The Wheel Cipher," Caller ID technicalities, "Hacking Honesty Tests," password cracking software, "Changing Your Grades," an overview of DSS1 and a review of Approaching Zero. Winter adds "Hackers in Jail, Part Two," "Cellular Phone Biopsy," "Elementary Switching," "Hacking Smartphone," NYNEX voice mail and digital locks.

Hacking at the End of the Universe, held on a Dutch campsite that August, is the second of the outdoor European gatherings the magazine covered, after the Galactic Hacker Party of 1989.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1994
description:
The 1994 volume, whose Summer issue reports the first Hackers On Planet Earth conference, the New York gathering 2600 organised that August and has run at intervals ever since.

Spring opens with "Crime Waves" and prints a DTMF decoder, NYNEX cards, "Hacking Health," "Software Piracy," facts on the Freedom of Information Act, blue boxing on CCITT System 5, "The Chrome Box" and reviews of Secrets of a Super Hacker and a UNIX security title. Summer covers HOPE itself along with "Life Under GTD5," "The Joys of Voice Mail," "Finger Follies," "Hacking Prodigy," keystroke monitoring and "Detecting Corporate Leaks." Autumn runs "Opening Doors," "Monitoring U.S. Mail," "Irish Telephones," "Hacking Netcash," "Generating an ESN," "The Ten Dollar Red Box" and "Breaking Windows." Winter reports the passage of the Digital Telephony bill and adds "Bypassing Protec," "The Risks of War Dialing," cellular hardware and "Janitor Privileges."

The Secrets of a Super Hacker reviewed in the Spring issue is the Loompanics manual published under the name The Knightmare, a copy of which is shelved in this wing.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1995
description:
The 1995 volume, dominated by two arrests: Kevin Mitnick in February and Ed Cummings, known to readers as Bernie S., a month later.

Spring leads with "The World vs. Kevin Mitnick" and runs "The Gold Card," ATM camera security, cellular interception techniques, "Hacking in Brazil," a 500 exchange guide and a review of Masters of Deception. Summer opens "The Bernie S. Saga" and adds new antiviral technologies, "The Gender Snooper," ATM tricks, "Hacking AS/400," war dialing and a second piece on cable denial. Autumn prints "No More Secrets," stealth trojans, "Military Madness," Macintosh key capturing, a COCOT resource guide, the mutation engine demystified, an ISDN overview and reviews of the films The Net and Hackers. Winter covers "What Happens on the AT&T Side," "A Spoofing Odyssey," "Infiltrating Disney," Ethernet sniffing, Verifone machines and the books The Fugitive Game and Takedown.

Both arrests became long campaigns in the magazine, and coverage of them continued in every volume for the rest of the decade.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1996
description:
The 1996 volume, the year the magazine's subject shifted from dial-up systems to the web, marked by the Spring editorial "Caught in the Web" and the Autumn "PHF Exploit."

Spring runs "Tap Alert," "Unshredding the Evidence," "Confessions of a Beige Boxer," "Hacking Caller ID Boxes," "The Alaskan Phone System," a Motorola cellular guide and "Avoiding Suspicion." Summer covers "Flood Warning," "Scanning Australia," "How To Create Encryption," RCONSOLE hacking, "Flightlink Fun," "Starting a Hacker Scene" and "And Justice For All." Autumn prints "Searches and Arrests," "Hacking the SCC OS," the Brazilian phone system, GTE voice prompts, "Hack Your High School," federal BBS lists, "Building the Cheese Box," "Spoofing Cellular Service" and "The Weird World of AOL." Winter adds "Toward More Secrets," "Chipcards Explained," "Craft Access Terminal," "Cracking AskSam," "Snooping Via MS-Mail," "Social Engineering Via Video" and "Defeating the W95 Screensaver."

"Starting a Hacker Scene" in the Summer issue is an early piece of organising advice. The magazine came back to it in the Summer 2008 issue with "Thirteen Years of Starting a Hacker Scene."

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1997
description:
The 1997 volume, which follows the arrival of GSM and cable modems in North America while the campaign for Kevin Mitnick runs through every issue.

Spring prints "Hacking LED Signs," "Use Your Skills to Escape Boot Camp," "Poor Man's Access," "Consequences of .gov/.mil Hacking," "Credit Card Numbers Via Calculators," cellular programming data, "How To Hack Tech Support," a letter from prison and "How To Legally Use a Red Box." Summer covers cable modem security holes, "GSM Comes to North America," "The Wonders of Net2Phone," "Those Pesky Mylar Strips," "Fortezza: The Next Clipper?," "Tricks and Treats of the Autovon" and "The Ins and Outs of Metrocard Gold." Autumn runs "How To Get Busted by the Feds," "Hacking Fedex," "Brute Forcing the World," "Hacking the Vote," "The EZPass System" and "Secrets of Walmart." Winter adds "The Medical Information Bureau," "TCP/IP Basics and Shortcomings," "The Ominous GETS," "The Potential of Mobil Speedpass," "The Argentinian Phone System" and "Spying on Yahoo."

The MetroCard and E-ZPass articles begin the magazine's long attention to transit fare systems, which runs on through "New York City's MTA Exposed" in 2005 and "Hacking NYC MTA Kiosks" in 2021.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1998
description:
The 1998 volume, whose Autumn issue carries a tutorial on Back Orifice, released by the Cult of the Dead Cow at DEF CON that August.

Spring covers the Defense Switched Network, "More on Military Phones" and "The Mysteries of SIPRnet." It also runs "Eggdropping," "Defeating Cyberpatrol," "A Brief History of Postal Hacking" and "Setting Up UNIX Trapdoors." Summer prints "Where Long Distance Charges Come From," a newbie guide to NT 4.0 and a modem diverter project. "The Tyranny of Project LUCID," "Millenium Payphones" and "How To Hack Your ISP" follow. Autumn adds homemade TCP packets, socket programming, "How To Probe A Remote Network" and "Cushioned Encryption and Deniability." Three articles follow on getting the better of Blockbuster, Moviefone and Radio Shack. Winter runs a touch memory primer, "The Facts of SSN," "Become a Radio Ninja," "Why Anonymous Phone Cards Aren't" and "The Cryptography of Today."

SIPRnet is followed across four volumes, from "The Mysteries of SIPRnet" in this Spring issue to "Still More on Siprnet" in Spring 2000.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 1999
description:
The 1999 volume, in which nmap, Netbus and Tripwire arrive in the pages beside the payphone and scanner articles the magazine had been running for fifteen years.

Spring covers vehicle tracking with AVI and ETTM, "Cracking the Time-Banc System," "Wreaking Havoc with Netbus," internet peering, "Fun with Tripwire," "A Hacker's Guide to Getting Busted," an overview of SS7, network scanning with nmap and hacking a Sony PlayStation. Summer prints "Securing Your Linux Box," "Fun at Costco," "Broad Band via the Earth," "Secrets of Copy Protection," two facing articles on parents spying on their children, "The Future of IPV6" and pushbutton lock hacking. Autumn runs "Upload Bombing," "The Terrorist of Orange, Texas," ITS prison phones, "Infiltrating Mediaone," forging ping packets, "Quantum Hacking," Protel COCOTs and an overview of Cellemetry. Winter adds "Accessing Forbidden NTFS Drives," "DATUs - The Tool of the New Age Phreak," "I Own Your Car!," POCSAG and FLEX interception, "Hack The Media" and "Why Redboxing Doesn't Work."

"Why Redboxing Doesn't Work" closes an argument the magazine had run since 1988. "Why Redboxing Still Works (sorta)" answered it four years later.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2000
description:
The 2000 volume, published while 2600 was itself the defendant in the case the major film studios brought over the DVD descrambling code DeCSS.

Spring runs "A Taste of Freedom," "How to Stay a Sysadmin," "Military Computer Secrets," "All About Securid," "AT&T's Gaping Hole," "How PSX Copy Protection Works," "How to Build a Coffee Box" and "How Does That DSS Card Really Work?" Summer covers system profiling, biometrics, "Strange Abuses For Your Home Phone," packet analysis, "Secrets of Dell," "How Domains Are Stolen," Java applet hacking and an interview with Jello Biafra. Autumn, under the editorial "A Summer of Trials," prints "DeCSS in Words," kernel modification with LKMs, "Hunting the Paper Carnivore," anomaly detection systems, "Accessing Federal Court Records" and "Build a Car Computer." Winter adds BellSouth's Mobitex network, Sub7, "Get Anyone's Credit Report For Free," "The DVD Paper Chain," "Hacking an NT Domain from the Desktop" and "Jury Nullification and The Hacker."

Universal City Studios v. Reimerdes was tried in New York that July and decided in August. "DeCSS in Words" and "The DVD Paper Chain" were both written under the injunction that came out of it.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2001
description:
The 2001 volume, whose Autumn issue, headed "Consequences," is the magazine's first after 11 September.

Spring prints "Police Searches of Computers," "The Future of PKI" and "Breaking the Windows Script Encoder," with "The Billboard Liberation Front" and "Declawing Your :CueCat." Summer covers "What is Carnivore, Really?" and "Everything Your Parents Told You About ESS was a Lie," alongside pieces on TCP wrappers, password authentication myths and "Snooping the Stack." Autumn runs "Passport Hacking," "How to Decrypt DirecTV," "Code Red 2" and "The Ultimate DRM Hack." It also carries "Defeating Intrusion Detection Systems," an introduction to ARP spoofing and "Hacking Kodak Picture Maker." Winter adds the security of the Inferno OS, "The Future of Enhanced 911," "Building a Floppy Based Router," "Build a Wooden Computer" and "Examining Student Databases."

The CueCat barcode reader, given away free to magazine subscribers that year, is taken apart here and again in Summer 2004 in "Passwords on a Cue Cat."

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2002
description:
The 2002 volume, in which 802.11b wireless networking becomes a subject of its own and the magazine begins tracking the surveillance law passed after 11 September.

Spring runs "Transaction Based Systems," "How to Regain Privacy on the Net," "Stupid Google Tricks" and "The Definitive Guide to Phreak Boxes." "CampusWide Wide Open" and "Defeating Network Address Translation" follow. Summer prints "The Comprehensive Guide to 802.11B Wireless Networks" and "How to Break Through a Proxy or Firewall," with "The Afghan Phone System" and "Getting Into Cisco Routers." Autumn covers "Lawfully Authorized Electronic Surveillance," "The Mysterious World of the Lerg" and "A History of '31337SP34K'," plus a review of Kevin Mitnick's The Art of Deception. Winter adds "Passport Hacking Revisited," "Warspying," "Honeypots: Building the Better Hacker," "Cracking Voter Fraud," "Linux on the Xbox" and "Exposing the Coinstar Network."

The Autumn editorial is "Freedom's Biggest Enemy." Together with "A New Era of Telecommunications Surveillance" in Summer and the Winter piece on the proposed CBDTPA, it sets out the legislative argument the magazine pursued for the decade.

Summer prints "The Comprehensive Guide to 802.11B Wireless Networks" and "How to Break Through a Proxy or Firewall," with "The Afghan Phone System" and "Getting Into Cisco Routers." Autumn covers "Lawfully Authorized Electronic Surveillance," "The Mysterious World of the Lerg" and "A History of '31337SP34K'," plus a review of Kevin Mitnick's The Art of Deception. Winter adds "Passport Hacking Revisited," "Warspying," "Honeypots: Building the Better Hacker," "Cracking Voter Fraud," "Linux on the Xbox" and "Exposing the Coinstar Network."

The Autumn editorial is "Freedom's Biggest Enemy." Together with "A New Era of Telecommunications Surveillance" in Summer and the Winter piece on the proposed CBDTPA, it sets out the legislative argument the magazine pursued for the decade.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2003
description:
The 2003 volume, published through the invasion of Iraq, opening with the editorial "Not in Our Name" and an article by a hacker sent there.

Spring runs "ANI and Caller ID Spoofing," "A Hacker Goes to Iraq" and "Getting Busted - Military Style," with "Fun with 802.11b at Kroger's" and "Best Buy Insecurities." Summer covers "Traversing the Corporate Firewall," "Staying Anonymous in the Information Age" and hardware key logging. It also prints "Microphones, Laptops, and Supertaps," "McWireless Exposed" and "Why Redboxing Still Works (sorta)." Autumn takes in "Getting to Know Your Neighbors," "Servers on a Ghetto ISP," "Case Mods Made Easy" and "More Xbox Fun and Mischief." "The Hacker Diet" and "The Threat of Biometrics" close the issue. Winter adds "Hacking the Genome," "Living Without an SSN," "WEP: Not For Me," "War Driving with a Pocket PC," "Verizon's Call Intercept" and "Unlocking GSM Handsets."

Wireless runs through the whole volume, from the supermarket article in Spring to three war driving and WEP pieces in Winter, and it is the volume's largest single subject.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2004
description:
The twentieth anniversary volume, opening with the editorial "Twenty Years After" and running the magazine's widest spread yet of articles on ordinary commercial systems.

Spring covers "Taking Advantage of Physical Access," "Hacking the Hilton," "Cruise Cracking" and "Hacking a Mercedes Benz with a Universal Remote." It also runs "Barcode Tricks," "Installing Debian on your Unmodded Xbox" and "Setting Your Music Free: iTunes Music Sans DRM." Summer prints "Scumware, Spyware, Adware, Sneakware," "Impromptu Lock Picks," "Magstripe Interfacing - A Lost Art" and "Passwords on a Cue Cat," with "A Guide to Internet Piracy." Autumn runs "Anti-Forensics: Make Secrets Stay Secret," "Digital CDMA Cloning," "Bit Torrent - The Future of the Internet?," "Hacking Soda Machines" and "Warwalking in Times Square." Winter adds "Hacking CDMA PRLs," "Catching Credit Card Fraud through Steganography," "Hacking LaGard ComboGard Locks," "Hacking Ticketmaster" and "Building Cheap ID Cards."

The Fifth HOPE was held in New York that July, fifth in the conference series 2600 began in 1994.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2005
description:
The 2005 volume, which opens with "New York City's MTA Exposed" and spends the year on Google, voice over IP, and the systems running inside chain stores.

Spring runs "Electronic Application Insecurity," "Voice Over Internet Protocol," "Hacking Cisco IP Phones" and "Hunting Wifi Leeches." It also prints "HP Printers: The Hidden Threat," "Magnetic Stripe Reading" and "Inside the Emergency Alert System." Summer is largely Google: "Hacking Google AdWords," "Hacking Google Map's Satellite Imagery" and "Googlejacking by Example," beside "Home Depot's Lousy Security" and "Spying on the Library." Autumn covers data destruction, "Getting More out of SSH," "Using Tor and SSH Tunneling," "Javascript Injection" and "A Peek Inside a Simple ATM Machine." Winter adds "Hacking a JP1 Remote Control," "The RedBox DVD Kiosk," "How to Track Any UK GSM Mobile Phone" and an introduction to the Asterisk PBX.

Tor appears in the magazine for the first time in the Autumn issue. It became a standing subject: its control protocol in 2009, running a hidden service in 2017, and the disappearance of hidden services in 2021.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2006
description:
The 2006 volume, in which the magazine acquired its named columns and, in the Winter issue, more pages than it had ever run.

Spring covers "Filesharing using TinyURL.com," "XSS'ing MySpace.com," "United Kingdom: The State of Surveillance" and "Hacking the Facebook," with "The Secrets of Cingular Wireless" and "A Look at Jabber/XMPP." Summer adds "More on Hacking Facebook," "Getting Screwed by PayPal," "Easy Access to T-Mobile and Cingular Accounts" and "Breaking Mac OS X Program Security." Autumn runs "Identity Theft: Misinformation Can Be Your Friend," "Where Have The Philes Gone?," "A Back Door to Your Oracle Database" and "Hacking Flickr." "Never Pay for WiFi Again!" and "Attacking Third Party Tracking" close it. Winter covers "Circumventing the DoD's SmartFilter," "Red Boxing Revealed for the New Age," "How to Build a Book Safe" and "The Not-So-Great Firewall of China."

TELECOM INFORMER, HACKER PERSPECTIVE and TECHNO-EXEGESIS all begin here. The HACKER PERSPECTIVE slot, a guest essay in every issue, was filled across the four issues by The Cheshire Catalyst, Bruce Schneier, Mark Abene and Phillip Torrone.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2007
description:
The 2007 volume, the first with TRANSMISSIONS running in every issue and the first in which web application security takes as much space as the telephone network.

Spring runs "Understanding Web Application Security," "RFID: Radio Freak-me-out Identification" and "Avoiding Internet Filtering," with "Hacking Your Own Front Door," "Dorking the DoorKing" and "Hacking My Ambulance." "Network Ninjitsu: Bypassing Firewalls and Web Filters" and "How to Cripple the FBI" close the issue. Summer covers "Discovering Vulns," "Enhancing Nortel IP Phones with Open Source Software," "Deobfuscation," "Internet Archaeology" and "Java Reverse Engineering." Autumn prints "VoIP Security: Shit or Get Off the POTS," "Social Engineering and Pretexts," "The RIAA's War on Terror," "Hacking an Election" and "The Trouble with Library Records." Winter adds "Building Your Own Networks," "Darknets," "An Introduction to Beige Boxing," "Hacking the SanDisk U3," "Facebook Applications Revealed" and "Zero-Knowledge Intrusion."

The Autumn HACKER PERSPECTIVE column is headed "YOU," an open call for the guest essay filled that year by Bill Squire, Mitch Altman and Rop Gonggrijp.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2008
description:
The 2008 volume, which runs a short story in each of its four issues and gives voice over IP, RFID and barcodes the space the magazine had once given to boxes.

Spring covers "Vhreaking with VoxALot," "Dirt-Cheap Phone Calls - The VoIP Way," "Gaming AT&T Mobility," "Hacking Two-Dimensional Barcodes," "Dissecting the EPC: RFID for the Commercial Sector," "Eavesdropping with LD_PRELOAD," "Remember CompUSA," "The EU Directive on Data Retention: Surveillance 2.0" and the story "To Kill an Atomic Subwoofer." Summer prints "Don't 'Locate Me'," "Exploring Road Runner's Internal Network," "The HughesNet FAP," "Hacking Society," "Thirteen Years of Starting a Hacker Scene," "Hacking: A Graffiti Writer's Perspective," "Capturing Botnet Malware Using a Honeypot," "JavaScript Password DOMination" and "The Geek Squad." Autumn runs "Bell's Mind Markup Language," "The TORminator," "The State of Cyberspace and Cyberwar," "Watching the Watchers," "Penetration Testing: The Red Team Way," "Blackhat SEO," "USB Antiforensics" and "Hacking Music." Winter adds an introduction to forensic data recovery, "Social Engineering the Stock Market," "Hack Thyself," "Anonymous SSH at the Library," "Pappy's Cheese Box," "Gaming Gamestop" and "Hacking WebCT."

The Last HOPE was held in New York that July. The year's guest essayists were Martin Eberhard, Barry Wels, Nick Farr and Bre Pettis.

Autumn runs "Bell's Mind Markup Language," "The TORminator," "The State of Cyberspace and Cyberwar," "Watching the Watchers," "Penetration Testing: The Red Team Way," "Blackhat SEO," "USB Antiforensics" and "Hacking Music." title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2009
description:
The 2009 volume, which prints a directory of hackerspaces across all four issues as the movement it documents spreads through North America and Europe.

Spring opens with "Year 26" and runs "ATA Security Exposed," "Outsourced," "MP3s: A Covert Means of Distributing Information" and "Inside Google Radio." "Network Neutrality Simplified" and "DNS Spoofing on a LAN" follow. Summer covers "Regaining Privacy in a Digital World," "Why the 'No-Fly List' is a Fraud," "Finding Information in the Library of Congress" and "Abusing Metadata." Autumn prints "Exploiting University Students using Rogue Access Points," "Post-Apocalyptic Communications," "Cracking WPA - PSK" and "Hard Disk Encryption, No Excuses." Winter adds "Pwning Past Whole Disk Encryption," "Hacking Tor's Control Protocol," "Underground Physical Network" and "Retail Automation - ABS."

The HACKER SPACES listings cover North America, Europe, the rest of the world and then new foreign entries, one section an issue. HACKER HAPPENINGS begins in the same volume.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2010
description:
The 2010 volume, whose Spring editorial "Cloudy Skies" opens the magazine's long argument with cloud computing.

Spring runs "Insecurities in Emergency Rescue," "The Grey Hat Manifesto," "The Hacker Enigma" and "An Introduction to CSRF Attacks," with "Dr. Jekyll and Mr. PayPass." Summer covers "Hacking Google Analytics," "My Second Implant," "Call the World for Free" and "Educational Wireless Honeypots." It also prints "Why You Need a Grimoire," "Hacking Boingo Wireless" and "Private Key Exchange Using Quantum Physics." Autumn takes in "Old School Hacking" and "How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Spam the Scammers." "Seven Things 'Hackers' Did Right" and "Life Without Walls: Circumventing Your Home Security System" follow. Winter adds "Bash Bash Bash!," "How to Cheat at Foursquare," "Android, You Broke My Heart," "Invisible ASCII: A Poor Person's Steganography" and "Phun with FOIA."

The Autumn editorial "Conflict in the Hacker World" and the following spring's "Abusing the Cloud" name the two arguments the magazine carried into the next decade.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2011
description:
The 2011 volume, published through the year of Anonymous, which the magazine covers twice under near-identical titles and from opposite directions.

Spring runs "Why I Like E-Books," "Who is Anonymous or How to Troll the Media for Fun and Profit" and "How to Accept Payments Anonymously." It also prints "How to Find Out What the Government Knows About You," "Virtual Anti-Forensics" and "Abusing the Cloud." Summer covers "Detecting and Tracking Stealth Satellites," "Pen Testing from a Mile Away," "Securing Online Voting" and "Mobile Hacking with Android," with "How I Escaped Google." Autumn prints "Introduction to Chrome OS," "Bypassing Shell Restrictions," "Network Anonymity Through 'MAC Swapping'," "Video Game Hacking" and the story "Kill Switch." Winter adds "Who is Anonymous?," "Free Phone Numbers with Google Voice," "MAC Spoofing Your Way to Free Internet," "Hacking Refog Keylogger," "Pirating the Caribbean" and "The Piracy Situation."

The Winter issue's "Simplex Locks: Illusion of Security, Version 2.0" returns to the Autumn 1991 article of the same name after twenty years. "The Piracy Situation," in the same issue, opened an exchange that filled three articles the following summer.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2012
description:
The 2012 volume, in which a reader argument about piracy runs on into a second year and Stuxnet gets its analysis.

Spring covers "A PHP Rootkit Case Study," "Denial of Service 2.0," "Spoofing MAC Addresses on Windows" and "GroupMe: A Modern Approach to Social Engineering." It also runs "Stupid 9-Volt Tricks," "Learning from Stratfor: Extracting a Salt from an MD5 Hash" and "Backdooring with Metasploit." Summer prints a Bluetooth hunter's guide, "Building a Cat-5 Cable Tap" and "NGFW - Not Grandpa's Firewall," together with three replies to the previous volume's piracy article. Autumn runs "Technology at the Federal Bureau of Prisons," "The Quadcopter Crash Course," "Hackers in Space," "Beware the Cyber Weapons Industrial Complex" and "Stuxnet: An Analysis." Winter adds "Basic Code Breaking," "Hardware Hacking - An Introduction Via Dev' Boards," "Steganography over Covert Channels" and "The Security Funnel: When OpenVPN Meets Tor."

The serialised fiction "Hacking the Naked Princess" begins in the Summer issue and ran, in numbered instalments, until 2020.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2013
description:
The thirtieth volume, published through the summer of the Snowden disclosures, with the Autumn editorial "The Right to Know."

Spring covers "Guest Networks: Protection Less Than WEP?," "Practical Cryptanalysis," "Social Engineering: Tactics for Prevention" and "Extra-Legal Harassment." It also runs "Fiddler - Never Trust the Client," "Hypercapitalism and Its Discontents" and "Cracking Push-Button Locks," with a review of Exploding the Phone. Summer prints "Splunking the Google Dork," "Fun with the Minuteman III Weapon System," "A Broad Spectrum of DRM" and "0-Day Adventures," beside "Cyber Attacks on Equities Markets." Autumn runs two articles on Bitcoin, "Hacking The Apple Collective," "Internet Trolls," "Access Tandem Codes and the Hidden Phone Network" and "Defeating Forensic Attacks on Full Disk Encryption." Winter adds "Privacy - A New Hope Through Tails," "Wi-Fi Security: Attack and Defense," "Pretty Good Privacy" and "The Growing Schism Between Hackers and the Law."

Bitcoin enters the magazine in the Autumn issue. One article introduces it, and a second asks whether it is the hacker currency, a question the volumes since have kept returning to.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2014
description:
The thirtieth anniversary volume, opening with "Thirty Years On" and closing with "The 21st Century Hacker Manifesto."

Spring covers "Lessons from 'Secret' History," "Asterisk: The Busy Box," "Robbing the Rich Using Bitcoin" and "The Night the ATM Went Down on Me." It also runs "Android Reversing Bootcamp" and "Hacking Commercial Maytag Washers and Dryers." Summer prints "Sabotage The System: Encryption as Surveillance State Monkey Wrench," "Crossover: Where Metal and Hacking Met and Mixed" and "Yippie Ki-Yay: Social Engineering and Film," beside "Toilet Hacking." Autumn runs "The Demoscene - Code, Graphics, and Music Hacking," "Bugging a Room with an IP Phone," "Writing Buffer Overflows for Non-Programmers" and "Covert War-Driving with WiGLE." Winter adds "Password Cracking in the Modern Age," "Format De-Shifting," "Home Depot Hacks," "Recon on Disney's Magic Band" and "Crypto Systems Which Resist Quantum Computers."

EFFECTING DIGITAL FREEDOM, written by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, begins in the Autumn issue and has run in every issue since.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2015
description:
The 2015 volume, in which the magazine reviews Mr. Robot, covers the Ashley Madison breach, and prints a reader's cipher next to the article that breaks it.

Spring runs "So, You Want to Be a Darknet Drug Lord....," "Brazil's Electronic Voting Booth," "Evolution of a Hack" and "McAfee Family Protection - Epic Fail!" Tapping a Nationwide Telecommunications Network," "Chiron and Me: Hacking Astronomy," "Library Security" and "Decoding a Carrier Pigeon." Autumn takes in "A Primer on Home Automation," "Dangerous Clouds," "Ashley Madison Military Sites," "Open Source Repository Abuse" and "The Dawn of the Crypto Age." Winter adds "USBkill - A Program for the Very Paranoid Computer User," "Circumventing Chrome and Firefox's Third Party Cookie Block," "Hackerspaces: A Definition" and "The Limits of Open Source Hardware."

"Yull Encryption" and "A Brief Cryptanalysis of Yull" run in the same Winter issue, a reader's cipher and its breaking printed side by side.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2016

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2017
description:
The 2017 volume, which introduces the CITIZEN ENGINEER column and finishes the five-part "Successful Network Attacks" series.

Spring runs "New U.K. Surveillance Laws," "Voices in the Sky: Satellite Communication Methods," "Lockbox PIN Code Generator" and "Hacking Free Wi-Fi on Delta Flights." It also prints "Telephones from Space," "Software Cracking with dotPeek," "Obfuscating Torrent Traffic" and "White House Phone Numbers." Summer covers "The Censorship Resistant Internet: How to Run a Tor Hidden Service," "Hacktivism to End Human Trafficking and Modern Day Slavery" and "A Declaration of Independence for Cyberspace." Autumn prints "Bypass Your ISP's DNS and Run A Private OpenNIC Server," "PHP Backdoors," "Inseparable: The Intersectionality of Hacking and Politics" and "(learn (LISP))." Winter adds "Using dnscat2 for Encrypted C&C over DNS," "What Happens When WHOIS Data Is Made Public," "Deauthing the Neighbors, or Ring Theory" and "Quantum Computers and Bitcoin."

"White House Phone Numbers" in the Spring issue reprints the kind of list the newsletter ran in its first year, thirty-three years after "White House Phone List."

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2018
description:
The 2018 volume, in which book reviews become a regular feature and the reporting turns to data protection law, IoT botnets and automated policing.

Spring covers "The Secrecy and Security of the Special Counsel," "Breaking Standards," "How to Run an I2P Hidden Service" and "A Review of CopperheadOS." It also runs "Unlocking the Secret of Keys," "Bluetooth Hacking 101," "Hidden ISPs" and "Extrapolating Phone Numbers Using Facebook and PayPal." Summer prints "A N00b's Guide to the Dark Web," "The IPv6 Delusion," "Serial Number Cracking For Fun and Profit" and "Automating a Police State." Autumn runs "Digital Sanctuary Cities," "Removing eBook DRM without OCR or GUIs" and "The Evolution of Ran$omware." "GDPR - Active Empowerment vs. Passive Consumerism" and "A Characteristic Study of IoT Botnets" follow. Winter adds "1979 Plus 40 Years," "AV1: One Giant Leap for Video-Kind," "Social Engineering from Prison" and "Thumbcache.db Primer."

Books are reviewed in two of the four issues. Kevin Mitnick's The Art of Invisibility comes in Autumn, then Surveillance Valley and Ten Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now together in Winter.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2019
description:
The 2019 volume, the last before the pandemic, with the Spring editorial "Preserving the Future" and a run of articles on Android internals and quantum computing.

Spring covers "Reverse Engineering Android Apps," "Android Smartphone Secret Codes: Revealed," "How to Make Your eBooks Inheritable" and "Second-Generation Quantum Computers." It also runs "In-Browser Cryptojacking," "Lights Out! Guerilla Radio" and "We Just Called Them Dialers," with a review of Weapons of Math Destruction. Summer prints "Porting IoT Malware to Windows," "There Is No Magic in the Clouds" and "Connecting to the Internet for Free Using Iodine," with a review of Broad Band. Autumn runs "Fully Homomorphic Encryption and Privacy," "The Mysteries of the Hidden Internet," "Breaking DirecTV's DVR Authentication" and "The Case Against Certified Ethical Hacking." Winter adds "Industrial Control with Modbus," "Cyberspelunking," "Steganographic Filesystems," "Death of a Scene" and "Body Key-Logging."

CITIZEN ENGINEER runs for the last time in the Winter issue. That issue also carries a correction to an earlier article, printed as "Student Privacy by Practice - Not by Policy (fixing our mistake)."

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2020
description:
The 2020 volume, whose Spring editorial "The New Social Disease" was written as the pandemic closed the offices its readers worked in.

Spring covers "Cracking Your Neighbor's Wi-Fi for $180," "Null-Routing Facebook Using Small Tech to Fight Big Tech" and "Hackerspace School." It also runs "Antique Malware Can Still Bite You," "Printers: The Overlooked Security Concerns," "Yahoo Groups and the Legacy of Internet Content" and "An Introduction to Chaff." Summer prints "Skimming Credit Card and ACH Payment Details from Tigerpaw Software Clients," "Towards a Secure Telephone Network" and "Ghosting an Operating System for Privacy," beside "OhNoDaddy: GoDaddy Compromised." Autumn runs "Smile, You're On Camera," "Hacking Rotary Dials," "QR Chaos," "Clean Rooms and Reverse Engineering" and "What's Old Is New Again - We Are Still Jackpotting ATMs." Winter adds "The TikTok Spyware Conspiracy," "Hacking Digital Signage Screens," "How To Write Malware in PowerShell" and "The Brazilian Phone System Revisited."

HOPE 2020 was held online that July and the Autumn issue carries the debrief. ARTIFICIAL INTERRUPTION begins in the Summer issue, which is also where "Hacking the Naked Princess" ends after eight years.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2021
description:
The 2021 volume, in which the magazine's arguments with cryptocurrency, quantum computing and machine learning take as much space as its network security coverage.

Spring runs "Anonymity, Privacy, and Reality," "Ham Radio, SMS, and the ISS," "Randomize Your Exit Node" and "Logging Discord Tokens." It also prints "A Layman's Intro to Quantum Computers," "Inside Job: Exploiting Alarm Systems and the People Who Monitor Them" and "A Proposal for the Elimination of Passwords." Summer covers "More Privacy and Better Security Through Email Diversification," "Fluc Google's FLoC," "The Demise of Network Security" and "Vulnerabilities in Deep Artificial Neural Networks." Autumn prints "Wherever You Go, There You Are," "Where Have All the Tor Sites Gone?," "The FBI Communications Breach of 2010" and "Hacking NYC MTA Kiosks." Winter adds "L-Band: Frequencies and Equipment You Need to Know About," "In the Trenches: Working as a Security Analyst," "Inside the New World of Cryptocurrency Phishing" and "leet.c."

"The Phreak's Field Guide to Identifying North American Phone Switches" begins in the Autumn issue and concludes in Spring 2022. The serial "An Atavistic Freak Out" starts in Summer and ran to a final episode two years later.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2023
description:
The fortieth volume, published in the year of ChatGPT, which the magazine argues with in every issue and names in the Summer editorial "Artificial Nonsense."

Spring covers "Sleuthing Google Apps Part 2," "Hacker Movies," "A Post-Soviet Payphone Trick" and "Organizing Music Files With SongRec and Shazam." It also runs "Hacking The Lenovo 11e Chromebook," "Known Plaintext Attacks Are Caesar-ous Business," "What is Futel?" and "AI For Content Generation." Summer prints "Programming of the Past," "Science Fair and Congressional Farce," "A Chain Addition Generator in AWK" and "The Metaverse Is a Solution Looking for a Problem." Autumn runs "Designing an OpenAI Powered IRC Chat Bot for Fun and Profit," "The Arrival of 2600 Digital Delivery," "But I Don't Want a Copilot" and "Diskless Malware." Winter adds "The Dark Side of DNA Data," "The BoneBox," "Adventures in Lockpicking," "A Quick Intro to Biohacking" and reviews of Pegasus and Fancy Bear Goes Phishing.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, Spring 2024
description:
The 2024 volume, the magazine's fortieth year, in which its long arguments about passwords, surveillance and machine learning all run in serial form.

Spring covers "How to Social Engineer AI to Bypass Learned Ethics," "A Brief Guide to Sci-Hub" and "Further Password Discourse - Fundamentals." It also runs "Listening to Your Computer," "Overcoming Toyota USB Filesystem Limits," "The Garden of Privacy" and "Reflections on Wikileaks and Snowden." Summer prints "Big Tech Is the New Soviet Union," "Cookie Monster," "Encoded Audio Capture The Flag" and "Payphone Extenders: The Access Numbers That Replaced Red Boxing." Autumn runs "Further Password Discourse - Better Practices," "Hacking the URL Schema," "Introduction to the Robot Operating System (ROS)" and "Ten Teens and a Server Room." Winter adds "A Brief Look at Apple's Gatekeeper," "Domain Name Battlefield," "TIS-100: What It Tasted Like," "Use OSINT to Investigate a Phishing Scam" and "City of Flint - Pwned Hard."

The volume's clearest reader exchange runs between two issues. "Big Tech Is the New Soviet Union" appears in Summer, and "Big Tech Is Not the Soviet Union - It's Capitalism Gone Wild" answers it in Winter.

title: Secrets of a Super Hacker
description:
A how-to manual on breaking into computer systems, written under the pseudonym The Knightmare and published by the fringe press Loompanics Unlimited in 1994. It gives step-by-step instructions for social engineering, password theft, and system infiltration from a home computer, aimed at a reader with no prior hacking experience.

The book's core subject is social engineering: talking legitimate users and system administrators into giving up passwords and access. The author calls its variants reverse social engineering, spoofing, and superuser abuse. Further chapters cover screen stealing, hidden data delivery, Trojan horses, trap doors, and dummy accounts. Appendixes explain database and operating-system structure and password-guessing strategy, and close with a glossary of hacking terms. A closing chapter surveys the state and federal computer-crime laws a reader risked breaking by using the techniques described. Gareth Branwyn, an editor associated with the cyberpunk-era magazine Mondo 2000 and later a founding writer at Wired, supplies the introduction; Dan Wend illustrated it.

Loompanics Unlimited, the book's publisher, specialized in manuals on subjects mainstream houses avoided, from lock picking to fake identification. Secrets of a Super Hacker fits that catalog: an early, plainly written primer on hacking methodology rather than a technical security text. Some sources identify the author behind the Knightmare pseudonym as Dennis Fiery, itself understood to be another assumed name rather than the writer's legal identity.

title: The Best of 2600: A Hacker Odyssey
description:
Twenty-four years of the hacker underground's own magazine, edited into one volume by the man who has run it since 1984.

Emmanuel Goldstein selected the articles from 2600: The Hacker Quarterly and arranged them by decade, from the 1984 monthlies through the 2000s. The 1980s section is payphones, blue and red boxes and the last years of the Bell system. The 1990s bring bulletin boards, CompuServe and the early commercial internet. The 2000s run to Unix, mobile networks and traffic control systems. Each section opens with a new introduction placing the pieces in the period that produced them, and the technical writing is reprinted as it was first printed, schematics and all. Also here are the founding of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, the insecurity of ordinary locks, the FBI raids of the early 1990s and the long Kevin Mitnick case.

Goldstein has edited and published 2600 since the first issue, hosts the weekly WBAI radio programme Off the Hook, and organises the HOPE conferences in New York. He was technical consultant on the 1995 film Hackers, has testified before Congress on hacking, and was the defendant in Universal City Studios v. Reimerdes, the 2000 case that asked whether linking to DeCSS was speech. The library holds the complete run of the magazine the book draws from.
